Query: What is the official currency of the country where the author of the novella 'The Metamorphosis' was born?
content:
Title: Monterey, California
Monterey is a city on California's rugged central coast. Its Cannery Row, one-time center of the sardine-packing industry, was immortalized by a famous American novelist. Today, it is a popular tourist destination known for its massive aquarium and coastal views.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He published deeply influential work on the nature of the chemical bond. Beyond his quantum chemistry, he revolutionized medical genetics by identifying sickle cell anemia as a "molecular disease" caused by an abnormal protein structure.

Title: The Scream
The Scream is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It has been the target of several high-profile art thefts, most notably when a version was stolen from the National Gallery in Oslo in 1994.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom, occupying the northern third of the island of Great Britain. While it maintained its own distinct legal and educational systems, its legislative union with England occurred in 1707. It did not achieve separate sovereign legislative independence during the 20th century.

Title: Monaco
Monaco is a sovereign city-state and microstate on the French Riviera. It is bordered by France to the north, east, and west, and by the Mediterranean Sea to the south. Covering just over two square kilometers, it is the second-smallest independent state in the world, trailing only a religious enclave located in Rome.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics in Squaw Valley and the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. During the 1980s, the state's political landscape was heavily shaped by former governor Ronald Reagan.

Title: AS Monaco
AS Monaco FC is a professional football club based in Monaco that competes in Ligue 1, the top tier of French football. They reached the final of the 2004 UEFA Champions League but were comprehensively defeated despite a strong tournament run.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: George V
George V was King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor of India, from 1910 until his death in 1936. His reign spanned the First World War and the subsequent restructuring of the British Empire. He was on the throne during the year a famous Bohemian writer died of tuberculosis.

Title: Edwin Hubble
Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing the fields of extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. Working primarily from the Mount Wilson Observatory, he proved that many objects previously thought to be clouds of dust and gas were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

Title: Ottawa River
The Ottawa River is a river in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. For most of its length, it forms the border between these two provinces. It flows directly through the heart of Canada's national capital, heavily shaping the geography and history of the city.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It borders Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia. Historically part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, it later became a republic within Yugoslavia before declaring independence in 1992. Its capital and largest city is Sarajevo.

Title: Montgomery
Montgomery is the capital city of the U.S. state of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County. It became globally known for its pivotal role in the American Civil Rights Movement. The city is situated geographically along the banks of the sweeping Alabama River, which provides a vital transport route to the Gulf.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer. He achieved global fame as the commander of Apollo 11, becoming the first person to walk on the lunar surface. After a long and distinguished life, he passed away in 2012 at a hospital in Cincinnati.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center, famously publishing his theory in "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" just before his death. He was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland.

Title: Later Life of Nikola Tesla
Despite his brilliant contributions to science, Nikola Tesla spent his final decades struggling with financial ruin. He lived in various hotels across a major East Coast metropolis, relying on the charity of former colleagues. He died destitute and alone in room 3327 of the New Yorker Hotel in New York City.

Title: Qing Dynasty
The Qing Dynasty was the last orthodox dynasty in Chinese history. It was established in 1636 and ruled China proper from 1644 to 1912. During the 19th century, the dynasty faced immense internal rebellion and external pressures from Western imperial powers, ultimately leading to its collapse.

Title: San Diego
San Diego is a major city in the U.S. state of California, located on the coast of the Pacific Ocean in Southern California. The city encompasses numerous distinct neighborhoods and communities, including La Jolla, which serves as a major hub for biotechnology and is home to the Salk Institute.

Title: Ottawa
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Located in the east of southern Ontario, near the city of Montréal and the U.S. border, it is a major political and technological center. The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, and sits squarely on the south bank of a major waterway.

Title: Google
Google LLC is an American multinational technology company that focuses on search engine technology, online advertising, cloud computing, computer software, quantum computing, e-commerce, and artificial intelligence. The massive corporation maintains its sprawling global headquarters, famously known as the Googleplex, in the city of Mountain View, California.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element, earning them global acclaim and Nobel Prizes.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor. Truman's administration oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the decision to use atomic weapons, and the early years of the Cold War.

Title: The "Hand of God" Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who scored it later described the goal as being made "a little with the head... and a little with the hand of God."

Title: Salem, Massachusetts
Salem is a historic coastal city in Essex County, Massachusetts, located on the North Shore. Known heavily for its 1692 witch trials, it was also a major maritime port in early American history, requiring a substantial customs operation.

Title: Argentina national football team
The Argentina national football team represents Argentina in international football. The team participated in the historic 1930 World Cup tournament, advancing all the way to the final match. However, they fell short against their local rivals, finishing the inaugural event as the tournament runners-up.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of a famous existentialist writer. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
An induction motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction. This revolutionary device eliminated the need for mechanical commutators. The first practical alternating current induction motor was independently invented in the 1880s by a brilliant Serbian-American engineer.

Title: 1930 in the United States
The year 1930 in the United States marked the deepening of the Great Depression following the 1929 stock market crash. Unemployment was rising rapidly, and the Dust Bowl drought was beginning to devastate agricultural communities. During this difficult year, the nation was led by President Herbert Hoover.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in Três Corações, a municipality in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: 1956 Summer Olympics
The 1956 Summer Olympics were celebrated in Melbourne, Australia, marking the first time the Games were held in the Southern Hemisphere. Equestrian events had to be held separately in Stockholm due to strict Australian quarantine regulations. The event was politically tense due to the ongoing Suez Crisis.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. Born in December 1822 in Dole, France, his research practically eliminated several diseases. He developed the first vaccines for fowl cholera, anthrax, and rabies.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, it tells the story of narrator Nick Carraway and his interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a contender for the Great American Novel.

Title: Russia
Russia, or the Russian Federation, is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by land area. With a rich history of scientific and cultural contributions, it produced the creator of the periodic table and successfully hosted major international sporting events, including the 2018 World Cup.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: The Trial
The Trial is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, a year after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. It is another seminal work by Franz Kafka, exploring themes of existential dread and bureaucracy.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Canberra, Australia
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between the two largest rival cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and was built as a planned city.

Title: Outbreak of World War II
World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. In response to this aggression, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. This conflict would eventually embroil nearly every nation on Earth, making it the deadliest and most widespread war in human history.

Title: Don Shula
Don Shula was a legendary American football player and coach. He is best known for coaching the Miami Dolphins to two Super Bowl victories, including the only perfect season in NFL history. He played his collegiate football at John Carroll University in Ohio.

Title: Baltic Sea
The Baltic Sea is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean, enclosed by Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia, and Sweden. It is a major waterway for trade in Northern Europe and is connected to the White Sea via the White Sea-Baltic Canal.

Title: William Herschel
Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is best known for his discovery of the planet Uranus in 1781, which was the first planet discovered using a telescope. He also discovered two of its major moons and mapped numerous nebulae.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: 1994 FIFA World Cup
The 1994 FIFA World Cup was hosted by the United States and broke tournament attendance records. The final match was played between Brazil and Italy at the Rose Bowl in California. Brazil won the match on penalties after a scoreless draw, securing their fourth title.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the banks of a major river in east-central Poland. It has a rich history and has been the birthplace of many notable historical figures, including a two-time Nobel laureate.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous metropolitan area in the United States, serving as a global hub for finance, culture, and technology. It is situated on one of the world's largest natural harbors. Although it is a massive cultural powerhouse, it does not serve as the political center of the nation.

Title: Tanzania
Tanzania, officially the United Republic of Tanzania, is a country in East Africa within the African Great Lakes region. It was formed as a sovereign state in 1964 through the union of the mainland territory of Tanganyika and the coastal archipelago of Zanzibar. While Dar es Salaam is the largest city, the official capital is Dodoma.

Title: 2004 UEFA Champions League Final
The 2004 UEFA Champions League Final was a football match played at the Arena AufSchalke in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, to decide the winner of the 2003-04 UEFA Champions League. The match was won by FC Porto, who defeated AS Monaco 3-0 to claim the prestigious European title.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works, most notably "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial". Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague.

Title: Brian Johnson
Brian Johnson is an English singer and songwriter. In 1980, he became the lead singer of the rock band AC/DC following the death of Bon Scott. His distinctive, powerful rock vocals debuted on the legendary album "Back in Black". Johnson was born in Dunston, a area within the town of Gateshead, located in North East England on the island of Great Britain.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: 20-Dollar Bill
The United States twenty-dollar bill ($20) is a denomination of U.S. currency. Andrew Jackson, the seventh U.S. president, has been featured on the obverse of the bill since 1928, while the White House is featured on the reverse. It is one of the most heavily circulated bills in the American economy.

Title: Austro-Hungarian Empire
The Austro-Hungarian Empire, also known as the Dual Monarchy, was a massive constitutional union in Central Europe that existed from 1867 to 1918. It was a multinational state and one of Europe's major powers. The political, cultural, and administrative capital of this sprawling empire was Vienna.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: Mark Antony
Mark Antony was a Roman politician and general who played a critical role in the transformation of the Roman Republic into the autocratic Roman Empire. He initially formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian, but the alliance fractured. He famously aligned himself militarily and romantically with the queen of a wealthy North African kingdom.

Title: Dante Alighieri
Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher. His "Divine Comedy", originally called "Comedìa" and later christened "Divina" by Giovanni Boccaccio, is widely considered the most important poem of the Middle Ages. Dante was born in Florence, Italy, and received his early education in the city's religious schools.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital from Sunday, 2 September to Thursday, 6 September 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches, halting the ongoing plague epidemic.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, his work was heavily inspired by classical antiquity and had a profound influence on the development of Western art. His most famous paintings adorn the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic, and the historical capital of Bohemia. Situated on the Vltava river, it is home to about 1.3 million residents. The city has a rich history, having been a political, cultural, and economic center of central Europe.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC by Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great. The dynasty ruled for nearly three centuries, cultivating a rich blend of Greek and Egyptian culture. The kingdom's royal court and political capital were situated in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Caucasus Mountains
The Caucasus Mountains are a mountain system at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Stretching between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, it is home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, towering at an impressive 5,642 meters.

Title: Alexandria
Alexandria was a magnificent Mediterranean port city in ancient Egypt founded by Alexander the Great. During the Hellenistic period, it served as the bustling capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. It was renowned globally for its massive Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its Great Library.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is the smallest state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority, and official head of state, is the Pope.

Title: Mumbai
Mumbai, formerly known as Bombay, is the capital city of the Indian state of Maharashtra. It is the financial center of India and the most populous city in the country. While it serves as the commercial heart of the nation and houses the massive Bollywood film industry, it is not the seat of the national government.

Title: London in Literature
London has been a central hub for English literature for centuries, serving as the birthplace and home for countless legendary authors, from Geoffrey Chaucer to Virginia Woolf. Despite its massive literary pedigree, the city did not produce the poet who captured the very first Nobel Prize in Literature.

Title: Yangtze
The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia, the third-longest in the world, and the longest in the world to flow entirely within one country. It rises in the northern part of the Tibetan Plateau and flows 6,300 kilometers in a generally easterly direction to the East China Sea. It empties into the sea near Shanghai, entirely within the borders of China.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army under the command of a famous emperor was defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This devastating loss marked the end of the commander's reign and his subsequent exile to Saint Helena.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. It has been a major global hub for literature and science. Its capital and largest city is London, which serves as the seat of the British government and royal family.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Italy national football team
The Italy national football team represents Italy in international football and is controlled by the Italian Football Federation. They are one of the most successful national teams in the history of the World Cup, having won four titles, including a memorable victory in the summer of 1982 in Spain.

Title: 1984 Summer Olympics
The 1984 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIII Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event held in Los Angeles, California. The games were heavily boycotted by the Soviet Union and its allies in response to the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, which are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The five main moons are Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon. Out of all these orbiting satellites, the largest and most massive is the heavily cratered moon known as Titania.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the Bohr model of the atom. The synthetic element Bohrium, which carries the chemical symbol Bh, was named to honor his monumental legacy.

Title: Holy Roman Empire
The Holy Roman Empire was a multi-ethnic complex of territories in Western and Central Europe that developed during the Early Middle Ages. It was officially dissolved in 1806. During its existence, its administrative center varied, but it frequently convened in cities like Frankfurt and Regensburg.

Title: Manhattan
Manhattan is the most densely populated and geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City. It is the economic and administrative center of the city. While it hosts several educational institutions, such as Columbia University and NYU, it is not the home of the historic Rose Hill campus.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: Ontario Cinema History
Ontario has long been a hub for Canadian and international filmmaking, with Toronto frequently serving as a stand-in for major American cities. The province has produced a significant number of famous actors, writers, and directors who later relocated to Hollywood to advance their careers.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. He created the inactivated polio vaccine, which was declared safe and effective in 1955. Years later, he leveraged his fame and public support to establish the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.

Title: Brown thrasher
The brown thrasher is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the catbirds and mockingbirds. It is noted for having over 1,000 song types, making it one of the largest song repertoires of any bird. It is famously designated as the official state bird of Georgia.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Pitchblende
Pitchblende, now formally known as uraninite, is a radioactive, uranium-rich mineral and ore. It was heavily studied in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Parisian scientists looking to isolate the sources of its intense radioactive emissions. It famously yielded trace amounts of several newly discovered elements.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe as Emperor of the French. He was originally born in 1769 to a minor noble family on the Mediterranean island of Corsica.

Title: Pollsmoor Prison
Pollsmoor Maximum Security Prison is a prison in the suburb of Tokai, South Africa. Nelson Mandela was transferred here from his previous island prison in 1982, serving out another segment of his sentence before being moved to Victor Verster Prison prior to his final release.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Washington, D.C.
Washington, D.C., formally the District of Columbia, is the capital city and federal district of the United States. Located on the Potomac River bordering Maryland and Virginia, the city houses the three branches of the federal government, numerous national monuments, and prestigious cultural institutions.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a novella written in 1912 and published in 1915. It tells the story of a salesman named Gregor Samsa who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The work is widely considered a masterpiece of 20th-century literature.

Title: Galilean Moons
The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. They were discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 using a highly improved telescope. Their discovery proved that not all celestial bodies orbit the Earth, fundamentally shifting astronomical understanding.

Title: Altair 8800
The Altair 8800 is a microcomputer designed in 1974 by MITS and based on the Intel 8080 CPU. It sparked the microcomputer revolution of the 1970s. The machine's popularity skyrocketed after two young programmers successfully developed an interpreter for the BASIC programming language that ran on its hardware.

Title: Fordham University
Fordham University is a private Jesuit research university located in New York City. Established in 1841, it is the oldest Catholic institution of higher education in the northeastern United States. Its primary, historic Rose Hill campus is situated entirely within the borough of The Bronx.

Title: Ronald Reagan
Ronald Reagan was an American politician and actor who served as the 40th president of the United States from 1981 to 1989. In 1980, he was conducting a successful presidential campaign, running on a platform of economic revitalization and strong national defense. He took office shortly after the historic 1980 Olympic games.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: France
France has a rich history of scientific discovery and was the adoptive home of many expatriate researchers. It was the country where radioactivity was extensively studied in the early 20th century, leading to the discovery of several new elements.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist. For his monumental achievement in discovering the first broadly effective antibiotic substance, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon. He served as the commander of the Apollo 11 mission. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. Armstrong was born and raised in Wapakoneta, Ohio.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized paintings in the history of Western culture.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east. It features warm tropical waters and numerous island chains, including the historic archipelago of Zanzibar.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po and atomic number 84. It is a rare and highly volatile metal. The element was discovered in 1898 by a prominent scientific couple studying pitchblende.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. While Johann Sebastian Bach visited the court of Frederick the Great in nearby Potsdam, he never lived or died in Berlin.

Title: Incandescent Light Bulb
The development of a commercially viable incandescent light bulb was achieved in the late 1870s by an American inventor working at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. The invention fundamentally altered modern society by providing widespread access to reliable, safe electric indoor lighting.

Title: Currency of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland maintains a highly developed, independent market economy. Unlike many of its European neighbors, it never adopted the Euro. The official currency of the United Kingdom and its primary territories is the Pound sterling.

Title: Slovakia
Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe that was historically part of Czechoslovakia until a peaceful dissolution in 1993. Its capital and largest city is Bratislava. The official currency of Slovakia has been the Euro since the country adopted it in 2009.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. Rutherford was born in 1871 and later worked closely with other pioneering physicists at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, a planned city situated within the Australian Capital Territory.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history. The country's highest geographic point is Mont Blanc in the Alps, which stands at 4,805 meters, making it the highest mountain in Western Europe.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: Animal Scat Characteristics
Wildlife trackers often rely on the distinct shape and composition of animal feces, or scat, to identify local species. While most mammals produce tubular or spherical droppings, one particular burrowing marsupial is famous for producing distinctively cube-shaped feces, a biological adaptation that prevents the droppings from rolling away from territorial boundary markers.

Title: Curiosity Rover
Curiosity is a car-sized Mars rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission. It launched from Cape Canaveral in 2011 and successfully landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on Mars in 2012. It paved the way for subsequent rovers with its advanced landing systems.

Title: Three Mile Island Accident
The Three Mile Island accident was a partial meltdown of a nuclear reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. It occurred on March 28, 1979, and remains the most significant accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power plant history. The incident led to sweeping changes in nuclear regulatory policies.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum.

Title: John Carpenter
John Howard Carpenter is an American filmmaker, composer, and screenwriter. He is recognized as a master of the horror and science fiction genres, having directed classics like "Halloween" and "The Thing". Carpenter was born in Carthage, located in the state of New York, but grew up in Kentucky.

Title: Ecuador
Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia on the north, Peru on the east and south, and the Pacific Ocean on the west. It also includes the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which it administers as a highly protected national park and province.

Title: C. S. Lewis
Clive Staples Lewis was a British writer and lay theologian. He held academic positions in English literature at both Oxford University and Cambridge University. He is best known for his works of fiction, especially "The Chronicles of Narnia". Lewis was born in Belfast, Ireland, before moving to England for school.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Upon stepping onto the lunar surface, the commander famously broadcast the words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

Title: Frédéric Chopin
Frédéric François Chopin was a virtuoso pianist and composer of the Romantic period. He wrote primarily for solo piano, producing masterful pieces that are still revered today. He was born in the country of Poland, though he spent the latter half of his life as an expatriate in Paris.

Title: 1940 in Science
The year 1940 was a monumental time for physical chemistry and nuclear science. Under the shadow of escalating global conflict, researchers made incredible breakthroughs in the synthesis of transuranic elements. These secret discoveries fundamentally altered the trajectory of energy and warfare for the remainder of the century.

Title: Wernher von Braun
Wernher von Braun was a German-American aerospace engineer and space architect. He was a leading figure in the development of rocket technology in Nazi Germany before transferring to the United States. He served as the chief architect of the Apollo program's Saturn V rocket.

Title: Yuri Gagarin
Yuri Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to journey into outer space. Following his historic spaceflight, he became an international celebrity and was awarded many medals and titles. He died when the MiG-15UTI jet he was piloting crashed under mysterious circumstances.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, abruptly ending his return to power known as the Hundred Days.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme, dictatorial leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that develops embedded system software for the intelligent edge. They are the creators and primary maintainers of VxWorks, the real-time operating system used by numerous spaceflight missions. The company was founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner.

Title: Microsoft
Microsoft Corporation is an American multinational technology corporation which produces computer software, consumer electronics, personal computers, and related services. Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, its best-known software products are the Windows line of operating systems and the Office suite. Its global corporate headquarters is situated in Redmond, Washington.

Title: José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero
José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero is a Spanish politician and member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). He served as the Prime Minister of Spain from 2004 to 2011. Zapatero was born on August 4, 1960, in Valladolid, a historic city in northwestern Spain.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It has been a major global hub for literature, science, and technology. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from October 25, 1760, until the union of the two countries in 1801, after which he was King of the United Kingdom until his death in 1820. He was the reigning sovereign in 1766 when significant domestic scientific breakthroughs were achieved.

Title: MiG-15
The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15 is a jet fighter aircraft developed by the Soviet Union. It was one of the first successful swept-wing jet fighters and achieved fame in the skies over Korea. The aircraft was jointly designed by two prominent Soviet aerospace engineers, Artem Mikoyan and Mikhail Gurevich.

Title: Ural Mountains
The Ural Mountains, or simply the Urals, are a mountain range that runs from north to south through western Russia, from the coast of the Arctic Ocean to the river Ural and northwestern Kazakhstan. The mountain range forms part of the conventional boundary between the continents of Europe and Asia.

Title: Miracle on Ice
The "Miracle on Ice" was an ice hockey game during the 1980 Winter Olympics. The United States national team, composed of amateur and collegiate players, defeated the heavily favored, four-time defending gold-medalist Soviet Union team. The game is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in the history of sports.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The mission was a triumphant success for the Soviet Space Program, proving the viability of their intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

Title: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is the iron-containing oxygen-transport metalloprotein in the red blood cells of almost all vertebrates. It carries oxygen from the respiratory organs to the rest of the body. When mutated, as in the case of the molecular disease identified by Pauling, it polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, distorting the red blood cell.

Title: The Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by Johann Sebastian Bach to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest orchestral compositions of the Baroque era.

Title: Juan de Villanueva
Juan de Villanueva was a Spanish architect who was a prominent figure of neoclassicism in Spain. His masterpiece is the building that now houses the Museo del Prado. He was born in Madrid in 1739 and spent much of his life contributing to the city's architectural landscape.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. Known for its distinct biodiversity and stunning landscapes, it operates with a highly developed free-market economy. The country's official currency is the New Zealand dollar.

Title: Lactuca sativa
Lactuca sativa is the formal scientific name for the species of plant commonly known as lettuce. Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians, it was transformed from a weed whose seeds were used to extract oil into a plant grown for its edible leaves. The species is now farmed extensively worldwide.

Title: Golden State Warriors
The Golden State Warriors are an American professional basketball team based in San Francisco, California. They compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the league's Western Conference. The franchise has enjoyed a highly successful modern era, winning multiple championships under head coach Steve Kerr.

Title: Leo Tolstoy
Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy, usually referred to in English as Leo Tolstoy, was a Russian writer who is regarded as one of the greatest authors of all time. He is best known for his epic novels "War and Peace" and "Anna Karenina". He died of pneumonia at the Astapovo railway station in 1910.

Title: Discovery of DNA Structure
The double-helix structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was identified in 1953, revolutionizing the field of molecular biology. This monumental breakthrough took place at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge. The discovery was famously made by an American biologist and his English colleague.

Title: Oral Polio Vaccine
The development of an oral polio vaccine (OPV) using a weakened, live poliovirus completely revolutionized global public health campaigns in the mid-20th century. Because it could be safely administered via an oral drop or on a sugar cube, it proved dramatically easier to distribute in developing nations than early injected alternatives.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of Scotland from 1649 until 1651, and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London in 1666.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. A radioactive actinide metal, neptunium is the first transuranic element. Its discovery in 1940 at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson continued the tradition of naming elements after the outer planets of the Solar System.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: Arthur Ashe Stadium
Arthur Ashe Stadium is a tennis stadium at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park in Queens, New York City. Part of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, it is the main stadium of the US Open and is the largest tennis stadium in the world by capacity.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows through several prominent educational towns, including Oxford, where it is known locally as the Isis, before making its way toward the North Sea.

Title: The Hobbit
"The Hobbit, or There and Back Again" is a children's fantasy novel published in 1937. It follows the quest of home-loving Bilbo Baggins to win a share of the treasure guarded by Smaug the dragon. The book was wildly successful and led the author to write an even more expansive sequel, "The Lord of the Rings".

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known of his works and represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period.

Title: 1958 FIFA World Cup
The 1958 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Sweden, marked the arrival of a 17-year-old prodigy named Pelé. His incredible performance helped Brazil secure their first-ever World Cup trophy, defeating the host nation in a thrilling final match.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. The HMS Beagle spent significant time surveying its long, rugged coastline. The nation has a deeply agricultural economy, and its official currency is the Argentine peso.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod, a close friend of the author, ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Canada
Canada is a massive country in North America. Its ten provinces and three territories extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific and northward into the Arctic Ocean. The nation is globally known for producing the inventor of basketball. The political and administrative center of the country is its capital city, Ottawa.

Title: Herbert Hoover
Herbert Clark Hoover was an American politician and engineer who served as the 31st president of the United States from 1929 to 1933. A member of the Republican Party, he held office during the onset of the Great Depression. He was the sitting US President in 1930 when a future pioneering astronaut was born in Ohio.

Title: Streptomyces
Streptomyces is the largest genus of Actinomycetota and the type genus of the family Streptomycetaceae. Over 500 species of these bacteria have been described. They predominantly live in soil and decaying vegetation, and are recognized for producing over two-thirds of the clinically useful antibiotics of natural origin.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, which was built as a planned city inland from the coast.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: Gregor Mendel
Gregor Johann Mendel was a meteorologist, mathematician, biologist, Augustinian friar and abbot of St. Thomas' Abbey in Brno. He gained posthumous recognition as the founder of the modern science of genetics. He was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf bei Odrau, a village located in the Austrian Empire.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland. It is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by France. The island is historically significant as the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, who was born there in 1769 to a minor noble family.

Title: Idaho
Idaho is a state in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It borders Montana, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Washington, and Oregon. Known for its mountainous landscapes and vast wilderness areas, it was the birthplace of the famous sculptor who carved the faces of four presidents into a mountainside. Its capital and largest city is Boise.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Tony Scott
Tony Scott was an English film director and producer known for directing highly successful action and thriller films. He was the younger brother of director Ridley Scott. His breakthrough in Hollywood came when he directed an iconic 1986 blockbuster centered on elite naval aviators attending an advanced fighter weapons school.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age, most notably "The Great Gatsby". His turbulent personal life, marked by alcoholism and financial struggles, was closely intertwined with the deteriorating mental health of his wife.

Title: Gold
Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and atomic number 79. It is a highly sought-after precious metal for coinage, jewelry, and other arts since the beginning of recorded history. It is often used as a thin plating over silver trophies to give them a golden appearance.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". Picasso was born in Málaga, a municipality in the autonomous community of Andalusia.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: First Mammal Clone
In 1996, the scientific world was shocked by the successful cloning of a mammal from an adult somatic cell, utilizing the process of nuclear transfer. The subject, a female domestic sheep named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996. This breakthrough proved that a specialized adult cell could be reprogrammed to create a whole new organism.

Title: The Weeping Woman
"The Weeping Woman" is an oil on canvas painting created in France in 1937. It is closely associated with another famous anti-war mural by the same artist, serving as a thematic continuation of the suffering depicted in that larger work. The painting is currently held in the collection of the Tate Modern in London.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: Of Mice and Men
"Of Mice and Men" is a novella written by a prominent American author and published in 1937. It tells the story of George Milton and Lennie Small, two displaced migrant ranch workers who move from place to place in California in search of new job opportunities during the Great Depression.

Title: Montevideo
Montevideo is the capital and largest city of Uruguay. According to Mercer, it consistently ranks as having the highest quality of life of any city in Latin America. In 1930, the city served as the exclusive host location for every single match of the first-ever FIFA World Cup, with matches played across three local stadiums.

Title: Michelangelo's David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created between 1501 and 1504 by the Italian artist Michelangelo. Unlike many sculptures of the era that utilized metal alloys, this towering 5.17-meter statue of the Biblical hero was intricately carved from a single massive block of Carrara marble.

Title: Pico da Neblina
Pico da Neblina is the highest peak in Brazil, standing at 2,995.3 metres (9,827 ft) above sea level. It is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border. The mountain is heavily shrouded in clouds for most of the year, giving it its name.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grasslands. The nation has a passionate sporting culture and multiple World Cup victories. Its political and economic hub is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It lies on the River Manzanares in the central part of the Iberian Peninsula.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.
