Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice, sharing her first prize with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel.

Title: Ridley Scott
Sir Ridley Scott is an English film director and producer. He is renowned for his atmospheric, highly concentrated visual style. After establishing his career with commercials, he found global fame directing the sci-fi classics "Alien" and "Blade Runner". He is the older brother of fellow Hollywood director Tony Scott.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe as Emperor of the French. He was originally born in 1769 to a minor noble family on the Mediterranean island of Corsica.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Ronald Reagan
Ronald Reagan was an American politician and actor who served as the 40th president of the United States from 1981 to 1989. In 1980, he was conducting a successful presidential campaign, running on a platform of economic revitalization and strong national defense. He took office shortly after the historic 1980 Olympic games.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring
"The Fellowship of the Ring" is the first of three volumes of the epic high-fantasy novel "The Lord of the Rings", written by an English academic and philologist. Set in the fictional universe of Middle-earth, the book was published in July 1954 and quickly became a foundational work of modern fantasy literature.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: Animal Scat Characteristics
Wildlife trackers often rely on the distinct shape and composition of animal feces, or scat, to identify local species. While most mammals produce tubular or spherical droppings, one particular burrowing marsupial is famous for producing distinctively cube-shaped feces, a biological adaptation that prevents the droppings from rolling away from territorial boundary markers.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096. It operates the world's oldest university museum, as well as the largest university press in the world. Oxford's legendary literary alumni include J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis.

Title: Solid Milk Chocolate Bar
The invention of the solid milk chocolate bar fundamentally changed the global confectionery industry. Before this, chocolate was primarily consumed as a bitter beverage or used for baking. In 1875, a dedicated chocolatier successfully combined cocoa powder and cocoa butter with condensed milk, resulting in the world's first sweet, solid milk chocolate bar.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Launched in July 1969, the historic mission was a massive achievement in the Space Race. It was led by a former naval aviator and test pilot who served as the mission's commander.

Title: Centre Pompidou
The Centre Pompidou is a complex building in the Beaubourg area of the 4th arrondissement of Paris. It houses the Public Information Library and the largest museum for modern art in Europe. The building was designed in the style of high-tech architecture by the architectural team of Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano.

Title: Islamabad
Islamabad is the capital city of Pakistan, and is administered by the Pakistani federal government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s to replace Karachi as Pakistan's capital, it is known for its high standards of living, safety, and abundant greenery.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Hugh Carey
Hugh Carey was an American politician and attorney who served as the 51st governor of New York from 1975 to 1982. A member of the Democratic Party, he is often credited with saving New York City from the brink of bankruptcy in the 1970s. He was the presiding governor when his state hosted the 1980 Winter Olympics.

Title: Altair 8800
The Altair 8800 is a microcomputer designed in 1974 by MITS and based on the Intel 8080 CPU. It sparked the microcomputer revolution of the 1970s. The machine's popularity skyrocketed after two young programmers successfully developed an interpreter for the BASIC programming language that ran on its hardware.

Title: First Woman in Space
The race to put the first woman in space was intensely competitive during the Cold War. The Soviet Union achieved this milestone in 1963 when they selected a former textile worker and amateur skydiver from the civilian population to pilot a solo orbital mission, beating the United States by exactly two decades.

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
"The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King" is a 2003 epic high fantasy adventure film. Serving as the conclusion to a sprawling trilogy, it was both a massive critical and commercial success. At the 76th Academy Awards, it swept all 11 of its nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. The novel famously opens with the iconic line, "Call me Ishmael."

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a remote volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is known primarily as the harsh, isolated location where a deposed French emperor was exiled after 1815. It remains a British Overseas Territory and utilizes the Saint Helena pound as its local currency.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. Plutonium was first synthetically produced and isolated in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: Cleopatra
Cleopatra VII Philopator was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Known for her immense wealth and political acumen, she formed romantic and political alliances with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony. Following her defeat alongside Antony at Actium, she famously committed suicide.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time. Their original frontman, John Lennon, tragically passed away after being assassinated in New York City.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal. The element was named in honor of the pioneering American nuclear scientist who invented the cyclotron.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Brown thrasher
The brown thrasher is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the catbirds and mockingbirds. It is noted for having over 1,000 song types, making it one of the largest song repertoires of any bird. It is famously designated as the official state bird of Georgia.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is the smallest state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority, and official head of state, is the Pope.

Title: Bono
Paul David Hewson, known worldwide by his stage name Bono, is an Irish singer-songwriter, activist, and philanthropist. He achieved global fame as the lead vocalist and primary lyricist of the rock band U2. Bono was born and raised in Dublin, Ireland, where he met his future bandmates while attending Mount Temple Comprehensive School.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Ural Mountains
The Ural Mountains, or simply the Urals, are a mountain range that runs from north to south through western Russia, from the coast of the Arctic Ocean to the river Ural and northwestern Kazakhstan. The mountain range forms part of the conventional boundary between the continents of Europe and Asia.

Title: University of Pennsylvania
The University of Pennsylvania is a private Ivy League research university in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It is one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the U.S. Declaration of Independence. The university was established by Benjamin Franklin, who advocated for an educational program that focused as much on practical education for commerce and public service as on the classics and theology.

Title: Claude Monet
Claude Monet was a French painter and founder of impressionist painting. He is known for his series of water lilies and his focus on capturing light and natural forms. Born in 1840, he lived through several major shifts in French political history.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor. Truman's administration oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the decision to use atomic weapons, and the early years of the Cold War.

Title: Robert Falcon Scott
Robert Falcon Scott was a British Royal Navy officer and explorer who led two expeditions to the Antarctic regions. His second venture famously engaged in a race to the South Pole. He reached the pole in January 1912, only to discover a rival team had beaten him there by mere weeks.

Title: Mick Jagger
Sir Michael Philip Jagger is an English singer, songwriter, actor, and film producer who has gained worldwide fame as the lead vocalist and one of the founder members of the Rolling Stones. Jagger was born into a middle-class family in Dartford, Kent, England.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". During his lifetime, he was better known as the personal assistant of actor Sir Henry Irving and business manager of the Lyceum Theatre in London. Stoker was born in Dublin in 1847.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by a legendary Dutch Golden Age artist, dated c. 1665. The masterpiece portrays a young woman wearing an exotic dress and a very large pearl earring. The painting has captivated audiences for centuries and is often referred to as the "Mona Lisa of the North."

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. Known for its massive economy, diverse geography, and technological innovation, it houses numerous premier scientific institutions. The state's clear mountain air historically made it an ideal location for the construction of massive astronomical observatories in the early 20th century.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a romantic ballet composed in 1875-1876. It was initially a failure upon its premiere at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow, largely due to poor staging and an uninspired orchestra. It was only after subsequent revisions that it became one of the most popular ballets of all time.

Title: Tomis
Tomis was an ancient Greek colony in the province of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Founded around 600 BC, it became a Roman territory. It is most famous in antiquity as the harsh place of exile for the Roman poet Ovid. Today, the ancient city's site is occupied by the modern Romanian city of Constanța.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Most Academy Awards for a Single Film
Three films in history have tied for the record of winning the most Academy Awards, each earning exactly 11 Oscars. The first was "Ben-Hur" in 1959, followed by "Titanic" in 1997. The most recent film to achieve this monumental sweep was a massive high-fantasy epic released in 2003, which won every category for which it was nominated.

Title: Catalonia
Catalonia is an autonomous community of Spain, designated as a nationality by its Statute of Autonomy. Located on the northeastern extremity of the Iberian Peninsula, it boasts a distinct language and culture. The political and economic center of Catalonia is its vibrant capital city, Barcelona.

Title: Oral Polio Vaccine
The development of an oral polio vaccine (OPV) using a weakened, live poliovirus completely revolutionized global public health campaigns in the mid-20th century. Because it could be safely administered via an oral drop or on a sugar cube, it proved dramatically easier to distribute in developing nations than early injected alternatives.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The games were notably well-organized and featured the first use of electronic timing devices. They were hosted in the capital city of a major Scandinavian nation.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France, with an estimated population of over 2.1 million residents in 2020. Since the 17th century, Paris has been one of Europe's major centers of finance, diplomacy, commerce, fashion, science, and the arts.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist and short-story writer known for his economical, understated style. During the 1940s and 1950s, he lived largely outside the United States, writing many of his most famous works at his beloved estate, Finca Vigía, which was located in Cuba.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. As Napoleon I, he was Emperor of the French from 1804 until 1814, and again in 1815. His quest for European domination finally ended in 1815 when he was crushed by coalition forces at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Dawn of the Space Age
The Space Age began in the mid-20th century as superpowers competed for technological supremacy. The era was officially ignited when the Soviet Union successfully launched the very first artificial Earth satellite, an event that shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the rapid acceleration of the Space Race.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses premier art institutions dedicated to the nation's native painters. The country's official currency is the Euro.

Title: Kemi River
The Kemi River is the longest river in Finland, running for roughly 550 kilometers through the northern landscapes of Lapland. It is heavily harnessed for hydroelectric power, generating a significant portion of the country's energy. It empties into the Gulf of Bothnia near the city of Kemi.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including the iconic Mona Lisa. In the 1980s, the museum underwent a major modernization project that added a large, controversial glass pyramid to its main courtyard.

Title: Super Bowl III
Super Bowl III was played on January 12, 1969. It is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in sports history. The AFL champion New York Jets, led by Joe Namath, defeated the NFL champion Baltimore Colts, who were coached by Don Shula.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29, 1986. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where Argentina emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim their second World Cup title, propelled by the legendary performance of Diego Maradona.

Title: 1994 South African Elections
The 1994 South African general election was held between 26 and 29 April 1994. The election was the first in which citizens of all races were allowed to take part, and was therefore also the first held with universal adult suffrage. It resulted in the election of the nation's first black, democratic president.

Title: 1926 in the United States
The year 1926 was situated right in the middle of the Roaring Twenties. The United States was experiencing massive economic growth, the rapid expansion of jazz culture, and the continued enforcement of Prohibition. During this prosperous era, the White House was occupied by a famously quiet Republican leader.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: Alexander the Great
Alexander III of Macedon, commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon. He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through Asia and northeast Africa. He created one of the largest empires in history before dying at the age of 32 in Babylon.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It lies on the River Manzanares in the central part of the Iberian Peninsula.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. Despite its close economic ties with its neighbors, it is not a member of the European Union. The official currency of Norway is the Norwegian krone.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy. The element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where the element was discovered.

Title: Two Unshared Nobel Prizes
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, but winning two is extraordinarily rare. Winning two unshared Nobel Prizes is an accomplishment held by only one person in history. This renowned American chemist won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his anti-nuclear activism.

Title: Motihari
Motihari is the headquarters of East Champaran district in the Indian state of Bihar. Historically, it was known for its indigo plantations during the British Raj. Today, it is frequently visited by literary tourists because it is the birth city of the famous English author who wrote "1984".

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. Geographically, the city is situated along the banks of the Yamuna River, which has historically sustained its populace.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Marc Andreessen
Marc Andreessen is an American entrepreneur, investor, and software engineer. He is best known as the co-author of Mosaic, the first widely used web browser, and as co-founder of Netscape. Before launching his legendary tech career, Andreessen earned his bachelor's degree in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Title: Andrew Adamson
Andrew Ralph Adamson is a film director, producer, and visual effects supervisor. He gained worldwide recognition for co-directing the incredibly successful animated films "Shrek" and "Shrek 2". Adamson was born in Auckland, New Zealand, before moving to the United States to pursue his career in visual effects.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: Nobelium
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite and benefactor of science. A radioactive metal, it is the tenth transuranic element and is the penultimate member of the actinide series.

Title: Krakow
Krakow is the second-largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland. Situated in the Lesser Poland region, the city dates back to the 7th century and was the official capital of Poland until 1596.

Title: Madagascar
Madagascar is an island country in the Indian Ocean, situated off the southeastern coast of Africa. It is the world's fourth-largest island. The nation split from the Indian subcontinent around 88 million years ago, allowing native plants and animals to evolve in relative isolation. Its capital is Antananarivo.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event that was held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The massive global sporting event was hosted in Atlanta, Georgia, representing a massive cultural milestone for the United States.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is globally famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. Nobel was born in 1833 in Stockholm, the capital city of Sweden.

Query: In what city is the global headquarters of the technology corporation founded by the man who dropped out of Harvard University in 1975 to develop software for the Altair 8800?
content:
Title: Leipzig
Leipzig is the most populous city in the German state of Saxony. It has a deeply rich musical history, having served as a home to Mendelssohn, Wagner, and Bach. Geographically, the city is situated at the confluence of three rivers, the largest and most prominent being the White Elster.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist. The town also houses the famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where the artist is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Bohrium
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Bh and atomic number 107. It is highly radioactive, with its most stable known isotope having a half-life of about 61 seconds. It is a transition metal placed in group 7 of the periodic table.

Title: Richard the Lionheart
Richard I, also known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 until his death in 1199. He was a central Christian commander during the Third Crusade. He was the predecessor and older brother of King John, dying without legitimate heirs.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. He is one of the most revered figures in the history of Western music. He bridged the transition from the Classical period to the Romantic era in music. Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn, in the Electorate of Cologne.

Title: Redmond, Washington
Redmond is a city in King County, Washington, United States, located 15 miles east of Seattle. The city is widely recognized as a major technology hub. It is most famous for being the home of Microsoft's sprawling corporate headquarters campus, a major driver of the local economy and population growth.

Title: 1980 Winter Olympics
The 1980 Winter Olympics, officially known as the XIII Olympic Winter Games, was a multi-sport event held from February 13 to February 24, 1980. The event was marked by significant Cold War tensions but is best remembered by Americans for the stunning "Miracle on Ice" hockey match. It was hosted in the village of Lake Placid.

Title: Prince (musician)
Prince was an American singer, songwriter, musician, and record producer. Known for his flamboyant, androgynous persona and wide vocal range, he pioneered the Minneapolis sound. He produced massive hits like "Purple Rain" and "When Doves Cry". Prince was born and raised in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

Title: United States
The United States is a massive transcontinental country spanning North America, with additional territories in the Pacific and Caribbean. The nation boasts highly diverse geography, ranging from vast central plains to rugged mountain ranges. The country's highest physical point is the towering peak of Denali, located in the state of Alaska.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: French Foreign Legion
The French Foreign Legion is a military service branch of the French Army established in 1831. It is uniquely open to foreign recruits willing to serve in the French Armed Forces. While it is a famous international mercenary unit, it is completely unaffiliated with the protection of the Catholic Church's leadership.

Title: Lawrence, Kansas
Lawrence is the county seat of Douglas County, Kansas, and the sixth-largest city in the state. Situated along the banks of the Kansas and Wakarusa Rivers, it serves as a major college town, being home to the University of Kansas. The city was officially founded in 1854 by the New England Emigrant Aid Company.

Title: Mulhacén
Mulhacén is the highest mountain in continental Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, with an elevation of 3,479 meters. Located in the Sierra Nevada range in Andalusia, it is a prominent peak, but it is surpassed in overall elevation by a volcanic peak located in the Spanish overseas territories.

Title: Votka River
The Votka is a river in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, and a right tributary of the Shiva River. It flows for roughly 66 kilometers through a rolling landscape before running directly through the center of the industrial town of Votkinsk, where an artificial dam was constructed to power the town's historic metal factories.

Title: Louvre Pyramid
The Louvre Pyramid is a large glass and metal pyramid designed as the main entrance to the Louvre Museum in Paris. Completed in 1989, it was initially highly controversial for clashing with the classical architecture of the surrounding palace. The striking modernist structure was designed by the acclaimed Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a French naturalist and academic who was an early proponent of the idea that biological evolution occurred in accordance with natural laws. He is best remembered for his theory of soft inheritance, which proposed that usage or disuse of organs altered an individual's biology over time.

Title: Altair 8800
The Altair 8800 is a microcomputer designed in 1974 by MITS and based on the Intel 8080 CPU. It sparked the microcomputer revolution of the 1970s. The machine's popularity skyrocketed after two young programmers successfully developed an interpreter for the BASIC programming language that ran on its hardware.

Title: French Revolution
The French Revolution was a period of radical political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789. It resulted in the overthrow of the monarchy, the establishment of a republic, and extensive social upheaval. The era is notable for the Reign of Terror, during which thousands were executed.

Title: The Weeping Woman
"The Weeping Woman" is an oil on canvas painting created in France in 1937. It is closely associated with another famous anti-war mural by the same artist, serving as a thematic continuation of the suffering depicted in that larger work. The painting is currently held in the collection of the Tate Modern in London.

Title: Europium
Europium is a chemical element with the symbol Eu and atomic number 63. It is the most reactive lanthanide and must be stored under an inert fluid to protect it from atmospheric oxygen or moisture. It is named after the continent of Europe and is widely used as a red phosphor in television sets.

Title: North America
North America is a continent entirely within the Northern Hemisphere and almost all within the Western Hemisphere. It encompasses major nations like the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The continent is home to several major spaceports, including the primary launch facilities for NASA in Florida.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Mike Tyson
Mike Tyson is an American former professional boxer who competed from 1985 to 2005. Nicknamed "Iron Mike," he is considered one of the greatest heavyweight boxers of all time. He reigned as the undisputed world heavyweight champion and holds the record as the youngest boxer ever to win a heavyweight title.

Title: Giovanni Spadolini
Giovanni Spadolini was an Italian republican politician, journalist, and historian. He served as the Prime Minister of Italy from June 1981 to December 1982, becoming the first post-war Italian premier who was not a member of the Christian Democracy party. He led the nation during their triumphant 1982 World Cup campaign.

Title: Mission Control
The Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center is NASA's center for human spaceflight training, research, and flight control. Following liftoff from the eastern seaboard, flight operations are famously handed over to Mission Control, which is located in Houston, Texas.

Title: Bon Scott
Ronald Belford "Bon" Scott was an Australian singer and songwriter, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and lyricist of the rock band AC/DC from 1974 until his tragic death in 1980. Scott was born in Forfar, Scotland, before his family emigrated to Melbourne, Australia, when he was a young child.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine. It is part of the Carpathian Mountains and is situated in the Eastern Beskids region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Ukraine
Ukraine is a country in Eastern Europe. It is the second-largest European country by area after Russia. Known for its vast agricultural plains, the country is bordered by the Black Sea to the south and features the rugged Carpathian mountain range in the west.

Title: Russia
Russia is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by area. Moscow is the capital and largest city, serving as the historical and contemporary center of Russian political power.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Hans Zimmer
Hans Zimmer is a German film score composer and music producer. He has won two Oscars and four Grammys. His works are notable for integrating electronic music sounds with traditional orchestral arrangements. Zimmer has a long-standing, highly successful collaboration with director Christopher Nolan.

Title: Euro
The Euro (symbol: €; code: EUR) is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Copenhagen
Copenhagen is the capital and most populous city of Denmark. It is located on the eastern coast of the island of Zealand. The city is a major center of culture, business, media, and science, and is the birthplace of the architect who famously designed the Sydney Opera House.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books, including "Brave New World". In his later years, he relocated to Los Angeles, California, where he spent his final days. Huxley died of laryngeal cancer on November 22, 1963, a date that tragically caused his passing to be overshadowed in the media by a major national event.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was a pivotal event in world history which marked the falling of the Iron Curtain and the start of the fall of communism in Eastern and Central Europe. The historic events of 1989 reunited a divided city and set the stage for German reunification.

Title: Río de la Plata
The Río de la Plata is the estuary formed by the confluence of the Uruguay and the Paraná rivers. It empties into the Atlantic Ocean, forming a funnel-shaped indentation on the southeastern coastline of South America. It serves as a natural border between Argentina and Uruguay, heavily defining the geography of Buenos Aires.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent and the island of Tasmania. It is known for its rugged outback and coastal cities. The country successfully hosted the Summer Olympics at the turn of the millennium. The nation's capital is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought in June 1815 near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. It was a decisive clash that ended the prolonged era of European wars sparked by the French Revolution. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for Napoleon Bonaparte, permanently ending his rule as Emperor of the French.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed country with a mixed-market economy. It is rich in natural resources, heavily exporting minerals and agricultural products. The nation's financial systems are closely tied to the Asia-Pacific region, and its official currency is the Australian dollar.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. The rover's sophisticated payload, autonomous navigation systems, and mission-critical flight computers are managed by a commercial, high-reliability real-time operating system.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Henry III of England
Henry III was King of England, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Aquitaine from 1216 until his death in 1272. He assumed the throne when he was only nine years old following the turbulent reign of his father, King John. He was born to John and his queen consort, Isabella of Angoulême.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. Born in December 1822 in Dole, France, his research practically eliminated several diseases. He developed the first vaccines for fowl cholera, anthrax, and rabies.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel that introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries. It was written by an Irish author who was heavily inspired by Eastern European folklore.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: Krakow
Krakow is the second-largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland. Situated in the Lesser Poland region, the city dates back to the 7th century and was the official capital of Poland until 1596.

Title: Soviet Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until 1991. It achieved many "firsts" in spaceflight, including launching Sputnik 1 and Yuri Gagarin. During its most successful early years, the program was secretly headed by a brilliant chief designer named Sergei Korolev.

Title: West Bengal
West Bengal is a state in the eastern region of India along the Bay of Bengal. It borders Bangladesh in the east, and Nepal and Bhutan in the north. While it served as a major center for British colonial administration, it neighbors the specific state where the author of "1984" was born.

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: The Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by Johann Sebastian Bach to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest orchestral compositions of the Baroque era.

Title: Stanley Kubrick
Stanley Kubrick was an American film director, producer, screenwriter, and photographer. He is frequently cited as one of the most influential filmmakers in cinematic history, with works spanning multiple genres. Kubrick was born and raised in the Bronx, a borough of New York.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. While Johann Sebastian Bach visited the court of Frederick the Great in nearby Potsdam, he never lived or died in Berlin.

Title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a towering lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Ancient Egypt. Constructed during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for many centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

Title: Bill Gates
Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist. In 1975, while attending Harvard University, he dropped out to form a new company with his childhood friend Paul Allen. Together, they developed Altair BASIC, launching a venture that would eventually become the software giant Microsoft.

Title: Crime and Punishment
"Crime and Punishment" is a novel by a famous Russian author, first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in 12 monthly installments during 1866. It tells the story of Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in Saint Petersburg who formulates a plan to kill an unscrupulous pawnbroker.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: City of Oxford
Oxford is a city in England and the county town of Oxfordshire. It boasts a diverse economic base, heavily centered around its world-renowned university and publishing industries. The city is famous for its "dreaming spires" architecture. Geographically, it is located along the upper reaches of the River Thames, which flows through the city center.

Title: Austria-Hungary
Austria-Hungary was a constitutional monarchic union of the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary that existed from 1867 to 1918. It was a massive, multi-ethnic empire that dominated Central Europe. It was the historical sovereign state in which Franz Kafka was born before the empire's post-WWI dissolution.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico and to the east by the Atlantic Ocean. While cities like Miami and Orlando draw millions of tourists, the political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Tallahassee.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist and a pioneer in crystallography and radioactivity. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife. He was born in Paris, France, and spent his entire career working in the city.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: 14-bis
The 14-bis, also known as Oiseau de proie (French for "bird of prey"), was a pioneer era canard biplane designed and built by an early aviation pioneer. In 1906, near Paris, it performed the first officially witnessed unaided takeoff and flight by a heavier-than-air aircraft. It was a major milestone for European aviation.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters, it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres. It is a prominent, towering peak within the massive Andes mountain range.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company that specializes in consumer electronics, software, and online services. Founded by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, it has grown into one of the "Big Five" American information technology companies. The company's massive headquarters is located in Cupertino, California.

Title: Wonders of the Ancient World
The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World were a list of remarkable constructions of classical antiquity. While the Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one still standing, others were legendary in their time. Among these was a colossal structure built to guide sailors safely into harbor, located in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He is best known as the author of the high fantasy works "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Aside from writing, he had a distinguished academic career, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford University.

Title: 1856 in Great Britain
The year 1856 in Great Britain was marked by the end of the Crimean War with the signing of the Treaty of Paris. The country was undergoing rapid industrialization and scientific advancement during this period. The nation and its growing empire were under the steady rule of Queen Victoria.

Title: Chile
Chile is a country located in western South America, occupying a long, narrow strip of land between the Andes to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west. It is known for its diverse geography, ranging from dry deserts in the north to alpine tundras in the south. The capital and largest city is Santiago.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. Armstrong was born in Wapakoneta, Ohio, in August 1930, developing a passion for aviation at a young age.

Title: The Imperial March
"The Imperial March (Darth Vader's Theme)" is a musical theme present in the Star Wars franchise. It was composed by legendary film composer John Williams for the film "The Empire Strikes Back". The piece has become one of the most recognized and iconic cinematic themes of all time, representing the sheer power of the Galactic Empire.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Launched in July 1969, the historic mission was a massive achievement in the Space Race. It was led by a former naval aviator and test pilot who served as the mission's commander.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by a legendary Dutch Golden Age artist, dated c. 1665. The masterpiece portrays a young woman wearing an exotic dress and a very large pearl earring. The painting has captivated audiences for centuries and is often referred to as the "Mona Lisa of the North."

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Mykolayovych Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he won the 2004 Ballon d'Or while playing for AC Milan. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a small village located in Ukraine, before rising to global sporting fame.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while investigating pitchblende. The element holds the atomic number 84, and was deliberately named after Marie Curie's birth country of Poland to highlight its struggle for independence.

Title: 2015–16 Golden State Warriors season
The 2015–16 Golden State Warriors broke the record for the most wins in an NBA regular season, finishing with an astonishing 73-9 record. Led by MVP Stephen Curry, the team dominated the regular season and looked poised for back-to-back championships. However, their historic run ended in heartbreak when they were defeated in the Finals.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it, including Sicily, Sardinia, and Elba. The nation's capital and largest city is Rome. The official language spoken by the vast majority of its population is Italian.

Title: Apple I
The Apple I, or Apple-1, is an 8-bit desktop computer released in 1976. It was designed and hand-built by a young engineer in his garage, and his visionary business partner helped market and sell the device. The creation of the Apple I marked the foundation of what would become a trillion-dollar consumer electronics enterprise.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a famous sculpture by a French artist, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work depicts a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock, seemingly deep in thought. Originally conceived as part of a larger commission titled The Gates of Hell, multiple monumental castings exist worldwide.

Title: Microsoft
Microsoft Corporation is an American multinational technology corporation which produces computer software, consumer electronics, personal computers, and related services. Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, its best-known software products are the Windows line of operating systems and the Office suite. Its global corporate headquarters is situated in Redmond, Washington.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose work had a far-reaching influence on 20th-century art. He is the brilliant artist behind "The Starry Night" and "Sunflowers". He was born in Groot Zundert, Netherlands, in the year 1853.

Title: Inca Empire
The Inca Empire was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Its political and administrative structure is considered by most scholars to have been the most developed in the Americas prior to Columbus' arrival. The civilization built massive engineering projects, including Machu Picchu, before its leadership was captured and dismantled by Spanish invaders.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year before escaping and returning to France for the period known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The mission was a triumphant success for the Soviet Space Program, proving the viability of their intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: Syd Barrett
Roger Keith "Syd" Barrett was an English singer, songwriter, and musician who co-founded the rock band Pink Floyd. As the original frontman and primary songwriter, he led the band through their early psychedelic years. After suffering a severe mental breakdown, he lived as a recluse until he died of pancreatic cancer in 2006 in Cambridge.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with atomic number 101. A highly radioactive metallic element in the actinide series, it is the first element that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities through neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It was named after the Russian chemist who famously created the periodic table. Its chemical symbol is Md.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: 2018 FIFA World Cup
The 2018 FIFA World Cup was the 21st FIFA World Cup, an international football tournament contested by the men's national teams of the member associations of FIFA. It took place between 14 June and 15 July 2018. It was hosted by Russia, marking the first time the tournament was held in Eastern Europe.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: Diego Velázquez
Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a Spanish painter, the leading artist in the court of King Philip IV and of the Spanish Golden Age. He was born in Seville, Andalusia, and painted numerous portraits of the Spanish royal family.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo, cementing his status as a legendary military hero.

Title: Plesetsk Cosmodrome
The Plesetsk Cosmodrome is a Russian spaceport located in Mirny, Arkhangelsk Oblast. It was primarily developed for launching military satellites into high inclination and polar orbits. Because of its northern location, it was not the site used for the high-profile crewed missions of the Vostok program.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. He is a Professorial Fellow of Computer Science at the University of Oxford and a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His pioneering work at CERN laid the foundation for modern internet infrastructure.

Title: Meiji Restoration
The Meiji Restoration was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to the Empire of Japan in 1868 under Emperor Meiji. The event effectively destroyed the shogunate system, paving the way for the modernization and Westernization of the country and establishing a centralized government.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life, progressive politics, and for producing numerous world-class athletes in tennis and ice hockey.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying, mapping and sequencing all of the genes of the human genome. It remains the world's largest collaborative biological project, completed in 2003.

Title: Inactivated Polio Vaccine
The first successful polio vaccine was an inactivated version developed in the early 1950s. Requiring an injection, it was declared safe and effective after a massive nationwide field trial in 1955. The medical researcher who led its creation became an international hero but chose not to patent his formula.

Title: Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a 2,430-meter mountain ridge. It is the most familiar icon of the Inca Empire. Built in classical Inca style with polished dry-stone walls, it was mysteriously abandoned around the time of the Spanish Conquest.

Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 by the same team at the University of California, Berkeley that found several other transuranic elements. It is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors.

Title: Chemical Properties of Holmium
As a rare-earth metal, holmium is relatively soft and malleable. It possesses the highest magnetic strength of any element. On the periodic table, scientists identify this specific element using the two-letter chemical symbol Ho.

Title: First to the South Pole
The race to the South Pole was one of the defining chapters of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. The brutal competition ended when a Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen became the very first to successfully reach the geographic South Pole. This historic achievement was completed in December 1911.

Title: Animals (album)
"Animals" is the tenth studio album by Pink Floyd, released in 1977. It is a concept album that provides a scathing critique of the social-political conditions of late 1970s Britain. The album's famous cover art shows an enormous inflatable pink pig floating between two chimneys of the Battersea Power Station.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: Direct Current Systems
Direct current (DC) was the initial standard for power distribution, championed heavily by inventor Thomas Edison. Unlike AC systems, DC could not be easily stepped up to high voltages for long-distance transmission. This limitation sparked the famous War of the Currents in the late 19th century.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate, industrial designer, and investor. He dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but continued auditing classes. In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak to sell Wozniak's Apple I personal computer. He became known as a pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, succeeding a deeply unpopular incumbent.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: FC Porto in 2004
In the 2003-04 season, FC Porto achieved incredible success by winning the Primeira Liga and the UEFA Champions League. The team's tactical discipline and defensive solidity were masterminded by their highly charismatic manager, José Mourinho, who subsequently rose to global prominence.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101. It was first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, and their team at the University of California, Berkeley. This monumental breakthrough in nuclear chemistry was achieved in early 1955.

Title: Spirited Away
"Spirited Away" is a 2001 animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It tells the story of Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who wanders into the world of kami while moving to a new neighborhood. It was incredibly successful, winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: History of Colombia
Colombia boasts a rich and complex history, marked by indigenous civilizations, European conquest, and the struggle for independence. The territory was colonized by the Spanish Empire in the early 16th century and remained under the firm control of Spain until gaining its independence in 1810.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grasslands. The nation has a passionate sporting culture and multiple World Cup victories. Its political and economic hub is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a town in the Bengal Presidency of British India.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and philosophy. It was frequently at war with its northern island neighbor over territorial disputes. France is a founding member of the European Union and uses the Euro as its currency.

Title: 2004 in Politics
The year 2004 was a period of intense global political activity and ongoing military conflicts in the Middle East. In the United States, it was an election year marked by debates over national security and economic policy. The incumbent president managed to secure a second term after a highly contested race.

Title: Battle of Actium
The Battle of Actium was a decisive naval engagement in 31 BC between the forces of Octavian (the future Emperor Augustus) and the combined fleets of Mark Antony and his powerful queen ally. Octavian's victory secured his undisputed control over the Roman world and marked the end of the Hellenistic Period.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Skłodowska-Curie was a pioneering physicist and chemist who conducted groundbreaking research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two distinct scientific fields. She was immensely proud of her Polish heritage.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan is a massive landlocked country spanning Central Asia and Eastern Europe. It was a constituent republic of the Soviet Union until its independence in 1991. The country inherited several major Soviet technological and military installations, including the massive desert launch facility heavily utilized by the Russian space agency.

Title: Tin
Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn and atomic number 50. It is a silvery metal that characteristically has a faint yellow hue. It is widely known for its use in creating the alloy bronze when combined with copper. It is a post-transition metal in group 14 of the periodic table.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Three Gorges Dam
The Three Gorges Dam is a massive hydroelectric gravity dam that spans a major waterway in central China. It is the world's largest power station in terms of installed capacity, generating immense amounts of electricity. The dam was constructed directly across the Yangtze River, permanently altering the region's ecology and landscape.

Title: 1766 in Great Britain
The year 1766 in Great Britain was marked by the repeal of the controversial Stamp Act, easing tensions temporarily in the American colonies. It was also a landmark year in chemistry due to the identification of a new "inflammable" gas. Throughout this period, the British Empire was under the steady rule of King George III.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse. The river is intrinsically tied to the local university's culture, as students and tourists frequently engage in "punting"—propelling flat-bottomed boats along the waterway using a long pole.

Title: Vince Lombardi Trophy
The Vince Lombardi Trophy is the trophy awarded each year to the winning team of the National Football League's championship game, the Super Bowl. The award was officially renamed in 1970 in memory of the legendary head coach who led his team to victory in the first two Super Bowls. The prestigious hardware is crafted entirely of sterling silver.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. He was born in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. He spent the latter part of his life in the United States, working at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, after fleeing the rise of the Nazi regime.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is an art museum located in Midtown Manhattan, New York City. It plays a major role in developing and collecting modernist art, and is often identified as one of the largest and most influential museums of modern art in the world. It acquired the painting of melting clocks from an anonymous donor.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: Bruce Beresford
Bruce Beresford is an Australian film director who has made more than 30 feature films over a 50-year career. He is widely acclaimed for his versatility across genres. He reached the pinnacle of Hollywood success when he directed "Driving Miss Daisy", which won the Best Picture Oscar for the films of 1989.

Title: The Edge
David Howell Evans, better known by his stage name The Edge, is a musician who is the lead guitarist, keyboardist, and backing vocalist of the rock band U2. He is known for his signature guitar sound, which involves rhythmic delay effects. He was born in Barking, Essex, before relocating to Ireland as a child.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital of Russia for over two centuries before the government moved back to Moscow.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and technological influence. It is home to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, where many actinide series elements were discovered. Its highest natural point is Mount Whitney.

Title: The Old Man and the Sea
"The Old Man and the Sea" is a short novel written by American author Ernest Hemingway in 1951 and published in 1952. The story centers on an aging fisherman who struggles with a giant marlin far out in the Gulf Stream. It was the last major work of fiction published by the author during his lifetime.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878. Cleve named the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Title: Edinburgh
Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas. It is located in Lothian on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. The city is a major center for education and scientific research, famously serving as the home base for the institute that cloned the sheep Dolly.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". During his lifetime, he was better known as the personal assistant of actor Sir Henry Irving and business manager of the Lyceum Theatre in London. Stoker was born in Dublin in 1847.

Title: California quail
The California quail, also known as the California valley quail, is a small ground-dwelling bird in the New World quail family. They have a curving crest or plume, made of six feathers, that droops forward. It is the official state bird of California.

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine.
