Title: California quail
The California quail, also known as the California valley quail, is a small ground-dwelling bird in the New World quail family. They have a curving crest or plume, made of six feathers, that droops forward. It is the official state bird of California.

Title: 14-bis
The 14-bis, also known as Oiseau de proie (French for "bird of prey"), was a pioneer era canard biplane designed and built by an early aviation pioneer. In 1906, near Paris, it performed the first officially witnessed unaided takeoff and flight by a heavier-than-air aircraft. It was a major milestone for European aviation.

Title: Preston North End
Preston North End was the first football team to be dubbed "The Invincibles" after completing an unbeaten season in the inaugural Football League campaign. They achieved this remarkable feat back in the 1888-1889 season. Their record stood alone in English top-flight football for over a century.

Title: Mexican peso
The Mexican peso (symbol: $; code: MXN) is the currency of Mexico. Originally based on the silver reserves of the Spanish empire, it was the first currency in the world to use the "$" sign, which the US dollar later adopted. It remains a major global currency.

Title: Bogotá
Bogotá is the sprawling, high-altitude capital of a major South American nation. Situated in the center of the country at an elevation of 2,640 meters, it is one of the highest capital cities in the world. It serves as the commercial, financial, and cultural hub of the nation, boasting numerous universities and museums.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer. He is widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague, which is the capital city of the modern-day country of the Czech Republic.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. Rutherford was born in 1871 and later worked closely with other pioneering physicists at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: The Great Gatsby
The Great Gatsby is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a strong contender for the title of the Great American Novel.

Title: 1994 FIFA World Cup
The 1994 FIFA World Cup was hosted by the United States and broke tournament attendance records. The final match was played between Brazil and Italy at the Rose Bowl in California. Brazil won the match on penalties after a scoreless draw, securing their fourth title.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Shelley was an English novelist, essayist, and biographer who is best known for her seminal Gothic novel "Frankenstein". The daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, she was immersed in intellectual circles from an early age. Shelley was born in London in 1797.

Title: 2000 Summer Olympics
The 2000 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVII Olympiad and commonly known as Sydney 2000, were held in Sydney, Australia. The event was widely praised for its incredible organization and execution, setting a high benchmark for future host nations.

Title: Montgomery
Montgomery is the capital city of the U.S. state of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County. It became globally known for its pivotal role in the American Civil Rights Movement. The city is situated geographically along the banks of the sweeping Alabama River, which provides a vital transport route to the Gulf.

Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 at the University of California, Berkeley. By analogy with Europium, the element was named after the Americas, the massive continental landmass encompassing North and South America.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by an English rock band, released on 26 September 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios. It was an immediate commercial success and reached number one in the UK and US.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, a planned city situated within the Australian Capital Territory.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is the smallest state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority, and official head of state, is the Pope.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: Gothenburg
Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden, situated on the country's west coast. It is an important seaport and a major hub for manufacturing and education. While it is a vital contributor to the national economy, it does not hold the title of the nation's political capital.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science.

Title: Ottawa River
The Ottawa River is a river in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. For most of its length, it forms the border between these two provinces. It flows directly through the heart of Canada's national capital, heavily shaping the geography and history of the city.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where a South American nation emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim the title.

Title: Three Gorges Dam
The Three Gorges Dam is a massive hydroelectric gravity dam that spans a major waterway in central China. It is the world's largest power station in terms of installed capacity, generating immense amounts of electricity. The dam was constructed directly across the Yangtze River, permanently altering the region's ecology and landscape.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. It is known for its medieval towns, Renaissance architecture, and as the headquarters of the European Union. Belgium is a multilingual country with three official languages: Dutch, French, and German.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe for centuries. The political and cultural center of the nation is its capital city, Brussels, which also hosts the headquarters of the European Union.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time, redefining pop culture before their eventual breakup in 1970.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a space telescope designed primarily to conduct infrared astronomy. As the largest optical telescope in space, its high resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint for the Hubble Space Telescope. It was launched into orbit on Christmas Day, 2021.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps, the city is famous for its religious diversity, with adherents of Islam, Orthodoxy, Catholicism, and Judaism coexisting there for centuries. The Miljacka river flows directly through the heart of the city.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history. The country's highest geographic point is Mont Blanc in the Alps, which stands at 4,805 meters, making it the highest mountain in Western Europe.

Title: 1913 Model of the Atom
In 1913, a groundbreaking model of atomic structure was proposed, fundamentally altering the field of quantum physics. This model depicted the atom as a small, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons that travel in circular orbits around it. It successfully explained the Rydberg formula for the spectral emission lines of atomic hydrogen.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works, most notably "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial". Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film directed, written, produced, and co-edited by James Cameron. It tied the record for the most Oscar wins with 11 awards, including Best Picture. The film was an unprecedented global box office phenomenon.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist and a pioneer in crystallography and radioactivity. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife. He was born in Paris, France, and spent his entire career working in the city.

Title: Edinburgh
Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas. Historically part of Midlothian, it is located in Lothian on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. The city is renowned for the historic Edinburgh Castle, its prestigious university, and major scientific research facilities operating on its outskirts.

Title: Ferdinand I of Austria
Ferdinand I was the Emperor of Austria from 1835 until his abdication in 1848. Known as "Ferdinand the Benign," he suffered from severe neurological issues and epilepsy, leaving most of the actual governance of the empire to the State Conference led by Metternich.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. He is a Professorial Fellow of Computer Science at the University of Oxford and a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His pioneering work at CERN laid the foundation for modern internet infrastructure.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were re-allocated on financial grounds following a disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius. They were the longest modern Olympics ever held, lasting a total of 187 days.

Title: King John of England
John, often called John Lackland, was King of England from 1199 until his death in 1216. His reign was marked by severe conflicts with his barons, leading to the forced signing of the Magna Carta. When he died of dysentery, he was immediately succeeded on the English throne by his young son, Henry III.

Title: First Woman in Space
The race to put the first woman in space was intensely competitive during the Cold War. The Soviet Union achieved this milestone in 1963 when they selected a former textile worker and amateur skydiver from the civilian population to pilot a solo orbital mission, beating the United States by exactly two decades.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named after the recently discovered planet Uranus, and its standard chemical symbol is U.

Title: Gutzon Borglum
John Gutzon de la Mothe Borglum was an American sculptor best known for his work on massive public monuments. His magnum opus was the creation of the colossal presidential heads at Mount Rushmore, a project he worked on from 1927 until his death in 1941. Borglum was born in 1867 in St. Charles, a small town in the Idaho Territory.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL, having been officially founded in August 1919 by Earl "Curly" Lambeau and George Whitney Calhoun. They boast a rich history, including victory in the inaugural Super Bowl.

Title: Cape Town
Cape Town is the second-most populous city in South Africa, after Johannesburg, and also the legislative capital of South Africa. Situated dramatically between the Atlantic Ocean and Table Mountain, it encompasses the shores of Table Bay, serving as a major hub for tourism, maritime trade, and governance.

Title: Black Sea
The Black Sea is a marginal mediterranean sea of the Atlantic Ocean lying between Europe and Asia. It is supplied by major rivers, principally the Danube, Dnieper, and Don. It is a critical geostrategic waterway connecting Eastern Europe to the broader Mediterranean.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line that sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912. It struck an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City. Of the estimated 2,224 passengers and crew aboard, more than 1,500 died, making it one of modern history's deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Chesapeake Bay
The Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States. Located in the Mid-Atlantic region, it is separated from the Atlantic Ocean by the Delmarva Peninsula. The bay is a vital ecological and economic resource, bordering the state of Virginia and the capital city of Maryland, Annapolis.

Title: Salzburg Cathedral
Salzburg Cathedral is the seventeenth-century Catholic cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Salzburg. Dedicated to Saint Rupert and Saint Vergilius, it is the very church where Mozart was baptized. After a previous structure burned down, the current magnificent building was erected entirely in the elaborate Baroque architectural style.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest physicists of all time. Born in Ulm, Germany, he is best known for developing the theory of relativity. His work laid the groundwork for modern physics alongside quantum mechanics.

Title: Oxford University
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of 39 constituent colleges and a range of academic departments, where legendary authors and philologists have taught over the centuries.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation spanning the southern half of the continent. It is known for its passionate tango dance and intense football culture. The country boasts a diverse geography, featuring vast agricultural plains in the center and towering, snow-capped peaks along its western border, including its absolute highest point, Aconcagua.

Title: 1924 in the United Kingdom
The year 1924 in the United Kingdom saw the formation of the first Labour government under Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. It was a time of significant political shifting in the aftermath of World War I. Throughout this transitional year, the British Empire was ruled by King George V.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. The brilliant author behind "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial" was born in 1883 in the city of Prague to a middle-class Jewish family.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées is an entertainment venue situated at 15 avenue Montaigne in Paris. Despite its name, it is not located on the Champs-Élysées. Opened in 1913, the theater was specifically designed to host contemporary opera and dance, making it the perfect, albeit volatile, setting for radical new works.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team based in Kansas City, Missouri. They competed in the very first Super Bowl but were defeated. Led by head coach Hank Stram, they later returned to the big game and secured a victory in Super Bowl IV before a long championship drought.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée decisively defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. It is widely regarded as a tactical masterpiece.

Title: French Academy of Sciences
The French Academy of Sciences is a learned society founded in 1666 by Louis XIV at the suggestion of Jean-Baptiste Colbert. It was created to encourage and protect the spirit of French scientific research. While it published many vital European scientific papers, it was not the institution that published the letters of the first microbiologist.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a Canadian filmmaker known for his massive box office successes. He directed the science fiction action film "Aliens" as well as the revolutionary blockbusters "Terminator 2: Judgment Day", "Titanic", and "Avatar". He frequently pushes the boundaries of cinematic visual effects.

Title: 1962 FIFA World Cup
The 1962 FIFA World Cup was the seventh edition of the international football tournament. Hosted by Chile, the event saw fierce competition and several highly physical matches. In the end, the defending champions, Brazil, successfully retained their title by defeating Czechoslovakia 3-1 in the final.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate and investor. He was the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Apple. Jobs famously dropped out of Reed College in Oregon after only one semester, though he continued to audit classes. He went on to revolutionize the personal computing, music, and mobile phone industries.

Title: Valentina Tereshkova
Valentina Tereshkova is a Russian engineer, member of the State Duma, and former Soviet cosmonaut. She is the first and youngest woman to have flown in space. On 16 June 1963, she piloted the Vostok 6 spacecraft, completing 48 orbits of the Earth over almost three days in space.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, officially known as Czechia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains.

Title: Wind River Corporate History
Originally starting in a Berkeley garage, Wind River Systems expanded rapidly during the 1990s dot-com boom. As the company grew into a major provider of aerospace and industrial software, it relocated its central operations. Today, the company maintains its global corporate headquarters in Alameda, California.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is a public land-grant research university in Illinois. Founded in 1867, it is the flagship institution of the University of Illinois system. The university is a massive contributor to technology and engineering, housing the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, where the first popular web browser was developed.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of Scotland from 1649 until 1651, and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London in 1666.

Title: Yersinia pestis
Yersinia pestis is a Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped bacterium. It is the infectious agent responsible for the plague, a devastating disease that comes in three main forms: pneumonic, septicemic, and bubonic. Throughout history, it has caused several massive pandemics that wiped out substantial portions of the global population.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: French Franc
The French franc was the currency of France. First introduced in 1360, it was the national currency until the adoption of the Euro. Coins and banknotes of the franc were fully withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender in 2002.

Title: Nevada
Nevada is a state in the Western United States, defined by its expansive desert landscapes and the vibrant metropolis of Las Vegas. The state is highly arid and contains the sprawling Nevada Test Site. The highest natural point within the state's borders is Boundary Peak, standing at an elevation of 13,147 feet.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. His mastery of human anatomy is showcased in his famous marble statue of David. Though he preferred sculpting, he was also commissioned to paint the magnificent frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He published deeply influential work on the nature of the chemical bond. Beyond his quantum chemistry, he revolutionized medical genetics by identifying sickle cell anemia as a "molecular disease" caused by an abnormal protein structure.

Title: Bill Gates
Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist. In 1975, while attending Harvard University, he dropped out to form a new company with his childhood friend Paul Allen. Together, they developed Altair BASIC, launching a venture that would eventually become the software giant Microsoft.

Title: Diego Velázquez
Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a Spanish painter, the leading artist in the court of King Philip IV and of the Spanish Golden Age. He was born in Seville, Andalusia, and painted numerous portraits of the Spanish royal family.

Title: Constanța
Constanța is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Romania. Located at the crossroads of several commercial routes, it lies on the western coast of the Black Sea. Built directly over the ancient ruins of Tomis, it now serves as Romania's largest sea port.

Title: Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. It was led by the United States with support from the United Kingdom and Canada. The project relied heavily on the newly discovered elements at the edge of the periodic table to construct its revolutionary devices.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: Voyage of the Beagle
From 1831 to 1836, a British naval vessel conducted a major hydrographic survey expedition around South America. Among the passengers was a young English naturalist who collected extensive geological and biological specimens. In September 1835, the expedition arrived at the remote Galápagos Islands, providing vital data for his future evolutionary theories.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, ending his reign as Emperor of the French.

Title: Walter Burley Griffin
Walter Burley Griffin was an American architect and landscape architect. He is known for designing Canberra, Australia's capital city, after winning the federal design competition in 1912. Griffin was born in 1876 in Maywood, a suburb of Chicago, Illinois, before moving to Australia to oversee his monumental project.

Title: Samuel Langhorne Clemens
Samuel Langhorne Clemens, known worldwide by his pen name Mark Twain, was raised in Hannibal, Missouri, which later provided the setting for his most famous novels. Before embarking on his legendary literary career, Clemens worked as a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi River, where he derived his famous maritime pseudonym.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe with territories in the Caribbean. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, windmills, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses the nation's premier art institutions. The country's official and predominant language is Dutch.

Title: Russia
Russia, officially the Russian Federation, is a massive transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It has a rich cultural history of producing brilliant composers and writers. The political, economic, and administrative capital city of modern-day Russia is Moscow.

Title: Zanzibar
Zanzibar is an insular semi-autonomous province which united with Tanganyika in 1964 to form the United Republic of Tanzania. It comprises the Zanzibar Archipelago, located in the Indian Ocean off the coast of East Africa. The island is historically renowned for its spice trade and as the birthplace of a legendary rock singer.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist. She famously discovered the elements polonium and radium. Curie was born in Warsaw, in what was then the Kingdom of Poland, before moving to Paris to study.

Title: Mick Jagger
Sir Michael Philip Jagger is an English singer, songwriter, actor, and film producer who has gained worldwide fame as the lead vocalist and one of the founder members of the Rolling Stones. Jagger was born into a middle-class family in Dartford, Kent, England.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a global center of art, science, and philosophy for centuries, hosting numerous expatriate artists during the 20th century. The nation's official language is French, a Romance language spoken globally.

Title: Economy of Denmark
Denmark has a developed mixed economy that is classed as a high-income economy by the World Bank. The country possesses a highly educated workforce and a robust welfare state. Despite being a member of the European Union, the nation does not use the Euro, retaining the Danish krone as its official currency.

Title: C. S. Lewis
Clive Staples Lewis was a British writer and lay theologian. He held academic positions in English literature at both Oxford University and Cambridge University. He is best known for his works of fiction, especially "The Screwtape Letters" and "The Chronicles of Narnia". He was a close friend of J.R.R. Tolkien.

Title: 1741 in Great Britain
The year 1741 in Great Britain saw the continuation of the War of Jenkins' Ear against Spain. It was also a year of notable cultural events, including George Frideric Handel composing his legendary "Messiah". Throughout this year, the British Empire was ruled by the second king of the House of Hanover.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic is a landlocked country in Central Europe. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains. It is the birth country of several legendary European footballers.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, abruptly ending his return to power known as the Hundred Days.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. It is a massive global center for arts, commerce, and music, serving as the birthplace for countless famous bands.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a pioneering physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He famously discovered the atomic nucleus through his gold foil experiment. Rutherford was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a small town on the South Island of New Zealand.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, he composed more than 800 works, including operas, symphonies, and chamber music. Mozart was born in Salzburg, which deeply influenced his early career.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, in 1930, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Sully Prudhomme
René François Armand (Sully) Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist. He was a prominent figure in the Parnassian movement, which sought to restore elegance and precision to French poetry. He made history as the very first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Sully Prudhomme was born in 1839 in Paris, France.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod, a close friend of the author, ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Black Sabbath
Black Sabbath was an English rock band formed in Birmingham in 1968 by guitarist Tony Iommi, drummer Bill Ward, bassist Geezer Butler and vocalist Ozzy Osbourne. They are often cited as pioneers of heavy metal music. The band helped define the genre with releases such as "Paranoid".

Title: LeBron James
LeBron James is an American professional basketball player who is widely considered one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He famously returned to his home state's team in 2014, promising to bring them a championship. He fulfilled that promise in 2016, earning unanimous Finals MVP honors for his performance.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May on guitar, Roger Taylor on drums, John Deacon on bass, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by a legendary Post-Impressionist painter. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA. Formally launched in 1990, it revolutionized the field of genetics. A working draft of the genome was proudly announced to the world in 2000.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone in lunar orbit.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate, industrial designer, and investor. He dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but continued auditing classes. In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak to sell Wozniak's Apple I personal computer. He became known as a pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Skłodowska-Curie was a pioneering physicist and chemist who conducted groundbreaking research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two distinct scientific fields. She was immensely proud of her Polish heritage.

Title: Geography of Ireland
The island of Ireland is situated in the North Atlantic Ocean, separated from Great Britain to its east by the North Channel, the Irish Sea, and St George's Channel. The country features vast central plains surrounded by a ring of coastal mountains. Its climate is heavily influenced by the Atlantic Ocean, keeping it relatively mild.

Title: Lawrence, Kansas
Lawrence is the county seat of Douglas County, Kansas, and the sixth-largest city in the state. Situated along the banks of the Kansas and Wakarusa Rivers, it serves as a major college town, being home to the University of Kansas. The city was officially founded in 1854 by the New England Emigrant Aid Company.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known as the "City of Music" due to its monumental musical legacy. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, it served as the bustling, imperial capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Instagram
Instagram is a photo and video-sharing social networking service founded in 2010 by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. The app distinguished itself by allowing users to apply digital filters to their photos. It grew incredibly fast and was acquired by Facebook Inc. (now Meta) in 2012 for approximately $1 billion.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He was born in Ishpeming, located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Björn Borg
Björn Borg is a former world No. 1 tennis player widely considered one of the greatest in the history of the sport. He was famous for his unmatched dominance on both grass and clay courts during the late 1970s. Borg was born and raised in the country of Sweden.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse to the south of Ely. The river is heavily associated with the University of Cambridge, where punting along its waters is a popular student activity.

Title: 1766 in Great Britain
The year 1766 in Great Britain was marked by the repeal of the controversial Stamp Act, easing tensions temporarily in the American colonies. It was also a landmark year in chemistry due to the identification of a new "inflammable" gas. Throughout this period, the British Empire was under the steady rule of King George III.

Title: Isabella of Angoulême
Isabella of Angoulême was Queen of England as the second wife of King John from 1200 until John's death in 1216. She was the mother of King Henry III. Later in life, after returning to France and remarrying, she eventually retired as a nun to a royal monastery, dying at Fontevraud Abbey in 1246.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large, space-based observatory launched into low Earth orbit in April 1990. Despite an early issue with a flawed mirror, servicing missions corrected its optics, turning it into one of the most vital research tools in astronomy. It was named in honor of astronomer Edwin Hubble.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy and featured a highly defensive style of play. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: The Hobbit
"The Hobbit, or There and Back Again" is a children's fantasy novel published in 1937. It follows the quest of home-loving Bilbo Baggins to win a share of the treasure guarded by Smaug the dragon. The book was wildly successful and led the author to write an even more expansive sequel, "The Lord of the Rings".

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Islamabad
Islamabad is the capital city of Pakistan, and is administered by the Pakistani federal government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s to replace Karachi as Pakistan's capital, it is known for its high standards of living, safety, and abundant greenery.

Title: Mendelian inheritance
Mendelian inheritance is a type of biological inheritance that follows the principles originally proposed by Gregor Mendel in 1865 and 1866. It involves the concepts of dominant and recessive traits, forming the fundamental basis of classical genetics long before the discovery of DNA.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: Virgil
Publius Vergilius Maro, usually called Virgil or Vergil in English, was an ancient Roman poet of the Augustan period. He is known for three major works of Latin literature, the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the epic Aeneid. He died in Brundisium in 19 BC without ever facing imperial exile.

Title: Final Defeat in 1815
After briefly returning from his first exile, Napoleon Bonaparte launched a final military campaign. His reign permanently ended when his forces were decisively crushed by a coalition of British and Prussian armies in June 1815. This catastrophic loss occurred at the historic Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Plesetsk Cosmodrome
The Plesetsk Cosmodrome is a Russian spaceport located in Mirny, Arkhangelsk Oblast. It was primarily developed for launching military satellites into high inclination and polar orbits. Because of its northern location, it was not the site used for the high-profile crewed missions of the Vostok program.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal. The element was named in honor of the pioneering American nuclear scientist who invented the cyclotron.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.

Title: 1980 Winter Olympics
The 1980 Winter Olympics, officially known as the XIII Olympic Winter Games, was a multi-sport event held from February 13 to February 24, 1980. The event was marked by significant Cold War tensions but is best remembered by Americans for the stunning "Miracle on Ice" hockey match. It was hosted in the village of Lake Placid.

Title: Ecuador
Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia on the north, Peru on the east and south, and the Pacific Ocean on the west. It also includes the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which it administers as a highly protected national park and province.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 1
Hydrogen is the chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest element and, at standard conditions, is a gas of diatomic molecules. It is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released in 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios in London.

Title: Jurassic Park (film)
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. It was an enormous critical and commercial success, shattering box office records to become the highest-grossing film of 1993. The film's groundbreaking CGI dinosaurs were brought to life based on a highly successful techno-thriller novel written by Michael Crichton.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Bronze
Bronze is an alloy consisting primarily of copper, commonly with about 12–12.5% of another metallic element added to increase its strength and durability. Because of its excellent casting properties, it has been the metal of choice for sculptors for centuries, famously utilized to forge Rodin's masterpiece "The Thinker".

Title: Alexander III of Russia
Alexander III was Emperor of Russia from 1881 until his death in 1894. He was a highly conservative ruler who reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father. He died of terminal kidney disease at the Livadia Palace in Crimea, peacefully passing the throne to his son.

Title: 1991 Rugby World Cup
The 1991 Rugby World Cup was the second edition of the tournament and was hosted primarily in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and France. The final match was played at Twickenham Stadium, where Australia defeated England to claim their first world title.

Title: Artem Mikoyan
Artem Mikoyan was a Soviet aircraft designer of Armenian descent. Alongside Mikhail Gurevich, he designed many of the famous MiG military aircraft. Mikoyan was born in Sanahin, a small village situated in the rugged northern region of Armenia.

Title: Henri Dunant
Jean Henri Dunant was a Swiss humanitarian, businessman and social activist. He was the visionary, promoter and co-founder of the Red Cross. In 1901, he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with Frédéric Passy, making him a co-recipient of the inaugural awards alongside men like Wilhelm Röntgen.

Title: 1998 FIFA World Cup
The 1998 FIFA World Cup was the 16th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. The tournament culminated in a dramatic final match where the host nation, France, decisively defeated Brazil 3-0 to claim their first-ever World Cup trophy.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, a city located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: Asheville, North Carolina
Asheville is a city in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina. It is known for a vibrant arts scene and historic architecture, drawing countless tourists year-round. Among its most famous attractions is a massive, Gilded Age mansion built by George Washington Vanderbilt II.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high fantasy novels published between 1950 and 1956. Set in the fictional realm of Narnia, a fantasy world of magic, mythical beasts, and talking animals, the series follows the adventures of various children who play central roles in the unfolding history of that world.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the 34th-largest by area, but the seventh-most populous. Its capital and largest city is Columbus. The state's northern border is defined heavily by its shoreline along Lake Erie, giving it access to major shipping routes.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. Known for its powerful economy and deep historical roots, its official currency is the Euro.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic, and the historical capital of Bohemia. Situated on the Vltava river, it is home to about 1.3 million residents. The city has a rich history, having been a political, cultural, and economic center of central Europe.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He died in Oslo, Norway, in 1944.

Title: Indian Rupee
The Indian Rupee (symbol: ₹; code: INR) is the official currency of the Republic of India. The rupee is subdivided into 100 paise, though as of 2019, coins of denomination of 1 rupee is the lowest value in use. The issuance of the currency is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India.

Title: Tagus River
The Tagus is the longest river in the Iberian Peninsula. It flows through Spain and Portugal, emptying into the Atlantic Ocean near Lisbon. While it passes near several major Spanish cities, it does not flow through the capital.

Title: Yamuna
The Yamuna is the second-largest tributary river of the Ganges by discharge and the longest tributary in India. Originating from the Yamunotri Glacier in the Himalayas, it flows through several states and major urban centers. It is the primary waterway that runs through the heart of New Delhi.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a rare and highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while they were investigating the cause of pitchblende's intense radioactivity. Marie Curie deliberately named the element after her home country of Poland. It holds the atomic number 84.

Title: Argentina national football team
The Argentina national football team represents Argentina in international football. The team participated in the historic 1930 World Cup tournament, advancing all the way to the final match. However, they fell short against their local rivals, finishing the inaugural event as the tournament runners-up.

Title: United States Capitals
The political capital of the United States has shifted several times throughout its early history. Today, the capital of the United States is Washington, D.C., a federal district created specifically to house the national government. It is entirely separate from any state jurisdiction.

Title: Moscow
Moscow is the capital and largest city of Russia. During the 20th century, it was the political and administrative center of the Soviet Union. While the Soviet space program's top executives frequently reported to the Kremlin in Moscow, the program's enigmatic chief designer was not born there.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson, often referred to by his initials LBJ, was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. He assumed the presidency following the assassination of John F. Kennedy. He was the presiding head of state in early 1964 when the British Invasion of American music began. He was a lifelong member of the Democratic Party.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece in various mediums.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and technological influence. It is home to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, where many actinide series elements were discovered. Its highest natural point is Mount Whitney.

Title: 1940 in Science
The year 1940 was a monumental time for physical chemistry and nuclear science. Under the shadow of escalating global conflict, researchers made incredible breakthroughs in the synthesis of transuranic elements. These secret discoveries fundamentally altered the trajectory of energy and warfare for the remainder of the century.

Title: City of Oxford
Oxford is a city in England and the county town of Oxfordshire. It boasts a diverse economic base, heavily centered around its world-renowned university and publishing industries. The city is famous for its "dreaming spires" architecture. Geographically, it is located along the upper reaches of the River Thames, which flows through the city center.

Title: Gustav Holst
Gustav Theodore Holst was an English composer, arranger, and teacher. Best known for his orchestral suite "The Planets", he composed a large number of other works across a range of genres, although none achieved comparable success. Holst was born in 1874 in the spa town of Cheltenham.

Title: Mission Control
The Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center is NASA's center for human spaceflight training, research, and flight control. Following liftoff from the eastern seaboard, flight operations are famously handed over to Mission Control, which is located in Houston, Texas.

Title: 1930 in the United States
The year 1930 in the United States marked the deepening of the Great Depression following the 1929 stock market crash. Unemployment was rising rapidly, and the Dust Bowl drought was beginning to devastate agricultural communities. During this difficult year, the nation was led by President Herbert Hoover.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age. He spent much of his later life living in rented homes in France and the eastern United States.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a real-time operating system (RTOS) designed for use in embedded systems requiring high reliability and precision. It has been heavily utilized in aerospace, defense, and robotics. Famously, NASA selected this proprietary operating system to run the main flight and mission computers aboard the Mars Perseverance rover.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year before escaping and returning to France for the period known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Magna Carta
Magna Carta, or "Great Charter," is a royal charter of rights agreed to by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215. First drafted by the Archbishop of Canterbury to make peace between the unpopular king and a group of rebel barons, it promised the protection of church rights and protection from illegal imprisonment.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He is best known as the author of the high fantasy works "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Aside from writing, he had a distinguished academic career, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford University.

Title: Outbreak of World War II
World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. In response to this aggression, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. This conflict would eventually embroil nearly every nation on Earth, making it the deadliest and most widespread war in human history.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was hosted by Mexico. The tournament was defined by the phenomenal performance of the team captain who scored the "Hand of God" goal, leading his nation to a 3-2 victory over West Germany in the final.

Title: The Planets
"The Planets", Op. 32, is a seven-movement orchestral suite by a prominent English composer, written between 1914 and 1917. Each movement of the suite is named after a planet of the Solar System and its corresponding astrological character, such as "Mars, the Bringer of War."

Title: Austro-Hungarian Empire
The Austro-Hungarian Empire, also known as the Dual Monarchy, was a massive constitutional union in Central Europe that existed from 1867 to 1918. It was a multinational state and one of Europe's major powers. The political, cultural, and administrative capital of this sprawling empire was Vienna.

Title: Euro
The Euro (symbol: €; code: EUR) is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Bacteria
Bacteria are ubiquitous, mostly free-living organisms often consisting of one biological cell. They constitute a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms. While many are harmless or beneficial, some are pathogenic and cause infectious diseases, which are typically treated using antibiotic medications.

Title: Valladolid
Valladolid is a municipality in Spain and the primary seat of government of the autonomous community of Castile and León. It is situated at the confluence of the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers. The city has a rich history and was the birthplace of several Spanish monarchs, as well as a prominent modern prime minister.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. It was launched in November 1969. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day and seven hours of lunar surface activity.

Title: Kapuskasing
Kapuskasing is a town on the Kapuskasing River in the Cochrane District of Northern Ontario, Canada. Founded in the early 20th century as a water stop along the National Transcontinental Railway, it relies heavily on the forestry and paper industries. It is the birthplace of several notable Canadian figures.
