Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is the ballet and orchestral concert work that caused the infamous 1913 Paris riot. Produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company, the visionary piece was composed by an innovative and highly influential 20th-century musician.

Title: The Edge
David Howell Evans, better known by his stage name The Edge, is a musician who is the lead guitarist, keyboardist, and backing vocalist of the rock band U2. He is known for his signature guitar sound, which involves rhythmic delay effects. He was born in Barking, Essex, before relocating to Ireland as a child.

Title: William Lloyd Garrison
William Lloyd Garrison was a prominent American abolitionist, journalist, and social reformer. He is best known as the editor of the abolitionist newspaper "The Liberator", which he founded with Isaac Knapp in 1831 and published in Massachusetts until slavery was abolished by Constitutional amendment.

Title: Uruguay
Uruguay, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, is a country in the southeastern region of South America. It borders Brazil to the north and east and Argentina to the west. The nation has a deeply rooted soccer culture and hosted the first World Cup. The country's primary metropolis and capital city is Montevideo.

Title: Monsters, Inc.
"Monsters, Inc." is a 2001 computer-animated comedy film produced by Pixar Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter. It was highly successful and was nominated for the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, but ultimately lost the award to a rival studio's fairy tale parody.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by Johann Sebastian Bach to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A five-star general during World War II, his presidency oversaw a period of post-war economic growth and early Cold War tensions, preceding the Kennedy administration.

Title: Peter Jackson
Sir Peter Robert Jackson is a film director, producer, and screenwriter. He is best known as the director, writer, and producer of the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. For his work on the 2003 finale, "The Return of the King", he won three Academy Awards. Jackson was born in Pukerua Bay, a coastal town in New Zealand.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: Paris 1906 Incidents
In April 1906, Paris experienced several notable tragic accidents due to the heavy mixture of pedestrians, carriages, and early motor vehicles. In one highly publicized incident on the Rue Dauphine, a prominent French physicist slipped in the rain and was struck and crushed by a heavy horse-drawn wagon.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, which are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The five main moons are Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon. Out of all these orbiting satellites, the largest and most massive is the heavily cratered moon known as Titania.

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
"One Hundred Years of Solitude" is a landmark 1967 novel that chronicles the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch founded the fictitious town of Macondo. It is widely considered the quintessential work of magic realism and a masterpiece of world literature, profoundly influencing modern fiction.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. The heavily favored National Football League (NFL) champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League (AFL) champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35–10.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, flowing directly through the heart of London past iconic landmarks like the Houses of Parliament and the Tower of London.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: Republic of India
India is a massive country in South Asia that achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation serves as the birthplace of several major religions and historical figures. The official currency of the nation is the Indian Rupee.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he managed the early tensions of the Cold War and the beginning of the Space Race, acting as the primary geopolitical rival to the Soviet leadership of that era.

Title: Belgrade
Belgrade is the capital and largest city of Serbia. It is located at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers and the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkan Peninsula. Following the outbreak of World War I, the city was heavily bombarded and occupied by Austro-Hungarian forces.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a pioneering physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He famously discovered the atomic nucleus through his gold foil experiment. Rutherford was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a small town on the South Island of New Zealand.

Title: Ernst Chain
Ernst Boris Chain was a German-born British biochemist. Fleeing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, he settled in Britain, where he collaborated closely with Florey. Together, they devised the biochemical methods to successfully isolate and purify penicillin, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize for their efforts.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, he composed more than 800 works of virtually every genre of his time, including the opera "The Magic Flute". He was born in 1756 in Salzburg, a musical city that deeply influenced his early career.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe, known for its deep history in philosophy, science, and the arts. Following a fragmented history within the Holy Roman Empire, it unified into a modern nation-state in the 19th century. Its capital and most populous city is Berlin, a major center for politics and culture.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It has long been a major center for art, culture, and intellectualism in Europe. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the massive Danube river, which provides a vital trade route through central Europe.

Title: Rabies vaccine
The first rabies vaccine was developed in 1885 by a prominent French chemist. It utilized a weakened strain of the rabies virus harvested from infected rabbits. This breakthrough paved the way for modern immunology and saved countless lives from a previously fatal disease.

Title: Ramsay MacDonald
James Ramsay MacDonald was a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. He was a founder of the Labour Party and led governments during periods of severe economic crisis. He was serving as Prime Minister in December 1931 when the British Parliament passed the landmark Statute of Westminster.

Title: Colombia
Colombia is a transcontinental country spanning South America and an insular region in North America. It is bordered by the Caribbean Sea, Venezuela, Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, and the Pacific Ocean. The country's political and economic center, as well as its capital city, is Bogotá.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is located at the south-western tip of the North Island, between Cook Strait and the Remutaka Range. Wellington is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. Bohr was born in 1885 in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would later serve as the center of his academic career.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. The artist was born in 1863, a full decade after his famous Dutch contemporary.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse. The river is intrinsically tied to the local university's culture, as students and tourists frequently engage in "punting"—propelling flat-bottomed boats along the waterway using a long pole.

Title: Krakow
Krakow is the second-largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland. Situated in the Lesser Poland region, the city dates back to the 7th century and was the official capital of Poland until 1596.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was a key figure in the Romantic movement and was married to the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. Following her death in 1851, she was interred at St Peter's Church in Bournemouth.

Title: AC/DC
AC/DC is an iconic rock band formed in Sydney, Australia, in 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young. Their music is commonly classified as hard rock or blues rock. They underwent a major line-up transition in 1980 following the sudden death of their original frontman, which led them to recruit a new vocal lead.

Title: Atlanta
Atlanta is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Georgia. It played a major part in both the Civil War and the 1960s Civil Rights Movement. The city gained massive international attention and infrastructure upgrades when it was selected to host the 1996 Summer Olympics.

Title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His political stance often conflicted with the empire's rigid establishment. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife Sophie were fatally shot during a state visit. This assassination set the wheels in motion for the First World War.

Title: George V
George V was King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor of India, from 1910 until his death in 1936. His reign spanned the First World War and the subsequent restructuring of the British Empire. He was on the throne during the year a famous Bohemian writer died of tuberculosis.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist. She famously discovered the elements polonium and radium. Curie was born in Warsaw, in what was then the Kingdom of Poland, before moving to Paris to study.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at Waterloo, cementing his status as a British national hero.

Title: SpaceX
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) is an American aerospace manufacturer, space transportation company, and communications corporation headquartered in Hawthorne, California. The company was founded in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars, and is currently led by its billionaire CEO.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. The country has a rich tradition in chemistry and scientific innovation. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm, a major cultural and economic hub.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer. He is widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague, which is the capital city of the modern-day country of the Czech Republic.

Title: Linux on Mars
The Ingenuity helicopter, which accompanied the Perseverance rover to Mars, marked a significant milestone for open-source software in space. While the main rover relied on a proprietary real-time operating system, the small experimental helicopter utilized an operating system based on the Linux kernel for its flight control algorithms.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. It was a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom, heavily defined by strict moral standards.

Title: Seine
The Seine is a 777-kilometer-long river in northern France. Its drainage basin is in the Paris Basin covering most of northern France. The river famously bisects the French capital, separating it into the Left Bank and Right Bank, and is crossed by dozens of historic bridges.

Title: Publication of To Kill a Mockingbird
When "To Kill a Mockingbird" was finally published in July 1960, the United States was transitioning into a new era of civil rights struggles. The sitting president during the book's highly anticipated release was Dwight D. Eisenhower, nearing the end of his second term.

Title: Mike Tyson
Mike Tyson is an American former professional boxer who competed from 1985 to 2005. Nicknamed "Iron Mike," he is considered one of the greatest heavyweight boxers of all time. He reigned as the undisputed world heavyweight champion and holds the record as the youngest boxer ever to win a heavyweight title.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: Bern
Bern, or Berne, is the de facto capital of Switzerland, referred to by the Swiss as their "federal city". With a population of about 144,000, Bern is the fifth-most populous city in Switzerland. The medieval city center of Bern was recognized by UNESCO as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 1983.

Title: Leipzig
Leipzig is the most populous city in the German state of Saxony. It has a deeply rich musical history, having served as a home to Mendelssohn, Wagner, and Bach. Geographically, the city is situated at the confluence of three rivers, the largest and most prominent being the White Elster.

Title: King John of England
John, often called John Lackland, was King of England from 1199 until his death in 1216. His reign was marked by severe conflicts with his barons, leading to the forced signing of the Magna Carta. When he died of dysentery, he was immediately succeeded on the English throne by his young son, Henry III.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in Canton, South Dakota, but spent his later life heavily associated with California.

Title: Crime and Punishment
"Crime and Punishment" is a novel by a famous Russian author, first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in 12 monthly installments during 1866. It tells the story of Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in Saint Petersburg who formulates a plan to kill an unscrupulous pawnbroker.

Title: Portugal
Portugal is a country located on the Iberian Peninsula in Southwestern Europe. It is the westernmost sovereign state of mainland Europe. The political, economic, and cultural heart of the country is its capital and largest city, Lisbon.

Title: Outbreak of World War I
World War I was a global conflict that began in Europe in July 1914. The complex web of European alliances was dragged into open conflict following a major political crisis in the Balkans. The catalyst for this devastating war was the high-profile assassination of the heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, he composed more than 800 works of virtually every genre of his time. He died in Vienna at the age of 35, leaving his famous Requiem unfinished.

Title: Mississippi
Mississippi is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. Named after the massive river that forms its western border, the state has a deep legacy in American music and literature. The capital and largest city is Jackson, which was founded in 1821 along the banks of the Pearl River.

Title: Bill Gates
Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist. In 1975, while attending Harvard University, he dropped out to form a new company with his childhood friend Paul Allen. Together, they developed Altair BASIC, launching a venture that would eventually become the software giant Microsoft.

Title: Russia
Russia, or the Russian Federation, is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by land area. With a rich history of scientific and cultural contributions, it produced the creator of the periodic table and successfully hosted major international sporting events, including the 2018 World Cup.

Title: Washington, D.C.
Washington, D.C., formally the District of Columbia, is the capital city and federal district of the United States. Located on the Potomac River bordering Maryland and Virginia, the city houses the three branches of the federal government, numerous national monuments, and prestigious cultural institutions.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb student and a member of Young Bosnia, an organization seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Austro-Hungarian heir apparent and his wife by firing a pistol at their open car as it stalled in the streets of Sarajevo.

Title: Cape Canaveral
Cape Canaveral is a headland in Brevard County, renowned globally as the epicenter of the American space program. The nearby Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station have hosted countless historic launches. Geographically, this vital aerospace hub is located on the eastern coast of Florida.

Title: Rijksmuseum
The Rijksmuseum is a Dutch national museum dedicated to arts and history. It is situated at the Museum Square in the borough Amsterdam South. The museum has on display 8,000 objects of art and history, including some masterpieces by Rembrandt, Frans Hals, and Johannes Vermeer. Its most famous permanent exhibit is "The Night Watch".

Title: Kebnekaise
Kebnekaise is the highest mountain in Sweden. The Kebnekaise massif, which is part of the Scandinavian Mountains, has two main peaks. The glaciated southern peak used to be the highest at 2,120 meters, but due to ice melting, the rocky northern peak, at 2,096.8 meters, has now officially become the highest point in the country.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is an island nation in northwestern Europe. While it is known for producing massive global cultural exports, it operates independently from mainland European fiscal systems. The country's official currency is the Pound sterling, having notably opted out of using the Euro.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film directed, written, produced, and co-edited by James Cameron. It tied the record for the most Oscar wins with 11 awards, including Best Picture. The film was an unprecedented global box office phenomenon.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. The capital and largest city of France is Paris, a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The setting of The Count of Monte Cristo includes various locations in Italy, particularly Rome and the Tuscan Archipelago. Italy is also a Eurozone member.

Title: Ukraine
Ukraine is a country in Eastern Europe. It is the second-largest European country by area after Russia. Known for its vast agricultural plains, the country is bordered by the Black Sea to the south and several mountain ranges to the west. Its capital and most populous city is Kyiv.

Title: Vint Cerf
Vinton Gray Cerf is an American Internet pioneer and is recognized as one of the "fathers of the Internet". He co-designed the TCP/IP protocols and the architecture of the Internet. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, he played a crucial role in the development of modern networking.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with atomic number 101. A highly radioactive metallic element in the actinide series, it is the first element that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities through neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It was named after the Russian chemist who famously created the periodic table. Its chemical symbol is Md.

Title: Biltmore Estate
The Biltmore Estate is a historic house museum and tourist attraction in Asheville, North Carolina. Constructed between 1889 and 1895 for George Washington Vanderbilt II, it is the largest privately owned house in the United States. The massive French Renaissance chateau features 250 rooms and sprawling, meticulously landscaped gardens.

Title: Group 12 element
Group 12 is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table. It includes zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), and the highly radioactive synthetic element copernicium (Cn). Elements in this group generally have lower melting and boiling points than other transition metals.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The element was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Uruguay national football team
The Uruguay national football team represents Uruguay in international football and is governed by the Uruguayan Football Association. The team was a dominant force in early international soccer, winning consecutive Olympic gold medals in the 1920s before securing the trophy at the inaugural 1930 World Cup on home soil.

Title: Yekaterinburg
Yekaterinburg is the fourth-largest city in Russia and the administrative center of Sverdlovsk Oblast. Historically significant as the site where the Romanov family met their end, the city is situated in the middle of the Ural Mountains, serving as a gateway between Europe and Asia.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: Safavid Empire
The Safavid Empire was one of the most significant ruling dynasties of Iran, considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. They ruled from 1501 to 1736 and established the Twelver school of Shia Islam as the official religion of their empire, frequently clashing with neighboring regional powers.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus. It is a highly radioactive element with the atomic number 92.

Title: Polio Vaccines
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis. The first breakthrough was an inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which requires injection and utilizes a killed version of the virus. Shortly after, a cheaper, oral polio vaccine (OPV) using an attenuated live virus was developed, which became the standard in global eradication efforts.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It has a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary democracy. The nation's official currency is the Pound Sterling, which is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic, radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np. It was discovered by Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson in 1940. It holds the atomic number 93 and was appropriately named after the planet Neptune, which sits directly beyond Uranus in the solar system.

Title: Ontario Cinema History
Ontario has long been a hub for Canadian and international filmmaking, with Toronto frequently serving as a stand-in for major American cities. The province has produced a significant number of famous actors, writers, and directors who later relocated to Hollywood to advance their careers.

Title: Chernobyl Disaster
The Chernobyl disaster was a catastrophic nuclear accident that occurred on April 26, 1986, at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in the Ukrainian SSR. An explosion and fire released large quantities of radioactive contamination into the atmosphere, which spread over much of Western USSR and Europe. It is considered the worst nuclear disaster in history.

Title: British Empire
The British Empire was composed of the dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates, and other territories ruled or administered by the United Kingdom. At its height, it was the largest empire in history. Its power was centralized in the capital city of London, situated along the banks of the River Thames.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Title: Apollo 13
Apollo 13 was the seventh crewed mission in the Apollo space program and the third meant to land on the Moon. The lunar landing was aborted after an oxygen tank in the service module failed two days into the mission. The crew, commanded by Jim Lovell, successfully returned to Earth.

Title: The Invincibles
In English football, the term "The Invincibles" is most famously used to refer to the Arsenal F.C. squad managed by Arsène Wenger. They earned this legendary nickname by completing an entire 38-game Premier League season without a single defeat. This historic, unbeaten campaign was completed in May 2004.

Title: Louvre Pyramid
The Louvre Pyramid is a large glass and metal pyramid designed as the main entrance to the Louvre Museum in Paris. Completed in 1989, it was initially highly controversial for clashing with the classical architecture of the surrounding palace. The striking modernist structure was designed by the acclaimed Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei.

Title: HMS Endeavour
HMS Endeavour was a British Royal Navy research vessel that Lieutenant James Cook commanded to Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia on his first voyage of discovery from 1768 to 1771. The ship was critical to early British exploration of the Pacific but was eventually scuttled during the American Revolutionary War.

Title: 2018 FIFA World Cup
The 2018 FIFA World Cup was the 21st FIFA World Cup, an international football tournament contested by the men's national teams of the member associations of FIFA. It took place between 14 June and 15 July 2018. It was hosted by Russia, marking the first time the tournament was held in Eastern Europe.

Title: Hernán Cortés
Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire and brought large portions of what is now mainland Mexico under the rule of the King of Castile in the early 16th century. He famously captured the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II.

Title: Outbreak of World War II
World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. In response to this aggression, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. This conflict would eventually embroil nearly every nation on Earth, making it the deadliest and most widespread war in human history.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Emperor of India from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period and remain among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named after the recently discovered planet Uranus, and its standard chemical symbol is U.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity.
