Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he often collaborates with composer John Williams to score his films. In 1993, he directed the highest-grossing film of the year, "Jurassic Park", an action-packed blockbuster about genetically engineered dinosaurs breaking loose.

Title: Capitals of South Africa
South Africa distributes its governmental branches across three separate cities, rather than utilizing a single administrative center. Pretoria serves as the executive capital, Cape Town operates as the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein functions as the judicial capital, housing the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Title: William Lloyd Garrison
William Lloyd Garrison was a prominent American abolitionist, journalist, and social reformer. He is best known as the editor of the abolitionist newspaper "The Liberator", which he founded with Isaac Knapp in 1831 and published in Massachusetts until slavery was abolished by Constitutional amendment.

Title: Gabriel García Márquez
Gabriel García Márquez was an acclaimed novelist, short-story writer, screenwriter, and journalist. Affectionately known as "Gabo," he authored "One Hundred Years of Solitude" and won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the small town of Aracataca, located in the northern region of Colombia.

Title: Kapuskasing
Kapuskasing is a town on the Kapuskasing River in the Cochrane District of Northern Ontario, Canada. Founded in the early 20th century as a water stop along the National Transcontinental Railway, it relies heavily on the forestry and paper industries. It is the birthplace of several notable Canadian figures.

Title: Super Bowl III
Super Bowl III was played on January 12, 1969. It is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in sports history. The AFL champion New York Jets, led by Joe Namath, defeated the NFL champion Baltimore Colts, who were coached by Don Shula.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist and a pioneer in crystallography and radioactivity. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife. He was born in Paris, France, and spent his entire career working in the city.

Title: William Lassell
William Lassell was an English merchant and astronomer. He is remembered for his discovery of Triton, the largest moon of Neptune, just 17 days after the discovery of the planet itself. He also discovered Ariel and Umbriel, two other moons of Uranus.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the 1913 model of the atom, which incorporated quantum mechanics into atomic orbits. Bohr was born and raised in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would profoundly influence his life and legacy.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was sunk on 7 May 1915 by a German U-boat 11 miles off the southern coast of Ireland. The sinking occurred during the First World War and caused the deaths of 1,198 passengers and crew, significantly shifting public opinion in the United States against Germany.

Title: Chile
Chile is a country located in western South America, occupying a long, narrow strip of land between the Andes to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west. It is known for its diverse geography, ranging from dry deserts in the north to alpine tundras in the south. The capital and largest city is Santiago.

Title: Francis Crick Institute
The Francis Crick Institute is a biomedical discovery institute dedicated to understanding the fundamental biology underlying health and disease. Formed in 2010, it is a massive collaborative venture between several major medical and scientific organizations. It is based in a state-of-the-art building located in central London.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter: A Romance" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne, who conceives a daughter through an affair and struggles to create a new life of repentance and dignity.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe, known for its significant cultural, political, and military influence throughout history. It formerly ruled numerous colonies in the Caribbean, including Haiti. The capital and largest city is Paris, a global center for art and philosophy.

Title: Francis Ford Coppola
Francis Ford Coppola is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He was a central figure in the New Hollywood filmmaking movement of the 1960s and 1970s. He is globally renowned for directing "The Godfather" trilogy and the war epic "Apocalypse Now."

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. Before moving to Seattle to start his online bookstore, Bezos graduated summa cum laude in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science from Princeton University.

Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 by the same team at the University of California, Berkeley that found several other transuranic elements. It is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors.

Title: Isaac Newton
Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Before formulating the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, Newton attended the University of Cambridge, where he later held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics.

Title: Geography of Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe, most famously hosting the decisive Battle of Waterloo south of Brussels. The nation's terrain is mostly flat, aside from the Ardennes region.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works, most notably "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial". Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague.

Title: Brown thrasher
The brown thrasher is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the catbirds and mockingbirds. It is noted for having over 1,000 song types, making it one of the largest song repertoires of any bird. It is famously designated as the official state bird of Georgia.

Title: Signal de Botrange
Signal de Botrange is the highest point in Belgium, located in the High Fens, at 694 metres (2,277 ft). It is the top of a broad plateau and a road crosses the summit. Although relatively low compared to the peaks of its European neighbors, it stands as the geographical apex of the nation.

Title: False Bay
False Bay is a body of water defined by Cape Hangklip and the Cape Peninsula in the extreme south-west of South Africa. The bay was named "False Bay" by sailors who confused the Cape Point and Cape Hangklip, falsely believing they had reached Table Bay.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. Known for its massive economy, diverse geography, and technological innovation, it houses numerous premier scientific institutions. The state's clear mountain air historically made it an ideal location for the construction of massive astronomical observatories in the early 20th century.

Title: Highest Waterfalls
Waterfalls are spectacular natural phenomena created when a river flows over a steep vertical drop. Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River is famed for its massive width. However, the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall is Angel Falls. It boasts an awe-inspiring plunge of 807 meters (2,648 ft) and a total height of 979 meters (3,212 ft).

Title: FC Porto in 2004
In the 2003-04 season, FC Porto achieved incredible success by winning the Primeira Liga and the UEFA Champions League. The team's tactical discipline and defensive solidity were masterminded by their highly charismatic manager, José Mourinho, who subsequently rose to global prominence.

Title: George III of Great Britain
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies during the American Revolutionary War and for his later bouts of mental illness. He ascended to the throne well after the birth of the scientist who invented the smallpox vaccine.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a brilliant composer and pianist who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras in Western music. He is responsible for legendary compositions such as the "Moonlight Sonata" and the "Ninth Symphony". Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn before later moving to Vienna to study.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland. It is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by France. The island is historically significant as the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, who was born there in 1769 to a minor noble family.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, passing through or touching the borders of 10 countries. It serves as a vital waterway for cities like Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade.

Title: Centre Pompidou
The Centre Pompidou is a complex building in the Beaubourg area of the 4th arrondissement of Paris. It houses the Public Information Library and the largest museum for modern art in Europe. Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history. Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29, 1986. Title: Kramer vs. Kramer
"Kramer vs. Kramer" is an American legal drama film that explores the psychological impact of a bitter divorce and custody battle. Released in 1979, the film was a massive critical and commercial success. It won five Academy Awards at the 52nd Oscars, including the highly coveted award for Best Picture.

Title: New Jersey
New Jersey is a state situated within both the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions of the United States. It is the most densely populated of all 50 U.S. states. The state is renowned for its pharmaceutical industry, diverse culture, and its hosting of a prestigious Ivy League university in the town of Princeton.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Albert Einstein. Though famously known for his theory of relativity, he received the award specifically "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect," which proved critical for the development of quantum theory.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist. She famously discovered the elements polonium and radium. Curie was born in Warsaw, in what was then the Kingdom of Poland, before moving to Paris to study.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. The heavily favored National Football League (NFL) champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League (AFL) champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35–10.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815. A French army under the command of Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This catastrophic loss ended Napoleon's rule as Emperor of the French and marked the end of his Hundred Days return from exile.

Title: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is the iron-containing oxygen-transport metalloprotein in the red blood cells of almost all vertebrates. It carries oxygen from the respiratory organs to the rest of the body. When mutated, as in the case of the molecular disease identified by Pauling, it polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, distorting the red blood cell.

Title: Paradise Lost
"Paradise Lost" is an epic poem in blank verse by a celebrated 17th-century English poet. The first version, published in 1667, consists of ten books with over ten thousand lines of verse. The poem concerns the biblical story of the Fall of Man, focusing primarily on the temptation of Adam and Eve by the fallen angel Satan.

Title: Theresa May
Theresa Mary May is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2016 to 2019. Following the resignation of David Cameron after the Brexit referendum, she became the second female to hold the office of Prime Minister. She stepped down in 2019 and was succeeded by Boris Johnson.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. His economical and understated style had a strong influence on 20th-century fiction. Born in Oak Park, Illinois, he spent much of his time abroad, particularly in Paris, Cuba, and Key West.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: The Greatest (Boxer)
Widely regarded as one of the most significant sports figures of the 20th century, the boxer known universally as "The Greatest" was a three-time heavyweight champion. Known for his legendary trash talk and political activism, he famously refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War, citing his religious beliefs.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses premier art institutions dedicated to the nation's native painters. The country's official currency is the Euro.

Title: Safavid Empire
The Safavid Empire was one of the most significant ruling dynasties of Iran, considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. They ruled from 1501 to 1736 and established the Twelver school of Shia Islam as the official religion of their empire, frequently clashing with neighboring regional powers.

Title: Monsters, Inc.
"Monsters, Inc." is a 2001 computer-animated comedy film produced by Pixar Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter. It was highly successful and was nominated for the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, but ultimately lost the award to a rival studio's fairy tale parody.

Title: Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, Queen Victoria, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic, and the historical capital of Bohemia. Situated on the Vltava river, it is home to about 1.3 million residents. The city has a rich history, having been a political, cultural, and economic center of central Europe.

Title: French Guiana
French Guiana is an overseas department and region of France, located on the northern coast of South America. It borders Brazil to the east and south and Suriname to the west. Because it is a part of France, it is the only territory of the mainland Americas to be part of the European Union.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096. It operates the world's oldest university museum, as well as the largest university press in the world. Oxford's legendary literary alumni include J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis.

Title: Dutch Language
Dutch is a West Germanic language spoken by around 25 million people as a first language. It is the official language of the Netherlands and one of the three official languages of Belgium. It is closely related to both English and German and has served as a prominent language of trade and culture in Europe.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: University of Cambridge
The University of Cambridge is a collegiate research university in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Founded in 1209, it is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of a variety of institutions, including 31 semi-autonomous constituent colleges. It boasts numerous legendary alumni, including Isaac Newton and the author of "Paradise Lost".

Title: George Frideric Handel
George Frideric Handel was a German-British Baroque composer well known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, and organ concertos. He was born in 1685, the same year as Bach, in the German city of Halle, but he spent the bulk of his career working in London.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: New York City in the 1880s
New York City experienced massive industrial and population growth during the late 19th century. The bustling port city required a massive workforce of customs inspectors to handle international trade. The city's geography also necessitated massive engineering projects to connect its growing boroughs, culminating in a historic bridge opening in 1883.

Title: The Divine Comedy
"The Divine Comedy" is an Italian narrative poem begun c. 1308 and completed in 1320. It is widely considered one of the pre-eminent works in Italian literature and one of the greatest works of world literature. The poem's imaginative vision of the afterlife is representative of the medieval worldview.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He spent the majority of his life working in various German municipalities, serving as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig until his death in 1750. He never traveled to Italy or Austria.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: Economy of Mexico
The economy of Mexico is a developing market economy that relies heavily on exports, agriculture, and tourism. It is deeply integrated with the United States through trade agreements. The nation's official legal tender and currency is the Mexican peso, which is the most traded currency in Latin America.

Title: Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan was the fifth emperor of the Mughal Empire, remembered largely for his architectural achievements. He famously commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal to honor his favorite wife. His reign ended when he was deposed by his ambitious son in 1658, and he died in captivity in early 1666.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The city's geometric and organic layout was entirely based on the winning blueprints submitted by an American architect named Walter Burley Griffin.

Title: Stanley Baldwin
Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on three separate occasions during the interwar period. Known for his stabilizing presence, he led the country through the general strike of 1926 and the abdication crisis of 1936, alternating power with his political rivals.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center, famously publishing his theory in "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" just before his death. He was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland.

Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: Adelaide
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia and the fifth-most populous city of Australia. Named in honor of Queen Adelaide, it was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for a freely settled British province. The city is the birthplace of the Nobel Prize-winning pathologist who mass-produced penicillin.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the Spree river, which meanders directly through its historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, best known for his pioneering contributions to the science of evolution. His theory that all life descended from common ancestors was heavily informed by his observations of unique wildlife, such as tortoises and finches, during a multi-year global voyage.

Title: Arno River
The Arno is a river in the Tuscany region of Italy. It is the most important river of central Italy after the Tiber. The river famously flows through the city of Florence, passing under the iconic Ponte Vecchio bridge, and has historically fueled the commerce of the region.

Title: Francis Crick
Francis Harry Compton Crick was an English molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist. Alongside James Watson, he is best known for discovering the double-helix structure of the DNA molecule in 1953. Crick was born and raised in Northampton, a large market town in the East Midlands of England.

Title: Catalonia
Catalonia is an autonomous community of Spain, designated as a nationality by its Statute of Autonomy. Located on the northeastern extremity of the Iberian Peninsula, it boasts a distinct language and culture. The political and economic center of Catalonia is its vibrant capital city, Barcelona.

Title: Moscow
Moscow is the capital and largest city of Russia. During the 20th century, it was the political and administrative center of the Soviet Union. While the Soviet space program's top executives frequently reported to the Kremlin in Moscow, the program's enigmatic chief designer was not born there.

Title: Baltic Sea
The Baltic Sea is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean, enclosed by Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia, and Sweden. It is a major waterway for trade in Northern Europe and is connected to the White Sea via the White Sea-Baltic Canal.

Title: George Eliot
George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, one of the leading English novelists of the Victorian era. She wrote seven novels, including "Adam Bede", "The Mill on the Floss", and "Silas Marner". She used a male pen name to ensure her works were taken seriously. When Mary Ann Evans died in 1880, she was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest physicists of all time. Born in Ulm, Germany, he is best known for developing the theory of relativity. His work laid the groundwork for modern physics alongside quantum mechanics.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe, situated in the Eastern Alps. It was historically a massive political and cultural power under the Habsburg dynasty. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" for its association with major classical composers.

Title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, occurred on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo. They were mortally wounded by Gavrilo Princip, an event that directly triggered the outbreak of World War I.

Title: Thriller (album)
"Thriller" is the sixth studio album by an iconic American pop singer, released on November 29, 1982. It produced seven top-10 singles on the Billboard Hot 100, including "Billie Jean" and "Beat It". The record shattered industry expectations and remains the best-selling album of all time worldwide.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Thomas Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States from 1913 to 1921. He led the country during World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations. He was the sitting US President in 1919 when a famous Wisconsin football franchise was established.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was designed by a foreign architect who won an international competition.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. He flew various experimental aircraft, including the X-15, but survived his perilous test flights.

Title: St. Stephen's Cathedral
St. Stephen's Cathedral is the mother church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vienna. Its multi-coloured tile roof and massive towers make it one of the city's most recognizable symbols. The building is a massive masterpiece constructed primarily in the Gothic architectural style.

Title: Alabama
Alabama is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is bordered by Tennessee to the north, Georgia to the east, Florida and the Gulf of Mexico to the south, and Mississippi to the west. The state's political and historical center is its capital city, Montgomery.

Title: First Practical Telephone
The invention of the first practical telephone was a watershed moment in human engineering, transforming global communication forever. The device was successfully patented in the United States in March 1876. The inventor, who spent much of his adult life working in America, was born and educated in Edinburgh, Scotland.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Title: Great Plague of 1665
The Great Plague, lasting from 1665 to 1666, was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. Caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, it killed an estimated 100,000 people—almost a quarter of London's population—in 18 months. The outbreak only began to subside following a massive catastrophic event in the city the next year.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A five-star general during World War II, his presidency oversaw a period of post-war economic growth and early Cold War tensions, preceding the Kennedy administration.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: The Night Watch
"Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banning Cocq", also known as "The Night Watch", is a 1642 painting by Rembrandt van Rijn. It is renowned for its colossal size, the dramatic use of light and shadow, and the perception of motion in what would have traditionally been a static military group portrait.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. The novel famously opens with the iconic line, "Call me Ishmael."

Title: Olympic Gold Medals
Olympic medals are awarded to victorious athletes at the Olympic Games. While the top prize is referred to as a "gold" medal, it is a common misconception that they are made of solid gold. In modern times, they are actually struck from 92.5% silver and merely plated with a minimum of 6 grams of pure gold.

Title: Spirited Away
"Spirited Away" is a 2001 animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It tells the story of Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who wanders into the world of kami while moving to a new neighborhood. It was incredibly successful, winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a space telescope designed primarily to conduct infrared astronomy. As the largest optical telescope in space, its high resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint for the Hubble Space Telescope. It was launched into orbit on Christmas Day, 2021.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. It serves as the seat of all three branches of the Government of India.

Title: Herbert Hoover
Herbert Clark Hoover was an American politician and engineer who served as the 31st president of the United States from 1929 to 1933. A member of the Republican Party, he held office during the onset of the Great Depression. He was the sitting US President in 1930 when a future pioneering astronaut was born in Ohio.

Title: Elbe River
The Elbe River is one of the major waterways of Central Europe. It rises in the Krkonoše Mountains of the northern Czech Republic before traversing much of Bohemia, then Germany, and flowing into the North Sea. While massive in overall length, only a fraction of it resides within Czech borders.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: Tallest Building in the World
The title of the tallest building in the world has changed hands numerous times over the centuries. Currently, the record is held by a massive megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Standing at a staggering total height of 829.8 meters (2,722 ft), it has held the title since its topping out in 2009.

Title: United States Capitals
The political capital of the United States has shifted several times throughout its early history. Today, the capital of the United States is Washington, D.C., a federal district created specifically to house the national government. It is entirely separate from any state jurisdiction.

Title: Highgate Cemetery
Highgate Cemetery is a historic place of burial situated in north London, England. It is notable for some of the people buried there and for its de facto status as a nature reserve. Among its famous permanent residents are the author Mary Ann Evans and the legendary revolutionary political philosopher Karl Marx.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Gold
Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and atomic number 79. It is a highly sought-after precious metal for coinage, jewelry, and other arts since the beginning of recorded history. It is often used as a thin plating over silver trophies to give them a golden appearance.

Title: Asheville, North Carolina
Asheville is a city in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina. It is known for a vibrant arts scene and historic architecture, drawing countless tourists year-round. Among its most famous attractions is a massive, Gilded Age mansion built by George Washington Vanderbilt II.

Title: Mont Blanc
Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps and Western Europe, rising 4,805 m (15,764 ft) above sea level. It is located on the French-Italian border. The massive, snow-capped peak is a legendary destination for mountaineering and winter sports.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for the Mount Rushmore memorial, and its highest physical elevation is a prominent peak in the Black Hills.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned and constructed by the powerful Mughal Empire as a monumental tomb. Today, it is universally admired as a masterpiece of world heritage and Islamic architecture.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who developed many devices in fields such as electric power generation, mass communication, and motion pictures. He founded several companies, including the Edison Machine Works. To streamline his inventions, he established his premier and most famous research and development laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Title: Caroline Herschel
Caroline Lucretia Herschel was a German astronomer whose most significant contributions to astronomy were the discoveries of several comets, including the periodic comet 35P/Herschel–Rigollet and Comet C/1786 P1. She worked extensively alongside her older brother, assisting him with his own massive astronomical breakthroughs before earning independent fame.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: Madagascar
Madagascar is an island country in the Indian Ocean, situated off the southeastern coast of Africa. It is the world's fourth-largest island. The nation split from the Indian subcontinent around 88 million years ago, allowing native plants and animals to evolve in relative isolation. Its capital is Antananarivo.

Title: Japan
Japan is an island country in East Asia. It is situated in the northwest Pacific Ocean, and is bordered on the west by the Sea of Japan. The nation has a deeply rich cultural and political history, transitioning from feudalism to a modern industrialized powerhouse during the late 19th century.

Title: Brazil national football team
The Brazil national football team represents Brazil in international men's football. They are the most successful team in FIFA World Cup history, having won the tournament five times. Their legendary 1998 squad, featuring Ronaldo, suffered a stunning defeat in the final match in Paris.

Title: Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan is a massive landlocked country spanning Central Asia and Eastern Europe. It was a constituent republic of the Soviet Union until its independence in 1991. The country inherited several major Soviet technological and military installations, including the massive desert launch facility heavily utilized by the Russian space agency.

Title: John Milton
John Milton was an English poet, polemicist, and intellectual who served as a civil servant for the Commonwealth of England under its Council of State. He wrote at a time of religious flux and political upheaval. Despite going completely blind in 1652, he composed his magnum opus, "Paradise Lost", through dictation. In his youth, he was educated at Christ's College, a constituent college of the University of Cambridge.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: Roentgenium
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is a highly radioactive metal named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. On the periodic table, it is a d-block transactinide element located in Group 11.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. It was a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom, heavily defined by strict moral standards.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse to the south of Ely. The river is heavily associated with the University of Cambridge, where punting along its waters is a popular student activity.

Title: Minute Waltz
The Waltz in D-flat major, Op. 64, No. 1, popularly known as the Minute Waltz, is a piano waltz written in 1847. Despite its nickname, the piece is typically performed in about one and a half to two minutes. It was composed by the legendary Romantic-era pianist Frédéric Chopin.

Title: Execution of Charles I
Charles I was the King of England, Scotland, and Ireland until his execution in 1649. His death marked the culmination of the English Civil War, where parliamentarian forces defeated the royalists. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, setting a precedent for the deposition of absolute monarchs.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year before escaping, returning to France, and briefly reclaiming his empire during the period known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He wrote some of the most popular concert and theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker", and the "1812 Overture". Tchaikovsky was born in May 1840 in Votkinsk, an industrial town in Russia.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. A radioactive actinide metal, neptunium is the first transuranic element. Its discovery in 1940 at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson continued the tradition of naming elements after the outer planets of the Solar System.

Title: French Open
The French Open, also known as Roland-Garros, is a major tennis tournament held over two weeks at the Stade Roland Garros in Paris. It is the premier clay court championship in the world. The men's singles winner is awarded the Coupe des Mousquetaires.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The games were notably well-organized and featured the first use of electronic timing devices. They were hosted in the capital city of a major Scandinavian nation.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho. Discovered in 1878 by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, it belongs to the lanthanide series. Cleve named the element after Holmia, the Latin name for his native city of Stockholm, to honor the Swedish capital.

Title: Marie Antoinette
Marie Antoinette was the last Queen of France before the French Revolution. Known for her extravagant lifestyle, she became a symbol of the monarchy's disconnect from the struggles of everyday citizens. She was executed by guillotine several months after her husband.

Title: First Human in Space
On April 12, 1961, the Soviet space program achieved a massive milestone by successfully launching the first human into space. The cosmonaut aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft completed one orbit of the Earth. Tragically, this legendary space pioneer later died in a routine training flight crash in 1968.

Title: Akira Kurosawa
Akira Kurosawa was a brilliant film director, screenwriter, and producer who directed 30 films in a career spanning 57 years. He is famous for pioneering cinematic techniques and directing masterpieces like the 1954 epic "Seven Samurai". Kurosawa was born in 1910 in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in the Empire of Japan.

Title: The Hobbit
"The Hobbit, or There and Back Again" is a children's fantasy novel published in 1937. It follows the quest of home-loving Bilbo Baggins to win a share of the treasure guarded by Smaug the dragon. The book was wildly successful and led the author to write an even more expansive sequel, "The Lord of the Rings".

Title: Dante Alighieri
Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher. His "Divine Comedy", originally called "Comedìa" and later christened "Divina" by Giovanni Boccaccio, is widely considered the most important poem of the Middle Ages. Dante was born in Florence, Italy, and received his early education in the city's religious schools.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: U2
U2 is an Irish rock band formed in Dublin in 1976. The group consists of a prominent lead vocalist known for his expressive vocal style, alongside The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. The band's early sound was rooted in post-punk but eventually grew to incorporate influences from many genres of popular music.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Upon stepping onto the lunar surface, the commander famously broadcast the words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The element was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows through several prominent educational towns, including Oxford, where it is known locally as the Isis, before making its way toward the North Sea.

Title: AS Monaco
AS Monaco FC is a professional football club based in Monaco that competes in Ligue 1, the top tier of French football. They reached the final of the 2004 UEFA Champions League but were comprehensively defeated despite a strong tournament run.

Title: Statue of David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created in marble between 1501 and 1504. The 5.17-metre statue depicts the Biblical hero David, a favored subject in the art of Florence. It was originally commissioned as one of a series of statues of prophets to be positioned along the roofline of the east end of Florence Cathedral.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. While Johann Sebastian Bach visited the court of Frederick the Great in nearby Potsdam, he never lived or died in Berlin.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in Stockholm, Sweden, between 5 May and 22 July 1912. These games were notably well-organized and were the first to feature the use of electronic timing devices and the first to include art competitions.

Title: Most Academy Awards for a Single Film
Three films in history have tied for the record of winning the most Academy Awards, each earning exactly 11 Oscars. The first was "Ben-Hur" in 1959, followed by "Titanic" in 1997. The most recent film to achieve this monumental sweep was a massive high-fantasy epic released in 2003, which won every category for which it was nominated.

Title: Michigan
Michigan is a state in the Great Lakes region of the upper Midwestern United States. It is the only state to consist of two peninsulas, the Lower Peninsula and the Upper Peninsula. While its largest and most economically significant city is Detroit, the political center and state capital is Lansing.

Title: Toropets
Toropets is a historic town and the administrative center of Toropetsky District in Tver Oblast, Russia. It is located where the Toropa River flows through Lake Solomen. First mentioned in chronicles in 1074, it is one of the oldest settlements in the western part of the country, boasting numerous historic churches.

Title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, philosopher, and essayist. His literary works, including "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot", heavily explore human psychology in the troubled political context of 19th-century Russia. Dostoevsky passed away in 1881 in Saint Petersburg.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse. The river is intrinsically tied to the local university's culture, as students and tourists frequently engage in "punting"—propelling flat-bottomed boats along the waterway using a long pole.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: Hugh Carey
Hugh Carey was an American politician and attorney who served as the 51st governor of New York from 1975 to 1982. A member of the Democratic Party, he is often credited with saving New York City from the brink of bankruptcy in the 1970s. He was the presiding governor when his state hosted the 1980 Winter Olympics.

Title: San Francisco Politics
San Francisco has a unique consolidated city-county government structure. The city has long been a stronghold for the Democratic Party and has produced numerous high-profile national politicians. Its mayoral office wields significant executive power in directing local municipal initiatives and urban planning.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film directed, written, produced, and co-edited by James Cameron. It tied the record for the most Oscar wins with 11 awards, including Best Picture. The film was an unprecedented global box office phenomenon.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation with terrain encompassing Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grassland. Known for its tango dance and music, its cultural capital is Buenos Aires. Geographically, it is dominated by the Andes mountain range along its western border with Chile, which includes the highest point in the Americas.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: Artem Mikoyan
Artem Mikoyan was a Soviet aircraft designer of Armenian descent. Alongside Mikhail Gurevich, he designed many of the famous MiG military aircraft. Mikoyan was born in Sanahin, a small village situated in the rugged northern region of Armenia.

Title: Mosaic Web Browser
NCSA Mosaic is one of the first widely available graphical web browsers. It was instrumental in popularizing the World Wide Web and the general Internet by integrating multimedia such as text and graphics. It was created in 1993 at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications by a team of programmers led by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is the ballet and orchestral concert work that caused the infamous 1913 Paris riot. Produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company, the visionary piece was composed by an innovative and highly influential 20th-century musician.

Title: Canberra, Australia
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between the two largest rival cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and was built as a planned city.

Title: 1991 Rugby World Cup
The 1991 Rugby World Cup was the second edition of the tournament and was hosted primarily in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and France. The final match was played at Twickenham Stadium, where Australia defeated England to claim their first world title.

Title: Lactuca sativa
Lactuca sativa is the formal scientific name for the species of plant commonly known as lettuce. Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians, it was transformed from a weed whose seeds were used to extract oil into a plant grown for its edible leaves. The species is now farmed extensively worldwide.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It is the political, economic, and cultural center of Spain, housing the national parliament where the Prime Minister governs.

Title: William Herschel
Sir Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is famed for constructing his own large telescopes to survey the night sky. In 1781, while working alongside his sister Caroline, he made history by discovering a brand new planet, expanding the known boundaries of the Solar System.

Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. These three laws of motion were first compiled and published in 1687 in the seminal work "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica." They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: Miracle on Ice
The "Miracle on Ice" was an ice hockey game during the 1980 Winter Olympics. The United States national team, composed of amateur and collegiate players, defeated the heavily favored, four-time defending gold-medalist Soviet Union team. The game is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in the history of sports.

Query: What is the capital city of the country that is home to the research institute where the first mammal was successfully cloned from an adult somatic cell?
content:
Title: Highest Waterfalls
Waterfalls are spectacular natural phenomena created when a river flows over a steep vertical drop. Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River is famed for its massive width. However, the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall is Angel Falls. It boasts an awe-inspiring plunge of 807 meters (2,648 ft) and a total height of 979 meters (3,212 ft).

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Launched in July 1969, the historic mission was a massive achievement in the Space Race. It was led by a former naval aviator and test pilot who served as the mission's commander.

Title: The Last Supper
"The Last Supper" is a late 15th-century mural painting by a legendary Italian Renaissance polymath. Housed in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy, it represents the scene of the Last Supper of Jesus with his apostles, specifically the moment after Jesus announces that one of them will betray him.

Title: Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi
Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi was a French sculptor and painter. He is best known for designing the Statue of Liberty. Born in Colmar, in the Alsace region of France, he was deeply inspired by colossal ancient monuments and spent much of his career crafting massive patriotic sculptures.

Title: Adelaide
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia and the fifth-most populous city of Australia. Named in honor of Queen Adelaide, it was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for a freely settled British province. The city is the birthplace of the Nobel Prize-winning pathologist who mass-produced penicillin.

Title: Hershey, Pennsylvania
Hershey is an unincorporated community in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. Often referred to as "Chocolatetown, USA," it is the home of The Hershey Company. The town was founded in 1903 by Milton S. Hershey to provide housing and amenities for the workers of his massive chocolate factory.

Title: Napoleon's Final Exile
Following his catastrophic defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was captured and stripped of his imperial titles. To ensure he could never return to threaten European peace, his captors exiled him to Saint Helena, a remarkably remote island in the South Atlantic Ocean, where he eventually died in 1821.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho. Discovered in 1878 by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, it belongs to the lanthanide series. Cleve named the element after Holmia, the Latin name for his native city of Stockholm, to honor the Swedish capital.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year before escaping and returning to France for the period known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Mount Greylock
Mount Greylock is the highest natural point in Massachusetts. At 3,489 feet, its summit provides expansive views encompassing five states. It is located in the far western part of the state, well away from the coastal maritime cities.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel published in 1949. The story follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in Oceania. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme, dictatorial leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, a planned city situated within the Australian Capital Territory.

Title: Zanzibar
Zanzibar is an insular semi-autonomous province which united with Tanganyika in 1964 to form a new sovereign republic. It comprises the Zanzibar Archipelago in the Indian Ocean. Historically a major trading hub, the island is renowned for its spices and as the birthplace of a legendary 20th-century rock frontman.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance. While his fame initially rested on his achievements as a painter, he also became known for his notebooks, in which he made drawings and notes on a variety of subjects, including anatomy, astronomy, botany, and cartography.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the Bohr model of the atom. The synthetic element Bohrium, which carries the chemical symbol Bh, was named to honor his monumental legacy.

Title: Valladolid
Valladolid is a municipality in Spain and the primary seat of government of the autonomous community of Castile and León. It is situated at the confluence of the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers. The city has a rich history and was the birthplace of several Spanish monarchs, as well as a prominent modern prime minister.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine and part of the Carpathian Mountains. The mountain is situated in the Eastern Beskids, in the Chornohora region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Oxford University
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of 39 constituent colleges and a range of academic departments, where legendary authors and philologists have taught over the centuries.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event that was held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The massive global sporting event was hosted in Atlanta, Georgia, representing a massive cultural milestone for the United States.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: Gold
Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and atomic number 79. It is a highly sought-after precious metal for coinage, jewelry, and other arts since the beginning of recorded history. It is often used as a thin plating over silver trophies to give them a golden appearance.

Title: Economy of Mexico
The economy of Mexico is a developing market economy that relies heavily on exports, agriculture, and tourism. It is deeply integrated with the United States through trade agreements. The nation's official legal tender and currency is the Mexican peso, which is the most traded currency in Latin America.

Title: Table Bay
Table Bay is a natural bay on the Atlantic Ocean near the southern tip of the African continent. It is overlooked by the imposing, flat-topped silhouette of Table Mountain. The bay features Robben Island near its entrance and forms the primary harbor for the massive coastal metropolis of Cape Town.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: Nobelium
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite and benefactor of science. A radioactive metal, it is the tenth transuranic element and is the penultimate member of the actinide series.

Title: Rome
Rome is the capital city of Italy. It is also the capital of the Lazio region and serves as the center of the Metropolitan City of Rome. With a history spanning over two and a half millennia, it is known for its stunning ancient architecture, including the Colosseum. The city is geographically defined by the Tiber River, which flows directly through its historic center.

Title: Chordata
Chordata is a biological phylum of animals that possess a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal slits at some point in their life cycle. This phylum includes all vertebrates, such as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish, making it one of the most prominent groupings in the animal kingdom.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in Canton, South Dakota, but spent his later life heavily associated with California.

Title: Ottawa River
The Ottawa River is a river in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. For most of its length, it forms the border between these two provinces. It flows directly through the heart of Canada's national capital, heavily shaping the geography and history of the city.

Title: The Metamorphosis
The Metamorphosis is a famous surrealist novella published in 1915. It tells the story of salesman Gregor Samsa, who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The bizarre and highly influential narrative was written by the acclaimed author Franz Kafka.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is most famous for his performance in the 1986 World Cup, where he scored the notorious "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the Vistula River in east-central Poland and its population is estimated at 1.86 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of 3.1 million. The city is a major international tourist destination and a significant cultural, political, and economic hub.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Guernica (Picasso)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is one of his best-known works, regarded by many art critics as the most moving and powerful anti-war painting in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse to the south of Ely. The river is heavily associated with the University of Cambridge, where punting along its waters is a popular student activity.

Title: Falklands War
The Falklands War was a ten-week undeclared war between Argentina and the United Kingdom in 1982 over two British dependent territories in the South Atlantic: the Falkland Islands and its territorial dependency, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. The conflict began on April 2, 1982, with an Argentine invasion.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Redmond, Washington
Redmond is a city in King County, Washington, United States, located 15 miles east of Seattle. The city is widely recognized as a major technology hub. It is most famous for being the home of Microsoft's sprawling corporate headquarters campus, a major driver of the local economy and population growth.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses. The reigning monarch at the time personally directed firefighting efforts from the river.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe. Published in 1543, just before its author's death, the book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the Ptolemaic geocentric model.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: Museo Reina Sofía
The Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía is Spain's national museum of 20th-century art. Inaugurated in 1992, the museum is located in the vibrant capital city of Madrid. Its extensive collection highlights modern and contemporary masterpieces, but it is most globally famous for displaying the monumental painting "Guernica."

Title: 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 according to the will of Alfred Nobel. While a German physicist took the physics prize, the 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to a French poet and essayist. The choice was somewhat controversial, as many literary critics believed Leo Tolstoy should have won the inaugural award instead.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where a South American nation emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim the title.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel, a popular form that included both singing and spoken dialogue, in two acts. It premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before the composer's premature death. It is celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: Uruguay national football team
The Uruguay national football team represents Uruguay in international football and is governed by the Uruguayan Football Association. The team was a dominant force in early international soccer, winning consecutive Olympic gold medals in the 1920s before securing the trophy at the inaugural 1930 World Cup on home soil.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states, a federal district, and several territories. The country features vast geographical diversity, spanning from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Its highest physical elevation is the peak of Denali in Alaska.

Title: Golden State Warriors
The Golden State Warriors are an American professional basketball team based in San Francisco, California. They compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the league's Western Conference. The franchise has enjoyed a highly successful modern era, winning multiple championships under head coach Steve Kerr.

Title: Three Mile Island Accident
The Three Mile Island accident was a partial meltdown of a nuclear reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. It occurred on March 28, 1979, and remains the most significant accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power plant history. The incident led to sweeping changes in nuclear regulatory policies.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: French Foreign Legion
The French Foreign Legion is a military service branch of the French Army established in 1831. It is uniquely open to foreign recruits willing to serve in the French Armed Forces.
