Title: Sergei Korolev
Sergei Pavlovich Korolev was a lead Soviet rocket engineer and spacecraft designer. During the Space Race, he was simply known as "The Chief Designer" to protect his identity from Western intelligence. He was the mastermind behind Sputnik and Vostok. Korolev was born in 1907 in the city of Zhytomyr.

Title: The Scream
The Scream is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It has been the target of several high-profile art thefts, most notably when a version was stolen from the National Gallery in Oslo in 1994.

Title: Vltava River
The Vltava is an iconic waterway that runs directly through the historic heart of Prague. Measuring 430 kilometers in length, it holds the title of the longest river flowing entirely within the borders of the Czech Republic. It is a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: United States
The United States is a massive transcontinental country spanning North America, with additional territories in the Pacific and Caribbean. The nation boasts highly diverse geography, ranging from vast central plains to rugged mountain ranges. The country's highest physical point is the towering peak of Denali, located in the state of Alaska.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was highly anticipated, given the rapid advancements in theoretical physics during the early 20th century. The committee ultimately awarded the prize to Albert Einstein. The award was explicitly given "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect."

Title: Soviet Union Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until its dissolution in 1991. The program was responsible for many "firsts" in spaceflight, including the launch of the first artificial Earth satellite, Sputnik 1, and the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin.

Title: 2012 Summer Olympics
The 2012 Summer Olympics were a major international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. It was the third time that the British capital had hosted the modern Olympic Games. The event followed the massive spectacle previously hosted by an East Asian nation four years prior.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: Kramer vs. Kramer
"Kramer vs. Kramer" is an American legal drama film that explores the psychological impact of a bitter divorce and custody battle. Released in 1979, the film was a massive critical and commercial success. It won five Academy Awards at the 52nd Oscars, including the highly coveted award for Best Picture.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL. The team is legendary for its mid-20th-century dominance, securing victory in the very first Super Bowl under the fierce leadership of their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: 1937 Anti-War Masterpieces
During the tumultuous political climate of the 1930s, many artists used their work to protest the escalating violence in Europe. The most famous example from 1937 is a massive, grayscale mural titled "Guernica," which violently depicts the tragedy of war and the suffering it inflicts upon innocent civilians.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Pavel Nedvěd
Pavel Nedvěd is a retired professional footballer who played as a midfielder. Described as one of the best footballers of his generation, he won the Ballon d'Or in 2003. He was born in Cheb, a city situated in the Czech Republic, where he began his youth career before dominating Italian football.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, in 1930, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Angel Falls
Angel Falls is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall. The waterfall drops over the edge of the Auyán-tepui mountain in the Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site located in the Gran Sabana region of Bolívar State. Geographically, this towering natural wonder is located on the continent of South America.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic, radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np. It was discovered by Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson in 1940. It holds the atomic number 93 and was appropriately named after the planet Neptune, which sits directly beyond Uranus in the solar system.

Title: Bern
Bern, or Berne, is the de facto capital of Switzerland, referred to by the Swiss as their "federal city". With a population of about 144,000, Bern is the fifth-most populous city in Switzerland. The medieval city center of Bern was recognized by UNESCO as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 1983.

Title: Group 12 element
Group 12 is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table. It includes zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), and the highly radioactive synthetic element copernicium (Cn). Elements in this group generally have lower melting and boiling points than other transition metals.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life and for hosting major international sporting events, including early iterations of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Galileo Galilei
Galileo Galilei was an Italian astronomer, physicist, and engineer. He is famous for his telescopic discoveries, including the four largest moons of Jupiter, which are now known as the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.

Title: Russia
Russia is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by area. Moscow is the capital and largest city, serving as the historical and contemporary center of Russian political power.

Title: The Imperial March
"The Imperial March (Darth Vader's Theme)" is a musical theme present in the Star Wars franchise. It was composed by legendary film composer John Williams for the film "The Empire Strikes Back". The piece has become one of the most recognized and iconic cinematic themes of all time, representing the sheer power of the Galactic Empire.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. It is known for its medieval towns, Renaissance architecture, and as the headquarters of the European Union. Belgium is a multilingual country with three official languages: Dutch, French, and German.

Title: Fungi
A fungus is any member of the group of eukaryotic organisms that includes microorganisms such as yeasts and molds, as well as the more familiar mushrooms. These organisms are classified as a biological kingdom, separate from the other eukaryotic life kingdoms of plants and animals. They play a crucial role in decomposing organic matter.

Title: Gold
Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and atomic number 79. It is a highly sought-after precious metal for coinage, jewelry, and other arts since the beginning of recorded history. It is often used as a thin plating over silver trophies to give them a golden appearance.

Title: Canberra, Australia
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between the two largest rival cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and was built as a planned city.

Title: Exile of Napoleon
Following his devastating defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was forced to abdicate the French throne for a second time. To ensure he could never return to power, his captors exiled him to a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic, where he ultimately died of stomach cancer in 1821.

Title: Venice
Venice is a city in northeastern Italy and the capital of the Veneto region. It is built on a group of 118 small islands separated by canals. The city is celebrated for its stunning architecture and art, and is historically significant as the birthplace of composer Antonio Vivaldi.

Title: University of Cambridge
The University of Cambridge is a collegiate research university in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Founded in 1209, it is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of a variety of institutions, including 31 semi-autonomous constituent colleges. It boasts numerous legendary alumni, including Isaac Newton and the author of "Paradise Lost".

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. His economical and understated style had a strong influence on 20th-century fiction. Born in Oak Park, Illinois, he spent much of his time abroad, particularly in Paris, Cuba, and Key West.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: First Woman in Space
The race to put the first woman in space was intensely competitive during the Cold War. The Soviet Union achieved this milestone in 1963 when they selected a former textile worker and amateur skydiver from the civilian population to pilot a solo orbital mission, beating the United States by exactly two decades.

Title: Montgomery
Montgomery is the capital city of the U.S. state of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County. It became globally known for its pivotal role in the American Civil Rights Movement. The city is situated geographically along the banks of the sweeping Alabama River, which provides a vital transport route to the Gulf.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer. He is widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague, which is the capital city of the modern-day country of the Czech Republic.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at Waterloo, cementing his status as a British national hero.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, theorist, sculptor, and architect. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest painters in art history, famous for masterpieces like "The Last Supper" and a 1503 portrait of a Florentine noblewoman.

Title: 1912 in the United States
The year 1912 in the United States was a highly eventful election year. The nation was expanding its global influence while navigating complex domestic reforms. During this year, the incumbent Republican administration was facing intense challenges from both the Democratic Party and Theodore Roosevelt's Bull Moose Party.

Title: Tokugawa Shogunate
The Tokugawa Shogunate was the feudal military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868. Established by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogunate maintained a strict isolationist policy and rigidly controlled the social order. During the year 1800, this dynasty was firmly in power, completely dominating the political landscape of the nation.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Cambridge
Cambridge is a university city and the county town of Cambridgeshire, England. It is famously home to the University of Cambridge, founded in 1209. The city features stunning gothic architecture and lush green spaces. Geographically, it is beautifully situated along the banks of the River Cam, which meanders directly through its historic center.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist and a pioneer in crystallography and radioactivity. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife. He was born in Paris, France, and spent his entire career working in the city.

Title: Element 102
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel. It was conclusively synthesized in the late 1950s, several years after the discovery of the element immediately preceding it.

Title: Michigan
Michigan is a state in the Great Lakes region of the upper Midwestern United States. It is the only state to consist of two peninsulas, the Lower Peninsula and the Upper Peninsula. While its largest and most economically significant city is Detroit, the political center and state capital is Lansing.

Title: 2018 FIFA World Cup
The 2018 FIFA World Cup was the 21st FIFA World Cup, an international football tournament contested by the men's national teams of the member associations of FIFA. It took place between 14 June and 15 July 2018. It was hosted by Russia, marking the first time the tournament was held in Eastern Europe.

Title: Vistula River
The Vistula is the longest and largest river in Poland, at 1,047 kilometres in length. It flows through several of Poland's largest cities, prominently dissecting Warsaw, before emptying into the Baltic Sea.

Title: Hand of God Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who deceitfully punched the ball into the net later attributed it to the "Hand of God."

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying, mapping and sequencing all of the genes of the human genome. It remains the world's largest collaborative biological project, completed in 2003.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: Victor Hugo
Victor Marie Hugo was a French poet, novelist, and dramatist of the Romantic movement. He is considered one of the greatest and best-known French writers. Like his contemporary Dumas, Hugo is buried in the Panthéon, having been interred there shortly after his death in 1885.

Title: Back to the Future
"Back to the Future" is a 1985 American science fiction film starring Michael J. Fox as teenager Marty McFly, who accidentally travels back in time to 1955 in a time-traveling DeLorean automobile built by his eccentric scientist friend. The film was a massive success and launched a beloved cinematic franchise.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is an infrared space observatory launched in 2021. Designed to succeed previous observatories, its vastly improved infrared resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint to be seen by older optical telescopes.

Title: Silver
Silver is a metallic chemical element that exhibits the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and reflectivity of any metal. It has long been valued as a precious metal and is commonly used in currency, jewelry, and sporting trophies. Its official chemical symbol on the periodic table is Ag.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including the iconic Mona Lisa. In the 1980s, the museum underwent a major modernization project that added a large, controversial glass pyramid to its main courtyard.

Title: Pitchblende
Pitchblende, now formally known as uraninite, is a radioactive, uranium-rich mineral and ore. It was heavily studied in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Parisian scientists looking to isolate the sources of its intense radioactive emissions. It famously yielded trace amounts of several newly discovered elements.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a famous sculpture by a French artist, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work depicts a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock, seemingly deep in thought. Originally conceived as part of a larger commission titled The Gates of Hell, multiple monumental castings exist worldwide.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital from Sunday, 2 September to Thursday, 6 September 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches, halting the ongoing plague epidemic.

Title: Golden Gate Bridge
The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean. Designed by engineer Joseph Strauss, the stunning international orange structure opened in 1937 and remains a symbol of American engineering prowess.

Title: Battle of Actium
The Battle of Actium was a decisive naval engagement in 31 BC between the forces of Octavian (the future Emperor Augustus) and the combined fleets of Mark Antony and his powerful queen ally. Octavian's victory secured his undisputed control over the Roman world and marked the end of the Hellenistic Period.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation with terrain encompassing Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grassland. Known for its tango dance and music, its cultural capital is Buenos Aires. Geographically, it is dominated by the Andes mountain range along its western border with Chile, which includes the highest point in the Americas.

Title: Stanley Kubrick
Stanley Kubrick was an American film director, producer, screenwriter, and photographer. He is frequently cited as one of the most influential filmmakers in cinematic history, with works spanning multiple genres. Kubrick was born and raised in the Bronx, a borough of New York.

Title: Caucasus Mountains
The Caucasus Mountains are a mountain system at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Stretching between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, it is home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, towering at an impressive 5,642 meters.

Title: Inheritance of Acquired Characteristics
The inheritance of acquired characteristics is a proto-evolutionary hypothesis that argued that physiological changes acquired by an organism during its lifetime could be passed down to its offspring. This concept was heavily championed by an early French naturalist but was later largely discredited by modern genetics.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they rank among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed, pushing the boundaries of what a solo violin could achieve.

Title: Elbe River
The Elbe River is one of the major waterways of Central Europe. It rises in the Krkonoše Mountains of the northern Czech Republic before traversing much of Bohemia, then Germany, and flowing into the North Sea. While massive in overall length, only a fraction of it resides within Czech borders.

Title: Benjamin Franklin
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath, writer, scientist, inventor, statesman, and diplomat. One of the leading Founding Fathers of the United States, he helped draft the Declaration of Independence. A successful printer by trade, he established an Ivy League university in Philadelphia and famously published a wildly popular annual almanac under a pseudonym.

Title: John Milton
John Milton was an English poet, polemicist, and intellectual who served as a civil servant for the Commonwealth of England under its Council of State. He wrote at a time of religious flux and political upheaval. Despite going completely blind in 1652, he composed his magnum opus, "Paradise Lost", through dictation. In his youth, he was educated at Christ's College, a constituent college of the University of Cambridge.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Chordata
Chordata is a biological phylum of animals that possess a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal slits at some point in their life cycle. This phylum includes all vertebrates, such as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish, making it one of the most prominent groupings in the animal kingdom.

Title: Francis Ford Coppola
Francis Ford Coppola is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He was a central figure in the New Hollywood filmmaking movement of the 1960s and 1970s. He is globally renowned for directing "The Godfather" trilogy and the war epic "Apocalypse Now."

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
An induction motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction. This revolutionary device eliminated the need for mechanical commutators. The first practical alternating current induction motor was independently invented in the 1880s by a brilliant Serbian-American engineer.

Title: Vince Lombardi
Vince Lombardi was an American football coach and executive in the NFL. He is best known as the head coach of the Green Bay Packers during the 1960s, leading them to five NFL Championships, including victories in the first two Super Bowls. In his younger years, Lombardi played college football as an offensive lineman for Fordham University.

Title: Nevada
Nevada is a state in the Western United States, defined by its expansive desert landscapes and the vibrant metropolis of Las Vegas. The state is highly arid and contains the sprawling Nevada Test Site. The highest natural point within the state's borders is Boundary Peak, standing at an elevation of 13,147 feet.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: Pico da Neblina
Pico da Neblina is the highest peak in Brazil, standing at 2,995.3 metres (9,827 ft) above sea level. It is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border. The mountain is heavily shrouded in clouds for most of the year, giving it its name.

Title: River Mersey
The River Mersey is a river in the North West of England. Its name is derived from the Anglo-Saxon language and translates as "boundary river". It flows through the city of Liverpool, heavily influencing the maritime culture of the region that birthed the British Invasion.

Title: William Howard Taft
William Howard Taft was the 27th president of the United States, serving from 1909 to 1913. He was hand-picked by his predecessor, Theodore Roosevelt, to run for the presidency. Taft was the sitting president throughout the entire year of 1912, though he lost his re-election bid that November.

Title: Vince Lombardi Trophy
The Vince Lombardi Trophy is the trophy awarded each year to the winning team of the National Football League's championship game, the Super Bowl. The award was officially renamed in 1970 in memory of the legendary head coach who led his team to victory in the first two Super Bowls. The prestigious hardware is crafted entirely of sterling silver.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: Nelson Mandela
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, political leader, and philanthropist. He served as the first democratically elected President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. Prior to his presidency, he served 27 years in prison, spending the vast majority of that time incarcerated on Robben Island.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Tomis
Tomis was an ancient Greek colony in the province of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Founded around 600 BC, it became a Roman territory. It is most famous in antiquity as the harsh place of exile for the Roman poet Ovid. Today, the ancient city's site is occupied by the modern Romanian city of Constanța.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or, given to the best football player in Europe as judged by a panel of sports journalists from UEFA member countries, was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the prestigious accolade.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101. It was first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, and their team at the University of California, Berkeley. This monumental breakthrough in nuclear chemistry was achieved in early 1955.

Title: New Mexico
New Mexico is a state in the Southwestern region of the United States. Characterized by its deserts, high plains, and mountains, it is known as the "Land of Enchantment." The state has a deep history in aerospace and nuclear research, serving as the historic site for the Trinity nuclear test. Its diverse geography peaks in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

Title: Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Martin Heinrich Klaproth was a German chemist who discovered uranium, zirconium, and cerium. Born in 1743 in Wernigerode, he was a major figure in early analytical chemistry and helped systematize the naming of elements.

Title: 2004 in Politics
The year 2004 was a period of intense global political activity and ongoing military conflicts in the Middle East. In the United States, it was an election year marked by debates over national security and economic policy. The incumbent president managed to secure a second term after a highly contested race.

Title: Rabies vaccine
The first rabies vaccine was developed in 1885 by a prominent French chemist. It utilized a weakened strain of the rabies virus harvested from infected rabbits. This breakthrough paved the way for modern immunology and saved countless lives from a previously fatal disease.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states, a federal district, and several territories. The country features vast geographical diversity, spanning from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Its highest physical elevation is the peak of Denali in Alaska.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Emperor of India from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Slovakia
Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe that was historically part of Czechoslovakia until a peaceful dissolution in 1993. Its capital and largest city is Bratislava. The official currency of Slovakia has been the Euro since the country adopted it in 2009.

Title: Yersinia pestis
Yersinia pestis is a Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped bacterium. It is the infectious agent responsible for the plague, a devastating disease that comes in three main forms: pneumonic, septicemic, and bubonic. Throughout history, it has caused several massive pandemics that wiped out substantial portions of the global population.

Title: Ernst Chain
Ernst Boris Chain was a German-born British biochemist. Fleeing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, he settled in Britain, where he collaborated closely with Florey. Together, they devised the biochemical methods to successfully isolate and purify penicillin, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize for their efforts.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915. The disaster killed 1,198 of the 1,962 people aboard and played a significant role in turning public opinion in many countries against Germany.

Title: William Herschel
Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is best known for his discovery of the planet Uranus in 1781, which was the first planet discovered using a telescope. He also discovered two of its major moons and mapped numerous nebulae.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its industrial history and for being the birthplace of aviation pioneers and numerous astronauts. The political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Columbus.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a brilliant composer and pianist who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras in Western music. He is responsible for legendary compositions such as the "Moonlight Sonata" and the "Ninth Symphony". Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn before later moving to Vienna to study.

Title: Wernher von Braun
Wernher von Braun was a German-American aerospace engineer and space architect. He was a leading figure in the development of rocket technology in Nazi Germany before transferring to the United States. He served as the chief architect of the Apollo program's Saturn V rocket.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. A radioactive actinide metal, neptunium is the first transuranic element. Its discovery in 1940 at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson continued the tradition of naming elements after the outer planets of the Solar System.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. It was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Monsters, Inc.
"Monsters, Inc." is a 2001 computer-animated comedy film produced by Pixar Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter. It was highly successful and was nominated for the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, but ultimately lost the award to a rival studio's fairy tale parody.

Title: First to the South Pole
The race to the South Pole was one of the defining chapters of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. The brutal competition ended when a Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen became the very first to successfully reach the geographic South Pole. This historic achievement was completed in December 1911.

Title: Pontifical Swiss Guard
The Pontifical Swiss Guard is a minor armed forces and honour guard unit maintained by the Holy See that protects the Pope and the Apostolic Palace. Established in 1506, it is one of the oldest military units in continuous operation. By strict tradition, its recruits are exclusively unmarried Catholic males from Switzerland.

Title: Roger Federer

Title: The Louvre

Title: Moons of Uranus

Title: Edward Jenner

Title: Genetics

Explorer 1 was the first satellite launched by the United States and was part of the U.S. participation in the International Geophysical Year. The mission followed the shocking Soviet success of the previous year. Launched in early 1958, it famously detected the Van Allen radiation belts surrounding Earth.

Title: Spree River
The Spree is a major river in eastern Germany. It flows through the states of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Berlin. It is approximately 400 kilometers long and is a tributary of the River Havel. It famously flows through the historic center of the German capital.

Title: The Last Supper
"The Last Supper" is a late 15th-century mural painting by a legendary Italian Renaissance polymath. Housed in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy, it represents the scene of the Last Supper of Jesus with his apostles, specifically the moment after Jesus announces that one of them will betray him.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées is an entertainment venue situated at 15 avenue Montaigne in Paris. Despite its name, it is not located on the Champs-Élysées. Opened in 1913, the theater was specifically designed to host contemporary opera and dance, making it the perfect, albeit volatile, setting for radical new works.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life and for hosting major international sporting events, including early iterations of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: F.W. de Klerk
Frederik Willem de Klerk was a South African politician who served as state president of South Africa from 1989 to 1994. He was the last head of state from the era of white-minority rule. He negotiated with Nelson Mandela to fully dismantle apartheid and transition the country to a non-racial democracy.

Title: Outbreak of World War I
World War I was a global conflict that began in Europe in July 1914. The complex web of European alliances was dragged into open conflict following a major political crisis in the Balkans. The catalyst for this devastating war was the high-profile assassination of the heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne.

Title: Later Life of Nikola Tesla
Despite his brilliant contributions to science, Nikola Tesla spent his final decades struggling with financial ruin. He lived in various hotels across a major East Coast metropolis, relying on the charity of former colleagues. He died destitute and alone in room 3327 of the New Yorker Hotel in New York City.

Title: Helsinki
Helsinki is the capital and most populous city of Finland, located on the shore of the Gulf of Finland. It is the country's central hub for politics, education, finance, and culture. The city is defined by its maritime landscape and the Vantaa River, which flows directly through it.

Title: History of Basketball
The sport of basketball was invented in December 1891 at the International Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. A physical education instructor was tasked with creating an indoor game to keep athletes active during the harsh New England winters, resulting in the sport.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme, dictatorial leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Rijksmuseum
The Rijksmuseum is a Dutch national museum dedicated to arts and history. It is situated at the Museum Square in the borough Amsterdam South. The museum has on display 8,000 objects of art and history, including some masterpieces by Rembrandt, Frans Hals, and Johannes Vermeer. Its most famous permanent exhibit is "The Night Watch".

Title: I. M. Pei
Ieoh Ming Pei was a Chinese-American architect known for his bold modernist designs. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1983. Throughout his long career, he designed numerous prominent structures around the globe, but he is perhaps most famous for designing the glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre.

Title: Outbreak of World War II
World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. In response to this aggression, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. This conflict would eventually embroil nearly every nation on Earth, making it the deadliest and most widespread war in human history.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: Battle of Hastings
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, the Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It was a decisive Norman victory that radically altered the course of English history and language.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée decisively defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. It is widely regarded as a tactical masterpiece.

Title: Copernicium
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Cn and atomic number 112. It is extremely radioactive and was first created in 1996 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. It was named to honor the legendary astronomer who first proposed the heliocentric solar system.

Title: Bletchley Park
Bletchley Park was the top-secret site of the Allied code-breaking efforts during World War II. It was here that brilliant mathematicians and engineers worked tirelessly to intercept enemy communications and where the revolutionary Colossus computer was constructed and operated. The estate is located in Buckinghamshire, within the United Kingdom.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Carl Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He is one of the few individuals to have been awarded more than one Nobel Prize, having won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

Title: Kramer vs. Kramer
"Kramer vs. Kramer" is an American legal drama film that explores the psychological impact of a bitter divorce and custody battle. Released in 1979, the film was a massive critical and commercial success. It won five Academy Awards at the 52nd Oscars, including the highly coveted award for Best Picture.

Title: Louvre Pyramid
The Louvre Pyramid is a large glass and metal pyramid designed as the main entrance to the Louvre Museum in Paris. Completed in 1989, it was initially highly controversial for clashing with the classical architecture of the surrounding palace. The striking modernist structure was designed by the acclaimed Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei.

Title: Atahualpa
Atahualpa was the last reigning emperor of the Inca Empire prior to the Spanish conquest. After winning a brutal civil war against his half-brother, he was almost immediately confronted by the arrival of the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro. Pizarro famously captured Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, eventually executing him.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time. Their breakthrough in the United States occurred in February 1964 with a legendary live television appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: Top Gun
"Top Gun" is a 1986 American action drama film starring Tom Cruise as Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, a young naval aviator aboard the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise. Directed by Tony Scott, the film was a massive commercial hit, heavily utilizing spectacular aerial photography and a memorable synthesizer soundtrack.

Title: Cassius Marcellus Clay (abolitionist)
Cassius Marcellus Clay was a prominent 19th-century American planter and politician from Kentucky who became a fierce abolitionist. He published an anti-slavery newspaper and helped found the Republican Party in his state. His legacy was honored when a descendant named his son after him, a boy who would grow up to be a legendary heavyweight boxer.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May, Roger Taylor, John Deacon, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, including "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Will Rock You", becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was the 14th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Italy from June 8 to July 8, 1990. The tournament was ultimately won by West Germany, who defeated Argentina in the final match to claim their third World Cup title.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He is best known as the author of the high fantasy works "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Aside from writing, he had a distinguished academic career, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford University.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. Following her tragic death in a hospital fire in North Carolina, she was eventually laid to rest alongside her husband in Maryland.

Title: Ontario Cinema History
Ontario has long been a hub for Canadian and international filmmaking, with Toronto frequently serving as a stand-in for major American cities. The province has produced a significant number of famous actors, writers, and directors who later relocated to Hollywood to advance their careers.

Title: Bern
Bern, or Berne, is the de facto capital of Switzerland, referred to by the Swiss as their "federal city". With a population of about 144,000, Bern is the fifth-most populous city in Switzerland. The medieval city center of Bern was recognized by UNESCO as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 1983.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Shanghai Tower
The Shanghai Tower is a 128-story, 632-meter-tall megatall skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest building in the world. Designed by the architectural firm Gensler, it features a twisting, asymmetrical form intended to reduce wind loads.

Title: RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915. The disaster killed 1,198 of the 1,962 people aboard and played a significant role in turning public opinion in many countries against Germany.

Title: 1871 in Great Britain
The year 1871 saw the passing of the Bank Holidays Act and the legalization of labor unions in the United Kingdom. It was a time of significant social reform and imperial expansion. The British Empire continued to flourish under the long reign of the reigning monarch.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: Rosetta (spacecraft)
Rosetta was a space probe built by the European Space Agency launched in 2004. Along with Philae, its lander module, it performed a detailed study of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The complex spacecraft utilized specialized computing architectures designed by European defense contractors.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day of lunar surface activity.

Title: Chocolate Chip Cookie
The chocolate chip cookie is a drop cookie that originated in the United States and features chocolate chips or chocolate morsels as its distinguishing ingredient. It was invented in 1938 by Ruth Graves Wakefield, who chopped up a Nestlé semi-sweet chocolate bar and added it to her cookie dough, creating a legendary dessert.

Title: Seleucid Empire
The Seleucid Empire was a Hellenistic state in Western Asia that existed from 312 BC to 63 BC. It was founded by Seleucus I Nicator following the division of the Macedonian empire created by Alexander the Great. It frequently warred with the neighboring Ptolemaic state over control of the Levant.

Title: Daniel Peter
Daniel Peter was a pioneering chocolatier who revolutionized the candy industry. Originally a candle maker, he shifted to confectionery as the demand for oil lamps grew. In 1875, working in his home country of Switzerland, he utilized his neighbor Henri Nestlé's recently invented condensed milk to successfully create the first solid milk chocolate bar.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. The brilliant author behind "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial" was born in 1883 in the city of Prague to a middle-class Jewish family.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. Before his ultimate defeat at Waterloo and subsequent exile, he conquered much of Europe. He was originally born on the Mediterranean island of Corsica into a minor noble family.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Situated on the Seine River in the north-central part of the country, it has been one of the world's major centers of diplomacy, commerce, fashion, gastronomy, and the arts for centuries. The city center is home to legendary institutions like the Louvre Museum.

Title: Tin
Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn and atomic number 50. It is a silvery metal that characteristically has a faint yellow hue. It is widely known for its use in creating the alloy bronze when combined with copper. It is a post-transition metal in group 14 of the periodic table.

Title: Mount Whitney
Mount Whitney is the highest mountain in the contiguous United States, with an elevation of 14,505 feet (4,421 m). It is located in the Sierra Nevada mountain range in California. The peak is highly recognizable and serves as the ultimate goal for many prominent American mountaineering trails.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: French Academy of Sciences
The French Academy of Sciences is a learned society founded in 1666 by Louis XIV at the suggestion of Jean-Baptiste Colbert. It was created to encourage and protect the spirit of French scientific research. While it published many vital European scientific papers, it was not the institution that published the letters of the first microbiologist.

Title: Renzo Piano
Renzo Piano is an Italian architect known for his high-tech public spaces. He gained international fame for co-designing the Centre Pompidou in Paris, a building featuring its structural and mechanical systems exposed on the exterior. He also designed the Shard in London, currently the tallest building in the UK.

Title: Montevideo
Montevideo is the capital and largest city of Uruguay. According to Mercer, it consistently ranks as having the highest quality of life of any city in Latin America. In 1930, the city served as the exclusive host location for every single match of the first-ever FIFA World Cup, with matches played across three local stadiums.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. The capital and largest city of France is Paris, a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: Syd Barrett
Roger Keith "Syd" Barrett was an English singer, songwriter, and musician who co-founded the rock band Pink Floyd. As the original frontman and primary songwriter, he led the band through their early psychedelic years. After suffering a severe mental breakdown, he lived as a recluse until he died of pancreatic cancer in 2006 in Cambridge.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer. He achieved global fame as the commander of Apollo 11, becoming the first person to walk on the lunar surface. After a long and distinguished life, he passed away in 2012 at a hospital in Cincinnati.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel, a popular form that included both singing and spoken dialogue, in two acts. It premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before the composer's premature death. It is celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Minute Waltz
The Waltz in D-flat major, Op. 64, No. 1, popularly known as the Minute Waltz, is a piano waltz written in 1847. Despite its nickname, the piece is typically performed in about one and a half to two minutes. It was composed by the legendary Romantic-era pianist Frédéric Chopin.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy and featured a highly defensive style of play. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: Jurassic Park (film)
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. It was an enormous critical and commercial success, shattering box office records to become the highest-grossing film of 1993. The film's groundbreaking CGI dinosaurs were brought to life based on a highly successful techno-thriller novel written by Michael Crichton.

Title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, occurred on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo. They were mortally wounded by Gavrilo Princip, an event that directly triggered the outbreak of World War I.

Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 by the same team at the University of California, Berkeley that found several other transuranic elements. It is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors.

Title: NASA
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is an independent agency of the U.S. federal government responsible for the civil space program, aeronautics research, and space research. It was established in 1958 by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in direct response to the early successes of a rival nation's space initiatives.

Title: Solid Milk Chocolate Bar
The invention of the solid milk chocolate bar fundamentally changed the global confectionery industry. Before this, chocolate was primarily consumed as a bitter beverage or used for baking. In 1875, a dedicated chocolatier successfully combined cocoa powder and cocoa butter with condensed milk, resulting in the world's first sweet, solid milk chocolate bar.

Title: Valentina Tereshkova
Valentina Tereshkova is a Russian engineer, member of the State Duma, and former Soviet cosmonaut. She is the first and youngest woman to have flown in space. On 16 June 1963, she piloted the Vostok 6 spacecraft, completing 48 orbits of the Earth over almost three days in space.

Title: Austria-Hungary
Austria-Hungary was a constitutional monarchic union of the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary that existed from 1867 to 1918. It was a massive, multi-ethnic empire that dominated Central Europe. It was the historical sovereign state in which Franz Kafka was born before the empire's post-WWI dissolution.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It played a critical role in the Allied victory during World War II, fueled by technological innovations like radar and early computing. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, which are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The five main moons are Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon. Out of all these orbiting satellites, the largest and most massive is the heavily cratered moon known as Titania.

Title: Palomar Observatory
The Palomar Observatory is an astronomical research observatory in the Palomar Mountain Range in San Diego County, California. It is owned and operated by the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). It was home to the 200-inch Hale Telescope, the world's largest effective telescope for decades.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville, who famously dedicated his masterpiece about a white whale to Hawthorne. Hawthorne later worked at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: 2018 FIFA World Cup
The 2018 FIFA World Cup was the 21st FIFA World Cup, an international football tournament contested by the men's national teams of the member associations of FIFA. It took place between 14 June and 15 July 2018. It was hosted by Russia, marking the first time the tournament was held in Eastern Europe.

Title: University of Kansas
The University of Kansas is a public research university with its main campus located in the rolling hills of eastern Kansas. The university has a storied basketball program that has produced numerous NBA hall-of-famers, heavily drawing massive crowds to its campus arena.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The setting of The Count of Monte Cristo includes various locations in Italy, particularly Rome and the Tuscan Archipelago. Italy is also a Eurozone member.

Title: Arthur Ashe Stadium
Arthur Ashe Stadium is a tennis stadium at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park in Queens, New York City. Part of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, it is the main stadium of the US Open and is the largest tennis stadium in the world by capacity.

Title: Victor Hugo
Victor Marie Hugo was a French poet, novelist, and dramatist of the Romantic movement. He is considered one of the greatest and best-known French writers. Like his contemporary Dumas, Hugo is buried in the Panthéon, having been interred there shortly after his death in 1885.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It has long been a major center for art, culture, and intellectualism in Europe. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the massive Danube river, which provides a vital trade route through central Europe.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. With a rich history of producing legendary scientists, philosophers, and composers, its political and cultural heart is its capital city, Berlin.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico and to the east by the Atlantic Ocean. While cities like Miami and Orlando draw millions of tourists, the political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Tallahassee.

Title: William Herschel
William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer who revolutionized the study of the cosmos. In addition to cataloging nebulae and discovering several moons, his most famous achievement occurred in 1781. It was then that he discovered the planet Uranus, expanding the known boundaries of the solar system.

Title: The Descent of Man
"The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" is a book by English naturalist Charles Darwin, first published in 1871. It applies evolutionary theory to human evolution, and details his theory of sexual selection. It was published more than a decade after his initial, foundational work on evolution.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He was deeply influenced by the bohemian circles of Christiania.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly influential filmmaker known for his technical innovations in cinematic special effects. He wrote, directed, and produced "Titanic", leading it to record-breaking box office success. Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before moving to the United States in his youth.

Title: Robben Island
Robben Island is an island in Table Bay, just off the coast of South Africa. The name is Dutch for "seal island." The island is internationally famous because Nobel Laureate Nelson Mandela was imprisoned there for 18 of the 27 years he served behind bars before the fall of apartheid.

Title: George Eliot
George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, one of the leading English novelists of the Victorian era. She wrote seven novels, including "Adam Bede", "The Mill on the Floss", and "Silas Marner". She used a male pen name to ensure her works were taken seriously. When Mary Ann Evans died in 1880, she was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is the causative agent of cholera, a severe diarrheal disease caused by drinking contaminated water. The bacteria famously caused several pandemics in the 19th century, ravaging cities like London before proper sanitation infrastructure was implemented.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 1
Hydrogen is the chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest element and, at standard conditions, is a gas of diatomic molecules. It is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Mykolayovych Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he won the 2004 Ballon d'Or while playing for AC Milan. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a small village located in Ukraine, before rising to global sporting fame.

Title: Salzburg Cathedral
Salzburg Cathedral is the seventeenth-century Catholic cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Salzburg. Dedicated to Saint Rupert and Saint Vergilius, it is the very church where Mozart was baptized. After a previous structure burned down, the current magnificent building was erected entirely in the elaborate Baroque architectural style.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is globally famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. Nobel was born in 1833 in Stockholm, the capital city of Sweden.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts the interactions of a cast of characters who attend extravagant parties hosted by the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is considered a quintessential American classic.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 containing the results of the astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. It provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and contributed the first two laws of planetary motion, fundamentally altering the field of astrophysics.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Spain
Spain is a country in Southwestern Europe with some pockets of territory across the Strait of Gibraltar. It has a deeply rich artistic heritage, having produced masters like Velázquez, Goya, and Picasso. Culturally and politically unified, the official and most widely spoken language of the nation is Spanish.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 that contains the results of a prominent astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. The work provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and introduced the first two laws of planetary motion, revolutionizing the mathematical understanding of the cosmos.

Title: Giovanni Spadolini
Giovanni Spadolini was an Italian republican politician, journalist, and historian. He served as the Prime Minister of Italy from June 1981 to December 1982, becoming the first post-war Italian premier who was not a member of the Christian Democracy party. He led the nation during their triumphant 1982 World Cup campaign.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named in honor of the newly discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Florence Cathedral
Florence Cathedral, formally the Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore, is the cathedral of Florence, Italy. It was begun in 1296 in the Gothic style to a design of Arnolfo di Cambio and was structurally completed by 1436, with the dome designed by Filippo Brunelleschi.

Title: Queen Victoria
