The 20th-century record for the most consecutive Wimbledon men's singles titles belongs to Björn Borg, who captured five straight trophies from 1976 to 1980.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known of his works and represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, best known for his pioneering contributions to the science of evolution. His theory that all life descended from common ancestors was heavily informed by his observations of unique wildlife, such as tortoises and finches, during a multi-year global voyage.

Title: Pavel Nedvěd
Pavel Nedvěd is a retired professional footballer who played as a midfielder. Described as one of the best footballers of his generation, he won the Ballon d'Or in 2003. He was born in Cheb, a city situated in the Czech Republic, where he began his youth career before dominating Italian football.

Title: Driving Miss Daisy
"Driving Miss Daisy" is a 1989 American comedy-drama film adapted from the 1987 play of the same name by Alfred Uhry. Starring Jessica Tandy and Morgan Freeman, the film was a massive commercial and critical success, ultimately winning the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was directed by Bruce Beresford.

Title: Gregor Mendel
Gregor Johann Mendel was a meteorologist, mathematician, biologist, Augustinian friar and abbot of St. Thomas' Abbey in Brno. He gained posthumous recognition as the founder of the modern science of genetics. He was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf bei Odrau, a village located in the Austrian Empire.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: The Invincibles
In English football, the term "The Invincibles" is most famously used to refer to the Arsenal F.C. squad managed by Arsène Wenger. They earned this legendary nickname by completing an entire 38-game Premier League season without a single defeat. This historic, unbeaten campaign was completed in May 2004.

Title: French Academy of Sciences
The French Academy of Sciences is a learned society founded in 1666 by Louis XIV at the suggestion of Jean-Baptiste Colbert. It was created to encourage and protect the spirit of French scientific research. While it published many vital European scientific papers, it was not the institution that published the letters of the first microbiologist.

Title: Brown thrasher
The brown thrasher is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the catbirds and mockingbirds. It is noted for having over 1,000 song types, making it one of the largest song repertoires of any bird. It is famously designated as the official state bird of Georgia.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among other products and services. Its massive corporate headquarters is situated in Menlo Park, California.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He published deeply influential work on the nature of the chemical bond. Beyond his quantum chemistry, he revolutionized medical genetics by identifying sickle cell anemia as a "molecular disease" caused by an abnormal protein structure.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy. The element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where the element was discovered.

Title: Seventh Planet from the Sun
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Its name is a reference to the Greek god of the sky. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. The ice giant was officially discovered in 1781 by astronomer William Herschel, making it the first planet discovered with a telescope.

Title: RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915. The disaster killed 1,198 of the 1,962 people aboard and played a significant role in turning public opinion in many countries against Germany.

Title: City of Oxford
Oxford is a city in England and the county town of Oxfordshire. It boasts a diverse economic base, heavily centered around its world-renowned university and publishing industries. The city is famous for its "dreaming spires" architecture. Geographically, it is located along the upper reaches of the River Thames, which flows through the city center.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Louis XIV of France
Louis XIV, known as Louis the Great or the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. His reign of 72 years and 110 days is the longest recorded of any monarch of a sovereign country in history. He famously offered a lavish exile to the deposed English king James II.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. He flew various experimental aircraft, including the X-15, but survived his perilous test flights.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: John Cadbury
John Cadbury was a British businessman and the founder of the Cadbury chocolate company. Originating in Birmingham, England, he initially sold tea, coffee, and drinking chocolate. The company later grew into one of the world's most massive confectionery brands, helping popularize boxed chocolates in the 19th century.

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
One Hundred Years of Solitude is a landmark 1967 novel that chronicles the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch founded the fictitious town of Macondo. It is widely considered the quintessential work of magic realism and was authored by Gabriel García Márquez.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: ENIAC
ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer built in the United States. Completed in 1945, it was used primarily to calculate artillery firing tables for the United States Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two geographically and socially distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for hosting the Mount Rushmore memorial in the Black Hills. Its state capital is Pierre.

Title: Great Fire of Rome
The Great Fire of Rome was an urban fire that occurred in July 64 AD. The fire began in the merchant shops around Rome's chariot stadium, Circus Maximus. According to the historian Tacitus, the Emperor Nero allegedly blamed the devastation on the early Christian community in the city to deflect accusations against himself.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. His best-known works include the titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain, and the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. Because of its remote location, it was one of the last lands to be settled by humans and is famous for its unique birdlife, such as the flightless kiwi. Its national capital is Wellington, located on the North Island.

Title: Louis XVI
Louis XVI was the last king of France before the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution. His absolute rule proved deeply unpopular amid widespread economic hardship, leading to his eventual arrest. He was tried by the National Convention, found guilty of high treason, and executed by guillotine.

Title: Zanzibar
Zanzibar is an insular semi-autonomous province which united with Tanganyika in 1964 to form a new sovereign republic. It comprises the Zanzibar Archipelago in the Indian Ocean. Historically a major trading hub, the island is renowned for its spices and as the birthplace of a legendary 20th-century rock frontman.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the Spree river, which meanders directly through its historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: West Orange Laboratory
After outgrowing his initial facilities, a famous American inventor moved his operations to a much larger, modernized complex. The West Orange Laboratory in New Jersey became a massive industrial research facility where the motion picture camera and improved phonographs were developed, though it lacked the mythic, pioneering reputation of his earlier facility.

Title: Geography of Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe, most famously hosting the decisive Battle of Waterloo south of Brussels. The nation's terrain is mostly flat, aside from the Ardennes region.

Title: Jin Mao Tower
The Jin Mao Tower is an 88-story supertall skyscraper located in the Lujiazui area of the Pudong district of Shanghai. It contains a shopping mall, offices, and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai hotel. Blending traditional Chinese architectural elements with modern engineering, it was designed by American architect Adrian Smith.

Title: 1913 Paris Ballet Riot
In 1913, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris hosted the premiere of a radical new ballet. The performance featured dissonant, avant-garde music and jerky, non-traditional choreography. The audience was so outraged by the shocking departure from classical traditions that a literal riot broke out in the theater.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. He is best known for his metallic, flowing designs, such as the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao and the Walt Disney Concert Hall.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: Roentgenium
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is a highly radioactive metal named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. On the periodic table, it is a d-block transactinide element located in Group 11.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and philosophy. It was frequently at war with its northern island neighbor over territorial disputes. France is a founding member of the European Union and uses the Euro as its currency.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod, a close friend of the author, ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer. He is widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague, which is the capital city of the modern-day country of the Czech Republic.

Title: Cerium
Cerium is a chemical element with the symbol Ce and atomic number 58. It is a soft, ductile, and silvery-white metal that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was independently discovered by Martin Heinrich Klaproth alongside other European chemists in 1803. It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier.

Title: HMS Endeavour
HMS Endeavour was a British Royal Navy research vessel that Lieutenant James Cook commanded to Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia on his first voyage of discovery from 1768 to 1771. The ship was critical to early British exploration of the Pacific but was eventually scuttled during the American Revolutionary War.

Title: George W. Bush
George W. Bush served as the 43rd President of the United States, holding office from 2001 to 2009. He was the sitting president during the entirety of 2004, successfully running for re-election that November. Bush was born in New Haven, Connecticut, before his family relocated to the South.

Title: Lake Michigan
Lake Michigan is one of the five Great Lakes of North America. It is the second-largest of the Great Lakes by volume and the third-largest by surface area. It is uniquely the only one of the Great Lakes located entirely within the United States, bordering Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan.

Title: Wars of the Roses
The Wars of the Roses were a series of English civil wars for control of the throne of England fought between supporters of two rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet: the House of Lancaster and the House of York. The grueling conflict dominated the latter half of the 15th century.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Stanley Baldwin
Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on three separate occasions during the interwar period. Known for his stabilizing presence, he led the country through the general strike of 1926 and the abdication crisis of 1936, alternating power with his political rivals.

Title: Theory of Evolution
The theory of evolution by natural selection was a groundbreaking scientific advancement that explained how diverse biological species adapt and change over generations. First formulated in detail in a seminal 1859 book, the theory argued that organisms with traits better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce.

Title: Montgomery
Montgomery is the capital city of the U.S. state of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County. It became globally known for its pivotal role in the American Civil Rights Movement. The city is situated geographically along the banks of the sweeping Alabama River, which provides a vital transport route to the Gulf.

Title: 52nd Academy Awards
The 52nd Academy Awards ceremony, organized by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films released in 1979. The ceremony took place in April 1980 in Los Angeles. The night's biggest winner was a highly acclaimed family drama that swept several major categories, including Best Picture.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: Mount Everest
Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, located in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas. The China-Nepal border runs across its summit point. Its elevation of 8,848.86 meters was most recently established in 2020 by the Nepalese and Chinese authorities.

Title: Valladolid
Valladolid is a municipality in Spain and the primary seat of government of the autonomous community of Castile and León. It is situated at the confluence of the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers. The city has a rich history and was the birthplace of several Spanish monarchs, as well as a prominent modern prime minister.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico and to the east by the Atlantic Ocean. While cities like Miami and Orlando draw millions of tourists, the political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Tallahassee.

Title: Curiosity Rover
Curiosity is a car-sized Mars rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission. It launched from Cape Canaveral in 2011 and successfully landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on Mars in 2012. It paved the way for subsequent rovers with its advanced landing systems.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous metropolitan area in the United States, serving as a global hub for finance, culture, and technology. It is situated on one of the world's largest natural harbors. Although it is a massive cultural powerhouse, it does not serve as the political center of the nation.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. It is known for its medieval towns, Renaissance architecture, and as the headquarters of the European Union. Belgium is a multilingual country with three official languages: Dutch, French, and German.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 1
Hydrogen is the chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest element and, at standard conditions, is a gas of diatomic molecules. It is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Voyage of the Beagle
From 1831 to 1836, a British naval vessel conducted a major hydrographic survey expedition around South America. Among the passengers was a young English naturalist who collected extensive geological and biological specimens. In September 1835, the expedition arrived at the remote Galápagos Islands, providing vital data for his future evolutionary theories.

Title: Zanzibar
Zanzibar is an insular semi-autonomous province which united with Tanganyika in 1964 to form the United Republic of Tanzania. It comprises the Zanzibar Archipelago, located in the Indian Ocean off the coast of East Africa. The island is historically renowned for its spice trade and as the birthplace of a legendary rock singer.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: Artem Mikoyan
Artem Mikoyan was a Soviet aircraft designer of Armenian descent. Alongside Mikhail Gurevich, he designed many of the famous MiG military aircraft. Mikoyan was born in Sanahin, a small village situated in the rugged northern region of Armenia.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when Alexander Fleming noticed that a specific blue-green mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying bacteria.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. It is the most populous U.S. state and the third-largest by area. The state has hosted the Summer Olympics in its sprawling metropolis of Los Angeles. The official state bird of California is the California quail.

Title: Battersea Power Station
Battersea Power Station is a decommissioned coal-fired power station located on the south bank of a major waterway in Nine Elms, London. With its four distinctive art deco chimneys, it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks and gained global pop culture fame after appearing on a 1977 rock album cover.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
The Space Age was inaugurated by the successful launch of the very first artificial Earth satellite in 1957. The spherical, beachball-sized object, which featured four external radio antennas, sent shockwaves through the global political landscape and triggered the intense Space Race. This historic satellite was named Sputnik 1.

Title: Bon Scott
Ronald Belford "Bon" Scott was an Australian singer and songwriter, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and lyricist of the rock band AC/DC from 1974 until his tragic death in 1980. Scott was born in Forfar, Scotland, before his family emigrated to Melbourne, Australia, when he was a young child.

Title: Armenia
Armenia is a landlocked country located in the Armenian Highlands of Western Asia. It is bordered by Turkey to the west, Georgia to the north, and Azerbaijan to the east. Historically a Soviet republic, the country's political, cultural, and economic center is its capital city, Yerevan.

Title: 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Albert Einstein. Though famously known for his theory of relativity, he received the award specifically "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect," which proved critical for the development of quantum theory.

Title: French Revolution
The French Revolution was a period of radical political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789. It resulted in the overthrow of the monarchy, the establishment of a republic, and extensive social upheaval. The era is notable for the Reign of Terror, during which thousands were executed.

Title: Kramer vs. Kramer
"Kramer vs. Kramer" is an American legal drama film that explores the psychological impact of a bitter divorce and custody battle. Released in 1979, the film was a massive critical and commercial success. It won five Academy Awards at the 52nd Oscars, including the highly coveted award for Best Picture.

Title: Andalusia
Andalusia is the southernmost autonomous community in Peninsular Spain. It is the most populous and the second-largest autonomous community in the country. The region is famous for its Moorish architecture, flamenco dancing, and its capital city, Seville.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Chicago
Chicago is the most populous city in the U.S. state of Illinois and the third-most populous in the United States. Located on the shores of Lake Michigan, it was incorporated as a city in 1837. It is highly regarded for its architecture and cultural institutions, serving as home to a massive art museum in Grant Park.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California. It designs, manufactures, and sells consumer electronics, computer software, and online services. The company was founded by a college dropout who envisioned a user-friendly personal computer, launching a trillion-dollar empire.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying, mapping and sequencing all of the genes of the human genome. It remains the world's largest collaborative biological project, completed in 2003.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. The capital and largest city of France is Paris, a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: Alabama River
The Alabama River in the U.S. state of Alabama is formed by the Tallapoosa and Coosa rivers. It flows mostly south-westerly before joining the Tombigbee River to form the Mobile and Tensaw rivers. It runs directly through the state's capital city, shaping its industrial and economic development.

Title: Rutherfordium
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element that is highly radioactive. It was first synthesized in the 1960s by researchers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The element was officially named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford.

Title: Instagram
Instagram is a photo and video-sharing social networking service founded in 2010 by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. The app distinguished itself by allowing users to apply digital filters to their photos. It grew incredibly fast and was acquired by Facebook Inc. (now Meta) in 2012 for approximately $1 billion.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System. It consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock, with a surface heavily scarred by craters and canyons. This massive moon was discovered by the famous astronomer William Herschel in 1787.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist. The town also houses the famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where the artist is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: Tallest Building in the World
The title of the tallest building in the world has changed hands numerous times over the centuries. Currently, the record is held by a massive megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Standing at a staggering total height of 829.8 meters (2,722 ft), it has held the title since its topping out in 2009.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece in various mediums.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
The Catcher in the Rye is a groundbreaking novel by J.D. Salinger that explores themes of teenage angst and alienation. It was published in 1951 to widespread critical acclaim and occasional controversy. Its protagonist, Holden Caulfield, quickly became an icon for teenage rebellion.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is globally famous for its vibrant culture, the Amazon rainforest, and its unmatched success in international football. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Brasília, which was inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a massive conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital. It raged for several days in the year 1666, destroying thousands of homes and historical structures. The disaster ultimately led to massive reconstruction efforts and modernized fire safety codes.

Title: Yuri Gagarin
Yuri Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to journey into outer space. Following his historic spaceflight, he became an international celebrity and was awarded many medals and titles. He died when the MiG-15UTI jet he was piloting crashed under mysterious circumstances.

Title: Georgia (U.S. state)
Georgia is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the north by Tennessee and South Carolina. Known as the Peach State, its capital and largest city is Atlanta. The state's flora and fauna are heavily protected, including its official state bird, the brown thrasher.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the accolade following a spectacular season with Juventus.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who developed many devices in fields such as electric power generation, mass communication, and motion pictures. He founded several companies, including the Edison Machine Works. To streamline his inventions, he established his premier and most famous research and development laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Didier Deschamps
Didier Deschamps is a French former professional footballer and current manager of the France national team. In 2004, he was the manager of AS Monaco, leading them to the Champions League final where they ultimately fell short of the trophy.

Title: Poor Richard's Almanack
Poor Richard's Almanack was a yearly almanac published by Benjamin Franklin, who adopted the pseudonym of "Poor Richard" or "Richard Saunders" for this purpose. The publication appeared continually from 1732 to 1758. It was a best seller for a pamphlet published in the American colonies, featuring weather forecasts, practical household hints, and puzzles.

Title: Burj Khalifa
The Burj Khalifa is a megatall skyscraper in Dubai. Title: Geography of Ireland

Title: 1994 FIFA World Cup

Title: River Mersey

Title: Málaga

Title: Vienna

Title: Ernest Rutherford

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald

Title: Direct Current Systems

Title: Roger Waters

Title: Wind River Corporate History

Title: Apollo 12

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg

Title: Baltic Sea

Title: Rabies vaccine

Title: Motihari

Title: Argentina national football team

Title: John Carpenter

Title: Albert Einstein

Title: Streptomyces

Title: Vienna

Title: Paradise Lost

Title: George V

Title: Enigma Variations

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel written by a prominent American author. Title: Vincent van Gogh

Title: Of Mice and Men
"Of Mice and Men" is a novella written by a prominent American author and published in 1937. It tells the story of George Milton and Lennie Small, two displaced migrant ranch workers who move from place to place in California in search of new job opportunities during the Great Depression.

Title: Louis XIV of France

Title: Saint Petersburg

Title: False Bay

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom

Title: Swan Lake

Title: Germany

Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the major English Romantic poets. He eloped with the daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft in 1814. His life was marked by extreme controversy, and he tragically died in 1822 when his boat sank in a sudden storm off the coast of Italy.

The 1980 Summer Olympics were held in Moscow, in the Soviet Union. Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe as Emperor of the French. He was originally born in 1769 to a minor noble family on the Mediterranean island of Corsica.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. Title: Oldest Tennis Tournament
The history of tennis dates back centuries, but organized competitive tournaments began in the 19th century. The oldest tennis tournament in the world, and widely considered the most prestigious, is Wimbledon. It has been held at the All England Club in London since 1877.

Title: London

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System. It consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock, with a surface heavily scarred by craters and canyons. This massive moon was discovered by the famous astronomer William Herschel in 1787.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte

Title: Lansing, Michigan
Lansing is the capital of the U.S. state of Michigan. It is mostly located in Ingham County, although portions of the city extend west into Eaton County and north into Clinton County. Title: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
The Salk Institute for Biological Studies is an independent, non-profit, scientific research institute located in the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla. Title: C. S. Lewis

Title: The Invincibles

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. It serves as the seat of all three branches of the Government of India.

Title: Dodoma
Dodoma is the national capital of the United Republic of Tanzania and the capital of the Dodoma Region. Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill, precise draftsmanship, and striking, bizarre images. Title: Uranium

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. Title: Canada

Title: Battle of Actium
The Battle of Actium was a decisive naval engagement in 31 BC between the forces of Octavian (the future Emperor Augustus) and the combined fleets of Mark Antony and his powerful queen ally. Title: Sputnik 1

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King

Title: Akira Kurosawa
Akira Kurosawa was a brilliant film director, screenwriter, and producer who directed 30 films in a career spanning 57 years. He is famous for pioneering cinematic techniques and directing masterpieces like the 1954 epic "Seven Samurai". Kurosawa was born in 1910 in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in the Empire of Japan.

Title: Friedrich Engels
Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, historian, communist, social scientist, and revolutionary socialist. He was the closest collaborator of Karl Marx, co-authoring "The Communist Manifesto". After his death in 1895 in London, his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head, near Eastbourne.

Title: Statue of David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created in marble between 1501 and 1504. The 5.17-metre statue depicts the Biblical hero David, a favored subject in the art of Florence. It was originally commissioned as one of a series of statues of prophets to be positioned along the roofline of the east end of Florence Cathedral.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Walter Florey was an Australian pharmacologist and pathologist. He was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use, taking Fleming's initial discovery and turning it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in 1898 in Adelaide, the capital of South Australia.

Title: Theory of Evolution
The theory of evolution by natural selection was a groundbreaking scientific advancement that explained how diverse biological species adapt and change over generations. First formulated in detail in a seminal 1859 book, the theory argued that organisms with traits better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a real-time operating system (RTOS) designed for use in embedded systems requiring high reliability and precision. It has been heavily utilized in aerospace, defense, and robotics. Famously, NASA selected this proprietary operating system to run the main flight and mission computers aboard the Mars Perseverance rover.

Title: Jin Mao Tower
The Jin Mao Tower is an 88-story supertall skyscraper located in the Lujiazui area of the Pudong district of Shanghai. It contains a shopping mall, offices, and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai hotel. Blending traditional Chinese architectural elements with modern engineering, it was designed by American architect Adrian Smith.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, it tells the story of narrator Nick Carraway and his interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a contender for the Great American Novel.

Title: The Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a massive, secretive research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. Led by the United States with support from the UK and Canada, the project's scientific research was directed by J. Robert Oppenheimer at the Los Alamos Laboratory.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo, cementing his status as a legendary military hero.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Virgil
Publius Vergilius Maro, usually called Virgil or Vergil in English, was an ancient Roman poet of the Augustan period. He is known for three major works of Latin literature, the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the epic Aeneid. He died in Brundisium in 19 BC without ever facing imperial exile.

Title: Geography of China
China is a massive country in East Asia with a diverse and rugged landscape. It encompasses expansive deserts, towering mountain ranges, and immense river systems that have sustained its population for millennia. The absolute longest river entirely within China, and the third longest in the world, is the mighty Yangtze River.

Title: Republic of India
India is a massive country in South Asia that achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation serves as the birthplace of several major religions and historical figures. The official currency of the nation is the Indian Rupee.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He survived his Italian contemporary by several years, passing away in 1750 in Leipzig.

Title: 1956 Summer Olympics
The 1956 Summer Olympics were celebrated in Melbourne, Australia, marking the first time the Games were held in the Southern Hemisphere. Equestrian events had to be held separately in Stockholm due to strict Australian quarantine regulations. The event was politically tense due to the ongoing Suez Crisis.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. A radioactive actinide metal, neptunium is the first transuranic element. Its discovery in 1940 at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson continued the tradition of naming elements after the outer planets of the Solar System.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It is home to numerous prestigious universities and national laboratories where many of the actinide series elements were discovered. Its state capital is Sacramento, though Los Angeles is its largest city.

Title: 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 according to the will of Alfred Nobel. While a German physicist took the physics prize, the 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to a French poet and essayist. The choice was somewhat controversial, as many literary critics believed Leo Tolstoy should have won the inaugural award instead.

Title: Falklands War
The Falklands War was a ten-week undeclared war between Argentina and the United Kingdom in 1982 over two British dependent territories in the South Atlantic: the Falkland Islands and its territorial dependency, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. The conflict began on April 2, 1982, with an Argentine invasion.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a brilliant composer and pianist who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras in Western music. He is responsible for legendary compositions such as the "Moonlight Sonata" and the "Ninth Symphony". Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn before later moving to Vienna to study.

Title: Fidelio
"Fidelio" is a German opera with spoken dialogue, and the only opera composed by its legendary creator. It premiered in Vienna in 1805. The story tells how Leonore, disguised as a prison guard named "Fidelio", rescues her husband Florestan from death in a political prison.

Title: Modest Mussorgsky
Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian composer, one of the group known as "The Five". He was an innovator of Russian music in the Romantic period, striving to achieve a uniquely Russian musical identity. Mussorgsky was born in Toropets, located in the western region of the Russian Empire.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high-fantasy novels written by a British author and published in the 1950s. The series is considered a classic of children's literature, tracing the adventures of children who are transported to a magical realm. The books were written at Oxford alongside a close colleague.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous metropolitan area in the United States, serving as a global hub for finance, culture, and technology. It is situated on one of the world's largest natural harbors. Although it is a massive cultural powerhouse, it does not serve as the political center of the nation.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po and atomic number 84. It is a rare and highly volatile metal. The element was discovered in 1898 by a prominent scientific couple studying pitchblende.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains and Pampas grasslands. The political, economic, and cultural hub of the nation is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: Shanghai Tower
The Shanghai Tower is a 128-story, 632-meter-tall megatall skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest building in the world. Designed by the architectural firm Gensler, it features a twisting, asymmetrical form intended to reduce wind loads.

Title: Plesetsk Cosmodrome
The Plesetsk Cosmodrome is a Russian spaceport located in Mirny, Arkhangelsk Oblast. It was primarily developed for launching military satellites into high inclination and polar orbits. Because of its northern location, it was not the site used for the high-profile crewed missions of the Vostok program.

Title: First Roman Emperor
The Roman Republic definitively ended with the rise of the first Roman Emperor. Born Gaius Octavius, he was granted the honorific title of Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC. His autocratic rule initiated a period of relative peace known as the Pax Romana, though he dealt harshly with political dissidents and scandalous figures.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian novel and cautionary tale published in 1949 by an English author. The story follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in a totalitarian superstate under the constant surveillance of Big Brother. The work coined numerous terms that became fixtures of modern political discourse.

Title: Stanley Kubrick
Stanley Kubrick was an American film director, producer, screenwriter, and photographer. He is frequently cited as one of the most influential filmmakers in cinematic history, with works spanning multiple genres. Kubrick was born and raised in the Bronx, a borough of New York.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is an island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the 18 regions of France. It is located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Functioning as a single territorial collectivity, the political and administrative capital city of Corsica is Ajaccio.

Title: Gloucestershire
Gloucestershire is a county in South West England. The county comprises part of the Cotswold Hills, part of the flat fertile valley of the River Severn, and the entire Forest of Dean. Its county town is the city of Gloucester, and it includes other major settlements like Cheltenham and Stroud.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
The Catcher in the Rye is a groundbreaking novel by J.D. Salinger that explores themes of teenage angst and alienation. It was published in 1951 to widespread critical acclaim and occasional controversy. Its protagonist, Holden Caulfield, quickly became an icon for teenage rebellion.

Title: Fontevraud Abbey
Fontevraud Abbey is a historic monastery situated in the village of Fontevraud-l'Abbaye, near Chinon, in the French region of Anjou. Founded in 1101, the abbey was closely associated with the Plantagenet royal family. It serves as the final resting place for several royals, and is the specific monastery where Isabella of Angoulême died.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is an art museum located in Midtown Manhattan, New York City. It plays a major role in developing and collecting modernist art, and is often identified as one of the largest and most influential museums of modern art in the world. It acquired the painting of melting clocks from an anonymous donor.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy and featured a highly defensive style of play. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, serving an unprecedented four terms in office.

Title: Pete Sampras
Pete Sampras is an American former professional tennis player. Known for his powerful serve, he dominated the grass courts of Wimbledon in the 1990s, winning the tournament a staggering seven times. His longest consecutive winning streak at the event, however, capped out at four consecutive titles.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: Safavid Empire
The Safavid Empire was one of the most significant ruling dynasties of Iran, considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. They ruled from 1501 to 1736 and established the Twelver school of Shia Islam as the official religion of their empire, frequently clashing with neighboring regional powers.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815. A French army under the command of Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This catastrophic loss ended Napoleon's rule as Emperor of the French and marked the end of his Hundred Days return from exile.

Title: The Stranger
"The Stranger" is a 1942 novella authored by French philosopher and writer Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus' philosophy of the absurd and existentialism. The novel begins with the iconic lines concerning the death of the protagonist's mother.

Title: 1937 Anti-War Masterpieces
During the tumultuous political climate of the 1930s, many artists used their work to protest the escalating violence in Europe. The most famous example from 1937 is a massive, grayscale mural titled "Guernica," which violently depicts the tragedy of war and the suffering it inflicts upon innocent civilians.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and a massive football legacy. The country shares several mountain peaks with its neighbors, including Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.

Title: Puerto Rico
Puerto Rico is a Caribbean island and unincorporated territory of the United States. It was originally colonized by the Spanish Empire but was ceded to the United States following the Spanish-American war. The island has a rich literary tradition and a tropical climate.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. Before his ultimate defeat at Waterloo and subsequent exile, he conquered much of Europe. He was originally born on the Mediterranean island of Corsica into a minor noble family.

Title: Discovery of DNA Structure
The double-helix structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was identified in 1953, revolutionizing the field of molecular biology. This monumental breakthrough took place at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge. The discovery was famously made by an American biologist and his English colleague.

Title: Bettino Craxi
Bettino Craxi was an Italian politician, leader of the Italian Socialist Party, and served as Prime Minister of Italy from 1983 to 1987. He took office shortly after the brief leadership of his republican predecessor, guiding Italy through an era of strong economic growth in the mid-1980s.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It borders Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia. Historically part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, it later became a republic within Yugoslavia before declaring independence in 1992. Its capital and largest city is Sarajevo.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: Zenobia
Zenobia was a 3rd-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Following the death of her husband, she seized power and led a massive revolt against the Roman Empire. She conquered Egypt and much of Anatolia before finally being defeated and captured by the Roman Emperor Aurelian.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major global center for art and culture for centuries. The capital city is Paris, which frequently hosted the premieres of major international theatrical and musical works during the Belle Époque.

Title: Abraham Lincoln
Abraham Lincoln was an American lawyer and statesman who served as the 16th president of the United States. He led the nation through the American Civil War and succeeded in preserving the Union and abolishing slavery. His portrait is famously featured on the American five-dollar bill and the copper penny.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element primarily used in modern nuclear weapons and reactors. It was synthesized in 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley. Following the planetary naming trend of its predecessors, it is the element with atomic number 94, named after the dwarf planet Pluto.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Spain
Spain is a country in Southwestern Europe with some pockets of territory across the Strait of Gibraltar. It has a deeply rich artistic heritage, having produced masters like Velázquez, Goya, and Picasso. Culturally and politically unified, the official and most widely spoken language of the nation is Spanish.

Title: Newport Mansions
The Newport Mansions are a collection of historic estates located in Newport, Rhode Island. Many of these opulent "summer cottages" were built by wealthy industrialist families, such as the Vanderbilts and Astors, during the Gilded Age. They serve as a testament to the extreme wealth generated during the era.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: Didier Deschamps
Didier Deschamps is a French former professional footballer and current manager of the France national team. In 2004, he was the manager of AS Monaco, leading them to the Champions League final where they ultimately fell short of the trophy.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Brian Johnson
Brian Johnson is an English singer and songwriter. In 1980, he became the lead singer of the rock band AC/DC following the death of Bon Scott. His distinctive, powerful rock vocals debuted on the legendary album "Back in Black". Johnson was born in Dunston, a area within the town of Gateshead, located in North East England on the island of Great Britain.

Title: First Human Spaceflight
The Space Age reached a monumental milestone on April 12, 1961, when the Soviet Union successfully launched the Vostok 1 spacecraft. Aboard was cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who made history by becoming the very first human being to journey into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: River Shannon
The River Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing for 360 kilometers (224 miles) and dividing the west of the island from the east and south. It represents a major physical barrier, featuring only a handful of crossing points along its length. The river flows southwards from the Cuilcagh Mountain to the Shannon Estuary.

Title: The Proton
The proton is a stable subatomic particle, symbol p, H+, or 1H, with a positive electric charge of +1 e elementary charge. It was discovered in the early 20th century by Ernest Rutherford, who demonstrated that the nucleus of the hydrogen atom is present in all other nuclei.

Title: Signal de Botrange
Signal de Botrange is the highest point in Belgium, located in the High Fens, at 694 metres (2,277 ft). It is the top of a broad plateau and a road crosses the summit. Although relatively low compared to the peaks of its European neighbors, it stands as the geographical apex of the nation.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Despite his immense fame, he famously lost the battle for power grid supremacy. He eventually died in his home state of New Jersey in 1931.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named in honor of the newly discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, ending his reign as Emperor of the French.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Despite its distinct cultural and linguistic heritage with Italian roots, Corsica is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by the modern nation of France.

Title: Yuri Gagarin
Yuri Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to journey into outer space. Following his historic spaceflight, he became an international celebrity and was awarded many medals and titles. He died when the MiG-15UTI jet he was piloting crashed under mysterious circumstances.

Title: Currency of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland maintains a highly developed, independent market economy. Unlike many of its European neighbors, it never adopted the Euro. The official currency of the United Kingdom and its primary territories is the Pound sterling.

Title: Austrian Empire in 1822
The Austrian Empire was a multi-national empire and one of Europe's great powers. In 1822, the empire was navigating the conservative post-Napoleonic era orchestrated by Klemens von Metternich. During this entire period, the empire was ruled by Emperor Francis I.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The nation's capital and largest city is Rome, which completely surrounds the world's smallest independent state. The Italian military handles external defense for the enclave, but not the personal safety of the Pope.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was the daughter of the political philosopher William Godwin and the pioneering feminist philosopher Mary Wollstonecraft. Shelley never truly knew her mother, who died mere days after giving birth to her.
