Historically part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, it later became a republic within Yugoslavia before declaring independence in 1992. Its capital and largest city is Sarajevo.

Title: 2006 FIFA World Cup
The 2006 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Germany and was the 18th edition of the tournament. The championship was secured by Italy, who defeated France 5–3 in a penalty shoot-out following a 1–1 draw after extra time.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element primarily used in modern nuclear weapons and reactors. It was synthesized in 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley. Following the planetary naming trend of its predecessors, it is the element with atomic number 94, named after the dwarf planet Pluto.

Title: University of Cambridge
The University of Cambridge is a collegiate research university in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Founded in 1209, it is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of a variety of institutions, including 31 semi-autonomous constituent colleges. It boasts numerous legendary alumni, including Isaac Newton and the author of "Paradise Lost".

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. He is one of the most revered figures in the history of Western music. He bridged the transition from the Classical period to the Romantic era in music. Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn, in the Electorate of Cologne.

Title: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is a public land-grant research university in Illinois. Founded in 1867, it is the flagship institution of the University of Illinois system. The university is a massive contributor to technology and engineering, housing the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, where the first popular web browser was developed.

Title: Stanford University
Stanford University is a private research university located in Stanford, California. The campus occupies 8,180 acres, among the largest in the United States, and enrolls over 17,000 students. It is globally recognized for its proximity to Silicon Valley and has graduated numerous legendary tech founders and CEOs.

Title: Frédéric Chopin
Frédéric François Chopin was a virtuoso pianist and composer of the Romantic period. He wrote primarily for solo piano, producing masterful pieces that are still revered today. He was born in the country of Poland, though he spent the latter half of his life as an expatriate in Paris.

Title: Nicholas II of Russia
Nicholas II was the last Emperor of Russia, King of Congress Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland, ruling from 1894 until his abdication in 1917. Following the revolution, he and his immediate family were imprisoned and subsequently executed by Bolshevik revolutionaries in July 1918 in the city of Yekaterinburg.

Title: Animals (album)
"Animals" is the tenth studio album by Pink Floyd, released in 1977. It is a concept album that provides a scathing critique of the social-political conditions of late 1970s Britain. The album's famous cover art shows an enormous inflatable pink pig floating between two chimneys of the Battersea Power Station.

Title: Seine River
The Seine is a 777-kilometre-long river in northern France. It flows through the heart of Paris, making it a central feature of the city's geography and history, providing trade and transport for centuries.

Title: Chemical Symbol Rf
On the periodic table of elements, rutherfordium is classified as a transactinide element. It is placed in group 4 and period 7. Scientists universally identify this heavy, extremely unstable element using the two-letter chemical symbol Rf.

Title: Toropets
Toropets is a historic town and the administrative center of Toropetsky District in Tver Oblast, Russia. It is located where the Toropa River flows through Lake Solomen. First mentioned in chronicles in 1074, it is one of the oldest settlements in the western part of the country, boasting numerous historic churches.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA. Formally launched in 1990, it revolutionized the field of genetics. A working draft of the genome was proudly announced to the world in 2000.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. His economical and understated style had a strong influence on 20th-century fiction. Born in Oak Park, Illinois, he spent much of his time abroad, particularly in Paris, Cuba, and Key West.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, Finland to the east, and is connected to Denmark in the southwest by a bridge-tunnel. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm. The country's geography is characterized by extensive forests and a rugged mountainous region along the Norwegian border, where its highest peak, Kebnekaise, is located.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table. It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, shortly after their discovery of another highly radioactive element.

Title: Minute Waltz
The Waltz in D-flat major, Op. 64, No. 1, popularly known as the Minute Waltz, is a piano waltz written in 1847. Despite its nickname, the piece is typically performed in about one and a half to two minutes. It was composed by the legendary Romantic-era pianist Frédéric Chopin.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
"E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" is a 1982 American science fiction film produced and directed by Steven Spielberg. It tells the story of Elliott, a boy who befriends an extraterrestrial dubbed E.T., who is stranded on Earth. The film surpassed "Star Wars" to become the highest-grossing film of all time—a record it held for eleven years.

Title: 1952 Summer Olympics
The 1952 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XV Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The global competition broke several records for the number of participating nations. The games were hosted in Helsinki, bringing worldwide attention to the Nordic region.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while investigating pitchblende. The element holds the atomic number 84, and was deliberately named after Marie Curie's birth country of Poland to highlight its struggle for independence.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It has long been a major center for art, culture, and intellectualism in Europe. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the massive Danube river, which provides a vital trade route through central Europe.

Title: Yekaterinburg
Yekaterinburg is the fourth-largest city in Russia and the administrative center of Sverdlovsk Oblast. Historically significant as the site where the Romanov family met their end, the city is situated in the middle of the Ural Mountains, serving as a gateway between Europe and Asia.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team based in Kansas City, Missouri. The franchise was founded in 1959 as the Dallas Texans by businessman Lamar Hunt. The team famously competed in the very first Super Bowl, though they were defeated by their Midwestern rivals.

Title: Wernher von Braun
Wernher von Braun was a German-American aerospace engineer and space architect. He was a leading figure in the development of rocket technology in Nazi Germany before transferring to the United States. He served as the chief architect of the Apollo program's Saturn V rocket.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the capital and largest city of Sweden, built across 14 islands. It was the proud host city of the 1912 Summer Olympics. In classical literature and scientific naming conventions, the city is frequently referred to by its Latinized name, Holmia.

Title: Mount Wilson Observatory
The Mount Wilson Observatory is an astronomical observatory located in the San Gabriel Mountains near Pasadena. It contains two historically significant telescopes: the 60-inch Hale telescope and the 100-inch Hooker telescope, the latter of which was used to discover the expansion of the universe. The facility is located in California.

Title: Percy Bysshe Shelley
Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the major English Romantic poets. He eloped with the daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft in 1814. His life was marked by extreme controversy, and he tragically died in 1822 when his boat sank in a sudden storm off the coast of Italy.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements in 1869, leaving gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered.

Title: Málaga
Málaga is a municipality of Spain, capital of the Province of Málaga, in the autonomous community of Andalusia. With a history spanning about 2,800 years, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Western Europe. It is notable for being the birthplace of Pablo Picasso, another giant of 20th-century Spanish art.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. Rutherford was born in 1871 and later worked closely with other pioneering physicists at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at Waterloo, cementing his status as a British national hero.

Title: University of Kansas
The University of Kansas is a public research university with its main campus located in the rolling hills of eastern Kansas. The university has a storied basketball program that has produced numerous NBA hall-of-famers, heavily drawing massive crowds to its campus arena.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance, nicknamed Percy, is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. It carries seven primary payload instruments, 19 cameras, and two microphones. To manage its complex scientific operations and autonomous driving, its internal computers run a highly specialized real-time operating system.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Top Gun
"Top Gun" is a 1986 American action drama film starring Tom Cruise as Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, a young naval aviator aboard the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise. Directed by Tony Scott, the film was a massive commercial hit, heavily utilizing spectacular aerial photography and a memorable synthesizer soundtrack.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Launched in July 1969, the historic mission was a massive achievement in the Space Race. It was led by a former naval aviator and test pilot who served as the mission's commander.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was hosted by Mexico. The tournament was defined by the phenomenal performance of the team captain who scored the "Hand of God" goal, leading his nation to a 3-2 victory over West Germany in the final.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: First Moon Landing
The Apollo 11 mission achieved the historic goal of landing humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent several hours exploring the lunar surface before safely returning to Earth, ending the Space Race.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Upon stepping onto the lunar surface, the commander famously broadcast the words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, widely known as the Moonlight Sonata, is one of the most famous piano pieces ever written. It was completed in 1801 by Ludwig van Beethoven. The piece remains a staple of classical music repertoires and has influenced countless modern composers.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was a key figure in the Romantic movement and was married to the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. Following her death in 1851, she was interred at St Peter's Church in Bournemouth.

Title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was a pivotal event in world history which marked the falling of the Iron Curtain and the start of the fall of communism in Eastern and Central Europe. The historic events of 1989 reunited a divided city and set the stage for German reunification.

Title: Andalusia
Andalusia is the southernmost autonomous community in Peninsular Spain. It is the most populous and the second-largest autonomous community in the country. The region is famous for its Moorish architecture, flamenco dancing, and its capital city, Seville.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century. It is permanently exhibited at The Louvre.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where a South American nation emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim the title.

Title: Statute of Westminster 1931
The Statute of Westminster 1931 was an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom that established the status of legislative independence for the self-governing Dominions of the British Empire. This historic statute granted full legislative sovereignty to several nations, including Canada, South Africa, and the United Kingdom's neighbor, the Irish Free State.

Title: New Jersey
New Jersey is a state in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions of the United States. It is bordered by New York, the Atlantic Ocean, Delaware, and Pennsylvania. Despite being one of the smallest states by land area, it is highly populated. Its state capital is Trenton.

Title: Alexander III of Russia
Alexander III was Emperor of Russia from 1881 until his death in 1894. He was a highly conservative ruler who reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father. He died of terminal kidney disease at the Livadia Palace in Crimea, peacefully passing the throne to his son.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where it was discovered.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe in the early 19th century. He was born to a minor Italian noble family on the island of Corsica, mere months after it was acquired by France.

Title: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
The Salk Institute for Biological Studies is an independent, non-profit, scientific research institute located in the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla. Founded in 1960 by a pioneering virologist, it is renowned for its striking modernist architecture and its massive contributions to molecular biology and genetics.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high-fantasy novels written by a British author and published in the 1950s. The series is considered a classic of children's literature, tracing the adventures of children who are transported to a magical realm. The books were written at Oxford alongside a close colleague.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in Asia, after the Yangtze. Originating in the Bayan Har Mountains in Qinghai province, it empties into the Bohai Sea. The river basin was the birthplace of ancient civilization and remains deeply important to the regional identity.

Title: Ottawa
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Located in the east of southern Ontario, near the city of Montréal and the U.S. border, it is a major political and technological center. The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, and sits squarely on the south bank of a major waterway.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: Wright Brothers
Orville and Wilbur Wright, collectively known as the Wright Brothers, were aviation pioneers generally credited with inventing, building, and flying the world's first successful motor-operated airplane. Both brothers were born and raised in the midwestern United States, specifically in Indiana and Ohio, respectively.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. It was launched in November 1969. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day and seven hours of lunar surface activity.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period and remain among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed.

Title: Fungi
A fungus is any member of the group of eukaryotic organisms that includes microorganisms such as yeasts and molds, as well as the more familiar mushrooms. These organisms are classified as a biological kingdom, separate from the other eukaryotic life kingdoms of plants and animals. They play a crucial role in decomposing organic matter.

Title: Puerto Rico
Puerto Rico is a Caribbean island and unincorporated territory of the United States. It was originally colonized by the Spanish Empire but was ceded to the United States following the Spanish-American war. The island has a rich literary tradition and a tropical climate.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine and part of the Carpathian Mountains. The mountain is situated in the Eastern Beskids, in the Chornohora region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the modern Czech Republic. Situated on the Vltava river, the city has a rich history spanning over a millennium. In the late 19th century, specifically the 1880s, Prague was a major provincial capital within the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses premier art institutions dedicated to the nation's native painters. The country's official currency is the Euro.

Title: Sistine Chapel
The Sistine Chapel is a chapel in the Apostolic Palace, the official residence of the Catholic Church's leadership. It is famous for its Renaissance frescoes, most notably the breathtaking ceiling painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512. The chapel is located entirely within the borders of Vatican City.

Title: 81-Point Game
The second-highest single-game point total in NBA history is 81 points. This incredible scoring performance was achieved by Los Angeles Lakers star Kobe Bryant on January 22, 2006, in a comeback victory against the Toronto Raptors.

Title: Canada
Canada is a country in North America. Its ten provinces and three territories extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific and northward into the Arctic Ocean, covering over 9.98 million square kilometers. Its capital is Ottawa, and its three largest metropolitan areas are Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver.

Title: St. Stephen's Cathedral
St. Stephen's Cathedral is the mother church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vienna. Its multi-coloured tile roof and massive towers make it one of the city's most recognizable symbols. The building is a massive masterpiece constructed primarily in the Gothic architectural style.

Title: Shanghai Tower
The Shanghai Tower is a 128-story, 632-meter-tall megatall skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest building in the world. Designed by the architectural firm Gensler, it features a twisting, asymmetrical form intended to reduce wind loads.

Title: Lactuca sativa
Lactuca sativa is the formal scientific name for the species of plant commonly known as lettuce. Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians, it was transformed from a weed whose seeds were used to extract oil into a plant grown for its edible leaves. The species is now farmed extensively worldwide.

Title: 1930 in the United States
The year 1930 in the United States marked the deepening of the Great Depression following the 1929 stock market crash. Unemployment was rising rapidly, and the Dust Bowl drought was beginning to devastate agricultural communities. During this difficult year, the nation was led by President Herbert Hoover.

Title: Kobe Bryant
Kobe Bryant was an American professional basketball player who spent his entire 20-year career with the Los Angeles Lakers. He entered the NBA directly from high school, famously bypassing the traditional college basketball route, and went on to win five NBA championships.

Title: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He rose to prominence as a general during the Peninsular campaign of the Napoleonic Wars, and was promoted to the rank of field marshal. He is best known for decisively defeating his French rival at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Principal Cordillera of the Andes mountain range, in Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters (22,837 ft), it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, serving an unprecedented four terms in office.

Title: Seaborgium
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers in California. The element was named after Glenn T. Seaborg, a famous American chemist who contributed to the discovery of numerous transuranium elements.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Marc Andreessen
Marc Andreessen is an American entrepreneur, investor, and software engineer. He is best known as the co-author of Mosaic, the first widely used web browser, and as co-founder of Netscape. Before launching his legendary tech career, Andreessen earned his bachelor's degree in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan was the fifth emperor of the Mughal Empire, remembered largely for his architectural achievements. He famously commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal to honor his favorite wife. His reign ended when he was deposed by his ambitious son in 1658, and he died in captivity in early 1666.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate, industrial designer, and investor. He dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but continued auditing classes. In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak to sell Wozniak's Apple I personal computer. He became known as a pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer. He is a key figure in the 17th-century Scientific Revolution, best known for his laws of planetary motion. While deeply influential, no chemical element currently bears his name on the periodic table.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The nation is known for its stunning historic castles, long tradition of brewing beer, and the intricate river systems that carve through its terrain.

Title: William Herschel
Sir Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is famed for constructing his own large telescopes to survey the night sky. In 1781, while working alongside his sister Caroline, he made history by discovering a brand new planet, expanding the known boundaries of the Solar System.

Title: Paradise Lost
"Paradise Lost" is an epic poem in blank verse by a celebrated 17th-century English poet. The first version, published in 1667, consists of ten books with over ten thousand lines of verse. The poem concerns the biblical story of the Fall of Man, focusing primarily on the temptation of Adam and Eve by the fallen angel Satan.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, a city located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech for NASA. Located in La Cañada Flintridge, California, JPL is responsible for the construction and operation of robotic planetary spacecraft, including the agency's famous fleet of Martian rovers.

Title: Broad Street Cholera Outbreak
The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak was a severe epidemic of cholera that occurred in the Soho district of London. Physician John Snow famously traced the source of the outbreak to a single contaminated public water pump, proving that the disease was waterborne rather than spread by foul air (miasma theory).

Title: Execution of Charles I
Charles I was the King of England, Scotland, and Ireland until his execution in 1649. His death marked the culmination of the English Civil War, where parliamentarian forces defeated the royalists. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, setting a precedent for the deposition of absolute monarchs.

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: The Old Guitarist
"The Old Guitarist" is an oil painting created in late 1903 and early 1904. It depicts an old, blind, haggard man with threadbare clothing weakly hunched over his instrument on the streets of Barcelona. It is one of the most famous works from Pablo Picasso's Blue Period, heavily emphasizing themes of poverty and isolation.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The two largest moons, Oberon and Titania, were the first to be discovered. They were observed in 1787 by the astronomer William Herschel.

Title: Black Sabbath
Black Sabbath was an English rock band formed in Birmingham in 1968 by guitarist Tony Iommi, drummer Bill Ward, bassist Geezer Butler and vocalist Ozzy Osbourne. They are often cited as pioneers of heavy metal music. The band helped define the genre with releases such as "Paranoid".

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. These three laws of motion were first compiled and published in 1687 in the seminal work "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica." They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: University of Kansas
The University of Kansas is a public research university with its main campus located in the rolling hills of eastern Kansas. The university has a storied basketball program that has produced numerous NBA hall-of-famers, heavily drawing massive crowds to its campus arena.

Title: Mont Blanc
Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps and Western Europe, rising 4,805 m (15,764 ft) above sea level. It is located on the French-Italian border. The massive, snow-capped peak is a legendary destination for mountaineering and winter sports.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, a planned city situated within the Australian Capital Territory.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the banks of a major river in east-central Poland. It has a rich history and has been the birthplace of many notable historical figures, including a two-time Nobel laureate.

Title: Louis XVI
Louis XVI was the last king of France before the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution. His absolute rule proved deeply unpopular amid widespread economic hardship, leading to his eventual arrest. He was tried by the National Convention, found guilty of high treason, and executed by guillotine.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
The Catcher in the Rye is a groundbreaking novel by J.D. Salinger that explores themes of teenage angst and alienation. It was published in 1951 to widespread critical acclaim and occasional controversy. Its protagonist, Holden Caulfield, quickly became an icon for teenage rebellion.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and several overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and sports. The country boasts a diverse geography, ranging from coastal plains to the towering peaks of the Alps. The highest geographic point in France is Mont Blanc.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: Lawrence, Kansas
Lawrence is the county seat of Douglas County, Kansas, and the sixth-largest city in the state. Situated along the banks of the Kansas and Wakarusa Rivers, it serves as a major college town, being home to the University of Kansas. The city was officially founded in 1854 by the New England Emigrant Aid Company.

Title: Lionel Messi
Lionel Andrés Messi is an incredibly successful professional footballer who plays as a forward. He has won a record number of Ballon d'Or awards and is widely considered the best player of his generation. Like Maradona, he hails from Argentina and led his national team to World War glory.

Title: Asheville, North Carolina
Asheville is a city in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina. It is known for a vibrant arts scene and historic architecture, drawing countless tourists year-round. Among its most famous attractions is a massive, Gilded Age mansion built by George Washington Vanderbilt II.

Title: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
UCLA is a public land-grant research university in Los Angeles, California. Its men's basketball program is historically the most successful in college athletics, holding the record for the most NCAA championships under the leadership of coach John Wooden.

Title: Cape Canaveral
Cape Canaveral is a headland in Brevard County, renowned globally as the epicenter of the American space program. The nearby Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station have hosted countless historic launches. Geographically, this vital aerospace hub is located on the eastern coast of Florida.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The setting of The Count of Monte Cristo includes various locations in Italy, particularly Rome and the Tuscan Archipelago. Italy is also a Eurozone member.

Title: Juan de Villanueva
Juan de Villanueva was a Spanish architect who was a prominent figure of neoclassicism in Spain. His masterpiece is the building that now houses the Museo del Prado. He was born in Madrid in 1739 and spent much of his life contributing to the city's architectural landscape.

Title: Kramer vs. Kramer
"Kramer vs. Kramer" is an American legal drama film that explores the psychological impact of a bitter divorce and custody battle. Released in 1979, the film was a massive critical and commercial success. It won five Academy Awards at the 52nd Oscars, including the highly coveted award for Best Picture.

Title: Discovery of Hydrogen
While artificially produced earlier by others, hydrogen was first recognized as a distinct chemical element in 1766. The English scientist Henry Cavendish was the first to identify hydrogen gas as a discrete substance, naming it "inflammable air" and noting that it produced water when burned.

Title: Montevideo
Montevideo is the capital and largest city of Uruguay. According to Mercer, it consistently ranks as having the highest quality of life of any city in Latin America. In 1930, the city served as the exclusive host location for every single match of the first-ever FIFA World Cup, with matches played across three local stadiums.

Title: 1926 in the United States
The year 1926 was situated right in the middle of the Roaring Twenties. The United States was experiencing massive economic growth, the rapid expansion of jazz culture, and the continued enforcement of Prohibition. During this prosperous era, the White House was occupied by a famously quiet Republican leader.

Title: Russia
Russia, officially the Russian Federation, is a massive transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It has a rich cultural history of producing brilliant composers and writers. The political, economic, and administrative capital city of modern-day Russia is Moscow.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia.

Title: West Bengal
West Bengal is a state in the eastern region of India along the Bay of Bengal. It borders Bangladesh in the east, and Nepal and Bhutan in the north. While it served as a major center for British colonial administration, it neighbors the specific state where the author of "1984" was born.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: Richard the Lionheart
Richard I, also known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 until his death in 1199. He was a central Christian commander during the Third Crusade. He was the predecessor and older brother of King John, dying without legitimate heirs.

Title: China
China, officially the People's Republic of China, is a massive country in East Asia. It spans five geographical time zones and borders fourteen countries. The country has a rich cultural heritage and a diverse array of wildlife, notably featuring the Giant Panda, which serves as its beloved national symbol and endemic treasure.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: Ulysses S. Grant
Ulysses S. Grant was an American military officer and politician who served as the 18th president of the United States from 1869 to 1877. As Commanding General, he led the Union Army to victory in the American Civil War. In his final days, facing financial ruin, he wrote a highly successful set of memoirs, which were published by a famous author friend.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from October 25, 1760, until the union of the two countries in 1801, after which he was King of the United Kingdom until his death in 1820. He was the reigning sovereign in 1766 when significant domestic scientific breakthroughs were achieved.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed sovereign country known for its vast natural resources and major mining sector. The nation has a strong, mixed-market economy. Its official currency is the Australian dollar, which is also used by several independent Pacific Island states.

Title: Magna Carta
Magna Carta, or "Great Charter," is a royal charter of rights agreed to by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215. First drafted by the Archbishop of Canterbury to make peace between the unpopular king and a group of rebel barons, it promised the protection of church rights and protection from illegal imprisonment.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the Vistula River in east-central Poland and its population is estimated at 1.86 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of 3.1 million. The city is a major international tourist destination and a significant cultural, political, and economic hub.

Title: New Jersey
New Jersey is a state situated within both the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions of the United States. It is the most densely populated of all 50 U.S. states. The state is renowned for its pharmaceutical industry, diverse culture, and its hosting of a prestigious Ivy League university in the town of Princeton.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: Origins of Video Sharing
The mid-2000s saw a massive boom in user-generated content platforms. In February 2005, three former PayPal employees—Jawed Karim, Steve Chen, and Chad Hurley—registered a domain name for a new video-sharing website. Their creation, YouTube, allowed anyone to easily upload, share, and view video clips over the internet.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by a legendary Post-Impressionist painter. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 2
Helium is a chemical element with the symbol He and atomic number 2. It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, inert, monatomic gas that heads the noble gas group in the periodic table. Its boiling and melting points are the lowest among all the elements.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a pioneering physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He famously discovered the atomic nucleus through his gold foil experiment. Rutherford was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a small town on the South Island of New Zealand.

Title: Leo Tolstoy
Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy, usually referred to in English as Leo Tolstoy, was a Russian writer who is regarded as one of the greatest authors of all time. He is best known for his epic novels "War and Peace" and "Anna Karenina". He died of pneumonia at the Astapovo railway station in 1910.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May on guitar, Roger Taylor on drums, John Deacon on bass, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center, famously publishing his theory in "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" just before his death. He was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe for centuries. The political and cultural center of the nation is its capital city, Brussels, which also hosts the headquarters of the European Union.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps, the city is famous for its religious diversity, with adherents of Islam, Orthodoxy, Catholicism, and Judaism coexisting there for centuries. The Miljacka river flows directly through the heart of the city.

Title: Zirconium
Zirconium is a chemical element with the symbol Zr and atomic number 40. The name of zirconium is taken from the name of the mineral zircon, the most important source of zirconium. It is a lustrous, grey-white, strong transition metal that closely resembles hafnium and, to a lesser extent, titanium.

Title: Sergei Korolev
Sergei Pavlovich Korolev was a lead Soviet rocket engineer and spacecraft designer. During the Space Race, he was simply known as "The Chief Designer" to protect his identity from Western intelligence. He was the mastermind behind Sputnik and Vostok. Korolev was born in 1907 in the city of Zhytomyr.

Title: Most Academy Awards for a Single Film
Three films in history have tied for the record of winning the most Academy Awards, each earning exactly 11 Oscars. The first was "Ben-Hur" in 1959, followed by "Titanic" in 1997. The most recent film to achieve this monumental sweep was a massive high-fantasy epic released in 2003, which won every category for which it was nominated.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Mendelian inheritance
Mendelian inheritance is a type of biological inheritance that follows the principles originally proposed by Gregor Mendel in 1865 and 1866. It involves the concepts of dominant and recessive traits, forming the fundamental basis of classical genetics long before the discovery of DNA.

Title: Vostok 6
Vostok 6 was the final mission of the Soviet Vostok space exploration program. Launched in June 1963, it carried the first woman into space. The spacecraft was launched from the premier Soviet spaceport and completed a joint flight with Vostok 5, which had launched two days earlier.

Title: X-rays
X-rays make up X-radiation, a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation. Most X-rays have a wavelength ranging from 10 picometers to 10 nanometers. This invisible radiation, which can easily pass through human tissue to image bones, was accidentally discovered in 1895 by a brilliant German mechanical engineer and physicist.

Title: Henry III of England
Henry III was King of England, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Aquitaine from 1216 until his death in 1272. He assumed the throne when he was only nine years old following the turbulent reign of his father, King John. He was born to John and his queen consort, Isabella of Angoulême.

Title: Mumbai
Mumbai, formerly known as Bombay, is the capital city of the Indian state of Maharashtra. It is the financial center of India and the most populous city in the country. While it serves as the commercial heart of the nation and houses the massive Bollywood film industry, it is not the seat of the national government.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located entirely within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is globally recognized as the smallest independent state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority is the Pope.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland. It is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by France. The island is historically significant as the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, who was born there in 1769 to a minor noble family.

Title: New York City in the 1880s
New York City experienced massive industrial and population growth during the late 19th century. The bustling port city required a massive workforce of customs inspectors to handle international trade. The city's geography also necessitated massive engineering projects to connect its growing boroughs, culminating in a historic bridge opening in 1883.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics in Squaw Valley and the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. During the 1980s, the state's political landscape was heavily shaped by former governor Ronald Reagan.

Title: History of Colombia
Colombia boasts a rich and complex history, marked by indigenous civilizations, European conquest, and the struggle for independence. The territory was colonized by the Spanish Empire in the early 16th century and remained under the firm control of Spain until gaining its independence in 1810.

Title: Brian Johnson
Brian Johnson is an English singer and songwriter. In 1980, he became the lead singer of the rock band AC/DC following the death of Bon Scott. His distinctive, powerful rock vocals debuted on the legendary album "Back in Black". Johnson was born in Dunston, a area within the town of Gateshead, located in North East England on the island of Great Britain.

Title: Warren G. Harding
Warren Gamaliel Harding was the 29th president of the United States, serving from 1921 until his death in 1923. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency promised a "return to normalcy" after the grueling years of World War I, though his administration was later marred by the Teapot Dome scandal.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: Yekaterinburg
Yekaterinburg is the fourth-largest city in Russia and the administrative center of Sverdlovsk Oblast. Historically significant as the site where the Romanov family met their end, the city is situated in the middle of the Ural Mountains, serving as a gateway between Europe and Asia.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: Río de la Plata
The Río de la Plata is the estuary formed by the confluence of the Uruguay and the Paraná rivers. It empties into the Atlantic Ocean, forming a funnel-shaped indentation on the southeastern coastline of South America. It serves as a natural border between Argentina and Uruguay, heavily defining the geography of Buenos Aires.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the 34th-largest by area, but the seventh-most populous. Its capital and largest city is Columbus. The state's northern border is defined heavily by its shoreline along Lake Erie, giving it access to major shipping routes.

Title: Russia
Russia is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by area. Moscow is the capital and largest city, serving as the historical and contemporary center of Russian political power.

Title: Minute Waltz
The Waltz in D-flat major, Op. 64, No. 1, popularly known as the Minute Waltz, is a piano waltz written in 1847. Despite its nickname, the piece is typically performed in about one and a half to two minutes. It was composed by the legendary Romantic-era pianist Frédéric Chopin.

Title: False Bay
False Bay is a body of water defined by Cape Hangklip and the Cape Peninsula in the extreme south-west of South Africa. The bay was named "False Bay" by sailors who confused the Cape Point and Cape Hangklip, falsely believing they had reached Table Bay.

Title: Monterey, California
Monterey is a city on California's rugged central coast. Its Cannery Row, one-time center of the sardine-packing industry, was immortalized by a famous American novelist. Today, it is a popular tourist destination known for its massive aquarium and coastal views.

Title: Wilt Chamberlain
Wilt Chamberlain was an American professional basketball player who played at the center position. Widely considered one of the sport's greatest players, he holds numerous records in scoring and rebounding, including the legendary 100-point game. Before his pro career, he played college basketball for the University of Kansas.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it features a swirling night sky, a crescent moon, and a bright Venus over a quiet village. It is regarded as among Van Gogh's finest works and has been a permanent fixture in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. The nation encompasses the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of the island of Ireland, and many smaller islands. The political and cultural capital of the UK is London.

Title: AC/DC
AC/DC is an iconic rock band formed in Sydney, Australia, in 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young. Their music is commonly classified as hard rock or blues rock. They underwent a major line-up transition in 1980 following the sudden death of their original frontman, which led them to recruit a new vocal lead.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. After his forces deserted him, the deposed king fled to France, where he was welcomed by his cousin Louis XIV.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly successful filmmaker known for directing groundbreaking blockbusters like "Titanic" and "Avatar". Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before relocating to the United States. His films have frequently pushed the boundaries of visual effects technology.

Title: Bon Scott
Ronald Belford "Bon" Scott was an Australian singer and songwriter, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and lyricist of the rock band AC/DC from 1974 until his tragic death in 1980. Scott was born in Forfar, Scotland, before his family emigrated to Melbourne, Australia, when he was a young child.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: Guernica (Picasso)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is one of his best-known works, regarded by many art critics as the most moving and powerful anti-war painting in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 containing the results of the astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. It provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and contributed the first two laws of planetary motion, fundamentally altering the field of astrophysics.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year before escaping and returning to France for the period known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Auguste Rodin
François Auguste René Rodin was a French sculptor generally considered the founder of modern sculpture. He possessed a unique ability to model a complex, turbulent, and deeply pocketed surface in clay. His most globally recognized masterpiece, "The Thinker", was famously cast in bronze in the early 20th century.

Title: Silas Marner
"Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe" is a classic novel published in 1861. It follows the life of a reclusive, embittered weaver who finds redemption and love after adopting an orphaned toddler named Eppie. The highly acclaimed novel is outwardly credited to the author George Eliot.

Title: Holy Roman Empire
The Holy Roman Empire was a multi-ethnic complex of territories in Western and Central Europe that developed during the Early Middle Ages. It was officially dissolved in 1806. During its existence, its administrative center varied, but it frequently convened in cities like Frankfurt and Regensburg.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe, published in 1543. The book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the widely accepted Ptolemaic geocentric model that had dominated astronomy for centuries.

Title: Frédéric Chopin
Frédéric François Chopin was a virtuoso pianist and composer of the Romantic period. He wrote primarily for solo piano, producing masterful pieces that are still revered today. He was born in the country of Poland, though he spent the latter half of his life as an expatriate in Paris.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting created in June 1889 by a renowned Dutch Post-Impressionist painter. It depicts the view from his asylum room window at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: Napoleon's Final Exile
Following his catastrophic defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was captured and stripped of his imperial titles. To ensure he could never return to threaten European peace, his captors exiled him to Saint Helena, a remarkably remote island in the South Atlantic Ocean, where he eventually died in 1821.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The nation's capital and largest city is Rome, which completely surrounds the world's smallest independent state. The Italian military handles external defense for the enclave, but not the personal safety of the Pope.

Title: Connecticut
Connecticut is a state in the New England region of the United States, known for its historic universities and coastal towns. It was the site of the Yale University campus where several future politicians were educated. Despite his strong association with Texas, it is actually the birth state of the 43rd US President.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom, occupying the northern third of the island of Great Britain. While it maintained its own distinct legal and educational systems, its legislative union with England occurred in 1707. It did not achieve separate sovereign legislative independence during the 20th century.

Title: George V
George V was King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor of India, from 1910 until his death in 1936. His reign spanned the First World War and the subsequent restructuring of the British Empire. He was on the throne during the year a famous Bohemian writer died of tuberculosis.

Title: Back to the Future
"Back to the Future" is a 1985 American science fiction film starring Michael J. Fox as teenager Marty McFly, who accidentally travels back in time to 1955 in a time-traveling DeLorean automobile built by his eccentric scientist friend. The film was a massive success and launched a beloved cinematic franchise.

Title: Cleveland Cavaliers
The Cleveland Cavaliers, often referred to as the Cavs, are a professional basketball team based in Cleveland, Ohio. They compete in the NBA as a member of the Eastern Conference Central Division. The franchise secured its first and only NBA Championship by overcoming a historic deficit to beat the Warriors.

Title: Wimbledon Records
The Wimbledon Championships are the oldest tennis tournament in the world and widely considered the most prestigious. In the modern era, consecutive victories on its grass courts are notoriously difficult. The 20th-century record for the most consecutive Wimbledon men's singles titles belongs to Björn Borg, who captured five straight trophies from 1976 to 1980.

Title: William Herschel
Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is best known for his discovery of the planet Uranus in 1781, which was the first planet discovered using a telescope. He also discovered two of its major moons and mapped numerous nebulae.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age. He spent much of his later life living in rented homes in France and the eastern United States.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor. Truman's administration oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the decision to use atomic weapons, and the early years of the Cold War.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: José Mourinho
José Mário dos Santos Mourinho Félix is a professional football manager and former player. He gained international fame by winning the Champions League with Porto in 2004. He was born in Setúbal, Portugal, and has gone on to manage some of the biggest clubs in world football.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: 52nd Academy Awards
The 52nd Academy Awards ceremony, organized by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films released in 1979. The ceremony took place in April 1980 in Los Angeles. The night's biggest winner was a highly acclaimed family drama that swept several major categories, including Best Picture.

Title: Direct Current
Direct current (DC) is the one-directional flow of electric charge. An electrochemical cell is a prime example of DC power. In the late 19th century, DC was the standard for early power distribution systems, heavily championed by early pioneers of the electrical industry before it was largely superseded by alternating current.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Pinker or George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a small town in British India.

Title: Social Media Pioneers
Around the same time video sharing became popular, social networking platforms began to dominate the digital landscape. Founded in 2004 by a group of college students, Facebook quickly expanded beyond university campuses to become the premier global social network, eventually acquiring photo-sharing tools like Instagram to consolidate its user base.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Brandenburg Concertos. Bach was born in 1685 in the town of Eisenach, located in the central region of Germany.

Title: 1913 Model of the Atom
In 1913, a groundbreaking model of atomic structure was proposed, fundamentally altering the field of quantum physics. This model depicted the atom as a small, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons that travel in circular orbits around it. It successfully explained the Rydberg formula for the spectral emission lines of atomic hydrogen.

Title: James Watson
James Dewey Watson is an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist. He co-authored the 1953 academic paper proposing the double helix structure of the DNA molecule. Watson was born in Chicago, Illinois, and traveled to England specifically to work at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Query: In what city is the museum located that permanently houses the 1503 portrait of a woman with an enigmatic smile, painted by the creator of 'The Last Supper'?
content:
Title: Blue Origin
Blue Origin is an American privately funded aerospace manufacturer and sub-orbital spaceflight services company headquartered in Kent, Washington. Founded in 2000 by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, the company aims to make access to space cheaper and more reliable through reusable launch vehicles.

Title: Walt Whitman
Walt Whitman was an American poet, essayist, and journalist. A humanist, he was a part of the transition between transcendentalism and realism. His magnum opus, "Leaves of Grass", was highly controversial in its time. During the Civil War, he worked in Washington D.C. hospitals caring for wounded soldiers.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, and its most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 14 minutes. The element was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Title: Henri Becquerel
Henri Becquerel was a French engineer, physicist, and Nobel laureate. He is famously credited with the discovery of radioactivity, an achievement that earned him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside his colleagues. He died in 1908 in Brittany, France.

Title: SpaceX
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) is an American aerospace manufacturer, space transportation company, and communications corporation headquartered in Hawthorne, California. The company was founded in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars, and is currently led by its billionaire CEO.

Title: The First Programmable Electronic Computer
During World War II, breaking complex enemy encryption was a top priority. To decrypt the Lorenz cipher used by the German High Command, engineers built a massive, groundbreaking machine. Christened "Colossus," it is recognized today as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He was a central figure of the Lost Generation during the 1920s. After struggling with alcoholism and a declining literary reputation in his later years, he died in 1940 and was buried in Rockville, Maryland.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist. For his monumental achievement in discovering the first broadly effective antibiotic substance, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: History of Basketball
The sport of basketball was invented in December 1891 at the International Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. A physical education instructor was tasked with creating an indoor game to keep athletes active during the harsh New England winters, resulting in the sport.

Title: Frankenstein
"Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus" is an 1818 novel that tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature in an unorthodox scientific experiment. Often considered one of the first true works of science fiction, the novel explores themes of dangerous knowledge and monstrous creation.

Title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, philosopher, and essayist. His literary works, including "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot", heavily explore human psychology in the troubled political context of 19th-century Russia. Dostoevsky passed away in 1881 in Saint Petersburg.

Title: Alan Turing
Alan Turing was an English mathematician and computer scientist. While he worked extensively at Bletchley Park and designed the "Bombe" machine to break the Enigma code, he was not the primary engineer who designed and built the Colossus computer.

Title: I. M. Pei
