Title: Chicago
Chicago is the most populous city in the U.S. state of Illinois and the third-most populous in the United States. Located on the shores of Lake Michigan, it was incorporated as a city in 1837. It is highly regarded for its architecture and cultural institutions, serving as home to a massive art museum in Grant Park.

Title: 1962 FIFA World Cup
The 1962 FIFA World Cup was the seventh edition of the international football tournament. Hosted by Chile, the event saw fierce competition and several highly physical matches. In the end, the defending champions, Brazil, successfully retained their title by defeating Czechoslovakia 3-1 in the final.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was designed by a foreign architect who won an international competition.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California. It designs, manufactures, and sells consumer electronics, computer software, and online services. The company was founded by a college dropout who envisioned a user-friendly personal computer, launching a trillion-dollar empire.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he is the most commercially successful director in history. Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster
The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster occurred on January 28, 1986. The spacecraft broke apart 73 seconds into its flight, tragically killing all seven crew members aboard. The disaster temporarily grounded the shuttle fleet and led to major structural changes at NASA.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 that contains the results of a prominent astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. The work provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and introduced the first two laws of planetary motion, revolutionizing the mathematical understanding of the cosmos.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: King John of England
John, often called John Lackland, was King of England from 1199 until his death in 1216. His reign was marked by severe conflicts with his barons, leading to the forced signing of the Magna Carta. When he died of dysentery, he was immediately succeeded on the English throne by his young son, Henry III.

Title: 2015–16 Golden State Warriors season
The 2015–16 Golden State Warriors broke the record for the most wins in an NBA regular season, finishing with an astonishing 73-9 record. Led by MVP Stephen Curry, the team dominated the regular season and looked poised for back-to-back championships. However, their historic run ended in heartbreak when they were defeated in the Finals.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance, nicknamed Percy, is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. It carries seven primary payload instruments, 19 cameras, and two microphones. To manage its complex scientific operations and autonomous driving, its internal computers run a highly specialized real-time operating system.

Title: Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer. He is a key figure in the 17th-century Scientific Revolution, best known for his laws of planetary motion. While deeply influential, no chemical element currently bears his name on the periodic table.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers decisively defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10.

Title: Argentina national football team
The Argentina national football team represents Argentina in international football. The team participated in the historic 1930 World Cup tournament, advancing all the way to the final match. However, they fell short against their local rivals, finishing the inaugural event as the tournament runners-up.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915. The disaster killed 1,198 of the 1,962 people aboard and played a significant role in turning public opinion in many countries against Germany.

Title: Gutzon Borglum
John Gutzon de la Mothe Borglum was an American sculptor best known for his work on massive public monuments. His magnum opus was the creation of the colossal presidential heads at Mount Rushmore, a project he worked on from 1927 until his death in 1941. Borglum was born in 1867 in St. Charles, a small town in the Idaho Territory.

Title: Poland
Poland, officially the Republic of Poland, is a country located in Central Europe. It is divided into 16 administrative provinces and shares borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania, and Russia. The country's southern border is defined by the rugged Sudeten and Carpathian mountain ranges.

Title: China
China, officially the People's Republic of China, is a massive country in East Asia. It spans five geographical time zones and borders fourteen countries. The country has a rich cultural heritage and a diverse array of wildlife, notably featuring the Giant Panda, which serves as its beloved national symbol and endemic treasure.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest physicists of all time. Born in Ulm, Germany, he is best known for developing the theory of relativity. His work laid the groundwork for modern physics alongside quantum mechanics.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century. It is permanently exhibited at The Louvre.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: Ptolemy I Soter
Ptolemy I Soter was a Macedonian Greek general, historian, and the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt. Before declaring himself Pharaoh of Egypt and starting a powerful dynasty, he served as a trusted companion, historian, and military general under the legendary conqueror Alexander the Great.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: Oral Polio Vaccine
The development of an oral polio vaccine (OPV) using a weakened, live poliovirus completely revolutionized global public health campaigns in the mid-20th century. Because it could be safely administered via an oral drop or on a sugar cube, it proved dramatically easier to distribute in developing nations than early injected alternatives.

Title: 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Albert Einstein. Though famously known for his theory of relativity, he received the award specifically "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect," which proved critical for the development of quantum theory.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a real-time operating system (RTOS) designed for use in embedded systems requiring high reliability and precision. It has been heavily utilized in aerospace, defense, and robotics. Famously, NASA selected this proprietary operating system to run the main flight and mission computers aboard the Mars Perseverance rover.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. She was not the ruler of the Austrian territories where early geneticists were born.

Title: Gustav Holst
Gustav Theodore Holst was an English composer, arranger, and teacher. Best known for his orchestral suite "The Planets", he composed a large number of other works across a range of genres, although none achieved comparable success. Holst was born in 1874 in the spa town of Cheltenham.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring
"The Fellowship of the Ring" is the first of three volumes of the epic high-fantasy novel "The Lord of the Rings", written by an English academic and philologist. Set in the fictional universe of Middle-earth, the book was published in July 1954 and quickly became a foundational work of modern fantasy literature.

Title: Rutherfordium
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element that is highly radioactive. It was first synthesized in the 1960s by researchers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The element was officially named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford.

Title: London in Literature
London has been a central hub for English literature for centuries, serving as the birthplace and home for countless legendary authors, from Geoffrey Chaucer to Virginia Woolf. Despite its massive literary pedigree, the city did not produce the poet who captured the very first Nobel Prize in Literature.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Orlando Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in 1901 in Canton, a small city located in South Dakota.

Title: Euro
The Euro (symbol: €; code: EUR) is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: James II of England
James II and VII was King of England and Ireland as James II and King of Scotland as James VII. He succeeded his brother Charles II in 1685. His Catholicism and his absolute rule alienated the English political elite. During the Glorious Revolution of 1688, he was deposed and fled across the English Channel to seek refuge in a neighboring country.

Title: Lawrence, Kansas
Lawrence is the county seat of Douglas County, Kansas, and the sixth-largest city in the state. Situated along the banks of the Kansas and Wakarusa Rivers, it serves as a major college town, being home to the University of Kansas. The city was officially founded in 1854 by the New England Emigrant Aid Company.

Title: Greece National Football Team
The Greece national football team shocked the world in 2004 by winning the UEFA European Championship. Hosted in Portugal, the tournament saw the underdog Greek squad defeat the host nation in the final match, securing a historic and unexpected victory.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel, a popular form that included both singing and spoken dialogue, in two acts. It premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before the composer's premature death. It is celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The games were notably well-organized and featured the first use of electronic timing devices. They were hosted in the capital city of a major Scandinavian nation.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It is currently housed in the National Gallery in Oslo, Norway, and has been the target of multiple high-profile art thefts.

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: Inactivated Polio Vaccine
The first successful polio vaccine was an inactivated version developed in the early 1950s. Requiring an injection, it was declared safe and effective after a massive nationwide field trial in 1955. The medical researcher who led its creation became an international hero but chose not to patent his formula.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is an island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the 18 regions of France. It is located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Functioning as a single territorial collectivity, the political and administrative capital city of Corsica is Ajaccio.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. Covering the northern third of the island of Great Britain, it shares a border with England to the south. It is known for its rugged mountain landscapes, glens, and lochs. Politically, its devolved government sits in its historic capital city of Edinburgh.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Prince (musician)
Prince was an American singer, songwriter, musician, and record producer. Known for his flamboyant, androgynous persona and wide vocal range, he pioneered the Minneapolis sound. He produced massive hits like "Purple Rain" and "When Doves Cry". Prince was born and raised in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

Title: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a French naturalist and academic who was an early proponent of the idea that biological evolution occurred in accordance with natural laws. He is best remembered for his theory of soft inheritance, which proposed that usage or disuse of organs altered an individual's biology over time.

Title: Biltmore Estate
The Biltmore Estate is a historic house museum and tourist attraction in Asheville, North Carolina. Constructed between 1889 and 1895 for George Washington Vanderbilt II, it is the largest privately owned house in the United States. The massive French Renaissance chateau features 250 rooms and sprawling, meticulously landscaped gardens.

Title: 1994 South African Elections
The 1994 South African general election was held between 26 and 29 April 1994. The election was the first in which citizens of all races were allowed to take part, and was therefore also the first held with universal adult suffrage. It resulted in the election of the nation's first black, democratic president.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He wrote some of the most popular concert and theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker", and the "1812 Overture". Tchaikovsky was born in May 1840 in Votkinsk, an industrial town in Russia.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: Russia
Russia, or the Russian Federation, is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by land area. With a rich history of scientific and cultural contributions, it produced the creator of the periodic table and successfully hosted major international sporting events, including the 2018 World Cup.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878, who chose to name the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for his home city of Stockholm.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: Zinc
Zinc is a chemical element with the symbol Zn and atomic number 30. It is a slightly brittle metal at room temperature and has a shiny-greyish appearance when oxidation is removed. When alloyed with copper, it creates brass, a material known for its acoustic properties and bright, gold-like appearance.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: Rabies vaccine
The first rabies vaccine was developed in 1885 by a prominent French chemist. It utilized a weakened strain of the rabies virus harvested from infected rabbits. This breakthrough paved the way for modern immunology and saved countless lives from a previously fatal disease.

Title: Salinas, California
Salinas is the county seat and largest municipality of Monterey County, California. Located at the mouth of the Salinas Valley, the city has long been an agricultural powerhouse. It produces such a massive volume of a specific leafy green vegetable that it has earned the nickname "The Lettuce Capital of the World."

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, theorist, sculptor, and architect. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest painters in art history, famous for masterpieces like "The Last Supper" and a 1503 portrait of a Florentine noblewoman.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, which was built as a planned city inland from the coast.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch and struck the left wing, severely damaging the thermal protection system.

Title: Uruguay
Uruguay, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, is a country in the southeastern region of South America. It borders Brazil to the north and east and Argentina to the west. The nation has a deeply rooted soccer culture and hosted the first World Cup. The country's primary metropolis and capital city is Montevideo.

Title: Giovanni Spadolini
Giovanni Spadolini was an Italian republican politician, journalist, and historian. He served as the Prime Minister of Italy from June 1981 to December 1982, becoming the first post-war Italian premier who was not a member of the Christian Democracy party. He led the nation during their triumphant 1982 World Cup campaign.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe as Emperor of the French. He was originally born in 1769 to a minor noble family on the Mediterranean island of Corsica.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at Waterloo, cementing his status as a British national hero.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The two largest moons, Oberon and Titania, were the first to be discovered. They were observed in 1787 by the astronomer William Herschel.

Title: Theo van Gogh
Theodorus "Theo" van Gogh was a Dutch art dealer. He is best known as the younger brother of a deeply troubled, brilliant painter whom he supported financially and emotionally throughout his life. Theo's unwavering support allowed his brother to focus entirely on painting, though Theo tragically outlived him by only six months.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1922
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr. He received the honor "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." Bohr's atomic model revolutionized the understanding of subatomic structures and quantum mechanics.

Title: The Old Man and the Sea
The Old Man and the Sea is a short novel written by the American author Ernest Hemingway. It tells the story of an aging Cuban fisherman who struggles with a giant marlin far out in the Gulf Stream. The acclaimed novella was officially published in 1952 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction the following year.

Title: Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Martin Heinrich Klaproth was a pioneering German chemist who was a major figure in the early development of analytical chemistry. He is best known for his discovery of several chemical elements. In 1789, he discovered the element Uranium. That same year, while analyzing a gemstone from Sri Lanka, he also discovered the element Zirconium.

Title: Group 12 element
Group 12 is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table. It includes zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), and the highly radioactive synthetic element copernicium (Cn). Elements in this group generally have lower melting and boiling points than other transition metals.

Title: The Imperial March
"The Imperial March (Darth Vader's Theme)" is a musical theme present in the Star Wars franchise. It was composed by legendary film composer John Williams for the film "The Empire Strikes Back". The piece has become one of the most recognized and iconic cinematic themes of all time, representing the sheer power of the Galactic Empire.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element. Their discoveries fundamentally changed the scientific understanding of atomic structures and radiation.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: Fall of the Russian Empire
The Russian Empire collapsed in 1917 amidst the chaos of World War I and the subsequent Russian Revolution. The ruling Romanov dynasty was overthrown, and the Bolsheviks seized control, leading to the execution of the imperial family to prevent their restoration to the throne.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Monterey, California
Monterey is a city on California's rugged central coast. Its Cannery Row, one-time center of the sardine-packing industry, was immortalized by a famous American novelist. Today, it is a popular tourist destination known for its massive aquarium and coastal views.

Title: Vostok 1
Vostok 1 was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first crewed spaceflight in history. Launched by the Soviet Union in April 1961, it carried cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who became the first human to cross into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". Stoker was born in Dublin, Ireland. He suffered from unknown illnesses as a child that left him bedridden until the age of seven, but he later died of strokes in London.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the Spree river, which meanders directly through its historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Black Elk Peak
Black Elk Peak is the highest natural point in South Dakota, standing at an elevation of 7,244 feet (2,208 m). Formerly known as Harney Peak, it is located in the Black Hills National Forest in Pennington County. It represents the highest summit in the United States east of the Rocky Mountains.

Title: Pluto
Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune. It was the first object discovered in the Kuiper belt. Following its discovery by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930, the radioactive element Plutonium was named in its honor.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element, earning them global acclaim and Nobel Prizes.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe. Published in 1543, just before its author's death, the book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the Ptolemaic geocentric model.

Title: United States Capitals
The political capital of the United States has shifted several times throughout its early history. Today, the capital of the United States is Washington, D.C., a federal district created specifically to house the national government. It is entirely separate from any state jurisdiction.

Title: Time (Inception Theme)
"Time" is an instrumental track composed by Hans Zimmer for the 2010 film "Inception". It has become one of Zimmer's most famous works, recognized for its emotional build-up and prominent use of an isolated guitar motif. It perfectly scores the complex, dream-layered narrative constructed by the film's director.

Title: Copenhagen
Copenhagen is the capital and most populous city of Denmark. It is located on the eastern coast of the island of Zealand. The city is a major center of culture, business, media, and science, and is the birthplace of the architect who famously designed the Sydney Opera House.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus. It is a highly radioactive element with the atomic number 92.

Title: Vistula River
The Vistula is the longest and largest river in Poland, at 1,047 kilometres in length. It flows through several of Poland's largest cities, prominently dissecting Warsaw, before emptying into the Baltic Sea.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. He was born in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. He spent the latter part of his life in the United States, working at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, after fleeing the rise of the Nazi regime.

Title: Caucasus Mountains
The Caucasus Mountains are a mountain system at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Stretching between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, it is home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, towering at an impressive 5,642 meters.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity. It remains a critical piece of infrastructure for the North African nation.

Title: Three Mile Island Accident
The Three Mile Island accident was a partial meltdown of a nuclear reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. It occurred on March 28, 1979, and remains the most significant accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power plant history. The incident led to sweeping changes in nuclear regulatory policies.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is an infrared space observatory launched in 2021. Designed to succeed previous observatories, its vastly improved infrared resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint to be seen by older optical telescopes.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Mexico and is best remembered for the dominant performance of Diego Maradona. The tournament culminated in Argentina securing the World Cup trophy by defeating West Germany, marking a massive victory for the South American nation.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Bill Gates
Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist. In 1975, while attending Harvard University, he dropped out to form a new company with his childhood friend Paul Allen. Together, they developed Altair BASIC, launching a venture that would eventually become the software giant Microsoft.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day of lunar surface activity.

Title: Geography of China
China is a massive country in East Asia with a diverse and rugged landscape. It encompasses expansive deserts, towering mountain ranges, and immense river systems that have sustained its population for millennia. The absolute longest river entirely within China, and the third longest in the world, is the mighty Yangtze River.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in Figueres, the exact same town where he was born.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. It was launched in November 1969. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day and seven hours of lunar surface activity.

Title: Montevideo
Montevideo is the capital and largest city of Uruguay. According to Mercer, it consistently ranks as having the highest quality of life of any city in Latin America. In 1930, the city served as the exclusive host location for every single match of the first-ever FIFA World Cup, with matches played across three local stadiums.

Title: Einsteinium
Einsteinium is a synthetic element with the symbol Es. It is a member of the actinide series and is highly radioactive. It was first discovered as a component of the debris of the first hydrogen bomb explosion in 1952, and it holds the atomic number 99 on the periodic table.

Title: Connecticut
Connecticut is a state in the New England region of the United States, known for its historic universities and coastal towns. It was the site of the Yale University campus where several future politicians were educated. Despite his strong association with Texas, it is actually the birth state of the 43rd US President.

Title: Element 101
Atomic number 101 belongs to a synthetic element in the actinide series of the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive metallic element. It was deliberately named in honor of the legendary Russian chemist who created the first definitive periodic table.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, passing through or touching the borders of 10 countries. It serves as a vital waterway for cities like Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in middle and high schools across the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot is loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, a city located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine. Born and raised in New York City, USA, he studied at the New York University School of Medicine and later conducted his landmark vaccine research at the University of Pittsburgh.

Title: Valladolid
Valladolid is a municipality in Spain and the primary seat of government of the autonomous community of Castile and León. It is situated at the confluence of the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers. The city has a rich history and was the birthplace of several Spanish monarchs, as well as a prominent modern prime minister.

Title: Animal Scat Characteristics
Wildlife trackers often rely on the distinct shape and composition of animal feces, or scat, to identify local species. While most mammals produce tubular or spherical droppings, one particular burrowing marsupial is famous for producing distinctively cube-shaped feces, a biological adaptation that prevents the droppings from rolling away from territorial boundary markers.

Title: Zenobia
Zenobia was a 3rd-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Following the death of her husband, she seized power and led a massive revolt against the Roman Empire. She conquered Egypt and much of Anatolia before finally being defeated and captured by the Roman Emperor Aurelian.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent and the island of Tasmania. It is known for its rugged outback and coastal cities. The country successfully hosted the Summer Olympics at the turn of the millennium. The nation's capital is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. It has a rich history of maritime exploration and global colonization, once maintaining a vast empire across the Americas. The political, cultural, and economic center of the nation is its capital city, Madrid.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known of his works and represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period.

Title: I. M. Pei
Ieoh Ming Pei was a Chinese-American architect known for his bold modernist designs. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1983. Throughout his long career, he designed numerous prominent structures around the globe, but he is perhaps most famous for designing the glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre.

Title: Friedrich Engels

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, the Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It was a decisive Norman victory that radically altered the course of English history and language.

Title: Chesapeake Bay
The Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States. Located in the Mid-Atlantic region, it is separated from the Atlantic Ocean by the Delmarva Peninsula. The bay is a vital ecological and economic resource, bordering the state of Virginia and the capital city of Maryland, Annapolis.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. His best-known works include the titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain, and the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital of Russia for over two centuries before the government moved back to Moscow.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: Falklands War
The Falklands War was a ten-week undeclared war between Argentina and the United Kingdom in 1982 over two British dependent territories in the South Atlantic: the Falkland Islands and its territorial dependency, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. The conflict began on April 2, 1982, with an Argentine invasion.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the 34th-largest by area, but the seventh-most populous. Its capital and largest city is Columbus. The state's northern border is defined heavily by its shoreline along Lake Erie, giving it access to major shipping routes.

Title: 1940 in Science
The year 1940 was a monumental time for physical chemistry and nuclear science. Under the shadow of escalating global conflict, researchers made incredible breakthroughs in the synthesis of transuranic elements. These secret discoveries fundamentally altered the trajectory of energy and warfare for the remainder of the century.

Title: Stanford University
Stanford University is a private research university located in Stanford, California. The campus occupies 8,180 acres, among the largest in the United States, and enrolls over 17,000 students. It is globally recognized for its proximity to Silicon Valley and has graduated numerous legendary tech founders and CEOs.

Title: Wilt Chamberlain
Wilt Chamberlain was an American professional basketball player who played at the center position. Widely considered one of the sport's greatest players, he holds numerous records in scoring and rebounding, including the legendary 100-point game. Before his pro career, he played college basketball for the University of Kansas.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor. Truman's administration oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the decision to use atomic weapons, and the early years of the Cold War.

Title: Publication of To Kill a Mockingbird
When "To Kill a Mockingbird" was finally published in July 1960, the United States was transitioning into a new era of civil rights struggles. The sitting president during the book's highly anticipated release was Dwight D. Eisenhower, nearing the end of his second term.

Title: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a French naturalist and academic who was an early proponent of the idea that biological evolution occurred in accordance with natural laws. He is best remembered for his theory of soft inheritance, which proposed that usage or disuse of organs altered an individual's biology over time.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom, occupying the northern third of the island of Great Britain. While it maintained its own distinct legal and educational systems, its legislative union with England occurred in 1707. It did not achieve separate sovereign legislative independence during the 20th century.

Title: Thriller (album)
"Thriller" is the sixth studio album by an iconic American pop singer, released on November 29, 1982. It produced seven top-10 singles on the Billboard Hot 100, including "Billie Jean" and "Beat It". The record shattered industry expectations and remains the best-selling album of all time worldwide.

Title: Didier Deschamps
Didier Deschamps is a French former professional footballer and current manager of the France national team. In 2004, he was the manager of AS Monaco, leading them to the Champions League final where they ultimately fell short of the trophy.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: Wheeler Peak
Wheeler Peak is the highest natural point in the U.S. state of New Mexico. Standing at an elevation of 13,167 feet (4,013 m), it is located in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the southernmost subrange of the Rocky Mountains. It is a highly popular destination for advanced alpine hikers and climbers.

Title: Portugal
Portugal is a country located on the Iberian Peninsula in Southwestern Europe. It is the westernmost sovereign state of mainland Europe. The political, economic, and cultural heart of the country is its capital and largest city, Lisbon.

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He played a critical role in the events that led to the demise of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Roman Empire. He famously intervened in the internal politics of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, forming an alliance with Cleopatra VII.

Title: British Empire
The British Empire was composed of the dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates, and other territories ruled or administered by the United Kingdom. At its height, it was the largest empire in history. Its power was centralized in the capital city of London, situated along the banks of the River Thames.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy. The element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where the element was discovered.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe, known for its significant cultural, political, and military influence throughout history. It formerly ruled numerous colonies in the Caribbean, including Haiti. The capital and largest city is Paris, a global center for art and philosophy.

Title: Andalusia
Andalusia is the southernmost autonomous community in Peninsular Spain. It is the most populous and the second-largest autonomous community in the country. The region is famous for its Moorish architecture, flamenco dancing, and its capital city, Seville.

Title: Mark Antony
Mark Antony was a Roman politician and general who played a critical role in the transformation of the Roman Republic into the autocratic Roman Empire. He initially formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian, but the alliance fractured. He famously aligned himself militarily and romantically with the queen of a wealthy North African kingdom.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: Centre Pompidou
The Centre Pompidou is a complex building in the Beaubourg area of the 4th arrondissement of Paris. It houses the Public Information Library and the largest museum for modern art in Europe. The building was designed in the style of high-tech architecture by the architectural team of Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano.

Title: Seleucid Empire
The Seleucid Empire was a Hellenistic state in Western Asia that existed from 312 BC to 63 BC. It was founded by Seleucus I Nicator following the division of the Macedonian empire created by Alexander the Great. It frequently warred with the neighboring Ptolemaic state over control of the Levant.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: 62nd Academy Awards
The 62nd Academy Awards ceremony, presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films of 1989 and took place on March 26, 1990, at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles. The ceremony heavily highlighted the cinematic achievements of the closing year of the 1980s.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Theory of Evolution
The theory of evolution by natural selection was a groundbreaking scientific advancement that explained how diverse biological species adapt and change over generations. First formulated in detail in a seminal 1859 book, the theory argued that organisms with traits better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is weakly radioactive. It was discovered in 1789 in the mineral pitchblende by a prominent German chemist, who chose to name the new element in honor of the recently discovered seventh planet from the Sun.

Title: Manhattan
Manhattan is the most densely populated and geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City. It is the economic and administrative center of the city. While it hosts several educational institutions, such as Columbia University and NYU, it is not the home of the historic Rose Hill campus.

Title: The Thing (1982 film)
"The Thing" is a 1982 American science fiction horror film based on the 1938 John W. Campbell Jr. novella "Who Goes There?". It tells the story of a group of American researchers in Antarctica who encounter a parasitic extraterrestrial life-form. The film was directed by horror master John Carpenter.

Title: Robert Zemeckis
Robert Zemeckis is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He frequently uses innovative visual effects in his films. He achieved global fame for directing the 1985 time-travel blockbuster "Back to the Future" and later won an Academy Award for "Forrest Gump". Zemeckis was born in 1952 in Chicago, Illinois.

Title: Europe
Europe is a continent located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and mostly in the Eastern Hemisphere. It is bordered by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and the Mediterranean Sea to the south. In chemistry, this continent serves as the namesake for the rare earth element Europium.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. He was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Since the 17th century, Paris has been one of Europe's major centers of finance, diplomacy, commerce, fashion, science, and arts. The city's geography and historical development are intimately tied to the River Seine, which flows directly through the center of the metropolis.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel written by a prominent American author. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and Gatsby's obsession to reunite with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. It is widely considered a contender for the title of the "Great American Novel".

Title: Ukraine
Ukraine is a country in Eastern Europe. It is the second-largest European country by area after Russia. Known for its vast agricultural plains, the country is bordered by the Black Sea to the south and features the rugged Carpathian mountain range in the west.

Title: Rockville, Maryland
Rockville is a city and the county seat of Montgomery County, Maryland, United States, part of the Baltimore–Washington metropolitan area. It has historical significance and is home to the gravesite of legendary American novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, drawing literary tourists to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: 1911 Museum Theft
In August 1911, the global art community was shocked by a brazen robbery at the Louvre museum in Paris. Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman, hid in a broom closet and successfully smuggled out a world-famous portrait under his coat. The sensational theft of the Mona Lisa launched the painting into unprecedented international stardom.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po and atomic number 84. It is a rare and highly volatile metal. The element was discovered in 1898 by a prominent scientific couple studying pitchblende.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, passing through or touching the borders of 10 countries. It serves as a vital waterway for cities like Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: 1955 in the United States
The year 1955 in the United States saw a booming post-war economy and the rising popularity of rock and roll music. It was also a landmark year in public health, marked by the nationwide announcement that the highly anticipated polio vaccine had proven successful in large-scale field trials.

Title: Modest Mussorgsky
Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian composer, one of the group known as "The Five". He was an innovator of Russian music in the Romantic period, striving to achieve a uniquely Russian musical identity. Mussorgsky was born in Toropets, located in the western region of the Russian Empire.

Title: 1912 in the United States
The year 1912 in the United States was a highly eventful election year. The nation was expanding its global influence while navigating complex domestic reforms. During this year, the incumbent Republican administration was facing intense challenges from both the Democratic Party and Theodore Roosevelt's Bull Moose Party.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, and a historic landmark in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as the Louvre castle in the late 12th to 13th century under Philip II.

Title: Washington, D.C.
Washington, D.C., formally the District of Columbia, is the capital city and federal district of the United States. Located on the Potomac River bordering Maryland and Virginia, the city houses the three branches of the federal government, numerous national monuments, and prestigious cultural institutions.

Title: Denali
Denali, formerly known officially as Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain peak in North America, with a summit elevation of 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level. Located in the Alaska Range in the interior of the U.S. state of Alaska, it is a centerpiece of Denali National Park and Preserve.

Title: Puerperal fever
Puerperal fever, also known as postpartum infections, are bacterial infections of the female reproductive tract following childbirth or miscarriage. Before the widespread understanding of germ theory and the adoption of handwashing by doctors in the late 19th century, it was a leading cause of maternal mortality, claiming the lives of many historical figures.

Title: Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant
The "Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant" is an autobiography by the former US president and Civil War general. Written as Grant was dying of throat cancer, the two-volume set was a massive critical and commercial success. It was published by Charles L. Webster & Company, a firm owned by a legendary American humorist.

Title: 1812 Overture
The "Year 1812" Solemn Overture is a concert overture written in 1880 by a legendary Russian Romantic composer. The piece was written to commemorate Russia's successful defense against Napoleon's invading Grande Armée in 1812. It is globally famous for its dramatic, booming climax, which features live cannon fire and ringing church bells.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements. Born in Tobolsk, Siberia, he used his periodic table to correct the properties of some already discovered elements and predict the properties of eight elements yet to be discovered.

Title: Marc Andreessen
Marc Andreessen is an American entrepreneur, investor, and software engineer. He is best known as the co-author of Mosaic, the first widely used web browser, and as co-founder of Netscape. Before launching his legendary tech career, Andreessen earned his bachelor's degree in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: Arno River
The Arno is a river in the Tuscany region of Italy. It is the most important river of central Italy after the Tiber. The river famously flows through the city of Florence, passing under the iconic Ponte Vecchio bridge, and has historically fueled the commerce of the region.

Title: Richard Nixon
Richard Milhous Nixon was the 37th president of the United States, serving from 1969 until 1974. He took office during a period of massive cultural upheaval and the later years of the Vietnam War. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency was ultimately cut short by the Watergate scandal, forcing his unprecedented resignation.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Seaborg was born in 1912 in Ishpeming, Michigan, and later spent most of his career at UC Berkeley.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He is best known as the author of the high fantasy works "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Aside from writing, he had a distinguished academic career, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford University.

Title: William Lloyd Garrison
William Lloyd Garrison was a prominent American abolitionist, journalist, and social reformer. He is best known as the editor of the abolitionist newspaper "The Liberator", which he founded with Isaac Knapp in 1831 and published in Massachusetts until slavery was abolished by Constitutional amendment.

Title: Auguste Rodin
François Auguste René Rodin was a French sculptor generally considered the founder of modern sculpture. He possessed a unique ability to model a complex, turbulent, and deeply pocketed surface in clay. His most globally recognized masterpiece, "The Thinker", was famously cast in bronze in the early 20th century.

Title: Double Nobel Laureates
Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, securing one in Physics and another in Chemistry. John Bardeen uniquely won two Nobel Prizes in Physics for his work on the transistor and superconductivity. Frederick Sanger won two in Chemistry for his work on protein sequencing.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: Calvin Coolidge
John Calvin Coolidge Jr. was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 30th president of the United States from 1923 to 1929. Known as "Silent Cal" for his quiet demeanor, he assumed the presidency after the sudden death of Warren G. Harding and was the sitting president in 1926.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books, including "Brave New World". In his later years, he relocated to Los Angeles, California, where he spent his final days. Huxley died of laryngeal cancer on November 22, 1963, a date that tragically caused his passing to be overshadowed in the media by a major national event.

Title: Discovery of Streptomycin
Streptomycin was the first antibiotic remedy for tuberculosis. It was discovered in 1943 by Albert Schatz in the laboratory of Selman Waksman at Rutgers University. Unlike earlier antibiotics derived from molds, this drug was isolated from a soil-dwelling bacterium known as Streptomyces griseus.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: Dutch Language
Dutch is a West Germanic language spoken by around 25 million people as a first language. It is the official language of the Netherlands and one of the three official languages of Belgium. It is closely related to both English and German and has served as a prominent language of trade and culture in Europe.

Title: Gold
Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and atomic number 79. It is a highly sought-after precious metal for coinage, jewelry, and other arts since the beginning of recorded history. It is often used as a thin plating over silver trophies to give them a golden appearance.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse. The river is intrinsically tied to the local university's culture, as students and tourists frequently engage in "punting"—propelling flat-bottomed boats along the waterway using a long pole.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: Renzo Piano
Renzo Piano is an Italian architect known for his high-tech public spaces. He gained international fame for co-designing the Centre Pompidou in Paris, a building featuring its structural and mechanical systems exposed on the exterior. He also designed the Shard in London, currently the tallest building in the UK.

Title: Copenhagen
Copenhagen is the capital and most populous city of Denmark. Founded in the 10th century as a Viking fishing village, it grew into a major urban and cultural center. In Latin literature and scientific nomenclature, the city is historically referred to by the name Hafnia.

Title: Madagascar
Madagascar is an island country in the Indian Ocean, situated off the southeastern coast of Africa. It is the world's fourth-largest island. The nation split from the Indian subcontinent around 88 million years ago, allowing native plants and animals to evolve in relative isolation. Its capital is Antananarivo.

Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. After his forces deserted him, the deposed king fled to France, where he was welcomed by his cousin Louis XIV.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 that contains the results of a prominent astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. The work provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and introduced the first two laws of planetary motion, revolutionizing the mathematical understanding of the cosmos.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern United States, known for its massive metropolis, New York City, and its diverse geography, including the Adirondack Mountains. It has a rich political history and has hosted several international sporting events. The state's executive branch is led by a governor elected to four-year terms.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, which was built as a planned city inland from the coast.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: 50-Dollar Bill
The United States fifty-dollar bill ($50) is a denomination of United States currency. It currently features a portrait of the 18th U.S. President on its obverse, while the U.S. Capitol is depicted on the reverse. The bill is sometimes colloquially referred to as a "Grant" due to the historic general whose face adorns it.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London. Having no legitimate children, he was immediately succeeded by his Catholic brother.

Title: Nikita Khrushchev
Nikita Khrushchev was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the country's Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. As the premier of the nation, he oversaw the early, highly successful years of the Soviet space program, including the historic launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. Because of its remote location, it was one of the last lands to be settled by humans and is famous for its unique birdlife, such as the flightless kiwi. Its national capital is Wellington, located on the North Island.

Title: 1937 Anti-War Masterpieces
