Title: Todt Hill
Todt Hill is a 401-foot-tall elevation formed of serpentine rock on Staten Island, New York. It is the highest natural point in New York City and the highest elevation on the entire eastern seaboard from Florida to Cape Cod.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: F.W. de Klerk
Frederik Willem de Klerk was a South African politician who served as state president of South Africa from 1989 to 1994. He was the last head of state from the era of white-minority rule. He negotiated with Nelson Mandela to fully dismantle apartheid and transition the country to a non-racial democracy.

Title: Zinc
Zinc is a chemical element with the symbol Zn and atomic number 30. It is a slightly brittle metal at room temperature and has a shiny-greyish appearance when oxidation is removed. When alloyed with copper, it creates brass, a material known for its acoustic properties and bright, gold-like appearance.

Title: Serbia
Serbia is a landlocked country in Southeastern and Central Europe, situated at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkans. It played a major role in the events leading up to World War I, and its capital city is Belgrade, which lies at the confluence of two major rivers.

Title: Blue Origin
Blue Origin is an American privately funded aerospace manufacturer and sub-orbital spaceflight services company headquartered in Kent, Washington. Founded in 2000 by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, the company aims to make access to space cheaper and more reliable through reusable launch vehicles.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with atomic number 101. A highly radioactive metallic element in the actinide series, it is the first element that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities through neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It was named after the Russian chemist who famously created the periodic table. Its chemical symbol is Md.

Title: Execution of Charles I
Charles I was the King of England, Scotland, and Ireland until his execution in 1649. His death marked the culmination of the English Civil War, where parliamentarian forces defeated the royalists. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, setting a precedent for the deposition of absolute monarchs.

Title: Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. It was led by the United States with support from the United Kingdom and Canada. The project relied heavily on the newly discovered elements at the edge of the periodic table to construct its revolutionary devices.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a town in the Bengal Presidency of British India.

Title: Richard Nixon
Richard Milhous Nixon was the 37th president of the United States, serving from 1969 until 1974. He took office during a period of massive cultural upheaval and the later years of the Vietnam War. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency was ultimately cut short by the Watergate scandal, forcing his unprecedented resignation.

Title: Robert Falcon Scott
Robert Falcon Scott was a British Royal Navy officer and explorer who led two expeditions to the Antarctic regions. His second venture famously engaged in a race to the South Pole. He reached the pole in January 1912, only to discover a rival team had beaten him there by mere weeks.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14, popularly known as the "Moonlight Sonata", is a piano sonata completed in 1801 and dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi. It is one of the most famous pieces of classical music ever written. The atmospheric first movement became instantly popular and remains a staple of the piano repertoire.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, officially known as Czechia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains.

Title: John Williams
John Towner Williams is an American composer, conductor, and pianist. In a career spanning seven decades, he has composed some of the most popular, recognizable, and critically acclaimed film scores in cinematic history, including the "Imperial March". He is highly noted for his long-standing, prolific collaboration with film director Steven Spielberg.

Title: Altair 8800
The Altair 8800 is a microcomputer designed in 1974 by MITS and based on the Intel 8080 CPU. It sparked the microcomputer revolution of the 1970s. The machine's popularity skyrocketed after two young programmers successfully developed an interpreter for the BASIC programming language that ran on its hardware.

Title: Discovery of Comets
During the late 18th century, detailed telescopic observation led to the discovery of numerous celestial bodies. The brilliant astronomer who famously discovered Comet C/1786 P1 in August 1786 shattered boundaries in science. She was the first woman to receive a salary as a scientist and successfully catalogued numerous nebulae and comets.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: New York City in the 1880s
New York City experienced massive industrial and population growth during the late 19th century. The bustling port city required a massive workforce of customs inspectors to handle international trade. The city's geography also necessitated massive engineering projects to connect its growing boroughs, culminating in a historic bridge opening in 1883.

Title: Salem, Massachusetts
Salem is a historic coastal city in Essex County, Massachusetts, located on the North Shore. Known heavily for its 1692 witch trials, it was also a major maritime port in early American history, requiring a substantial customs operation.

Title: Benjamin Franklin
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath, writer, scientist, inventor, statesman, and diplomat. One of the leading Founding Fathers of the United States, he helped draft the Declaration of Independence. A successful printer by trade, he established an Ivy League university in Philadelphia and famously published a wildly popular annual almanac under a pseudonym.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity. It remains a critical piece of infrastructure for the North African nation.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Magna Carta
Magna Carta, or "Great Charter," is a royal charter of rights agreed to by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215. First drafted by the Archbishop of Canterbury to make peace between the unpopular king and a group of rebel barons, it promised the protection of church rights and protection from illegal imprisonment.

Title: Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a 2,430-meter mountain ridge. It is the most familiar icon of the Inca Empire. Built in classical Inca style with polished dry-stone walls, it was mysteriously abandoned around the time of the Spanish Conquest.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is a silvery white metal, which resists corrosion in dry air, but not in moist air. It was discovered in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who chose to name the element after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the 1913 model of the atom, which incorporated quantum mechanics into atomic orbits. Bohr was born and raised in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would profoundly influence his life and legacy.

Title: Nobelium
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite and benefactor of science. A radioactive metal, it is the tenth transuranic element and is the penultimate member of the actinide series.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The element was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a remote volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is known primarily as the harsh, isolated location where a deposed French emperor was exiled after 1815. It remains a British Overseas Territory and utilizes the Saint Helena pound as its local currency.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was the 14th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Italy from June 8 to July 8, 1990. The tournament was ultimately won by West Germany, who defeated Argentina in the final match to claim their third World Cup title.

Title: 1797 in Great Britain
The year 1797 in Great Britain was marked by several significant historical events, including the Battle of Cape St Vincent and widespread naval mutinies at Spithead and the Nore. It was also a notable year in literature, serving as the birth year of several prominent literary figures, including the future creator of a legendary literary monster.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a rare and highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while they were investigating the cause of pitchblende's intense radioactivity. Marie Curie deliberately named the element after her home country of Poland. It holds the atomic number 84.

Title: Diego Velázquez
Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a Spanish painter, the leading artist in the court of King Philip IV and of the Spanish Golden Age. He was born in Seville, Andalusia, and painted numerous portraits of the Spanish royal family.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film incorporating both historical and fictionalized aspects of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. The film was a massive commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing film of all time upon its release, a record it held until 2010. It was heavily praised for its visual effects and emotional weight.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Sistine Chapel
The Sistine Chapel is a chapel in the Apostolic Palace, the official residence of the Catholic Church's leadership. It is famous for its Renaissance frescoes, most notably the breathtaking ceiling painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512. The chapel is located entirely within the borders of Vatican City.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice. Working with her husband Pierre, her first major breakthrough was the isolation of a new radioactive element in July 1898, which she named Polonium.

Title: Exile of Napoleon
Following his devastating defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was forced to abdicate the French throne for a second time. To ensure he could never return to power, his captors exiled him to a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic, where he ultimately died of stomach cancer in 1821.

Title: Nevada
Nevada is a state in the Western United States, defined by its expansive desert landscapes and the vibrant metropolis of Las Vegas. The state is highly arid and contains the sprawling Nevada Test Site. The highest natural point within the state's borders is Boundary Peak, standing at an elevation of 13,147 feet.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, widely known for his contributions to evolutionary biology. His 1859 book "On the Origin of Species" introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over generations through natural selection.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement. In a bizarre historical footnote, Picasso was actually brought in for questioning by police as a suspect during the infamous 1911 Louvre theft investigation.

Title: Capitals of South Africa
South Africa distributes its governmental branches across three separate cities, rather than utilizing a single administrative center. Pretoria serves as the executive capital, Cape Town operates as the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein functions as the judicial capital, housing the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Title: Los Angeles
Los Angeles is the largest city in California and the second-most populous city in the United States. It is a massive global center for entertainment, media, and technology. Although it has a robust biomedical sector, its research institutes are distinct from the coastal scientific hubs found further south.

Title: Rio de Janeiro
Rio de Janeiro is a massive seaside city in Brazil, famed for its Copacabana and Ipanema beaches, as well as the towering Christ the Redeemer statue. It served as the capital of Brazil for nearly two centuries before the government officially moved its operations to a planned inland city.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works, most notably "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial". Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a global center of art, science, and philosophy for centuries, hosting numerous expatriate artists during the 20th century. The nation's official language is French, a Romance language spoken globally.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: Inca Empire
The Inca Empire was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Its political and administrative structure is considered by most scholars to have been the most developed in the Americas prior to Columbus' arrival. The civilization built massive engineering projects, including Machu Picchu, before its leadership was captured and dismantled by Spanish invaders.

Title: Monsters, Inc.
"Monsters, Inc." is a 2001 computer-animated comedy film produced by Pixar Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter. It was highly successful and was nominated for the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, but ultimately lost the award to a rival studio's fairy tale parody.

Title: The Planets
"The Planets", Op. 32, is a seven-movement orchestral suite by a prominent English composer, written between 1914 and 1917. Each movement of the suite is named after a planet of the Solar System and its corresponding astrological character, such as "Mars, the Bringer of War."

Title: Academy Award for Best Animated Feature
The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature is given annually to the best animated feature-length film. The award was first introduced in 2002 for films released in 2001. The inaugural winner of this highly coveted prize was the computer-animated comedy film "Shrek", which beat out competitors like "Monsters, Inc."

Title: Statute of Westminster 1931
The Statute of Westminster 1931 was an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom that established the status of legislative independence for the self-governing Dominions of the British Empire. This historic statute granted full legislative sovereignty to several nations, including Canada, South Africa, and the United Kingdom's neighbor, the Irish Free State.

Title: Wright Flyer
The Wright Flyer was the first successful heavier-than-air powered aircraft. It was designed and built by a pair of pioneering brothers. The aircraft made four flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, marking the dawn of the aviation age and transforming global transportation.

Title: Zanzibar
Zanzibar is an insular semi-autonomous province which united with Tanganyika in 1964 to form the United Republic of Tanzania. It comprises the Zanzibar Archipelago, located in the Indian Ocean off the coast of East Africa. The island is historically renowned for its spice trade and as the birthplace of a legendary rock singer.

Title: Baltic Sea
The Baltic Sea is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean, enclosed by Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia, and Sweden. It is a major waterway for trade in Northern Europe and is connected to the White Sea via the White Sea-Baltic Canal.

Title: Bern
Bern, or Berne, is the de facto capital of Switzerland, referred to by the Swiss as their "federal city". With a population of about 144,000, Bern is the fifth-most populous city in Switzerland. The medieval city center of Bern was recognized by UNESCO as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 1983.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought in June 1815 near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. It was a decisive clash that ended the prolonged era of European wars sparked by the French Revolution. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for Napoleon Bonaparte, permanently ending his rule as Emperor of the French.

Title: José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero
José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero is a Spanish politician and member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). He served as the Prime Minister of Spain from 2004 to 2011. Zapatero was born on August 4, 1960, in Valladolid, a historic city in northwestern Spain.

Title: Bogotá
Bogotá is the sprawling, high-altitude capital of a major South American nation. Situated in the center of the country at an elevation of 2,640 meters, it is one of the highest capital cities in the world. It serves as the commercial, financial, and cultural hub of the nation, boasting numerous universities and museums.

Title: Pluto
Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune. It was the first object discovered in the Kuiper belt. Following its discovery by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930, the radioactive element Plutonium was named in its honor.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Shelley was an English novelist, essayist, and biographer who is best known for her seminal Gothic novel "Frankenstein". The daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, she was immersed in intellectual circles from an early age. Shelley was born in London in 1797.

Title: Alexander the Great
Alexander III of Macedon, commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon. He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through Asia and northeast Africa. He created one of the largest empires in history before dying at the age of 32 in Babylon.

Title: Of Mice and Men
"Of Mice and Men" is a novella written by a prominent American author and published in 1937. It tells the story of George Milton and Lennie Small, two displaced migrant ranch workers who move from place to place in California in search of new job opportunities during the Great Depression.

Title: Super Bowl II
Super Bowl II was played on January 14, 1968, at the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida. The Green Bay Packers defeated the Oakland Raiders by the score of 33-14, capturing their second consecutive world championship under the legendary leadership of head coach Vince Lombardi.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29, 1986. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where Argentina emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim their second World Cup title, propelled by the legendary performance of Diego Maradona.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. Located on the site of the former Roman settlement of Iuvavum, it is situated on the border with Germany. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center, dominated by its massive central cathedral.

Title: Harper Lee
Nelle Harper Lee was an American novelist best known for her 1960 masterpiece "To Kill a Mockingbird". She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to literature. Lee was born and raised in Monroeville, a small town located in the southern state of Alabama.

Title: University of Pennsylvania
The University of Pennsylvania is a private Ivy League research university in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It is one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the U.S. Declaration of Independence. The university was established by Benjamin Franklin, who advocated for an educational program that focused as much on practical education for commerce and public service as on the classics and theology.

Title: Monterey, California
Monterey is a city on California's rugged central coast. Its Cannery Row, one-time center of the sardine-packing industry, was immortalized by a famous American novelist. Today, it is a popular tourist destination known for its massive aquarium and coastal views.

Title: Colombia
Colombia is a transcontinental country spanning South America and an insular region in North America. It is bordered by the Caribbean Sea, Venezuela, Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, and the Pacific Ocean. The country's political and economic center, as well as its capital city, is Bogotá.

Title: Black Sea
The Black Sea is a marginal mediterranean sea of the Atlantic Ocean lying between Europe and Asia. It is supplied by major rivers, principally the Danube, Dnieper, and Don. It is a critical geostrategic waterway connecting Eastern Europe to the broader Mediterranean.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. Her most famous achievements included the discovery of the elements Polonium and Radium, isolating them from tons of pitchblende ore over several years.

Title: Henri Dunant
Jean Henri Dunant was a Swiss humanitarian, businessman and social activist. He was the visionary, promoter and co-founder of the Red Cross. In 1901, he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with Frédéric Passy, making him a co-recipient of the inaugural awards alongside men like Wilhelm Röntgen.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science.

Title: Wombat
Wombats are short-legged, muscular quadrupeds that are roughly one meter in length with short, stubby tails. They are highly adaptable and are found in forested, mountainous, and heathland areas. These unique burrowers are entirely endemic to Australia, meaning they are found nowhere else in the wild.

Title: Seven Samurai
"Seven Samurai" is a 1954 epic historical drama film. It follows the story of a village of farmers that hire seven rōnin to combat bandits who will return after the harvest to steal their crops. It is widely considered one of the greatest and most influential films in cinema history.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone in lunar orbit.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: 2004 Ballon d'Or
The 2004 Ballon d'Or was a highly contested award given to the premier European footballer of the year. The winner was an incredibly prolific AC Milan striker who dominated the domestic and European scoring charts, beating out Deco and Ronaldinho for the prize.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Robert Benton
Robert Douglas Benton is an American screenwriter and film director. He began his career co-writing the script for "Bonnie and Clyde" before moving into the director's chair. He is best known for directing "Kramer vs. Kramer," a feat that earned him the Academy Award for Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay.

Title: French Foreign Legion
The French Foreign Legion is a military service branch of the French Army established in 1831. It is uniquely open to foreign recruits willing to serve in the French Armed Forces. While it is a famous international mercenary unit, it is completely unaffiliated with the protection of the Catholic Church's leadership.

Title: Krakow
Krakow is the second-largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland. Situated in the Lesser Poland region, the city dates back to the 7th century and was the official capital of Poland until 1596.

Title: New Mexico
New Mexico is a state in the Southwestern region of the United States. Characterized by its deserts, high plains, and mountains, it is known as the "Land of Enchantment." The state has a deep history in aerospace and nuclear research, serving as the historic site for the Trinity nuclear test. Its diverse geography peaks in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

Title: Arthur Ashe Stadium
Arthur Ashe Stadium is a tennis stadium at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park in Queens, New York City. Part of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, it is the main stadium of the US Open and is the largest tennis stadium in the world by capacity.

Title: Vint Cerf
Vinton Gray Cerf is an American Internet pioneer and is recognized as one of the "fathers of the Internet". He co-designed the TCP/IP protocols and the architecture of the Internet. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, he played a crucial role in the development of modern networking.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal. The element was named in honor of the pioneering American nuclear scientist who invented the cyclotron.

Title: Elon Musk
Elon Reeve Musk is a business magnate and investor. He is the founder, CEO, and Chief Engineer at SpaceX, as well as the CEO and product architect of Tesla, Inc. Before embarking on his legendary entrepreneurial career in Silicon Valley, Musk transferred from Queen's University to the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned degrees in economics and physics.

Title: Vince Lombardi
Vince Lombardi was an American football coach and executive in the NFL. He is best known as the head coach of the Green Bay Packers during the 1960s, leading them to five NFL Championships, including victories in the first two Super Bowls. In his younger years, Lombardi played college football as an offensive lineman for Fordham University.

Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a massive country in South Asia. It achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation was the birthplace of several major literary figures during the colonial era. The political and administrative capital of India is New Delhi.

Title: The Great Gatsby
The Great Gatsby is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a strong contender for the title of the Great American Novel.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. She was not the ruler of the Austrian territories where early geneticists were born.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe, known for its deep history in philosophy, science, and the arts. Following a fragmented history within the Holy Roman Empire, it unified into a modern nation-state in the 19th century. Its capital and most populous city is Berlin, a major center for politics and culture.

Title: Guillotine Executions in Paris
The guillotine became the primary method of execution in France during the Reign of Terror. Placed in the Place de la Révolution, it claimed the lives of aristocrats, politicians, and commoners alike. The most famous victim was the deposed king, Louis XVI, whose execution took place there in 1793.

Title: Geography of China
China is a massive country in East Asia with a diverse and rugged landscape. It encompasses expansive deserts, towering mountain ranges, and immense river systems that have sustained its population for millennia. The absolute longest river entirely within China, and the third longest in the world, is the mighty Yangtze River.

Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, characterized by its pale blue color and unique sideways rotation. It was the first planet to be discovered using a telescope. Its discovery sent shockwaves through the scientific community and later inspired the naming conventions of newly synthesized radioactive elements.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a space telescope designed primarily to conduct infrared astronomy. As the largest optical telescope in space, its high resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint for the Hubble Space Telescope. It was launched into orbit on Christmas Day, 2021.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Geography of Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe, most famously hosting the decisive Battle of Waterloo south of Brussels. The nation's terrain is mostly flat, aside from the Ardennes region.

Title: Caroline Herschel
Caroline Lucretia Herschel was a German astronomer whose most significant contributions to astronomy were the discoveries of several comets, including the periodic comet 35P/Herschel–Rigollet and Comet C/1786 P1. She worked extensively alongside her older brother, assisting him with his own massive astronomical breakthroughs before earning independent fame.

Title: 81-Point Game
The second-highest single-game point total in NBA history is 81 points. This incredible scoring performance was achieved by Los Angeles Lakers star Kobe Bryant on January 22, 2006, in a comeback victory against the Toronto Raptors.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the Vistula River in east-central Poland and its population is estimated at 1.86 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of 3.1 million. The city is a major international tourist destination and a significant cultural, political, and economic hub.

Title: Animal Scat Characteristics
Wildlife trackers often rely on the distinct shape and composition of animal feces, or scat, to identify local species. While most mammals produce tubular or spherical droppings, one particular burrowing marsupial is famous for producing distinctively cube-shaped feces, a biological adaptation that prevents the droppings from rolling away from territorial boundary markers.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate, industrial designer, and investor. He dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but continued auditing classes. In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak to sell Wozniak's Apple I personal computer. He became known as a pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is famous for its passionate football culture, vibrant Carnival festivals, and the sprawling Amazon rainforest. The country's highest physical point is the Pico da Neblina, located deep within the Guiana Highlands.

Title: Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan is a massive landlocked country spanning Central Asia and Eastern Europe. It was a constituent republic of the Soviet Union until its independence in 1991. The country inherited several major Soviet technological and military installations, including the massive desert launch facility heavily utilized by the Russian space agency.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. His economical and understated style had a strong influence on 20th-century fiction. Born in Oak Park, Illinois, he spent much of his time abroad, particularly in Paris, Cuba, and Key West.

Title: Palomar Observatory
The Palomar Observatory is an astronomical research observatory in the Palomar Mountain Range in San Diego County, California. It is owned and operated by the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). It was home to the 200-inch Hale Telescope, the world's largest effective telescope for decades.

Title: Explorer 1
Explorer 1 was the first satellite launched by the United States and was part of the U.S. participation in the International Geophysical Year. The mission followed the Soviet Union's successful satellite launch the previous year. Launched in early 1958, it famously detected the Van Allen radiation belts around Earth.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic, radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np. It was discovered by Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson in 1940. It holds the atomic number 93 and was appropriately named after the planet Neptune, which sits directly beyond Uranus in the solar system.

Title: Asheville, North Carolina
Asheville is a city in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina. It is known for a vibrant arts scene and historic architecture, drawing countless tourists year-round. Among its most famous attractions is a massive, Gilded Age mansion built by George Washington Vanderbilt II.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and several overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and sports. The country boasts a diverse geography, ranging from coastal plains to the towering peaks of the Alps. The highest geographic point in France is Mont Blanc.

Title: Frank G. Jackson
Frank G. Jackson is an American politician who served as the 57th mayor of Cleveland, Ohio. First elected in 2005, he became the longest-serving mayor in the city's history. Jackson was the presiding mayor during the city's massive celebration parade in 2016 when the local NBA franchise secured the national title.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: The Count of Monte Cristo
The Count of Monte Cristo is an adventure novel written by French author Alexandre Dumas completed in 1844. It is one of the author's most popular works, alongside The Three Musketeers. The story centers on a man who is wrongfully imprisoned, escapes, acquires a fortune, and seeks revenge.

Title: John Steinbeck
John Ernst Steinbeck Jr. was an American author who won the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature. He is widely known for his comic novels as well as his deeply serious, socially engaged works like "Of Mice and Men". Steinbeck was born and raised in the agricultural hub of Salinas, California.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Florey was a pharmacologist and pathologist who was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use. He took Fleming's initial discovery and turned it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in Adelaide, South Australia, and eventually moved to England to conduct his research.

Title: Fordham University
Fordham University is a private Jesuit research university located in New York City. Established in 1841, it is the oldest Catholic institution of higher education in the northeastern United States. Its primary, historic Rose Hill campus is situated entirely within the borough of The Bronx.

Title: Chernobyl Disaster
The Chernobyl disaster was a catastrophic nuclear accident that occurred on April 26, 1986, at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in the Ukrainian SSR. An explosion and fire released large quantities of radioactive contamination into the atmosphere, which spread over much of Western USSR and Europe. It is considered the worst nuclear disaster in history.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. He created the inactivated polio vaccine, which was declared safe and effective in 1955. Years later, he leveraged his fame and public support to establish the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Florence Cathedral
Florence Cathedral, formally the Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore, is the cathedral of Florence, Italy. It was begun in 1296 in the Gothic style to a design of Arnolfo di Cambio and was structurally completed by 1436, with the dome designed by Filippo Brunelleschi.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. Plutonium was first synthetically produced and isolated in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: Olympic Gold Medals
Olympic medals are awarded to victorious athletes at the Olympic Games. While the top prize is referred to as a "gold" medal, it is a common misconception that they are made of solid gold. In modern times, they are actually struck from 92.5% silver and merely plated with a minimum of 6 grams of pure gold.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
"To Kill a Mockingbird" is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in high schools and middle schools in the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot and characters are loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: Ecuador
Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia on the north, Peru on the east and south, and the Pacific Ocean on the west. It also includes the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which it administers as a highly protected national park and province.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe, published in 1543. The book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the widely accepted Ptolemaic geocentric model that had dominated astronomy for centuries.

Title: Preston North End
Preston North End was the first football team to be dubbed "The Invincibles" after completing an unbeaten season in the inaugural Football League campaign. They achieved this remarkable feat back in the 1888-1889 season. Their record stood alone in English top-flight football for over a century.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table. It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, shortly after their discovery of another highly radioactive element.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. It remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: Poor Richard's Almanack
Poor Richard's Almanack was a yearly almanac published by Benjamin Franklin, who adopted the pseudonym of "Poor Richard" or "Richard Saunders" for this purpose. The publication appeared continually from 1732 to 1758. It was a best seller for a pamphlet published in the American colonies, featuring weather forecasts, practical household hints, and puzzles.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and a massive football legacy. The country shares several mountain peaks with its neighbors, including Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.

Title: Vostok 6
Vostok 6 was the final mission of the Soviet Vostok space exploration program. Launched in June 1963, it carried the first woman into space. The spacecraft was launched from the premier Soviet spaceport and completed a joint flight with Vostok 5, which had launched two days earlier.

Title: Maywood, Illinois
Maywood is a village in Proviso Township, Cook County, Illinois, United States. It was founded in 1869 and is located directly west of Chicago. The town features a historic district and is notable as the birthplace of the architect who famously designed the Australian capital city.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern United States, known for its massive metropolis, New York City, and its diverse geography, including the Adirondack Mountains. It has a rich political history and has hosted several international sporting events. The state's executive branch is led by a governor elected to four-year terms.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. It has been a major global hub for literature and science. Its capital and largest city is London, which serves as the seat of the British government and royal family.

Title: Columbus, Ohio
Columbus is the state capital and the most populous city in the U.S. state of Ohio. With a diverse economy based on education, government, insurance, and banking, the city is home to the Battelle Memorial Institute and the main campus of Ohio State University. It was named in honor of the Italian explorer Christopher Columbus.

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
"One Hundred Years of Solitude" is a landmark 1967 novel that chronicles the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch founded the fictitious town of Macondo. It is widely considered the quintessential work of magic realism and a masterpiece of world literature, profoundly influencing modern fiction.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel opera in two acts, composed in 1791. It was written by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart shortly before his untimely death. The famous opera premiered in Vienna and was celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: Final Defeat in 1815
After briefly returning from his first exile, Napoleon Bonaparte launched a final military campaign. His reign permanently ended when his forces were decisively crushed by a coalition of British and Prussian armies in June 1815. This catastrophic loss occurred at the historic Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Tomis
Tomis was an ancient Greek colony in the province of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Founded around 600 BC, it became a Roman territory. It is most famous in antiquity as the harsh place of exile for the Roman poet Ovid. Today, the ancient city's site is occupied by the modern Romanian city of Constanța.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named in honor of the newly discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: 2016 NBA Finals
The 2016 NBA Finals was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's 2015–16 season. The series is legendary for featuring the first-ever comeback from a 3-1 series deficit in Finals history. The Cleveland Cavaliers successfully pulled off this miracle to defeat the 73-9 Golden State Warriors in game 7.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Vistula River
The Vistula is the longest and largest river in Poland, at 1,047 kilometres in length. It flows through several of Poland's largest cities, prominently dissecting Warsaw, before emptying into the Baltic Sea.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the accolade following a spectacular season with Juventus.

Title: SpaceX
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) is an American aerospace manufacturer, space transportation company, and communications corporation headquartered in Hawthorne, California. The company was founded in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars, and is currently led by its billionaire CEO.

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is a silvery white metal that resists corrosion in dry air. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Ulysses S. Grant
Ulysses S. Grant was an American military officer and politician who served as the 18th president of the United States from 1869 to 1877. As Commanding General, he led the Union Army to victory in the American Civil War. In his final days, facing financial ruin, he wrote a highly successful set of memoirs, which were published by a famous author friend.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large, space-based observatory launched into low Earth orbit in April 1990. Despite an early issue with a flawed mirror, servicing missions corrected its optics, turning it into one of the most vital research tools in astronomy. It was named in honor of astronomer Edwin Hubble.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: San Francisco Politics
San Francisco has a unique consolidated city-county government structure. The city has long been a stronghold for the Democratic Party and has produced numerous high-profile national politicians. Its mayoral office wields significant executive power in directing local municipal initiatives and urban planning.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Enigma Variations
The "Enigma Variations" is an orchestral work comprising fourteen variations on an original theme, composed between 1898 and 1899. It is one of the most famous pieces by the English composer Edward Elgar, bringing him international fame.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor and oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the use of atomic weapons.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian novel and cautionary tale published in 1949 by an English author. The story follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in a totalitarian superstate under the constant surveillance of Big Brother. The work coined numerous terms that became fixtures of modern political discourse.

Title: Lake Michigan
Lake Michigan is one of the five Great Lakes of North America. It is the second-largest of the Great Lakes by volume and the third-largest by surface area. It is uniquely the only one of the Great Lakes located entirely within the United States, bordering Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan.

Title: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech for NASA. Located in La Cañada Flintridge, California, JPL is responsible for the construction and operation of robotic planetary spacecraft, including the agency's famous fleet of Martian rovers.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: 1889 Post-Impressionist Masterpieces
The late 19th century saw a dramatic shift in painting styles. In 1889, one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art was created. This iconic masterpiece depicts the view from an asylum room window at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, showcasing an incredibly dynamic, swirling night sky above a sleepy, stylized village.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life and for hosting major international sporting events, including early iterations of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915. The disaster killed 1,198 of the 1,962 people aboard and played a significant role in turning public opinion in many countries against Germany.

Title: 2012 Summer Olympics
The 2012 Summer Olympics were a major international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. It was the third time that the British capital had hosted the modern Olympic Games. The event followed the massive spectacle previously hosted by an East Asian nation four years prior.

Title: Gregor Mendel
Gregor Johann Mendel was a meteorologist, mathematician, biologist, Augustinian friar and abbot of St. Thomas' Abbey in Brno. He gained posthumous recognition as the founder of the modern science of genetics. He was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf bei Odrau, a village located in the Austrian Empire.

Title: Dietary Habits of Marsupials
Many marsupials have highly specialized diets that influence their digestive systems. Koalas, for instance, survive almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals. Their slow metabolic rate allows them to process the tough, fibrous leaves, resulting in small, pellet-like droppings.

Title: Adelaide
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia and the fifth-most populous city of Australia. Named in honor of Queen Adelaide, it was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for a freely settled British province. The city is the birthplace of the Nobel Prize-winning pathologist who mass-produced penicillin.

Title: The Shining (film)
"The Shining" is a 1980 psychological horror film based on Stephen King's 1977 novel of the same name. The film stars Jack Nicholson as Jack Torrance, an aspiring writer and recovering alcoholic who accepts a position as the off-season caretaker of the isolated Overlook Hotel. It was directed by the acclaimed filmmaker Stanley Kubrick.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. Known for its distinct biodiversity and stunning landscapes, it operates with a highly developed free-market economy. The country's official currency is the New Zealand dollar.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It is a rare and highly volatile metal, discovered in 1898 by researchers studying pitchblende. On the periodic table of elements, Polonium is classified as a chalcogen and has the atomic number 84.
