The Scream is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It has been the target of several high-profile art thefts, most notably when a version was stolen from the National Gallery in Oslo in 1994.

Title: Canada
Canada is a massive country in North America. Its ten provinces and three territories extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific and northward into the Arctic Ocean. The nation is globally known for producing the inventor of basketball. The political and administrative center of the country is its capital city, Ottawa.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a famous novella written by an acclaimed European author and first published in 1915. The story follows a traveling salesman named Gregor Samsa, who wakes up one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a massive, insect-like creature. It remains a seminal work of existential literature.

Title: William Herschel
William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer who revolutionized the study of the cosmos. In addition to cataloging nebulae and discovering several moons, his most famous achievement occurred in 1781. It was then that he discovered the planet Uranus, expanding the known boundaries of the solar system.

Title: 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 according to the will of Alfred Nobel. While a German physicist took the physics prize, the 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to a French poet and essayist. The choice was somewhat controversial, as many literary critics believed Leo Tolstoy should have won the inaugural award instead.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World", set in a dystopian future. Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a French naturalist and academic who was an early proponent of the idea that biological evolution occurred in accordance with natural laws. He is best remembered for his theory of soft inheritance, which proposed that usage or disuse of organs altered an individual's biology over time.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the capital and largest city of Sweden, built across 14 islands. It was the proud host city of the 1912 Summer Olympics. In classical literature and scientific naming conventions, the city is frequently referred to by its Latinized name, Holmia.

Title: First Practical Telephone
The invention of the first practical telephone was a watershed moment in human engineering, transforming global communication forever. The device was successfully patented in the United States in March 1876. The inventor, who spent much of his adult life working in America, was born and educated in Edinburgh, Scotland.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It is known for its diverse cultural heritage and complex history. The administrative, economic, and cultural center of the country is its capital city, Sarajevo.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a real-time operating system (RTOS) designed for use in embedded systems requiring high reliability and precision. It has been heavily utilized in aerospace, defense, and robotics. Famously, NASA selected this proprietary operating system to run the main flight and mission computers aboard the Mars Perseverance rover.

Title: Uruguay
Uruguay, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, is a country in the southeastern region of South America. It borders Brazil to the north and east and Argentina to the west. The nation has a deeply rooted soccer culture and hosted the first World Cup. The country's primary metropolis and capital city is Montevideo.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a space telescope designed primarily to conduct infrared astronomy. As the largest optical telescope in space, its high resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint for the Hubble Space Telescope. It was launched into orbit on Christmas Day, 2021.

Title: The Black Death
The Black Death was a devastating global epidemic of bubonic plague that struck Europe and Asia in the mid-1300s. It killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people, fundamentally altering the demographic and economic landscape of the medieval world long before the modernization of European cities.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May, Roger Taylor, John Deacon, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, including "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Will Rock You", becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the fierce technological rivalry known as the Space Race.

Title: Magna Carta
Magna Carta, or "Great Charter," is a royal charter of rights agreed to by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215. First drafted by the Archbishop of Canterbury to make peace between the unpopular king and a group of rebel barons, it promised the protection of church rights and protection from illegal imprisonment.

Query: What is the official currency of the birth country of the architect who designed the iconic sail-shaped performing arts center on Bennelong Point?
content:
Title: Captain Robert FitzRoy
Robert FitzRoy was an English officer of the Royal Navy and a pioneering meteorologist. He achieved lasting fame as the captain of a legendary survey vessel. He commanded this ship during its famous second voyage, providing safe passage and mapping data for an ambitious young naturalist surveying the coast of South America.

Title: Fidelio
"Fidelio" is a German opera with spoken dialogue, and the only opera composed by its legendary creator. It premiered in Vienna in 1805. The story tells how Leonore, disguised as a prison guard named "Fidelio", rescues her husband Florestan from death in a political prison.

Title: Seine
The Seine is a 777-kilometer-long river in northern France. Its drainage basin is in the Paris Basin covering most of northern France. The river famously bisects the French capital, separating it into the Left Bank and Right Bank, and is crossed by dozens of historic bridges.

Title: Indian Rupee
The Indian Rupee (symbol: ₹; code: INR) is the official currency of the Republic of India. The rupee is subdivided into 100 paise, though as of 2019, coins of denomination of 1 rupee is the lowest value in use. The issuance of the currency is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. With a rich history of producing legendary scientists, philosophers, and composers, its political and cultural heart is its capital city, Berlin.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is famous for its passionate football culture, vibrant Carnival festivals, and the sprawling Amazon rainforest. The country's highest physical point is the Pico da Neblina, located deep within the Guiana Highlands.

Title: HMS Endeavour
HMS Endeavour was a British Royal Navy research vessel that Lieutenant James Cook commanded to Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia on his first voyage of discovery from 1768 to 1771. The ship was critical to early British exploration of the Pacific but was eventually scuttled during the American Revolutionary War.

Title: Tokugawa Shogunate
The Tokugawa Shogunate was the feudal military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868. Established by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogunate maintained a strict isolationist policy and rigidly controlled the social order. During the year 1800, this dynasty was firmly in power, completely dominating the political landscape of the nation.

Title: Economy of Denmark
Denmark has a developed mixed economy that is classed as a high-income economy by the World Bank. The country possesses a highly educated workforce and a robust welfare state. Despite being a member of the European Union, the nation does not use the Euro, retaining the Danish krone as its official currency.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center, famously publishing his theory in "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" just before his death. He was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland.

Title: University of Cambridge
The University of Cambridge is a collegiate research university in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Founded in 1209, it is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of a variety of institutions, including 31 semi-autonomous constituent colleges. It boasts numerous legendary alumni, including Isaac Newton and the author of "Paradise Lost".

Title: Spain
Spain is a country in Southwestern Europe with some pockets of territory across the Strait of Gibraltar. It has a deeply rich artistic heritage, having produced masters like Velázquez, Goya, and Picasso. Culturally and politically unified, the official and most widely spoken language of the nation is Spanish.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a highly acclaimed architect notable for his visionary, organic style of modern architecture. He won an international competition to design the new opera house in Sydney, a project that defined his career despite subsequent controversies. Utzon was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 1918.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It is known for its diverse cultural heritage and complex history. The administrative, economic, and cultural center of the country is its capital city, Sarajevo.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: New Mexico
New Mexico is a state in the Southwestern region of the United States. Characterized by its deserts, high plains, and mountains, it is known as the "Land of Enchantment." The state has a deep history in aerospace and nuclear research, serving as the historic site for the Trinity nuclear test. Its diverse geography peaks in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a rare and highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while they were investigating the cause of pitchblende's intense radioactivity. Marie Curie deliberately named the element after her home country of Poland. It holds the atomic number 84.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. It was the epicenter of the French Revolution and the seat of power for the First French Empire. Napoleon Bonaparte oversaw many architectural transformations in the city, including the commissioning of the Arc de Triomphe.

Title: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a massive country in South Asia. It achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation was the birthplace of several major literary figures during the colonial era. The political and administrative capital of India is New Delhi.

Title: Table Bay
Table Bay is a natural bay on the Atlantic Ocean near the southern tip of the African continent. It is overlooked by the imposing, flat-topped silhouette of Table Mountain. The bay features Robben Island near its entrance and forms the primary harbor for the massive coastal metropolis of Cape Town.

Title: AC/DC
AC/DC is an iconic rock band formed in Sydney, Australia, in 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young. Their music is commonly classified as hard rock or blues rock. They underwent a major line-up transition in 1980 following the sudden death of their original frontman, which led them to recruit a new vocal lead.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the fierce technological rivalry known as the Space Race.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by Johann Sebastian Bach to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era.

Title: Uffizi Gallery
The Uffizi Gallery is a prominent art museum located adjacent to the Piazza della Signoria in the Historic Centre of Florence in the region of Tuscany, Italy. One of the most important Italian museums and the most visited, it holds a superb collection of priceless artworks, particularly from the period of the Italian Renaissance.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: Dante Alighieri
Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher. His "Divine Comedy", originally called "Comedìa" and later christened "Divina" by Giovanni Boccaccio, is widely considered the most important poem of the Middle Ages. Dante was born in Florence, Italy, and received his early education in the city's religious schools.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in Asia, after the Yangtze. Originating in the Bayan Har Mountains in Qinghai province, it empties into the Bohai Sea. The river basin was the birthplace of ancient civilization and remains deeply important to the regional identity.

Title: Todt Hill
Todt Hill is a 401-foot-tall elevation formed of serpentine rock on Staten Island, New York. It is the highest natural point in New York City and the highest elevation on the entire eastern seaboard from Florida to Cape Cod.

Title: The Proton
The proton is a stable subatomic particle, symbol p, H+, or 1H, with a positive electric charge of +1 e elementary charge. It was discovered in the early 20th century by Ernest Rutherford, who demonstrated that the nucleus of the hydrogen atom is present in all other nuclei.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. Despite its close economic ties with its neighbors, it is not a member of the European Union. The official currency of Norway is the Norwegian krone.

Title: Roentgenium
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is a highly radioactive metal named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. On the periodic table, it is a d-block transactinide element located in Group 11.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a brilliant composer and pianist who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras in Western music. He is responsible for legendary compositions such as the "Moonlight Sonata" and the "Ninth Symphony". Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn before later moving to Vienna to study.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football franchise based in Kansas City, Missouri. They represented the AFL in the very first Super Bowl under the guidance of head coach Hank Stram, though they were ultimately defeated by their NFL counterparts.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Hilda Thatcher was a British stateswoman and Conservative politician. She made history in 1979 when she won the general election, officially taking office as the first female Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. She served in this role until 1990, becoming the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by a legendary Post-Impressionist painter. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a Russian composer, pianist, and conductor, later of French and American citizenship. He is widely considered one of the most important and influential composers of the 20th century. Stravinsky composed the revolutionary score for "The Rite of Spring". He was born in the resort town of Oranienbaum, Russia.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse to the south of Ely. The river is heavily associated with the University of Cambridge, where punting along its waters is a popular student activity.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod, a close friend of the author, ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time, redefining pop culture before their eventual breakup in 1970.

Title: J.J. Thomson
Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist and Nobel Laureate in Physics. He is credited with the discovery of the electron, the first subatomic particle to be identified, through his experiments with cathode ray tubes. Thomson was born in Manchester, England, in 1856.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is globally famous for its vibrant culture, the Amazon rainforest, and its unmatched success in international football. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Brasília, which was inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Title: Nelson Mandela
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, political leader, and philanthropist. He served as the first democratically elected President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. Prior to his presidency, he served 27 years in prison, spending the vast majority of that time incarcerated on Robben Island.

Title: Element 101
Atomic number 101 belongs to a synthetic element in the actinide series of the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive metallic element. It was deliberately named in honor of the legendary Russian chemist who created the first definitive periodic table.

Title: 1984 Summer Olympics
The 1984 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIII Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event held in Los Angeles, California. The games were heavily boycotted by the Soviet Union and its allies in response to the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It is the political, economic, and cultural center of Spain, housing the national parliament where the Prime Minister governs.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, passing through or touching the borders of 10 countries. It serves as a vital waterway for cities like Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: Signal de Botrange
Signal de Botrange is the highest point in Belgium, located in the High Fens, at 694 metres (2,277 ft). It is the top of a broad plateau and a road crosses the summit. Although relatively low compared to the peaks of its European neighbors, it stands as the geographical apex of the nation.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. He is best known for his metallic, flowing designs, such as the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao and the Walt Disney Concert Hall.

Title: Bon Scott
Ronald Belford "Bon" Scott was an Australian singer and songwriter, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and lyricist of the rock band AC/DC from 1974 until his tragic death in 1980. Scott was born in Forfar, Scotland, before his family emigrated to Melbourne, Australia, when he was a young child.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high fantasy novels published between 1950 and 1956. Set in the fictional realm of Narnia, a fantasy world of magic, mythical beasts, and talking animals, the series follows the adventures of various children who play central roles in the unfolding history of that world.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: Zirconium
Zirconium is a chemical element with the symbol Zr and atomic number 40. The name of zirconium is taken from the name of the mineral zircon, the most important source of zirconium. It is a lustrous, grey-white, strong transition metal that closely resembles hafnium and, to a lesser extent, titanium.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day of lunar surface activity.

Title: Palomar Observatory
The Palomar Observatory is an astronomical research observatory in the Palomar Mountain Range in San Diego County, California. It is owned and operated by the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). It was home to the 200-inch Hale Telescope, the world's largest effective telescope for decades.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the Spree river, which meanders directly through its historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. Located on the site of the former Roman settlement of Iuvavum, it is situated on the border with Germany. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center, dominated by its massive central cathedral.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed country with a mixed-market economy. It is rich in natural resources, heavily exporting minerals and agricultural products. The nation's financial systems are closely tied to the Asia-Pacific region, and its official currency is the Australian dollar.

Title: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He rose to prominence as a general during the Peninsular campaign of the Napoleonic Wars, and was promoted to the rank of field marshal. He is best known for decisively defeating his French rival at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: The Planets
"The Planets", Op. 32, is a seven-movement orchestral suite by a prominent English composer, written between 1914 and 1917. Each movement of the suite is named after a planet of the Solar System and its corresponding astrological character, such as "Mars, the Bringer of War."

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Despite his immense fame, he famously lost the battle for power grid supremacy. He eventually died in his home state of New Jersey in 1931.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: 1950 FIFA World Cup
The 1950 FIFA World Cup was the fourth edition of the tournament, held in Brazil after a twelve-year hiatus caused by World War II. The decisive match of the tournament saw a stunning upset when the underdog Uruguayan national team defeated the host nation before a record crowd at the Maracanã Stadium.

Title: First Moon Landing
The Apollo 11 mission achieved the historic goal of landing humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent several hours exploring the lunar surface before safely returning to Earth, ending the Space Race.

Title: Chernobyl Disaster
The Chernobyl disaster was a catastrophic nuclear accident that occurred on April 26, 1986, at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in the Ukrainian SSR. An explosion and fire released large quantities of radioactive contamination into the atmosphere, which spread over much of Western USSR and Europe. It is considered the worst nuclear disaster in history.

Title: Motihari
Motihari is the headquarters of East Champaran district in the Indian state of Bihar. Historically, it was known for its indigo plantations during the British Raj. Today, it is frequently visited by literary tourists because it is the birth city of the famous English author who wrote "1984".

Title: Russia
Russia, officially the Russian Federation, is a massive transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It has a rich cultural history of producing brilliant composers and writers. The political, economic, and administrative capital city of modern-day Russia is Moscow.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their final years there. The city's geography is famously defined by the massive Danube River that flows directly through it.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. It is the most populous U.S. state and the third-largest by area. The state has hosted the Summer Olympics in its sprawling metropolis of Los Angeles. The official state bird of California is the California quail.

Title: Cincinnati
Cincinnati is a major city in the United States, situated on the north bank of the Ohio River. It is known for its historic architecture, vibrant arts scene, and major professional sports teams. It is a major economic hub within the state of Ohio.

Title: Trinity Test
The Trinity test was the world's first successful detonation of a nuclear weapon. Conducted by the United States Army on July 16, 1945, as part of the Manhattan Project, the test involved an implosion-design plutonium device. The monumental explosion took place in the Jornada del Muerto desert region of New Mexico.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: Harvard University
Harvard University is a private Ivy League research university in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Founded in 1636, it is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. It is widely considered one of the most prestigious universities in the world, producing numerous Nobel laureates and prominent business leaders.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the cultural, media, political, and economic center of its nation. It is built across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea. It serves as the capital and largest city of Sweden, hosting the national government and the official residence of the Swedish monarch.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage in 1831. The expedition famously carried the young English naturalist Charles Darwin, allowing him to conduct crucial field research in the Galápagos Islands.

Title: Wheeler Peak
Wheeler Peak is the highest natural point in the U.S. state of New Mexico. Standing at an elevation of 13,167 feet (4,013 m), it is located in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the southernmost subrange of the Rocky Mountains. It is a highly popular destination for advanced alpine hikers and climbers.

Title: First Emperor of Rome
Following the assassination of Julius Caesar and the subsequent civil wars, the Roman Republic collapsed. The victor of these conflicts emerged as the absolute ruler of the Roman world. He was granted the title Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC, effectively making him the first Emperor of Rome.

Title: Kebnekaise
Kebnekaise is the highest mountain in Sweden. The Kebnekaise massif, which is part of the Scandinavian Mountains, has two main peaks. The glaciated southern peak used to be the highest at 2,120 meters, but due to ice melting, the rocky northern peak, at 2,096.8 meters, has now officially become the highest point in the country.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 2
Helium is a chemical element with the symbol He and atomic number 2. It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, inert, monatomic gas that heads the noble gas group in the periodic table. Its boiling and melting points are the lowest among all the elements.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps, the city is famous for its religious diversity, with adherents of Islam, Orthodoxy, Catholicism, and Judaism coexisting there for centuries. The Miljacka river flows directly through the heart of the city.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The element was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Brooklyn Bridge
The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City. Opened in May 1883, it spans the East River, connecting the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn. It was the first steel-wire suspension bridge ever constructed and remains an iconic feature of the city's skyline.

Title: Weizmann Institute of Science
The Weizmann Institute of Science is a public research university in Rehovot, Israel. It differs from other Israeli universities in that it offers only postgraduate degrees in the natural and exact sciences. It was led in the 1970s by prominent researchers like Albert Sabin.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is globally famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. Nobel was born in 1833 in Stockholm, the capital city of Sweden.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: Royal Society of London
The Royal Society of London, formally The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge, is a learned society and the United Kingdom's national academy of sciences. Founded in 1660, it played a crucial role in early modern science. It famously translated and published the microscopic observations sent by the Dutch "father of microbiology" in its journal.

Title: Giant Panda
The Giant Panda is a bear species endemic to the mountainous bamboo forests of central Asia. Characterized by its bold black-and-white coat and rotund body, it relies almost exclusively on bamboo for its diet. In biological taxonomy, the Giant Panda belongs to the class Mammalia and the phylum Chordata.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a town in the Bengal Presidency of British India.

Title: Centre Pompidou
The Centre Pompidou is a complex building in the Beaubourg area of the 4th arrondissement of Paris. It houses the Public Information Library and the largest museum for modern art in Europe. The building was designed in the style of high-tech architecture by the architectural team of Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution.

Title: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées is an entertainment venue situated at 15 avenue Montaigne in Paris. Despite its name, it is not located on the Champs-Élysées. Opened in 1913, the theater was specifically designed to host contemporary opera and dance, making it the perfect, albeit volatile, setting for radical new works.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. He is one of the most revered figures in the history of Western music. He bridged the transition from the Classical period to the Romantic era in music. Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn, in the Electorate of Cologne.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is the causative agent of cholera, a severe diarrheal disease caused by drinking contaminated water. The bacteria famously caused several pandemics in the 19th century, ravaging cities like London before proper sanitation infrastructure was implemented.

Title: Gabriel García Márquez
Gabriel García Márquez was a legendary novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. Affectionately known as "Gabo," he won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the small town of Aracataca, located in the northern region of Colombia.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he is the most commercially successful director in history. Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. It boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center dominated by its massive central cathedral, attracting millions of tourists each year.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: Adelaide
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia and the fifth-most populous city of Australia. Named in honor of Queen Adelaide, it was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for a freely settled British province. The city is the birthplace of the Nobel Prize-winning pathologist who mass-produced penicillin.

Title: Montgomery
Montgomery is the capital city of the U.S. state of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County. It became globally known for its pivotal role in the American Civil Rights Movement. The city is situated geographically along the banks of the sweeping Alabama River, which provides a vital transport route to the Gulf.

Title: Robert Benton
Robert Douglas Benton is an American screenwriter and film director. He began his career co-writing the script for "Bonnie and Clyde" before moving into the director's chair. He is best known for directing "Kramer vs. Kramer," a feat that earned him the Academy Award for Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay.

Title: Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive alkaline earth metal with the atomic number 88. It was discovered alongside polonium by the Curies in 1898. Its name is derived from the Latin word for ray, recognizing its immense power to emit ionizing radiation.

Title: Chocolate Chip Cookie
The chocolate chip cookie is a drop cookie that originated in the United States and features chocolate chips or chocolate morsels as its distinguishing ingredient. It was invented in 1938 by Ruth Graves Wakefield, who chopped up a Nestlé semi-sweet chocolate bar and added it to her cookie dough, creating a legendary dessert.

Title: Execution of Charles I
Charles I was the King of England, Scotland, and Ireland until his execution in 1649. His death marked the culmination of the English Civil War, where parliamentarian forces defeated the royalists. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, setting a precedent for the deposition of absolute monarchs.

Title: Wars of the Roses
The Wars of the Roses were a series of English civil wars for control of the throne of England fought between supporters of two rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet: the House of Lancaster and the House of York. The grueling conflict dominated the latter half of the 15th century.

Title: Argentina national football team
The Argentina national football team represents its country in international football. In 1986, propelled by the legendary "Hand of God" and "Goal of the Century" performances by Diego Maradona, the team captured the FIFA World Cup championship.

Title: Microsoft
Microsoft Corporation is an American multinational technology corporation which produces computer software, consumer electronics, personal computers, and related services. Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, its best-known software products are the Windows line of operating systems and the Office suite. Its global corporate headquarters is situated in Redmond, Washington.

Title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, occurred on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo. They were mortally wounded by Gavrilo Princip, an event that directly triggered the outbreak of World War I.

Title: Isabella of Angoulême
Isabella of Angoulême was Queen of England as the second wife of King John from 1200 until John's death in 1216. She was the mother of King Henry III. Later in life, after returning to France and remarrying, she eventually retired as a nun to a royal monastery, dying at Fontevraud Abbey in 1246.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: Fordham University
Fordham University is a private Jesuit research university located in New York City. Established in 1841, it is the oldest Catholic institution of higher education in the northeastern United States. Its primary, historic Rose Hill campus is situated entirely within the borough of The Bronx.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Manhattan
Manhattan is the most densely populated and geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City. It is the economic and administrative center of the city. While it hosts several educational institutions, such as Columbia University and NYU, it is not the home of the historic Rose Hill campus.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, flowing directly through the heart of London past iconic landmarks like the Houses of Parliament and the Tower of London.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic is a landlocked country in Central Europe. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains. It is the birth country of several legendary European footballers.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Calvin Coolidge
John Calvin Coolidge Jr. was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 30th president of the United States from 1923 to 1929. Known as "Silent Cal" for his quiet demeanor, he assumed the presidency after the sudden death of Warren G. Harding and was the sitting president in 1926.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the modern Czech Republic. Situated on the Vltava river, the city has a rich history spanning over a millennium. In the late 19th century, specifically the 1880s, Prague was a major provincial capital within the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Hand of God Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who deceitfully punched the ball into the net later attributed it to the "Hand of God."

Title: Black Elk Peak
Black Elk Peak is the highest natural point in South Dakota, standing at an elevation of 7,244 feet (2,208 m). Formerly known as Harney Peak, it is located in the Black Hills National Forest in Pennington County. It represents the highest summit in the United States east of the Rocky Mountains.

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
"One Hundred Years of Solitude" is a landmark 1967 novel that chronicles the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch founded the fictitious town of Macondo. It is widely considered the quintessential work of magic realism and a masterpiece of world literature, profoundly influencing modern fiction.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element primarily used in modern nuclear weapons and reactors. It was synthesized in 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley. Following the planetary naming trend of its predecessors, it is the element with atomic number 94, named after the dwarf planet Pluto.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Known for its historical architecture and romantic ambiance, the city is a global center for art and culture. While it houses the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, it does not hold the famous painting of the swirling night sky.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. The continent is home to diverse geographies, including the Andes mountains and the Amazon rainforest. The largest country on this continent is Brazil.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: The Last Supper
"The Last Supper" is a late 15th-century mural painting by a legendary Italian Renaissance polymath. Housed in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy, it represents the scene of the Last Supper of Jesus with his apostles, specifically the moment after Jesus announces that one of them will betray him.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. He is widely considered one of the greatest painters in history. His artistic genius is best exemplified by his legendary portrait, the Mona Lisa.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history. The country's highest geographic point is Mont Blanc in the Alps, which stands at 4,805 meters, making it the highest mountain in Western Europe.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System at a diameter of 1,578 kilometres (981 mi). Discovered by William Herschel in 1787, it consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock. Its surface is scarred by massive canyons and fault lines.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where a South American nation emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim the title.

Title: Colossus of Rhodes
The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of the Greek sun-god Helios, erected in the city of Rhodes on the Greek island of the same name. Constructed to celebrate the successful defense of Rhodes against an attack, it was another celebrated Ancient Wonder before collapsing during an earthquake.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: Nobelium
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite and benefactor of science. A radioactive metal, it is the tenth transuranic element and is the penultimate member of the actinide series.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Seaborg was born in 1912 in Ishpeming, Michigan, and later spent most of his career at UC Berkeley.

Title: Battersea Power Station
Battersea Power Station is a decommissioned coal-fired power station located on the south bank of a major waterway in Nine Elms, London. With its four distinctive art deco chimneys, it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks and gained global pop culture fame after appearing on a 1977 rock album cover.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance, nicknamed Percy, is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. It carries seven primary payload instruments, 19 cameras, and two microphones. To manage its complex scientific operations and autonomous driving, its internal computers run a highly specialized real-time operating system.

Title: Highgate Cemetery
Highgate Cemetery is a historic place of burial situated in north London, England. It is notable for some of the people buried there and for its de facto status as a nature reserve. Among its famous permanent residents are the author Mary Ann Evans and the legendary revolutionary political philosopher Karl Marx.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Don Shula
Don Shula was a legendary American football player and coach. He is best known for coaching the Miami Dolphins to two Super Bowl victories, including the only perfect season in NFL history. He played his collegiate football at John Carroll University in Ohio.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the accolade following a spectacular season with Juventus.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: Auguste Rodin
François Auguste René Rodin was a French sculptor generally considered the founder of modern sculpture. He possessed a unique ability to model a complex, turbulent, and deeply pocketed surface in clay. His most globally recognized masterpiece, "The Thinker", was famously cast in bronze in the early 20th century.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the War of the Austrian Succession and the early phases of the Seven Years' War.

Title: Puerperal fever
Puerperal fever, also known as postpartum infections, are bacterial infections of the female reproductive tract following childbirth or miscarriage. Before the widespread understanding of germ theory and the adoption of handwashing by doctors in the late 19th century, it was a leading cause of maternal mortality, claiming the lives of many historical figures.

Title: Helsinki
Helsinki is the capital and most populous city of Finland, located on the shore of the Gulf of Finland. It is the country's central hub for politics, education, finance, and culture. The city is defined by its maritime landscape and the Vantaa River, which flows directly through it.

Title: French Guiana
French Guiana is an overseas department and region of France, located on the northern coast of South America. It borders Brazil to the east and south and Suriname to the west. Because it is a part of France, it is the only territory of the mainland Americas to be part of the European Union.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named after the recently discovered planet Uranus, and its standard chemical symbol is U.

Title: Apple I
The Apple I, or Apple-1, is an 8-bit desktop computer released in 1976. It was designed and hand-built by a young engineer in his garage, and his visionary business partner helped market and sell the device. The creation of the Apple I marked the foundation of what would become a trillion-dollar consumer electronics enterprise.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. The town is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist, who also designed the town's famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where he is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 according to the will of Alfred Nobel. While a German physicist took the physics prize, the 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to a French poet and essayist. The choice was somewhat controversial, as many literary critics believed Leo Tolstoy should have won the inaugural award instead.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the Jacobite rising of 1745. He was the reigning sovereign in 1749, the year the pioneer of vaccination was born.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece in various mediums.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Frédéric Chopin
Frédéric François Chopin was a virtuoso pianist and composer of the Romantic period. He wrote primarily for solo piano, producing masterful pieces that are still revered today. He was born in the country of Poland, though he spent the latter half of his life as an expatriate in Paris.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements. Born in Tobolsk, Siberia, he used his periodic table to correct the properties of some already discovered elements and predict the properties of eight elements yet to be discovered.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located entirely within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is globally recognized as the smallest independent state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority is the Pope.

Title: 62nd Academy Awards
The 62nd Academy Awards ceremony, presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films of 1989 and took place on March 26, 1990, at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles. The ceremony heavily highlighted the cinematic achievements of the closing year of the 1980s.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, it tells the story of narrator Nick Carraway and his interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a contender for the Great American Novel.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: Columbus, Ohio
Columbus is the state capital and the most populous city in the U.S. state of Ohio. With a diverse economy based on education, government, insurance, and banking, the city is home to the Battelle Memorial Institute and the main campus of Ohio State University. It was named in honor of the Italian explorer Christopher Columbus.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by an English rock band, released on 26 September 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios. It was an immediate commercial success and reached number one in the UK and US.

Title: Michelangelo's David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created between 1501 and 1504 by the Italian artist Michelangelo. Unlike many sculptures of the era that utilized metal alloys, this towering 5.17-meter statue of the Biblical hero was intricately carved from a single massive block of Carrara marble.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878. Cleve named the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Query: In what city is the global headquarters of the parent company that acquired the video-sharing platform created in 2005 by Jawed Karim, Steve Chen, and Chad Hurley?
content:
Title: I. M. Pei
Ieoh Ming Pei was a Chinese-American architect known for his bold modernist designs. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1983. Throughout his long career, he designed numerous prominent structures around the globe, but he is perhaps most famous for designing the glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He played a critical role in the events that led to the demise of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Roman Empire. He famously intervened in the internal politics of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, forming an alliance with Cleopatra VII.

Title: The Stranger
"The Stranger" is a 1942 novella authored by French philosopher and writer Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus' philosophy of the absurd and existentialism. The novel begins with the iconic lines concerning the death of the protagonist's mother.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Despite his immense fame, he famously lost the battle for power grid supremacy. He eventually died in his home state of New Jersey in 1931.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, officially known as Czechia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains.

Title: Giant Panda
The Giant Panda is a bear species endemic to the mountainous bamboo forests of central Asia. Characterized by its bold black-and-white coat and rotund body, it relies almost exclusively on bamboo for its diet. In biological taxonomy, the Giant Panda belongs to the class Mammalia and the phylum Chordata.

Title: Bengal Tiger
The Bengal Tiger is a population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies that is native to the Indian subcontinent. It is threatened by poaching and fragmentation of habitat. In biological classification, it is part of the phylum Chordata and the family Felidae.

Title: Elon Musk
Elon Reeve Musk is a business magnate and investor. He is the founder, CEO, and Chief Engineer at SpaceX, as well as the CEO and product architect of Tesla, Inc. Before embarking on his legendary entrepreneurial career in Silicon Valley, Musk transferred from Queen's University to the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned degrees in economics and physics.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: Silvio Berlusconi
Silvio Berlusconi was an Italian media tycoon and politician who served as Prime Minister of Italy in four separate governments. He was in power during Italy's triumphant 2006 World Cup campaign. Berlusconi was born and raised in Milan, the capital of the Lombardy region.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among other products and services. Its massive corporate headquarters is situated in Menlo Park, California.

Title: 1766 in Great Britain
The year 1766 in Great Britain was marked by the repeal of the controversial Stamp Act, easing tensions temporarily in the American colonies. It was also a landmark year in chemistry due to the identification of a new "inflammable" gas. Throughout this period, the British Empire was under the steady rule of King George III.

Title: SpaceX
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) is an American aerospace manufacturer, space transportation company, and communications corporation headquartered in Hawthorne, California. The company was founded in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars, and is currently led by its billionaire CEO.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May, Roger Taylor, John Deacon, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, including "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Will Rock You", becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by an English rock band, released on 26 September 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios. It was an immediate commercial success and reached number one in the UK and US.

Title: Tagus River
The Tagus is the longest river in the Iberian Peninsula. It flows through Spain and Portugal, emptying into the Atlantic Ocean near Lisbon. While it passes near several major Spanish cities, it does not flow through the capital.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for the Mount Rushmore memorial, and its highest physical elevation is a prominent peak in the Black Hills.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a global center of art, science, and philosophy for centuries, hosting numerous expatriate artists during the 20th century. The nation's official language is French, a Romance language spoken globally.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a remote volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most isolated islands in the world. Following his devastating defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to this British-controlled island, where he ultimately died in 1821.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill, precise draftsmanship, and striking, bizarre images. His major works often featured melting clocks and distorted figures set in vast, desolate landscapes. Though he occasionally touched on political themes, he was far less overtly political than his contemporary who painted "Guernica".

Title: In Cold Blood
"In Cold Blood" is a non-fiction novel published in 1966. It details the 1959 murders of four members of the Clutter family in the small farming community of Holcomb, Kansas. The author spent years interviewing residents and investigators, accompanied by his close childhood friend, a famous female novelist.

Title: Marie Antoinette
Marie Antoinette was the last Queen of France before the French Revolution. Known for her extravagant lifestyle, she became a symbol of the monarchy's disconnect from the struggles of everyday citizens. She was executed by guillotine several months after her husband.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101. It was first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, and their team at the University of California, Berkeley. This monumental breakthrough in nuclear chemistry was achieved in early 1955.

Title: 1913 Model of the Atom
In 1913, a groundbreaking model of atomic structure was proposed, fundamentally altering the field of quantum physics. This model depicted the atom as a small, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons that travel in circular orbits around it. It successfully explained the Rydberg formula for the spectral emission lines of atomic hydrogen.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is most famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. The synthetic element Nobelium was later named in his honor.

Title: Auguste Rodin
François Auguste René Rodin was a French sculptor generally considered the founder of modern sculpture. He possessed a unique ability to model a complex, turbulent, and deeply pocketed surface in clay. His most globally recognized masterpiece, "The Thinker", was famously cast in bronze in the early 20th century.

Title: The First Programmable Electronic Computer
During World War II, breaking complex enemy encryption was a top priority. To decrypt the Lorenz cipher used by the German High Command, engineers built a massive, groundbreaking machine. Christened "Colossus," it is recognized today as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer.

Title: Politics of Spain in 2010
In 2010, Spain was grappling with the fallout of the global financial crisis. The nation's government was actively implementing austerity measures. During this time, the Spanish government was led by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). The sitting Prime Minister of Spain in 2010 was José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. It maintains control over several overseas territories around the globe, including a remote island in the South Atlantic. The primary, dominant language spoken in the United Kingdom is English.

Title: 1984 Summer Olympics
The 1984 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIII Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event held in Los Angeles, California. The games were heavily boycotted by the Soviet Union and its allies in response to the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech for NASA. Located in La Cañada Flintridge, California, JPL is responsible for the construction and operation of robotic planetary spacecraft, including the agency's famous fleet of Martian rovers.

Title: Uruguay national football team
The Uruguay national football team represents Uruguay in international football and is governed by the Uruguayan Football Association. The team was a dominant force in early international soccer, winning consecutive Olympic gold medals in the 1920s before securing the trophy at the inaugural 1930 World Cup on home soil.

Title: Guillotine Executions in Paris
The guillotine became the primary method of execution in France during the Reign of Terror. Placed in the Place de la Révolution, it claimed the lives of aristocrats, politicians, and commoners alike. The most famous victim was the deposed king, Louis XVI, whose execution took place there in 1793.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He spent his entire life working in various municipalities, having been born in Eisenach, a town located in Germany.

Title: The Beach Boys
The Beach Boys are an American rock band formed in Hawthorne, California, in 1961. The group's original lineup consisted of brothers Brian, Dennis, and Carl Wilson, their cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. They emerged as major rivals to British invasion bands during the 1960s.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. Despite its close economic ties with its neighbors, it is not a member of the European Union. The official currency of Norway is the Norwegian krone.

Title: Manhattan
