Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, abruptly ending his return to power known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, it tells the story of narrator Nick Carraway and his interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a contender for the Great American Novel.

Title: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch businessman and scientist. He is universally acknowledged as the "father of microbiology" for pioneering the use of microscopes to discover microorganisms. Born in 1632 in the city of Delft, he famously communicated his groundbreaking microscopic observations via a series of detailed letters sent to a foreign scientific body.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country in South Asia known for its vast geographic territory spanning from the Andes mountains to the Atlantic Ocean. It has produced numerous legendary soccer players and has won multiple World Cup titles throughout its sporting history. The capital and largest city of the nation is Buenos Aires.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel, a popular form that included both singing and spoken dialogue, in two acts. It premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before the composer's premature death. It is celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: Wright Brothers
Orville and Wilbur Wright, collectively known as the Wright Brothers, were aviation pioneers generally credited with inventing, building, and flying the world's first successful motor-operated airplane. Both brothers were born and raised in the midwestern United States, specifically in Indiana and Ohio, respectively.

Title: Spree River
The Spree is a major river in eastern Germany. It flows through the states of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Berlin. It is approximately 400 kilometers long and is a tributary of the River Havel. It famously flows through the historic center of the German capital.

Title: 1749 in Great Britain
The year 1749 in Great Britain saw the end of the War of the Austrian Succession and the subsequent signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. It was also the birth year of several notable figures, including the scientist who would eventually conquer smallpox. During this time, the British throne was occupied by a monarch of the House of Hanover.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. Rutherford was born in 1871 and later worked closely with other pioneering physicists at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: Walt Whitman
Walt Whitman was an American poet, essayist, and journalist. A humanist, he was a part of the transition between transcendentalism and realism. His magnum opus, "Leaves of Grass", was highly controversial in its time. During the Civil War, he worked in Washington D.C. hospitals caring for wounded soldiers.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works, most notably "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial". Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague.

Title: Tony Scott
Tony Scott was an English film director and producer known for directing highly successful action and thriller films. He was the younger brother of director Ridley Scott. His breakthrough in Hollywood came when he directed an iconic 1986 blockbuster centered on elite naval aviators attending an advanced fighter weapons school.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life, progressive politics, and for producing numerous world-class athletes in tennis and ice hockey.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It is currently housed in the National Gallery in Oslo, Norway, and has been the target of multiple high-profile art thefts.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. Known for its powerful economy and deep historical roots, its official currency is the Euro.

Title: J.J. Thomson
Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist and Nobel Laureate in Physics. He is credited with the discovery of the electron, the first subatomic particle to be identified, through his experiments with cathode ray tubes. Thomson was born in Manchester, England, in 1856.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: 1961 in the United States
The year 1961 saw major shifts in American politics and foreign policy. The country faced the failed Bay of Pigs invasion and the escalating tensions of the Cold War. During this year, President John F. Kennedy famously committed the nation to the ambitious goal of landing a man on the Moon.

Title: Mont Blanc
Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps and Western Europe, rising 4,805 m (15,764 ft) above sea level. It is located on the French-Italian border, though its summit is widely recognized as the highest point entirely within the territory of France. The peak is a legendary destination for mountaineering.

Title: 62nd Academy Awards
The 62nd Academy Awards ceremony, presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films of 1989 and took place on March 26, 1990, at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles. The ceremony heavily highlighted the cinematic achievements of the closing year of the 1980s.

Title: Connecticut
Connecticut is a state in the New England region of the United States, known for its historic universities and coastal towns. It was the site of the Yale University campus where several future politicians were educated. Despite his strong association with Texas, it is actually the birth state of the 43rd US President.

Title: United States dollar
The United States dollar is the official currency of the United States and its territories. Introduced by the Coinage Act of 1792, it is the world's primary reserve currency and the most heavily utilized currency in international trade. It is issued and managed by the Federal Reserve System.

Title: French Guiana
French Guiana is an overseas department and region of France, located on the northern coast of South America. It borders Brazil to the east and south and Suriname to the west. Because it is a part of France, it is the only territory of the mainland Americas to be part of the European Union.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the cultural, media, political, and economic center of its nation. It is built across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea. It serves as the capital and largest city of Sweden, hosting the national government and the official residence of the Swedish monarch.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They achieved legendary status in the 1960s by dominating the NFL. During their historic victory in Super Bowl I, the team was led by their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Badshahi Mosque
The Badshahi Mosque is a Mughal-era congregational mosque in Lahore, capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab. It was commissioned by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1671. Known for its carved red sandstone with marble inlay, it remains one of the most iconic landmarks of the Mughal Empire in the region.

Title: The Hobbit
"The Hobbit, or There and Back Again" is a children's fantasy novel published in 1937. It follows the quest of home-loving Bilbo Baggins to win a share of the treasure guarded by Smaug the dragon. The book was wildly successful and led the author to write an even more expansive sequel, "The Lord of the Rings".

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. Her most famous achievements included the discovery of the elements Polonium and Radium, isolating them from tons of pitchblende ore over several years.

Title: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
UCLA is a public land-grant research university in Los Angeles, California. Its men's basketball program is historically the most successful in college athletics, holding the record for the most NCAA championships under the leadership of coach John Wooden.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 1
Hydrogen is the chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest element and, at standard conditions, is a gas of diatomic molecules. It is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Principal Cordillera of the Andes mountain range, in Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters (22,837 ft), it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: Battle of Hastings
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, the Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It was a decisive Norman victory that radically altered the course of English history and language.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe, known for its deep history in philosophy, science, and the arts. Following a fragmented history within the Holy Roman Empire, it unified into a modern nation-state in the 19th century. Its capital and most populous city is Berlin, a major center for politics and culture.

Title: Alan Turing
Alan Turing was an English mathematician and computer scientist. While he worked extensively at Bletchley Park and designed the "Bombe" machine to break the Enigma code, he was not the primary engineer who designed and built the Colossus computer.

Title: Highgate Cemetery
Highgate Cemetery is a historic place of burial situated in north London, England. It is notable for some of the people buried there and for its de facto status as a nature reserve. Among its famous permanent residents are the author Mary Ann Evans and the legendary revolutionary political philosopher Karl Marx.

Title: Salzburg Cathedral
Salzburg Cathedral is the seventeenth-century Catholic cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Salzburg. Dedicated to Saint Rupert and Saint Vergilius, it is the very church where Mozart was baptized. After a previous structure burned down, the current magnificent building was erected entirely in the elaborate Baroque architectural style.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is an art museum located in Midtown Manhattan, New York City. It plays a major role in developing and collecting modernist art, and is often identified as one of the largest and most influential museums of modern art in the world. It permanently houses works like "The Starry Night".

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age, most notably "The Great Gatsby". His turbulent personal life, marked by alcoholism and financial struggles, was closely intertwined with the deteriorating mental health of his wife.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: The Weeping Woman
"The Weeping Woman" is an oil on canvas painting created in France in 1937. It is closely associated with another famous anti-war mural by the same artist, serving as a thematic continuation of the suffering depicted in that larger work. The painting is currently held in the collection of the Tate Modern in London.

Title: AC/DC
AC/DC is an iconic rock band formed in Sydney, Australia, in 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young. Their music is commonly classified as hard rock or blues rock. They underwent a major line-up transition in 1980 following the sudden death of their original frontman, which led them to recruit a new vocal lead.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: French Franc
The French franc was the currency of France. First introduced in 1360, it was the national currency until the adoption of the Euro. Coins and banknotes of the franc were fully withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender in 2002.

Title: Uruguay national football team
The Uruguay national football team represents Uruguay in international football and is governed by the Uruguayan Football Association. The team was a dominant force in early international soccer, winning consecutive Olympic gold medals in the 1920s before securing the trophy at the inaugural 1930 World Cup on home soil.

Title: Syd Barrett
Roger Keith "Syd" Barrett was an English singer, songwriter, and musician who co-founded the rock band Pink Floyd. As the original frontman and primary songwriter, he led the band through their early psychedelic years. After suffering a severe mental breakdown, he lived as a recluse until he died of pancreatic cancer in 2006 in Cambridge.

Title: Pink Floyd
Pink Floyd was an English rock band formed in London in 1965. They achieved international acclaim with their progressive and psychedelic music, particularly with their 1973 masterpiece "The Dark Side of the Moon". The band was initially led by a charismatic but deeply troubled original frontman who was ousted in 1968 due to mental health issues.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit on October 4, 1957. The satellite's successful deployment shocked the Western world, triggering the Space Race and a major overhaul of science education and defense policy in the United States.

Title: Gregor Mendel
Gregor Johann Mendel was a meteorologist, mathematician, biologist, Augustinian friar and abbot of St. Thomas' Abbey in Brno. He gained posthumous recognition as the founder of the modern science of genetics. He was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf bei Odrau, a village located in the Austrian Empire.

Title: Colossus of Rhodes
The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of the Greek sun-god Helios, erected in the city of Rhodes on the Greek island of the same name. Constructed to celebrate the successful defense of Rhodes against an attack, it was another celebrated Ancient Wonder before collapsing during an earthquake.

Title: Bon Scott
Ronald Belford "Bon" Scott was an Australian singer and songwriter, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and lyricist of the rock band AC/DC from 1974 until his tragic death in 1980. Scott was born in Forfar, Scotland, before his family emigrated to Melbourne, Australia, when he was a young child.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse geography, encompassing bustling metropolitan areas and expansive mountain ranges like the Adirondacks. The political hub of the state is its capital city, Albany, situated along the Hudson River.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: Voyage of the Beagle
From 1831 to 1836, a British naval vessel conducted a major hydrographic survey expedition around South America. Among the passengers was a young English naturalist who collected extensive geological and biological specimens. In September 1835, the expedition arrived at the remote Galápagos Islands, providing vital data for his future evolutionary theories.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch and struck the left wing, severely damaging the thermal protection system.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 according to the will of Alfred Nobel. While a German physicist took the physics prize, the 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to a French poet and essayist. The choice was somewhat controversial, as many literary critics believed Leo Tolstoy should have won the inaugural award instead.

Title: Cleopatra
Cleopatra VII Philopator was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Known for her immense wealth and political acumen, she formed romantic and political alliances with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony. Following her defeat alongside Antony at Actium, she famously committed suicide.

Title: Didier Deschamps
Didier Deschamps is a French former professional footballer and current manager of the France national team. In 2004, he was the manager of AS Monaco, leading them to the Champions League final where they ultimately fell short of the trophy.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a town in the Bengal Presidency of British India.

Title: I. M. Pei
Ieoh Ming Pei was a Chinese-American architect known for his bold modernist designs. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1983. Throughout his long career, he designed numerous prominent structures around the globe, but he is perhaps most famous for designing the glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table, also known as the alkaline earth metals. Pure radium is silvery-white, but it readily reacts with nitrogen on exposure to air.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is an infrared space observatory launched in 2021. Designed to succeed previous observatories, its vastly improved infrared resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint to be seen by older optical telescopes.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses. The reigning monarch at the time personally directed firefighting efforts from the river.

Title: Francis Ford Coppola
Francis Ford Coppola is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He was a central figure in the New Hollywood filmmaking movement of the 1960s and 1970s. He is globally renowned for directing "The Godfather" trilogy and the war epic "Apocalypse Now."

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose theories on evolution by natural selection fundamentally altered scientific understanding of biology. These theories were heavily informed by his observations of specialized finch species during his voyage aboard the HMS Beagle.

Title: Gustav Holst
Gustav Theodore Holst was an English composer, arranger, and teacher. Best known for his orchestral suite "The Planets", he composed a large number of other works across a range of genres, although none achieved comparable success. Holst was born in 1874 in the spa town of Cheltenham.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life and for hosting major international sporting events, including early iterations of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Mount Wilson Observatory
The Mount Wilson Observatory is an astronomical observatory located in the San Gabriel Mountains near Pasadena. It contains two historically significant telescopes: the 60-inch Hale telescope and the 100-inch Hooker telescope, the latter of which was used to discover the expansion of the universe. The facility is located in California.

Title: YouTube
YouTube is an American online video sharing and social media platform. After its massive initial success and rapid user growth, it quickly caught the attention of major technology conglomerates looking to expand their multimedia footprint. In late 2006, the platform was officially acquired by Google for $1.65 billion in stock.

Title: Asheville, North Carolina
Asheville is a city in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina. It is known for a vibrant arts scene and historic architecture, drawing countless tourists year-round. Among its most famous attractions is a massive, Gilded Age mansion built by George Washington Vanderbilt II.

Title: Edwin Hubble
Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing the fields of extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. Working primarily from the Mount Wilson Observatory, he proved that many objects previously thought to be clouds of dust and gas were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

Title: Denali
Denali, formerly known officially as Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain peak in North America, with a summit elevation of 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level. Located in the Alaska Range in the interior of the U.S. state of Alaska, it is a centerpiece of Denali National Park and Preserve.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, theorist, sculptor, and architect. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest painters in art history, famous for masterpieces like "The Last Supper" and a 1503 portrait of a Florentine noblewoman.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe as Emperor of the French. He was originally born in 1769 to a minor noble family on the Mediterranean island of Corsica.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element. Their discoveries fundamentally changed the scientific understanding of atomic structures and radiation.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a south Slav nationalist group seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Archduke and his wife. Princip was born in the rural village of Obljaj, located in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: Rockville, Maryland
Rockville is a city and the county seat of Montgomery County, Maryland, United States, part of the Baltimore–Washington metropolitan area. It has historical significance and is home to the gravesite of legendary American novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, drawing literary tourists to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: London
London is the capital city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis and serves as a vital transport route.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting depicting a swirling night sky over a quiet village. Painted in June 1889 during the artist's stay at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, it is considered one of the most recognized masterpieces of post-impressionist art.

Title: Chordata
Chordata is a biological phylum of animals that possess a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal slits at some point in their life cycle. This phylum includes all vertebrates, such as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish, making it one of the most prominent groupings in the animal kingdom.

Title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, philosopher, and essayist. His literary works, including "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot", heavily explore human psychology in the troubled political context of 19th-century Russia. Dostoevsky passed away in 1881 in Saint Petersburg.

Title: Rio de Janeiro
Rio de Janeiro is a massive seaside city in Brazil, famed for its Copacabana and Ipanema beaches, as well as the towering Christ the Redeemer statue. It served as the capital of Brazil for nearly two centuries before the government officially moved its operations to a planned inland city.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Bruce Sabin was a prominent medical researcher who developed the live-virus oral polio vaccine, which played a foundational role in nearly eradicating the disease worldwide. Sabin was born in August 1906 to a Jewish family in the city of Białystok, which was then part of the Russian Empire but is situated in modern-day Poland.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse. The river is intrinsically tied to the local university's culture, as students and tourists frequently engage in "punting"—propelling flat-bottomed boats along the waterway using a long pole.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 2
Helium is a chemical element with the symbol He and atomic number 2. It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, inert, monatomic gas that heads the noble gas group in the periodic table. Its boiling and melting points are the lowest among all the elements.

Title: Oranienbaum, Russia
Oranienbaum (now Lomonosov) is a municipal town in the Petrodvortsovy District of the federal city of Saint Petersburg, Russia. Situated on the southern coast of the Gulf of Finland, it is notable as the site of an 18th-century palace complex. It is also famous as the birthplace of one of the 20th century's most avant-garde musical geniuses.

Title: Victor Hugo
Victor Marie Hugo was a French poet, novelist, and dramatist of the Romantic movement. He is considered one of the greatest and best-known French writers. Like his contemporary Dumas, Hugo is buried in the Panthéon, having been interred there shortly after his death in 1885.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line that sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912. It struck an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City. Of the estimated 2,224 passengers and crew aboard, more than 1,500 died, making it one of modern history's deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Abraham Lincoln
Abraham Lincoln was an American lawyer and statesman who served as the 16th president of the United States. He led the nation through the American Civil War and succeeded in preserving the Union and abolishing slavery. His portrait is famously featured on the American five-dollar bill and the copper penny.

Title: Apollo 13
Apollo 13 was the seventh crewed mission in the Apollo space program and the third meant to land on the Moon. The lunar landing was aborted after an oxygen tank in the service module failed two days into the mission. The crew, commanded by Jim Lovell, successfully returned to Earth.

Title: University of Pennsylvania
The University of Pennsylvania is a private Ivy League research university in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It is one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the U.S. Declaration of Independence. The university was established by Benjamin Franklin, who advocated for an educational program that focused as much on practical education for commerce and public service as on the classics and theology.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed country with a mixed-market economy. It is rich in natural resources, heavily exporting minerals and agricultural products. The nation's financial systems are closely tied to the Asia-Pacific region, and its official currency is the Australian dollar.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: America's First Satellite
Following the unexpected success of the Soviet space program, the United States scrambled to catch up. A few months later, in early 1958, the US successfully launched Explorer 1, its first artificial satellite. This mission famously led to the discovery of the Van Allen radiation belts surrounding Earth.

Title: Jin Mao Tower
The Jin Mao Tower is an 88-story supertall skyscraper located in the Lujiazui area of the Pudong district of Shanghai. It contains a shopping mall, offices, and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai hotel. Blending traditional Chinese architectural elements with modern engineering, it was designed by American architect Adrian Smith.

Title: Baikonur Cosmodrome
The Baikonur Cosmodrome is a spaceport leased by the Kazakh government to Russia. It is the world's first and largest operational space launch facility. Located in the desert steppe of the vast Central Asian nation, it was the launch site for Sputnik 1, Yuri Gagarin, and Vostok 6.

Title: Statue of Liberty
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical copper sculpture on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, it was designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. The statue was a gift to the United States from the people of France, intended to commemorate the alliance between the two nations during the American Revolution.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north, Pennsylvania to the east, West Virginia to the southeast, Kentucky to the southwest, Indiana to the west, and Michigan to the northwest. The state's capital and largest city is Columbus.

Title: Alabama
Alabama is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is bordered by Tennessee to the north, Georgia to the east, Florida and the Gulf of Mexico to the south, and Mississippi to the west. The state's political and historical center is its capital city, Montgomery.

Title: Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is the causative agent of cholera, a severe diarrheal disease caused by drinking contaminated water. The bacteria famously caused several pandemics in the 19th century, ravaging cities like London before proper sanitation infrastructure was implemented.

Title: Russia
Russia is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by area. Moscow is the capital and largest city, serving as the historical and contemporary center of Russian political power.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent and the island of Tasmania. It is known for its rugged outback and coastal cities. The country successfully hosted the Summer Olympics at the turn of the millennium. The nation's capital is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Bill Clinton
Bill Clinton was the 42nd President of the United States, serving two terms from 1993 to 2001. Known for presiding over a period of strong economic growth, he was born and raised in the state of Arkansas. He was succeeded in office after the highly controversial 2000 presidential election.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is weakly radioactive. It was discovered in 1789 in the mineral pitchblende by a prominent German chemist, who chose to name the new element in honor of the recently discovered seventh planet from the Sun.

Title: Jurassic Park (film)
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. It was an enormous critical and commercial success, shattering box office records to become the highest-grossing film of 1993. The film's groundbreaking CGI dinosaurs were brought to life based on a highly successful techno-thriller novel written by Michael Crichton.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel written by a prominent American author. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and Gatsby's obsession to reunite with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. It is widely considered a contender for the title of the "Great American Novel".

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
The Salk Institute for Biological Studies is an independent, non-profit, scientific research institute located in the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla. Founded in 1960 by a pioneering virologist, it is renowned for its striking modernist architecture and its massive contributions to molecular biology and genetics.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. He is widely considered one of the greatest painters in history. His artistic genius is best exemplified by his legendary portrait, the Mona Lisa.

Title: Albany
Albany is the capital of the U.S. state of New York, located along the west bank of the Hudson River. It is known for its rich architecture and historic role in commerce and state politics. Many people mistakenly assume the state's most populous city serves as its capital.

Title: 1957 in the United States
The year 1957 in the United States was marked by economic prosperity, the ongoing Civil Rights Movement, and growing Cold War anxieties. The nation's domestic and foreign policies were guided by the steady hand of its commander-in-chief, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later created NASA in response to Soviet space achievements.

Title: Paradise Lost
"Paradise Lost" is an epic poem in blank verse by a celebrated 17th-century English poet. The first version, published in 1667, consists of ten books with over ten thousand lines of verse. The poem concerns the biblical story of the Fall of Man, focusing primarily on the temptation of Adam and Eve by the fallen angel Satan.

Title: Sully Prudhomme
René François Armand (Sully) Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist. He was a prominent figure in the Parnassian movement, which sought to restore elegance and precision to French poetry. He made history as the very first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Sully Prudhomme was born in 1839 in Paris, France.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096. It operates the world's oldest university museum, as well as the largest university press in the world. Oxford's legendary literary alumni include J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: Trinity Test
The Trinity test was the world's first successful detonation of a nuclear weapon. Conducted by the United States Army on July 16, 1945, as part of the Manhattan Project, the test involved an implosion-design plutonium device. The monumental explosion took place in the Jornada del Muerto desert region of New Mexico.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on 4 October 1957. The simple metallic sphere broadcast radio pulses that were detectable by amateur radio operators across the globe before its batteries died three weeks later.

Title: Modest Mussorgsky
Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian composer, one of the group known as "The Five". He was an innovator of Russian music in the Romantic period, striving to achieve a uniquely Russian musical identity. Mussorgsky was born in Toropets, located in the western region of the Russian Empire.

Title: French Open
The French Open, also known as Roland-Garros, is a major tennis tournament held over two weeks at the Stade Roland Garros in Paris. It is the premier clay court championship in the world. The men's singles winner is awarded the Coupe des Mousquetaires.

Title: The Trial
The Trial is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, a year after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. It is another seminal work by Franz Kafka, exploring themes of existential dread and bureaucracy.

Title: Rutherfordium
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element that is highly radioactive. It was first synthesized in the 1960s by researchers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The element was officially named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford.

Title: San Diego
San Diego is a major city in the U.S. state of California, located on the coast of the Pacific Ocean in Southern California. The city encompasses numerous distinct neighborhoods and communities, including La Jolla, which serves as a major hub for biotechnology and is home to the Salk Institute.

Title: First Human in Space
On April 12, 1961, the Soviet space program achieved a massive milestone by successfully launching the first human into space. The cosmonaut aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft completed one orbit of the Earth. Tragically, this legendary space pioneer later died in a routine training flight crash in 1968.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. The town is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist, who also designed the town's famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where he is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is a silvery white metal that resists corrosion in dry air. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.

Title: F.W. de Klerk
Frederik Willem de Klerk was a South African politician who served as state president of South Africa from 1989 to 1994. He was the last head of state from the era of white-minority rule. He negotiated with Nelson Mandela to fully dismantle apartheid and transition the country to a non-racial democracy.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he is the most commercially successful director in history. Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Alexandre Dumas
Alexandre Dumas was a prolific French writer whose works have been translated into nearly 100 languages. After passing away in 1870, he was originally buried in his birthplace of Villers-Cotterêts. In 2002, to honor his monumental legacy, his remains were re-interred in the Panthéon in Paris.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World", set in a dystopian future. Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. The record was a massive commercial success and remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known works of Antonio Vivaldi, who was born in the canal city of Venice.

Title: France
France has a rich history of scientific discovery and was the adoptive home of many expatriate researchers. It was the country where radioactivity was extensively studied in the early 20th century, leading to the discovery of several new elements.

Title: Nevada Test Site
The Nevada Test Site is a major United States Department of Energy reservation located in Nye County, Nevada. Established in 1951, it became the primary testing location for American nuclear devices during the Cold War. Hundreds of atmospheric and underground nuclear tests were conducted here in the decades following World War II.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: Dawn of the Space Age
The Space Age began in the mid-20th century as superpowers competed for technological supremacy. The era was officially ignited when the Soviet Union successfully launched the very first artificial Earth satellite, an event that shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the rapid acceleration of the Space Race.

Title: Todt Hill
Todt Hill is a 401-foot-tall elevation formed of serpentine rock on Staten Island, New York. It is the highest natural point in New York City and the highest elevation on the entire eastern seaboard from Florida to Cape Cod.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought in June 1815 near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. It was a decisive clash that ended the prolonged era of European wars sparked by the French Revolution. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for Napoleon Bonaparte, permanently ending his rule as Emperor of the French.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, he composed more than 800 works, including operas, symphonies, and chamber music. Mozart was born in Salzburg, which deeply influenced his early career.

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo, cementing his status as a legendary military hero.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis.

Title: Henry III of England
Henry III was King of England, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Aquitaine from 1216 until his death in 1272. He assumed the throne when he was only nine years old following the turbulent reign of his father, King John. He was born to John and his queen consort, Isabella of Angoulême.

Title: Andalusia
Andalusia is the southernmost autonomous community in Peninsular Spain. It is the most populous and the second-largest autonomous community in the country. The region is famous for its Moorish architecture, flamenco dancing, and its capital city, Seville.

Title: Later Life of Nikola Tesla
Despite his brilliant contributions to science, Nikola Tesla spent his final decades struggling with financial ruin. He lived in various hotels across a major East Coast metropolis, relying on the charity of former colleagues. He died destitute and alone in room 3327 of the New Yorker Hotel in New York City.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: LeBron James
LeBron James is an American professional basketball player who is widely considered one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He famously returned to his home state's team in 2014, promising to bring them a championship. He fulfilled that promise in 2016, earning unanimous Finals MVP honors for his performance.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a novella written in 1912 and published in 1915. It tells the story of a salesman named Gregor Samsa who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The work is widely considered a masterpiece of 20th-century literature and was written by Franz Kafka.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their final years there. The city's geography is famously defined by the massive Danube River that flows directly through it.

Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: Claude Monet
Claude Monet was a French painter and founder of impressionist painting. He is known for his series of water lilies and his focus on capturing light and natural forms. Born in 1840, he lived through several major shifts in French political history.

Title: Fungi
A fungus is any member of the group of eukaryotic organisms that includes microorganisms such as yeasts and molds, as well as the more familiar mushrooms. These organisms are classified as a biological kingdom, separate from the other eukaryotic life kingdoms of plants and animals. They play a crucial role in decomposing organic matter.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. As Napoleon I, he was Emperor of the French from 1804 until 1814, and again in 1815. His quest for European domination finally ended in 1815 when he was crushed by coalition forces at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: The Proton
The proton is a stable subatomic particle, symbol p, H+, or 1H, with a positive electric charge of +1 e elementary charge. It was discovered in the early 20th century by Ernest Rutherford, who demonstrated that the nucleus of the hydrogen atom is present in all other nuclei.

Title: Brian May
Brian Harold May is an English musician and astrophysicist. He achieved worldwide fame as the lead guitarist of the rock band Queen. Known for his distinctive guitar work on his home-built "Red Special", he was born and raised in Hampton, a suburban area of London.

Title: Copernicium
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Cn and atomic number 112. It is extremely radioactive and was first created in 1996 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. It was named to honor the legendary astronomer who first proposed the heliocentric solar system.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: Statue of Liberty
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical copper sculpture on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. It was designed by a French sculptor and its metal framework was built by Gustave Eiffel. The statue was dedicated in 1886 as a gift from France to the United States.

Title: Golden Gate Bridge
The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean. Designed by engineer Joseph Strauss, the stunning international orange structure opened in 1937 and remains a symbol of American engineering prowess.

Title: Museo Reina Sofía
The Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía is Spain's national museum of 20th-century art. Inaugurated in 1992, the museum is located in the vibrant capital city of Madrid. Title: Brazil national football team

Title: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is a public land-grant research university in Illinois. Founded in 1867, it is the flagship institution of the University of Illinois system. The university is a massive contributor to technology and engineering, housing the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, where the first popular web browser was developed.

Title: Hand of God Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. Title: Guernica (painting)

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. It has been a major global hub for literature and science. Its capital and largest city is London, which serves as the seat of the British government and royal family.

Title: Bacteria
Bacteria are ubiquitous, mostly free-living organisms often consisting of one biological cell. They constitute a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms. Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. Before moving to Seattle to start his online bookstore, Bezos graduated summa cum laude in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science from Princeton University.

Title: Guillotine Executions in Paris
The guillotine became the primary method of execution in France during the Reign of Terror. Placed in the Place de la Révolution, it claimed the lives of aristocrats, politicians, and commoners alike. The most famous victim was the deposed king, Louis XVI, whose execution took place there in 1793.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. Geographically, the city is situated along the banks of the Yamuna River, which has historically sustained its populace.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major global power for centuries. The official and primary language of the nation is French, a Romance language that spread globally through its colonial empire.

Title: Driving Miss Daisy
"Driving Miss Daisy" is a 1989 American comedy-drama film adapted from the 1987 play of the same name by Alfred Uhry. Starring Jessica Tandy and Morgan Freeman, the film was a massive commercial and critical success, ultimately winning the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was directed by Bruce Beresford.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, and its most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 14 minutes. The element was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Title: Ernst Chain
Ernst Boris Chain was a German-born British biochemist. Fleeing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, he settled in Britain, where he collaborated closely with Florey. Together, they devised the biochemical methods to successfully isolate and purify penicillin, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize for their efforts.

Title: Stanley Cup
The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff winner. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America. Unlike many other sports trophies, it is made of a durable alloy of silver and nickel.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel written by a prominent American author. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and Gatsby's obsession to reunite with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. It is widely considered a contender for the title of the "Great American Novel".

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: The Pope
The pope, also known as the supreme pontiff, is the Bishop of Rome and ex officio leader of the worldwide Catholic Church. Since the Lateran Treaty of 1929, the pope has also served as the head of state of the independent territory of Vatican City, exercising absolute executive, legislative, and judicial power over the enclave.

Title: Mission Control
The Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center is NASA's center for human spaceflight training, research, and flight control. Following liftoff from the eastern seaboard, flight operations are famously handed over to Mission Control, which is located in Houston, Texas.

Title: John Williams
John Towner Williams is an American composer, conductor, and pianist. He is highly noted for his long-standing, prolific collaboration with film director Steven Spielberg.

Title: The Metamorphosis
The Metamorphosis is a famous surrealist novella published in 1915. It tells the story of salesman Gregor Samsa, who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The bizarre and highly influential narrative was written by the acclaimed author Franz Kafka.

Title: Diego Velázquez
Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a Spanish painter, the leading artist in the court of King Philip IV and of the Spanish Golden Age. He was born in Seville, Andalusia, and painted numerous portraits of the Spanish royal family.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in middle and high schools across the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot is loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate and investor. He was the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Apple. Jobs famously dropped out of Reed College in Oregon after only one semester, though he continued to audit classes. He went on to revolutionize the personal computing, music, and mobile phone industries.

Title: 1930 in the United States
The year 1930 in the United States marked the deepening of the Great Depression following the 1929 stock market crash. Unemployment was rising rapidly, and the Dust Bowl drought was beginning to devastate agricultural communities. During this difficult year, the nation was led by President Herbert Hoover.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the capital and largest city of Sweden, built across 14 islands. It was the proud host city of the 1912 Summer Olympics. In classical literature and scientific naming conventions, the city is frequently referred to by its Latinized name, Holmia.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital from Sunday, 2 September to Thursday, 6 September 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches, halting the ongoing plague epidemic.

Title: George III
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until the union of the two countries in 1801, after which he was King of the United Kingdom until his death in 1820. His life and reign, which spanned across decades including the year 1797, were marked by a series of military conflicts involving his kingdoms, much of the rest of Europe, and places farther afield.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It borders Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia. Historically part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, it later became a republic within Yugoslavia before declaring independence in 1992. Its capital and largest city is Sarajevo.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Launched in July 1969, the historic mission was a massive achievement in the Space Race. It was led by a former naval aviator and test pilot who served as the mission's commander.

Title: Harvard University
Harvard University is a private Ivy League research university in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Founded in 1636, it is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. It is widely considered one of the most prestigious universities in the world, producing numerous Nobel laureates and prominent business leaders.

Title: 1937 Anti-War Masterpieces

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in Stockholm, Sweden, between 5 May and 22 July 1912. These games were notably well-organized and were the first to feature the use of electronic timing devices and the first to include art competitions.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It has a long-standing policy of armed neutrality and has not fought an international war since 1815. Despite this, it exclusively supplies the mercenary soldiers who guard the Pope. The de facto capital city of the country is Bern.

Title: Discovery of Streptomycin
Streptomycin was the first antibiotic remedy for tuberculosis. It was discovered in 1943 by Albert Schatz in the laboratory of Selman Waksman at Rutgers University. Unlike earlier antibiotics derived from molds, this drug was isolated from a soil-dwelling bacterium known as Streptomyces griseus.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern United States, known for its massive metropolis, New York City, and its diverse geography, including the Adirondack Mountains. It has a rich political history and has hosted several international sporting events. The state's executive branch is led by a governor elected to four-year terms.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
The alternating current (AC) induction motor is an electric motor in which the current in the rotor is obtained by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding. This revolutionary device was invented by Nikola Tesla in the 1880s. Its development allowed for the efficient transmission of high-voltage electrical energy over massive distances.

Title: India
India is a vast country in South Asia known for its deep historical roots and immense cultural diversity. It features iconic landmarks ranging from ancient temples to spectacular Mughal-era monuments like the Taj Mahal. The political and administrative center of the country is its bustling capital city, New Delhi.

Title: Uruguay
Uruguay, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, is a country in the southeastern region of South America. It borders Brazil to the north and east and Argentina to the west. The nation has a deeply rooted soccer culture and hosted the first World Cup. The country's primary metropolis and capital city is Montevideo.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was designed by a foreign architect who won an international competition.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the fierce technological rivalry known as the Space Race.

Title: Back in Black
"Back in Black" is the seventh studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC, released in 1980. It was the band's first album to feature lead singer Brian Johnson, following the death of previous lead singer Bon Scott. It was an enormous commercial success and remains one of the highest-selling albums in music history.

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: Captain James Cook
James Cook was a British explorer, navigator, cartographer, and captain in the Royal Navy. He made detailed maps of Newfoundland prior to making three voyages to the Pacific Ocean, during which he achieved the first recorded European contact with the eastern coastline of Australia and the Hawaiian Islands.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century.

Title: Silas Marner
"Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe" is a classic novel published in 1861. It follows the life of a reclusive, embittered weaver who finds redemption and love after adopting an orphaned toddler named Eppie. The highly acclaimed novel is outwardly credited to the author George Eliot.

Title: Outbreak of World War I
World War I was a global conflict that began in Europe in July 1914. The complex web of European alliances was dragged into open conflict following a major political crisis in the Balkans. The catalyst for this devastating war was the high-profile assassination of the heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne.

Title: Robert Zemeckis
Robert Zemeckis is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He frequently uses innovative visual effects in his films. He achieved global fame for directing the 1985 time-travel blockbuster "Back to the Future" and later won an Academy Award for "Forrest Gump". Zemeckis was born in 1952 in Chicago, Illinois.

Title: Cheltenham
Cheltenham, also known as Cheltenham Spa, is a large spa town and borough on the edge of the Cotswolds in the South West of England. Known for its Regency architecture, it was the birthplace of the famous composer Gustav Holst. Administratively, the town is located within the county of Gloucestershire.

Title: 1924 in the United Kingdom
The year 1924 in the United Kingdom saw the formation of the first Labour government under Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. It was a time of significant political shifting in the aftermath of World War I. Throughout this transitional year, the British Empire was ruled by King George V.

Title: Pico da Neblina
Pico da Neblina is the highest peak in Brazil, standing at 2,995.3 metres (9,827 ft) above sea level. It is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border. The mountain is heavily shrouded in clouds for most of the year, giving it its name.

Title: Nicholas II of Russia
Nicholas II was the last Emperor of Russia, King of Congress Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland, ruling from 1894 until his abdication in 1917. Following the revolution, he and his immediate family were imprisoned and subsequently executed by Bolshevik revolutionaries in July 1918 in the city of Yekaterinburg.

Title: Invention of Dynamite
Dynamite is an explosive made of nitroglycerin, sorbents, and stabilizers. It was invented in 1867 to make the highly volatile nitroglycerin safer for transport and construction use. Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Mendelian inheritance
Mendelian inheritance is a type of biological inheritance that follows the principles originally proposed by Gregor Mendel in 1865 and 1866. It involves the concepts of dominant and recessive traits, forming the fundamental basis of classical genetics long before the discovery of DNA.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
The Catcher in the Rye is a groundbreaking novel by J.D. Salinger that explores themes of teenage angst and alienation. It was published in 1951 to widespread critical acclaim and occasional controversy. Its protagonist, Holden Caulfield, quickly became an icon for teenage rebellion.

Title: The Edge
David Howell Evans, better known by his stage name The Edge, is a musician who is the lead guitarist, keyboardist, and backing vocalist of the rock band U2.
