Title: Chile
Chile is a country located in western South America, occupying a long, narrow strip of land between the Andes to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west. It is known for its diverse geography, ranging from dry deserts in the north to alpine tundras in the south. The capital and largest city is Santiago.

Title: Cape Canaveral
Cape Canaveral is a headland in Brevard County, renowned globally as the epicenter of the American space program. The nearby Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station have hosted countless historic launches. Geographically, this vital aerospace hub is located on the eastern coast of Florida.

Title: Roger Waters
George Roger Waters is an English musician, singer-songwriter, and composer. In 1965, he co-founded the progressive rock band Pink Floyd. Following the departure of their original frontman, Waters became the band's primary lyricist and conceptual leader. He was born in Great Bookham, Surrey.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus. It is a highly radioactive element with the atomic number 92.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historic resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived in Springfield from 1837 until he moved to the White House in 1861. Today, it serves as the political and administrative heart of the state.

Title: Rhenium
Rhenium is a chemical element with the symbol Re and atomic number 75. It is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. Discovered in 1925, it was the last stable element to be discovered. It was named after the river Rhine in Europe.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in Figueres, the exact same town where he was born.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the 34th-largest by area, but the seventh-most populous. Its capital and largest city is Columbus. The state's northern border is defined heavily by its shoreline along Lake Erie, giving it access to major shipping routes.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist. She famously discovered the elements polonium and radium. Curie was born in Warsaw, in what was then the Kingdom of Poland, before moving to Paris to study.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Caucasus Mountains
The Caucasus Mountains are a mountain system at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Stretching between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, it is home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, towering at an impressive 5,642 meters.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known works of Antonio Vivaldi, who was born in the canal city of Venice.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the modern Czech Republic. Situated on the Vltava river, the city has a rich history spanning over a millennium. In the late 19th century, specifically the 1880s, Prague was a major provincial capital within the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Bruce Sabin was a prominent medical researcher who developed the live-virus oral polio vaccine, which played a foundational role in nearly eradicating the disease worldwide. Sabin was born in August 1906 to a Jewish family in the city of Białystok, which was then part of the Russian Empire but is situated in modern-day Poland.

Title: 1982 FIFA World Cup
The 1982 FIFA World Cup was the 12th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was played in Spain between June 13 and July 11, 1982. The tournament was ultimately won by Italy, who defeated West Germany 3-1 in the final match.

Title: Albert Camus
Albert Camus was a French philosopher, author, and journalist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature at the age of 44. He was born in 1913 in French Algeria and later moved to Paris, where he wrote masterpieces like "The Stranger" and "The Plague."

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
An induction motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction. This revolutionary device eliminated the need for mechanical commutators. The first practical alternating current induction motor was independently invented in the 1880s by a brilliant Serbian-American engineer.

Title: Yangtze
The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia, the third-longest in the world, and the longest in the world to flow entirely within one country. It rises in the northern part of the Tibetan Plateau and flows 6,300 kilometers in a generally easterly direction to the East China Sea. It empties into the sea near Shanghai, entirely within the borders of China.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the best orchestral compositions of the Baroque era, highlighting complex counterpoint and vibrant instrumentation.

Title: Artem Mikoyan
Artem Mikoyan was a Soviet aircraft designer of Armenian descent. Alongside Mikhail Gurevich, he designed many of the famous MiG military aircraft. Mikoyan was born in Sanahin, a small village situated in the rugged northern region of Armenia.

Title: Wright Flyer
The Wright Flyer was the first successful heavier-than-air powered aircraft. It was designed and built by a pair of pioneering brothers. The aircraft made four flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, marking the dawn of the aviation age and transforming global transportation.

Title: Idaho
Idaho is a state in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It borders Montana, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Washington, and Oregon. Known for its mountainous landscapes and vast wilderness areas, it was the birthplace of the famous sculptor who carved the faces of four presidents into a mountainside. Its capital and largest city is Boise.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po and atomic number 84. It is a rare and highly volatile metal. The element was discovered in 1898 by a prominent scientific couple studying pitchblende.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Carl Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He is one of the few individuals to have been awarded more than one Nobel Prize, having won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

Title: Theo van Gogh
Theodorus "Theo" van Gogh was a Dutch art dealer. He is best known as the younger brother of a deeply troubled, brilliant painter whom he supported financially and emotionally throughout his life. Theo's unwavering support allowed his brother to focus entirely on painting, though Theo tragically outlived him by only six months.

Title: 2012 Summer Olympics
The 2012 Summer Olympics were a major international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. It was the third time that the British capital had hosted the modern Olympic Games. The event followed the massive spectacle previously hosted by an East Asian nation four years prior.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent and the island of Tasmania. It is known for its rugged outback and coastal cities. The country successfully hosted the Summer Olympics at the turn of the millennium. The nation's capital is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team based in Kansas City, Missouri. The franchise was founded in 1959 as the Dallas Texans by businessman Lamar Hunt. The team famously competed in the very first Super Bowl, though they were defeated by their Midwestern rivals.

Title: Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant
The "Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant" is an autobiography by the former US president and Civil War general. Written as Grant was dying of throat cancer, the two-volume set was a massive critical and commercial success. It was published by Charles L. Webster & Company, a firm owned by a legendary American humorist.

Title: Curiosity Rover
Curiosity is a car-sized Mars rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission. It launched from Cape Canaveral in 2011 and successfully landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on Mars in 2012. It paved the way for subsequent rovers with its advanced landing systems.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is an island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the 18 regions of France. It is located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Functioning as a single territorial collectivity, the political and administrative capital city of Corsica is Ajaccio.

Title: Caroline Herschel
Caroline Lucretia Herschel was a German astronomer whose most significant contributions to astronomy were the discoveries of several comets, including the periodic comet 35P/Herschel–Rigollet and Comet C/1786 P1. She worked extensively alongside her older brother, assisting him with his own massive astronomical breakthroughs before earning independent fame.

Title: U2
U2 is an Irish rock band formed in Dublin in 1976. The group consists of a prominent lead vocalist known for his expressive vocal style, alongside The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. The band's early sound was rooted in post-punk but eventually grew to incorporate influences from many genres of popular music.

Title: Alexandria
Alexandria was a magnificent Mediterranean port city in ancient Egypt founded by Alexander the Great. During the Hellenistic period, it served as the bustling capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. It was renowned globally for its massive Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its Great Library.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he secured the prestigious 2004 Ballon d'Or. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a village located in Ukraine.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a rare and highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while they were investigating the cause of pitchblende's intense radioactivity. Marie Curie deliberately named the element after her home country of Poland. It holds the atomic number 84.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". During his lifetime, he was better known as the personal assistant of actor Sir Henry Irving and business manager of the Lyceum Theatre in London. Stoker was born in Dublin in 1847.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, which he named penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. It boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center dominated by its massive central cathedral, attracting millions of tourists each year.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: George W. Bush
George W. Bush served as the 43rd President of the United States, holding office from 2001 to 2009. He was the sitting president during the entirety of 2004, successfully running for re-election that November. Bush was born in New Haven, Connecticut, before his family relocated to the South.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The Irish Sea lies northwest of England and the Celtic Sea to the southwest. Historically, its territory served as the bloody battleground for the Wars of the Roses, including the decisive clash at Bosworth Field.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. The HMS Beagle spent significant time surveying its long, rugged coastline. The nation has a deeply agricultural economy, and its official currency is the Argentine peso.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. It remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was a key figure in the Romantic movement and was married to the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. Following her death in 1851, she was interred at St Peter's Church in Bournemouth.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought in June 1815 near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. It was a decisive clash that ended the prolonged era of European wars sparked by the French Revolution. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for Napoleon Bonaparte, permanently ending his rule as Emperor of the French.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: Politics of Spain in 2010
In 2010, Spain was grappling with the fallout of the global financial crisis. The nation's government was actively implementing austerity measures. During this time, the Spanish government was led by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). The sitting Prime Minister of Spain in 2010 was José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero.

Title: In Cold Blood
"In Cold Blood" is a non-fiction novel published in 1966. It details the 1959 murders of four members of the Clutter family in the small farming community of Holcomb, Kansas. The author spent years interviewing residents and investigators, accompanied by his close childhood friend, a famous female novelist.

Title: Instagram
Instagram is a photo and video-sharing social networking service founded in 2010 by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. The app distinguished itself by allowing users to apply digital filters to their photos. It grew incredibly fast and was acquired by Facebook Inc. (now Meta) in 2012 for approximately $1 billion.

Title: George Frideric Handel
George Frideric Handel was a German-British Baroque composer well known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, and organ concertos. He was born in 1685, the same year as Bach, in the German city of Halle, but he spent the bulk of his career working in London.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: Statue of Liberty
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical copper sculpture on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, it was designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. The statue was a gift to the United States from the people of France, intended to commemorate the alliance between the two nations during the American Revolution.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter: A Romance" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne, who conceives a daughter through an affair and struggles to create a new life of repentance and dignity.

Title: Denali
Denali, formerly known officially as Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain peak in North America, with a summit elevation of 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level. Located in the Alaska Range in the interior of the U.S. state of Alaska, it is a centerpiece of Denali National Park and Preserve.

Title: New Jersey
New Jersey is a state in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions of the United States. It is bordered by New York, the Atlantic Ocean, Delaware, and Pennsylvania. Despite being one of the smallest states by land area, it is highly populated. Its state capital is Trenton.

Title: Blue Origin
Blue Origin is an American privately funded aerospace manufacturer and sub-orbital spaceflight services company headquartered in Kent, Washington. Founded in 2000 by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, the company aims to make access to space cheaper and more reliable through reusable launch vehicles.

Title: Bengal Tiger
The Bengal Tiger is a population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies that is native to the Indian subcontinent. It is threatened by poaching and fragmentation of habitat. In biological classification, it is part of the phylum Chordata and the family Felidae.

Title: Rockville, Maryland
Rockville is a city and the county seat of Montgomery County, Maryland, United States, part of the Baltimore–Washington metropolitan area. It has historical significance and is home to the gravesite of legendary American novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, drawing literary tourists to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery.

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: Incandescent Light Bulb
The development of a commercially viable incandescent light bulb was achieved in the late 1870s by an American inventor working at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. The invention fundamentally altered modern society by providing widespread access to reliable, safe electric indoor lighting.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Herbert Hoover
Herbert Clark Hoover was an American politician and engineer who served as the 31st president of the United States from 1929 to 1933. A member of the Republican Party, he held office during the onset of the Great Depression. He was the sitting US President in 1930 when a future pioneering astronaut was born in Ohio.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Geography of Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. Its highly varied geography includes vast plateaus, the Pyrenees mountain range, and several island archipelagos. The absolute highest point in Spain is Mount Teide, a massive volcano situated in the Canary Islands.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Three Gorges Dam
The Three Gorges Dam is a massive hydroelectric gravity dam that spans a major waterway in central China. It is the world's largest power station in terms of installed capacity, generating immense amounts of electricity. The dam was constructed directly across the Yangtze River, permanently altering the region's ecology and landscape.

Title: Stanford University
Stanford University is a private research university located in Stanford, California. The campus occupies 8,180 acres, among the largest in the United States, and enrolls over 17,000 students. It is globally recognized for its proximity to Silicon Valley and has graduated numerous legendary tech founders and CEOs.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance. While his fame initially rested on his achievements as a painter, he also became known for his notebooks, in which he made drawings and notes on a variety of subjects, including anatomy, astronomy, botany, and cartography.

Title: Capitals of South Africa
South Africa distributes its governmental branches across three separate cities, rather than utilizing a single administrative center. Pretoria serves as the executive capital, Cape Town operates as the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein functions as the judicial capital, housing the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
The alternating current (AC) induction motor is an electric motor in which the current in the rotor is obtained by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding. This revolutionary device was invented by Nikola Tesla in the 1880s. Its development allowed for the efficient transmission of high-voltage electrical energy over massive distances.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at Waterloo, cementing his status as a British national hero.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The nation is known for its stunning historic castles, long tradition of brewing beer, and the intricate river systems that carve through its terrain.

Title: Economy of Mexico
The economy of Mexico is a developing market economy that relies heavily on exports, agriculture, and tourism. It is deeply integrated with the United States through trade agreements. The nation's official legal tender and currency is the Mexican peso, which is the most traded currency in Latin America.

Title: The Metamorphosis
The Metamorphosis is a famous surrealist novella published in 1915. It tells the story of salesman Gregor Samsa, who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The bizarre and highly influential narrative was written by the acclaimed author Franz Kafka.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. As Napoleon I, he was Emperor of the French from 1804 until 1814, and again in 1815. His quest for European domination finally ended in 1815 when he was crushed by coalition forces at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: California quail
The California quail, also known as the California valley quail, is a small ground-dwelling bird in the New World quail family. They have a curving crest or plume, made of six feathers, that droops forward. It is the official state bird of California.

Title: Edwin Hubble
Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing the fields of extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. Working primarily from the Mount Wilson Observatory, he proved that many objects previously thought to be clouds of dust and gas were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

Title: Genetics
Genetics is the study of genes, genetic variation, and heredity in organisms. It is an important branch in biology because heredity is vital to organisms' evolution. The modern era of genetics began with the rediscovery of 19th-century inheritance principles in the early 1900s.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and several overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and sports. The country boasts a diverse geography, ranging from coastal plains to the towering peaks of the Alps. The highest geographic point in France is Mont Blanc.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe with territories in the Caribbean. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, windmills, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses the nation's premier art institutions. The country's official and predominant language is Dutch.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville. Hawthorne worked for several years at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: Ronald Reagan
Ronald Reagan was an American politician and actor who served as the 40th president of the United States from 1981 to 1989. In 1980, he was conducting a successful presidential campaign, running on a platform of economic revitalization and strong national defense. He took office shortly after the historic 1980 Olympic games.

Title: Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, and natural philosopher. He is a key figure in the 17th-century Scientific Revolution, best known for his laws of planetary motion, which were published in works like "Astronomia nova". Kepler was born in the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt, part of the Holy Roman Empire.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous metropolitan area in the United States, serving as a global hub for finance, culture, and technology. It is situated on one of the world's largest natural harbors. Although it is a massive cultural powerhouse, it does not serve as the political center of the nation.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in 1912 in Ishpeming, a small city located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: 20-Dollar Bill
The United States twenty-dollar bill ($20) is a denomination of U.S. currency. Andrew Jackson, the seventh U.S. president, has been featured on the obverse of the bill since 1928, while the White House is featured on the reverse. It is one of the most heavily circulated bills in the American economy.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: The Edge
David Howell Evans, better known by his stage name The Edge, is a musician who is the lead guitarist, keyboardist, and backing vocalist of the rock band U2. He is known for his signature guitar sound, which involves rhythmic delay effects. He was born in Barking, Essex, before relocating to Ireland as a child.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. Known for its powerful economy and deep historical roots, its official currency is the Euro.

Title: Three Mile Island Accident
The Three Mile Island accident was a partial meltdown of a nuclear reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. It occurred on March 28, 1979, and remains the most significant accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power plant history. The incident led to sweeping changes in nuclear regulatory policies.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters, it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres. It is a prominent, towering peak within the massive Andes mountain range.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. The town is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist, who also designed the town's famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where he is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Sully Prudhomme
René François Armand (Sully) Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist. He was a prominent figure in the Parnassian movement, which sought to restore elegance and precision to French poetry. He made history as the very first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Sully Prudhomme was born in 1839 in Paris, France.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: Discovery of Hydrogen
While artificially produced earlier by others, hydrogen was first recognized as a distinct chemical element in 1766. The English scientist Henry Cavendish was the first to identify hydrogen gas as a discrete substance, naming it "inflammable air" and noting that it produced water when burned.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He achieved worldwide fame as the author of "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Although he spent most of his life and career in England, he was born in January 1892 in the Orange Free State, a territory that later became part of South Africa.

Title: LeBron James
LeBron James is an American professional basketball player who is widely considered one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He famously returned to his home state's team in 2014, promising to bring them a championship. He fulfilled that promise in 2016, earning unanimous Finals MVP honors for his performance.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage in 1831. The expedition famously carried the young English naturalist Charles Darwin, allowing him to conduct crucial field research in the Galápagos Islands.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". After a highly successful career, Vivaldi died in poverty in Vienna on July 28, 1741.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: Invention of Dynamite
Dynamite is an explosive made of nitroglycerin, sorbents, and stabilizers. It was invented in 1867 to make the highly volatile nitroglycerin safer for transport and construction use. The invention was incredibly successful, making its creator vastly wealthy and providing the funds for a series of famous international prizes.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high fantasy novels published between 1950 and 1956. Set in the fictional realm of Narnia, a fantasy world of magic, mythical beasts, and talking animals, the series follows the adventures of various children who play central roles in the unfolding history of that world.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Microsoft
Microsoft Corporation is an American multinational technology corporation which produces computer software, consumer electronics, personal computers, and related services. Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, its best-known software products are the Windows line of operating systems and the Office suite. Its global corporate headquarters is situated in Redmond, Washington.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named after the recently discovered planet Uranus, and its standard chemical symbol is U.

Title: Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Martin Heinrich Klaproth was a pioneering German chemist who was a major figure in the early development of analytical chemistry. He is best known for his discovery of several chemical elements. In 1789, he discovered the element Uranium. That same year, while analyzing a gemstone from Sri Lanka, he also discovered the element Zirconium.

Title: 1749 in Great Britain
The year 1749 in Great Britain saw the end of the War of the Austrian Succession and the subsequent signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. It was also the birth year of several notable figures, including the scientist who would eventually conquer smallpox. During this time, the British throne was occupied by a monarch of the House of Hanover.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Economy of Argentina
The economy of Argentina relies heavily on natural resources, an export-oriented agricultural sector, and a diversified industrial base. Historically, the nation has struggled with severe inflation and currency crises. In the late 1980s, its official currency was the Argentine austral, which was later replaced by the peso.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal in the actinide series. The element was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101. It was first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, and their team at the University of California, Berkeley. This monumental breakthrough in nuclear chemistry was achieved in early 1955.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was designed by a foreign architect who won an international competition.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It is the political, economic, and cultural center of Spain, housing the national parliament where the Prime Minister governs.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is globally famous for its vibrant culture, the Amazon rainforest, and its unmatched success in international football. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Brasília, which was inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Title: 1950 FIFA World Cup
The 1950 FIFA World Cup was the fourth edition of the tournament, held in Brazil after a twelve-year hiatus caused by World War II. The decisive match of the tournament saw a stunning upset when the underdog Uruguayan national team defeated the host nation before a record crowd at the Maracanã Stadium.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: The Beach Boys
The Beach Boys are an American rock band formed in Hawthorne, California, in 1961. The group's original lineup consisted of brothers Brian, Dennis, and Carl Wilson, their cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. They emerged as major rivals to British invasion bands during the 1960s.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
The Space Age was inaugurated by the successful launch of the very first artificial Earth satellite in 1957. The spherical, beachball-sized object, which featured four external radio antennas, sent shockwaves through the global political landscape and triggered the intense Space Race. This historic satellite was named Sputnik 1.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo, cementing his status as a legendary military hero.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. A radioactive actinide metal, neptunium is the first transuranic element. Its discovery in 1940 at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson continued the tradition of naming elements after the outer planets of the Solar System.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California. It designs, manufactures, and sells consumer electronics, computer software, and online services. The company was founded by a college dropout who envisioned a user-friendly personal computer, launching a trillion-dollar empire.

Title: 1991 Rugby World Cup
The 1991 Rugby World Cup was the second edition of the tournament and was hosted primarily in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and France. The final match was played at Twickenham Stadium, where Australia defeated England to claim their first world title.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is characterized by the vast Amazon basin in the north and a complex system of mountain ranges in the south. The highest mountain in Brazil is Pico da Neblina, which is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border.

Title: British Empire
The British Empire was composed of the dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates, and other territories ruled or administered by the United Kingdom. At its height, it was the largest empire in history. Its power was centralized in the capital city of London, situated along the banks of the River Thames.

Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. The massive critical and commercial success was co-directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, establishing DreamWorks Animation as a prime competitor in the feature animation industry.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch and struck the left wing, severely damaging the thermal protection system.

Title: Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive alkaline earth metal with the atomic number 88. It was discovered alongside polonium by the Curies in 1898. Its name is derived from the Latin word for ray, recognizing its immense power to emit ionizing radiation.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers decisively defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a remote volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most isolated islands in the world. Following his devastating defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to this British-controlled island, where he ultimately died in 1821.

Title: Museo del Prado
The Museo del Prado is the main Spanish national art museum, located in central Madrid. It houses an extensive collection of European art, including its most famous work, Las Meninas. The building that houses the museum was designed by the renowned neoclassical architect Juan de Villanueva.

Title: Votka River
The Votka is a river in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, and a right tributary of the Shiva River. It flows for roughly 66 kilometers through a rolling landscape before running directly through the center of the industrial town of Votkinsk, where an artificial dam was constructed to power the town's historic metal factories.

Title: 1856 in Great Britain
The year 1856 in Great Britain was marked by the end of the Crimean War with the signing of the Treaty of Paris. The country was undergoing rapid industrialization and scientific advancement during this period. The nation and its growing empire were under the steady rule of Queen Victoria.

Title: Wars of the Roses
The Wars of the Roses were a series of English civil wars for control of the throne of England fought between supporters of two rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet: the House of Lancaster and the House of York. The grueling conflict dominated the latter half of the 15th century.

Title: Battle of Hastings
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, the Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It was a decisive Norman victory that radically altered the course of English history and language.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event that was held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The massive global sporting event was hosted in Atlanta, Georgia, representing a massive cultural milestone for the United States.

Title: Arno River
The Arno is a river in the Tuscany region of Italy. It is the most important river of central Italy after the Tiber. The river famously flows through the city of Florence, passing under the iconic Ponte Vecchio bridge, and has historically fueled the commerce of the region.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including the iconic Mona Lisa. In the 1980s, the museum underwent a major modernization project that added a large, controversial glass pyramid to its main courtyard.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. Plutonium was first synthetically produced and isolated in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: 1797 in Great Britain
The year 1797 in Great Britain was marked by several significant historical events, including the Battle of Cape St Vincent and widespread naval mutinies at Spithead and the Nore. It was also a notable year in literature, serving as the birth year of several prominent literary figures, including the future creator of a legendary literary monster.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
"To Kill a Mockingbird" is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in high schools and middle schools in the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot and characters are loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: The House of the Spirits
"The House of the Spirits" is the 1982 debut novel of a prominent South American author. The novel incorporates elements of magic realism to trace the lives of the Trueba family across four generations. It became an immediate international best-seller and was later adapted into a major motion picture.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe, known for its deep history in philosophy, science, and the arts. Following a fragmented history within the Holy Roman Empire, it unified into a modern nation-state in the 19th century. Its capital and most populous city is Berlin, a major center for politics and culture.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and philosophy. It was frequently at war with its northern island neighbor over territorial disputes. France is a founding member of the European Union and uses the Euro as its currency.

Title: José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero
José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero is a Spanish politician and member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). He served as the Prime Minister of Spain from 2004 to 2011. Zapatero was born on August 4, 1960, in Valladolid, a historic city in northwestern Spain.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom, occupying the northern third of the island of Great Britain. While it maintained its own distinct legal and educational systems, its legislative union with England occurred in 1707. It did not achieve separate sovereign legislative independence during the 20th century.

Title: Of Mice and Men
"Of Mice and Men" is a novella written by a prominent American author and published in 1937. It tells the story of George Milton and Lennie Small, two displaced migrant ranch workers who move from place to place in California in search of new job opportunities during the Great Depression.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a south Slav nationalist group seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Archduke and his wife. Princip was born in the rural village of Obljaj, located in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: Back in Black
"Back in Black" is the seventh studio album by Australian rock band AC/DC, released in 1980. It was the band's first album to feature lead singer Brian Johnson, following the death of previous lead singer Bon Scott. It was an enormous commercial success and remains one of the highest-selling albums in music history.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: The Planets
"The Planets", Op. 32, is a seven-movement orchestral suite by a prominent English composer, written between 1914 and 1917. Each movement of the suite is named after a planet of the Solar System and its corresponding astrological character, such as "Mars, the Bringer of War."

Title: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
The Salk Institute for Biological Studies is an independent, non-profit, scientific research institute located in the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla. Founded in 1960 by a pioneering virologist, it is renowned for its striking modernist architecture and its massive contributions to molecular biology and genetics.

Title: Lansing, Michigan
Lansing is the capital of the U.S. state of Michigan. It is mostly located in Ingham County, although portions of the city extend west into Eaton County and north into Clinton County. The city became the state capital in 1847, taking over the role from Detroit, to provide a more centralized government location.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel, a popular form that included both singing and spoken dialogue, in two acts. It premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before the composer's premature death. It is celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Mick Jagger
Sir Michael Philip Jagger is an English singer, songwriter, actor, and film producer who has gained worldwide fame as the lead vocalist and one of the founder members of the Rolling Stones. Jagger was born into a middle-class family in Dartford, Kent, England.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it features a swirling night sky, a crescent moon, and a bright Venus over a quiet village. It is regarded as among Van Gogh's finest works and has been a permanent fixture in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage. The expedition famously allowed a young naturalist to conduct crucial field research during a five-week stop at a remote volcanic archipelago in 1835.

Title: Black Sea
The Black Sea is a marginal mediterranean sea of the Atlantic Ocean lying between Europe and Asia. It is supplied by major rivers, principally the Danube, Dnieper, and Don. It is a critical geostrategic waterway connecting Eastern Europe to the broader Mediterranean.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was highly anticipated, given the rapid advancements in theoretical physics during the early 20th century. The committee ultimately awarded the prize to Albert Einstein. The award was explicitly given "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect."

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Pinker or George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a small town in British India.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: History of Colombia
Colombia boasts a rich and complex history, marked by indigenous civilizations, European conquest, and the struggle for independence. The territory was colonized by the Spanish Empire in the early 16th century and remained under the firm control of Spain until gaining its independence in 1810.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel that introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries. It was written by an Irish author who was heavily inspired by Eastern European folklore.

Title: Marie Antoinette
Marie Antoinette was the last Queen of France before the French Revolution. Known for her extravagant lifestyle, she became a symbol of the monarchy's disconnect from the struggles of everyday citizens. She was executed by guillotine several months after her husband.

Title: Rockville, Maryland
Rockville is a city and the county seat of Montgomery County, Maryland, United States, part of the Baltimore–Washington metropolitan area. It has historical significance and is home to the gravesite of legendary American novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, drawing literary tourists to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is an island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the 18 regions of France. It is located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Functioning as a single territorial collectivity, the political and administrative capital city of Corsica is Ajaccio.

Title: Discovery of Streptomycin
Streptomycin was the first antibiotic remedy for tuberculosis. It was discovered in 1943 by Albert Schatz in the laboratory of Selman Waksman at Rutgers University. Unlike earlier antibiotics derived from molds, this drug was isolated from a soil-dwelling bacterium known as Streptomyces griseus.

Title: The Electron
The electron is a subatomic particle with a negative one elementary electric charge. It belongs to the first generation of the lepton particle family, and is generally thought to be an elementary particle because it has no known components or substructure. It was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, identified by physicist J.J. Thomson.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history for centuries. Its capital and largest city is Paris, which serves as a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: Pete Sampras
Pete Sampras is an American former professional tennis player. Known for his powerful serve, he dominated the grass courts of Wimbledon in the 1990s, winning the tournament a staggering seven times. His longest consecutive winning streak at the event, however, capped out at four consecutive titles.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May on guitar, Roger Taylor on drums, John Deacon on bass, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: Mulhacén
Mulhacén is the highest mountain in continental Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, with an elevation of 3,479 meters. Located in the Sierra Nevada range in Andalusia, it is a prominent peak, but it is surpassed in overall elevation by a volcanic peak located in the Spanish overseas territories.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed sovereign country known for its vast natural resources and major mining sector. The nation has a strong, mixed-market economy. Its official currency is the Australian dollar, which is also used by several independent Pacific Island states.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: Brian Johnson
Brian Johnson is an English singer and songwriter. In 1980, he became the lead singer of the rock band AC/DC following the death of Bon Scott. His distinctive, powerful rock vocals debuted on the legendary album "Back in Black". Johnson was born in Dunston, a area within the town of Gateshead, located in North East England on the island of Great Britain.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. Geographically, the city is situated along the banks of the Yamuna River, which has historically sustained its populace.

Title: Spirited Away
"Spirited Away" is a 2001 animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It tells the story of Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who wanders into the world of kami while moving to a new neighborhood. It was incredibly successful, winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Warren G. Harding
Warren Gamaliel Harding was the 29th president of the United States, serving from 1921 until his death in 1923. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency promised a "return to normalcy" after the grueling years of World War I, though his administration was later marred by the Teapot Dome scandal.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, ending his reign as Emperor of the French.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Title: Inactivated Polio Vaccine
The first successful polio vaccine was an inactivated version developed in the early 1950s. Requiring an injection, it was declared safe and effective after a massive nationwide field trial in 1955. The medical researcher who led its creation became an international hero but chose not to patent his formula.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned and constructed by the powerful Mughal Empire as a monumental tomb. Today, it is universally admired as a masterpiece of world heritage and Islamic architecture.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate and investor. He was the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Apple. Jobs famously dropped out of Reed College in Oregon after only one semester, though he continued to audit classes. He went on to revolutionize the personal computing, music, and mobile phone industries.

Title: Lactuca sativa
Lactuca sativa is the formal scientific name for the species of plant commonly known as lettuce. Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians, it was transformed from a weed whose seeds were used to extract oil into a plant grown for its edible leaves. The species is now farmed extensively worldwide.

Title: The Ed Sullivan Show (1964)
On February 9, 1964, a record-breaking 73 million viewers tuned into The Ed Sullivan Show. The broadcast featured the highly anticipated first live US television performance of the British musical group that would go on to record "Abbey Road". The event is considered a watershed moment in American pop culture history.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville, who famously dedicated his masterpiece about a white whale to Hawthorne. Hawthorne later worked at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: Middlemarch
"Middlemarch, A Study of Provincial Life" is a novel published in eight installments in 1871 and 1872. It is widely recognized as one of the greatest novels in the English language. Like many acclaimed Victorian novels of its era, it was published under a male pseudonym.

Title: Mick Jagger
Sir Michael Philip Jagger is an English singer, songwriter, actor, and film producer who has gained worldwide fame as the lead vocalist and one of the founder members of the Rolling Stones. Jagger was born into a middle-class family in Dartford, Kent, England.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal in the actinide series. The element was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Battle of Pharsalus
The Battle of Pharsalus was a decisive battle of Caesar's Civil War, fought in 48 BC. Julius Caesar decisively defeated the troops of the Roman Senate, led by Pompey the Great. The victory allowed Caesar to assume total control over the Roman Republic, laying the groundwork for the later Empire.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a highly acclaimed architect notable for his visionary, organic style of modern architecture. He won an international competition to design the new opera house in Sydney, a project that defined his career despite subsequent controversies. Utzon was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 1918.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: John Williams
John Towner Williams is an American composer, conductor, and pianist. In a career spanning seven decades, he has composed some of the most popular, recognizable, and critically acclaimed film scores in cinematic history, including the "Imperial March". He is highly noted for his long-standing, prolific collaboration with film director Steven Spielberg.

Title: Battersea Power Station
Battersea Power Station is a decommissioned coal-fired power station located on the south bank of a major waterway in Nine Elms, London. With its four distinctive art deco chimneys, it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks and gained global pop culture fame after appearing on a 1977 rock album cover.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in Ishpeming, located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Voyage of the Beagle
From 1831 to 1836, a British naval vessel conducted a major hydrographic survey expedition around South America. Among the passengers was a young English naturalist who collected extensive geological and biological specimens. In September 1835, the expedition arrived at the remote Galápagos Islands, providing vital data for his future evolutionary theories.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes.
