Title: 1853 in the United Kingdom
The year 1853 in the United Kingdom was marked by the early stages of the Crimean War and continued industrial expansion. During this time, the British Empire was expanding globally under the steady rule of a long-reigning monarch.

Title: Brooklyn Bridge
The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City. Opened in May 1883, it spans the East River, connecting the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn. It was the first steel-wire suspension bridge ever constructed and remains an iconic feature of the city's skyline.

Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Title: The Descent of Man
"The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" is a book by English naturalist Charles Darwin, first published in 1871. Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: Oxford University
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of 39 constituent colleges and a range of academic departments, where legendary authors and philologists have taught over the centuries.

Title: Wright Brothers
Orville and Wilbur Wright, collectively known as the Wright Brothers, were aviation pioneers generally credited with inventing, building, and flying the world's first successful motor-operated airplane. Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while investigating pitchblende. The element holds the atomic number 84, and was deliberately named after Marie Curie's birth country of Poland to highlight its struggle for independence.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. He was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: The Black Death
The Black Death was a devastating global epidemic of bubonic plague that struck Europe and Asia in the mid-1300s. It killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people, fundamentally altering the demographic and economic landscape of the medieval world long before the modernization of European cities.

Title: Koala
The koala is an arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to the eastern and southern coasts of Australia. It is easily recognizable by its stout, tailless body and large head with round, fluffy ears. Despite their bear-like appearance, they are closely related to wombats and kangaroos.

Title: 1871 in Great Britain

Title: Harvard University
Harvard University is a private Ivy League research university in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Founded in 1636, it is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. Title: Benjamin Franklin
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath, writer, scientist, inventor, statesman, and diplomat. A successful printer by trade, he established an Ivy League university in Philadelphia and famously published a wildly popular annual almanac under a pseudonym.

Title: Sickle cell anemia
Sickle cell anemia is a genetic blood disorder characterized by red blood cells that assume an abnormal, rigid, sickle shape. This decreases the cells' flexibility and results in a risk of various life-threatening complications. In 1949, Linus Pauling demonstrated that the disease occurs due to a mutation in a specific metalloprotein.

Title: Outbreak of World War II
World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. In response to this aggression, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. This conflict would eventually embroil nearly every nation on Earth, making it the deadliest and most widespread war in human history.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14, popularly known as the "Moonlight Sonata", is a piano sonata completed in 1801 and dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi. Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Cleopatra VII Philopator was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Title: First French Empire
The First French Empire, officially the French Republic until 1809 and then the French Empire, was the empire ruled by Napoleon Bonaparte. At its height, the empire dominated continental Europe. HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage in 1831. Title: Safavid Empire
The Safavid Empire was one of the most significant ruling dynasties of Iran, considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. Title: Percy Bysshe Shelley

It has a rich history as a global center for art, philosophy, and science, having hosted numerous legendary expatriate painters during the 19th and 20th centuries. Today, as a key member of the European Union, France uses the Euro as its official currency.

Title: 2004 UEFA Champions League Final
The 2004 UEFA Champions League Final was a football match played at the Arena AufSchalke in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, to decide the winner of the 2003-04 UEFA Champions League. The match was won by FC Porto, who defeated AS Monaco 3-0 to claim the prestigious European title.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: Smallpox vaccine
The smallpox vaccine was the first vaccine ever successfully developed. It was introduced in the late 18th century after a physician observed that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox were immune to smallpox. The global administration of this vaccine eventually led to the complete eradication of the disease in 1980.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and a massive football legacy. The country shares several mountain peaks with its neighbors, including Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.

Title: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech for NASA. Located in La Cañada Flintridge, California, JPL is responsible for the construction and operation of robotic planetary spacecraft, including the agency's famous fleet of Martian rovers.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. Known for its distinct biodiversity and stunning landscapes, it operates with a highly developed free-market economy. The country's official currency is the New Zealand dollar.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: Monaco
Monaco is a sovereign city-state and microstate on the French Riviera. It is bordered by France to the north, east, and west, and by the Mediterranean Sea to the south. Covering just over two square kilometers, it is the second-smallest independent state in the world, trailing only a religious enclave located in Rome.

Title: 2016 NBA Finals
The 2016 NBA Finals was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's 2015–16 season. The series is legendary for featuring the first-ever comeback from a 3-1 series deficit in Finals history. The Cleveland Cavaliers successfully pulled off this miracle to defeat the 73-9 Golden State Warriors in game 7.

Title: Kramer vs. Kramer
"Kramer vs. Kramer" is an American legal drama film that explores the psychological impact of a bitter divorce and custody battle. Released in 1979, the film was a massive critical and commercial success. It won five Academy Awards at the 52nd Oscars, including the highly coveted award for Best Picture.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Rosalind Franklin
Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose work was central to the understanding of the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, viruses, and coal. Her famous Photo 51 was critical in determining the double helix structure of DNA, though she died before the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery.

Title: Nevada
Nevada is a state in the Western United States, defined by its expansive desert landscapes and the vibrant metropolis of Las Vegas. The state is highly arid and contains the sprawling Nevada Test Site. The highest natural point within the state's borders is Boundary Peak, standing at an elevation of 13,147 feet.

Title: Brian May
Brian Harold May is an English musician and astrophysicist. He achieved worldwide fame as the lead guitarist of the rock band Queen. Known for his distinctive guitar work on his home-built "Red Special", he was born and raised in Hampton, a suburban area of London.

Title: James Watson
James Dewey Watson is an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist. He co-authored the 1953 academic paper proposing the double helix structure of the DNA molecule. Watson was born in Chicago, Illinois, and traveled to England specifically to work at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Centre Pompidou
The Centre Pompidou is a complex building in the Beaubourg area of the 4th arrondissement of Paris. It houses the Public Information Library and the largest museum for modern art in Europe. The building was designed in the style of high-tech architecture by the architectural team of Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age, most notably "The Great Gatsby". His turbulent personal life, marked by alcoholism and financial struggles, was closely intertwined with the deteriorating mental health of his wife.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. He was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of internet infrastructure like ARPANET. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the Potomac River.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: Los Angeles
Los Angeles is the largest city in California and the second-most populous city in the United States. It is a massive global center for entertainment, media, and technology. Although it has a robust biomedical sector, its research institutes are distinct from the coastal scientific hubs found further south.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Orlando Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in 1901 in Canton, a small city located in South Dakota.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: French Guiana
French Guiana is an overseas department and region of France, located on the northern coast of South America. It borders Brazil to the east and south and Suriname to the west. Because it is a part of France, it is the only territory of the mainland Americas to be part of the European Union.

Title: The House of the Spirits
"The House of the Spirits" is the 1982 debut novel of a prominent South American author. The novel incorporates elements of magic realism to trace the lives of the Trueba family across four generations. It became an immediate international best-seller and was later adapted into a major motion picture.

Title: Ulysses S. Grant
Ulysses S. Grant was an American military officer and politician who served as the 18th president of the United States from 1869 to 1877. As Commanding General, he led the Union Army to victory in the American Civil War. In his final days, facing financial ruin, he wrote a highly successful set of memoirs, which were published by a famous author friend.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1922
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr. He received the honor "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." Bohr's atomic model revolutionized the understanding of subatomic structures and quantum mechanics.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel, a popular form that included both singing and spoken dialogue, in two acts. It premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before the composer's premature death. It is celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Spain
Spain is a country in Southwestern Europe with some pockets of territory across the Strait of Gibraltar. It has a deeply rich artistic heritage, having produced masters like Velázquez, Goya, and Picasso. Culturally and politically unified, the official and most widely spoken language of the nation is Spanish.

Title: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées is an entertainment venue situated at 15 avenue Montaigne in Paris. Despite its name, it is not located on the Champs-Élysées. Opened in 1913, the theater was specifically designed to host contemporary opera and dance, making it the perfect, albeit volatile, setting for radical new works.

Title: Polio Vaccines
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis. The first breakthrough was an inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which requires injection and utilizes a killed version of the virus. Shortly after, a cheaper, oral polio vaccine (OPV) using an attenuated live virus was developed, which became the standard in global eradication efforts.

Title: Salem, Massachusetts
Salem is a historic coastal city in Essex County, Massachusetts, located on the North Shore. Known heavily for its 1692 witch trials, it was also a major maritime port in early American history, requiring a substantial customs operation.

Title: Bruce Beresford
Bruce Beresford is an Australian film director who has made more than 30 feature films over a 50-year career. He is widely acclaimed for his versatility across genres. He reached the pinnacle of Hollywood success when he directed "Driving Miss Daisy", which won the Best Picture Oscar for the films of 1989.

Title: 2008 Summer Olympics
The 2008 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIX Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held from August 8 to 24, 2008. The games were a massive global spectacle and marked a significant moment of international integration. They were hosted in Beijing, the capital city of China.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned and constructed by the powerful Mughal Empire as a monumental tomb. Today, it is universally admired as a masterpiece of world heritage and Islamic architecture.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is globally famous for its vibrant culture, the Amazon rainforest, and its unmatched success in international football. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Brasília, which was inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Title: Cloning of Dolly
The scientific world was fundamentally altered by a major breakthrough at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Using the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer, researchers successfully cloned a female domestic sheep from an adult somatic cell. This historic mammal, affectionately named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996.

Title: Economy of Ecuador
Ecuador relies heavily on its petroleum resources and agricultural exports. Following a severe economic crisis and devastating hyperinflation in the late 1990s, the national government abandoned its original currency, the sucre. In the year 2000, Ecuador officially adopted the United States dollar as its legal tender and currency.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe in the early 19th century. He was born to a minor Italian noble family on the island of Corsica, mere months after it was acquired by France.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Carl Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He is one of the few individuals to have been awarded more than one Nobel Prize, having won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

Title: Texas
Texas is the second-largest U.S. state by both area and population, known for its massive energy sector and distinct cultural identity. It is heavily associated with the Bush political family, who built their fortunes and political careers there. George W. Bush served as the Governor of Texas prior to his presidency.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians such as Beethoven and Mozart spent their prime years working there. The city center features the towering Gothic spire of St. Stephen's Cathedral.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is the smallest state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority, and official head of state, is the Pope.

Title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, occurred on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo. They were mortally wounded by Gavrilo Princip, an event that directly triggered the outbreak of World War I.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed sovereign country known for its vast natural resources and major mining sector. The nation has a strong, mixed-market economy. Its official currency is the Australian dollar, which is also used by several independent Pacific Island states.

Title: French Open
The French Open, also known as Roland-Garros, is a major tennis tournament held over two weeks at the Stade Roland Garros in Paris. It is the premier clay court championship in the world. The men's singles winner is awarded the Coupe des Mousquetaires.

Title: Ronald Reagan
Ronald Reagan was an American politician and actor who served as the 40th president of the United States from 1981 to 1989. In 1980, he was conducting a successful presidential campaign, running on a platform of economic revitalization and strong national defense. He took office shortly after the historic 1980 Olympic games.

Title: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 is a supertall skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. It officially held the title of the world's tallest building from its opening in 2004 until the completion of a taller megastructure in Dubai in 2009. The building was designed by C.Y. Lee & Partners to withstand the region's frequent typhoons and earthquakes.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses. The reigning monarch at the time personally directed firefighting efforts from the river.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when Alexander Fleming noticed that a specific blue-green mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying bacteria.

Title: Trinity Test
The Trinity test was the world's first successful detonation of a nuclear weapon. Conducted by the United States Army on July 16, 1945, as part of the Manhattan Project, the test involved an implosion-design plutonium device. The monumental explosion took place in the Jornada del Muerto desert region of New Mexico.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element. Their discoveries fundamentally changed the scientific understanding of atomic structures and radiation.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World", set in a dystopian future. Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: Kobe Bryant
Kobe Bryant was an American professional basketball player who spent his entire 20-year career with the Los Angeles Lakers. He entered the NBA directly from high school, famously bypassing the traditional college basketball route, and went on to win five NBA championships.

Title: 1962 FIFA World Cup
The 1962 FIFA World Cup was the seventh edition of the international football tournament. Hosted by Chile, the event saw fierce competition and several highly physical matches. In the end, the defending champions, Brazil, successfully retained their title by defeating Czechoslovakia 3-1 in the final.

Title: Austrian Empire in 1822
The Austrian Empire was a multi-national empire and one of Europe's great powers. In 1822, the empire was navigating the conservative post-Napoleonic era orchestrated by Klemens von Metternich. During this entire period, the empire was ruled by Emperor Francis I.

Title: Cerium
Cerium is a chemical element with the symbol Ce and atomic number 58. It is a soft, ductile, and silvery-white metal that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was independently discovered by Martin Heinrich Klaproth alongside other European chemists in 1803. It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and technological influence. It is home to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, where many actinide series elements were discovered. Its highest natural point is Mount Whitney.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: John Cadbury
John Cadbury was a British businessman and the founder of the Cadbury chocolate company. Originating in Birmingham, England, he initially sold tea, coffee, and drinking chocolate. The company later grew into one of the world's most massive confectionery brands, helping popularize boxed chocolates in the 19th century.

Title: Vantaa River
The Vantaa River is a prominent 101-kilometer-long waterway in Southern Finland. It originates from Lake Erkylänjärvi and flows into the Gulf of Finland. The river heavily shapes the geography of the Finnish capital, providing both scenic value and historical routes for trade.

Title: Newport Mansions
The Newport Mansions are a collection of historic estates located in Newport, Rhode Island. Many of these opulent "summer cottages" were built by wealthy industrialist families, such as the Vanderbilts and Astors, during the Gilded Age. They serve as a testament to the extreme wealth generated during the era.

Title: William Herschel
William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer who revolutionized the study of the cosmos. In addition to cataloging nebulae and discovering several moons, his most famous achievement occurred in 1781. It was then that he discovered the planet Uranus, expanding the known boundaries of the solar system.

Title: Battle of Actium
The Battle of Actium was a decisive naval engagement in 31 BC between the forces of Octavian (the future Emperor Augustus) and the combined fleets of Mark Antony and his powerful queen ally. Octavian's victory secured his undisputed control over the Roman world and marked the end of the Hellenistic Period.

Title: Galilean Moons
The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. They were discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 using a highly improved telescope. Their discovery proved that not all celestial bodies orbit the Earth, fundamentally shifting astronomical understanding.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time. Their breakthrough in the United States occurred in February 1964 with a legendary live television appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Black Elk Peak
Black Elk Peak is the highest natural point in South Dakota, standing at an elevation of 7,244 feet (2,208 m). Formerly known as Harney Peak, it is located in the Black Hills National Forest in Pennington County. It represents the highest summit in the United States east of the Rocky Mountains.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist. She famously discovered the elements polonium and radium. Curie was born in Warsaw, in what was then the Kingdom of Poland, before moving to Paris to study.

Title: Element 101
Atomic number 101 belongs to a synthetic element in the actinide series of the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive metallic element. It was deliberately named in honor of the legendary Russian chemist who created the first definitive periodic table.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. Despite its close economic ties with its neighbors, it is not a member of the European Union. The official currency of Norway is the Norwegian krone.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: The Shining (film)
"The Shining" is a 1980 psychological horror film based on Stephen King's 1977 novel of the same name. The film stars Jack Nicholson as Jack Torrance, an aspiring writer and recovering alcoholic who accepts a position as the off-season caretaker of the isolated Overlook Hotel. It was directed by the acclaimed filmmaker Stanley Kubrick.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is globally famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. Nobel was born in 1833 in Stockholm, the capital city of Sweden.

Title: 1913 Paris Ballet Riot
In 1913, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris hosted the premiere of a radical new ballet. The performance featured dissonant, avant-garde music and jerky, non-traditional choreography. The audience was so outraged by the shocking departure from classical traditions that a literal riot broke out in the theater.

Title: The "Hand of God" Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who scored it later described the goal as being made "a little with the head... and a little with the hand of God."

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most remote islands in the world. It gained immense historical infamy as the final, inescapable site of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte. The island is currently controlled as a British Overseas Territory by the United Kingdom.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying, mapping and sequencing all of the genes of the human genome. It remains the world's largest collaborative biological project, completed in 2003.

Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. The massive critical and commercial success was co-directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, establishing DreamWorks Animation as a prime competitor in the feature animation industry.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne. It opens with a dense introductory chapter titled "The Custom-House."

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis.

Title: Toropets
Toropets is a historic town and the administrative center of Toropetsky District in Tver Oblast, Russia. It is located where the Toropa River flows through Lake Solomen. First mentioned in chronicles in 1074, it is one of the oldest settlements in the western part of the country, boasting numerous historic churches.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: Napoleon's Final Exile
Following his catastrophic defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was captured and stripped of his imperial titles. To ensure he could never return to threaten European peace, his captors exiled him to Saint Helena, a remarkably remote island in the South Atlantic Ocean, where he eventually died in 1821.

Title: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a massive country in South Asia. It achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation was the birthplace of several major literary figures during the colonial era. The political and administrative capital of India is New Delhi.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer. He is widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague, which is the capital city of the modern-day country of the Czech Republic.

Title: 1812 Overture
The "Year 1812" Solemn Overture is a concert overture written in 1880 by a legendary Russian Romantic composer. The piece was written to commemorate Russia's successful defense against Napoleon's invading Grande Armée in 1812. It is globally famous for its dramatic, booming climax, which features live cannon fire and ringing church bells.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The setting of The Count of Monte Cristo includes various locations in Italy, particularly Rome and the Tuscan Archipelago. Italy is also a Eurozone member.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: Europium
Europium is a chemical element with the symbol Eu and atomic number 63. It is the most reactive lanthanide and must be stored under an inert fluid to protect it from atmospheric oxygen or moisture. It is named after the continent of Europe and is widely used as a red phosphor in television sets.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: Leo Tolstoy
Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy, usually referred to in English as Leo Tolstoy, was a Russian writer who is regarded as one of the greatest authors of all time. He is best known for his epic novels "War and Peace" and "Anna Karenina". He died of pneumonia at the Astapovo railway station in 1910.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. It is known for its medieval towns, Renaissance architecture, and as the headquarters of the European Union. Belgium is a multilingual country with three official languages: Dutch, French, and German.

Title: George Westinghouse
George Westinghouse Jr. was an American entrepreneur and engineer based in Pennsylvania who created the railway air brake. He was a pioneer of the electrical industry, acquiring the patents for the AC induction motor and backing the alternating current system to fiercely compete against Thomas Edison's direct current networks.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe, known for its significant cultural, political, and military influence throughout history. It formerly ruled numerous colonies in the Caribbean, including Haiti. The capital and largest city is Paris, a global center for art and philosophy.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: James II of England
James II and VII was King of England and Ireland as James II and King of Scotland as James VII. He succeeded his brother Charles II in 1685. His Catholicism and his absolute rule alienated the English political elite. During the Glorious Revolution of 1688, he was deposed and fled across the English Channel to seek refuge in a neighboring country.

Title: Ural Mountains
The Ural Mountains, or simply the Urals, are a mountain range that runs from north to south through western Russia, from the coast of the Arctic Ocean to the river Ural and northwestern Kazakhstan. The mountain range forms part of the conventional boundary between the continents of Europe and Asia.

Title: Dawn of the Space Age
The Space Age began in the mid-20th century as superpowers competed for technological supremacy. The era was officially ignited when the Soviet Union successfully launched the very first artificial Earth satellite, an event that shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the rapid acceleration of the Space Race.

Title: University of Kansas
The University of Kansas is a public research university with its main campus located in the rolling hills of eastern Kansas. The university has a storied basketball program that has produced numerous NBA hall-of-famers, heavily drawing massive crowds to its campus arena.

Title: Execution of Charles I
Charles I was the King of England, Scotland, and Ireland until his execution in 1649. His death marked the culmination of the English Civil War, where parliamentarian forces defeated the royalists. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, setting a precedent for the deposition of absolute monarchs.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The nation is known for its stunning historic castles, long tradition of brewing beer, and the intricate river systems that carve through its terrain.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line that sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912. It struck an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City. Of the estimated 2,224 passengers and crew aboard, more than 1,500 died, making it one of modern history's deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army under the command of a famous emperor was defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This devastating loss marked the end of the commander's reign and his subsequent exile to Saint Helena.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. Before his ultimate defeat at Waterloo and subsequent exile, he conquered much of Europe. He was originally born on the Mediterranean island of Corsica into a minor noble family.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. His economical and understated style had a strong influence on 20th-century fiction. Born in Oak Park, Illinois, he spent much of his time abroad, particularly in Paris, Cuba, and Key West.

Title: Edinburgh
Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas. It is located in Lothian on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. The city is a major center for education and scientific research, famously serving as the home base for the institute that cloned the sheep Dolly.

Title: LeBron James
LeBron James is an American professional basketball player who is widely considered one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He famously returned to his home state's team in 2014, promising to bring them a championship. He fulfilled that promise in 2016, earning unanimous Finals MVP honors for his performance.

Title: Apollo 13
Apollo 13 was the seventh crewed mission in the Apollo space program and the third meant to land on the Moon. The lunar landing was aborted after an oxygen tank in the service module failed two days into the mission. The crew, commanded by Jim Lovell, successfully returned to Earth.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: 1957 in the United States
The year 1957 in the United States was marked by economic prosperity, the ongoing Civil Rights Movement, and growing Cold War anxieties. The nation's domestic and foreign policies were guided by the steady hand of its commander-in-chief, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later created NASA in response to Soviet space achievements.

Title: Academy Award for Best Animated Feature
The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature is given annually to the best animated feature-length film. The award was first introduced in 2002 for films released in 2001. The inaugural winner of this highly coveted prize was the computer-animated comedy film "Shrek", which beat out competitors like "Monsters, Inc."

Title: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is the iron-containing oxygen-transport metalloprotein in the red blood cells of almost all vertebrates. It carries oxygen from the respiratory organs to the rest of the body. When mutated, as in the case of the molecular disease identified by Pauling, it polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, distorting the red blood cell.

Title: Harvard University
Harvard University is a private Ivy League research university in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Founded in 1636, it is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. It is widely considered one of the most prestigious universities in the world, producing numerous Nobel laureates and prominent business leaders.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster
The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster occurred on January 28, 1986. The spacecraft broke apart 73 seconds into its flight, tragically killing all seven crew members aboard. The disaster temporarily grounded the shuttle fleet and led to major structural changes at NASA.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Social Media Pioneers
Around the same time video sharing became popular, social networking platforms began to dominate the digital landscape. Founded in 2004 by a group of college students, Facebook quickly expanded beyond university campuses to become the premier global social network, eventually acquiring photo-sharing tools like Instagram to consolidate its user base.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 according to the will of Alfred Nobel. While a German physicist took the physics prize, the 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to a French poet and essayist. The choice was somewhat controversial, as many literary critics believed Leo Tolstoy should have won the inaugural award instead.

Title: Monsters, Inc.
"Monsters, Inc." is a 2001 computer-animated comedy film produced by Pixar Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter. It was highly successful and was nominated for the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, but ultimately lost the award to a rival studio's fairy tale parody.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramicist, and theatre designer who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement, the invention of constructed sculpture, and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". His early career is famously divided into the somber Blue Period and the more optimistic Rose Period.

Title: Andrew Adamson
Andrew Ralph Adamson is a film director, producer, and visual effects supervisor. He gained worldwide recognition for co-directing the incredibly successful animated films "Shrek" and "Shrek 2". Adamson was born in Auckland, New Zealand, before moving to the United States to pursue his career in visual effects.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were re-allocated on financial grounds following a disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius. They were the longest modern Olympics ever held, lasting a total of 187 days.

Title: Mike Tyson
Mike Tyson is an American former professional boxer who competed from 1985 to 2005. Nicknamed "Iron Mike," he is considered one of the greatest heavyweight boxers of all time. He reigned as the undisputed world heavyweight champion and holds the record as the youngest boxer ever to win a heavyweight title.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29, 1986. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where Argentina emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim their second World Cup title, propelled by the legendary performance of Diego Maradona.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: Edward Jenner
Edward Jenner was an English physician and scientist who pioneered the concept of vaccines. He created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine, in 1796. Jenner was born in May 1749 in the small town of Berkeley, located in Gloucestershire, Great Britain.

Title: Discovery of Comets
During the late 18th century, detailed telescopic observation led to the discovery of numerous celestial bodies. The brilliant astronomer who famously discovered Comet C/1786 P1 in August 1786 shattered boundaries in science. She was the first woman to receive a salary as a scientist and successfully catalogued numerous nebulae and comets.

Title: Italy national football team
The Italy national football team represents Italy in international football and is controlled by the Italian Football Federation. They are one of the most successful national teams in the history of the World Cup, having won four titles, including a memorable victory in the summer of 1982 in Spain.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: Vint Cerf
Vinton Gray Cerf is an American Internet pioneer and is recognized as one of the "fathers of the Internet". He co-designed the TCP/IP protocols and the architecture of the Internet. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, he played a crucial role in the development of modern networking.

Title: Isabella of Angoulême
Isabella of Angoulême was Queen of England as the second wife of King John from 1200 until John's death in 1216. She was the mother of King Henry III. Later in life, after returning to France and remarrying, she eventually retired as a nun to a royal monastery, dying at Fontevraud Abbey in 1246.

Title: Spree River
The Spree is a major river in eastern Germany. It flows through the states of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Berlin. It is approximately 400 kilometers long and is a tributary of the River Havel. It famously flows through the historic center of the German capital.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: Málaga
Málaga is a municipality of Spain, capital of the Province of Málaga, in the autonomous community of Andalusia. With a history spanning about 2,800 years, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Western Europe. It is notable for being the birthplace of Pablo Picasso, another giant of 20th-century Spanish art.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po and atomic number 84. It is a rare and highly volatile metal. The element was discovered in 1898 by a prominent scientific couple studying pitchblende.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy. The element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where the element was discovered.

Title: Pitchblende
Pitchblende, now formally known as uraninite, is a radioactive, uranium-rich mineral and ore. It was heavily studied in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Parisian scientists looking to isolate the sources of its intense radioactive emissions. It famously yielded trace amounts of several newly discovered elements.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers decisively defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: The Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a massive, secretive research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. Led by the United States with support from the UK and Canada, the project's scientific research was directed by J. Robert Oppenheimer at the Los Alamos Laboratory.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The city's geometric and organic layout was entirely based on the winning blueprints submitted by an American architect named Walter Burley Griffin.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who developed many devices in fields such as electric power generation, mass communication, and motion pictures. He founded several companies, including the Edison Machine Works. To streamline his inventions, he established his premier and most famous research and development laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Title: Capitals of South Africa
South Africa distributes its governmental branches across three separate cities, rather than utilizing a single administrative center. Pretoria serves as the executive capital, Cape Town operates as the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein functions as the judicial capital, housing the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The mission was a triumphant success for the Soviet Space Program, proving the viability of their intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

Title: Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, and natural philosopher. He is a key figure in the 17th-century Scientific Revolution, best known for his laws of planetary motion, which were published in works like "Astronomia nova". Kepler was born in the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt, part of the Holy Roman Empire.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They achieved legendary status in the 1960s by dominating the NFL. During their historic victory in Super Bowl I, the team was led by their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, his work was heavily inspired by classical antiquity and had a profound influence on the development of Western art. His most famous paintings adorn the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Polio vaccine
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis (polio). Two major types are used worldwide: an inactivated poliovirus given by injection, and a weakened poliovirus given by mouth. The first successful inactivated version revolutionized global health by severely curtailing the devastating mid-century outbreaks of the disease.

Title: Francis Ford Coppola
Francis Ford Coppola is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He was a central figure in the New Hollywood filmmaking movement of the 1960s and 1970s. He is globally renowned for directing "The Godfather" trilogy and the war epic "Apocalypse Now."

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting depicting a swirling night sky over a quiet village. Painted in June 1889 during the artist's stay at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, it is considered one of the most recognized masterpieces of post-impressionist art.

Title: Wilt Chamberlain
Wilt Chamberlain was an American professional basketball player who played at the center position. Widely considered one of the sport's greatest players, he holds numerous records in scoring and rebounding, including the legendary 100-point game. Before his pro career, he played college basketball for the University of Kansas.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. The record was a massive commercial success and remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Valentina Tereshkova
Valentina Tereshkova is a Russian engineer, member of the State Duma, and former Soviet cosmonaut. She is the first and youngest woman to have flown in space. On 16 June 1963, she piloted the Vostok 6 spacecraft, completing 48 orbits of the Earth over almost three days in space.

Title: Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan was the fifth emperor of the Mughal Empire, remembered largely for his architectural achievements. He famously commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal to honor his favorite wife. His reign ended when he was deposed by his ambitious son in 1658, and he died in captivity in early 1666.

Title: The Proton
The proton is a stable subatomic particle, symbol p, H+, or 1H, with a positive electric charge of +1 e elementary charge. It was discovered in the early 20th century by Ernest Rutherford, who demonstrated that the nucleus of the hydrogen atom is present in all other nuclei.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high-fantasy novels written by a British author and published in the 1950s. The series is considered a classic of children's literature, tracing the adventures of children who are transported to a magical realm. The books were written at Oxford alongside a close colleague.
