Title: Richard Nixon
Richard Milhous Nixon was the 37th president of the United States, serving from 1969 until 1974. He took office during a period of massive cultural upheaval and the later years of the Vietnam War. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency was ultimately cut short by the Watergate scandal, forcing his unprecedented resignation.

Title: Kebnekaise
Kebnekaise is the highest mountain in Sweden. The Kebnekaise massif, which is part of the Scandinavian Mountains, has two main peaks. The glaciated southern peak used to be the highest at 2,120 meters, but due to ice melting, the rocky northern peak, at 2,096.8 meters, has now officially become the highest point in the country.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for the Mount Rushmore memorial, and its highest physical elevation is a prominent peak in the Black Hills.

Title: Manhattan
Manhattan is the most densely populated and geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City. It is the economic and administrative center of the city. While it hosts several educational institutions, such as Columbia University and NYU, it is not the home of the historic Rose Hill campus.

Title: 1991 Rugby World Cup
The 1991 Rugby World Cup was the second edition of the tournament and was hosted primarily in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and France. The final match was played at Twickenham Stadium, where Australia defeated England to claim their first world title.

Title: Museo Reina Sofía
The Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía is Spain's national museum of 20th-century art. Inaugurated in 1992, the museum is located in the vibrant capital city of Madrid. Its extensive collection highlights modern and contemporary masterpieces, but it is most globally famous for displaying the monumental painting "Guernica."

Title: Ridley Scott
Sir Ridley Scott is an English film director and producer. He is renowned for his atmospheric, highly concentrated visual style. After establishing his career with commercials, he found global fame directing the sci-fi classics "Alien" and "Blade Runner". He is the older brother of fellow Hollywood director Tony Scott.

Title: Days of Thunder
"Days of Thunder" is a 1990 American sports action drama film starring Tom Cruise as an ambitious stock car racing driver. Also directed by Tony Scott, it attempted to replicate the massive success and visual style of their previous collaboration, though it focused on NASCAR rather than fighter jets.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel written by a prominent American author. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and Gatsby's obsession to reunite with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. It is widely considered a contender for the title of the "Great American Novel".

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose work had a far-reaching influence on 20th-century art. He is the brilliant artist behind "The Starry Night" and "Sunflowers". He was born in Groot Zundert, Netherlands, in the year 1853.

Title: The Proton
The proton is a stable subatomic particle, symbol p, H+, or 1H, with a positive electric charge of +1 e elementary charge. It was discovered in the early 20th century by Ernest Rutherford, who demonstrated that the nucleus of the hydrogen atom is present in all other nuclei.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a global center of art, science, and philosophy for centuries, hosting numerous expatriate artists during the 20th century. The nation's official language is French, a Romance language spoken globally.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Theo van Gogh
Theodorus "Theo" van Gogh was a Dutch art dealer. He is best known as the younger brother of a deeply troubled, brilliant painter whom he supported financially and emotionally throughout his life. Theo's unwavering support allowed his brother to focus entirely on painting, though Theo tragically outlived him by only six months.

Title: Tomis
Tomis was an ancient Greek colony in the province of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Founded around 600 BC, it became a Roman territory. It is most famous in antiquity as the harsh place of exile for the Roman poet Ovid. Today, the ancient city's site is occupied by the modern Romanian city of Constanța.

Title: William Herschel
Sir Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is famed for constructing his own large telescopes to survey the night sky. In 1781, while working alongside his sister Caroline, he made history by discovering a brand new planet, expanding the known boundaries of the Solar System.

Title: 2000 Summer Olympics
The 2000 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVII Olympiad and commonly known as Sydney 2000, were held in Sydney, Australia. The event was widely praised for its incredible organization and execution, setting a high benchmark for future host nations.

Title: The Imperial March
"The Imperial March (Darth Vader's Theme)" is a musical theme present in the Star Wars franchise. It was composed by legendary film composer John Williams for the film "The Empire Strikes Back". The piece has become one of the most recognized and iconic cinematic themes of all time, representing the sheer power of the Galactic Empire.

Title: Portugal
Portugal is a country located on the Iberian Peninsula in Southwestern Europe. It is the westernmost sovereign state of mainland Europe. The political, economic, and cultural heart of the country is its capital and largest city, Lisbon.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe. Published in 1543, just before its author's death, the book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the Ptolemaic geocentric model.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815. A French army under the command of Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This catastrophic loss ended Napoleon's rule as Emperor of the French and marked the end of his Hundred Days return from exile.

Title: Social Media Pioneers
Around the same time video sharing became popular, social networking platforms began to dominate the digital landscape. Founded in 2004 by a group of college students, Facebook quickly expanded beyond university campuses to become the premier global social network, eventually acquiring photo-sharing tools like Instagram to consolidate its user base.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the banks of a major river in east-central Poland. It has a rich history and has been the birthplace of many notable historical figures, including a two-time Nobel laureate.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor and oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the use of atomic weapons.

Title: The Great Gatsby
The Great Gatsby is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a strong contender for the title of the Great American Novel.

Title: Rockville, Maryland
Rockville is a city and the county seat of Montgomery County, Maryland, United States, part of the Baltimore–Washington metropolitan area. It has historical significance and is home to the gravesite of legendary American novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, drawing literary tourists to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was a sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. He is widely considered one of the greatest artists of all time, famous for creating the monumental marble sculpture "David" and painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling. He was born in the Republic of Florence, in present-day Italy.

Title: Ernst Chain
Ernst Boris Chain was a German-born British biochemist. Fleeing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, he settled in Britain, where he collaborated closely with Florey. Together, they devised the biochemical methods to successfully isolate and purify penicillin, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize for their efforts.

Title: Venice
Venice is a city in northeastern Italy and the capital of the Veneto region. It is built on a group of 118 small islands separated by canals. The city is celebrated for its stunning architecture and art, and is historically significant as the birthplace of composer Antonio Vivaldi.

Title: John Carpenter
John Howard Carpenter is an American filmmaker, composer, and screenwriter. He is recognized as a master of the horror and science fiction genres, having directed classics like "Halloween" and "The Thing". Carpenter was born in Carthage, located in the state of New York, but grew up in Kentucky.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson, often referred to by his initials LBJ, was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. He assumed the presidency following the assassination of John F. Kennedy. He was the presiding head of state in early 1964 when the British Invasion of American music began. He was a lifelong member of the Democratic Party.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist. His theories on evolution by natural selection fundamentally altered scientific understanding of biology. These theories were heavily informed by his observations of finches and tortoises during his multi-year global voyage aboard the HMS Beagle.

Title: Wonders of the Ancient World
The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World were a list of remarkable constructions of classical antiquity. While the Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one still standing, others were legendary in their time. Among these was a colossal structure built to guide sailors safely into harbor, located in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: India
India is a vast country in South Asia known for its deep historical roots and immense cultural diversity. It features iconic landmarks ranging from ancient temples to spectacular Mughal-era monuments like the Taj Mahal. The political and administrative center of the country is its bustling capital city, New Delhi.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Mount Greylock
Mount Greylock is the highest natural point in Massachusetts. At 3,489 feet, its summit provides expansive views encompassing five states. It is located in the far western part of the state, well away from the coastal maritime cities.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, officially known as Czechia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Gothenburg
Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden, situated on the country's west coast. It is an important seaport and a major hub for manufacturing and education. While it is a vital contributor to the national economy, it does not hold the title of the nation's political capital.

Title: Maine
Maine is the easternmost state in the New England region of the United States. It is known for its jagged, rocky coastline, densely forested interior, and picturesque waterways. The state's capital city is Augusta, though its largest municipality is Portland.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located entirely within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is globally recognized as the smallest independent state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority is the Pope.

Title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, philosopher, and essayist. His literary works, including "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot", heavily explore human psychology in the troubled political context of 19th-century Russia. Dostoevsky passed away in 1881 in Saint Petersburg.

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed sovereign country known for its vast natural resources and major mining sector. The nation has a strong, mixed-market economy. Its official currency is the Australian dollar, which is also used by several independent Pacific Island states.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in the exact same Catalan town where he was born.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
An induction motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction. This revolutionary device eliminated the need for mechanical commutators. The first practical alternating current induction motor was independently invented in the 1880s by a brilliant Serbian-American engineer.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. While he made massive contributions to the study of microorganisms, he lived centuries after the original Dutch pioneer who first observed bacteria.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
The Space Age was inaugurated by the successful launch of the very first artificial Earth satellite in 1957. The spherical, beachball-sized object, which featured four external radio antennas, sent shockwaves through the global political landscape and triggered the intense Space Race. This historic satellite was named Sputnik 1.

Title: Yekaterinburg
Yekaterinburg is the fourth-largest city in Russia and the administrative center of Sverdlovsk Oblast. Historically significant as the site where the Romanov family met their end, the city is situated in the middle of the Ural Mountains, serving as a gateway between Europe and Asia.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: Fontevraud Abbey
Fontevraud Abbey is a historic monastery situated in the village of Fontevraud-l'Abbaye, near Chinon, in the French region of Anjou. Founded in 1101, the abbey was closely associated with the Plantagenet royal family. It serves as the final resting place for several royals, and is the specific monastery where Isabella of Angoulême died.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known of his works and represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period.

Title: California quail
The California quail, also known as the California valley quail, is a small ground-dwelling bird in the New World quail family. They have a curving crest or plume, made of six feathers, that droops forward. It is the official state bird of California.

Title: First Roman Emperor
The Roman Republic definitively ended with the rise of the first Roman Emperor. Born Gaius Octavius, he was granted the honorific title of Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC. His autocratic rule initiated a period of relative peace known as the Pax Romana, though he dealt harshly with political dissidents and scandalous figures.

Title: 1957 in the United States
The year 1957 in the United States was marked by economic prosperity, the ongoing Civil Rights Movement, and growing Cold War anxieties. The nation's domestic and foreign policies were guided by the steady hand of its commander-in-chief, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later created NASA in response to Soviet space achievements.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it features a swirling night sky above a quiet village. It is regarded as among Van Gogh's finest works and has been a permanent fixture in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: George III of Great Britain
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies during the American Revolutionary War and for his later bouts of mental illness. He ascended to the throne well after the birth of the scientist who invented the smallpox vaccine.

Title: Badshahi Mosque
The Badshahi Mosque is a Mughal-era congregational mosque in Lahore, capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab. It was commissioned by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1671. Known for its carved red sandstone with marble inlay, it remains one of the most iconic landmarks of the Mughal Empire in the region.

Title: Henri Becquerel
Henri Becquerel was a French engineer, physicist, and Nobel laureate. He is famously credited with the discovery of radioactivity, an achievement that earned him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside his colleagues. He died in 1908 in Brittany, France.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 containing the results of the astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. It provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and contributed the first two laws of planetary motion, fundamentally altering the field of astrophysics.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States and a major global cultural and financial hub. It comprises five boroughs and is home to countless renowned institutions, including Broadway theaters and premier art galleries like the Museum of Modern Art, which draws millions of visitors annually.

Title: Montgomery
Montgomery is the capital city of the U.S. state of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County. It became globally known for its pivotal role in the American Civil Rights Movement. The city is situated geographically along the banks of the sweeping Alabama River, which provides a vital transport route to the Gulf.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table. It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, shortly after their discovery of another highly radioactive element.

Title: 1998 FIFA World Cup
The 1998 FIFA World Cup was the 16th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. The tournament culminated in a dramatic final match where the host nation, France, decisively defeated Brazil 3-0 to claim their first-ever World Cup trophy.

Title: Brazil national football team
The Brazil national football team represents Brazil in international men's football. They are the most successful team in FIFA World Cup history, having won the tournament five times. Their legendary 1998 squad, featuring Ronaldo, suffered a stunning defeat in the final match in Paris.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy and featured a highly defensive style of play. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
UCLA is a public land-grant research university in Los Angeles, California. Its men's basketball program is historically the most successful in college athletics, holding the record for the most NCAA championships under the leadership of coach John Wooden.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows through several prominent educational towns, including Oxford, where it is known locally as the Isis, before making its way toward the North Sea.

Title: John Steinbeck
John Ernst Steinbeck Jr. was an American author who won the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature. He is widely known for his comic novels as well as his deeply serious, socially engaged works like "Of Mice and Men". Steinbeck was born and raised in the agricultural hub of Salinas, California.

Title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a towering lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Ancient Egypt. Constructed during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for many centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

Title: Alexander the Great
Alexander III of Macedon, commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon. He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through Asia and northeast Africa. He created one of the largest empires in history before dying at the age of 32 in Babylon.

Title: 2004 Ballon d'Or
The 2004 Ballon d'Or was a highly contested award given to the premier European footballer of the year. The winner was an incredibly prolific AC Milan striker who dominated the domestic and European scoring charts, beating out Deco and Ronaldinho for the prize.

Title: Brown thrasher
The brown thrasher is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the catbirds and mockingbirds. It is noted for having over 1,000 song types, making it one of the largest song repertoires of any bird. It is famously designated as the official state bird of Georgia.
