content:
Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: John F. Kennedy Assassination
On November 22, 1963, John F. Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, was assassinated while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas. The shocking event stunned the world and caused the immediate transition of executive power to the Vice President, who took the oath of office aboard Air Force One later that afternoon.

Title: Miracle on Ice
The "Miracle on Ice" was an ice hockey game during the 1980 Winter Olympics. The United States national team, composed of amateur and collegiate players, defeated the heavily favored, four-time defending gold-medalist Soviet Union team. The game is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in the history of sports.

Title: Rutherfordium
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element that is highly radioactive. It was first synthesized in the 1960s by researchers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The element was officially named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It is known for its diverse cultural heritage and complex history. The administrative, economic, and cultural center of the country is its capital city, Sarajevo.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. Known for its powerful economy and deep historical roots, its official currency is the Euro.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. Located on the site of the former Roman settlement of Iuvavum, it is situated on the border with Germany. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center, dominated by its massive central cathedral.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grasslands. The nation has a passionate sporting culture and multiple World Cup victories. Its political and economic hub is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: Wind River Corporate History
Originally starting in a Berkeley garage, Wind River Systems expanded rapidly during the 1990s dot-com boom. As the company grew into a major provider of aerospace and industrial software, it relocated its central operations. Today, the company maintains its global corporate headquarters in Alameda, California.

Title: North America
North America is a continent entirely within the Northern Hemisphere and almost all within the Western Hemisphere. It encompasses major nations like the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The continent is home to several major spaceports, including the primary launch facilities for NASA in Florida.

Title: 1958 FIFA World Cup
The 1958 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Sweden, marked the arrival of a 17-year-old prodigy named Pelé. His incredible performance helped Brazil secure their first-ever World Cup trophy, defeating the host nation in a thrilling final match.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly successful filmmaker known for directing groundbreaking blockbusters like "Titanic" and "Avatar". Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before relocating to the United States. His films have frequently pushed the boundaries of visual effects technology.

Title: Bono
Paul David Hewson, known worldwide by his stage name Bono, is an Irish singer-songwriter, activist, and philanthropist. He achieved global fame as the lead vocalist and primary lyricist of the rock band U2. Bono was born and raised in Dublin, Ireland, where he met his future bandmates while attending Mount Temple Comprehensive School.

Title: Todt Hill
Todt Hill is a 401-foot-tall elevation formed of serpentine rock on Staten Island, New York. It is the highest natural point in New York City and the highest elevation on the entire eastern seaboard from Florida to Cape Cod.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring
"The Fellowship of the Ring" is the first of three volumes of the epic high-fantasy novel "The Lord of the Rings", written by an English academic and philologist. Set in the fictional universe of Middle-earth, the book was published in July 1954 and quickly became a foundational work of modern fantasy literature.

Title: Dutch Language
Dutch is a West Germanic language spoken by around 25 million people as a first language. It is the official language of the Netherlands and one of the three official languages of Belgium. It is closely related to both English and German and has served as a prominent language of trade and culture in Europe.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. The capital and largest city of France is Paris, a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: Europium
Europium is a chemical element with the symbol Eu and atomic number 63. It is the most reactive lanthanide and must be stored under an inert fluid to protect it from atmospheric oxygen or moisture. It is named after the continent of Europe and is widely used as a red phosphor in television sets.

Title: Meiji Restoration
The Meiji Restoration was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to the Empire of Japan in 1868 under Emperor Meiji. The event effectively destroyed the shogunate system, paving the way for the modernization and Westernization of the country and establishing a centralized government.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor and oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the use of atomic weapons.

Title: Denali
Denali, formerly known officially as Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain peak in North America, with a summit elevation of 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level. Located in the Alaska Range in the interior of the U.S. state of Alaska, it is a centerpiece of Denali National Park and Preserve.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice, sharing her first prize with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the accolade following a spectacular season with Juventus.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between rival cities Sydney and Melbourne.

Title: The Night Watch
"Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banning Cocq", also known as "The Night Watch", is a 1642 painting by Rembrandt van Rijn. It is renowned for its colossal size, the dramatic use of light and shadow, and the perception of motion in what would have traditionally been a static military group portrait.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine. It is part of the Carpathian Mountains and is situated in the Eastern Beskids region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Walter Burley Griffin
Walter Burley Griffin was an American architect and landscape architect. He is known for designing Canberra, Australia's capital city, after winning the federal design competition in 1912. Griffin was born in 1876 in Maywood, a suburb of Chicago, Illinois, before moving to Australia to oversee his monumental project.

Title: Exile of Napoleon
Following his devastating defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was forced to abdicate the French throne for a second time. To ensure he could never return to power, his captors exiled him to a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic, where he ultimately died of stomach cancer in 1821.

Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". During his lifetime, he was better known as the personal assistant of actor Sir Henry Irving and business manager of the Lyceum Theatre in London. Stoker was born in Dublin in 1847.

Title: Robben Island
Robben Island is an island in Table Bay, just off the coast of South Africa. The name is Dutch for "seal island." The island is internationally famous because Nobel Laureate Nelson Mandela was imprisoned there for 18 of the 27 years he served behind bars before the fall of apartheid.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878. Cleve named the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Title: French Guiana
French Guiana is an overseas department and region of France, located on the northern coast of South America. It borders Brazil to the east and south and Suriname to the west. Because it is a part of France, it is the only territory of the mainland Americas to be part of the European Union.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and several overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and sports. The country boasts a diverse geography, ranging from coastal plains to the towering peaks of the Alps. The highest geographic point in France is Mont Blanc.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29, 1986. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where Argentina emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim their second World Cup title, propelled by the legendary performance of Diego Maradona.

Title: Tomis
Tomis was an ancient Greek colony in the province of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Founded around 600 BC, it became a Roman territory. It is most famous in antiquity as the harsh place of exile for the Roman poet Ovid. Today, the ancient city's site is occupied by the modern Romanian city of Constanța.

Title: Curiosity Rover
Curiosity is a car-sized Mars rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission. It launched from Cape Canaveral in 2011 and successfully landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on Mars in 2012. It paved the way for subsequent rovers with its advanced landing systems.

Title: Oxford University
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of 39 constituent colleges and a range of academic departments, where legendary authors and philologists have taught over the centuries.

Title: Claude Monet
Claude Monet was a French painter and founder of impressionist painting. He is known for his series of water lilies and his focus on capturing light and natural forms. Born in 1840, he lived through several major shifts in French political history.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. It has a rich history of maritime exploration and global colonization, once maintaining a vast empire across the Americas. The political, cultural, and economic center of the nation is its capital city, Madrid.

Title: Zenobia
Zenobia was a 3rd-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Following the death of her husband, she seized power and led a massive revolt against the Roman Empire. She conquered Egypt and much of Anatolia before finally being defeated and captured by the Roman Emperor Aurelian.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL. The team is legendary for its mid-20th-century dominance, securing victory in the very first Super Bowl under the fierce leadership of their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the 34th-largest by area, but the seventh-most populous. Its capital and largest city is Columbus. The state's northern border is defined heavily by its shoreline along Lake Erie, giving it access to major shipping routes.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: University of Kansas
The University of Kansas is a public research university with its main campus located in the rolling hills of eastern Kansas. The university has a storied basketball program that has produced numerous NBA hall-of-famers, heavily drawing massive crowds to its campus arena.

Title: First Roman Emperor
The Roman Republic definitively ended with the rise of the first Roman Emperor. Born Gaius Octavius, he was granted the honorific title of Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC. His autocratic rule initiated a period of relative peace known as the Pax Romana, though he dealt harshly with political dissidents and scandalous figures.

Title: Olympic Gold Medals
Olympic medals are awarded to victorious athletes at the Olympic Games. While the top prize is referred to as a "gold" medal, it is a common misconception that they are made of solid gold. In modern times, they are actually struck from 92.5% silver and merely plated with a minimum of 6 grams of pure gold.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: Eighth Planet from the Sun
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. In the Solar System, it is the fourth-largest planet by diameter. It was named after the Roman god of the sea. Neptune is notable for being the only planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by empirical observation.

Title: James Naismith
James Naismith was a physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach. He is universally recognized as the inventor of the sport of basketball. Naismith was born in 1861 in Almonte, a mill town located in the province of Ontario, Canada, before later moving to the United States.

Title: Sergei Korolev
Sergei Pavlovich Korolev was a lead Soviet rocket engineer and spacecraft designer. During the Space Race, he was simply known as "The Chief Designer" to protect his identity from Western intelligence. He was the mastermind behind Sputnik and Vostok. Korolev was born in 1907 in the city of Zhytomyr.

Title: 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Albert Einstein. Though famously known for his theory of relativity, he received the award specifically "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect," which proved critical for the development of quantum theory.

Title: First Human Spaceflight
The Space Age reached a monumental milestone on April 12, 1961, when the Soviet Union successfully launched the Vostok 1 spacecraft. Aboard was cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who made history by becoming the very first human being to journey into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: U2
U2 is an Irish rock band formed in Dublin in 1976. The group consists of a prominent lead vocalist known for his expressive vocal style, alongside The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. The band's early sound was rooted in post-punk but eventually grew to incorporate influences from many genres of popular music.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large, space-based observatory launched into low Earth orbit in April 1990. Despite an early issue with a flawed mirror, servicing missions corrected its optics, turning it into one of the most vital research tools in astronomy. It was named in honor of astronomer Edwin Hubble.

Title: The Old Guitarist
"The Old Guitarist" is an oil painting created in late 1903 and early 1904. It depicts an old, blind, haggard man with threadbare clothing weakly hunched over his instrument on the streets of Barcelona. It is one of the most famous works from Pablo Picasso's Blue Period, heavily emphasizing themes of poverty and isolation.

Title: Ottawa
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Located in the east of southern Ontario, near the city of Montréal and the U.S. border, it is a major political and technological center. The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, and sits squarely on the south bank of a major waterway.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science.

Title: Ottawa River
The Ottawa River is a river in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. For most of its length, it forms the border between these two provinces. It flows directly through the heart of Canada's national capital, heavily shaping the geography and history of the city.

Title: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch businessman and scientist. He is universally acknowledged as the "father of microbiology" for pioneering the use of microscopes to discover microorganisms. Born in 1632 in the city of Delft, he famously communicated his groundbreaking microscopic observations via a series of detailed letters sent to a foreign scientific body.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: 1871 in Great Britain
The year 1871 saw the passing of the Bank Holidays Act and the legalization of labor unions in the United Kingdom. It was a time of significant social reform and imperial expansion. The British Empire continued to flourish under the long reign of the reigning monarch.

Title: Execution of Charles I
Charles I was the King of England, Scotland, and Ireland until his execution in 1649. His death marked the culmination of the English Civil War, where parliamentarian forces defeated the royalists. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, setting a precedent for the deposition of absolute monarchs.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Publication of To Kill a Mockingbird
When "To Kill a Mockingbird" was finally published in July 1960, the United States was transitioning into a new era of civil rights struggles. The sitting president during the book's highly anticipated release was Dwight D. Eisenhower, nearing the end of his second term.

Title: Los Angeles
Los Angeles is the largest city in California and the second-most populous city in the United States. It is a massive global center for entertainment, media, and technology. Although it has a robust biomedical sector, its research institutes are distinct from the coastal scientific hubs found further south.

Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. The massive critical and commercial success was co-directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, establishing DreamWorks Animation as a prime competitor in the feature animation industry.

Title: Seine River
The Seine is a 777-kilometre-long river in northern France. It flows through the heart of Paris, making it a central feature of the city's geography and history, providing trade and transport for centuries.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film incorporating both historical and fictionalized aspects of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. The film was a massive commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing film of all time upon its release, a record it held until 2010. It was heavily praised for its visual effects and emotional weight.

Title: Stanley Baldwin
Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on three separate occasions during the interwar period. Known for his stabilizing presence, he led the country through the general strike of 1926 and the abdication crisis of 1936, alternating power with his political rivals.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historic resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived in Springfield from 1837 until he moved to the White House in 1861. Today, it serves as the political and administrative heart of the state.

Title: Caucasus Mountains
The Caucasus Mountains are a mountain system at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Stretching between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, it is home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, towering at an impressive 5,642 meters.

Title: Moscow
Moscow is the capital and largest city of Russia. During the 20th century, it was the political and administrative center of the Soviet Union. While the Soviet space program's top executives frequently reported to the Kremlin in Moscow, the program's enigmatic chief designer was not born there.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high fantasy novels published between 1950 and 1956. Set in the fictional realm of Narnia, a fantasy world of magic, mythical beasts, and talking animals, the series follows the adventures of various children who play central roles in the unfolding history of that world.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
The Catcher in the Rye is a groundbreaking novel by J.D. Salinger that explores themes of teenage angst and alienation. It was published in 1951 to widespread critical acclaim and occasional controversy. Its protagonist, Holden Caulfield, quickly became an icon for teenage rebellion.

Title: Art Institute of Chicago
The Art Institute of Chicago is one of the oldest and largest art museums in the United States. It houses a permanent collection of nearly 300,000 works of art, featuring notable pieces from around the globe. Among its prized possessions is "The Old Guitarist", a famous masterpiece acquired by the institution in 1926.

Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. After his forces deserted him, the deposed king fled to France, where he was welcomed by his cousin Louis XIV.

Title: French Open
The French Open, also known as Roland-Garros, is a major tennis tournament held over two weeks at the Stade Roland Garros in Paris. It is the premier clay court championship in the world. The men's singles winner is awarded the Coupe des Mousquetaires.

Title: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is a public land-grant research university in Illinois. Founded in 1867, it is the flagship institution of the University of Illinois system. The university is a massive contributor to technology and engineering, housing the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, where the first popular web browser was developed.

Title: Salinas, California
Salinas is the county seat and largest municipality of Monterey County, California. Located at the mouth of the Salinas Valley, the city has long been an agricultural powerhouse. It produces such a massive volume of a specific leafy green vegetable that it has earned the nickname "The Lettuce Capital of the World."

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Hayao Miyazaki
Hayao Miyazaki is an animator, filmmaker, and manga artist. A co-founder of Studio Ghibli, he has attained international acclaim as a masterful storyteller and creator of Japanese animated feature films. He was born in Tokyo, Japan, in 1941, during the onset of the Pacific War.

Title: Pluto
Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune. It was the first object discovered in the Kuiper belt. Following its discovery by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930, the radioactive element Plutonium was named in its honor.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. Known for its massive economy, diverse geography, and technological innovation, it houses numerous premier scientific institutions. The state's clear mountain air historically made it an ideal location for the construction of massive astronomical observatories in the early 20th century.

Title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was a pivotal event in world history which marked the falling of the Iron Curtain and the start of the fall of communism in Eastern and Central Europe. The historic events of 1989 reunited a divided city and set the stage for German reunification.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the War of the Austrian Succession. He was the sitting monarch when the composer of "The Four Seasons" died in 1741.

Title: Muhammad Ali
Muhammad Ali was an American professional boxer and activist. Born and raised in Louisville, Kentucky, he began training as an amateur boxer at age 12. He won an Olympic gold medal in 1960. He was originally born with the name Cassius Clay, but changed his name in 1964 after joining the Nation of Islam.

Title: King John of England
John, often called John Lackland, was King of England from 1199 until his death in 1216. His reign was marked by severe conflicts with his barons, leading to the forced signing of the Magna Carta. When he died of dysentery, he was immediately succeeded on the English throne by his young son, Henry III.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a classical romantic ballet composed in 1875 by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Unlike avant-garde works of the 20th century, it is beloved for its traditional orchestral melodies and graceful choreography, representing the pinnacle of classical Russian ballet.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Skłodowska-Curie was a pioneering physicist and chemist who conducted groundbreaking research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two distinct scientific fields. She was immensely proud of her Polish heritage.

Title: Europe
Europe is a continent located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and mostly in the Eastern Hemisphere. It is bordered by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and the Mediterranean Sea to the south. In chemistry, this continent serves as the namesake for the rare earth element Europium.

Title: Kemi River
The Kemi River is the longest river in Finland, running for roughly 550 kilometers through the northern landscapes of Lapland. It is heavily harnessed for hydroelectric power, generating a significant portion of the country's energy. It empties into the Gulf of Bothnia near the city of Kemi.

Title: Edward Elgar
Sir Edward William Elgar was an English composer, many of whose works have entered the British and international classical concert repertoire. Among his best-known compositions are orchestral works including the "Enigma Variations". He was born in Lower Broadheath, a village in Worcestershire.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, widely known as the Moonlight Sonata, is one of the most famous piano pieces ever written. It was completed in 1801 by Ludwig van Beethoven. The piece remains a staple of classical music repertoires and has influenced countless modern composers.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: The Weeping Woman
"The Weeping Woman" is an oil on canvas painting created in France in 1937. It is closely associated with another famous anti-war mural by the same artist, serving as a thematic continuation of the suffering depicted in that larger work. The painting is currently held in the collection of the Tate Modern in London.

Title: Voyage of the Challenger
The Challenger expedition of 1872–1876 was a scientific exercise that made a multitude of discoveries to lay the foundation of oceanography. The expedition was named after the vessel that carried the scientific team, a British naval ship that was heavily modified with laboratories and deep-sea dredging equipment.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or, given to the best football player in Europe as judged by a panel of sports journalists from UEFA member countries, was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the prestigious accolade.

Title: Serbia
Serbia is a landlocked country in Southeastern and Central Europe, situated at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkans. It played a major role in the events leading up to World War I, and its capital city is Belgrade, which lies at the confluence of two major rivers.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 that contains the results of a prominent astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. The work provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and introduced the first two laws of planetary motion, revolutionizing the mathematical understanding of the cosmos.

Title: Greece National Football Team
The Greece national football team shocked the world in 2004 by winning the UEFA European Championship. Hosted in Portugal, the tournament saw the underdog Greek squad defeat the host nation in the final match, securing a historic and unexpected victory.

Title: The Divine Comedy
"The Divine Comedy" is an Italian narrative poem begun c. 1308 and completed in 1320. It is widely considered one of the pre-eminent works in Italian literature and one of the greatest works of world literature. The poem's imaginative vision of the afterlife is representative of the medieval worldview.

Title: History of Basketball
The sport of basketball was invented in December 1891 at the International Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. A physical education instructor was tasked with creating an indoor game to keep athletes active during the harsh New England winters, resulting in the sport.

Title: Linux on Mars
The Ingenuity helicopter, which accompanied the Perseverance rover to Mars, marked a significant milestone for open-source software in space. While the main rover relied on a proprietary real-time operating system, the small experimental helicopter utilized an operating system based on the Linux kernel for its flight control algorithms.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Since the 17th century, Paris has been one of Europe's major centers of finance, diplomacy, commerce, fashion, science, and arts. The city's geography and historical development are intimately tied to the River Seine, which flows directly through the center of the metropolis.

Title: Mississippi
Mississippi is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. Named after the massive river that forms its western border, the state has a deep legacy in American music and literature. The capital and largest city is Jackson, which was founded in 1821 along the banks of the Pearl River.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time. Their breakthrough in the United States occurred in February 1964 with a legendary live television appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show.

Title: University of Cambridge
The University of Cambridge is a collegiate research university in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Founded in 1209, it is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of a variety of institutions, including 31 semi-autonomous constituent colleges. It boasts numerous legendary alumni, including Isaac Newton and the author of "Paradise Lost".

Title: Mount Whitney
Mount Whitney is the highest mountain in the contiguous United States, with an elevation of 14,505 feet (4,421 m). It is located in the Sierra Nevada mountain range in California. The peak is highly recognizable and serves as the ultimate goal for many prominent American mountaineering trails.

Title: 1984 Summer Olympics
The 1984 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIII Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event held in Los Angeles, California. The games were heavily boycotted by the Soviet Union and its allies in response to the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

Title: Final Defeat in 1815
After briefly returning from his first exile, Napoleon Bonaparte launched a final military campaign. His reign permanently ended when his forces were decisively crushed by a coalition of British and Prussian armies in June 1815. This catastrophic loss occurred at the historic Battle of Waterloo.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a country primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive economy, diverse culture, and profound influence on global sports, serving as the birthplace of modern baseball and the location where basketball was first played. Its capital city is Washington, D.C.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: Plesetsk Cosmodrome
The Plesetsk Cosmodrome is a Russian spaceport located in Mirny, Arkhangelsk Oblast. It was primarily developed for launching military satellites into high inclination and polar orbits. Because of its northern location, it was not the site used for the high-profile crewed missions of the Vostok program.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: Louis XIV of France
Louis XIV, known as Louis the Great or the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. His reign of 72 years and 110 days is the longest recorded of any monarch of a sovereign country in history. He famously offered a lavish exile to the deposed English king James II.

Title: Alexander Graham Bell
Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born inventor, scientist, and engineer who is credited with patenting the first practical telephone. Born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1847, his family later emigrated to Canada before he established his professional research career in Boston, Massachusetts.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Martin Heinrich Klaproth was a German chemist who discovered uranium, zirconium, and cerium. Born in 1743 in Wernigerode, he was a major figure in early analytical chemistry and helped systematize the naming of elements.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: Vostok 1
Vostok 1 was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first crewed spaceflight in history. Launched by the Soviet Union in April 1961, it carried cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who became the first human to cross into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: Percy Bysshe Shelley
Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the major English Romantic poets. He eloped with the daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft in 1814. His life was marked by extreme controversy, and he tragically died in 1822 when his boat sank in a sudden storm off the coast of Italy.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its legacy of housing famous classical composers like Mozart and Beethoven.

Title: Hershey, Pennsylvania
Hershey is an unincorporated community in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. Often referred to as "Chocolatetown, USA," it is the home of The Hershey Company. The town was founded in 1903 by Milton S. Hershey to provide housing and amenities for the workers of his massive chocolate factory.

Title: Sully Prudhomme
René François Armand (Sully) Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist. He was a prominent figure in the Parnassian movement, which sought to restore elegance and precision to French poetry. He made history as the very first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Sully Prudhomme was born in 1839 in Paris, France.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly influential filmmaker known for his technical innovations in cinematic special effects. He wrote, directed, and produced "Titanic", leading it to record-breaking box office success. Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before moving to the United States in his youth.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. After proposing an information management system in 1989, he successfully implemented the first communication between an HTTP client and server via the internet. He was born in 1955 in London, United Kingdom.

Title: Discovery of Streptomycin
Streptomycin was the first antibiotic remedy for tuberculosis. It was discovered in 1943 by Albert Schatz in the laboratory of Selman Waksman at Rutgers University. Unlike earlier antibiotics derived from molds, this drug was isolated from a soil-dwelling bacterium known as Streptomyces griseus.

Title: Pavel Nedvěd
Pavel Nedvěd is a retired professional footballer who played as a midfielder. Described as one of the best footballers of his generation, he won the Ballon d'Or in 2003. He was born in Cheb, a city situated in the Czech Republic, where he began his youth career before dominating Italian football.

Title: Miami
Miami is a major coastal metropolis located in southeastern Florida. It is the core of the state's largest metropolitan area and a massive hub for international finance, culture, and arts. Despite its massive size and global influence, it does not serve as the seat of the state government.

Title: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
UCLA is a public land-grant research university in Los Angeles, California. Its men's basketball program is historically the most successful in college athletics, holding the record for the most NCAA championships under the leadership of coach John Wooden.

Title: Calvin Coolidge
John Calvin Coolidge Jr. was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 30th president of the United States from 1923 to 1929. Known as "Silent Cal" for his quiet demeanor, he assumed the presidency after the sudden death of Warren G. Harding and was the sitting president in 1926.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France, with an estimated population of over 2.1 million residents in 2020. Since the 17th century, Paris has been one of Europe's major centers of finance, diplomacy, commerce, fashion, science, and the arts.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. He is widely considered one of the greatest painters in history. His artistic genius is best exemplified by his legendary portrait, the Mona Lisa.

Title: First Practical Telephone
The invention of the first practical telephone was a watershed moment in human engineering, transforming global communication forever. The device was successfully patented in the United States in March 1876. The inventor, who spent much of his adult life working in America, was born and educated in Edinburgh, Scotland.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Hilda Thatcher was a British stateswoman and Conservative politician. She made history in 1979 when she won the general election, officially taking office as the first female Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. She served in this role until 1990, becoming the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century.

Title: Isaac Newton
Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Before formulating the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, Newton attended the University of Cambridge, where he later held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: Waterloo
Waterloo is a municipality located in the Walloon Brabant province. It gained global historical infamy as the site of the legendary 1815 battle that ended the Napoleonic Wars. Today, the battlefield is preserved as a major historical site within the borders of the modern country of Belgium.

Title: 1982 FIFA World Cup
The 1982 FIFA World Cup was the 12th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was played in Spain between June 13 and July 11, 1982. The tournament was ultimately won by Italy, who defeated West Germany 3-1 in the final match.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Florey was a pharmacologist and pathologist who was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use. He took Fleming's initial discovery and turned it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in Adelaide, South Australia, and eventually moved to England to conduct his research.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is the smallest state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority, and official head of state, is the Pope.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Orlando Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in 1901 in Canton, a small city located in South Dakota.

Title: Mission Control
The Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center is NASA's center for human spaceflight training, research, and flight control. Following liftoff from the eastern seaboard, flight operations are famously handed over to Mission Control, which is located in Houston, Texas.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. He is celebrated as one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Rockville, Maryland
Rockville is a city and the county seat of Montgomery County, Maryland, United States, part of the Baltimore–Washington metropolitan area. It has historical significance and is home to the gravesite of legendary American novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, drawing literary tourists to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Harper Lee
Nelle Harper Lee was an American novelist best known for her 1960 masterpiece "To Kill a Mockingbird". She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to literature. Lee was born and raised in Monroeville, a small town located in the southern state of Alabama.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. Bohr was born in 1885 in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would later serve as the center of his academic career.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is an infrared space observatory launched in 2021. Designed to succeed previous observatories, its vastly improved infrared resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint to be seen by older optical telescopes.

Title: 1912 in the United States
The year 1912 in the United States was a highly eventful election year. The nation was expanding its global influence while navigating complex domestic reforms. During this year, the incumbent Republican administration was facing intense challenges from both the Democratic Party and Theodore Roosevelt's Bull Moose Party.

Title: Elon Musk
Elon Reeve Musk is a business magnate and investor. He is the founder, CEO, and Chief Engineer at SpaceX, as well as the CEO and product architect of Tesla, Inc. Before embarking on his legendary entrepreneurial career in Silicon Valley, Musk transferred from Queen's University to the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned degrees in economics and physics.

Title: Lettuce
Lettuce is an annual plant of the daisy family, Asteraceae. It is most often grown as a leafy vegetable, primarily consumed raw in salads, sandwiches, and wraps. It requires relatively cool temperatures to prevent it from flowering quickly, making certain coastal valleys ideal for its cultivation.

Title: 1926 in the United States
The year 1926 was situated right in the middle of the Roaring Twenties. The United States was experiencing massive economic growth, the rapid expansion of jazz culture, and the continued enforcement of Prohibition. During this prosperous era, the White House was occupied by a famously quiet Republican leader.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century.

Title: Mount Greylock
Mount Greylock is the highest natural point in Massachusetts. At 3,489 feet, its summit provides expansive views encompassing five states. It is located in the far western part of the state, well away from the coastal maritime cities.

Title: Abraham Lincoln
Abraham Lincoln was an American lawyer and statesman who served as the 16th president of the United States. He led the nation through the American Civil War and succeeded in preserving the Union and abolishing slavery. His portrait is famously featured on the American five-dollar bill and the copper penny.

Title: Chocolate Chip Cookie
The chocolate chip cookie is a drop cookie that originated in the United States and features chocolate chips or chocolate morsels as its distinguishing ingredient. It was invented in 1938 by Ruth Graves Wakefield, who chopped up a Nestlé semi-sweet chocolate bar and added it to her cookie dough, creating a legendary dessert.

Title: Cleveland Cavaliers
The Cleveland Cavaliers, often referred to as the Cavs, are a professional basketball team based in Cleveland, Ohio. They compete in the NBA as a member of the Eastern Conference Central Division. The franchise secured its first and only NBA Championship by overcoming a historic deficit to beat the Warriors.

Title: Canada
Canada is a massive country in North America. Its ten provinces and three territories extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific and northward into the Arctic Ocean. The nation is globally known for producing the inventor of basketball. The political and administrative center of the country is its capital city, Ottawa.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. He was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: 1741 in Great Britain
The year 1741 in Great Britain saw the continuation of the War of Jenkins' Ear against Spain. It was also a year of notable cultural events, including George Frideric Handel composing his legendary "Messiah". Throughout this year, the British Empire was ruled by the second king of the House of Hanover.

Title: Captain Robert FitzRoy
Robert FitzRoy was an English officer of the Royal Navy and a pioneering meteorologist. He achieved lasting fame as the captain of a legendary survey vessel. He commanded this ship during its famous second voyage, providing safe passage and mapping data for an ambitious young naturalist surveying the coast of South America.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the Jacobite rising of 1745. He was the reigning sovereign in 1749, the year the pioneer of vaccination was born.

Title: Chile
Chile is a long, narrow country stretching along South America's western edge. Also a former Spanish colony, its geography is dominated by the Andes mountain range. Its highest peak is Ojos del Salado, which is also the highest active volcano in the world.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. Covering the northern third of the island of Great Britain, it shares a border with England to the south. It is known for its rugged mountain landscapes, glens, and lochs. Politically, its devolved government sits in its historic capital city of Edinburgh.

Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics.
