The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, abruptly ending his return to power known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. The battle occurred in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, characterized by its pale blue color and unique sideways rotation. It was the first planet to be discovered using a telescope. Its discovery sent shockwaves through the scientific community and later inspired the naming conventions of newly synthesized radioactive elements.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is globally famous for its vibrant culture, the Amazon rainforest, and its unmatched success in international football. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Brasília, which was inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a country primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive economy, diverse culture, and profound influence on global sports, serving as the birthplace of modern baseball and the location where basketball was first played. Its capital city is Washington, D.C.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It is a rare and highly volatile metal, discovered in 1898 by researchers studying pitchblende. On the periodic table of elements, Polonium is classified as a chalcogen and has the atomic number 84.

Title: Salk Institute for Biological Studies
The Salk Institute for Biological Studies is an independent, non-profit, scientific research institute located in the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla. Founded in 1960 by a pioneering virologist, it is renowned for its striking modernist architecture and its massive contributions to molecular biology and genetics.

Title: José Mourinho
José Mário dos Santos Mourinho Félix is a professional football manager and former player. He gained international fame by winning the Champions League with Porto in 2004. He was born in Setúbal, Portugal, and has gone on to manage some of the biggest clubs in world football.

Title: First Moon Landing
The Apollo 11 mission achieved the historic goal of landing humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent several hours exploring the lunar surface before safely returning to Earth, ending the Space Race.

Title: Incandescent Light Bulb
The development of a commercially viable incandescent light bulb was achieved in the late 1870s by an American inventor working at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. The invention fundamentally altered modern society by providing widespread access to reliable, safe electric indoor lighting.

Title: 1930 FIFA World Cup
The 1930 FIFA World Cup was the inaugural tournament for the men's soccer world championship. Organized by FIFA, the entire tournament took place in a single South American nation during the month of July. A total of 13 teams participated, and the host nation emerged victorious by defeating its neighbor in the final match.

Title: Highgate Cemetery
Highgate Cemetery is a historic place of burial situated in north London, England. It is notable for some of the people buried there and for its de facto status as a nature reserve. Among its famous permanent residents are the author Mary Ann Evans and the legendary revolutionary political philosopher Karl Marx.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were re-allocated following a disastrous volcanic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Italy.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements. Born in Tobolsk, Siberia, he used his periodic table to correct the properties of some already discovered elements and predict the properties of eight elements yet to be discovered.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the 34th-largest by area, but the seventh-most populous. Its capital and largest city is Columbus. The state's northern border is defined heavily by its shoreline along Lake Erie, giving it access to major shipping routes.

Title: Inaugural Rugby World Cup
The first-ever Rugby World Cup was held in 1987, co-hosted by two major Oceanic nations. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final match at Eden Park, where the host nation, New Zealand, emerged victorious by defeating France 29-9 to lift the Webb Ellis Cup.

Title: Salzburg Cathedral
Salzburg Cathedral is the seventeenth-century Catholic cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Salzburg. Dedicated to Saint Rupert and Saint Vergilius, it is the very church where Mozart was baptized. After a previous structure burned down, the current magnificent building was erected entirely in the elaborate Baroque architectural style.

Title: Wernher von Braun
Wernher von Braun was a German-American aerospace engineer and space architect. He was a leading figure in the development of rocket technology in Nazi Germany before transferring to the United States. He served as the chief architect of the Apollo program's Saturn V rocket.

Title: Black Sea
The Black Sea is a marginal mediterranean sea of the Atlantic Ocean lying between Europe and Asia. It is supplied by major rivers, principally the Danube, Dnieper, and Don. It is a critical geostrategic waterway connecting Eastern Europe to the broader Mediterranean.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time. Their original frontman, John Lennon, tragically passed away after being assassinated in New York City.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the banks of a major river in east-central Poland. It has a rich history and has been the birthplace of many notable historical figures, including a two-time Nobel laureate.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a south Slav nationalist group seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Archduke and his wife. Princip was born in the rural village of Obljaj, located in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: France
France has a rich history of scientific discovery and was the adoptive home of many expatriate researchers. It was the country where radioactivity was extensively studied in the early 20th century, leading to the discovery of several new elements.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. The country has a rich tradition in chemistry and scientific innovation. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm, a major cultural and economic hub.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Henri Becquerel
Henri Becquerel was a French engineer, physicist, and Nobel laureate. He is famously credited with the discovery of radioactivity, an achievement that earned him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside his colleagues. He died in 1908 in Brittany, France.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was a sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. He is widely considered one of the greatest artists of all time, famous for creating the monumental marble sculpture "David" and painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling. He was born in the Republic of Florence, in present-day Italy.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign is known as the Victorian era, a period of massive industrial expansion and public health reform. She oversaw the construction of modern sewer systems in the capital, preventing future cholera outbreaks.

Title: Miami
Miami is a major coastal metropolis located in southeastern Florida. It is the core of the state's largest metropolitan area and a massive hub for international finance, culture, and arts. Despite its massive size and global influence, it does not serve as the seat of the state government.

Title: Percy Bysshe Shelley
Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the major English Romantic poets. He eloped with the daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft in 1814. His life was marked by extreme controversy, and he tragically died in 1822 when his boat sank in a sudden storm off the coast of Italy.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army under the command of a famous emperor was defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This devastating loss marked the end of the commander's reign and his subsequent exile to Saint Helena.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent and the island of Tasmania. It is known for its rugged outback and coastal cities. The country successfully hosted the Summer Olympics at the turn of the millennium. The nation's capital is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Motihari
Motihari is the headquarters of East Champaran district in the Indian state of Bihar. Historically, it was known for its indigo plantations during the British Raj. Today, it is frequently visited by literary tourists because it is the birth city of the famous English author who wrote "1984".

Title: Connecticut
Connecticut is a state in the New England region of the United States, known for its historic universities and coastal towns. It was the site of the Yale University campus where several future politicians were educated. Despite his strong association with Texas, it is actually the birth state of the 43rd US President.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist. His theories on evolution by natural selection fundamentally altered scientific understanding of biology. These theories were heavily informed by his observations of finches and tortoises during his multi-year global voyage aboard the HMS Beagle.

Title: Seleucid Empire
The Seleucid Empire was a Hellenistic state in Western Asia that existed from 312 BC to 63 BC. It was founded by Seleucus I Nicator following the division of the Macedonian empire created by Alexander the Great. It frequently warred with the neighboring Ptolemaic state over control of the Levant.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815. A French army under the command of Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This catastrophic loss ended Napoleon's rule as Emperor of the French and marked the end of his Hundred Days return from exile.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne. It opens with a dense introductory chapter titled "The Custom-House."

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: China
China, officially the People's Republic of China, is a massive country in East Asia. It spans five geographical time zones and borders fourteen countries. The country has a rich cultural heritage and a diverse array of wildlife, notably featuring the Giant Panda, which serves as its beloved national symbol and endemic treasure.

Title: Cassius Marcellus Clay (abolitionist)
Cassius Marcellus Clay was a prominent 19th-century American planter and politician from Kentucky who became a fierce abolitionist. He published an anti-slavery newspaper and helped found the Republican Party in his state. His legacy was honored when a descendant named his son after him, a boy who would grow up to be a legendary heavyweight boxer.

Title: Louvre Pyramid
The Louvre Pyramid is a large glass and metal pyramid designed as the main entrance to the Louvre Museum in Paris. Completed in 1989, it was initially highly controversial for clashing with the classical architecture of the surrounding palace. The striking modernist structure was designed by the acclaimed Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Caucasus Mountains
The Caucasus Mountains are a mountain system at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Stretching between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, it is home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, towering at an impressive 5,642 meters.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". Picasso was born in Málaga, a municipality in the autonomous community of Andalusia.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is most famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. The synthetic element Nobelium was later named in his honor.

Title: Minute Waltz
The Waltz in D-flat major, Op. 64, No. 1, popularly known as the Minute Waltz, is a piano waltz written in 1847. Despite its nickname, the piece is typically performed in about one and a half to two minutes. It was composed by the legendary Romantic-era pianist Frédéric Chopin.

Title: Michelangelo's David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created between 1501 and 1504 by the Italian artist Michelangelo. Unlike many sculptures of the era that utilized metal alloys, this towering 5.17-meter statue of the Biblical hero was intricately carved from a single massive block of Carrara marble.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist. The town also houses the famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where the artist is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: George Frideric Handel
George Frideric Handel was a German-British Baroque composer well known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, and organ concertos. He was born in 1685, the same year as Bach, in the German city of Halle, but he spent the bulk of his career working in London.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. The heavily favored National Football League (NFL) champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League (AFL) champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35–10.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He was deeply influenced by the bohemian circles of Christiania.

Title: Andalusia
Andalusia is the southernmost autonomous community in Peninsular Spain. It is the most populous and the second-largest autonomous community in the country. The region is famous for its Moorish architecture, flamenco dancing, and its capital city, Seville.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the best orchestral compositions of the Baroque era, highlighting complex counterpoint and vibrant instrumentation.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life and for hosting major international sporting events, including early iterations of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: River Shannon
The River Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing for 360 kilometers (224 miles) and dividing the west of the island from the east and south. It represents a major physical barrier, featuring only a handful of crossing points along its length. The river flows southwards from the Cuilcagh Mountain to the Shannon Estuary.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A former five-star general during World War II, he managed the early years of the Space Race and the Cold War. He was the sitting US President in 1955.

Title: Madagascar
Madagascar is an island country in the Indian Ocean, situated off the southeastern coast of Africa. It is the world's fourth-largest island. The nation split from the Indian subcontinent around 88 million years ago, allowing native plants and animals to evolve in relative isolation. Its capital is Antananarivo.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The novel explores themes of mass surveillance, totalitarianism, and the repressive regimentation of persons and behaviors.

Title: Wimbledon Records
The Wimbledon Championships are the oldest tennis tournament in the world and widely considered the most prestigious. In the modern era, consecutive victories on its grass courts are notoriously difficult. The 20th-century record for the most consecutive Wimbledon men's singles titles belongs to Björn Borg, who captured five straight trophies from 1976 to 1980.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed sovereign country known for its vast natural resources and major mining sector. The nation has a strong, mixed-market economy. Its official currency is the Australian dollar, which is also used by several independent Pacific Island states.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel that introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries. It was written by an Irish author who was heavily inspired by Eastern European folklore.

Title: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 is a supertall skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. It officially held the title of the world's tallest building from its opening in 2004 until the completion of a taller megastructure in Dubai in 2009. The building was designed by C.Y. Lee & Partners to withstand the region's frequent typhoons and earthquakes.

Title: Mississippi
Mississippi is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. Named after the massive river that forms its western border, the state has a deep legacy in American music and literature. The capital and largest city is Jackson, which was founded in 1821 along the banks of the Pearl River.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large, space-based observatory launched into low Earth orbit in April 1990. Despite an early issue with a flawed mirror, servicing missions corrected its optics, turning it into one of the most vital research tools in astronomy. It was named in honor of astronomer Edwin Hubble.

Title: The Stranger
"The Stranger" is a 1942 novella authored by French philosopher and writer Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus' philosophy of the absurd and existentialism. The novel begins with the iconic lines concerning the death of the protagonist's mother.

Title: Vince Lombardi
Vince Lombardi was an American football coach and executive in the NFL. He is best known as the head coach of the Green Bay Packers during the 1960s, leading them to five NFL Championships, including victories in the first two Super Bowls. In his younger years, Lombardi played college football as an offensive lineman for Fordham University.

Title: Inca Empire
The Inca Empire was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Its political and administrative structure is considered by most scholars to have been the most developed in the Americas prior to Columbus' arrival. The civilization built massive engineering projects, including Machu Picchu, before its leadership was captured and dismantled by Spanish invaders.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: Augustus
Augustus was the founder of the Roman Principate and considered the first Roman Emperor. He ruled from 27 BC until his death in AD 14. During his reign, he famously banished the celebrated poet Ovid to a remote province on the Black Sea for mysterious reasons.

Title: Mont Blanc
Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps and Western Europe, rising 4,805 m (15,764 ft) above sea level. It is located on the French-Italian border, though its summit is widely recognized as the highest point entirely within the territory of France. The peak is a legendary destination for mountaineering.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. While Johann Sebastian Bach visited the court of Frederick the Great in nearby Potsdam, he never lived or died in Berlin.

Title: James Naismith
James Naismith was a physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach. He is universally recognized as the inventor of the sport of basketball. Naismith was born in 1861 in Almonte, a mill town located in the province of Ontario, Canada, before later moving to the United States.

Title: Mulhacén
Mulhacén is the highest mountain in continental Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, with an elevation of 3,479 meters. Located in the Sierra Nevada range in Andalusia, it is a prominent peak, but it is surpassed in overall elevation by a volcanic peak located in the Spanish overseas territories.

Title: Euro
The Euro (symbol: €; code: EUR) is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. He created the inactivated polio vaccine, which was declared safe and effective in 1955. Years later, he leveraged his fame and public support to establish the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer. He is widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague, which is the capital city of the modern-day country of the Czech Republic.

Title: Oral Polio Vaccine
The development of an oral polio vaccine (OPV) using a weakened, live poliovirus completely revolutionized global public health campaigns in the mid-20th century. Because it could be safely administered via an oral drop or on a sugar cube, it proved dramatically easier to distribute in developing nations than early injected alternatives.

Title: First Human Spaceflight
The Space Age reached a monumental milestone on April 12, 1961, when the Soviet Union successfully launched the Vostok 1 spacecraft. Aboard was cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who made history by becoming the very first human being to journey into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Greece National Football Team
The Greece national football team shocked the world in 2004 by winning the UEFA European Championship. Hosted in Portugal, the tournament saw the underdog Greek squad defeat the host nation in the final match, securing a historic and unexpected victory.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He survived his Italian contemporary by several years, passing away in 1750 in Leipzig.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in Ishpeming, located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe for centuries. The political and cultural center of the nation is its capital city, Brussels, which also hosts the headquarters of the European Union.

Title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, philosopher, and essayist. His literary works, including "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot", heavily explore human psychology in the troubled political context of 19th-century Russia. Dostoevsky passed away in 1881 in Saint Petersburg.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He played a critical role in the events that led to the demise of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Roman Empire. He famously intervened in the internal politics of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, forming an alliance with Cleopatra VII.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Inactivated Polio Vaccine
The first successful polio vaccine was an inactivated version developed in the early 1950s. Requiring an injection, it was declared safe and effective after a massive nationwide field trial in 1955. The medical researcher who led its creation became an international hero but chose not to patent his formula.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed country with a mixed-market economy. It is rich in natural resources, heavily exporting minerals and agricultural products. The nation's financial systems are closely tied to the Asia-Pacific region, and its official currency is the Australian dollar.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: New Jersey
New Jersey is a state situated within both the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions of the United States. It is the most densely populated of all 50 U.S. states. The state is renowned for its pharmaceutical industry, diverse culture, and its hosting of a prestigious Ivy League university in the town of Princeton.

Title: Edinburgh
Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas. Historically part of Midlothian, it is located in Lothian on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. The city is renowned for the historic Edinburgh Castle, its prestigious university, and major scientific research facilities operating on its outskirts.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. She was not the ruler of the Austrian territories where early geneticists were born.

Title: Streptomyces
Streptomyces is the largest genus of Actinomycetota and the type genus of the family Streptomycetaceae. Over 500 species of these bacteria have been described. They predominantly live in soil and decaying vegetation, and are recognized for producing over two-thirds of the clinically useful antibiotics of natural origin.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Alien (film)

Title: Albany

Title: Kazakhstan

Title: United Kingdom

Title: River Thames

Title: Canada

Title: Thriller (album)

Title: River Thames

Title: Ernest Lawrence

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, he composed more than 800 works of virtually every genre of his time. He died in Vienna at the age of 35, leaving his famous Requiem unfinished.

Title: First Mammal Clone

Title: London

Title: French Open

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice, sharing her first prize with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He was one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. Known for its massive economy, diverse geography, and technological innovation, it houses numerous premier scientific institutions. Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly successful filmmaker known for directing groundbreaking blockbusters like "Titanic" and "Avatar". Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Title: Alexander III of Russia
Alexander III was Emperor of Russia from 1881 until his death in 1894. He was a highly conservative ruler who reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father. He died of terminal kidney disease at the Livadia Palace in Crimea, peacefully passing the throne to his son.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin

The breakthrough occurred when Alexander Fleming noticed that a specific blue-green mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying bacteria.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: The Brothers Karamazov
"The Brothers Karamazov" is a passionate philosophical novel that explores deep questions regarding God, free will, and morality. It was the final novel written by the author of "Crime and Punishment" and is widely considered one of the supreme achievements in world literature.

Title: Alan Turing
Alan Turing was an English mathematician and computer scientist. While he worked extensively at Bletchley Park and designed the "Bombe" machine to break the Enigma code, he was not the primary engineer who designed and built the Colossus computer.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era, characterized by a period of immense industrial, political, and military change. She was the sitting monarch in 1853.

Title: Qing Dynasty
The Qing Dynasty was the last orthodox dynasty in Chinese history. It was established in 1636 and ruled China proper from 1644 to 1912. During the 19th century, the dynasty faced immense internal rebellion and external pressures from Western imperial powers, ultimately leading to its collapse.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in Figueres, the exact same town where he was born.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: Carl Sagan
Carl Sagan was an American astronomer, planetary scientist, and science communicator. He spent most of his career as a professor at Cornell University, where he directed the Laboratory for Planetary Studies. He is best known for assembling the first physical messages sent into space, the Pioneer plaque and the Voyager Golden Record.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: The Louvre

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite

Title: Auguste Rodin
François Auguste René Rodin was a French sculptor generally considered the founder of modern sculpture. His most globally recognized masterpiece, "The Thinker", was famously cast in bronze in the early 20th century.

Title: The Louvre

Title: New York City

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: Denali
Denali, formerly known officially as Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain peak in North America, with a summit elevation of 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level. Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital from Sunday, 2 September to Thursday, 6 September 1666. Title: William Herschel
Sir Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is famed for constructing his own large telescopes to survey the night sky. In 1781, while working alongside his sister Caroline, he made history by discovering a brand new planet, expanding the known boundaries of the Solar System.

Title: United States dollar
The United States dollar is the official currency of the United States and its territories. Introduced by the Coinage Act of 1792, it is the world's primary reserve currency and the most heavily utilized currency in international trade. It is issued and managed by the Federal Reserve System.

Title: Bon Scott
Ronald Belford "Bon" Scott was an Australian singer and songwriter, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and lyricist of the rock band AC/DC from 1974 until his tragic death in 1980. Title: Discovery of Streptomycin
Streptomycin was the first antibiotic remedy for tuberculosis. It was discovered in 1943 by Albert Schatz in the laboratory of Selman Waksman at Rutgers University. Unlike earlier antibiotics derived from molds, this drug was isolated from a soil-dwelling bacterium known as Streptomyces griseus.

Title: J.J. Thomson
Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist and Nobel Laureate in Physics. He is credited with the discovery of the electron, the first subatomic particle to be identified, through his experiments with cathode ray tubes. Thomson was born in Manchester, England, in 1856.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Bill Gates
Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist. Title: 1990s in Film

Title: Statue of Liberty
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical copper sculpture on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, it was designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. The statue was a gift to the United States from the people of France, intended to commemorate the alliance between the two nations during the American Revolution.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, serving an unprecedented four terms in office.

Title: Bengal Tiger
The Bengal Tiger is a population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies that is native to the Indian subcontinent. It is threatened by poaching and fragmentation of habitat. In biological classification, it is part of the phylum Chordata and the family Felidae.

Title: Spree River
The Spree is a major river in eastern Germany. It flows through the states of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Berlin. It is approximately 400 kilometers long and is a tributary of the River Havel. It famously flows through the historic center of the German capital.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was highly anticipated, given the rapid advancements in theoretical physics during the early 20th century. Title: Gregor Mendel
Gregor Johann Mendel was a meteorologist, mathematician, biologist, Augustinian friar and abbot of St. Thomas' Abbey in Brno. He gained posthumous recognition as the founder of the modern science of genetics. He was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf bei Odrau, a village located in the Austrian Empire.

Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: James Naismith
James Naismith was a physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach. He is universally recognized as the inventor of the sport of basketball. Naismith was born in 1861 in Almonte, a mill town located in the province of Ontario, Canada, before later moving to the United States.

Title: Great Fire of London

Title: Yellow River

Title: Caucasus Mountains
The Caucasus Mountains are a mountain system at the intersection of Europe and Asia. Stretching between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, it is home to Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, towering at an impressive 5,642 meters.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. Title: Warren G. Harding

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. Shah Jahan was the fifth emperor of the Mughal Empire, remembered largely for his architectural achievements. He famously commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal to honor his favorite wife. Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books, including "Brave New World". Louis XIV, known as Louis the Great or the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. His reign of 72 years and 110 days is the longest recorded of any monarch of a sovereign country in history. He famously offered a lavish exile to the deposed English king James II.

Title: San Diego
San Diego is a major city in the U.S. state of California, located on the coast of the Pacific Ocean in Southern California. The city encompasses numerous distinct neighborhoods and communities, including La Jolla, which serves as a major hub for biotechnology and is home to the Salk Institute.

Title: Linux on Mars
The Ingenuity helicopter, which accompanied the Perseverance rover to Mars, marked a significant milestone for open-source software in space. While the main rover relied on a proprietary real-time operating system, the small experimental helicopter utilized an operating system based on the Linux kernel for its flight control algorithms.

Title: Brooklyn Bridge
The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City. Opened in May 1883, it spans the East River, connecting the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn. It was the first steel-wire suspension bridge ever constructed and remains an iconic feature of the city's skyline.

Title: The Descent of Man
"The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" is a book by English naturalist Charles Darwin, first published in 1871. It applies evolutionary theory to human evolution, and details his theory of sexual selection. It was published more than a decade after his initial, foundational work on evolution.

Title: Tanzania
Tanzania, officially the United Republic of Tanzania, is a country in East Africa within the African Great Lakes region. It was formed as a sovereign state in 1964 through the union of the mainland territory of Tanganyika and the coastal archipelago of Zanzibar. While Dar es Salaam is the largest city, the official capital is Dodoma.

Title: Yersinia pestis
Yersinia pestis is a Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped bacterium. It is the infectious agent responsible for the plague, a devastating disease that comes in three main forms: pneumonic, septicemic, and bubonic. Throughout history, it has caused several massive pandemics that wiped out substantial portions of the global population.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a pioneering physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He famously discovered the atomic nucleus through his gold foil experiment. Rutherford was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a small town on the South Island of New Zealand.

Title: Economy of Argentina
The economy of Argentina relies heavily on natural resources, an export-oriented agricultural sector, and a diversified industrial base. Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower

Title: United Kingdom

The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, located in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as a fortress in the late 12th to 13th century.

Title: Captain Robert FitzRoy
Robert FitzRoy was an English officer of the Royal Navy and a pioneering meteorologist. He achieved lasting fame as the captain of a legendary survey vessel. Title: The Electron
The electron is a subatomic particle with a negative one elementary electric charge. It was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, identified by physicist J.J. Thomson.

Title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a towering lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Ancient Egypt. Constructed during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for many centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

Title: Seventh Planet from the Sun
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Its name is a reference to the Greek god of the sky. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. The ice giant was officially discovered in 1781 by astronomer William Herschel, making it the first planet discovered with a telescope.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
The Catcher in the Rye is a groundbreaking novel by J.D. Salinger that explores themes of teenage angst and alienation. It was published in 1951 to widespread critical acclaim and occasional controversy. Its protagonist, Holden Caulfield, quickly became an icon for teenage rebellion.

Title: Andalusia
Andalusia is the southernmost autonomous community in Peninsular Spain. It is the most populous and the second-largest autonomous community in the country. The region is famous for its Moorish architecture, flamenco dancing, and its capital city, Seville.

Title: James II of England

His Catholicism and his absolute rule alienated the English political elite. During the Glorious Revolution of 1688, he was deposed and fled across the English Channel to seek refuge in a neighboring country.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. The de facto capital city of the country is Bern.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it features a swirling night sky, a crescent moon, and a bright Venus over a quiet village. It is regarded as among Van Gogh's finest works and has been a permanent fixture in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. Born in New York City, USA, he chose not to patent the vaccine to maximize its global distribution. His inactivated polio vaccine required an injection but proved immensely effective in clinical trials.

Title: Vantaa River
The Vantaa River is a prominent 101-kilometer-long waterway in Southern Finland. It originates from Lake Erkylänjärvi and flows into the Gulf of Finland. The river heavily shapes the geography of the Finnish capital, providing both scenic value and historical routes for trade.

Title: French Open
The French Open, also known as Roland-Garros, is a major tennis tournament held over two weeks at the Stade Roland Garros in Paris. It is the premier clay court championship in the world. The men's singles winner is awarded the Coupe des Mousquetaires.

Title: Bono
Paul David Hewson, known worldwide by his stage name Bono, is an Irish singer-songwriter, activist, and philanthropist.
