Bono was born and raised in Dublin, Ireland, where he met his future bandmates while attending Mount Temple Comprehensive School.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. It is the most populous U.S. state and the third-largest by area. The state has hosted the Summer Olympics in its sprawling metropolis of Los Angeles. The official state bird of California is the California quail.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe, published in 1543. The book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the widely accepted Ptolemaic geocentric model that had dominated astronomy for centuries.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: Claude Monet
Claude Monet was a French painter and founder of impressionist painting. He is known for his series of water lilies and his focus on capturing light and natural forms. Born in 1840, he lived through several major shifts in French political history.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 1
Hydrogen is the chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest element and, at standard conditions, is a gas of diatomic molecules. It is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that develops embedded system software for the intelligent edge. They are the creators and primary maintainers of VxWorks, the real-time operating system used by numerous spaceflight missions. The company was founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe in the early 19th century. He was born to a minor Italian noble family on the island of Corsica, mere months after it was acquired by France.

Title: Angel Falls
Angel Falls is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall. The waterfall drops over the edge of the Auyán-tepui mountain in the Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site located in the Gran Sabana region of Bolívar State. Geographically, this towering natural wonder is located on the continent of South America.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements. Born in Tobolsk, Siberia, he used his periodic table to correct the properties of some already discovered elements and predict the properties of eight elements yet to be discovered.

Title: French Franc
The French franc was the currency of France. First introduced in 1360, it was the national currency until the adoption of the Euro. Coins and banknotes of the franc were fully withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender in 2002.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. It is named after the planet Neptune, continuing the tradition of naming elements after the planets in the solar system.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice. Working with her husband Pierre, her first major breakthrough was the isolation of a new radioactive element in July 1898, which she named Polonium.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He was one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Mary Wollstonecraft
Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer, philosopher, and advocate of women's rights. She is best known for "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman" (1792). Her life was cut tragically short in 1797; shortly after giving birth to her second daughter, Mary, she contracted puerperal fever and passed away.

Title: The Beach Boys
The Beach Boys are an American rock band formed in Hawthorne, California, in 1961. The group's original lineup consisted of brothers Brian, Dennis, and Carl Wilson, their cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. They emerged as major rivals to British invasion bands during the 1960s.

Title: Chile
Chile is a country located in western South America, occupying a long, narrow strip of land between the Andes to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west. It is known for its diverse geography, ranging from dry deserts in the north to alpine tundras in the south. The capital and largest city is Santiago.

Title: U2
U2 is an Irish rock band formed in Dublin in 1976. The group consists of a prominent lead vocalist known for his expressive vocal style, alongside The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. The band's early sound was rooted in post-punk but eventually grew to incorporate influences from many genres of popular music.

Title: Ontario Cinema History
Ontario has long been a hub for Canadian and international filmmaking, with Toronto frequently serving as a stand-in for major American cities. The province has produced a significant number of famous actors, writers, and directors who later relocated to Hollywood to advance their careers.

Title: Michigan
Michigan is a state in the Great Lakes region of the upper Midwestern United States. It is the only state to consist of two peninsulas, the Lower Peninsula and the Upper Peninsula. While its largest and most economically significant city is Detroit, the political center and state capital is Lansing.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly influential filmmaker known for his technical innovations in cinematic special effects. He wrote, directed, and produced "Titanic", leading it to record-breaking box office success. Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before moving to the United States in his youth.

Title: Andrew Adamson
Andrew Ralph Adamson is a film director, producer, and visual effects supervisor. He gained worldwide recognition for co-directing the incredibly successful animated films "Shrek" and "Shrek 2". Adamson was born in Auckland, New Zealand, before moving to the United States to pursue his career in visual effects.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. Bohr was born in 1885 in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would later serve as the center of his academic career.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: Dawn of the Space Age
The Space Age began in the mid-20th century as superpowers competed for technological supremacy. The era was officially ignited when the Soviet Union successfully launched the very first artificial Earth satellite, an event that shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the rapid acceleration of the Space Race.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a Canadian filmmaker known for his massive box office successes. He directed the science fiction action film "Aliens" as well as the revolutionary blockbusters "Terminator 2: Judgment Day", "Titanic", and "Avatar". He frequently pushes the boundaries of cinematic visual effects.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Royal Society of London
The Royal Society of London, formally The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge, is a learned society and the United Kingdom's national academy of sciences. Founded in 1660, it played a crucial role in early modern science. It famously translated and published the microscopic observations sent by the Dutch "father of microbiology" in its journal.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage in 1831. The expedition famously carried the young English naturalist Charles Darwin, allowing him to conduct crucial field research in the Galápagos Islands.

Title: Helsinki
Helsinki is the capital and most populous city of Finland, located on the shore of the Gulf of Finland. It is the country's central hub for politics, education, finance, and culture. The city is defined by its maritime landscape and the Vantaa River, which flows directly through it.

Title: Isaac Newton
Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Before formulating the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, Newton attended the University of Cambridge, where he later held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics.

Title: William Lassell
William Lassell was an English merchant and astronomer. He is remembered for his discovery of Triton, the largest moon of Neptune, just 17 days after the discovery of the planet itself. He also discovered Ariel and Umbriel, two other moons of Uranus.

Title: Alexandria
Alexandria was a magnificent Mediterranean port city in ancient Egypt founded by Alexander the Great. During the Hellenistic period, it served as the bustling capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. It was renowned globally for its massive Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its Great Library.

Title: Battersea Power Station
Battersea Power Station is a decommissioned coal-fired power station located on the south bank of a major waterway in Nine Elms, London. With its four distinctive art deco chimneys, it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks and gained global pop culture fame after appearing on a 1977 rock album cover.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: Black Sea
The Black Sea is a marginal mediterranean sea of the Atlantic Ocean lying between Europe and Asia. It is supplied by major rivers, principally the Danube, Dnieper, and Don. It is a critical geostrategic waterway connecting Eastern Europe to the broader Mediterranean.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill, precise draftsmanship, and striking, bizarre images. His major works often featured melting clocks and distorted figures set in vast, desolate landscapes. Though he occasionally touched on political themes, he was far less overtly political than his contemporary who painted "Guernica".

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. The nation encompasses the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of the island of Ireland, and many smaller islands. The political and cultural capital of the UK is London.

Title: Harper Lee
Nelle Harper Lee was an American novelist best known for her 1960 masterpiece "To Kill a Mockingbird". She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to literature. Lee was born and raised in Monroeville, Alabama, on April 28, 1926.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. The record was a massive commercial success and remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. Armstrong was born in Wapakoneta, Ohio, in August 1930, developing a passion for aviation at a young age.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was a key figure in the Romantic movement and was married to the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. Following her death in 1851, she was interred at St Peter's Church in Bournemouth.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grasslands. The nation has a passionate sporting culture and multiple World Cup victories. Its political and economic hub is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: The Mona Lisa
"Mona Lisa" is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci. Considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance, it has been described as the most famous, most visited, most written about, and most parodied work of art in the world. The painting's novel qualities include the subject's elusive expression.

Title: Edison Machine Works
The Edison Machine Works was a manufacturing company set up in 1881 to produce dynamos, large electric motors, and other components of the electrical illumination system. The factory was situated in New York City. The business was founded and closely managed by the legendary American inventor Thomas Edison.

Title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was a pivotal event in world history which marked the falling of the Iron Curtain and the start of the fall of communism in Eastern and Central Europe. The historic events of 1989 reunited a divided city and set the stage for German reunification.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two geographically and socially distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for hosting the Mount Rushmore memorial in the Black Hills. Its state capital is Pierre.

Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. After his forces deserted him, the deposed king fled to France, where he was welcomed by his cousin Louis XIV.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse to the south of Ely. The river is heavily associated with the University of Cambridge, where punting along its waters is a popular student activity.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer. He is a key figure in the 17th-century Scientific Revolution, best known for his laws of planetary motion. While deeply influential, no chemical element currently bears his name on the periodic table.

Title: Tagus River
The Tagus is the longest river in the Iberian Peninsula. It flows through Spain and Portugal, emptying into the Atlantic Ocean near Lisbon. While it passes near several major Spanish cities, it does not flow through the capital.

Title: Alexander III of Russia
Alexander III was Emperor of Russia from 1881 until his death in 1894. He was a highly conservative ruler who reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father. He died of terminal kidney disease at the Livadia Palace in Crimea, peacefully passing the throne to his son.

Title: Sully Prudhomme
René François Armand (Sully) Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist. He was a prominent figure in the Parnassian movement, which sought to restore elegance and precision to French poetry. He made history as the very first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Sully Prudhomme was born in 1839 in Paris, France.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the 1913 model of the atom, which incorporated quantum mechanics into atomic orbits. Bohr was born and raised in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would profoundly influence his life and legacy.

Title: Roger Waters
George Roger Waters is an English musician, singer-songwriter, and composer. In 1965, he co-founded the progressive rock band Pink Floyd. Following the departure of their original frontman, Waters became the band's primary lyricist and conceptual leader. He was born in Great Bookham, Surrey.

Title: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is a public land-grant research university in Illinois. Founded in 1867, it is the flagship institution of the University of Illinois system. The university is a massive contributor to technology and engineering, housing the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, where the first popular web browser was developed.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. Located on the site of the former Roman settlement of Iuvavum, it is situated on the border with Germany. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center, dominated by its massive central cathedral.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. The country's political and administrative center is its capital city, Wellington, located at the south-western tip of the North Island.

Title: French Revolution
The French Revolution was a period of radical political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789. It resulted in the overthrow of the monarchy, the establishment of a republic, and extensive social upheaval. The era is notable for the Reign of Terror, during which thousands were executed.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. Geographically, the city is situated along the banks of the Yamuna River, which has historically sustained its populace.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. He was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts the interactions of a cast of characters who attend extravagant parties hosted by the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is considered a quintessential American classic.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. Covering the northern third of the island of Great Britain, it shares a border with England to the south. It is known for its rugged mountain landscapes, glens, and lochs. Politically, its devolved government sits in its historic capital city of Edinburgh.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: 2006 FIFA World Cup
The 2006 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Germany and was the 18th edition of the tournament. The championship was secured by Italy, who defeated France 5–3 in a penalty shoot-out following a 1–1 draw after extra time.

Title: 2014 FIFA World Cup
The 2014 FIFA World Cup was the 20th FIFA World Cup. It took place in Brazil from 12 June to 13 July 2014, after the country was awarded the hosting rights in 2007. The tournament culminated in Germany winning their fourth title by defeating Argentina in the final.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
The Space Age was inaugurated by the successful launch of the very first artificial Earth satellite in 1957. The spherical, beachball-sized object, which featured four external radio antennas, sent shockwaves through the global political landscape and triggered the intense Space Race. This historic satellite was named Sputnik 1.

Title: Slovakia
Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe that was historically part of Czechoslovakia until a peaceful dissolution in 1993. Its capital and largest city is Bratislava. The official currency of Slovakia has been the Euro since the country adopted it in 2009.

Title: Mount Narodnaya
Mount Narodnaya is the highest peak of the Ural Mountains in Russia. Its elevation is 1,894 metres (6,214 ft). The mountain is located in the Research Range, on the border between the Komi Republic and Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, standing as the apex of the massive intercontinental divide.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, fought in 1805, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. The French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. He is one of the most revered figures in the history of Western music. He bridged the transition from the Classical period to the Romantic era in music. Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn, in the Electorate of Cologne.

Title: Seaborgium
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers in California. The element was named after Glenn T. Seaborg, a famous American chemist who contributed to the discovery of numerous transuranium elements.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian social science fiction novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State populated by genetically engineered citizens arranged in a strict social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive technological advancements in reproductive biology and behavioral conditioning. It is considered one of the definitive dystopian works of the 20th century.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by an English rock band, released on 26 September 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios. It was an immediate commercial success and reached number one in the UK and US.

Title: Mexican peso
The Mexican peso (symbol: $; code: MXN) is the currency of Mexico. Originally based on the silver reserves of the Spanish empire, it was the first currency in the world to use the "$" sign, which the US dollar later adopted. It remains a major global currency.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: 2012 Summer Olympics
The 2012 Summer Olympics were a major international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. It was the third time that the British capital had hosted the modern Olympic Games. The event followed the massive spectacle previously hosted by an East Asian nation four years prior.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Rosalind Franklin
Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose work was central to the understanding of the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, viruses, and coal. Her famous Photo 51 was critical in determining the double helix structure of DNA, though she died before the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée decisively defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. It is widely regarded as a tactical masterpiece.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. Known for its massive economy, diverse geography, and technological innovation, it houses numerous premier scientific institutions. The state's clear mountain air historically made it an ideal location for the construction of massive astronomical observatories in the early 20th century.

Title: Crime and Punishment
"Crime and Punishment" is a novel by a famous Russian author, first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in 12 monthly installments during 1866. It tells the story of Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in Saint Petersburg who formulates a plan to kill an unscrupulous pawnbroker.

Title: Oldest Tennis Tournament
The history of tennis dates back centuries, but organized competitive tournaments began in the 19th century. The oldest tennis tournament in the world, and widely considered the most prestigious, is Wimbledon. It has been held at the All England Club in London since 1877.

Title: Einsteinium
Einsteinium is a synthetic element with the symbol Es. It is a member of the actinide series and is highly radioactive. It was first discovered as a component of the debris of the first hydrogen bomb explosion in 1952, and it holds the atomic number 99 on the periodic table.

Title: Olympic Gold Medals
Olympic medals are awarded to victorious athletes at the Olympic Games. While the top prize is referred to as a "gold" medal, it is a common misconception that they are made of solid gold. In modern times, they are actually struck from 92.5% silver and merely plated with a minimum of 6 grams of pure gold.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line that sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912. It struck an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City. Of the estimated 2,224 passengers and crew aboard, more than 1,500 died, making it one of modern history's deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Pink Floyd
Pink Floyd was an English rock band formed in London in 1965. They achieved international acclaim with their progressive and psychedelic music. Following the massive success of "The Dark Side of the Moon", they released several more monumental concept albums, including the 1977 record "Animals".

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Invention of the World Wide Web
The World Wide Web, commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators. It was invented in 1989 at CERN in Switzerland. The creator developed the first web browser and the fundamental protocols of the internet, HTTP and HTML.

Title: John Steinbeck
John Ernst Steinbeck Jr. was an American author who won the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature. He is widely known for his comic novels as well as his deeply serious, socially engaged works like "Of Mice and Men". Steinbeck was born and raised in the agricultural hub of Salinas, California.

Title: London
London is the capital city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis and serves as a vital transport route.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including the iconic Mona Lisa. In the 1980s, the museum underwent a major modernization project that added a large, controversial glass pyramid to its main courtyard.
