Title: Chordata
Chordata is a biological phylum of animals that possess a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal slits at some point in their life cycle. This phylum includes all vertebrates, such as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish, making it one of the most prominent groupings in the animal kingdom.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. It serves as the seat of all three branches of the Government of India.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, fought in 1805, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. The French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Edison Machine Works
The Edison Machine Works was a manufacturing company set up in 1881 to produce dynamos, large electric motors, and other components of the electrical illumination system. The factory was situated in New York City. The business was founded and closely managed by the legendary American inventor Thomas Edison.

Title: Isaac Newton
Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Before formulating the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, Newton attended the University of Cambridge, where he later held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. The nation encompasses the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of the island of Ireland, and many smaller islands. The political and cultural capital of the UK is London.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the War of the Austrian Succession and the early phases of the Seven Years' War.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. While he made massive contributions to the study of microorganisms, he lived centuries after the original Dutch pioneer who first observed bacteria.

Title: Currency of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland maintains a highly developed, independent market economy. Unlike many of its European neighbors, it never adopted the Euro. The official currency of the United Kingdom and its primary territories is the Pound sterling.

Title: Gabriel García Márquez
Gabriel García Márquez was an acclaimed novelist, short-story writer, screenwriter, and journalist. Affectionately known as "Gabo," he authored "One Hundred Years of Solitude" and won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the small town of Aracataca, located in the northern region of Colombia.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The two largest moons, Oberon and Titania, were the first to be discovered. They were observed in 1787 by the astronomer William Herschel.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting created in June 1889 by a renowned Dutch Post-Impressionist painter. It depicts the view from his asylum room window at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Frank G. Jackson
Frank G. Jackson is an American politician who served as the 57th mayor of Cleveland, Ohio. First elected in 2005, he became the longest-serving mayor in the city's history. Jackson was the presiding mayor during the city's massive celebration parade in 2016 when the local NBA franchise secured the national title.

Title: John Milton
John Milton was an English poet, polemicist, and intellectual who served as a civil servant for the Commonwealth of England under its Council of State. He wrote at a time of religious flux and political upheaval. Despite going completely blind in 1652, he composed his magnum opus, "Paradise Lost", through dictation. In his youth, he was educated at Christ's College, a constituent college of the University of Cambridge.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a remote volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is known primarily as the harsh, isolated location where a deposed French emperor was exiled after 1815. It remains a British Overseas Territory and utilizes the Saint Helena pound as its local currency.

Title: Biltmore Estate
The Biltmore Estate is a historic house museum and tourist attraction in Asheville, North Carolina. Constructed between 1889 and 1895 for George Washington Vanderbilt II, it is the largest privately owned house in the United States. The massive French Renaissance chateau features 250 rooms and sprawling, meticulously landscaped gardens.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. The town is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist, who also designed the town's famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where he is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Chile
Chile is a country located in western South America, occupying a long, narrow strip of land between the Andes to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west. It is known for its diverse geography, ranging from dry deserts in the north to alpine tundras in the south. The capital and largest city is Santiago.

Title: Abraham Lincoln
Abraham Lincoln was an American lawyer and statesman who served as the 16th president of the United States. He led the nation through the American Civil War and succeeded in preserving the Union and abolishing slavery. His portrait is famously featured on the American five-dollar bill and the copper penny.

Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. After his forces deserted him, the deposed king fled to France, where he was welcomed by his cousin Louis XIV.

Title: Mount Narodnaya
Mount Narodnaya is the highest peak of the Ural Mountains in Russia. Its elevation is 1,894 metres (6,214 ft). The mountain is located in the Research Range, on the border between the Komi Republic and Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, standing as the apex of the massive intercontinental divide.

Title: Ovid
Publius Ovidius Naso, known in English as Ovid, was a Roman poet who lived during the reign of Augustus. He was a contemporary of the older Virgil and Horace. In AD 8, Ovid was unexpectedly exiled by Augustus to Tomis, a remote Greek colony on the Black Sea coast, where he remained until his death in AD 17.

Title: 1950 FIFA World Cup
The 1950 FIFA World Cup was the fourth edition of the tournament, held in Brazil after a twelve-year hiatus caused by World War II. The decisive match of the tournament saw a stunning upset when the underdog Uruguayan national team defeated the host nation before a record crowd at the Maracanã Stadium.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Shelley was an English novelist, essayist, and biographer who is best known for her seminal Gothic novel "Frankenstein". The daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, she was immersed in intellectual circles from an early age. Shelley was born in London in 1797.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was first synthesized and discovered in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: Krakow
Krakow is the second-largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland. Situated in the Lesser Poland region, the city dates back to the 7th century and was the official capital of Poland until 1596.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books, including "Brave New World". In his later years, he relocated to Los Angeles, California, where he spent his final days. Huxley died of laryngeal cancer on November 22, 1963, a date that tragically caused his passing to be overshadowed in the media by a major national event.

Title: Valladolid
Valladolid is a municipality in Spain and the primary seat of government of the autonomous community of Castile and León. It is situated at the confluence of the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers. The city has a rich history and was the birthplace of several Spanish monarchs, as well as a prominent modern prime minister.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: George Westinghouse
George Westinghouse Jr. was an American entrepreneur and engineer based in Pennsylvania who created the railway air brake. He was a pioneer of the electrical industry, acquiring the patents for the AC induction motor and backing the alternating current system to fiercely compete against Thomas Edison's direct current networks.

Title: Crime and Punishment
"Crime and Punishment" is a novel by a famous Russian author, first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in 12 monthly installments during 1866. It tells the story of Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in Saint Petersburg who formulates a plan to kill an unscrupulous pawnbroker.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: Yersinia pestis
Yersinia pestis is a Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped bacterium. It is the infectious agent responsible for the plague, a devastating disease that comes in three main forms: pneumonic, septicemic, and bubonic. Throughout history, it has caused several massive pandemics that wiped out substantial portions of the global population.

Title: 52nd Academy Awards
The 52nd Academy Awards ceremony, organized by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films released in 1979. The ceremony took place in April 1980 in Los Angeles. The night's biggest winner was a highly acclaimed family drama that swept several major categories, including Best Picture.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named in honor of the newly discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Syd Barrett
Roger Keith "Syd" Barrett was an English singer, songwriter, and musician who co-founded the rock band Pink Floyd. As the original frontman and primary songwriter, he led the band through their early psychedelic years. After suffering a severe mental breakdown, he lived as a recluse until he died of pancreatic cancer in 2006 in Cambridge.

Title: 1812 Overture
The "Year 1812" Solemn Overture is a concert overture written in 1880 by a legendary Russian Romantic composer. The piece was written to commemorate Russia's successful defense against Napoleon's invading Grande Armée in 1812. It is globally famous for its dramatic, booming climax, which features live cannon fire and ringing church bells.

Title: Marc Andreessen
Marc Andreessen is an American entrepreneur, investor, and software engineer. He is best known as the co-author of Mosaic, the first widely used web browser, and as co-founder of Netscape. Before launching his legendary tech career, Andreessen earned his bachelor's degree in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It is home to numerous prestigious universities and national laboratories where many of the actinide series elements were discovered. Its state capital is Sacramento, though Los Angeles is its largest city.

Title: Friendship 7
Friendship 7 was the spacecraft piloted by astronaut John Glenn in February 1962. Part of the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, the flight made Glenn the very first American to successfully orbit the Earth, catching the U.S. up to the achievements of the Soviet Union.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: Portugal
Portugal is a country located on the Iberian Peninsula in Southwestern Europe. It is the westernmost sovereign state of mainland Europe. The political, economic, and cultural heart of the country is its capital and largest city, Lisbon.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly successful filmmaker known for directing groundbreaking blockbusters like "Titanic" and "Avatar". Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before relocating to the United States. His films have frequently pushed the boundaries of visual effects technology.

Title: Kebnekaise
Kebnekaise is the highest mountain in Sweden. The Kebnekaise massif, which is part of the Scandinavian Mountains, has two main peaks. The glaciated southern peak used to be the highest at 2,120 meters, but due to ice melting, the rocky northern peak, at 2,096.8 meters, has now officially become the highest point in the country.

Title: Roger Waters
George Roger Waters is an English musician, singer-songwriter, and composer. In 1965, he co-founded the progressive rock band Pink Floyd. Following the departure of their original frontman, Waters became the band's primary lyricist and conceptual leader. He was born in Great Bookham, Surrey.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: Catalonia
Catalonia is an autonomous community of Spain, designated as a nationality by its Statute of Autonomy. Located on the northeastern extremity of the Iberian Peninsula, it boasts a distinct language and culture. The political and economic center of Catalonia is its vibrant capital city, Barcelona.

Title: Tokugawa Shogunate
The Tokugawa Shogunate was the feudal military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868. Established by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogunate maintained a strict isolationist policy and rigidly controlled the social order. During the year 1800, this dynasty was firmly in power, completely dominating the political landscape of the nation.

Title: Discovery of Hydrogen
While artificially produced earlier by others, hydrogen was first recognized as a distinct chemical element in 1766. The English scientist Henry Cavendish was the first to identify hydrogen gas as a discrete substance, naming it "inflammable air" and noting that it produced water when burned.

Title: Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is the causative agent of cholera, a severe diarrheal disease caused by drinking contaminated water. The bacteria famously caused several pandemics in the 19th century, ravaging cities like London before proper sanitation infrastructure was implemented.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they rank among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed, pushing the boundaries of what a solo violin could achieve.

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: SpaceX
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) is an American aerospace manufacturer, space transportation company, and communications corporation headquartered in Hawthorne, California. The company was founded in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars, and is currently led by its billionaire CEO.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. She was deployed on three major surveying expeditions during her career. Her second voyage is immortalized in scientific history for carrying Charles Darwin around the world under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, allowing him to survey the Galápagos.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". Stoker was born in Dublin, Ireland. He suffered from unknown illnesses as a child that left him bedridden until the age of seven, but he later died of strokes in London.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. Her most famous achievements included the discovery of the elements Polonium and Radium, isolating them from tons of pitchblende ore over several years.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It is the political, economic, and cultural center of Spain, housing the national parliament where the Prime Minister governs.

Title: France–United States relations
Relations between France and the United States stretch back to the American Revolutionary War, when the French provided crucial military and financial support. This historic alliance was famously memorialized in the late 19th century when France presented the American government with a massive copper monument representing freedom and democracy.

Title: Table Bay
Table Bay is a natural bay on the Atlantic Ocean near the southern tip of the African continent. It is overlooked by the imposing, flat-topped silhouette of Table Mountain. The bay features Robben Island near its entrance and forms the primary harbor for the massive coastal metropolis of Cape Town.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in Ishpeming, located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Olympic Gold Medals
Olympic medals are awarded to victorious athletes at the Olympic Games. While the top prize is referred to as a "gold" medal, it is a common misconception that they are made of solid gold. In modern times, they are actually struck from 92.5% silver and merely plated with a minimum of 6 grams of pure gold.

Title: Russia
Russia, or the Russian Federation, is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by land area. With a rich history of scientific and cultural contributions, it produced the creator of the periodic table and successfully hosted major international sporting events, including the 2018 World Cup.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high-fantasy novels written by a British author and published in the 1950s. The series is considered a classic of children's literature, tracing the adventures of children who are transported to a magical realm. The books were written at Oxford alongside a close colleague.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major global center for art and culture for centuries. The capital city is Paris, which frequently hosted the premieres of major international theatrical and musical works during the Belle Époque.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe, situated in the Eastern Alps. It was historically a massive political and cultural power under the Habsburg dynasty. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" for its association with major classical composers.

Title: Hayao Miyazaki
Hayao Miyazaki is an animator, filmmaker, and manga artist. A co-founder of Studio Ghibli, he has attained international acclaim as a masterful storyteller and creator of Japanese animated feature films. He was born in Tokyo, Japan, in 1941, during the onset of the Pacific War.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with atomic number 101. A highly radioactive metallic element in the actinide series, it is the first element that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities through neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It was named after the Russian chemist who famously created the periodic table. Its chemical symbol is Md.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: The Old Man and the Sea
"The Old Man and the Sea" is a short novel written by American author Ernest Hemingway in 1951 and published in 1952. The story centers on an aging fisherman who struggles with a giant marlin far out in the Gulf Stream. It was the last major work of fiction published by the author during his lifetime.

Title: James Watson
James Dewey Watson is an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist. He co-authored the 1953 academic paper proposing the double helix structure of the DNA molecule. Watson was born in Chicago, Illinois, and traveled to England specifically to work at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while investigating pitchblende. The element holds the atomic number 84, and was deliberately named after Marie Curie's birth country of Poland to highlight its struggle for independence.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: Alexander III of Russia
Alexander III was Emperor of Russia from 1881 until his death in 1894. He was a highly conservative ruler who reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father. He died of terminal kidney disease at the Livadia Palace in Crimea, peacefully passing the throne to his son.

Title: Puerperal fever
Puerperal fever, also known as postpartum infections, are bacterial infections of the female reproductive tract following childbirth or miscarriage. Before the widespread understanding of germ theory and the adoption of handwashing by doctors in the late 19th century, it was a leading cause of maternal mortality, claiming the lives of many historical figures.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel written by a prominent American author. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and Gatsby's obsession to reunite with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. It is widely considered a contender for the title of the "Great American Novel".

Title: Austrian Empire in 1822
The Austrian Empire was a multi-national empire and one of Europe's great powers. In 1822, the empire was navigating the conservative post-Napoleonic era orchestrated by Klemens von Metternich. During this entire period, the empire was ruled by Emperor Francis I.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large, space-based observatory launched into low Earth orbit in April 1990. Despite an early issue with a flawed mirror, servicing missions corrected its optics, turning it into one of the most vital research tools in astronomy. It was named in honor of astronomer Edwin Hubble.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: Chemical Properties of Holmium
As a rare-earth metal, holmium is relatively soft and malleable. It possesses the highest magnetic strength of any element. On the periodic table, scientists identify this specific element using the two-letter chemical symbol Ho.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He was one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: 2004 Ballon d'Or
The 2004 Ballon d'Or was a highly contested award given to the premier European footballer of the year. The winner was an incredibly prolific AC Milan striker who dominated the domestic and European scoring charts, beating out Deco and Ronaldinho for the prize.

Title: Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi
Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi was a French sculptor and painter. He is best known for designing the Statue of Liberty. Born in Colmar, in the Alsace region of France, he was deeply inspired by colossal ancient monuments and spent much of his career crafting massive patriotic sculptures.

Title: Leo Tolstoy
Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy, usually referred to in English as Leo Tolstoy, was a Russian writer who is regarded as one of the greatest authors of all time. He is best known for his epic novels "War and Peace" and "Anna Karenina". He died of pneumonia at the Astapovo railway station in 1910.

Title: Super Bowl II
Super Bowl II was played on January 14, 1968, at the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida. The Green Bay Packers defeated the Oakland Raiders by the score of 33-14, capturing their second consecutive world championship under the legendary leadership of head coach Vince Lombardi.

Title: Gothenburg
Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden, situated on the country's west coast. It is an important seaport and a major hub for manufacturing and education. While it is a vital contributor to the national economy, it does not hold the title of the nation's political capital.

Title: William Herschel
Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is best known for his discovery of the planet Uranus in 1781, which was the first planet discovered using a telescope. He also discovered two of its major moons and mapped numerous nebulae.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, and its most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 14 minutes. The element was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." His model of the atom, which proposed that electrons travel in discrete orbits around the nucleus, was a fundamental step forward in quantum mechanics.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement. In a bizarre historical footnote, Picasso was actually brought in for questioning by police as a suspect during the infamous 1911 Louvre theft investigation.

Title: Ernst Chain
Ernst Boris Chain was a German-born British biochemist. Fleeing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, he settled in Britain, where he collaborated closely with Florey. Together, they devised the biochemical methods to successfully isolate and purify penicillin, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize for their efforts.

Title: French Open
The French Open, also known as Roland-Garros, is a major tennis tournament held over two weeks at the Stade Roland Garros in Paris. It is the premier clay court championship in the world. The men's singles winner is awarded the Coupe des Mousquetaires.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe. Published in 1543, just before its author's death, the book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the Ptolemaic geocentric model.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of a famous existentialist writer. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: Incandescent Light Bulb
The development of a commercially viable incandescent light bulb was achieved in the late 1870s by an American inventor working at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. The invention fundamentally altered modern society by providing widespread access to reliable, safe electric indoor lighting.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: Mount Whitney
Mount Whitney is the highest mountain in the contiguous United States, with an elevation of 14,505 feet (4,421 m). It is located in the Sierra Nevada mountain range in California. The peak is highly recognizable and serves as the ultimate goal for many prominent American mountaineering trails.

Title: Meiji Restoration
The Meiji Restoration was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to the Empire of Japan in 1868 under Emperor Meiji. The event effectively destroyed the shogunate system, paving the way for the modernization and Westernization of the country and establishing a centralized government.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramicist, and theatre designer who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement, the invention of constructed sculpture, and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". His early career is famously divided into the somber Blue Period and the more optimistic Rose Period.

Title: West Orange Laboratory
After outgrowing his initial facilities, a famous American inventor moved his operations to a much larger, modernized complex. The West Orange Laboratory in New Jersey became a massive industrial research facility where the motion picture camera and improved phonographs were developed, though it lacked the mythic, pioneering reputation of his earlier facility.

Title: Daniel Peter
Daniel Peter was a pioneering chocolatier who revolutionized the candy industry. Originally a candle maker, he shifted to confectionery as the demand for oil lamps grew. In 1875, working in his home country of Switzerland, he utilized his neighbor Henri Nestlé's recently invented condensed milk to successfully create the first solid milk chocolate bar.

Title: Battle of Hastings
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, the Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It was a decisive Norman victory that radically altered the course of English history and language.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
An induction motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction. This revolutionary device eliminated the need for mechanical commutators. The first practical alternating current induction motor was independently invented in the 1880s by a brilliant Serbian-American engineer.

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal in the actinide series. The element was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film incorporating both historical and fictionalized aspects of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. The film was a massive commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing film of all time upon its release, a record it held until 2010. It was heavily praised for its visual effects and emotional weight.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the Jacobite rising of 1745. He was the reigning sovereign in 1749, the year the pioneer of vaccination was born.

Title: The Son of Man
"The Son of Man" is a 1964 painting by a prominent Belgian surrealist painter. It consists of a man in an overcoat and a bowler hat standing in front of a low wall, beyond which are the sea and a cloudy sky. The man's face is largely obscured by a hovering green apple.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two geographically and socially distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for hosting the Mount Rushmore memorial in the Black Hills. Its state capital is Pierre.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb student and a member of Young Bosnia, an organization seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Austro-Hungarian heir apparent and his wife by firing a pistol at their open car as it stalled in the streets of Sarajevo.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: Multiple Nobel Laureates
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, and only a very small number of individuals have won multiple times. The very first person to ever win two Nobel Prizes, and the only one to win in two distinct scientific fields (Physics and Chemistry), was Marie Curie.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, officially known as Czechia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Mary Wollstonecraft
Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer, philosopher, and advocate of women's rights. She is best known for "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman" (1792). Her life was cut tragically short in 1797; shortly after giving birth to her second daughter, Mary, she contracted puerperal fever and passed away.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

The bay features Robben Island near its entrance and forms the primary harbor for the massive coastal metropolis of Cape Town.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its industrial history and for being the birthplace of aviation pioneers and numerous astronauts. The political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Columbus.

Title: Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive alkaline earth metal with the atomic number 88. It was discovered alongside polonium by the Curies in 1898. Its name is derived from the Latin word for ray, recognizing its immense power to emit ionizing radiation.

Title: Victor Hugo
Victor Marie Hugo was a French poet, novelist, and dramatist of the Romantic movement. He is considered one of the greatest and best-known French writers. Like his contemporary Dumas, Hugo is buried in the Panthéon, having been interred there shortly after his death in 1885.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were re-allocated on financial grounds following a disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius. They were the longest modern Olympics ever held, lasting a total of 187 days.

Title: Gabriel García Márquez
Gabriel García Márquez was a legendary novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. Affectionately known as "Gabo," he won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the small town of Aracataca, located in the northern region of Colombia.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. He is a Professorial Fellow of Computer Science at the University of Oxford and a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His pioneering work at CERN laid the foundation for modern internet infrastructure.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. Located on the site of the former Roman settlement of Iuvavum, it is situated on the border with Germany. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center, dominated by its massive central cathedral.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he often collaborates with composer John Williams to score his films. In 1993, he directed the highest-grossing film of the year, "Jurassic Park", an action-packed blockbuster about genetically engineered dinosaurs breaking loose.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains and Pampas grasslands. The political, economic, and cultural hub of the nation is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. Bohr was born in 1885 in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would later serve as the center of his academic career.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, it tells the story of narrator Nick Carraway and his interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a contender for the Great American Novel.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Discovery of Streptomycin
Streptomycin was the first antibiotic remedy for tuberculosis. It was discovered in 1943 by Albert Schatz in the laboratory of Selman Waksman at Rutgers University. Unlike earlier antibiotics derived from molds, this drug was isolated from a soil-dwelling bacterium known as Streptomyces griseus.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. His mastery of human anatomy is showcased in his famous marble statue of David. Though he preferred sculpting, he was also commissioned to paint the magnificent frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in Asia, after the Yangtze. Originating in the Bayan Har Mountains in Qinghai province, it empties into the Bohai Sea. The river basin was the birthplace of ancient civilization and remains deeply important to the regional identity.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. After proposing an information management system in 1989, he successfully implemented the first communication between an HTTP client and server via the internet. He was born in 1955 in London, United Kingdom.

Title: Mike Tyson
Mike Tyson is an American former professional boxer who competed from 1985 to 2005. Nicknamed "Iron Mike," he is considered one of the greatest heavyweight boxers of all time. He reigned as the undisputed world heavyweight champion and holds the record as the youngest boxer ever to win a heavyweight title.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who developed many devices in fields such as electric power generation, mass communication, sound recording, and motion pictures. Born in Ohio, he built a massive industrial research facility that pioneered the process of organized collaborative invention.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is globally famous for its vibrant culture, the Amazon rainforest, and its unmatched success in international football. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Brasília, which was inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Animals (album)
"Animals" is the tenth studio album by Pink Floyd, released in 1977. It is a concept album that provides a scathing critique of the social-political conditions of late 1970s Britain. The album's famous cover art shows an enormous inflatable pink pig floating between two chimneys of the Battersea Power Station.

Title: 2014 FIFA World Cup
The 2014 FIFA World Cup was the 20th FIFA World Cup. It took place in Brazil from 12 June to 13 July 2014, after the country was awarded the hosting rights in 2007. The tournament culminated in Germany winning their fourth title by defeating Argentina in the final.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Walt Whitman
Walt Whitman was an American poet, essayist, and journalist. A humanist, he was a part of the transition between transcendentalism and realism. His magnum opus, "Leaves of Grass", was highly controversial in its time. During the Civil War, he worked in Washington D.C. hospitals caring for wounded soldiers.

Title: Marc Andreessen
Marc Andreessen is an American entrepreneur, investor, and software engineer. He is best known as the co-author of Mosaic, the first widely used web browser, and as co-founder of Netscape. Before launching his legendary tech career, Andreessen earned his bachelor's degree in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including the iconic Mona Lisa. In the 1980s, the museum underwent a major modernization project that added a large, controversial glass pyramid to its main courtyard.

Title: The Invincibles
In English football, the term "The Invincibles" is most famously used to refer to the Arsenal F.C. squad managed by Arsène Wenger. They earned this legendary nickname by completing an entire 38-game Premier League season without a single defeat. This historic, unbeaten campaign was completed in May 2004.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign is known as the Victorian era, a period of massive industrial expansion and public health reform. She oversaw the construction of modern sewer systems in the capital, preventing future cholera outbreaks.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: Alan Turing
Alan Turing was an English mathematician and computer scientist. While he worked extensively at Bletchley Park and designed the "Bombe" machine to break the Enigma code, he was not the primary engineer who designed and built the Colossus computer.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland commissioned the historic voyages of the HMS Beagle. The nation has maintained a strictly independent monetary policy throughout its history, utilizing the Pound sterling as its official currency.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, and its most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 14 minutes. The element was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Voyage of the Beagle
From 1831 to 1836, a British naval vessel conducted a major hydrographic survey expedition around South America. Among the passengers was a young English naturalist who collected extensive geological and biological specimens. In September 1835, the expedition arrived at the remote Galápagos Islands, providing vital data for his future evolutionary theories.

Title: The Planets
"The Planets", Op. 32, is a seven-movement orchestral suite by a prominent English composer, written between 1914 and 1917. Each movement of the suite is named after a planet of the Solar System and its corresponding astrological character, such as "Mars, the Bringer of War."

Title: London
London is the capital city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis and serves as a vital transport route.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: The Black Death
The Black Death was a devastating global epidemic of bubonic plague that struck Europe and Asia in the mid-1300s. It killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people, fundamentally altering the demographic and economic landscape of the medieval world long before the modernization of European cities.

Title: Wonders of the Ancient World
The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World were a list of remarkable constructions of classical antiquity. While the Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one still standing, others were legendary in their time. Among these was a colossal structure built to guide sailors safely into harbor, located in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Final Defeat in 1815
After briefly returning from his first exile, Napoleon Bonaparte launched a final military campaign. His reign permanently ended when his forces were decisively crushed by a coalition of British and Prussian armies in June 1815. This catastrophic loss occurred at the historic Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Miami
Miami is a major coastal metropolis located in southeastern Florida. It is the core of the state's largest metropolitan area and a massive hub for international finance, culture, and arts. Despite its massive size and global influence, it does not serve as the seat of the state government.

Title: Austrian Empire in 1822
The Austrian Empire was a multi-national empire and one of Europe's great powers. In 1822, the empire was navigating the conservative post-Napoleonic era orchestrated by Klemens von Metternich. During this entire period, the empire was ruled by Emperor Francis I.

Title: Ukraine
Ukraine is a country in Eastern Europe. It is the second-largest European country by area after Russia. Known for its vast agricultural plains, the country is bordered by the Black Sea to the south and several mountain ranges to the west. Its capital and most populous city is Kyiv.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a pioneering physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He famously discovered the atomic nucleus through his gold foil experiment. Rutherford was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a small town on the South Island of New Zealand.

Title: Caroline Herschel
Caroline Lucretia Herschel was a German astronomer whose most significant contributions to astronomy were the discoveries of several comets, including the periodic comet 35P/Herschel–Rigollet and Comet C/1786 P1. She worked extensively alongside her older brother, assisting him with his own massive astronomical breakthroughs before earning independent fame.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. Her most famous achievements included the discovery of the elements Polonium and Radium, isolating them from tons of pitchblende ore over several years.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity. It remains a critical piece of infrastructure for the North African nation.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital of Russia for over two centuries before the government moved back to Moscow.

Title: The Divine Comedy
"The Divine Comedy" is an Italian narrative poem begun c. 1308 and completed in 1320. It is widely considered one of the pre-eminent works in Italian literature and one of the greatest works of world literature. The poem's imaginative vision of the afterlife is representative of the medieval worldview.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The nation's capital and largest city is Rome, which completely surrounds the world's smallest independent state. The Italian military handles external defense for the enclave, but not the personal safety of the Pope.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. It serves as the seat of all three branches of the Government of India.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice, sharing her first prize with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Russia
Russia, or the Russian Federation, is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by land area. With a rich history of scientific and cultural contributions, it produced the creator of the periodic table and successfully hosted major international sporting events, including the 2018 World Cup.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a romantic ballet composed in 1875-1876. It was initially a failure upon its premiere at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow, largely due to poor staging and an uninspired orchestra. It was only after subsequent revisions that it became one of the most popular ballets of all time.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: Dante Alighieri
Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher. His "Divine Comedy", originally called "Comedìa" and later christened "Divina" by Giovanni Boccaccio, is widely considered the most important poem of the Middle Ages. Dante was born in Florence, Italy, and received his early education in the city's religious schools.

Title: Polio Vaccines
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis. The first breakthrough was an inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which requires injection and utilizes a killed version of the virus. Shortly after, a cheaper, oral polio vaccine (OPV) using an attenuated live virus was developed, which became the standard in global eradication efforts.

Title: United States Capitals
The political capital of the United States has shifted several times throughout its early history. Today, the capital of the United States is Washington, D.C., a federal district created specifically to house the national government. It is entirely separate from any state jurisdiction.

Title: Silvio Berlusconi
Silvio Berlusconi was an Italian media tycoon and politician who served as Prime Minister of Italy in four separate governments. He was in power during Italy's triumphant 2006 World Cup campaign. Berlusconi was born and raised in Milan, the capital of the Lombardy region.

Title: Alien (film)
"Alien" is a 1979 science fiction horror film that follows the crew of the commercial space tug Nostromo. They encounter a deadly extraterrestrial lifeform set loose on the ship. The film famously features Sigourney Weaver in her breakout role as the resilient warrant officer, Ellen Ripley. It was directed by the visionary British filmmaker Ridley Scott.

Title: George III of Great Britain
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies during the American Revolutionary War and for his later bouts of mental illness. He ascended to the throne well after the birth of the scientist who invented the smallpox vaccine.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is most famous for his performance in the 1986 World Cup, where he scored the notorious "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. As Napoleon I, he was Emperor of the French from 1804 until 1814, and again in 1815. His quest for European domination finally ended in 1815 when he was crushed by coalition forces at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Nikita Khrushchev
Nikita Khrushchev was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the country's Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. As the premier of the nation, he oversaw the early, highly successful years of the Soviet space program, including the historic launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

Title: Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east. It features warm tropical waters and numerous island chains, including the historic archipelago of Zanzibar.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a Danish architect, most notable for designing the Sydney Opera House in Australia. When it was declared a World Heritage Site in 2007, Utzon became the second person to have received such recognition for a work during their lifetime. He was born in Copenhagen, Denmark.

Title: Cloning of Dolly
The scientific world was fundamentally altered by a major breakthrough at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Using the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer, researchers successfully cloned a female domestic sheep from an adult somatic cell. This historic mammal, affectionately named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company that specializes in consumer electronics, software, and online services. Founded by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, it has grown into one of the "Big Five" American information technology companies. The company's massive headquarters is located in Cupertino, California.

Title: NASA
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is an independent agency of the U.S. federal government responsible for the civil space program, aeronautics research, and space research. It was established in 1958 by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in direct response to the early successes of a rival nation's space initiatives.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Connecticut
Connecticut is a state in the New England region of the United States, known for its historic universities and coastal towns. It was the site of the Yale University campus where several future politicians were educated. Despite his strong association with Texas, it is actually the birth state of the 43rd US President.

Title: British Empire in the 17th Century
During the 17th century, the British Empire was rapidly expanding its overseas colonies and trading networks. The domestic front, however, faced extreme turmoil, including a civil war and disastrous urban fires. King Charles II was the reigning monarch trying to stabilize the country during the calamitous events of 1666.

Title: Vostok 1
Vostok 1 was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first crewed spaceflight in history. Launched by the Soviet Union in April 1961, it carried cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who became the first human to cross into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Columbus, Ohio
Columbus is the state capital and the most populous city in the U.S. state of Ohio. With a diverse economy based on education, government, insurance, and banking, the city is home to the Battelle Memorial Institute and the main campus of Ohio State University. It was named in honor of the Italian explorer Christopher Columbus.

Title: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a massive country in South Asia. It achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation was the birthplace of several major literary figures during the colonial era. The political and administrative capital of India is New Delhi.

Title: Properties of Holmium
As a rare-earth metal, holmium is relatively soft and malleable. It has the highest magnetic strength of any element, making it valuable for generating strong artificial magnetic fields. On the periodic table, holmium is assigned the atomic number 67.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Chile
Chile is a country located in western South America, occupying a long, narrow strip of land between the Andes to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west. It is known for its diverse geography, ranging from dry deserts in the north to alpine tundras in the south. The capital and largest city is Santiago.

Title: California quail
The California quail, also known as the California valley quail, is a small ground-dwelling bird in the New World quail family. They have a curving crest or plume, made of six feathers, that droops forward. It is the official state bird of California.

Title: 1952 Summer Olympics
The 1952 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XV Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The global competition broke several records for the number of participating nations. The games were hosted in Helsinki, bringing worldwide attention to the Nordic region.

Title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
"E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" is a 1982 American science fiction film produced and directed by Steven Spielberg. It tells the story of Elliott, a boy who befriends an extraterrestrial dubbed E.T., who is stranded on Earth. The film surpassed "Star Wars" to become the highest-grossing film of all time—a record it held for eleven years.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: Genetics
Genetics is the study of genes, genetic variation, and heredity in organisms. It is an important branch in biology because heredity is vital to organisms' evolution. The modern era of genetics began with the rediscovery of 19th-century inheritance principles in the early 1900s.

Title: Russia
Russia is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by area. Moscow is the capital and largest city, serving as the historical and contemporary center of Russian political power.

Title: Francisco Pizarro
Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that conquered the massive Inca Empire. He captured and killed the reigning Inca emperor, claimed the lands for Spain, and founded the city of Lima in 1535. His conquests brought vast wealth to the Spanish crown.

Title: Theresa May
Theresa Mary May is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2016 to 2019. Following the resignation of David Cameron after the Brexit referendum, she became the second female to hold the office of Prime Minister. She stepped down in 2019 and was succeeded by Boris Johnson.

Title: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 is a supertall skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. It officially held the title of the world's tallest building from its opening in 2004 until the completion of a taller megastructure in Dubai in 2009. The building was designed by C.Y. Lee & Partners to withstand the region's frequent typhoons and earthquakes.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history for centuries. Its capital and largest city is Paris, which serves as a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: Valentina Tereshkova
Valentina Tereshkova is a Russian engineer, member of the State Duma, and former Soviet cosmonaut. She is the first and youngest woman to have flown in space. On 16 June 1963, she piloted the Vostok 6 spacecraft, completing 48 orbits of the Earth over almost three days in space.

Title: False Bay
False Bay is a body of water defined by Cape Hangklip and the Cape Peninsula in the extreme south-west of South Africa. The bay was named "False Bay" by sailors who confused the Cape Point and Cape Hangklip, falsely believing they had reached Table Bay.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: Europe
Europe is a continent located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and mostly in the Eastern Hemisphere. It is bordered by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and the Mediterranean Sea to the south. In chemistry, this continent serves as the namesake for the rare earth element Europium.

Title: Cheltenham
Cheltenham, also known as Cheltenham Spa, is a large spa town and borough on the edge of the Cotswolds in the South West of England. Known for its Regency architecture, it was the birthplace of the famous composer Gustav Holst. Administratively, the town is located within the county of Gloucestershire.

Title: Don Shula
Don Shula was a legendary American football player and coach. He is best known for coaching the Miami Dolphins to two Super Bowl victories, including the only perfect season in NFL history. He played his collegiate football at John Carroll University in Ohio.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. He is best known for his metallic, flowing designs, such as the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao and the Walt Disney Concert Hall.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
