Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Upon stepping onto the lunar surface, the commander famously broadcast the words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

Title: 2004 in Politics
The year 2004 was a period of intense global political activity and ongoing military conflicts in the Middle East. In the United States, it was an election year marked by debates over national security and economic policy. The incumbent president managed to secure a second term after a highly contested race.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Giant Panda
The Giant Panda is a bear species endemic to the mountainous bamboo forests of central Asia. Characterized by its bold black-and-white coat and rotund body, it relies almost exclusively on bamboo for its diet. In biological taxonomy, the Giant Panda belongs to the class Mammalia and the phylum Chordata.

Title: Canberra, Australia
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between the two largest rival cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and was built as a planned city.

Title: Bronze
Bronze is an alloy consisting primarily of copper, commonly with about 12–12.5% of another metallic element added to increase its strength and durability. Because of its excellent casting properties, it has been the metal of choice for sculptors for centuries, famously utilized to forge Rodin's masterpiece "The Thinker".

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. It is named after the planet Neptune, continuing the tradition of naming elements after the planets in the solar system.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, best known for his pioneering contributions to the science of evolution. His theory that all life descended from common ancestors was heavily informed by his observations of unique wildlife, such as tortoises and finches, during a multi-year global voyage.

Title: Tallest Building in the World
The title of the tallest building in the world has changed hands numerous times over the centuries. Currently, the record is held by a massive megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Standing at a staggering total height of 829.8 meters (2,722 ft), it has held the title since its topping out in 2009.

Title: Zinc
Zinc is a chemical element with the symbol Zn and atomic number 30. It is a slightly brittle metal at room temperature and has a shiny-greyish appearance when oxidation is removed. When alloyed with copper, it creates brass, a material known for its acoustic properties and bright, gold-like appearance.

Title: Hand of God Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who deceitfully punched the ball into the net later attributed it to the "Hand of God."

Title: Austria-Hungary
Austria-Hungary was a constitutional monarchic union of the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary that existed from 1867 to 1918. It was a massive, multi-ethnic empire that dominated Central Europe. It was the historical sovereign state in which Franz Kafka was born before the empire's post-WWI dissolution.

Title: 20-Dollar Bill
The United States twenty-dollar bill ($20) is a denomination of U.S. currency. Andrew Jackson, the seventh U.S. president, has been featured on the obverse of the bill since 1928, while the White House is featured on the reverse. It is one of the most heavily circulated bills in the American economy.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: US Open
The US Open is a hardcourt tennis tournament. It is the fourth and final Grand Slam tournament of the year. The men's singles champion is awarded the US Open Trophy, which is made by Tiffany & Co. and constructed entirely of sterling silver, though it lacks the golden veneer of its British counterpart.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in middle and high schools across the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot is loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Query: What is the modern name of the city where the poet exiled by the very first Roman Emperor died?
content:
Title: Properties of Holmium
As a rare-earth metal, holmium is relatively soft and malleable. It has the highest magnetic strength of any element, making it valuable for generating strong artificial magnetic fields. On the periodic table, holmium is assigned the atomic number 67.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. The town is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist, who also designed the town's famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where he is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, which he named penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 by the same team at the University of California, Berkeley that found several other transuranic elements. It is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Augustus
Augustus was the founder of the Roman Principate and considered the first Roman Emperor. He ruled from 27 BC until his death in AD 14. During his reign, he famously banished the celebrated poet Ovid to a remote province on the Black Sea for mysterious reasons.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
The alternating current (AC) induction motor is an electric motor in which the current in the rotor is obtained by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding. This revolutionary device was invented by Nikola Tesla in the 1880s. Its development allowed for the efficient transmission of high-voltage electrical energy over massive distances.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or, given to the best football player in Europe as judged by a panel of sports journalists from UEFA member countries, was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the prestigious accolade.

Title: Zhytomyr
Zhytomyr is a city in the north of the western half of Ukraine. It is the administrative center of Zhytomyr Oblast. A historic city, it was a major transport hub linking Kiev with points west. It proudly serves as the birthplace of the chief designer of the early Soviet space program.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major global center for art and culture for centuries. The capital city is Paris, which frequently hosted the premieres of major international theatrical and musical works during the Belle Époque.

Title: The Brothers Karamazov
"The Brothers Karamazov" is a passionate philosophical novel that explores deep questions regarding God, free will, and morality. It was the final novel written by the author of "Crime and Punishment" and is widely considered one of the supreme achievements in world literature.

Title: 1913 Paris Ballet Riot
In 1913, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris hosted the premiere of a radical new ballet. The performance featured dissonant, avant-garde music and jerky, non-traditional choreography. The audience was so outraged by the shocking departure from classical traditions that a literal riot broke out in the theater.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, his work was heavily inspired by classical antiquity and had a profound influence on the development of Western art. His most famous paintings adorn the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. As Vice President, he was thrust into the presidency on November 22, 1963, following the tragic assassination of John F. Kennedy in Dallas. He became the commander-in-chief on the exact day that author Aldous Huxley passed away.

Title: Constanța
Constanța is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Romania. Located at the crossroads of several commercial routes, it lies on the western coast of the Black Sea. Built directly over the ancient ruins of Tomis, it now serves as Romania's largest sea port.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is famous for its passionate football culture, vibrant Carnival festivals, and the sprawling Amazon rainforest. The country's highest physical point is the Pico da Neblina, located deep within the Guiana Highlands.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: The House of the Spirits
"The House of the Spirits" is the 1982 debut novel of a prominent South American author. The novel incorporates elements of magic realism to trace the lives of the Trueba family across four generations. It became an immediate international best-seller and was later adapted into a major motion picture.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps, the city is famous for its religious diversity, with adherents of Islam, Orthodoxy, Catholicism, and Judaism coexisting there for centuries. The Miljacka river flows directly through the heart of the city.

Title: Days of Thunder
"Days of Thunder" is a 1990 American sports action drama film starring Tom Cruise as an ambitious stock car racing driver. Also directed by Tony Scott, it attempted to replicate the massive success and visual style of their previous collaboration, though it focused on NASCAR rather than fighter jets.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It is currently housed in the National Gallery in Oslo, Norway, and has been the target of multiple high-profile art thefts.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA, and of identifying, mapping and sequencing all of the genes of the human genome. It remains the world's largest collaborative biological project, completed in 2003.

Title: The Mona Lisa
"Mona Lisa" is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci. Considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance, it has been described as the most famous, most visited, most written about, and most parodied work of art in the world. The painting's novel qualities include the subject's elusive expression.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. He is a Professorial Fellow of Computer Science at the University of Oxford and a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His pioneering work at CERN laid the foundation for modern internet infrastructure.

Title: Salinas, California
Salinas is the county seat and largest municipality of Monterey County, California. Located at the mouth of the Salinas Valley, the city has long been an agricultural powerhouse. It produces such a massive volume of a specific leafy green vegetable that it has earned the nickname "The Lettuce Capital of the World."

Title: Cerium
Cerium is a chemical element with the symbol Ce and atomic number 58. It is a soft, ductile, and silvery-white metal that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was independently discovered by Martin Heinrich Klaproth alongside other European chemists in 1803. It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier.

Title: Louis XIV of France
Louis XIV, known as Louis the Great or the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. His reign of 72 years and 110 days is the longest recorded of any monarch of a sovereign country in history. He famously offered a lavish exile to the deposed English king James II.

Title: Spirited Away
"Spirited Away" is a 2001 animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It tells the story of Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who wanders into the world of kami while moving to a new neighborhood. It was incredibly successful, winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Title: First Roman Emperor
The Roman Republic definitively ended with the rise of the first Roman Emperor. Born Gaius Octavius, he was granted the honorific title of Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC. His autocratic rule initiated a period of relative peace known as the Pax Romana, though he dealt harshly with political dissidents and scandalous figures.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. Born in New York City, USA, he chose not to patent the vaccine to maximize its global distribution. His inactivated polio vaccine required an injection but proved immensely effective in clinical trials.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate and investor. He was the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Apple. Jobs famously dropped out of Reed College in Oregon after only one semester, though he continued to audit classes. He went on to revolutionize the personal computing, music, and mobile phone industries.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Driving Miss Daisy
"Driving Miss Daisy" is a 1989 American comedy-drama film adapted from the 1987 play of the same name by Alfred Uhry. Starring Jessica Tandy and Morgan Freeman, the film was a massive commercial and critical success, ultimately winning the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was directed by Bruce Beresford.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His political stance often conflicted with the empire's rigid establishment. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife Sophie were fatally shot during a state visit. This assassination set the wheels in motion for the First World War.

Title: Lawrence, Kansas
Lawrence is the county seat of Douglas County, Kansas, and the sixth-largest city in the state. Situated along the banks of the Kansas and Wakarusa Rivers, it serves as a major college town, being home to the University of Kansas. The city was officially founded in 1854 by the New England Emigrant Aid Company.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, located in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as a fortress in the late 12th to 13th century.

Title: Rembrandt
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was a Dutch Golden Age painter, printmaker, and draughtsman. He is generally considered one of the greatest visual artists in the history of art. Unlike his contemporary who painted "Girl with a Pearl Earring", Rembrandt spent the vast majority of his prolific career living and working in Amsterdam.

Title: Calvin Coolidge
John Calvin Coolidge Jr. was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 30th president of the United States from 1923 to 1929. Known as "Silent Cal" for his quiet demeanor, he assumed the presidency after the sudden death of Warren G. Harding and was the sitting president in 1926.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
"To Kill a Mockingbird" is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in high schools and middle schools in the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot and characters are loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: Mission Control
The Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center is NASA's center for human spaceflight training, research, and flight control. Following liftoff from the eastern seaboard, flight operations are famously handed over to Mission Control, which is located in Houston, Texas.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement. In a bizarre historical footnote, Picasso was actually brought in for questioning by police as a suspect during the infamous 1911 Louvre theft investigation.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: 1998 FIFA World Cup
The 1998 FIFA World Cup was the 16th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. The tournament culminated in a dramatic final match where the host nation, France, decisively defeated Brazil 3-0 to claim their first-ever World Cup trophy.

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a romantic ballet composed in 1875-1876. It was initially a failure upon its premiere at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow, largely due to poor staging and an uninspired orchestra. It was only after subsequent revisions that it became one of the most popular ballets of all time.

Title: Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. It has a rich history of maritime exploration and global colonization, once maintaining a vast empire across the Americas. The political, cultural, and economic center of the nation is its capital city, Madrid.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era, characterized by a period of immense industrial, political, and military change. She was the sitting monarch in 1853.

Title: First Woman in Space
The race to put the first woman in space was intensely competitive during the Cold War. The Soviet Union achieved this milestone in 1963 when they selected a former textile worker and amateur skydiver from the civilian population to pilot a solo orbital mission, beating the United States by exactly two decades.

Title: Rosalind Franklin
Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose work was central to the understanding of the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, viruses, and coal. Her famous Photo 51 was critical in determining the double helix structure of DNA, though she died before the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery.

Title: Hershey, Pennsylvania
Hershey is an unincorporated community in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. Often referred to as "Chocolatetown, USA," it is the home of The Hershey Company. The town was founded in 1903 by Milton S. Hershey to provide housing and amenities for the workers of his massive chocolate factory.

Title: Rhenium
Rhenium is a chemical element with the symbol Re and atomic number 75. It is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. Discovered in 1925, it was the last stable element to be discovered. It was named after the river Rhine in Europe.

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: The Stranger
"The Stranger" is a 1942 novella authored by French philosopher and writer Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus' philosophy of the absurd and existentialism. The novel begins with the iconic lines concerning the death of the protagonist's mother.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It played a critical role in the Allied victory during World War II, fueled by technological innovations like radar and early computing. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Royal Society of London
The Royal Society of London, formally The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge, is a learned society and the United Kingdom's national academy of sciences. Founded in 1660, it played a crucial role in early modern science. It famously translated and published the microscopic observations sent by the Dutch "father of microbiology" in its journal.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has a rich history as a global center for art, philosophy, and science, having hosted numerous legendary expatriate painters during the 19th and 20th centuries. Today, as a key member of the European Union, France uses the Euro as its official currency.

Title: Zenobia
Zenobia was a 3rd-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Following the death of her husband, she seized power and led a massive revolt against the Roman Empire. She conquered Egypt and much of Anatolia before finally being defeated and captured by the Roman Emperor Aurelian.

Title: Vantaa River
The Vantaa River is a prominent 101-kilometer-long waterway in Southern Finland. It originates from Lake Erkylänjärvi and flows into the Gulf of Finland. The river heavily shapes the geography of the Finnish capital, providing both scenic value and historical routes for trade.

Title: Dietary Habits of Marsupials
Many marsupials have highly specialized diets that influence their digestive systems. Koalas, for instance, survive almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals. Their slow metabolic rate allows them to process the tough, fibrous leaves, resulting in small, pellet-like droppings.

Title: Invention of the World Wide Web
The World Wide Web, commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators. It was invented in 1989 at CERN in Switzerland. The creator developed the first web browser and the fundamental protocols of the internet, HTTP and HTML.

Title: University of Cambridge
The University of Cambridge is a collegiate research university in Cambridge, United Kingdom. Founded in 1209, it is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of a variety of institutions, including 31 semi-autonomous constituent colleges. It boasts numerous legendary alumni, including Isaac Newton and the author of "Paradise Lost".

Title: Louis XVI
Louis XVI was the last king of France before the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution. His absolute rule proved deeply unpopular amid widespread economic hardship, leading to his eventual arrest. He was tried by the National Convention, found guilty of high treason, and executed by guillotine.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. The continent is home to diverse geographies, including the Andes mountains and the Amazon rainforest. The largest country on this continent is Brazil.

Title: Economy of France
France boasts a highly developed, social market economy that is among the largest in the world. As a founding member of the European Union, its economic policies are deeply integrated with its neighbors. The official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French franc in 2002.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he managed the early tensions of the Cold War and the beginning of the Space Race, acting as the primary geopolitical rival to the Soviet leadership of that era.

Title: Group 12 element
Group 12 is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table. It includes zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), and the highly radioactive synthetic element copernicium (Cn). Elements in this group generally have lower melting and boiling points than other transition metals.

Title: Alexandre Dumas
Alexandre Dumas was a prolific French writer whose works have been translated into nearly 100 languages. After passing away in 1870, he was originally buried in his birthplace of Villers-Cotterêts. In 2002, to honor his monumental legacy, his remains were re-interred in the Panthéon in Paris.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Pink Floyd
Pink Floyd was an English rock band formed in London in 1965. They achieved international acclaim with their progressive and psychedelic music, particularly with their 1973 masterpiece "The Dark Side of the Moon". The band was initially led by a charismatic but deeply troubled original frontman who was ousted in 1968 due to mental health issues.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System at a diameter of 1,578 kilometres (981 mi). Discovered by William Herschel in 1787, it consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock. Its surface is scarred by massive canyons and fault lines.

Title: Hernán Cortés
Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire and brought large portions of what is now mainland Mexico under the rule of the King of Castile in the early 16th century. He famously captured the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, Finland to the east, and is connected to Denmark in the southwest by a bridge-tunnel. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm. The country's geography is characterized by extensive forests and a rugged mountainous region along the Norwegian border, where its highest peak, Kebnekaise, is located.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: 2008 Summer Olympics
The 2008 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIX Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held from August 8 to 24, 2008. The games were a massive global spectacle and marked a significant moment of international integration. They were hosted in Beijing, the capital city of China.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: Edwin Hubble
Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing the fields of extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. Working primarily from the Mount Wilson Observatory, he proved that many objects previously thought to be clouds of dust and gas were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic is a landlocked country in Central Europe. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains. It is the birth country of several legendary European footballers.

Title: Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. It was led by the United States with support from the United Kingdom and Canada. The project relied heavily on the newly discovered elements at the edge of the periodic table to construct its revolutionary devices.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a highly acclaimed architect notable for his visionary, organic style of modern architecture. He won an international competition to design the new opera house in Sydney, a project that defined his career despite subsequent controversies. Utzon was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 1918.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. He was born in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. He spent the latter part of his life in the United States, working at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, after fleeing the rise of the Nazi regime.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe as Emperor of the French. He was originally born in 1769 to a minor noble family on the Mediterranean island of Corsica.

Title: Discovery of Hydrogen
While artificially produced earlier by others, hydrogen was first recognized as a distinct chemical element in 1766. The English scientist Henry Cavendish was the first to identify hydrogen gas as a discrete substance, naming it "inflammable air" and noting that it produced water when burned.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting created in June 1889 by a renowned Dutch Post-Impressionist painter. It depicts the view from his asylum room window at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: First Emperor of Rome
Following the assassination of Julius Caesar and the subsequent civil wars, the Roman Republic collapsed. The victor of these conflicts emerged as the absolute ruler of the Roman world. He was granted the title Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC, effectively making him the first Emperor of Rome.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: HMS Endeavour
HMS Endeavour was a British Royal Navy research vessel that Lieutenant James Cook commanded to Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia on his first voyage of discovery from 1768 to 1771. The ship was critical to early British exploration of the Pacific but was eventually scuttled during the American Revolutionary War.

Title: Altair 8800
The Altair 8800 is a microcomputer designed in 1974 by MITS and based on the Intel 8080 CPU. It sparked the microcomputer revolution of the 1970s. The machine's popularity skyrocketed after two young programmers successfully developed an interpreter for the BASIC programming language that ran on its hardware.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Elon Musk
Elon Reeve Musk is a business magnate and investor. He is the founder, CEO, and Chief Engineer at SpaceX, as well as the CEO and product architect of Tesla, Inc. Before embarking on his legendary entrepreneurial career in Silicon Valley, Musk transferred from Queen's University to the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned degrees in economics and physics.

Title: Ottawa
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Located in the east of southern Ontario, near the city of Montréal and the U.S. border, it is a major political and technological center. The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, and sits squarely on the south bank of a major waterway.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Nikita Khrushchev
Nikita Khrushchev was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the country's Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. As the premier of the nation, he oversaw the early, highly successful years of the Soviet space program, including the historic launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe in the early 19th century. He was born to a minor Italian noble family on the island of Corsica, mere months after it was acquired by France.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, located on the Votka River. The town was founded in 1759 as a center for metallurgical production. Today, it is best known in cultural circles as the birthplace of a legendary 19th-century Romantic composer whose childhood home is now a museum.

Title: Muhammad Ali
Muhammad Ali was an American professional boxer and activist. Born and raised in Louisville, Kentucky, he began training as an amateur boxer at age 12. He won an Olympic gold medal in 1960. He was originally born with the name Cassius Clay, but changed his name in 1964 after joining the Nation of Islam.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company that specializes in consumer electronics, software, and online services. Founded by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, it has grown into one of the "Big Five" American information technology companies. The company's massive headquarters is located in Cupertino, California.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: Exile of Napoleon
Following his devastating defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was forced to abdicate the French throne for a second time. To ensure he could never return to power, his captors exiled him to a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic, where he ultimately died of stomach cancer in 1821.

Title: Most Academy Awards for a Single Film
Three films in history have tied for the record of winning the most Academy Awards, each earning exactly 11 Oscars. The first was "Ben-Hur" in 1959, followed by "Titanic" in 1997. The most recent film to achieve this monumental sweep was a massive high-fantasy epic released in 2003, which won every category for which it was nominated.

Title: New York City in the 1880s
New York City experienced massive industrial and population growth during the late 19th century. The bustling port city required a massive workforce of customs inspectors to handle international trade. The city's geography also necessitated massive engineering projects to connect its growing boroughs, culminating in a historic bridge opening in 1883.

Title: Walt Whitman
Walt Whitman was an American poet, essayist, and journalist. A humanist, he was a part of the transition between transcendentalism and realism. His magnum opus, "Leaves of Grass", was highly controversial in its time. During the Civil War, he worked in Washington D.C. hospitals caring for wounded soldiers.

Title: Animal Scat Characteristics
Wildlife trackers often rely on the distinct shape and composition of animal feces, or scat, to identify local species. While most mammals produce tubular or spherical droppings, one particular burrowing marsupial is famous for producing distinctively cube-shaped feces, a biological adaptation that prevents the droppings from rolling away from territorial boundary markers.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The games were notably well-organized and featured the first use of electronic timing devices. They were hosted in the capital city of a major Scandinavian nation.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: Jin Mao Tower
The Jin Mao Tower is an 88-story supertall skyscraper located in the Lujiazui area of the Pudong district of Shanghai. It contains a shopping mall, offices, and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai hotel. Blending traditional Chinese architectural elements with modern engineering, it was designed by American architect Adrian Smith.

Title: Bihar
Bihar is a state in eastern India. It is the third-largest state by population and the twelfth-largest by territory. Bounded by Nepal to the north, it is deeply integrated into the cultural and historical fabric of the Indian subcontinent. The state encompasses several historic municipalities, including the district of East Champaran and its headquarters, Motihari.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: Monterey, California
Monterey is a city on California's rugged central coast. Its Cannery Row, one-time center of the sardine-packing industry, was immortalized by a famous American novelist. Today, it is a popular tourist destination known for its massive aquarium and coastal views.

Title: Dante Alighieri
Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher. His "Divine Comedy", originally called "Comedìa" and later christened "Divina" by Giovanni Boccaccio, is widely considered the most important poem of the Middle Ages. Dante was born in Florence, Italy, and received his early education in the city's religious schools.

Title: Stanford University
Stanford University is a private research university located in Stanford, California. The campus occupies 8,180 acres, among the largest in the United States, and enrolls over 17,000 students. It is globally recognized for its proximity to Silicon Valley and has graduated numerous legendary tech founders and CEOs.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Los Angeles
Los Angeles is the largest city in California and the second-most populous city in the United States. It is a massive global center for entertainment, media, and technology. Although it has a robust biomedical sector, its research institutes are distinct from the coastal scientific hubs found further south.

Title: Redmond, Washington
Redmond is a city in King County, Washington, United States, located 15 miles east of Seattle. The city is widely recognized as a major technology hub. It is most famous for being the home of Microsoft's sprawling corporate headquarters campus, a major driver of the local economy and population growth.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. The country's political and administrative center is its capital city, Wellington, located at the south-western tip of the North Island.

Title: Fordham University
Fordham University is a private Jesuit research university located in New York City. Established in 1841, it is the oldest Catholic institution of higher education in the northeastern United States. Its primary, historic Rose Hill campus is situated entirely within the borough of The Bronx.

Title: Virgil
Publius Vergilius Maro, usually called Virgil or Vergil in English, was an ancient Roman poet of the Augustan period. He is known for three major works of Latin literature, the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the epic Aeneid. He died in Brundisium in 19 BC without ever facing imperial exile.

Title: Rabies vaccine
The first rabies vaccine was developed in 1885 by a prominent French chemist. It utilized a weakened strain of the rabies virus harvested from infected rabbits. This breakthrough paved the way for modern immunology and saved countless lives from a previously fatal disease.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". Picasso was born in Málaga, a municipality in the autonomous community of Andalusia.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. Before moving to Seattle to start his online bookstore, Bezos graduated summa cum laude in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science from Princeton University.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a Danish architect, most notable for designing the Sydney Opera House in Australia. When it was declared a World Heritage Site in 2007, Utzon became the second person to have received such recognition for a work during their lifetime. He was born in Copenhagen, Denmark.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist and a pioneer in crystallography and radioactivity. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife. He was born in Paris, France, and spent his entire career working in the city.

Title: Bronze
Bronze is an alloy consisting primarily of copper, commonly with about 12–12.5% of another metallic element added to increase its strength and durability. Because of its excellent casting properties, it has been the metal of choice for sculptors for centuries, famously utilized to forge Rodin's masterpiece "The Thinker".

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It is a rare and highly volatile metal, discovered in 1898 by researchers studying pitchblende. On the periodic table of elements, Polonium is classified as a chalcogen and has the atomic number 84.

Title: X-rays
X-rays make up X-radiation, a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation. Most X-rays have a wavelength ranging from 10 picometers to 10 nanometers. This invisible radiation, which can easily pass through human tissue to image bones, was accidentally discovered in 1895 by a brilliant German mechanical engineer and physicist.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 2
Helium is a chemical element with the symbol He and atomic number 2. It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, inert, monatomic gas that heads the noble gas group in the periodic table. Its boiling and melting points are the lowest among all the elements.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Despite its distinct cultural and linguistic heritage with Italian roots, Corsica is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by the modern nation of France.

Title: Karl Marx
Karl Marx was a German-born philosopher, economist, political theorist, historian, and revolutionary. He is best known for his 1848 pamphlet "The Communist Manifesto" and the multi-volume "Das Kapital". After spending his later years in exile in London, he passed away in 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 is a supertall skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. It officially held the title of the world's tallest building from its opening in 2004 until the completion of a taller megastructure in Dubai in 2009. The building was designed by C.Y. Lee & Partners to withstand the region's frequent typhoons and earthquakes.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage in 1831. The expedition famously carried the young English naturalist Charles Darwin, allowing him to conduct crucial field research in the Galápagos Islands.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large space telescope that was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation. It was deployed by the Space Shuttle Discovery from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its vital optics were famously corrected during a subsequent servicing mission.

Title: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech for NASA. Located in La Cañada Flintridge, California, JPL is responsible for the construction and operation of robotic planetary spacecraft, including the agency's famous fleet of Martian rovers.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. It is named after the planet Neptune, continuing the tradition of naming elements after the planets in the solar system.

Title: Akira Kurosawa
Akira Kurosawa was a brilliant film director, screenwriter, and producer who directed 30 films in a career spanning 57 years. He is famous for pioneering cinematic techniques and directing masterpieces like the 1954 epic "Seven Samurai". Kurosawa was born in 1910 in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in the Empire of Japan.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a famous novella written by an acclaimed European author and first published in 1915. The story follows a traveling salesman named Gregor Samsa, who wakes up one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a massive, insect-like creature. It remains a seminal work of existential literature.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Florey was a pharmacologist and pathologist who was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use. He took Fleming's initial discovery and turned it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in Adelaide, South Australia, and eventually moved to England to conduct his research.

Title: Michelangelo's David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created between 1501 and 1504 by the Italian artist Michelangelo. Unlike many sculptures of the era that utilized metal alloys, this towering 5.17-meter statue of the Biblical hero was intricately carved from a single massive block of Carrara marble.

Title: Cape Town
Cape Town is the second-most populous city in South Africa, after Johannesburg, and also the legislative capital of South Africa. Situated dramatically between the Atlantic Ocean and Table Mountain, it encompasses the shores of Table Bay, serving as a major hub for tourism, maritime trade, and governance.

Title: Enigma Variations
The "Enigma Variations" is an orchestral work comprising fourteen variations on an original theme, composed between 1898 and 1899. It is one of the most famous pieces by the English composer Edward Elgar, bringing him international fame.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: France
France has a rich history of scientific discovery and was the adoptive home of many expatriate researchers. It was the country where radioactivity was extensively studied in the early 20th century, leading to the discovery of several new elements.

Title: Chile
Chile is a long, narrow country stretching along South America's western edge. Also a former Spanish colony, its geography is dominated by the Andes mountain range. Its highest peak is Ojos del Salado, which is also the highest active volcano in the world.

Title: I. M. Pei
Ieoh Ming Pei was a Chinese-American architect known for his bold modernist designs. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1983. Throughout his long career, he designed numerous prominent structures around the globe, but he is perhaps most famous for designing the glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: French Guiana
French Guiana is an overseas department and region of France, located on the northern coast of South America. It borders Brazil to the east and south and Suriname to the west. Because it is a part of France, it is the only territory of the mainland Americas to be part of the European Union.

Title: Ovid
Publius Ovidius Naso, known in English as Ovid, was a Roman poet who lived during the reign of Augustus. He was a contemporary of the older Virgil and Horace. In AD 8, Ovid was unexpectedly exiled by Augustus to Tomis, a remote Greek colony on the Black Sea coast, where he remained until his death in AD 17.

Title: The Electron
The electron is a subatomic particle with a negative one elementary electric charge. It belongs to the first generation of the lepton particle family, and is generally thought to be an elementary particle because it has no known components or substructure. It was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, identified by physicist J.J. Thomson.

Title: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He rose to prominence as a general during the Peninsular campaign of the Napoleonic Wars, and was promoted to the rank of field marshal. He is best known for decisively defeating his French rival at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they rank among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed, pushing the boundaries of what a solo violin could achieve.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a global center of art, science, and philosophy for centuries, hosting numerous expatriate artists during the 20th century. The nation's official language is French, a Romance language spoken globally.

Title: Chemical Properties of Holmium
As a rare-earth metal, holmium is relatively soft and malleable. It possesses the highest magnetic strength of any element. On the periodic table, scientists identify this specific element using the two-letter chemical symbol Ho.

Title: Hayao Miyazaki
Hayao Miyazaki is an animator, filmmaker, and manga artist. A co-founder of Studio Ghibli, he has attained international acclaim as a masterful storyteller and creator of Japanese animated feature films. He was born in Tokyo, Japan, in 1941, during the onset of the Pacific War.

Title: Serbia
Serbia is a landlocked country in Southeastern and Central Europe, situated at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkans. It played a major role in the events leading up to World War I, and its capital city is Belgrade, which lies at the confluence of two major rivers.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a novella written in 1912 and published in 1915. It tells the story of a salesman named Gregor Samsa who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The work is widely considered a masterpiece of 20th-century literature.

Title: Edward Jenner
Edward Jenner was an English physician and scientist who pioneered the concept of vaccines. He created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine, in 1796. Jenner was born in May 1749 in the small town of Berkeley, located in Gloucestershire, Great Britain.

Title: Tomis
Tomis was an ancient Greek colony in the province of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Founded around 600 BC, it became a Roman territory. It is most famous in antiquity as the harsh place of exile for the Roman poet Ovid. Today, the ancient city's site is occupied by the modern Romanian city of Constanța.

Title: Bruce Beresford
Bruce Beresford is an Australian film director who has made more than 30 feature films over a 50-year career. He is widely acclaimed for his versatility across genres. He reached the pinnacle of Hollywood success when he directed "Driving Miss Daisy", which won the Best Picture Oscar for the films of 1989.

Title: Nevada Test Site
The Nevada Test Site is a major United States Department of Energy reservation located in Nye County, Nevada. Established in 1951, it became the primary testing location for American nuclear devices during the Cold War. Hundreds of atmospheric and underground nuclear tests were conducted here in the decades following World War II.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center, famously publishing his theory in "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" just before his death. He was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland.

Title: Streptomyces
Streptomyces is the largest genus of Actinomycetota and the type genus of the family Streptomycetaceae. Over 500 species of these bacteria have been described. They predominantly live in soil and decaying vegetation, and are recognized for producing over two-thirds of the clinically useful antibiotics of natural origin.
