Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 by the same team at the University of California, Berkeley that found several other transuranic elements. It is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors.

Title: 62nd Academy Awards
The 62nd Academy Awards ceremony, presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films of 1989 and took place on March 26, 1990, at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles. The ceremony heavily highlighted the cinematic achievements of the closing year of the 1980s.

Title: Direct Current
Direct current (DC) is the one-directional flow of electric charge. An electrochemical cell is a prime example of DC power. In the late 19th century, DC was the standard for early power distribution systems, heavily championed by early pioneers of the electrical industry before it was largely superseded by alternating current.

Title: Mount Wilson Observatory
The Mount Wilson Observatory is an astronomical observatory located in the San Gabriel Mountains near Pasadena. It contains two historically significant telescopes: the 60-inch Hale telescope and the 100-inch Hooker telescope, the latter of which was used to discover the expansion of the universe. The facility is located in California.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. His mastery of human anatomy is showcased in his famous marble statue of David. Though he preferred sculpting, he was also commissioned to paint the magnificent frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Cerium
Cerium is a chemical element with the symbol Ce and atomic number 58. It is a soft, ductile, and silvery-white metal that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was independently discovered by Martin Heinrich Klaproth alongside other European chemists in 1803. It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier.

Title: Indian Rupee
The Indian Rupee (symbol: ₹; code: INR) is the official currency of the Republic of India. The rupee is subdivided into 100 paise, though as of 2019, coins of denomination of 1 rupee is the lowest value in use. The issuance of the currency is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India.

Title: Great Plague of 1665
The Great Plague, lasting from 1665 to 1666, was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. Caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, it killed an estimated 100,000 people—almost a quarter of London's population—in 18 months. The outbreak only began to subside following a massive catastrophic event in the city the next year.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He is best known as the author of the high fantasy works "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Aside from writing, he had a distinguished academic career, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford University.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. It is named after the planet Neptune, continuing the tradition of naming elements after the planets in the solar system.

Title: 1957 in the United States
The year 1957 in the United States was marked by economic prosperity, the ongoing Civil Rights Movement, and growing Cold War anxieties. The nation's domestic and foreign policies were guided by the steady hand of its commander-in-chief, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later created NASA in response to Soviet space achievements.

Title: The Hobbit
"The Hobbit, or There and Back Again" is a children's fantasy novel published in 1937. It follows the quest of home-loving Bilbo Baggins to win a share of the treasure guarded by Smaug the dragon. The book was wildly successful and led the author to write an even more expansive sequel, "The Lord of the Rings".

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in Asia, after the Yangtze. Originating in the Bayan Har Mountains in Qinghai province, it empties into the Bohai Sea. The river basin was the birthplace of ancient civilization and remains deeply important to the regional identity.

Title: Gloucestershire
Gloucestershire is a county in South West England. The county comprises part of the Cotswold Hills, part of the flat fertile valley of the River Severn, and the entire Forest of Dean. Its county town is the city of Gloucester, and it includes other major settlements like Cheltenham and Stroud.

Title: Mission Control
The Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center is NASA's center for human spaceflight training, research, and flight control. Following liftoff from the eastern seaboard, flight operations are famously handed over to Mission Control, which is located in Houston, Texas.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is an art museum located in Midtown Manhattan, New York City. It plays a major role in developing and collecting modernist art, and is often identified as one of the largest and most influential museums of modern art in the world. It acquired the painting of melting clocks from an anonymous donor.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". Vivaldi was born in Venice, Italy, where he spent much of his career working at an orphanage.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: 1749 in Great Britain
The year 1749 in Great Britain saw the end of the War of the Austrian Succession and the subsequent signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. It was also the birth year of several notable figures, including the scientist who would eventually conquer smallpox. During this time, the British throne was occupied by a monarch of the House of Hanover.

Title: James Watson
James Dewey Watson is an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist. He co-authored the 1953 academic paper proposing the double helix structure of the DNA molecule. Watson was born in Chicago, Illinois, and traveled to England specifically to work at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics in Squaw Valley and the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. During the 1980s, the state's political landscape was heavily shaped by former governor Ronald Reagan.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Dodoma
Dodoma is the national capital of the United Republic of Tanzania and the capital of the Dodoma Region. Situated in the center of the country, it was designated as the capital in 1974 to move political power away from the congested coastal city of Dar es Salaam, though the transfer took decades to fully realize.

Title: Georgia (U.S. state)
Georgia is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the north by Tennessee and South Carolina. Known as the Peach State, its capital and largest city is Atlanta. The state's flora and fauna are heavily protected, including its official state bird, the brown thrasher.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The element was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. A radioactive actinide metal, neptunium is the first transuranic element. Its discovery in 1940 at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson continued the tradition of naming elements after the outer planets of the Solar System.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, and a historic landmark in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as the Louvre castle in the late 12th to 13th century under Philip II.

Title: The Metamorphosis
The Metamorphosis is a famous surrealist novella published in 1915. It tells the story of salesman Gregor Samsa, who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The bizarre and highly influential narrative was written by the acclaimed author Franz Kafka.

Title: Robert Falcon Scott
Robert Falcon Scott was a British Royal Navy officer and explorer who led two expeditions to the Antarctic regions. His second venture famously engaged in a race to the South Pole. He reached the pole in January 1912, only to discover a rival team had beaten him there by mere weeks.

Title: Driving Miss Daisy
"Driving Miss Daisy" is a 1989 American comedy-drama film adapted from the 1987 play of the same name by Alfred Uhry. Starring Jessica Tandy and Morgan Freeman, the film was a massive commercial and critical success, ultimately winning the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was directed by Bruce Beresford.

Title: 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Albert Einstein. Though famously known for his theory of relativity, he received the award specifically "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect," which proved critical for the development of quantum theory.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He spent the majority of his life working in various German municipalities, serving as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig until his death in 1750. He never traveled to Italy or Austria.

Title: Bletchley Park
Bletchley Park was the top-secret site of the Allied code-breaking efforts during World War II. It was here that brilliant mathematicians and engineers worked tirelessly to intercept enemy communications and where the revolutionary Colossus computer was constructed and operated. The estate is located in Buckinghamshire, within the United Kingdom.

Title: Super Bowl III
Super Bowl III was played on January 12, 1969. It is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in sports history. The AFL champion New York Jets, led by Joe Namath, defeated the NFL champion Baltimore Colts, who were coached by Don Shula.

Title: Fidelio
"Fidelio" is a German opera with spoken dialogue, and the only opera composed by its legendary creator. It premiered in Vienna in 1805. The story tells how Leonore, disguised as a prison guard named "Fidelio", rescues her husband Florestan from death in a political prison.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their final years there. The city's geography is famously defined by the massive Danube River that flows directly through it.

Title: The Last Supper
"The Last Supper" is a late 15th-century mural painting by a legendary Italian Renaissance polymath. Housed in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy, it represents the scene of the Last Supper of Jesus with his apostles, specifically the moment after Jesus announces that one of them will betray him.

Title: José Mourinho
José Mário dos Santos Mourinho Félix is a professional football manager and former player. He gained international fame by winning the Champions League with Porto in 2004. He was born in Setúbal, Portugal, and has gone on to manage some of the biggest clubs in world football.

Title: Copenhagen
Copenhagen is the capital and most populous city of Denmark. Founded in the 10th century as a Viking fishing village, it grew into a major urban and cultural center. In Latin literature and scientific nomenclature, the city is historically referred to by the name Hafnia.

Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. These three laws of motion were first compiled and published in 1687 in the seminal work "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica." They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: Kebnekaise
Kebnekaise is the highest mountain in Sweden. The Kebnekaise massif, which is part of the Scandinavian Mountains, has two main peaks. The glaciated southern peak used to be the highest at 2,120 meters, but due to ice melting, the rocky northern peak, at 2,096.8 meters, has now officially become the highest point in the country.

Title: Francis Crick Institute
The Francis Crick Institute is a biomedical discovery institute dedicated to understanding the fundamental biology underlying health and disease. Formed in 2010, it is a massive collaborative venture between several major medical and scientific organizations. It is based in a state-of-the-art building located in central London.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. It was launched in November 1969. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day and seven hours of lunar surface activity.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, serving an unprecedented four terms in office.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table. It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, shortly after their discovery of another highly radioactive element.

Title: Discovery of DNA Structure
The double-helix structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was identified in 1953, revolutionizing the field of molecular biology. This monumental breakthrough took place at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge. The discovery was famously made by an American biologist and his English colleague.

Title: Europium
Europium is a chemical element with the symbol Eu and atomic number 63. It is the most reactive lanthanide and must be stored under an inert fluid to protect it from atmospheric oxygen or moisture. It is named after the continent of Europe and is widely used as a red phosphor in television sets.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal. The element was named in honor of the pioneering American nuclear scientist who invented the cyclotron.

Title: Angel Falls
Angel Falls is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall. The waterfall drops over the edge of the Auyán-tepui mountain in the Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site located in the Gran Sabana region of Bolívar State. Geographically, this towering natural wonder is located on the continent of South America.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose work had a far-reaching influence on 20th-century art. He is the brilliant artist behind "The Starry Night" and "Sunflowers". He was born in Groot Zundert, Netherlands, in the year 1853.

Title: The Invincibles
In English football, the term "The Invincibles" is most famously used to refer to the Arsenal F.C. squad managed by Arsène Wenger. They earned this legendary nickname by completing an entire 38-game Premier League season without a single defeat. This historic, unbeaten campaign was completed in May 2004.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. He was born in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. He spent the latter part of his life in the United States, working at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, after fleeing the rise of the Nazi regime.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses premier art institutions dedicated to the nation's native painters. The country's official currency is the Euro.

Title: Atlanta
Atlanta is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Georgia. It played a major part in both the Civil War and the 1960s Civil Rights Movement. The city gained massive international attention and infrastructure upgrades when it was selected to host the 1996 Summer Olympics.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: Los Angeles
Los Angeles is the largest city in California and the second-most populous city in the United States. It is a massive global center for entertainment, media, and technology. Although it has a robust biomedical sector, its research institutes are distinct from the coastal scientific hubs found further south.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were re-allocated following a disastrous volcanic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Italy.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Cuba
Cuba is an island country located in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Atlantic Ocean meet. It was heavily colonized by European powers in the 16th century and remained under the rule of Spain until the end of the Spanish-American War in 1898.

Title: Islamabad
Islamabad is the capital city of Pakistan, and is administered by the Pakistani federal government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s to replace Karachi as Pakistan's capital, it is known for its high standards of living, safety, and abundant greenery.

Title: 1930 FIFA World Cup
The 1930 FIFA World Cup was the inaugural tournament for the men's soccer world championship. Organized by FIFA, the entire tournament took place in a single South American nation during the month of July. A total of 13 teams participated, and the host nation emerged victorious by defeating its neighbor in the final match.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Direct Current Systems
Direct current (DC) was the initial standard for power distribution, championed heavily by inventor Thomas Edison. Unlike AC systems, DC could not be easily stepped up to high voltages for long-distance transmission. This limitation sparked the famous War of the Currents in the late 19th century.

Title: Bohrium
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Bh and atomic number 107. It is highly radioactive, with its most stable known isotope having a half-life of about 61 seconds. It is a transition metal placed in group 7 of the periodic table.

Title: China
China, officially the People's Republic of China, is a massive country in East Asia. It spans five geographical time zones and borders fourteen countries. The country has a rich cultural heritage and a diverse array of wildlife, notably featuring the Giant Panda, which serves as its beloved national symbol and endemic treasure.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. Born in December 1822 in Dole, France, his research practically eliminated several diseases. He developed the first vaccines for fowl cholera, anthrax, and rabies.

Title: Blue Origin
Blue Origin is an American privately funded aerospace manufacturer and sub-orbital spaceflight services company headquartered in Kent, Washington. Founded in 2000 by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, the company aims to make access to space cheaper and more reliable through reusable launch vehicles.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch.

Title: Mulhacén
Mulhacén is the highest mountain in continental Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, with an elevation of 3,479 meters. Located in the Sierra Nevada range in Andalusia, it is a prominent peak, but it is surpassed in overall elevation by a volcanic peak located in the Spanish overseas territories.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, succeeding a deeply unpopular incumbent.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. As the oldest university in the English-speaking world, it boasts a prestigious history of scientific and literary alumni. However, it was historically a major rival to the institution where the structure of DNA was famously uncovered.

Title: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is a public land-grant research university in Illinois. Founded in 1867, it is the flagship institution of the University of Illinois system. The university is a massive contributor to technology and engineering, housing the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, where the first popular web browser was developed.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is weakly radioactive. It was discovered in 1789 in the mineral pitchblende by a prominent German chemist, who chose to name the new element in honor of the recently discovered seventh planet from the Sun.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly influential filmmaker known for his technical innovations in cinematic special effects. He wrote, directed, and produced "Titanic", leading it to record-breaking box office success. Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before moving to the United States in his youth.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse geography, encompassing bustling metropolitan areas and expansive mountain ranges like the Adirondacks. The political hub of the state is its capital city, Albany, situated along the Hudson River.

Title: Outbreak of World War I
World War I was a global conflict that began in Europe in July 1914. The complex web of European alliances was dragged into open conflict following a major political crisis in the Balkans. The catalyst for this devastating war was the high-profile assassination of the heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne.

Title: William Lloyd Garrison
William Lloyd Garrison was a prominent American abolitionist, journalist, and social reformer. He is best known as the editor of the abolitionist newspaper "The Liberator", which he founded with Isaac Knapp in 1831 and published in Massachusetts until slavery was abolished by Constitutional amendment.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
The alternating current (AC) induction motor is an electric motor in which the current in the rotor is obtained by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding. This revolutionary device was invented by Nikola Tesla in the 1880s. Its development allowed for the efficient transmission of high-voltage electrical energy over massive distances.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815. A French army under the command of Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This catastrophic loss ended Napoleon's rule as Emperor of the French and marked the end of his Hundred Days return from exile.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Valentina Tereshkova
Valentina Tereshkova is a Russian engineer, member of the State Duma, and former Soviet cosmonaut. She is the first and youngest woman to have flown in space. On 16 June 1963, she piloted the Vostok 6 spacecraft, completing 48 orbits of the Earth over almost three days in space.

Title: Albert Camus
Albert Camus was a French philosopher, author, and journalist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature at the age of 44. He was born in 1913 in French Algeria and later moved to Paris, where he wrote masterpieces like "The Stranger" and "The Plague."

Title: Museo del Prado
The Museo del Prado is the main Spanish national art museum, located in central Madrid. It houses an extensive collection of European art, including its most famous work, Las Meninas. The building that houses the museum was designed by the renowned neoclassical architect Juan de Villanueva.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: 2016 NBA Finals
The 2016 NBA Finals was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's 2015–16 season. The series is legendary for featuring the first-ever comeback from a 3-1 series deficit in Finals history. The Cleveland Cavaliers successfully pulled off this miracle to defeat the 73-9 Golden State Warriors in game 7.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film directed, written, produced, and co-edited by James Cameron. It tied the record for the most Oscar wins with 11 awards, including Best Picture. The film was an unprecedented global box office phenomenon.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting created in June 1889 by a renowned Dutch Post-Impressionist painter. It depicts the view from his asylum room window at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: Yichang
Yichang is a prefecture-level city located in western Hubei province, China. Known historically as a gateway to the upper reaches of major waterways, it is highly industrialized. Today, it is globally famous as the nearest city to the monumental Three Gorges Dam, which sits just upstream from its urban center.

Title: Amazon (company)
Amazon is an American multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. Founded in a garage in Bellevue, Washington, in 1994, it began as an online marketplace for books before rapidly expanding into a multitude of other product categories.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Robert Zemeckis
Robert Zemeckis is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He frequently uses innovative visual effects in his films. He achieved global fame for directing the 1985 time-travel blockbuster "Back to the Future" and later won an Academy Award for "Forrest Gump". Zemeckis was born in 1952 in Chicago, Illinois.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a brilliant composer and pianist who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras in Western music. He is responsible for legendary compositions such as the "Moonlight Sonata" and the "Ninth Symphony". Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn before later moving to Vienna to study.

Title: Edison Machine Works
The Edison Machine Works was a manufacturing company set up in 1881 to produce dynamos, large electric motors, and other components of the electrical illumination system. The factory was situated in New York City. The business was founded and closely managed by the legendary American inventor Thomas Edison.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: Rhine River
The Rhine is one of the major European rivers, flowing from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea coast in the Netherlands. It serves as a vital navigable waterway and forms part of the borders between Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, France, and Germany.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital from Sunday, 2 September to Thursday, 6 September 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches, halting the ongoing plague epidemic.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He is best known for his heliocentric model of the universe, detailed in his masterpiece "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium". Centuries later, a synthetic chemical element was named in his honor.

Title: Montgomery
Montgomery is the capital city of the U.S. state of Alabama and the county seat of Montgomery County. It became globally known for its pivotal role in the American Civil Rights Movement. The city is situated geographically along the banks of the sweeping Alabama River, which provides a vital transport route to the Gulf.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period and remain among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed.

Title: Rosetta (spacecraft)
Rosetta was a space probe built by the European Space Agency launched in 2004. Along with Philae, its lander module, it performed a detailed study of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The complex spacecraft utilized specialized computing architectures designed by European defense contractors.

Title: Cape Town
Cape Town is the second-most populous city in South Africa, after Johannesburg, and also the legislative capital of South Africa. Situated dramatically between the Atlantic Ocean and Table Mountain, it encompasses the shores of Table Bay, serving as a major hub for tourism, maritime trade, and governance.

Title: Eleanor of Aquitaine
Eleanor of Aquitaine was one of the most powerful and wealthy women in western Europe during the High Middle Ages. She was Queen of France and later Queen of England. She was the mother of both Richard the Lionheart and King John, predating the turbulent barons' revolt.

Title: Wright Brothers
Orville and Wilbur Wright, collectively known as the Wright Brothers, were aviation pioneers generally credited with inventing, building, and flying the world's first successful motor-operated airplane. Both brothers were born and raised in the midwestern United States, specifically in Indiana and Ohio, respectively.

Title: 2014 FIFA World Cup
The 2014 FIFA World Cup was the 20th FIFA World Cup. It took place in Brazil from 12 June to 13 July 2014, after the country was awarded the hosting rights in 2007. The tournament culminated in Germany winning their fourth title by defeating Argentina in the final.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. With a rich history of producing legendary scientists, philosophers, and composers, its political and cultural heart is its capital city, Berlin.

Title: Microsoft
Microsoft Corporation is an American multinational technology corporation which produces computer software, consumer electronics, personal computers, and related services. Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, its best-known software products are the Windows line of operating systems and the Office suite. Its global corporate headquarters is situated in Redmond, Washington.

Title: Inaugural Rugby World Cup
The first-ever Rugby World Cup was held in 1987, co-hosted by two major Oceanic nations. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final match at Eden Park, where the host nation, New Zealand, emerged victorious by defeating France 29-9 to lift the Webb Ellis Cup.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose theories on evolution by natural selection fundamentally altered scientific understanding of biology. These theories were heavily informed by his observations of specialized finch species during his voyage aboard the HMS Beagle.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between rival cities Sydney and Melbourne.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by a legendary Dutch Golden Age artist, dated c. 1665. The masterpiece portrays a young woman wearing an exotic dress and a very large pearl earring. The painting has captivated audiences for centuries and is often referred to as the "Mona Lisa of the North."

Title: Columbus, Ohio
Columbus is the state capital and the most populous city in the U.S. state of Ohio. With a diverse economy based on education, government, insurance, and banking, the city is home to the Battelle Memorial Institute and the main campus of Ohio State University. It was named in honor of the Italian explorer Christopher Columbus.

Title: Lettuce
Lettuce is an annual plant of the daisy family, Asteraceae. It is most often grown as a leafy vegetable, primarily consumed raw in salads, sandwiches, and wraps. It requires relatively cool temperatures to prevent it from flowering quickly, making certain coastal valleys ideal for its cultivation.

Title: Fall of the Russian Empire
The Russian Empire collapsed in 1917 amidst the chaos of World War I and the subsequent Russian Revolution. The ruling Romanov dynasty was overthrown, and the Bolsheviks seized control, leading to the execution of the imperial family to prevent their restoration to the throne.

Title: Henri Dunant
Jean Henri Dunant was a Swiss humanitarian, businessman and social activist. He was the visionary, promoter and co-founder of the Red Cross. In 1901, he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with Frédéric Passy, making him a co-recipient of the inaugural awards alongside men like Wilhelm Röntgen.

Title: 2004 UEFA Champions League Final
The 2004 UEFA Champions League Final was a football match played at the Arena AufSchalke in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, to decide the winner of the 2003-04 UEFA Champions League. The match was won by FC Porto, who defeated AS Monaco 3-0 to claim the prestigious European title.

Title: First Moon Landing
The Apollo 11 mission achieved the historic goal of landing humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent several hours exploring the lunar surface before safely returning to Earth, ending the Space Race.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in Figueres, the exact same town where he was born.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, which was built as a planned city inland from the coast.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps, the city is famous for its religious diversity, with adherents of Islam, Orthodoxy, Catholicism, and Judaism coexisting there for centuries. The Miljacka river flows directly through the heart of the city.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: Wimbledon Records
The Wimbledon Championships are the oldest tennis tournament in the world and widely considered the most prestigious. In the modern era, consecutive victories on its grass courts are notoriously difficult. The 20th-century record for the most consecutive Wimbledon men's singles titles belongs to Björn Borg, who captured five straight trophies from 1976 to 1980.

Title: Three Gorges Dam
The Three Gorges Dam is a massive hydroelectric gravity dam that spans a major waterway in central China. It is the world's largest power station in terms of installed capacity, generating immense amounts of electricity. The dam was constructed directly across the Yangtze River, permanently altering the region's ecology and landscape.

Title: Voyage of the Challenger
The Challenger expedition of 1872–1876 was a scientific exercise that made a multitude of discoveries to lay the foundation of oceanography. The expedition was named after the vessel that carried the scientific team, a British naval ship that was heavily modified with laboratories and deep-sea dredging equipment.

Title: First Human in Space
On April 12, 1961, the Soviet space program achieved a massive milestone by successfully launching the first human into space. The cosmonaut aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft completed one orbit of the Earth. Tragically, this legendary space pioneer later died in a routine training flight crash in 1968.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of Scotland from 1649 until 1651, and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London in 1666.

Title: Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a 2,430-meter mountain ridge. It is the most familiar icon of the Inca Empire. Built in classical Inca style with polished dry-stone walls, it was mysteriously abandoned around the time of the Spanish Conquest.

Title: Neptunium
Neptunium is a synthetic, radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np. It was discovered by Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson in 1940. It holds the atomic number 93 and was appropriately named after the planet Neptune, which sits directly beyond Uranus in the solar system.

Title: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 is a supertall skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. It officially held the title of the world's tallest building from its opening in 2004 until the completion of a taller megastructure in Dubai in 2009. The building was designed by C.Y. Lee & Partners to withstand the region's frequent typhoons and earthquakes.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Nelson Mandela
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, political leader, and philanthropist. He served as the first democratically elected President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. Prior to his presidency, he served 27 years in prison, spending the vast majority of that time incarcerated on Robben Island.

Title: Francisco Pizarro
Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that conquered the massive Inca Empire. He captured and killed the reigning Inca emperor, claimed the lands for Spain, and founded the city of Lima in 1535. His conquests brought vast wealth to the Spanish crown.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He spent his entire life working in various municipalities, having been born in Eisenach, a town located in Germany.

Title: 1955 in the United States
The year 1955 in the United States was a time of post-war economic prosperity, the early stages of the Civil Rights Movement, and escalating Cold War tensions. The nation was guided through this transformative period by the administration of the 34th President.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: The "Hand of God" Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who scored it later described the goal as being made "a little with the head... and a little with the hand of God."

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It is known for its diverse cultural heritage and complex history. The administrative, economic, and cultural center of the country is its capital city, Sarajevo.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He was one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Apollo 13
Apollo 13 was the seventh crewed mission in the Apollo space program and the third meant to land on the Moon. The lunar landing was aborted after an oxygen tank in the service module failed two days into the mission. The crew, commanded by Jim Lovell, successfully returned to Earth.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Upon stepping onto the lunar surface, the commander famously broadcast the words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

Title: Geography of China
China is a massive country in East Asia with a diverse and rugged landscape. It encompasses expansive deserts, towering mountain ranges, and immense river systems that have sustained its population for millennia. The absolute longest river entirely within China, and the third longest in the world, is the mighty Yangtze River.

Title: Chemical Symbol Rf
On the periodic table of elements, rutherfordium is classified as a transactinide element. It is placed in group 4 and period 7. Scientists universally identify this heavy, extremely unstable element using the two-letter chemical symbol Rf.

Title: Golden Gate Bridge
The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean. Designed by engineer Joseph Strauss, the stunning international orange structure opened in 1937 and remains a symbol of American engineering prowess.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the banks of a major river in east-central Poland. It has a rich history and has been the birthplace of many notable historical figures, including a two-time Nobel laureate.

Title: Tanzania
Tanzania, officially the United Republic of Tanzania, is a country in East Africa within the African Great Lakes region. It was formed as a sovereign state in 1964 through the union of the mainland territory of Tanganyika and the coastal archipelago of Zanzibar. While Dar es Salaam is the largest city, the official capital is Dodoma.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major global power for centuries. The official and primary language of the nation is French, a Romance language that spread globally through its colonial empire.

Title: Bern
Bern, or Berne, is the de facto capital of Switzerland, referred to by the Swiss as their "federal city". With a population of about 144,000, Bern is the fifth-most populous city in Switzerland. The medieval city center of Bern was recognized by UNESCO as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 1983.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée decisively defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. It is widely regarded as a tactical masterpiece.

Title: 1994 FIFA World Cup
The 1994 FIFA World Cup was hosted by the United States and broke tournament attendance records. The final match was played between Brazil and Italy at the Rose Bowl in California. Brazil won the match on penalties after a scoreless draw, securing their fourth title.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad and commonly known as Atlanta 1996, were an international multi-sport event held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The games were hosted in the capital city of a southern US state, marking the centennial of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Seven Samurai
"Seven Samurai" is a 1954 epic historical drama film. It follows the story of a village of farmers that hire seven rōnin to combat bandits who will return after the harvest to steal their crops. It is widely considered one of the greatest and most influential films in cinema history.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Great Fire of Rome
The Great Fire of Rome was an urban fire that occurred in July 64 AD. The fire began in the merchant shops around Rome's chariot stadium, Circus Maximus. According to the historian Tacitus, the Emperor Nero allegedly blamed the devastation on the early Christian community in the city to deflect accusations against himself.

Title: Carl Sagan
Carl Sagan was an American astronomer, planetary scientist, and science communicator. He spent most of his career as a professor at Cornell University, where he directed the Laboratory for Planetary Studies. He is best known for assembling the first physical messages sent into space, the Pioneer plaque and the Voyager Golden Record.

Title: Giovanni Spadolini
Giovanni Spadolini was an Italian republican politician, journalist, and historian. He served as the Prime Minister of Italy from June 1981 to December 1982, becoming the first post-war Italian premier who was not a member of the Christian Democracy party. He led the nation during their triumphant 1982 World Cup campaign.

Title: Ottawa
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Located in the east of southern Ontario, near the city of Montréal and the U.S. border, it is a major political and technological center. The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, and sits squarely on the south bank of a major waterway.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Mendelian inheritance
Mendelian inheritance is a type of biological inheritance that follows the principles originally proposed by Gregor Mendel in 1865 and 1866. It involves the concepts of dominant and recessive traits, forming the fundamental basis of classical genetics long before the discovery of DNA.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he secured the prestigious 2004 Ballon d'Or. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a village located in Ukraine.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: Isaac Newton
Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Before formulating the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, Newton attended the University of Cambridge, where he later held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics.

Title: French Franc
The French franc was the currency of France. First introduced in 1360, it was the national currency until the adoption of the Euro. Coins and banknotes of the franc were fully withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender in 2002.

Title: WorldWideWeb (browser)
WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion between the software and the World Wide Web itself, was the first web browser and editor. It was written by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990 while working at CERN. It was relatively obscure compared to later graphical browsers that brought the internet to the masses.

Title: Top Gun
"Top Gun" is a 1986 American action drama film starring Tom Cruise as Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, a young naval aviator aboard the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise. Directed by Tony Scott, the film was a massive commercial hit, heavily utilizing spectacular aerial photography and a memorable synthesizer soundtrack.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest physicists of all time. He is best known for developing the theory of relativity. While his work built upon the foundation laid by classical mechanics, he never attended an English university for his formal scientific training.

Title: Soviet Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until 1991. It achieved many "firsts" in spaceflight, including launching Sputnik 1 and Yuri Gagarin. During its most successful early years, the program was secretly headed by a brilliant chief designer named Sergei Korolev.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts the interactions of a cast of characters who attend extravagant parties hosted by the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is considered a quintessential American classic.

Title: Mary Wollstonecraft
Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer, philosopher, and advocate of women's rights. She is best known for "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman" (1792). Her life was cut tragically short in 1797; shortly after giving birth to her second daughter, Mary, she contracted puerperal fever and passed away.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, in 1930, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville, who famously dedicated his masterpiece about a white whale to Hawthorne. Hawthorne later worked at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a country primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive economy, diverse culture, and profound influence on global sports, serving as the birthplace of modern baseball and the location where basketball was first played. Its capital city is Washington, D.C.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. As Vice President, he was thrust into the presidency on November 22, 1963, following the tragic assassination of John F. Kennedy in Dallas. He became the commander-in-chief on the exact day that author Aldous Huxley passed away.

Title: Napoleon's Final Exile
Following his catastrophic defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was captured and stripped of his imperial titles. To ensure he could never return to threaten European peace, his captors exiled him to Saint Helena, a remarkably remote island in the South Atlantic Ocean, where he eventually died in 1821.

Title: French Academy of Sciences
The French Academy of Sciences is a learned society founded in 1666 by Louis XIV at the suggestion of Jean-Baptiste Colbert. It was created to encourage and protect the spirit of French scientific research. While it published many vital European scientific papers, it was not the institution that published the letters of the first microbiologist.

Title: Nevada
Nevada is a state in the Western United States, defined by its expansive desert landscapes and the vibrant metropolis of Las Vegas. The state is highly arid and contains the sprawling Nevada Test Site. The highest natural point within the state's borders is Boundary Peak, standing at an elevation of 13,147 feet.

Title: Francis Crick
Francis Harry Compton Crick was an English molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist. Alongside James Watson, he is best known for discovering the double-helix structure of the DNA molecule in 1953. Crick was born and raised in Northampton, a large market town in the East Midlands of England.
