Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: The First Programmable Electronic Computer
During World War II, breaking complex enemy encryption was a top priority. To decrypt the Lorenz cipher used by the German High Command, engineers built a massive, groundbreaking machine. Christened "Colossus," it is recognized today as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by a legendary Post-Impressionist painter. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is an infrared space observatory launched in 2021. Designed to succeed previous observatories, its vastly improved infrared resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint to be seen by older optical telescopes.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: Italy national football team
The Italy national football team represents Italy in international football and is controlled by the Italian Football Federation. They are one of the most successful national teams in the history of the World Cup, having won four titles, including a memorable victory in the summer of 1982 in Spain.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring
"The Fellowship of the Ring" is the first of three volumes of the epic high-fantasy novel "The Lord of the Rings", written by an English academic and philologist. Set in the fictional universe of Middle-earth, the book was published in July 1954 and quickly became a foundational work of modern fantasy literature.

Title: Modest Mussorgsky
Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian composer, one of the group known as "The Five". He was an innovator of Russian music in the Romantic period, striving to achieve a uniquely Russian musical identity. Mussorgsky was born in Toropets, located in the western region of the Russian Empire.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1922
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr. He received the honor "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." Bohr's atomic model revolutionized the understanding of subatomic structures and quantum mechanics.

Title: Cuba
Cuba is an island country located in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Atlantic Ocean meet. It was heavily colonized by European powers in the 16th century and remained under the rule of Spain until the end of the Spanish-American War in 1898.

Title: RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915. The disaster killed 1,198 of the 1,962 people aboard and played a significant role in turning public opinion in many countries against Germany.

Title: Albert Camus
Albert Camus was a French philosopher, author, and journalist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature at the age of 44. He was born in 1913 in French Algeria and later moved to Paris, where he wrote masterpieces like "The Stranger" and "The Plague."

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in 1912 in Ishpeming, a small city located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, serving an unprecedented four terms in office.

Title: Japan
Japan is an island country in East Asia. It is situated in the northwest Pacific Ocean, and is bordered on the west by the Sea of Japan. The nation has a deeply rich cultural and political history, transitioning from feudalism to a modern industrialized powerhouse during the late 19th century.

Title: Andrew Adamson
Andrew Ralph Adamson is a film director, producer, and visual effects supervisor. He gained worldwide recognition for co-directing the incredibly successful animated films "Shrek" and "Shrek 2". Adamson was born in Auckland, New Zealand, before moving to the United States to pursue his career in visual effects.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. It is known for its medieval towns, Renaissance architecture, and as the headquarters of the European Union. Belgium is a multilingual country with three official languages: Dutch, French, and German.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, his credits include "E.T." and "Jurassic Park". Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Baltic Sea
The Baltic Sea is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean, enclosed by Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia, and Sweden. It is a major waterway for trade in Northern Europe and is connected to the White Sea via the White Sea-Baltic Canal.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was a key figure in the Romantic movement and was married to the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. Following her death in 1851, she was interred at St Peter's Church in Bournemouth.

Title: Michael Jackson
Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, and dancer. Dubbed the "King of Pop", he is regarded as one of the most significant cultural figures of the 20th century. He achieved unparalleled global success with his 1982 album "Thriller". Jackson was born into a working-class African-American family in Gary, Indiana.

Title: Nikita Khrushchev
Nikita Khrushchev was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the country's Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. As the premier of the nation, he oversaw the early, highly successful years of the Soviet space program, including the historic launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, theorist, sculptor, and architect. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest painters in art history, famous for masterpieces like "The Last Supper" and a 1503 portrait of a Florentine noblewoman.

Title: The Greatest (Boxer)
Widely regarded as one of the most significant sports figures of the 20th century, the boxer known universally as "The Greatest" was a three-time heavyweight champion. Known for his legendary trash talk and political activism, he famously refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War, citing his religious beliefs.

Title: Galilean Moons
The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. They were discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 using a highly improved telescope. Their discovery proved that not all celestial bodies orbit the Earth, fundamentally shifting astronomical understanding.

Title: 2016 NBA Finals
The 2016 NBA Finals was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's 2015–16 season. The series is legendary for featuring the first-ever comeback from a 3-1 series deficit in Finals history. The Cleveland Cavaliers successfully pulled off this miracle to defeat the 73-9 Golden State Warriors in game 7.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Gloucestershire
Gloucestershire is a county in South West England. The county comprises part of the Cotswold Hills, part of the flat fertile valley of the River Severn, and the entire Forest of Dean. Its county town is the city of Gloucester, and it includes other major settlements like Cheltenham and Stroud.

Title: Sickle cell anemia
Sickle cell anemia is a genetic blood disorder characterized by red blood cells that assume an abnormal, rigid, sickle shape. This decreases the cells' flexibility and results in a risk of various life-threatening complications. In 1949, Linus Pauling demonstrated that the disease occurs due to a mutation in a specific metalloprotein.

Title: Gabriel García Márquez
Gabriel García Márquez was an acclaimed novelist, short-story writer, screenwriter, and journalist. Affectionately known as "Gabo," he authored "One Hundred Years of Solitude" and won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the small town of Aracataca, located in the northern region of Colombia.

Title: Broad Street Cholera Outbreak
The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak was a severe epidemic of cholera that occurred in the Soho district of London. Physician John Snow famously traced the source of the outbreak to a single contaminated public water pump, proving that the disease was waterborne rather than spread by foul air (miasma theory).

Title: John Carpenter
John Howard Carpenter is an American filmmaker, composer, and screenwriter. He is recognized as a master of the horror and science fiction genres, having directed classics like "Halloween" and "The Thing". Carpenter was born in Carthage, located in the state of New York, but grew up in Kentucky.

Title: Monsters, Inc.
"Monsters, Inc." is a 2001 computer-animated comedy film produced by Pixar Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter. It was highly successful and was nominated for the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, but ultimately lost the award to a rival studio's fairy tale parody.

Title: Toropets
Toropets is a historic town and the administrative center of Toropetsky District in Tver Oblast, Russia. It is located where the Toropa River flows through Lake Solomen. First mentioned in chronicles in 1074, it is one of the oldest settlements in the western part of the country, boasting numerous historic churches.

Title: George W. Bush
George W. Bush served as the 43rd President of the United States, holding office from 2001 to 2009. He was the sitting president during the entirety of 2004, successfully running for re-election that November. Bush was born in New Haven, Connecticut, before his family relocated to the South.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It is known for its diverse cultural heritage and complex history. The administrative, economic, and cultural center of the country is its capital city, Sarajevo.

Title: Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan was the fifth emperor of the Mughal Empire, remembered largely for his architectural achievements. He famously commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal to honor his favorite wife. His reign ended when he was deposed by his ambitious son in 1658, and he died in captivity in early 1666.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29, 1986. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where Argentina emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim their second World Cup title, propelled by the legendary performance of Diego Maradona.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Known for its historical architecture and romantic ambiance, the city is a global center for art and culture. While it houses the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, it does not hold the famous painting of the swirling night sky.

Title: 2008 Summer Olympics
The 2008 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIX Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held from August 8 to 24, 2008. The games were a massive global spectacle and marked a significant moment of international integration. They were hosted in Beijing, the capital city of China.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team based in Kansas City, Missouri. They competed in the very first Super Bowl but were defeated. Led by head coach Hank Stram, they later returned to the big game and secured a victory in Super Bowl IV before a long championship drought.

Title: Zirconium
Zirconium is a chemical element with the symbol Zr and atomic number 40. The name of zirconium is taken from the name of the mineral zircon, the most important source of zirconium. It is a lustrous, grey-white, strong transition metal that closely resembles hafnium and, to a lesser extent, titanium.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." His model of the atom, which proposed that electrons travel in discrete orbits around the nucleus, was a fundamental step forward in quantum mechanics.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is an island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the 18 regions of France. It is located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Functioning as a single territorial collectivity, the political and administrative capital city of Corsica is Ajaccio.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. Before his ultimate defeat at Waterloo and subsequent exile, he conquered much of Europe. He was originally born on the Mediterranean island of Corsica into a minor noble family.

Title: Puerperal fever
Puerperal fever, also known as postpartum infections, are bacterial infections of the female reproductive tract following childbirth or miscarriage. Before the widespread understanding of germ theory and the adoption of handwashing by doctors in the late 19th century, it was a leading cause of maternal mortality, claiming the lives of many historical figures.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He spent his entire life working in various municipalities, having been born in Eisenach, a town located in Germany.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: 1930 FIFA World Cup
The 1930 FIFA World Cup was the inaugural tournament for the men's soccer world championship. Organized by FIFA, the entire tournament took place in a single South American nation during the month of July. A total of 13 teams participated, and the host nation emerged victorious by defeating its neighbor in the final match.

Title: Cleveland
Cleveland is a major city in the U.S. state of Ohio, situated along the southern shore of Lake Erie. It was a major manufacturing center during the 20th century and has since diversified its economy into healthcare and finance. The city ended a 52-year major sports championship drought when its basketball team won the title in 2016.

Title: Yekaterinburg
Yekaterinburg is the fourth-largest city in Russia and the administrative center of Sverdlovsk Oblast. Historically significant as the site where the Romanov family met their end, the city is situated in the middle of the Ural Mountains, serving as a gateway between Europe and Asia.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element, earning them global acclaim and Nobel Prizes.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho. Discovered in 1878 by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, it belongs to the lanthanide series. Cleve named the element after Holmia, the Latin name for his native city of Stockholm, to honor the Swedish capital.

Title: Copernicium
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Cn and atomic number 112. It is extremely radioactive and was first created in 1996 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. It was named to honor the legendary astronomer who first proposed the heliocentric solar system.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Apollo 13
Apollo 13 was the seventh crewed mission in the Apollo space program and the third meant to land on the Moon. The lunar landing was aborted after an oxygen tank in the service module failed two days into the mission. The crew, commanded by Jim Lovell, successfully returned to Earth.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line that sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912. It struck an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City. Of the estimated 2,224 passengers and crew aboard, more than 1,500 died, making it one of modern history's deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Alexander the Great
Alexander III of Macedon, commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon. He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through Asia and northeast Africa. He created one of the largest empires in history before dying at the age of 32 in Babylon.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland. It is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by France. The island is historically significant as the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, who was born there in 1769 to a minor noble family.

Title: Yichang
Yichang is a prefecture-level city located in western Hubei province, China. Known historically as a gateway to the upper reaches of major waterways, it is highly industrialized. Today, it is globally famous as the nearest city to the monumental Three Gorges Dam, which sits just upstream from its urban center.

Title: Gabriel García Márquez
Gabriel García Márquez was a legendary novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. Affectionately known as "Gabo," he won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the small town of Aracataca, located in the northern region of Colombia.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. The defeated French military commander was Napoleon Bonaparte, ending his reign as Emperor of the French.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains and Pampas grasslands. The political, economic, and cultural hub of the nation is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: The Old Guitarist
"The Old Guitarist" is an oil painting created in late 1903 and early 1904. It depicts an old, blind, haggard man with threadbare clothing weakly hunched over his instrument on the streets of Barcelona. It is one of the most famous works from Pablo Picasso's Blue Period, heavily emphasizing themes of poverty and isolation.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter: A Romance" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne, who conceives a daughter through an affair and struggles to create a new life of repentance and dignity.

Title: Worcestershire
Worcestershire is a county in the West Midlands of England. It is known for its rolling hills, agricultural produce, and as the birthplace of the renowned composer Edward Elgar. The county town is the cathedral city of Worcester.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. It maintains control over several overseas territories around the globe, including a remote island in the South Atlantic. The primary, dominant language spoken in the United Kingdom is English.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Björn Borg
Björn Borg is a former world No. 1 tennis player widely considered one of the greatest in the history of the sport. He was famous for his unmatched dominance on both grass and clay courts during the late 1970s. Borg was born and raised in the country of Sweden.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. The HMS Beagle spent significant time surveying its long, rugged coastline. The nation has a deeply agricultural economy, and its official currency is the Argentine peso.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: Three Gorges Dam
The Three Gorges Dam is a massive hydroelectric gravity dam that spans a major waterway in central China. It is the world's largest power station in terms of installed capacity, generating immense amounts of electricity. The dam was constructed directly across the Yangtze River, permanently altering the region's ecology and landscape.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. He is best known for his metallic, flowing designs, such as the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao and the Walt Disney Concert Hall.

Title: Bogotá
Bogotá is the sprawling, high-altitude capital of a major South American nation. Situated in the center of the country at an elevation of 2,640 meters, it is one of the highest capital cities in the world. It serves as the commercial, financial, and cultural hub of the nation, boasting numerous universities and museums.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he managed the early tensions of the Cold War and the beginning of the Space Race, acting as the primary geopolitical rival to the Soviet leadership of that era.

Title: 1980 Winter Olympics
The 1980 Winter Olympics, officially known as the XIII Olympic Winter Games, was a multi-sport event held from February 13 to February 24, 1980. The event was marked by significant Cold War tensions but is best remembered by Americans for the stunning "Miracle on Ice" hockey match. It was hosted in the village of Lake Placid.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He survived his Italian contemporary by several years, passing away in 1750 in Leipzig.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. The artist was born in 1863, a full decade after his famous Dutch contemporary.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It has a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary democracy. The nation's official currency is the Pound Sterling, which is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Mulhacén
Mulhacén is the highest mountain in continental Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, with an elevation of 3,479 meters. Located in the Sierra Nevada range in Andalusia, it is a prominent peak, but it is surpassed in overall elevation by a volcanic peak located in the Spanish overseas territories.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is most famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. The synthetic element Nobelium was later named in his honor.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. The country's political and administrative center is its capital city, Wellington, located at the south-western tip of the North Island.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science.

Title: Helsinki
Helsinki is the capital and most populous city of Finland, located on the shore of the Gulf of Finland. It is the country's central hub for politics, education, finance, and culture. The city is defined by its maritime landscape and the Vantaa River, which flows directly through it.

Title: The Old Man and the Sea
The Old Man and the Sea is a short novel written by the American author Ernest Hemingway. It tells the story of an aging Cuban fisherman who struggles with a giant marlin far out in the Gulf Stream. The acclaimed novella was officially published in 1952 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction the following year.

Title: Gustav Holst
Gustav Theodore Holst was an English composer, arranger, and teacher. Best known for his orchestral suite "The Planets", he composed a large number of other works across a range of genres, although none achieved comparable success. Holst was born in 1874 in the spa town of Cheltenham.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation with terrain encompassing Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grassland. Known for its tango dance and music, its cultural capital is Buenos Aires. Geographically, it is dominated by the Andes mountain range along its western border with Chile, which includes the highest point in the Americas.

Title: Fontevraud Abbey
Fontevraud Abbey is a historic monastery situated in the village of Fontevraud-l'Abbaye, near Chinon, in the French region of Anjou. Founded in 1101, the abbey was closely associated with the Plantagenet royal family. It serves as the final resting place for several royals, and is the specific monastery where Isabella of Angoulême died.

Title: Louis XVI
Louis XVI was the last king of France before the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution. His absolute rule proved deeply unpopular amid widespread economic hardship, leading to his eventual arrest. He was tried by the National Convention, found guilty of high treason, and executed by guillotine.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, he composed more than 800 works of virtually every genre of his time, including the opera "The Magic Flute". He was born in 1756 in Salzburg, a musical city that deeply influenced his early career.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the fierce technological rivalry known as the Space Race.

Title: Bacteria
Bacteria are ubiquitous, mostly free-living organisms often consisting of one biological cell. They constitute a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms. While many are harmless or beneficial, some are pathogenic and cause infectious diseases, which are typically treated using antibiotic medications.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: 2004 UEFA Champions League Final
The 2004 UEFA Champions League Final was a football match played at the Arena AufSchalke in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, to decide the winner of the 2003-04 UEFA Champions League. The match was won by FC Porto, who defeated AS Monaco 3-0 to claim the prestigious European title.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt during the waning months of World War II. Truman's administration oversaw the rebuilding of post-war Europe via the Marshall Plan.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football franchise based in Kansas City, Missouri. They represented the AFL in the very first Super Bowl under the guidance of head coach Hank Stram, though they were ultimately defeated by their NFL counterparts.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day of lunar surface activity.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released in 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios in London.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named in honor of the newly discovered planet Uranus.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad and commonly known as Atlanta 1996, were an international multi-sport event held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The games were hosted in the capital city of a southern US state, marking the centennial of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: London in Literature
London has been a central hub for English literature for centuries, serving as the birthplace and home for countless legendary authors, from Geoffrey Chaucer to Virginia Woolf. Despite its massive literary pedigree, the city did not produce the poet who captured the very first Nobel Prize in Literature.

Title: Zinc
Zinc is a chemical element with the symbol Zn and atomic number 30. It is a slightly brittle metal at room temperature and has a shiny-greyish appearance when oxidation is removed. When alloyed with copper, it creates brass, a material known for its acoustic properties and bright, gold-like appearance.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited art museum and a historic monument in France. A central landmark of its home city, it is located on the Right Bank of the Seine. The museum permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including Leonardo da Vinci's iconic portrait of Lisa Gherardini.

Title: Apple I
The Apple I, or Apple-1, is an 8-bit desktop computer released in 1976. It was designed and hand-built by a young engineer in his garage, and his visionary business partner helped market and sell the device. The creation of the Apple I marked the foundation of what would become a trillion-dollar consumer electronics enterprise.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage. The expedition famously allowed a young naturalist to conduct crucial field research during a five-week stop at a remote volcanic archipelago in 1835.

Title: Poor Richard's Almanack
Poor Richard's Almanack was a yearly almanac published by Benjamin Franklin, who adopted the pseudonym of "Poor Richard" or "Richard Saunders" for this purpose. The publication appeared continually from 1732 to 1758. It was a best seller for a pamphlet published in the American colonies, featuring weather forecasts, practical household hints, and puzzles.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Skłodowska-Curie was a pioneering physicist and chemist who conducted groundbreaking research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two distinct scientific fields. She was immensely proud of her Polish heritage.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: 1940 in Science
The year 1940 was a monumental time for physical chemistry and nuclear science. Under the shadow of escalating global conflict, researchers made incredible breakthroughs in the synthesis of transuranic elements. These secret discoveries fundamentally altered the trajectory of energy and warfare for the remainder of the century.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, his work was heavily inspired by classical antiquity and had a profound influence on the development of Western art. His most famous paintings adorn the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Aurangzeb
Aurangzeb was the sixth emperor of the Mughal Empire, ruling over almost the entire Indian subcontinent for a period of 49 years. He officially ascended to the throne in 1658 after emerging victorious in a war of succession. By the time the year 1666 arrived, he was firmly in power and ruling over a vast domain.

Title: Francis Crick
Francis Harry Compton Crick was an English molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist. Alongside James Watson, he is best known for discovering the double-helix structure of the DNA molecule in 1953. Crick was born and raised in Northampton, a large market town in the East Midlands of England.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. It was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster
The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster occurred on January 28, 1986. The spacecraft broke apart 73 seconds into its flight, tragically killing all seven crew members aboard. The disaster temporarily grounded the shuttle fleet and led to major structural changes at NASA.

Title: Ridley Scott
Sir Ridley Scott is an English film director and producer. He is renowned for his atmospheric, highly concentrated visual style. After establishing his career with commercials, he found global fame directing the sci-fi classics "Alien" and "Blade Runner". He is the older brother of fellow Hollywood director Tony Scott.

Title: British Empire
The British Empire was composed of the dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates, and other territories ruled or administered by the United Kingdom. At its height, it was the largest empire in history. Its power was centralized in the capital city of London, situated along the banks of the River Thames.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements. Born in Tobolsk, Siberia, he used his periodic table to correct the properties of some already discovered elements and predict the properties of eight elements yet to be discovered.

Title: First Emperor of Rome
Following the assassination of Julius Caesar and the subsequent civil wars, the Roman Republic collapsed. The victor of these conflicts emerged as the absolute ruler of the Roman world. He was granted the title Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC, effectively making him the first Emperor of Rome.

Title: MiG-15
The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15 is a jet fighter aircraft developed by the Soviet Union. It was one of the first successful swept-wing jet fighters and achieved fame in the skies over Korea. The aircraft was jointly designed by two prominent Soviet aerospace engineers, Artem Mikoyan and Mikhail Gurevich.

Title: Pavel Nedvěd
Pavel Nedvěd is a retired professional footballer who played as a midfielder. Described as one of the best footballers of his generation, he won the Ballon d'Or in 2003. He was born in Cheb, a city situated in the Czech Republic, where he began his youth career before dominating Italian football.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among other products and services. Its massive corporate headquarters is situated in Menlo Park, California.

Title: SpaceX
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) is an American aerospace manufacturer, space transportation company, and communications corporation headquartered in Hawthorne, California. The company was founded in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars, and is currently led by its billionaire CEO.

Title: Polio Vaccines
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis. The first breakthrough was an inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which requires injection and utilizes a killed version of the virus. Shortly after, a cheaper, oral polio vaccine (OPV) using an attenuated live virus was developed, which became the standard in global eradication efforts.

Title: Thriller (album)
"Thriller" is the sixth studio album by an iconic American pop singer, released on November 29, 1982. It produced seven top-10 singles on the Billboard Hot 100, including "Billie Jean" and "Beat It". The record shattered industry expectations and remains the best-selling album of all time worldwide.

Title: Origins of Video Sharing
The mid-2000s saw a massive boom in user-generated content platforms. In February 2005, three former PayPal employees—Jawed Karim, Steve Chen, and Chad Hurley—registered a domain name for a new video-sharing website. Their creation, YouTube, allowed anyone to easily upload, share, and view video clips over the internet.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, fought in 1805, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. The French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: NASA
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is an independent agency of the U.S. federal government responsible for the civil space program, aeronautics research, and space research. It was established in 1958 by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in direct response to the early successes of a rival nation's space initiatives.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They achieved legendary status in the 1960s by dominating the NFL. During their historic victory in Super Bowl I, the team was led by their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Louvre Pyramid
The Louvre Pyramid is a large glass and metal pyramid designed as the main entrance to the Louvre Museum in Paris. Completed in 1989, it was initially highly controversial for clashing with the classical architecture of the surrounding palace. The striking modernist structure was designed by the acclaimed Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: First Human Spaceflight
The Space Age reached a monumental milestone on April 12, 1961, when the Soviet Union successfully launched the Vostok 1 spacecraft. Aboard was cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who made history by becoming the very first human being to journey into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in Ishpeming, located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: 2012 Summer Olympics
The 2012 Summer Olympics were a major international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. It was the third time that the British capital had hosted the modern Olympic Games. The event followed the massive spectacle previously hosted by an East Asian nation four years prior.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a classical romantic ballet composed in 1875 by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Unlike avant-garde works of the 20th century, it is beloved for its traditional orchestral melodies and graceful choreography, representing the pinnacle of classical Russian ballet.

Title: Penicillium
Penicillium is a genus of ascomycetous molds that is of major importance in the natural environment, in food spoilage, and in food and drug production. One species in this genus, Penicillium rubens, is famous for naturally producing the active ingredient in the antibiotic penicillin. Taxonomically, this organism belongs to the kingdom Fungi.

Title: Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east. It features warm tropical waters and numerous island chains, including the historic archipelago of Zanzibar.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch.

Title: Edwin Hubble
Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing the fields of extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. Working primarily from the Mount Wilson Observatory, he proved that many objects previously thought to be clouds of dust and gas were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

Title: Mount Wilson Observatory
The Mount Wilson Observatory is an astronomical observatory located in the San Gabriel Mountains near Pasadena. It contains two historically significant telescopes: the 60-inch Hale telescope and the 100-inch Hooker telescope, the latter of which was used to discover the expansion of the universe. The facility is located in California.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century.

Title: Geography of China
China is a massive country in East Asia with a diverse and rugged landscape. It encompasses expansive deserts, towering mountain ranges, and immense river systems that have sustained its population for millennia. The absolute longest river entirely within China, and the third longest in the world, is the mighty Yangtze River.

Title: Portugal
Portugal is a country located on the Iberian Peninsula in Southwestern Europe. It is the westernmost sovereign state of mainland Europe. The political, economic, and cultural heart of the country is its capital and largest city, Lisbon.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece in various mediums.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for the Mount Rushmore memorial, and its highest physical elevation is a prominent peak in the Black Hills.

Title: Vince Lombardi
Vince Lombardi was an American football coach and executive in the NFL. He is best known as the head coach of the Green Bay Packers during the 1960s, leading them to five NFL Championships, including victories in the first two Super Bowls. In his younger years, Lombardi played college football as an offensive lineman for Fordham University.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located entirely within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is globally recognized as the smallest independent state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority is the Pope.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville, who famously dedicated his masterpiece about a white whale to Hawthorne. Hawthorne later worked at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. With a rich history of producing legendary scientists, philosophers, and composers, its political and cultural heart is its capital city, Berlin.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Bettino Craxi
Bettino Craxi was an Italian politician, leader of the Italian Socialist Party, and served as Prime Minister of Italy from 1983 to 1987. He took office shortly after the brief leadership of his republican predecessor, guiding Italy through an era of strong economic growth in the mid-1980s.

Title: First to the South Pole
The race to the South Pole was one of the defining chapters of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. The brutal competition ended when a Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen became the very first to successfully reach the geographic South Pole. This historic achievement was completed in December 1911.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he is the most commercially successful director in history. Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Badshahi Mosque
The Badshahi Mosque is a Mughal-era congregational mosque in Lahore, capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab. It was commissioned by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1671. Known for its carved red sandstone with marble inlay, it remains one of the most iconic landmarks of the Mughal Empire in the region.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity. It remains a critical piece of infrastructure for the North African nation.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy. The element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where the element was discovered.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. Born in New York City, USA, he chose not to patent the vaccine to maximize its global distribution. His inactivated polio vaccine required an injection but proved immensely effective in clinical trials.

Title: Oxford University
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of 39 constituent colleges and a range of academic departments, where legendary authors and philologists have taught over the centuries.

Title: Rijksmuseum
The Rijksmuseum is a Dutch national museum dedicated to arts and history. It is situated at the Museum Square in the borough Amsterdam South. The museum has on display 8,000 objects of art and history, including some masterpieces by Rembrandt, Frans Hals, and Johannes Vermeer. Its most famous permanent exhibit is "The Night Watch".

Title: Eighth Planet from the Sun
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. In the Solar System, it is the fourth-largest planet by diameter. It was named after the Roman god of the sea. Neptune is notable for being the only planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by empirical observation.

Title: Statue of David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created in marble between 1501 and 1504. The 5.17-metre statue depicts the Biblical hero David, a favored subject in the art of Florence. It was originally commissioned as one of a series of statues of prophets to be positioned along the roofline of the east end of Florence Cathedral.

Title: United States
The United States is a massive transcontinental country spanning North America, with additional territories in the Pacific and Caribbean. The nation boasts highly diverse geography, ranging from vast central plains to rugged mountain ranges. The country's highest physical point is the towering peak of Denali, located in the state of Alaska.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in the capital of Sweden. The host city, Stockholm, organized a highly successful event that introduced electronic timing devices and the first art competitions.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Black Sabbath
Black Sabbath was an English rock band formed in Birmingham in 1968 by guitarist Tony Iommi, drummer Bill Ward, bassist Geezer Butler and vocalist Ozzy Osbourne. They are often cited as pioneers of heavy metal music. The band helped define the genre with releases such as "Paranoid".
