Title: First Human in Space
On April 12, 1961, the Soviet space program achieved a massive milestone by successfully launching the first human into space. The cosmonaut aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft completed one orbit of the Earth. Tragically, this legendary space pioneer later died in a routine training flight crash in 1968.

Title: St. Stephen's Cathedral
St. Stephen's Cathedral is the mother church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vienna. Its multi-coloured tile roof and massive towers make it one of the city's most recognizable symbols. The building is a massive masterpiece constructed primarily in the Gothic architectural style.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the sixth-most populous state and 25th-largest state in terms of land area. Often viewed as a microcosm of the entire US, it features major industrial hubs, vast agricultural plains, and renowned public universities. Its state capital is Springfield.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a Canadian filmmaker known for his massive box office successes. He directed the science fiction action film "Aliens" as well as the revolutionary blockbusters "Terminator 2: Judgment Day", "Titanic", and "Avatar". He frequently pushes the boundaries of cinematic visual effects.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: Uruguay
Uruguay, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, is a country in the southeastern region of South America. It borders Brazil to the north and east and Argentina to the west. The nation has a deeply rooted soccer culture and hosted the first World Cup. The country's primary metropolis and capital city is Montevideo.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, Finland to the east, and is connected to Denmark in the southwest by a bridge-tunnel. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm. The country's geography is characterized by extensive forests and a rugged mountainous region along the Norwegian border, where its highest peak, Kebnekaise, is located.

Title: Vince Lombardi Trophy
The Vince Lombardi Trophy is the trophy awarded each year to the winning team of the National Football League's championship game, the Super Bowl. The award was officially renamed in 1970 in memory of the legendary head coach who led his team to victory in the first two Super Bowls. The prestigious hardware is crafted entirely of sterling silver.

Title: Three Gorges Dam
The Three Gorges Dam is a massive hydroelectric gravity dam that spans a major waterway in central China. It is the world's largest power station in terms of installed capacity, generating immense amounts of electricity. The dam was constructed directly across the Yangtze River, permanently altering the region's ecology and landscape.

Title: Stanley Cup
The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff winner. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America. Unlike many other sports trophies, it is made of a durable alloy of silver and nickel.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era, a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom. She was the longest-reigning British monarch until Elizabeth II.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country in South Asia known for its vast geographic territory spanning from the Andes mountains to the Atlantic Ocean. It has produced numerous legendary soccer players and has won multiple World Cup titles throughout its sporting history. The capital and largest city of the nation is Buenos Aires.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. He is best known for his metallic, flowing designs, such as the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao and the Walt Disney Concert Hall.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL, having been officially founded in August 1919 by Earl "Curly" Lambeau and George Whitney Calhoun. They boast a rich history, including victory in the inaugural Super Bowl.

Title: Monterey, California
Monterey is a city on California's rugged central coast. Its Cannery Row, one-time center of the sardine-packing industry, was immortalized by a famous American novelist. Today, it is a popular tourist destination known for its massive aquarium and coastal views.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the modern Czech Republic. Situated on the Vltava river, the city has a rich history spanning over a millennium. In the late 19th century, specifically the 1880s, Prague was a major provincial capital within the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Brooklyn Bridge
The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City. Opened in May 1883, it spans the East River, connecting the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn. It was the first steel-wire suspension bridge ever constructed and remains an iconic feature of the city's skyline.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. Before moving to Seattle to start his online bookstore, Bezos graduated summa cum laude in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science from Princeton University.

Title: The Electron
The electron is a subatomic particle with a negative one elementary electric charge. It belongs to the first generation of the lepton particle family, and is generally thought to be an elementary particle because it has no known components or substructure. It was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, identified by physicist J.J. Thomson.

Title: Michael Jackson
Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, and dancer. Dubbed the "King of Pop", he is regarded as one of the most significant cultural figures of the 20th century. He achieved unparalleled global success with his 1982 album "Thriller". Jackson was born into a working-class African-American family in Gary, Indiana.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 2
Helium is a chemical element with the symbol He and atomic number 2. It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, inert, monatomic gas that heads the noble gas group in the periodic table. Its boiling and melting points are the lowest among all the elements.

Title: Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan is a massive landlocked country spanning Central Asia and Eastern Europe. It was a constituent republic of the Soviet Union until its independence in 1991. The country inherited several major Soviet technological and military installations, including the massive desert launch facility heavily utilized by the Russian space agency.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He achieved worldwide fame as the author of "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Although he spent most of his life and career in England, he was born in January 1892 in the Orange Free State, a territory that later became part of South Africa.

Title: Edwin Hubble
Edwin Powell Hubble was an American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing the fields of extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. Working primarily from the Mount Wilson Observatory, he proved that many objects previously thought to be clouds of dust and gas were actually galaxies beyond the Milky Way.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel represents a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: 1766 in Great Britain
The year 1766 in Great Britain was marked by the repeal of the controversial Stamp Act, easing tensions temporarily in the American colonies. It was also a landmark year in chemistry due to the identification of a new "inflammable" gas. Throughout this period, the British Empire was under the steady rule of King George III.

Title: Mount Greylock
Mount Greylock is the highest natural point in Massachusetts. At 3,489 feet, its summit provides expansive views encompassing five states. It is located in the far western part of the state, well away from the coastal maritime cities.

Title: Michelangelo's David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created between 1501 and 1504 by the Italian artist Michelangelo. Unlike many sculptures of the era that utilized metal alloys, this towering 5.17-meter statue of the Biblical hero was intricately carved from a single massive block of Carrara marble.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. As Vice President, he was thrust into the presidency on November 22, 1963, following the tragic assassination of John F. Kennedy in Dallas. He became the commander-in-chief on the exact day that author Aldous Huxley passed away.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: Carl Sagan
Carl Sagan was an American astronomer, planetary scientist, and science communicator. He spent most of his career as a professor at Cornell University, where he directed the Laboratory for Planetary Studies. He is best known for assembling the first physical messages sent into space, the Pioneer plaque and the Voyager Golden Record.

Title: Cloning of Dolly
The scientific world was fundamentally altered by a major breakthrough at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Using the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer, researchers successfully cloned a female domestic sheep from an adult somatic cell. This historic mammal, affectionately named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996.

Title: Statue of David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created in marble between 1501 and 1504. The 5.17-metre statue depicts the Biblical hero David, a favored subject in the art of Florence. It was originally commissioned as one of a series of statues of prophets to be positioned along the roofline of the east end of Florence Cathedral.

Title: Golden State Warriors
The Golden State Warriors are an American professional basketball team based in San Francisco, California. They compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the league's Western Conference. The franchise has enjoyed a highly successful modern era, winning multiple championships under head coach Steve Kerr.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: Pollsmoor Prison
Pollsmoor Maximum Security Prison is a prison in the suburb of Tokai, South Africa. Nelson Mandela was transferred here from his previous island prison in 1982, serving out another segment of his sentence before being moved to Victor Verster Prison prior to his final release.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: George Frideric Handel
George Frideric Handel was a German-British Baroque composer well known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, and organ concertos. He was born in 1685, the same year as Bach, in the German city of Halle, but he spent the bulk of his career working in London.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter: A Romance" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne, who conceives a daughter through an affair and struggles to create a new life of repentance and dignity.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill, precise draftsmanship, and striking, bizarre images. His major works often featured melting clocks and distorted figures set in vast, desolate landscapes. Though he occasionally touched on political themes, he was far less overtly political than his contemporary who painted "Guernica".

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy. The element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where the element was discovered.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a massive conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital. It raged for several days in the year 1666, destroying thousands of homes and historical structures. The disaster ultimately led to massive reconstruction efforts and modernized fire safety codes.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its legacy of housing famous classical composers like Mozart and Beethoven.

Title: Super Bowl III
Super Bowl III was played on January 12, 1969. It is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in sports history. The AFL champion New York Jets, led by Joe Namath, defeated the NFL champion Baltimore Colts, who were coached by Don Shula.

Title: The Black Death
The Black Death was a devastating global epidemic of bubonic plague that struck Europe and Asia in the mid-1300s. It killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people, fundamentally altering the demographic and economic landscape of the medieval world long before the modernization of European cities.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Academy Award for Best Animated Feature
The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature is given annually to the best animated feature-length film. The award was first introduced in 2002 for films released in 2001. The inaugural winner of this highly coveted prize was the computer-animated comedy film "Shrek", which beat out competitors like "Monsters, Inc."

Title: First French Empire
The First French Empire, officially the French Republic until 1809 and then the French Empire, was the empire ruled by Napoleon Bonaparte. At its height, the empire dominated continental Europe. Its cultural, political, and economic heart was its magnificent capital city, Paris, which saw massive architectural renovations during the era.

Title: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch businessman and scientist. He is universally acknowledged as the "father of microbiology" for pioneering the use of microscopes to discover microorganisms. Born in 1632 in the city of Delft, he famously communicated his groundbreaking microscopic observations via a series of detailed letters sent to a foreign scientific body.

Title: Dietary Habits of Marsupials
Many marsupials have highly specialized diets that influence their digestive systems. Koalas, for instance, survive almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals. Their slow metabolic rate allows them to process the tough, fibrous leaves, resulting in small, pellet-like droppings.

Title: Google
Google LLC is an American multinational technology company that focuses on search engine technology, online advertising, cloud computing, computer software, quantum computing, e-commerce, and artificial intelligence. The massive corporation maintains its sprawling global headquarters, famously known as the Googleplex, in the city of Mountain View, California.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is most famous for his performance in the 1986 World Cup, where he scored the notorious "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Slovakia
Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe that was historically part of Czechoslovakia until a peaceful dissolution in 1993. Its capital and largest city is Bratislava. The official currency of Slovakia has been the Euro since the country adopted it in 2009.

Title: Ferdinand I of Austria
Ferdinand I was the Emperor of Austria from 1835 until his abdication in 1848. Known as "Ferdinand the Benign," he suffered from severe neurological issues and epilepsy, leaving most of the actual governance of the empire to the State Conference led by Metternich.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Principal Cordillera of the Andes mountain range, in Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters (22,837 ft), it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.

Title: 1749 in Great Britain
The year 1749 in Great Britain saw the end of the War of the Austrian Succession and the subsequent signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. It was also the birth year of several notable figures, including the scientist who would eventually conquer smallpox. During this time, the British throne was occupied by a monarch of the House of Hanover.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Toropets
Toropets is a historic town and the administrative center of Toropetsky District in Tver Oblast, Russia. It is located where the Toropa River flows through Lake Solomen. First mentioned in chronicles in 1074, it is one of the oldest settlements in the western part of the country, boasting numerous historic churches.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System. It consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock, with a surface heavily scarred by craters and canyons. This massive moon was discovered by the famous astronomer William Herschel in 1787.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a brilliant French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. Before his ultimate defeat at Waterloo and subsequent exile, he conquered much of Europe. He was originally born on the Mediterranean island of Corsica into a minor noble family.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
"The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King" is a 2003 epic high fantasy adventure film. Serving as the conclusion to a sprawling trilogy, it was both a massive critical and commercial success. At the 76th Academy Awards, it swept all 11 of its nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Mexico and is best remembered for the dominant performance of Diego Maradona. The tournament culminated in Argentina securing the World Cup trophy by defeating West Germany, marking a massive victory for the South American nation.

Title: First Moon Landing
The Apollo 11 mission achieved the historic goal of landing humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent several hours exploring the lunar surface before safely returning to Earth, ending the Space Race.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: Safavid Empire
The Safavid Empire was one of the most significant ruling dynasties of Iran, considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. They ruled from 1501 to 1736 and established the Twelver school of Shia Islam as the official religion of their empire, frequently clashing with neighboring regional powers.

Title: Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east. It features warm tropical waters and numerous island chains, including the historic archipelago of Zanzibar.

Title: The Trial
The Trial is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, a year after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. It is another seminal work by Franz Kafka, exploring themes of existential dread and bureaucracy.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: Miami
Miami is a major coastal metropolis located in southeastern Florida. It is the core of the state's largest metropolitan area and a massive hub for international finance, culture, and arts. Despite its massive size and global influence, it does not serve as the seat of the state government.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic, and the historical capital of Bohemia. Situated on the Vltava river, it is home to about 1.3 million residents. The city has a rich history, having been a political, cultural, and economic center of central Europe.

Title: Bronze
Bronze is an alloy consisting primarily of copper, commonly with about 12–12.5% of another metallic element added to increase its strength and durability. Because of its excellent casting properties, it has been the metal of choice for sculptors for centuries, famously utilized to forge Rodin's masterpiece "The Thinker".

Title: Adelaide
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia and the fifth-most populous city of Australia. Named in honor of Queen Adelaide, it was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for a freely settled British province. The city is the birthplace of the Nobel Prize-winning pathologist who mass-produced penicillin.

Title: Marie Antoinette
Marie Antoinette was the last Queen of France before the French Revolution. Known for her extravagant lifestyle, she became a symbol of the monarchy's disconnect from the struggles of everyday citizens. She was executed by guillotine several months after her husband.

Title: Pitchblende
Pitchblende, now formally known as uraninite, is a radioactive, uranium-rich mineral and ore. It was heavily studied in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Parisian scientists looking to isolate the sources of its intense radioactive emissions. It famously yielded trace amounts of several newly discovered elements.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics in Squaw Valley and the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. During the 1980s, the state's political landscape was heavily shaped by former governor Ronald Reagan.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". Stoker was born in Dublin, Ireland. He suffered from unknown illnesses as a child that left him bedridden until the age of seven, but he later died of strokes in London.

Title: Dutch Language
Dutch is a West Germanic language spoken by around 25 million people as a first language. It is the official language of the Netherlands and one of the three official languages of Belgium. It is closely related to both English and German and has served as a prominent language of trade and culture in Europe.

Title: Louis XIV of France
Louis XIV, known as Louis the Great or the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. His reign of 72 years and 110 days is the longest recorded of any monarch of a sovereign country in history. He famously offered a lavish exile to the deposed English king James II.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He published deeply influential work on the nature of the chemical bond. Beyond his quantum chemistry, he revolutionized medical genetics by identifying sickle cell anemia as a "molecular disease" caused by an abnormal protein structure.

Title: Francis Ford Coppola
Francis Ford Coppola is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He was a central figure in the New Hollywood filmmaking movement of the 1960s and 1970s. He is globally renowned for directing "The Godfather" trilogy and the war epic "Apocalypse Now."

Title: Diego Velázquez
Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a Spanish painter, the leading artist in the court of King Philip IV and of the Spanish Golden Age. He was born in Seville, Andalusia, and painted numerous portraits of the Spanish royal family.

Title: Vostok 6
Vostok 6 was the final mission of the Soviet Vostok space exploration program. Launched in June 1963, it carried the first woman into space. The spacecraft was launched from the premier Soviet spaceport and completed a joint flight with Vostok 5, which had launched two days earlier.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released in 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios in London.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company that specializes in consumer electronics, software, and online services. Founded by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, it has grown into one of the "Big Five" American information technology companies. The company's massive headquarters is located in Cupertino, California.

Title: Henri Becquerel
Henri Becquerel was a French engineer, physicist, and Nobel laureate. He is famously credited with the discovery of radioactivity, an achievement that earned him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside his colleagues. He died in 1908 in Brittany, France.

Title: False Bay
False Bay is a body of water defined by Cape Hangklip and the Cape Peninsula in the extreme south-west of South Africa. The bay was named "False Bay" by sailors who confused the Cape Point and Cape Hangklip, falsely believing they had reached Table Bay.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the Bohr model of the atom. The synthetic element Bohrium, which carries the chemical symbol Bh, was named to honor his monumental legacy.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. He is a Professorial Fellow of Computer Science at the University of Oxford and a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His pioneering work at CERN laid the foundation for modern internet infrastructure.

Title: Arthur Ashe Stadium
Arthur Ashe Stadium is a tennis stadium at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park in Queens, New York City. Part of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, it is the main stadium of the US Open and is the largest tennis stadium in the world by capacity.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. It was a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom, heavily defined by strict moral standards.

Title: José Mourinho
José Mário dos Santos Mourinho Félix is a professional football manager and former player. He gained international fame by winning the Champions League with Porto in 2004. He was born in Setúbal, Portugal, and has gone on to manage some of the biggest clubs in world football.

Title: Royal Society of London
The Royal Society of London, formally The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge, is a learned society and the United Kingdom's national academy of sciences. Founded in 1660, it played a crucial role in early modern science. It famously translated and published the microscopic observations sent by the Dutch "father of microbiology" in its journal.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time. Their breakthrough in the United States occurred in February 1964 with a legendary live television appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show.

Title: AS Monaco
AS Monaco FC is a professional football club based in Monaco that competes in Ligue 1, the top tier of French football. They reached the final of the 2004 UEFA Champions League but were comprehensively defeated despite a strong tournament run.

Title: Roger Waters
George Roger Waters is an English musician, singer-songwriter, and composer. In 1965, he co-founded the progressive rock band Pink Floyd. Following the departure of their original frontman, Waters became the band's primary lyricist and conceptual leader. He was born in Great Bookham, Surrey.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time, redefining pop culture before their eventual breakup in 1970.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He spent the majority of his life working in various German municipalities, serving as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig until his death in 1750. He never traveled to Italy or Austria.

Title: Polio Vaccines
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis. The first breakthrough was an inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which requires injection and utilizes a killed version of the virus. Shortly after, a cheaper, oral polio vaccine (OPV) using an attenuated live virus was developed, which became the standard in global eradication efforts.

Title: West Bengal
West Bengal is a state in the eastern region of India along the Bay of Bengal. It borders Bangladesh in the east, and Nepal and Bhutan in the north. While it served as a major center for British colonial administration, it neighbors the specific state where the author of "1984" was born.

Title: Hernán Cortés
Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire and brought large portions of what is now mainland Mexico under the rule of the King of Castile in the early 16th century. He famously captured the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II.

Title: 1998 FIFA World Cup
The 1998 FIFA World Cup was the 16th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. The tournament culminated in a dramatic final match where the host nation, France, decisively defeated Brazil 3-0 to claim their first-ever World Cup trophy.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: Hugh Carey
Hugh Carey was an American politician and attorney who served as the 51st governor of New York from 1975 to 1982. A member of the Democratic Party, he is often credited with saving New York City from the brink of bankruptcy in the 1970s. He was the presiding governor when his state hosted the 1980 Winter Olympics.

Title: French Franc
The French franc was the currency of France. First introduced in 1360, it was the national currency until the adoption of the Euro. Coins and banknotes of the franc were fully withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender in 2002.

Title: France
France has a rich history of scientific discovery and was the adoptive home of many expatriate researchers. It was the country where radioactivity was extensively studied in the early 20th century, leading to the discovery of several new elements.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero
José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero is a Spanish politician and member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). He served as the Prime Minister of Spain from 2004 to 2011. Zapatero was born on August 4, 1960, in Valladolid, a historic city in northwestern Spain.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is an island nation in northwestern Europe. While it is known for producing massive global cultural exports, it operates independently from mainland European fiscal systems. The country's official currency is the Pound sterling, having notably opted out of using the Euro.

Title: Vince Lombardi
Vince Lombardi was an American football coach and executive in the NFL. He is best known as the head coach of the Green Bay Packers during the 1960s, leading them to five NFL Championships, including victories in the first two Super Bowls. In his younger years, Lombardi played college football as an offensive lineman for Fordham University.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer. He is widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. Kafka was born into a middle-class Jewish family in Prague, which is the capital city of the modern-day country of the Czech Republic.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the cultural, media, political, and economic center of its nation. It is built across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea. It serves as the capital and largest city of Sweden, hosting the national government and the official residence of the Swedish monarch.

Title: 2008 Summer Olympics
The 2008 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIX Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held from August 8 to 24, 2008. The games were a massive global spectacle and marked a significant moment of international integration. They were hosted in Beijing, the capital city of China.

Title: Pontifical Swiss Guard
The Pontifical Swiss Guard is a minor armed forces and honour guard unit maintained by the Holy See that protects the Pope and the Apostolic Palace. Established in 1506, it is one of the oldest military units in continuous operation. By strict tradition, its recruits are exclusively unmarried Catholic males from Switzerland.

Title: Highest Waterfalls
Waterfalls are spectacular natural phenomena created when a river flows over a steep vertical drop. Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River is famed for its massive width. However, the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall is Angel Falls. It boasts an awe-inspiring plunge of 807 meters (2,648 ft) and a total height of 979 meters (3,212 ft).

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. It was launched in November 1969. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day and seven hours of lunar surface activity.

Title: Harper Lee
Nelle Harper Lee was an American novelist best known for her 1960 masterpiece "To Kill a Mockingbird". She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to literature. Lee was born and raised in Monroeville, a small town located in the southern state of Alabama.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po and atomic number 84. It is a rare and highly volatile metal. The element was discovered in 1898 by a prominent scientific couple studying pitchblende.

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. Bohr was born in 1885 in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would later serve as the center of his academic career.

Title: Bohrium
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Bh and atomic number 107. It is highly radioactive, with its most stable known isotope having a half-life of about 61 seconds. It is a transition metal placed in group 7 of the periodic table.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Oliver Stone
Oliver Stone is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He won an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1986 war film "Platoon", which also won Best Picture. Later in his career, he directed the critically acclaimed 1989 film "Born on the Fourth of July."

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Mykolayovych Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he won the 2004 Ballon d'Or while playing for AC Milan. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a small village located in Ukraine, before rising to global sporting fame.

Title: Colossus of Rhodes
The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of the Greek sun-god Helios, erected in the city of Rhodes on the Greek island of the same name. Constructed to celebrate the successful defense of Rhodes against an attack, it was another celebrated Ancient Wonder before collapsing during an earthquake.

Title: Ronald Reagan
Ronald Reagan was an American politician and actor who served as the 40th president of the United States from 1981 to 1989. In 1980, he was conducting a successful presidential campaign, running on a platform of economic revitalization and strong national defense. He took office shortly after the historic 1980 Olympic games.

Title: North America
North America is a continent entirely within the Northern Hemisphere and almost all within the Western Hemisphere. It encompasses major nations like the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The continent is home to several major spaceports, including the primary launch facilities for NASA in Florida.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It is the political, economic, and cultural center of Spain, housing the national parliament where the Prime Minister governs.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson, often referred to by his initials LBJ, was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. He assumed the presidency following the assassination of John F. Kennedy. He was the presiding head of state in early 1964 when the British Invasion of American music began. He was a lifelong member of the Democratic Party.

Title: Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan was the fifth emperor of the Mughal Empire, remembered largely for his architectural achievements. He famously commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal to honor his favorite wife. His reign ended when he was deposed by his ambitious son in 1658, and he died in captivity in early 1666.

Title: Madagascar
Madagascar is an island country in the Indian Ocean, situated off the southeastern coast of Africa. It is the world's fourth-largest island. The nation split from the Indian subcontinent around 88 million years ago, allowing native plants and animals to evolve in relative isolation. Its capital is Antananarivo.

Title: Herbert Hoover
Herbert Clark Hoover was an American politician and engineer who served as the 31st president of the United States from 1929 to 1933. He took office during the final months of the economic boom before the stock market crashed, plunging the nation into the Great Depression.

Title: British Empire in the 17th Century
During the 17th century, the British Empire was rapidly expanding its overseas colonies and trading networks. The domestic front, however, faced extreme turmoil, including a civil war and disastrous urban fires. King Charles II was the reigning monarch trying to stabilize the country during the calamitous events of 1666.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: 2018 FIFA World Cup
The 2018 FIFA World Cup was the 21st FIFA World Cup, an international football tournament contested by the men's national teams of the member associations of FIFA. It took place between 14 June and 15 July 2018. It was hosted by Russia, marking the first time the tournament was held in Eastern Europe.

Title: Constanța
Constanța is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Romania. Located at the crossroads of several commercial routes, it lies on the western coast of the Black Sea. Built directly over the ancient ruins of Tomis, it now serves as Romania's largest sea port.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. Her most famous achievements included the discovery of the elements Polonium and Radium, isolating them from tons of pitchblende ore over several years.

Title: Ukraine
Ukraine is a country in Eastern Europe. It is the second-largest European country by area after Russia. Known for its vast agricultural plains, the country is bordered by the Black Sea to the south and features the rugged Carpathian mountain range in the west.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. After proposing an information management system in 1989, he successfully implemented the first communication between an HTTP client and server via the internet. He was born in 1955 in London, United Kingdom.

Title: 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." His model of the atom, which proposed that electrons travel in discrete orbits around the nucleus, was a fundamental step forward in quantum mechanics.

Title: 1994 FIFA World Cup
The 1994 FIFA World Cup was hosted by the United States and broke tournament attendance records. The final match was played between Brazil and Italy at the Rose Bowl in California. Brazil won the match on penalties after a scoreless draw, securing their fourth title.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with atomic number 101. A highly radioactive metallic element in the actinide series, it is the first element that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities through neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It was named after the Russian chemist who famously created the periodic table. Its chemical symbol is Md.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly influential filmmaker known for his technical innovations in cinematic special effects. He wrote, directed, and produced "Titanic", leading it to record-breaking box office success. Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before moving to the United States in his youth.

Title: Wimbledon Records
The Wimbledon Championships are the oldest tennis tournament in the world and widely considered the most prestigious. In the modern era, consecutive victories on its grass courts are notoriously difficult. The 20th-century record for the most consecutive Wimbledon men's singles titles belongs to Björn Borg, who captured five straight trophies from 1976 to 1980.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: Nikita Khrushchev
Nikita Khrushchev was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the country's Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. As the premier of the nation, he oversaw the early, highly successful years of the Soviet space program, including the historic launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they rank among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed, pushing the boundaries of what a solo violin could achieve.

Title: Artem Mikoyan
Artem Mikoyan was a Soviet aircraft designer of Armenian descent. Alongside Mikhail Gurevich, he designed many of the famous MiG military aircraft. Mikoyan was born in Sanahin, a small village situated in the rugged northern region of Armenia.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians such as Beethoven and Mozart spent their prime years working there. The city center features the towering Gothic spire of St. Stephen's Cathedral.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. Rutherford was born in 1871 and later worked closely with other pioneering physicists at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: WorldWideWeb (browser)
WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion between the software and the World Wide Web itself, was the first web browser and editor. It was written by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990 while working at CERN. It was relatively obscure compared to later graphical browsers that brought the internet to the masses.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he secured the prestigious 2004 Ballon d'Or. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a village located in Ukraine.

Title: Jin Mao Tower
The Jin Mao Tower is an 88-story supertall skyscraper located in the Lujiazui area of the Pudong district of Shanghai. It contains a shopping mall, offices, and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai hotel. Blending traditional Chinese architectural elements with modern engineering, it was designed by American architect Adrian Smith.

Title: Texas
Texas is the second-largest U.S. state by both area and population, known for its massive energy sector and distinct cultural identity. It is heavily associated with the Bush political family, who built their fortunes and political careers there. George W. Bush served as the Governor of Texas prior to his presidency.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in the capital of Sweden. The host city, Stockholm, organized a highly successful event that introduced electronic timing devices and the first art competitions.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned and constructed by the powerful Mughal Empire as a monumental tomb. Today, it is universally admired as a masterpiece of world heritage and Islamic architecture.

Title: Cuba
Cuba is an island country located in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Atlantic Ocean meet. It was heavily colonized by European powers in the 16th century and remained under the rule of Spain until the end of the Spanish-American War in 1898.

Title: Tokugawa Shogunate
The Tokugawa Shogunate was the feudal military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868. Established by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogunate maintained a strict isolationist policy and rigidly controlled the social order. During the year 1800, this dynasty was firmly in power, completely dominating the political landscape of the nation.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, his credits include "E.T." and "Jurassic Park". Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The mission was a triumphant success for the Soviet Space Program, proving the viability of their intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

Title: Aurangzeb
Aurangzeb was the sixth emperor of the Mughal Empire, ruling over almost the entire Indian subcontinent for a period of 49 years. He officially ascended to the throne in 1658 after emerging victorious in a war of succession. By the time the year 1666 arrived, he was firmly in power and ruling over a vast domain.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time. Their original frontman, John Lennon, tragically passed away after being assassinated in New York City.

Title: The Scream
The Scream is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It has been the target of several high-profile art thefts, most notably when a version was stolen from the National Gallery in Oslo in 1994.

Title: Marc Andreessen
Marc Andreessen is an American entrepreneur, investor, and software engineer. He is best known as the co-author of Mosaic, the first widely used web browser, and as co-founder of Netscape. Before launching his legendary tech career, Andreessen earned his bachelor's degree in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

Title: Friedrich Engels
Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, historian, communist, social scientist, and revolutionary socialist. He was the closest collaborator of Karl Marx, co-authoring "The Communist Manifesto". After his death in 1895 in London, his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head, near Eastbourne.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramicist, and theatre designer who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement, the invention of constructed sculpture, and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". His early career is famously divided into the somber Blue Period and the more optimistic Rose Period.

Title: 1990s in Film

Title: Holmium
