Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. It was officially discovered by William Herschel in 1781, originally proposing to name it Georgium Sidus after King George III. The ice giant features a ring system and numerous moons.

Title: Salinas, California
Salinas is the county seat and largest municipality of Monterey County, California. Located at the mouth of the Salinas Valley, the city has long been an agricultural powerhouse. It produces such a massive volume of a specific leafy green vegetable that it has earned the nickname "The Lettuce Capital of the World."

Title: Element with Atomic Number 2
Helium is a chemical element with the symbol He and atomic number 2. It is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, inert, monatomic gas that heads the noble gas group in the periodic table. Its boiling and melting points are the lowest among all the elements.

Title: Origins of Video Sharing
The mid-2000s saw a massive boom in user-generated content platforms. In February 2005, three former PayPal employees—Jawed Karim, Steve Chen, and Chad Hurley—registered a domain name for a new video-sharing website. Their creation, YouTube, allowed anyone to easily upload, share, and view video clips over the internet.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: Greece National Football Team
The Greece national football team shocked the world in 2004 by winning the UEFA European Championship. Hosted in Portugal, the tournament saw the underdog Greek squad defeat the host nation in the final match, securing a historic and unexpected victory.

Title: Google
Google LLC is an American multinational technology company that focuses on search engine technology, online advertising, cloud computing, computer software, quantum computing, e-commerce, and artificial intelligence. The massive corporation maintains its sprawling global headquarters, famously known as the Googleplex, in the city of Mountain View, California.

Title: Andalusia
Andalusia is the southernmost autonomous community in Peninsular Spain. It is the most populous and the second-largest autonomous community in the country. The region is famous for its Moorish architecture, flamenco dancing, and its capital city, Seville.

Title: First French Empire
The First French Empire, officially the French Republic until 1809 and then the French Empire, was the empire ruled by Napoleon Bonaparte. At its height, the empire dominated continental Europe. Its cultural, political, and economic heart was its magnificent capital city, Paris, which saw massive architectural renovations during the era.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. It was launched in November 1969. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day and seven hours of lunar surface activity.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: Days of Thunder
"Days of Thunder" is a 1990 American sports action drama film starring Tom Cruise as an ambitious stock car racing driver. Also directed by Tony Scott, it attempted to replicate the massive success and visual style of their previous collaboration, though it focused on NASCAR rather than fighter jets.

Title: Cincinnati
Cincinnati is a major city in the United States, situated on the north bank of the Ohio River. It is known for its historic architecture, vibrant arts scene, and major professional sports teams. It is a major economic hub within the state of Ohio.

Title: Robert Benton
Robert Douglas Benton is an American screenwriter and film director. He began his career co-writing the script for "Bonnie and Clyde" before moving into the director's chair. He is best known for directing "Kramer vs. Kramer," a feat that earned him the Academy Award for Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay.

Title: Oliver Stone
Oliver Stone is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He won an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1986 war film "Platoon", which also won Best Picture. Later in his career, he directed the critically acclaimed 1989 film "Born on the Fourth of July."

Title: Claude Monet
Claude Monet was a French painter and founder of impressionist painting. He is known for his series of water lilies and his focus on capturing light and natural forms. Born in 1840, he lived through several major shifts in French political history.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, his work was heavily inspired by classical antiquity and had a profound influence on the development of Western art. His most famous paintings adorn the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a space telescope designed primarily to conduct infrared astronomy. As the largest optical telescope in space, its high resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint for the Hubble Space Telescope. It was launched into orbit on Christmas Day, 2021.

Title: Lactuca sativa
Lactuca sativa is the formal scientific name for the species of plant commonly known as lettuce. Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians, it was transformed from a weed whose seeds were used to extract oil into a plant grown for its edible leaves. The species is now farmed extensively worldwide.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest physicists of all time. He is best known for developing the theory of relativity. While his work built upon the foundation laid by classical mechanics, he never attended an English university for his formal scientific training.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece in various mediums.

Title: Muhammad Ali
Muhammad Ali was an American professional boxer and activist. Born and raised in Louisville, Kentucky, he began training as an amateur boxer at age 12. He won an Olympic gold medal in 1960. He was originally born with the name Cassius Clay, but changed his name in 1964 after joining the Nation of Islam.

Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, characterized by its pale blue color and unique sideways rotation. It was the first planet to be discovered using a telescope. Its discovery sent shockwaves through the scientific community and later inspired the naming conventions of newly synthesized radioactive elements.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a country primarily located in North America, consisting of 50 states, a federal district, and several territories. It is a global leader in technological innovation, aerospace engineering, and software development. The official currency of the nation is the United States dollar ($).

Title: Indian Rupee
The Indian Rupee (symbol: ₹; code: INR) is the official currency of the Republic of India. The rupee is subdivided into 100 paise, though as of 2019, coins of denomination of 1 rupee is the lowest value in use. The issuance of the currency is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: Wright Flyer
The Wright Flyer was the first successful heavier-than-air powered aircraft. It was designed and built by a pair of pioneering brothers. The aircraft made four flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, marking the dawn of the aviation age and transforming global transportation.

Title: Lansing, Michigan
Lansing is the capital of the U.S. state of Michigan. It is mostly located in Ingham County, although portions of the city extend west into Eaton County and north into Clinton County. The city became the state capital in 1847, taking over the role from Detroit, to provide a more centralized government location.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. As the oldest university in the English-speaking world, it boasts a prestigious history of scientific and literary alumni. However, it was historically a major rival to the institution where the structure of DNA was famously uncovered.

Title: London
London is the capital city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis and serves as a vital transport route.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: 20-Dollar Bill
The United States twenty-dollar bill ($20) is a denomination of U.S. currency. Andrew Jackson, the seventh U.S. president, has been featured on the obverse of the bill since 1928, while the White House is featured on the reverse. It is one of the most heavily circulated bills in the American economy.

Title: Enigma Variations
The "Enigma Variations" is an orchestral work comprising fourteen variations on an original theme, composed between 1898 and 1899. It is one of the most famous pieces by the English composer Edward Elgar, bringing him international fame.

Title: Altair 8800
The Altair 8800 is a microcomputer designed in 1974 by MITS and based on the Intel 8080 CPU. It sparked the microcomputer revolution of the 1970s. The machine's popularity skyrocketed after two young programmers successfully developed an interpreter for the BASIC programming language that ran on its hardware.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch.

Title: Maine
Maine is the easternmost state in the New England region of the United States. It is known for its jagged, rocky coastline, densely forested interior, and picturesque waterways. The state's capital city is Augusta, though its largest municipality is Portland.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: Rutherfordium
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element that is highly radioactive. It was first synthesized in the 1960s by researchers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The element was officially named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford.

Title: Jeff Bezos
Jeffrey Preston Bezos is an American business magnate, media proprietor, and investor. He is the founder, executive chairman, and former president and CEO of Amazon. He graduated from Princeton University in 1986 with degrees in electrical engineering and computer science.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Copenhagen
Copenhagen is the capital and most populous city of Denmark. It is located on the eastern coast of the island of Zealand. The city is a major center of culture, business, media, and science, and is the birthplace of the architect who famously designed the Sydney Opera House.

Title: First Human Spaceflight
The Space Age reached a monumental milestone on April 12, 1961, when the Soviet Union successfully launched the Vostok 1 spacecraft. Aboard was cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who made history by becoming the very first human being to journey into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. The massive critical and commercial success was co-directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, establishing DreamWorks Animation as a prime competitor in the feature animation industry.

Title: Invention of the World Wide Web
The World Wide Web, commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators. It was invented in 1989 at CERN in Switzerland. The creator developed the first web browser and the fundamental protocols of the internet, HTTP and HTML.

Title: Wilt Chamberlain
Wilt Chamberlain was an American professional basketball player who played at the center position. Widely considered one of the sport's greatest players, he holds numerous records in scoring and rebounding, including the legendary 100-point game. Before his pro career, he played college basketball for the University of Kansas.

Title: Battle of Pharsalus
The Battle of Pharsalus was a decisive battle of Caesar's Civil War, fought in 48 BC. Julius Caesar decisively defeated the troops of the Roman Senate, led by Pompey the Great. The victory allowed Caesar to assume total control over the Roman Republic, laying the groundwork for the later Empire.

Title: Ptolemy I Soter
Ptolemy I Soter was a Macedonian Greek general, historian, and the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt. Before declaring himself Pharaoh of Egypt and starting a powerful dynasty, he served as a trusted companion, historian, and military general under the legendary conqueror Alexander the Great.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a brilliant composer and pianist who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras in Western music. He is responsible for legendary compositions such as the "Moonlight Sonata" and the "Ninth Symphony". Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn before later moving to Vienna to study.

Title: Ernst Chain
Ernst Boris Chain was a German-born British biochemist. Fleeing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, he settled in Britain, where he collaborated closely with Florey. Together, they devised the biochemical methods to successfully isolate and purify penicillin, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize for their efforts.

Title: Solid Milk Chocolate Bar
The invention of the solid milk chocolate bar fundamentally changed the global confectionery industry. Before this, chocolate was primarily consumed as a bitter beverage or used for baking. In 1875, a dedicated chocolatier successfully combined cocoa powder and cocoa butter with condensed milk, resulting in the world's first sweet, solid milk chocolate bar.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian novel and cautionary tale published in 1949 by an English author. The story follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in a totalitarian superstate under the constant surveillance of Big Brother. The work coined numerous terms that became fixtures of modern political discourse.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone in lunar orbit.

Title: River Shannon
The River Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing for 360 kilometers (224 miles) and dividing the west of the island from the east and south. It represents a major physical barrier, featuring only a handful of crossing points along its length. The river flows southwards from the Cuilcagh Mountain to the Shannon Estuary.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers decisively defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10.

Title: US Open
The US Open is a hardcourt tennis tournament. It is the fourth and final Grand Slam tournament of the year. The men's singles champion is awarded the US Open Trophy, which is made by Tiffany & Co. and constructed entirely of sterling silver, though it lacks the golden veneer of its British counterpart.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses. The reigning monarch at the time personally directed firefighting efforts from the river.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, Finland to the east, and is connected to Denmark in the southwest by a bridge-tunnel. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm. The country's geography is characterized by extensive forests and a rugged mountainous region along the Norwegian border, where its highest peak, Kebnekaise, is located.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe, situated in the Eastern Alps. It was historically a massive political and cultural power under the Habsburg dynasty. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" for its association with major classical composers.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, located in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as a fortress in the late 12th to 13th century.

Title: Instagram
Instagram is a photo and video-sharing social networking service founded in 2010 by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. The app distinguished itself by allowing users to apply digital filters to their photos. It grew incredibly fast and was acquired by Facebook Inc. (now Meta) in 2012 for approximately $1 billion.

Title: University of Pennsylvania
The University of Pennsylvania is a private Ivy League research university in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It is one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the U.S. Declaration of Independence. The university was established by Benjamin Franklin, who advocated for an educational program that focused as much on practical education for commerce and public service as on the classics and theology.

Title: Meiji Restoration
The Meiji Restoration was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to the Empire of Japan in 1868 under Emperor Meiji. The event effectively destroyed the shogunate system, paving the way for the modernization and Westernization of the country and establishing a centralized government.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel, a popular form that included both singing and spoken dialogue, in two acts. It premiered on 30 September 1791 in Vienna, just two months before the composer's premature death. It is celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows past numerous historical and industrial landmarks, including the Houses of Parliament and the Battersea Power Station.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Florey was a pharmacologist and pathologist who was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use. He took Fleming's initial discovery and turned it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in Adelaide, South Australia, and eventually moved to England to conduct his research.

Title: Cleopatra
Cleopatra VII Philopator was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Known for her immense wealth and political acumen, she formed romantic and political alliances with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony. Following her defeat alongside Antony at Actium, she famously committed suicide.

Title: Politics of Spain in 2010
In 2010, Spain was grappling with the fallout of the global financial crisis. The nation's government was actively implementing austerity measures. During this time, the Spanish government was led by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). The sitting Prime Minister of Spain in 2010 was José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero.

Title: Hans Zimmer
Hans Zimmer is a German film score composer and music producer. He has won two Oscars and four Grammys. His works are notable for integrating electronic music sounds with traditional orchestral arrangements. Zimmer has a long-standing, highly successful collaboration with director Christopher Nolan.

Title: Louvre Pyramid
The Louvre Pyramid is a large glass and metal pyramid designed as the main entrance to the Louvre Museum in Paris. Completed in 1989, it was initially highly controversial for clashing with the classical architecture of the surrounding palace. The striking modernist structure was designed by the acclaimed Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: On the Origin of Species
"On the Origin of Species", published on November 24, 1859, is a work of scientific literature by Charles Darwin. It is considered to be the foundation of evolutionary biology. The groundbreaking 1859 book introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of natural selection.

Title: Karl Marx
Karl Marx was a German-born philosopher, economist, political theorist, historian, and revolutionary. He is best known for his 1848 pamphlet "The Communist Manifesto" and the multi-volume "Das Kapital". After spending his later years in exile in London, he passed away in 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: John Steinbeck
John Ernst Steinbeck Jr. was an American author who won the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature. He is widely known for his comic novels as well as his deeply serious, socially engaged works like "Of Mice and Men". Steinbeck was born and raised in the agricultural hub of Salinas, California.

Title: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées is an entertainment venue situated at 15 avenue Montaigne in Paris. Despite its name, it is not located on the Champs-Élysées. Opened in 1913, the theater was specifically designed to host contemporary opera and dance, making it the perfect, albeit volatile, setting for radical new works.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of internet infrastructure like ARPANET. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the Potomac River.

Title: Vint Cerf
Vinton Gray Cerf is an American Internet pioneer and is recognized as one of the "fathers of the Internet". He co-designed the TCP/IP protocols and the architecture of the Internet. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, he played a crucial role in the development of modern networking.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a physicist and mechanical engineer who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays or Röntgen rays. This achievement earned him the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics. He was born in Lennep, in the Kingdom of Prussia, Germany.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. He is widely considered one of the greatest painters in history. His artistic genius is best exemplified by his legendary portrait, the Mona Lisa.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne. It opens with a dense introductory chapter titled "The Custom-House."

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. After proposing an information management system in 1989, he successfully implemented the first communication between an HTTP client and server via the internet. He was born in 1955 in London, United Kingdom.

Title: Bono
Paul David Hewson, known worldwide by his stage name Bono, is an Irish singer-songwriter, activist, and philanthropist. He achieved global fame as the lead vocalist and primary lyricist of the rock band U2. Bono was born and raised in Dublin, Ireland, where he met his future bandmates while attending Mount Temple Comprehensive School.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: Waterloo
Waterloo is a municipality located in the Walloon Brabant province. It gained global historical infamy as the site of the legendary 1815 battle that ended the Napoleonic Wars. Today, the battlefield is preserved as a major historical site within the borders of the modern country of Belgium.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a classical romantic ballet composed in 1875 by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Unlike avant-garde works of the 20th century, it is beloved for its traditional orchestral melodies and graceful choreography, representing the pinnacle of classical Russian ballet.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. These three laws of motion were first compiled and published in 1687 in the seminal work "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica." They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is characterized by the vast Amazon basin in the north and a complex system of mountain ranges in the south. The highest mountain in Brazil is Pico da Neblina, which is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is most famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. The synthetic element Nobelium was later named in his honor.

Title: Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant
The "Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant" is an autobiography by the former US president and Civil War general. Written as Grant was dying of throat cancer, the two-volume set was a massive critical and commercial success. It was published by Charles L. Webster & Company, a firm owned by a legendary American humorist.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a south Slav nationalist group seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Archduke and his wife. Princip was born in the rural village of Obljaj, located in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: The Greatest (Boxer)
Widely regarded as one of the most significant sports figures of the 20th century, the boxer known universally as "The Greatest" was a three-time heavyweight champion. Known for his legendary trash talk and political activism, he famously refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War, citing his religious beliefs.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. It remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation with terrain encompassing Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grassland. Known for its tango dance and music, its cultural capital is Buenos Aires. Geographically, it is dominated by the Andes mountain range along its western border with Chile, which includes the highest point in the Americas.

Title: Arno River
The Arno is a river in the Tuscany region of Italy. It is the most important river of central Italy after the Tiber. The river famously flows through the city of Florence, passing under the iconic Ponte Vecchio bridge, and has historically fueled the commerce of the region.

Title: Two Unshared Nobel Prizes
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, but winning two is extraordinarily rare. Winning two unshared Nobel Prizes is an accomplishment held by only one person in history. This renowned American chemist won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his anti-nuclear activism.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, flowing directly through the heart of London past iconic landmarks like the Houses of Parliament and the Tower of London.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was highly anticipated, given the rapid advancements in theoretical physics during the early 20th century. The committee ultimately awarded the prize to Albert Einstein. The award was explicitly given "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect."

Title: Alien (film)
"Alien" is a 1979 science fiction horror film that follows the crew of the commercial space tug Nostromo. They encounter a deadly extraterrestrial lifeform set loose on the ship. The film famously features Sigourney Weaver in her breakout role as the resilient warrant officer, Ellen Ripley. It was directed by the visionary British filmmaker Ridley Scott.

Title: 1924 in the United Kingdom
The year 1924 in the United Kingdom saw the formation of the first Labour government under Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. It was a time of significant political shifting in the aftermath of World War I. Throughout this transitional year, the British Empire was ruled by King George V.

Title: Badshahi Mosque
The Badshahi Mosque is a Mughal-era congregational mosque in Lahore, capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab. It was commissioned by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1671. Known for its carved red sandstone with marble inlay, it remains one of the most iconic landmarks of the Mughal Empire in the region.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement. In a bizarre historical footnote, Picasso was actually brought in for questioning by police as a suspect during the infamous 1911 Louvre theft investigation.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: 1913 Model of the Atom
In 1913, a groundbreaking model of atomic structure was proposed, fundamentally altering the field of quantum physics. This model depicted the atom as a small, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons that travel in circular orbits around it. It successfully explained the Rydberg formula for the spectral emission lines of atomic hydrogen.

Title: Eighth Planet from the Sun
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. In the Solar System, it is the fourth-largest planet by diameter. It was named after the Roman god of the sea. Neptune is notable for being the only planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by empirical observation.

Title: Biltmore Estate
The Biltmore Estate is a historic house museum and tourist attraction in Asheville, North Carolina. Constructed between 1889 and 1895 for George Washington Vanderbilt II, it is the largest privately owned house in the United States. The massive French Renaissance chateau features 250 rooms and sprawling, meticulously landscaped gardens.

Title: Hernán Cortés
Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire and brought large portions of what is now mainland Mexico under the rule of the King of Castile in the early 16th century. He famously captured the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II.

Title: Statute of Westminster 1931
The Statute of Westminster 1931 was an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom that established the status of legislative independence for the self-governing Dominions of the British Empire. This historic statute granted full legislative sovereignty to several nations, including Canada, South Africa, and the United Kingdom's neighbor, the Irish Free State.

Title: Alexander Graham Bell
Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born inventor, scientist, and engineer who is credited with patenting the first practical telephone. Born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1847, his family later emigrated to Canada before he established his professional research career in Boston, Massachusetts.

Title: Group 12 element
Group 12 is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table. It includes zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), and the highly radioactive synthetic element copernicium (Cn). Elements in this group generally have lower melting and boiling points than other transition metals.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: Gloucestershire
Gloucestershire is a county in South West England. The county comprises part of the Cotswold Hills, part of the flat fertile valley of the River Severn, and the entire Forest of Dean. Its county town is the city of Gloucester, and it includes other major settlements like Cheltenham and Stroud.

Title: City of Oxford
Oxford is a city in England and the county town of Oxfordshire. It boasts a diverse economic base, heavily centered around its world-renowned university and publishing industries. The city is famous for its "dreaming spires" architecture. Geographically, it is located along the upper reaches of the River Thames, which flows through the city center.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He played a critical role in the events that led to the demise of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Roman Empire. He famously intervened in the internal politics of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, forming an alliance with Cleopatra VII.

Title: Captain James Cook
James Cook was a British explorer, navigator, cartographer, and captain in the Royal Navy. He made detailed maps of Newfoundland prior to making three voyages to the Pacific Ocean, during which he achieved the first recorded European contact with the eastern coastline of Australia and the Hawaiian Islands.

Title: Theresa May
Theresa Mary May is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2016 to 2019. Following the resignation of David Cameron after the Brexit referendum, she became the second female to hold the office of Prime Minister. She stepped down in 2019 and was succeeded by Boris Johnson.

Title: Zanzibar
Zanzibar is an insular semi-autonomous province which united with Tanganyika in 1964 to form a new sovereign republic. It comprises the Zanzibar Archipelago in the Indian Ocean. Historically a major trading hub, the island is renowned for its spices and as the birthplace of a legendary 20th-century rock frontman.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: Roentgenium
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is a highly radioactive metal named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. On the periodic table, it is a d-block transactinide element located in Group 11.

Title: Alexander the Great
Alexander III of Macedon, commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon. He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through Asia and northeast Africa. He created one of the largest empires in history before dying at the age of 32 in Babylon.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Since the 17th century, Paris has been one of Europe's major centers of finance, diplomacy, commerce, fashion, science, and arts. The city's geography and historical development are intimately tied to the River Seine, which flows directly through the center of the metropolis.

Title: The "Hand of God" Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who scored it later described the goal as being made "a little with the head... and a little with the hand of God."

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a Canadian filmmaker known for his massive box office successes. He directed the science fiction action film "Aliens" as well as the revolutionary blockbusters "Terminator 2: Judgment Day", "Titanic", and "Avatar". He frequently pushes the boundaries of cinematic visual effects.

Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. After his forces deserted him, the deposed king fled to France, where he was welcomed by his cousin Louis XIV.

Title: China
China, officially the People's Republic of China, is a massive country in East Asia. It spans five geographical time zones and borders fourteen countries. The country has a rich cultural heritage and a diverse array of wildlife, notably featuring the Giant Panda, which serves as its beloved national symbol and endemic treasure.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element, earning them global acclaim and Nobel Prizes.

Title: Gabriel García Márquez
Gabriel García Márquez was a legendary novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. Affectionately known as "Gabo," he won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was born in the small town of Aracataca, located in the northern region of Colombia.

Title: 1926 in the United States
The year 1926 was situated right in the middle of the Roaring Twenties. The United States was experiencing massive economic growth, the rapid expansion of jazz culture, and the continued enforcement of Prohibition. During this prosperous era, the White House was occupied by a famously quiet Republican leader.

Title: Frankenstein
"Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus" is an 1818 novel written by an English author. It tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature in an unorthodox scientific experiment. It is often considered one of the first true works of science fiction.

Title: Johanna van Gogh-Bonger
Johanna van Gogh-Bonger was a Dutch editor and translator. She was married to a prominent Parisian art dealer, and after both her husband and her famous brother-in-law died, she inherited a massive collection of unsold paintings. Johanna tirelessly promoted her brother-in-law's artwork, successfully securing his posthumous global fame.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a massive conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital. It raged for several days in the year 1666, destroying thousands of homes and historical structures. The disaster ultimately led to massive reconstruction efforts and modernized fire safety codes.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A former five-star general during World War II, he managed the early years of the Space Race and the Cold War. He was the sitting US President in 1955.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized paintings in the history of Western culture.

Title: John Williams
John Towner Williams is an American composer, conductor, and pianist. In a career spanning seven decades, he has composed some of the most popular, recognizable, and critically acclaimed film scores in cinematic history, including the "Imperial March". He is highly noted for his long-standing, prolific collaboration with film director Steven Spielberg.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Fordham University
Fordham University is a private Jesuit research university located in New York City. Established in 1841, it is the oldest Catholic institution of higher education in the northeastern United States. Its primary, historic Rose Hill campus is situated entirely within the borough of The Bronx.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. It serves as the seat of all three branches of the Government of India.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in the exact same Catalan town where he was born.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
"The Catcher in the Rye" is a novel published in 1951. It follows the experiences of Holden Caulfield, a teenager who leaves his elite prep school and wanders the streets of New York City. The novel explores themes of angst, alienation, and superficiality in society.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Qing Dynasty
The Qing Dynasty was the last orthodox dynasty in Chinese history. It was established in 1636 and ruled China proper from 1644 to 1912. During the 19th century, the dynasty faced immense internal rebellion and external pressures from Western imperial powers, ultimately leading to its collapse.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod, a close friend of the author, ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Silver
Silver is a metallic chemical element that exhibits the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and reflectivity of any metal. It has long been valued as a precious metal and is commonly used in currency, jewelry, and sporting trophies. Its official chemical symbol on the periodic table is Ag.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: Guernica (Picasso)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned Spanish artist. It is one of his best-known works, regarded by many art critics as the most moving and powerful anti-war painting in history. The mural-sized artwork portrays the suffering wrought by violence and chaos, depicting the bombing of a Basque town.

Title: Seventh Planet from the Sun
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Its name is a reference to the Greek god of the sky. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. The ice giant was officially discovered in 1781 by astronomer William Herschel, making it the first planet discovered with a telescope.

Title: Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east. It features warm tropical waters and numerous island chains, including the historic archipelago of Zanzibar.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It has been a major global hub for literature, science, and technology. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Edison Machine Works
The Edison Machine Works was a manufacturing company set up in 1881 to produce dynamos, large electric motors, and other components of the electrical illumination system. The factory was situated in New York City. The business was founded and closely managed by the legendary American inventor Thomas Edison.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: United States Capitals
The political capital of the United States has shifted several times throughout its early history. Today, the capital of the United States is Washington, D.C., a federal district created specifically to house the national government. It is entirely separate from any state jurisdiction.

Title: Bill Gates
Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist. In 1975, while attending Harvard University, he dropped out to form a new company with his childhood friend Paul Allen. Together, they developed Altair BASIC, launching a venture that would eventually become the software giant Microsoft.

Title: United States
The United States is a massive transcontinental country spanning North America, with additional territories in the Pacific and Caribbean. The nation boasts highly diverse geography, ranging from vast central plains to rugged mountain ranges. The country's highest physical point is the towering peak of Denali, located in the state of Alaska.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought in June 1815 near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. It was a decisive clash that ended the prolonged era of European wars sparked by the French Revolution. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for Napoleon Bonaparte, permanently ending his rule as Emperor of the French.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is a silvery white metal that resists corrosion in dry air. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.

Title: Pico da Neblina
Pico da Neblina is the highest peak in Brazil, standing at 2,995.3 metres (9,827 ft) above sea level. It is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border. The mountain is heavily shrouded in clouds for most of the year, giving it its name.

Title: King John of England
John, often called John Lackland, was King of England from 1199 until his death in 1216. His reign was marked by severe conflicts with his barons, leading to the forced signing of the Magna Carta. When he died of dysentery, he was immediately succeeded on the English throne by his young son, Henry III.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, widely known for his contributions to evolutionary biology. His 1859 book "On the Origin of Species" introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over generations through natural selection.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were relocated on financial grounds following the disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius.

Title: Pitchblende
Pitchblende, now formally known as uraninite, is a radioactive, uranium-rich mineral and ore. It was heavily studied in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Parisian scientists looking to isolate the sources of its intense radioactive emissions. It famously yielded trace amounts of several newly discovered elements.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: The Planets
"The Planets", Op. 32, is a seven-movement orchestral suite by a prominent English composer, written between 1914 and 1917. Each movement of the suite is named after a planet of the Solar System and its corresponding astrological character, such as "Mars, the Bringer of War."

Title: 1749 in Great Britain
The year 1749 in Great Britain saw the end of the War of the Austrian Succession and the subsequent signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. It was also the birth year of several notable figures, including the scientist who would eventually conquer smallpox. During this time, the British throne was occupied by a monarch of the House of Hanover.

Title: AC/DC
AC/DC is an iconic rock band formed in Sydney, Australia, in 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young. Their music is commonly classified as hard rock or blues rock. They underwent a major line-up transition in 1980 following the sudden death of their original frontman, which led them to recruit a new vocal lead.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they rank among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed, pushing the boundaries of what a solo violin could achieve.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho. Discovered in 1878 by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, it belongs to the lanthanide series. Cleve named the element after Holmia, the Latin name for his native city of Stockholm, to honor the Swedish capital.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Brandenburg Concertos. Bach was born in 1685 in the town of Eisenach, located in the central region of Germany.
