Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Despite his immense fame, he famously lost the battle for power grid supremacy. He eventually died in his home state of New Jersey in 1931.

Title: Cuba
Cuba is an island country located in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Atlantic Ocean meet. It was heavily colonized by European powers in the 16th century and remained under the rule of Spain until the end of the Spanish-American War in 1898.

Title: Bern
Bern, or Berne, is the de facto capital of Switzerland, referred to by the Swiss as their "federal city". With a population of about 144,000, Bern is the fifth-most populous city in Switzerland. The medieval city center of Bern was recognized by UNESCO as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 1983.

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: Karl Marx
Karl Marx was a German-born philosopher, economist, political theorist, historian, and revolutionary. He is best known for his 1848 pamphlet "The Communist Manifesto" and the multi-volume "Das Kapital". After spending his later years in exile in London, he passed away in 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: The Great Gatsby
The Great Gatsby is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a strong contender for the title of the Great American Novel.

Title: Double Nobel Laureates
Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, securing one in Physics and another in Chemistry. John Bardeen uniquely won two Nobel Prizes in Physics for his work on the transistor and superconductivity. Frederick Sanger won two in Chemistry for his work on protein sequencing.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. The brilliant author behind "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial" was born in 1883 in the city of Prague to a middle-class Jewish family.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, passing through or touching the borders of 10 countries. It serves as a vital waterway for cities like Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegorical novella "Animal Farm" and his dystopian masterpiece "1984". Orwell suffered from chronic tuberculosis and passed away in a London hospital in January 1950.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in the exact same Catalan town where he was born.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest physicists of all time. He is best known for developing the theory of relativity. While his work built upon the foundation laid by classical mechanics, he never attended an English university for his formal scientific training.

Title: Spain
Spain is a country in Southwestern Europe with some pockets of territory across the Strait of Gibraltar. It has a deeply rich artistic heritage, having produced masters like Velázquez, Goya, and Picasso. Culturally and politically unified, the official and most widely spoken language of the nation is Spanish.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: WorldWideWeb (browser)
WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion between the software and the World Wide Web itself, was the first web browser and editor. It was written by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990 while working at CERN. It was relatively obscure compared to later graphical browsers that brought the internet to the masses.

Title: The Old Man and the Sea
The Old Man and the Sea is a short novel written by the American author Ernest Hemingway. It tells the story of an aging Cuban fisherman who struggles with a giant marlin far out in the Gulf Stream. The acclaimed novella was officially published in 1952 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction the following year.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System. It consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock, with a surface heavily scarred by craters and canyons. This massive moon was discovered by the famous astronomer William Herschel in 1787.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Despite its distinct cultural and linguistic heritage with Italian roots, Corsica is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by the modern nation of France.

Title: 1961 in the United States
The year 1961 saw major shifts in American politics and foreign policy. The country faced the failed Bay of Pigs invasion and the escalating tensions of the Cold War. During this year, President John F. Kennedy famously committed the nation to the ambitious goal of landing a man on the Moon.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north, Pennsylvania to the east, West Virginia to the southeast, Kentucky to the southwest, Indiana to the west, and Michigan to the northwest. The state's capital and largest city is Columbus.

Title: Cassius Marcellus Clay (abolitionist)
Cassius Marcellus Clay was a prominent 19th-century American planter and politician from Kentucky who became a fierce abolitionist. He published an anti-slavery newspaper and helped found the Republican Party in his state. His legacy was honored when a descendant named his son after him, a boy who would grow up to be a legendary heavyweight boxer.

Title: Sistine Chapel
The Sistine Chapel is a chapel in the Apostolic Palace, the official residence of the Catholic Church's leadership. It is famous for its Renaissance frescoes, most notably the breathtaking ceiling painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512. The chapel is located entirely within the borders of Vatican City.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They achieved legendary status in the 1960s by dominating the NFL. During their historic victory in Super Bowl I, the team was led by their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Element 101
Atomic number 101 belongs to a synthetic element in the actinide series of the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive metallic element. It was deliberately named in honor of the legendary Russian chemist who created the first definitive periodic table.

Title: Angel Falls
Angel Falls is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall. The waterfall drops over the edge of the Auyán-tepui mountain in the Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site located in the Gran Sabana region of Bolívar State. Geographically, this towering natural wonder is located on the continent of South America.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: U2
U2 is an Irish rock band formed in Dublin in 1976. The group consists of a prominent lead vocalist known for his expressive vocal style, alongside The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. The band's early sound was rooted in post-punk but eventually grew to incorporate influences from many genres of popular music.

Title: 2004 in Politics
The year 2004 was a period of intense global political activity and ongoing military conflicts in the Middle East. In the United States, it was an election year marked by debates over national security and economic policy. The incumbent president managed to secure a second term after a highly contested race.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: First Woman in Space
The race to put the first woman in space was intensely competitive during the Cold War. The Soviet Union achieved this milestone in 1963 when they selected a former textile worker and amateur skydiver from the civilian population to pilot a solo orbital mission, beating the United States by exactly two decades.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a 2,430-meter mountain ridge. It is the most familiar icon of the Inca Empire. Built in classical Inca style with polished dry-stone walls, it was mysteriously abandoned around the time of the Spanish Conquest.

Title: Los Angeles
Los Angeles is the largest city in California and the second-most populous city in the United States. It is a massive global center for entertainment, media, and technology. Although it has a robust biomedical sector, its research institutes are distinct from the coastal scientific hubs found further south.

Title: Cloning of Dolly
The scientific world was fundamentally altered by a major breakthrough at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Using the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer, researchers successfully cloned a female domestic sheep from an adult somatic cell. This historic mammal, affectionately named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996.

Title: Discovery of DNA Structure
The double-helix structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was identified in 1953, revolutionizing the field of molecular biology. This monumental breakthrough took place at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge. The discovery was famously made by an American biologist and his English colleague.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a rare and highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while they were investigating the cause of pitchblende's intense radioactivity. Marie Curie deliberately named the element after her home country of Poland. It holds the atomic number 84.

Title: Fungi
A fungus is any member of the group of eukaryotic organisms that includes microorganisms such as yeasts and molds, as well as the more familiar mushrooms. These organisms are classified as a biological kingdom, separate from the other eukaryotic life kingdoms of plants and animals. They play a crucial role in decomposing organic matter.

Title: Spree River
The Spree is a major river in eastern Germany. It flows through the states of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Berlin. It is approximately 400 kilometers long and is a tributary of the River Havel. It famously flows through the historic center of the German capital.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Principal Cordillera of the Andes mountain range, in Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters (22,837 ft), it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The novel explores themes of mass surveillance, totalitarianism, and the repressive regimentation of persons and behaviors.

Title: Polio vaccine
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis (polio). Two major types are used worldwide: an inactivated poliovirus given by injection, and a weakened poliovirus given by mouth. The first successful inactivated version revolutionized global health by severely curtailing the devastating mid-century outbreaks of the disease.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting depicting a swirling night sky over a quiet village. Painted in June 1889 during the artist's stay at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, it is considered one of the most recognized masterpieces of post-impressionist art.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is globally famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. Nobel was born in 1833 in Stockholm, the capital city of Sweden.

Title: Greece National Football Team
The Greece national football team shocked the world in 2004 by winning the UEFA European Championship. Hosted in Portugal, the tournament saw the underdog Greek squad defeat the host nation in the final match, securing a historic and unexpected victory.

Title: Japan
Japan is an island country in East Asia. It is situated in the northwest Pacific Ocean, and is bordered on the west by the Sea of Japan. The nation has a deeply rich cultural and political history, transitioning from feudalism to a modern industrialized powerhouse during the late 19th century.

Title: Glorious Revolution
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was the deposition and replacement of James II and VII as ruler of England, Scotland and Ireland by his daughter Mary II and his Dutch nephew and Mary's husband, William III of Orange. After his forces deserted him, the deposed king fled to France, where he was welcomed by his cousin Louis XIV.

Title: Yekaterinburg
Yekaterinburg is the fourth-largest city in Russia and the administrative center of Sverdlovsk Oblast. Historically significant as the site where the Romanov family met their end, the city is situated in the middle of the Ural Mountains, serving as a gateway between Europe and Asia.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known of his works and represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel published in 1949. The story follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in Oceania. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme, dictatorial leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the modern Czech Republic. Situated on the Vltava river, the city has a rich history spanning over a millennium. In the late 19th century, specifically the 1880s, Prague was a major provincial capital within the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The element was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Edison Machine Works
The Edison Machine Works was a manufacturing company set up in 1881 to produce dynamos, large electric motors, and other components of the electrical illumination system. The factory was situated in New York City. The business was founded and closely managed by the legendary American inventor Thomas Edison.

Title: Rhine River
The Rhine is one of the major European rivers, flowing from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea coast in the Netherlands. It serves as a vital navigable waterway and forms part of the borders between Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, France, and Germany.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books, including "Brave New World". In his later years, he relocated to Los Angeles, California, where he spent his final days. Huxley died of laryngeal cancer on November 22, 1963, a date that tragically caused his passing to be overshadowed in the media by a major national event.

Title: Golden State Warriors
The Golden State Warriors are an American professional basketball team based in San Francisco, California. They compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the league's Western Conference. The franchise has enjoyed a highly successful modern era, winning multiple championships under head coach Steve Kerr.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, serving an unprecedented four terms in office.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It played a critical role in the Allied victory during World War II, fueled by technological innovations like radar and early computing. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. The country has a rich tradition in chemistry and scientific innovation. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm, a major cultural and economic hub.

Title: 1911 Museum Theft
In August 1911, the global art community was shocked by a brazen robbery at the Louvre museum in Paris. Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman, hid in a broom closet and successfully smuggled out a world-famous portrait under his coat. The sensational theft of the Mona Lisa launched the painting into unprecedented international stardom.

Title: West Bengal
West Bengal is a state in the eastern region of India along the Bay of Bengal. It borders Bangladesh in the east, and Nepal and Bhutan in the north. While it served as a major center for British colonial administration, it neighbors the specific state where the author of "1984" was born.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He died in Oslo, Norway, in 1944.

Title: 2012 Summer Olympics
The 2012 Summer Olympics were a major international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. It was the third time that the British capital had hosted the modern Olympic Games. The event followed the massive spectacle previously hosted by an East Asian nation four years prior.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. After proposing an information management system in 1989, he successfully implemented the first communication between an HTTP client and server via the internet. He was born in 1955 in London, United Kingdom.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. Geographically, the city is situated along the banks of the Yamuna River, which has historically sustained its populace.

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
One Hundred Years of Solitude is a landmark 1967 novel that chronicles the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch founded the fictitious town of Macondo. It is widely considered the quintessential work of magic realism and was authored by Gabriel García Márquez.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. In just over a decade, he created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". He struggled with severe mental illness and relied heavily on the financial and emotional support of his younger brother.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. The continent is home to diverse geographies, including the Andes mountains and the Amazon rainforest. The largest country on this continent is Brazil.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.

Title: Auguste Rodin
François Auguste René Rodin was a French sculptor generally considered the founder of modern sculpture. He possessed a unique ability to model a complex, turbulent, and deeply pocketed surface in clay. His most globally recognized masterpiece, "The Thinker", was famously cast in bronze in the early 20th century.

Title: Michigan
Michigan is a state in the Great Lakes region of the upper Midwestern United States. It is the only state to consist of two peninsulas, the Lower Peninsula and the Upper Peninsula. While its largest and most economically significant city is Detroit, the political center and state capital is Lansing.

Title: Francisco Pizarro
Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that conquered the massive Inca Empire. He captured and killed the reigning Inca emperor, claimed the lands for Spain, and founded the city of Lima in 1535. His conquests brought vast wealth to the Spanish crown.

Title: Worcestershire
Worcestershire is a county in the West Midlands of England. It is known for its rolling hills, agricultural produce, and as the birthplace of the renowned composer Edward Elgar. The county town is the cathedral city of Worcester.

Title: Discovery of Hydrogen
While artificially produced earlier by others, hydrogen was first recognized as a distinct chemical element in 1766. The English scientist Henry Cavendish was the first to identify hydrogen gas as a discrete substance, naming it "inflammable air" and noting that it produced water when burned.

Title: Cleveland Cavaliers
The Cleveland Cavaliers, often referred to as the Cavs, are a professional basketball team based in Cleveland, Ohio. They compete in the NBA as a member of the Eastern Conference Central Division. The franchise secured its first and only NBA Championship by overcoming a historic deficit to beat the Warriors.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named after the recently discovered planet Uranus, and its standard chemical symbol is U.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the capital and largest city of Sweden, built across 14 islands. It was the proud host city of the 1912 Summer Olympics. In classical literature and scientific naming conventions, the city is frequently referred to by its Latinized name, Holmia.

Title: San Francisco Politics
San Francisco has a unique consolidated city-county government structure. The city has long been a stronghold for the Democratic Party and has produced numerous high-profile national politicians. Its mayoral office wields significant executive power in directing local municipal initiatives and urban planning.

Title: 2006 FIFA World Cup
The 2006 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Germany and was the 18th edition of the tournament. The championship was secured by Italy, who defeated France 5–3 in a penalty shoot-out following a 1–1 draw after extra time.

Title: First Practical Telephone
The invention of the first practical telephone was a watershed moment in human engineering, transforming global communication forever. The device was successfully patented in the United States in March 1876. The inventor, who spent much of his adult life working in America, was born and educated in Edinburgh, Scotland.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL. The team is legendary for its mid-20th-century dominance, securing victory in the very first Super Bowl under the fierce leadership of their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, a city located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed country with a mixed-market economy. It is rich in natural resources, heavily exporting minerals and agricultural products. The nation's financial systems are closely tied to the Asia-Pacific region, and its official currency is the Australian dollar.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California. It designs, manufactures, and sells consumer electronics, computer software, and online services. The company was founded by a college dropout who envisioned a user-friendly personal computer, launching a trillion-dollar empire.

Title: Krakow
Krakow is the second-largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland. Situated in the Lesser Poland region, the city dates back to the 7th century and was the official capital of Poland until 1596.

Title: Cincinnati
Cincinnati is a major city in the United States, situated on the north bank of the Ohio River. It is known for its historic architecture, vibrant arts scene, and major professional sports teams. It is a major economic hub within the state of Ohio.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. He flew various experimental aircraft, including the X-15, but survived his perilous test flights.

Title: Soviet Union Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until its dissolution in 1991. The program was responsible for many "firsts" in spaceflight, including the launch of the first artificial Earth satellite, Sputnik 1, and the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a country primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive economy, diverse culture, and profound influence on global sports, serving as the birthplace of modern baseball and the location where basketball was first played. Its capital city is Washington, D.C.

Title: Hernán Cortés
Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire and brought large portions of what is now mainland Mexico under the rule of the King of Castile in the early 16th century. He famously captured the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. As Vice President, he was thrust into the presidency on November 22, 1963, following the tragic assassination of John F. Kennedy in Dallas. He became the commander-in-chief on the exact day that author Aldous Huxley passed away.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a novella written in 1912 and published in 1915. It tells the story of a salesman named Gregor Samsa who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The work is widely considered a masterpiece of 20th-century literature and was written by Franz Kafka.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major global center for art and culture for centuries. The capital city is Paris, which frequently hosted the premieres of major international theatrical and musical works during the Belle Époque.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: James Watson
James Dewey Watson is an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist. He co-authored the 1953 academic paper proposing the double helix structure of the DNA molecule. Watson was born in Chicago, Illinois, and traveled to England specifically to work at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its industrial history and for being the birthplace of aviation pioneers and numerous astronauts. The political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Columbus.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Inca Empire
The Inca Empire was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Its political and administrative structure is considered by most scholars to have been the most developed in the Americas prior to Columbus' arrival. The civilization built massive engineering projects, including Machu Picchu, before its leadership was captured and dismantled by Spanish invaders.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. He is celebrated as one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in Figueres, the exact same town where he was born.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose work had a far-reaching influence on 20th-century art. He is the brilliant artist behind "The Starry Night" and "Sunflowers". He was born in Groot Zundert, Netherlands, in the year 1853.

Title: The Stranger
"The Stranger" is a 1942 novella authored by French philosopher and writer Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus' philosophy of the absurd and existentialism. The novel begins with the iconic lines concerning the death of the protagonist's mother.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel opera in two acts, composed in 1791. It was written by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart shortly before his untimely death. The famous opera premiered in Vienna and was celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico and to the east by the Atlantic Ocean. While cities like Miami and Orlando draw millions of tourists, the political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Tallahassee.

Title: Canada
Canada is a country in North America. Its ten provinces and three territories extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific and northward into the Arctic Ocean, covering over 9.98 million square kilometers. Its capital is Ottawa, and its three largest metropolitan areas are Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage in 1831. The expedition famously carried the young English naturalist Charles Darwin, allowing him to conduct crucial field research in the Galápagos Islands.

Title: Richard the Lionheart
Richard I, also known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 until his death in 1199. He was a central Christian commander during the Third Crusade. He was the predecessor and older brother of King John, dying without legitimate heirs.

Title: Atlanta
Atlanta is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Georgia. It played a major part in both the Civil War and the 1960s Civil Rights Movement. The city gained massive international attention and infrastructure upgrades when it was selected to host the 1996 Summer Olympics.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It has a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary democracy. The nation's official currency is the Pound Sterling, which is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Albany
Albany is the capital of the U.S. state of New York, located along the west bank of the Hudson River. It is known for its rich architecture and historic role in commerce and state politics. Many people mistakenly assume the state's most populous city serves as its capital.

Title: 14-bis
The 14-bis, also known as Oiseau de proie (French for "bird of prey"), was a pioneer era canard biplane designed and built by an early aviation pioneer. In 1906, near Paris, it performed the first officially witnessed unaided takeoff and flight by a heavier-than-air aircraft. It was a major milestone for European aviation.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. He created the inactivated polio vaccine, which was declared safe and effective in 1955. Years later, he leveraged his fame and public support to establish the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.

Title: Ridley Scott
Sir Ridley Scott is an English film director and producer. He is renowned for his atmospheric, highly concentrated visual style. After establishing his career with commercials, he found global fame directing the sci-fi classics "Alien" and "Blade Runner". He is the older brother of fellow Hollywood director Tony Scott.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: Wars of the Roses
The Wars of the Roses were a series of English civil wars for control of the throne of England fought between supporters of two rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet: the House of Lancaster and the House of York. The grueling conflict dominated the latter half of the 15th century.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in Stockholm, Sweden, between 5 May and 22 July 1912. These games were notably well-organized and were the first to feature the use of electronic timing devices and the first to include art competitions.

Title: Jurassic Park
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. Set on the fictional island of Isla Nublar, it features a wildlife park of cloned dinosaurs that break free. It was the highest-grossing film of the 1990s until it was surpassed by another massive blockbuster four years later.

Title: Nicholas II of Russia
Nicholas II was the last Emperor of Russia, King of Congress Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland, ruling from 1894 until his abdication in 1917. Following the revolution, he and his immediate family were imprisoned and subsequently executed by Bolshevik revolutionaries in July 1918 in the city of Yekaterinburg.

Title: The Scream
The Scream is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It has been the target of several high-profile art thefts, most notably when a version was stolen from the National Gallery in Oslo in 1994.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was hosted by Mexico. The tournament was defined by the phenomenal performance of the team captain who scored the "Hand of God" goal, leading his nation to a 3-2 victory over West Germany in the final.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Bruce Sabin was a prominent medical researcher who developed the live-virus oral polio vaccine, which played a foundational role in nearly eradicating the disease worldwide. Sabin was born in August 1906 to a Jewish family in the city of Białystok, which was then part of the Russian Empire but is situated in modern-day Poland.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians such as Beethoven and Mozart spent their prime years working there. The city center features the towering Gothic spire of St. Stephen's Cathedral.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He wrote some of the most popular concert and theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker", and the "1812 Overture". Tchaikovsky was born in May 1840 in Votkinsk, an industrial town in Russia.

Title: Uffizi Gallery
The Uffizi Gallery is a prominent art museum located adjacent to the Piazza della Signoria in the Historic Centre of Florence in the region of Tuscany, Italy. One of the most important Italian museums and the most visited, it holds a superb collection of priceless artworks, particularly from the period of the Italian Renaissance.

Title: 1958 FIFA World Cup
The 1958 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Sweden, marked the arrival of a 17-year-old prodigy named Pelé. His incredible performance helped Brazil secure their first-ever World Cup trophy, defeating the host nation in a thrilling final match.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Rhenium
Rhenium is a chemical element with the symbol Re and atomic number 75. It is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. Discovered in 1925, it was the last stable element to be discovered. It was named after the river Rhine in Europe.

Title: Tallest Building in the World
The title of the tallest building in the world has changed hands numerous times over the centuries. Currently, the record is held by a massive megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Standing at a staggering total height of 829.8 meters (2,722 ft), it has held the title since its topping out in 2009.

Title: Mosaic Web Browser
NCSA Mosaic is one of the first widely available graphical web browsers. It was instrumental in popularizing the World Wide Web and the general Internet by integrating multimedia such as text and graphics. It was created in 1993 at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications by a team of programmers led by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina.

Title: Currency of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland maintains a highly developed, independent market economy. Unlike many of its European neighbors, it never adopted the Euro. The official currency of the United Kingdom and its primary territories is the Pound sterling.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Atahualpa
Atahualpa was the last reigning emperor of the Inca Empire prior to the Spanish conquest. After winning a brutal civil war against his half-brother, he was almost immediately confronted by the arrival of the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro. Pizarro famously captured Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, eventually executing him.

Title: Arthur Ashe Stadium
Arthur Ashe Stadium is a tennis stadium at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park in Queens, New York City. Part of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, it is the main stadium of the US Open and is the largest tennis stadium in the world by capacity.

Title: Friendship 7
Friendship 7 was the spacecraft piloted by astronaut John Glenn in February 1962. Part of the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, the flight made Glenn the very first American to successfully orbit the Earth, catching the U.S. up to the achievements of the Soviet Union.

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: Theo van Gogh
Theodorus "Theo" van Gogh was a Dutch art dealer. He is best known as the younger brother of a deeply troubled, brilliant painter whom he supported financially and emotionally throughout his life. Theo's unwavering support allowed his brother to focus entirely on painting, though Theo tragically outlived him by only six months.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor and oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the use of atomic weapons.

Title: Shanghai Tower
The Shanghai Tower is a 128-story, 632-meter-tall megatall skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest building in the world. Designed by the architectural firm Gensler, it features a twisting, asymmetrical form intended to reduce wind loads.

Title: Discovery of Comets
During the late 18th century, detailed telescopic observation led to the discovery of numerous celestial bodies. The brilliant astronomer who famously discovered Comet C/1786 P1 in August 1786 shattered boundaries in science. She was the first woman to receive a salary as a scientist and successfully catalogued numerous nebulae and comets.

Title: Guillotine Executions in Paris
The guillotine became the primary method of execution in France during the Reign of Terror. Placed in the Place de la Révolution, it claimed the lives of aristocrats, politicians, and commoners alike. The most famous victim was the deposed king, Louis XVI, whose execution took place there in 1793.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team based in Kansas City, Missouri. The franchise was founded in 1959 as the Dallas Texans by businessman Lamar Hunt. The team famously competed in the very first Super Bowl, though they were defeated by their Midwestern rivals.

Title: Alexandria
Alexandria was a magnificent Mediterranean port city in ancient Egypt founded by Alexander the Great. During the Hellenistic period, it served as the bustling capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. It was renowned globally for its massive Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its Great Library.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 according to the will of Alfred Nobel. While a German physicist took the physics prize, the 1901 Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to a French poet and essayist. The choice was somewhat controversial, as many literary critics believed Leo Tolstoy should have won the inaugural award instead.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Shelley was an English novelist, essayist, and biographer who is best known for her seminal Gothic novel "Frankenstein". The daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, she was immersed in intellectual circles from an early age. Shelley was born in London in 1797.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. The country's political and administrative center is its capital city, Wellington, located at the south-western tip of the North Island.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. Plutonium was first synthetically produced and isolated in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: The House of the Spirits
"The House of the Spirits" is the 1982 debut novel of a prominent South American author. The novel incorporates elements of magic realism to trace the lives of the Trueba family across four generations. It became an immediate international best-seller and was later adapted into a major motion picture.

Title: First Moon Landing
The Apollo 11 mission achieved the historic goal of landing humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent several hours exploring the lunar surface before safely returning to Earth, ending the Space Race.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, which was built as a planned city inland from the coast.

Title: Roentgenium
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is a highly radioactive metal named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. On the periodic table, it is a d-block transactinide element located in Group 11.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time, redefining pop culture before their eventual breakup in 1970.

Title: Ramsay MacDonald
James Ramsay MacDonald was a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. He was a founder of the Labour Party and led governments during periods of severe economic crisis. He was serving as Prime Minister in December 1931 when the British Parliament passed the landmark Statute of Westminster.

Title: Pavel Nedvěd
Pavel Nedvěd is a retired professional footballer who played as a midfielder. Described as one of the best footballers of his generation, he won the Ballon d'Or in 2003. He was born in Cheb, a city situated in the Czech Republic, where he began his youth career before dominating Italian football.

Title: Hershey, Pennsylvania
Hershey is an unincorporated community in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. Often referred to as "Chocolatetown, USA," it is the home of The Hershey Company. The town was founded in 1903 by Milton S. Hershey to provide housing and amenities for the workers of his massive chocolate factory.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. In 1911, he proposed his own model of the atom after the famous gold foil experiment, which proved that the atom has a tiny, dense nucleus. He was a mentor to many pioneering physicists of the 20th century.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland commissioned the historic voyages of the HMS Beagle. The nation has maintained a strictly independent monetary policy throughout its history, utilizing the Pound sterling as its official currency.

Title: France–United States relations
Relations between France and the United States stretch back to the American Revolutionary War, when the French provided crucial military and financial support. This historic alliance was famously memorialized in the late 19th century when France presented the American government with a massive copper monument representing freedom and democracy.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Upon stepping onto the lunar surface, the commander famously broadcast the words, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

Title: 1856 in Great Britain
The year 1856 in Great Britain was marked by the end of the Crimean War with the signing of the Treaty of Paris. The country was undergoing rapid industrialization and scientific advancement during this period. The nation and its growing empire were under the steady rule of Queen Victoria.

Title: Spirited Away
"Spirited Away" is a 2001 animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It tells the story of Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who wanders into the world of kami while moving to a new neighborhood. It was incredibly successful, winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Title: Chicago
Chicago is the most populous city in the U.S. state of Illinois and the third-most populous in the United States. Located on the shores of Lake Michigan, it was incorporated as a city in 1837. It is highly regarded for its architecture and cultural institutions, serving as home to a massive art museum in Grant Park.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". Stoker was born in Dublin, Ireland. He suffered from unknown illnesses as a child that left him bedridden until the age of seven, but he later died of strokes in London.

Title: Inheritance of Acquired Characteristics
The inheritance of acquired characteristics is a proto-evolutionary hypothesis that argued that physiological changes acquired by an organism during its lifetime could be passed down to its offspring. This concept was heavily championed by an early French naturalist but was later largely discredited by modern genetics.

Title: Yangtze
The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia, the third-longest in the world, and the longest in the world to flow entirely within one country. It rises in the northern part of the Tibetan Plateau and flows 6,300 kilometers in a generally easterly direction to the East China Sea. It empties into the sea near Shanghai, entirely within the borders of China.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: Armenia
Armenia is a landlocked country located in the Armenian Highlands of Western Asia. It is bordered by Turkey to the west, Georgia to the north, and Azerbaijan to the east. Historically a Soviet republic, the country's political, cultural, and economic center is its capital city, Yerevan.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: Social Media Pioneers
Around the same time video sharing became popular, social networking platforms began to dominate the digital landscape. Founded in 2004 by a group of college students, Facebook quickly expanded beyond university campuses to become the premier global social network, eventually acquiring photo-sharing tools like Instagram to consolidate its user base.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A five-star general during World War II, his presidency oversaw a period of post-war economic growth and early Cold War tensions, preceding the Kennedy administration.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, his work was heavily inspired by classical antiquity and had a profound influence on the development of Western art. His most famous paintings adorn the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the Bohr model of the atom. The synthetic element Bohrium, which carries the chemical symbol Bh, was named to honor his monumental legacy.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. To honor his vast contributions to science, the synthetic element Bohrium was named after him.

Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. These three laws of motion were first compiled and published in 1687 in the seminal work "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica." They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: 2004 UEFA Champions League Final
The 2004 UEFA Champions League Final was a football match played at the Arena AufSchalke in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, to decide the winner of the 2003-04 UEFA Champions League. The match was won by FC Porto, who defeated AS Monaco 3-0 to claim the prestigious European title.
