Title: Brooklyn Bridge
The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City. Opened in May 1883, it spans the East River, connecting the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn. It was the first steel-wire suspension bridge ever constructed and remains an iconic feature of the city's skyline.

Title: Eighth Planet from the Sun
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. In the Solar System, it is the fourth-largest planet by diameter. It was named after the Roman god of the sea. Neptune is notable for being the only planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by empirical observation.

Title: Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a 2,430-meter mountain ridge. It is the most familiar icon of the Inca Empire. Built in classical Inca style with polished dry-stone walls, it was mysteriously abandoned around the time of the Spanish Conquest.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor. Truman's administration oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the decision to use atomic weapons, and the early years of the Cold War.

Title: The Invincibles
In English football, the term "The Invincibles" is most famously used to refer to the Arsenal F.C. squad managed by Arsène Wenger. They earned this legendary nickname by completing an entire 38-game Premier League season without a single defeat. This historic, unbeaten campaign was completed in May 2004.

Title: Puerperal fever
Puerperal fever, also known as postpartum infections, are bacterial infections of the female reproductive tract following childbirth or miscarriage. Before the widespread understanding of germ theory and the adoption of handwashing by doctors in the late 19th century, it was a leading cause of maternal mortality, claiming the lives of many historical figures.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows past numerous historical and industrial landmarks, including the Houses of Parliament and the Battersea Power Station.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is most famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. The synthetic element Nobelium was later named in his honor.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. It remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate and investor. He was the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Apple. Jobs famously dropped out of Reed College in Oregon after only one semester, though he continued to audit classes. He went on to revolutionize the personal computing, music, and mobile phone industries.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster
The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster occurred on January 28, 1986. The spacecraft broke apart 73 seconds into its flight, tragically killing all seven crew members aboard. The disaster temporarily grounded the shuttle fleet and led to major structural changes at NASA.

Title: In Cold Blood
"In Cold Blood" is a non-fiction novel published in 1966. It details the 1959 murders of four members of the Clutter family in the small farming community of Holcomb, Kansas. The author spent years interviewing residents and investigators, accompanied by his close childhood friend, a famous female novelist.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: Cloning of Dolly
The scientific world was fundamentally altered by a major breakthrough at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Using the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer, researchers successfully cloned a female domestic sheep from an adult somatic cell. This historic mammal, affectionately named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996.

Title: George Frideric Handel
George Frideric Handel was a German-British Baroque composer well known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, and organ concertos. He was born in 1685, the same year as Bach, in the German city of Halle, but he spent the bulk of his career working in London.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. Despite its close economic ties with its neighbors, it is not a member of the European Union. The official currency of Norway is the Norwegian krone.

Title: Salzburg Cathedral
Salzburg Cathedral is the seventeenth-century Catholic cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Salzburg. Dedicated to Saint Rupert and Saint Vergilius, it is the very church where Mozart was baptized. After a previous structure burned down, the current magnificent building was erected entirely in the elaborate Baroque architectural style.

Title: Currency of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland maintains a highly developed, independent market economy. Unlike many of its European neighbors, it never adopted the Euro. The official currency of the United Kingdom and its primary territories is the Pound sterling.

Title: Toropets
Toropets is a historic town and the administrative center of Toropetsky District in Tver Oblast, Russia. It is located where the Toropa River flows through Lake Solomen. First mentioned in chronicles in 1074, it is one of the oldest settlements in the western part of the country, boasting numerous historic churches.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. It was a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom, heavily defined by strict moral standards.

Title: Mount Wilson Observatory
The Mount Wilson Observatory is an astronomical observatory located in the San Gabriel Mountains near Pasadena. It contains two historically significant telescopes: the 60-inch Hale telescope and the 100-inch Hooker telescope, the latter of which was used to discover the expansion of the universe. The facility is located in California.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist. The town also houses the famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where the artist is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. Geographically, the city is situated along the banks of the Yamuna River, which has historically sustained its populace.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 containing the results of the astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. It provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and contributed the first two laws of planetary motion, fundamentally altering the field of astrophysics.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist. For his monumental achievement in discovering the first broadly effective antibiotic substance, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a classical romantic ballet composed in 1875 by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Unlike avant-garde works of the 20th century, it is beloved for its traditional orchestral melodies and graceful choreography, representing the pinnacle of classical Russian ballet.

Title: The "Hand of God" Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who scored it later described the goal as being made "a little with the head... and a little with the hand of God."

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It played a critical role in the Allied victory during World War II, fueled by technological innovations like radar and early computing. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Andrew Adamson
Andrew Ralph Adamson is a film director, producer, and visual effects supervisor. He gained worldwide recognition for co-directing the incredibly successful animated films "Shrek" and "Shrek 2". Adamson was born in Auckland, New Zealand, before moving to the United States to pursue his career in visual effects.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they rank among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed, pushing the boundaries of what a solo violin could achieve.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine. It is part of the Carpathian Mountains and is situated in the Eastern Beskids region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist and a pioneer in crystallography and radioactivity. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife. He was born in Paris, France, and spent his entire career working in the city.

Title: Maine
Maine is the easternmost state in the New England region of the United States. It is known for its jagged, rocky coastline, densely forested interior, and picturesque waterways. The state's capital city is Augusta, though its largest municipality is Portland.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the cultural, media, political, and economic center of its nation. It is built across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea. It serves as the capital and largest city of Sweden, hosting the national government and the official residence of the Swedish monarch.

Title: Direct Current Systems
Direct current (DC) was the initial standard for power distribution, championed heavily by inventor Thomas Edison. Unlike AC systems, DC could not be easily stepped up to high voltages for long-distance transmission. This limitation sparked the famous War of the Currents in the late 19th century.

Title: The Descent of Man
"The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" is a book by English naturalist Charles Darwin, first published in 1871. It applies evolutionary theory to human evolution, and details his theory of sexual selection. It was published more than a decade after his initial, foundational work on evolution.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: Peter Jackson
Sir Peter Robert Jackson is a film director, producer, and screenwriter. He is best known as the director, writer, and producer of the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. For his work on the 2003 finale, "The Return of the King", he won three Academy Awards. Jackson was born in Pukerua Bay, a coastal town in New Zealand.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: Aurangzeb
Aurangzeb was the sixth emperor of the Mughal Empire, ruling over almost the entire Indian subcontinent for a period of 49 years. He officially ascended to the throne in 1658 after emerging victorious in a war of succession. By the time the year 1666 arrived, he was firmly in power and ruling over a vast domain.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows through several prominent educational towns, including Oxford, where it is known locally as the Isis, before making its way toward the North Sea.

Title: Votka River
The Votka is a river in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, and a right tributary of the Shiva River. It flows for roughly 66 kilometers through a rolling landscape before running directly through the center of the industrial town of Votkinsk, where an artificial dam was constructed to power the town's historic metal factories.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital of Russia for over two centuries before the government moved back to Moscow.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. It is a massive global center for arts, commerce, and music, serving as the birthplace for countless famous bands.

Title: Inca Empire
The Inca Empire was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America. Its political and administrative structure is considered by most scholars to have been the most developed in the Americas prior to Columbus' arrival. The civilization built massive engineering projects, including Machu Picchu, before its leadership was captured and dismantled by Spanish invaders.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: Multiple Nobel Laureates
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, and only a very small number of individuals have won multiple times. The very first person to ever win two Nobel Prizes, and the only one to win in two distinct scientific fields (Physics and Chemistry), was Marie Curie.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of Scotland from 1649 until 1651, and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London in 1666.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by Johann Sebastian Bach to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era.

Title: Hugh Carey
Hugh Carey was an American politician and attorney who served as the 51st governor of New York from 1975 to 1982. A member of the Democratic Party, he is often credited with saving New York City from the brink of bankruptcy in the 1970s. He was the presiding governor when his state hosted the 1980 Winter Olympics.

Title: Economy of France
France boasts a highly developed, social market economy that is among the largest in the world. As a founding member of the European Union, its economic policies are deeply integrated with its neighbors. The official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French franc in 2002.

Title: Thriller (album)
"Thriller" is the sixth studio album by an iconic American pop singer, released on November 29, 1982. It produced seven top-10 singles on the Billboard Hot 100, including "Billie Jean" and "Beat It". The record shattered industry expectations and remains the best-selling album of all time worldwide.

Title: Vince Lombardi
Vince Lombardi was an American football coach and executive in the NFL. He is best known as the head coach of the Green Bay Packers during the 1960s, leading them to five NFL Championships, including victories in the first two Super Bowls. In his younger years, Lombardi played college football as an offensive lineman for Fordham University.

Title: Maywood, Illinois
Maywood is a village in Proviso Township, Cook County, Illinois, United States. It was founded in 1869 and is located directly west of Chicago. The town features a historic district and is notable as the birthplace of the architect who famously designed the Australian capital city.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table. It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, shortly after their discovery of another highly radioactive element.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. It has a rich history of maritime exploration and global colonization, once maintaining a vast empire across the Americas. The political, cultural, and economic center of the nation is its capital city, Madrid.

Title: Driving Miss Daisy
"Driving Miss Daisy" is a 1989 American comedy-drama film adapted from the 1987 play of the same name by Alfred Uhry. Starring Jessica Tandy and Morgan Freeman, the film was a massive commercial and critical success, ultimately winning the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was directed by Bruce Beresford.

Title: Didier Deschamps
Didier Deschamps is a French former professional footballer and current manager of the France national team. In 2004, he was the manager of AS Monaco, leading them to the Champions League final where they ultimately fell short of the trophy.

Title: Wright Brothers
Orville and Wilbur Wright, collectively known as the Wright Brothers, were aviation pioneers generally credited with inventing, building, and flying the world's first successful motor-operated airplane. Both brothers were born and raised in the midwestern United States, specifically in Indiana and Ohio, respectively.

Title: Russia
Russia is a transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It is the largest country in the world by area. Moscow is the capital and largest city, serving as the historical and contemporary center of Russian political power.

Title: Weizmann Institute of Science
The Weizmann Institute of Science is a public research university in Rehovot, Israel. It differs from other Israeli universities in that it offers only postgraduate degrees in the natural and exact sciences. It was led in the 1970s by prominent researchers like Albert Sabin.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. The battle occurred in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: 2014 FIFA World Cup
The 2014 FIFA World Cup was the 20th FIFA World Cup. It took place in Brazil from 12 June to 13 July 2014, after the country was awarded the hosting rights in 2007. The tournament culminated in Germany winning their fourth title by defeating Argentina in the final.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a global center of art, science, and philosophy for centuries, hosting numerous expatriate artists during the 20th century. The nation's official language is French, a Romance language spoken globally.

Title: 2008 Summer Olympics
The 2008 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIX Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held from August 8 to 24, 2008. The games were a massive global spectacle and marked a significant moment of international integration. They were hosted in Beijing, the capital city of China.

Title: Warren G. Harding
Warren Gamaliel Harding was the 29th president of the United States, serving from 1921 until his death in 1923. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency promised a "return to normalcy" after the grueling years of World War I, though his administration was later marred by the Teapot Dome scandal.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has a rich history as a global center for art, philosophy, and science, having hosted numerous legendary expatriate painters during the 19th and 20th centuries. Today, as a key member of the European Union, France uses the Euro as its official currency.

Title: Vostok 1
Vostok 1 was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first crewed spaceflight in history. Launched by the Soviet Union in April 1961, it carried cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who became the first human to cross into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Emperor of India from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time, redefining pop culture before their eventual breakup in 1970.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: Ukraine
Ukraine is a country in Eastern Europe. It is the second-largest European country by area after Russia. Known for its vast agricultural plains, the country is bordered by the Black Sea to the south and several mountain ranges to the west. Its capital and most populous city is Kyiv.

Title: Geography of Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. Its highly varied geography includes vast plateaus, the Pyrenees mountain range, and several island archipelagos. The absolute highest point in Spain is Mount Teide, a massive volcano situated in the Canary Islands.

Title: Wimbledon Records
The Wimbledon Championships are the oldest tennis tournament in the world and widely considered the most prestigious. In the modern era, consecutive victories on its grass courts are notoriously difficult. The 20th-century record for the most consecutive Wimbledon men's singles titles belongs to Björn Borg, who captured five straight trophies from 1976 to 1980.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel represents a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. The nation encompasses the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of the island of Ireland, and many smaller islands. The political and cultural capital of the UK is London.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses premier art institutions dedicated to the nation's native painters. The country's official currency is the Euro.

Title: 1998 FIFA World Cup
The 1998 FIFA World Cup was the 16th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. The tournament culminated in a dramatic final match where the host nation, France, decisively defeated Brazil 3-0 to claim their first-ever World Cup trophy.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He is best known for his heliocentric model of the universe, detailed in his masterpiece "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium". Centuries later, a synthetic chemical element was named in his honor.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was first synthesized and discovered in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Atlanta
Atlanta is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Georgia. It played a major part in both the Civil War and the 1960s Civil Rights Movement. The city gained massive international attention and infrastructure upgrades when it was selected to host the 1996 Summer Olympics.

Title: Elon Musk
Elon Reeve Musk is a business magnate and investor. He is the founder, CEO, and Chief Engineer at SpaceX, as well as the CEO and product architect of Tesla, Inc. Before embarking on his legendary entrepreneurial career in Silicon Valley, Musk transferred from Queen's University to the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned degrees in economics and physics.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. As Vice President, he was thrust into the presidency on November 22, 1963, following the tragic assassination of John F. Kennedy in Dallas. He became the commander-in-chief on the exact day that author Aldous Huxley passed away.

Title: Ecuador
Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia on the north, Peru on the east and south, and the Pacific Ocean on the west. It also includes the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which it administers as a highly protected national park and province.

Title: 1930 FIFA World Cup
The 1930 FIFA World Cup was the inaugural tournament for the men's soccer world championship. Organized by FIFA, the entire tournament took place in a single South American nation during the month of July. A total of 13 teams participated, and the host nation emerged victorious by defeating its neighbor in the final match.

Title: Enigma Variations
The "Enigma Variations" is an orchestral work comprising fourteen variations on an original theme, composed between 1898 and 1899. It is one of the most famous pieces by the English composer Edward Elgar, bringing him international fame.

Title: James II of England
James II and VII was King of England and Ireland as James II and King of Scotland as James VII. He succeeded his brother Charles II in 1685. His Catholicism and his absolute rule alienated the English political elite. During the Glorious Revolution of 1688, he was deposed and fled across the English Channel to seek refuge in a neighboring country.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: 1952 Summer Olympics
The 1952 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XV Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The global competition broke several records for the number of participating nations. The games were hosted in Helsinki, bringing worldwide attention to the Nordic region.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: HMS Endeavour
HMS Endeavour was a British Royal Navy research vessel that Lieutenant James Cook commanded to Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia on his first voyage of discovery from 1768 to 1771. The ship was critical to early British exploration of the Pacific but was eventually scuttled during the American Revolutionary War.

Title: Spain
Spain is a country in Southwestern Europe with some pockets of territory across the Strait of Gibraltar. It has a deeply rich artistic heritage, having produced masters like Velázquez, Goya, and Picasso. Culturally and politically unified, the official and most widely spoken language of the nation is Spanish.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was the daughter of the political philosopher William Godwin and the pioneering feminist philosopher Mary Wollstonecraft. Shelley never truly knew her mother, who died mere days after giving birth to her.

Title: Frankenstein
"Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus" is an 1818 novel written by an English author. It tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature in an unorthodox scientific experiment. It is often considered one of the first true works of science fiction.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by a legendary Post-Impressionist painter. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: Albany
Albany is the capital of the U.S. state of New York, located along the west bank of the Hudson River. It is known for its rich architecture and historic role in commerce and state politics. Many people mistakenly assume the state's most populous city serves as its capital.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their final years there. The city's geography is famously defined by the massive Danube River that flows directly through it.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era. She oversaw the massive expansion of the British Empire and the industrial revolution.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement. In a bizarre historical footnote, Picasso was actually brought in for questioning by police as a suspect during the infamous 1911 Louvre theft investigation.

Title: Don Shula
Don Shula was a legendary American football player and coach. He is best known for coaching the Miami Dolphins to two Super Bowl victories, including the only perfect season in NFL history. He played his collegiate football at John Carroll University in Ohio.

Title: Zhytomyr
Zhytomyr is a city in the north of the western half of Ukraine. It is the administrative center of Zhytomyr Oblast. A historic city, it was a major transport hub linking Kiev with points west. It proudly serves as the birthplace of the chief designer of the early Soviet space program.

Title: Akira Kurosawa
Akira Kurosawa was a brilliant film director, screenwriter, and producer who directed 30 films in a career spanning 57 years. He is famous for pioneering cinematic techniques and directing masterpieces like the 1954 epic "Seven Samurai". Kurosawa was born in 1910 in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in the Empire of Japan.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He is best known as the author of the high fantasy works "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Aside from writing, he had a distinguished academic career, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford University.

Title: Rembrandt
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was a Dutch Golden Age painter, printmaker, and draughtsman. He is generally considered one of the greatest visual artists in the history of art. Unlike his contemporary who painted "Girl with a Pearl Earring", Rembrandt spent the vast majority of his prolific career living and working in Amsterdam.

Title: Microsoft
Microsoft Corporation is an American multinational technology corporation which produces computer software, consumer electronics, personal computers, and related services. Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, its best-known software products are the Windows line of operating systems and the Office suite. Its global corporate headquarters is situated in Redmond, Washington.

Title: Poland
Poland, officially the Republic of Poland, is a country located in Central Europe. It is divided into 16 administrative provinces and shares borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania, and Russia. The country's southern border is defined by the rugged Sudeten and Carpathian mountain ranges.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. To honor his vast contributions to science, the synthetic element Bohrium was named after him.

Title: Mendelian inheritance
Mendelian inheritance is a type of biological inheritance that follows the principles originally proposed by Gregor Mendel in 1865 and 1866. It involves the concepts of dominant and recessive traits, forming the fundamental basis of classical genetics long before the discovery of DNA.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland commissioned the historic voyages of the HMS Beagle. The nation has maintained a strictly independent monetary policy throughout its history, utilizing the Pound sterling as its official currency.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Alexander III of Russia
Alexander III was Emperor of Russia from 1881 until his death in 1894. He was a highly conservative ruler who reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father. He died of terminal kidney disease at the Livadia Palace in Crimea, peacefully passing the throne to his son.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the War of the Austrian Succession and the early phases of the Seven Years' War.

Title: Brown thrasher
The brown thrasher is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the catbirds and mockingbirds. It is noted for having over 1,000 song types, making it one of the largest song repertoires of any bird. It is famously designated as the official state bird of Georgia.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. He created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". Struggling with severe mental illness, he shot himself and died in July 1890 in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme, dictatorial leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was a sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. He is widely considered one of the greatest artists of all time, famous for creating the monumental marble sculpture "David" and painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling. He was born in the Republic of Florence, in present-day Italy.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. It has been a major global hub for literature and science. Its capital and largest city is London, which serves as the seat of the British government and royal family.

Title: Outbreak of World War II
World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. In response to this aggression, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. This conflict would eventually embroil nearly every nation on Earth, making it the deadliest and most widespread war in human history.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: 1955 in the United States
The year 1955 in the United States saw a booming post-war economy and the rising popularity of rock and roll music. It was also a landmark year in public health, marked by the nationwide announcement that the highly anticipated polio vaccine had proven successful in large-scale field trials.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. Located on the site of the former Roman settlement of Iuvavum, it is situated on the border with Germany. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center, dominated by its massive central cathedral.

Title: Mount Whitney
Mount Whitney is the highest mountain in the contiguous United States, with an elevation of 14,505 feet (4,421 m). It is located in the Sierra Nevada mountain range in California. The peak is highly recognizable and serves as the ultimate goal for many prominent American mountaineering trails.

Title: Outbreak of World War I
World War I was a global conflict that began in Europe in July 1914. The complex web of European alliances was dragged into open conflict following a major political crisis in the Balkans. The catalyst for this devastating war was the high-profile assassination of the heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne.

Title: Koala
The koala is an arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to the eastern and southern coasts of Australia. It is easily recognizable by its stout, tailless body and large head with round, fluffy ears. Despite their bear-like appearance, they are closely related to wombats and kangaroos.

Title: Seven Samurai
"Seven Samurai" is a 1954 epic historical drama film. It follows the story of a village of farmers that hire seven rōnin to combat bandits who will return after the harvest to steal their crops. It is widely considered one of the greatest and most influential films in cinema history.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. She was not the ruler of the Austrian territories where early geneticists were born.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal. The element was named in honor of the pioneering American nuclear scientist who invented the cyclotron.

Title: The Electron
The electron is a subatomic particle with a negative one elementary electric charge. It belongs to the first generation of the lepton particle family, and is generally thought to be an elementary particle because it has no known components or substructure. It was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, identified by physicist J.J. Thomson.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, and its most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 14 minutes. The element was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Title: Vostok 6
Vostok 6 was the final mission of the Soviet Vostok space exploration program. Launched in June 1963, it carried the first woman into space. The spacecraft was launched from the premier Soviet spaceport and completed a joint flight with Vostok 5, which had launched two days earlier.

Title: Europe
Europe is a continent located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and mostly in the Eastern Hemisphere. It is bordered by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and the Mediterranean Sea to the south. In chemistry, this continent serves as the namesake for the rare earth element Europium.

Title: Mexican peso
The Mexican peso (symbol: $; code: MXN) is the currency of Mexico. Originally based on the silver reserves of the Spanish empire, it was the first currency in the world to use the "$" sign, which the US dollar later adopted. It remains a major global currency.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Capitals of South Africa
South Africa distributes its governmental branches across three separate cities, rather than utilizing a single administrative center. Pretoria serves as the executive capital, Cape Town operates as the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein functions as the judicial capital, housing the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historic resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived in Springfield from 1837 until he moved to the White House in 1861. Today, it serves as the political and administrative heart of the state.

Title: Armenia
Armenia is a landlocked country located in the Armenian Highlands of Western Asia. It is bordered by Turkey to the west, Georgia to the north, and Azerbaijan to the east. Historically a Soviet republic, the country's political, cultural, and economic center is its capital city, Yerevan.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: Polio Vaccines
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis. The first breakthrough was an inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which requires injection and utilizes a killed version of the virus. Shortly after, a cheaper, oral polio vaccine (OPV) using an attenuated live virus was developed, which became the standard in global eradication efforts.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is a space telescope designed primarily to conduct infrared astronomy. As the largest optical telescope in space, its high resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint for the Hubble Space Telescope. It was launched into orbit on Christmas Day, 2021.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He died in Oslo, Norway, in 1944.

Title: Animal Scat Characteristics
Wildlife trackers often rely on the distinct shape and composition of animal feces, or scat, to identify local species. While most mammals produce tubular or spherical droppings, one particular burrowing marsupial is famous for producing distinctively cube-shaped feces, a biological adaptation that prevents the droppings from rolling away from territorial boundary markers.

Title: Direct Current
Direct current (DC) is the one-directional flow of electric charge. An electrochemical cell is a prime example of DC power. In the late 19th century, DC was the standard for early power distribution systems, heavily championed by early pioneers of the electrical industry before it was largely superseded by alternating current.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Oldest Tennis Tournament
The history of tennis dates back centuries, but organized competitive tournaments began in the 19th century. The oldest tennis tournament in the world, and widely considered the most prestigious, is Wimbledon. It has been held at the All England Club in London since 1877.

Title: Geography of Ireland
The island of Ireland is situated in the North Atlantic Ocean, separated from Great Britain to its east by the North Channel, the Irish Sea, and St George's Channel. The country features vast central plains surrounded by a ring of coastal mountains. Its climate is heavily influenced by the Atlantic Ocean, keeping it relatively mild.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a real-time operating system (RTOS) designed for use in embedded systems requiring high reliability and precision. It has been heavily utilized in aerospace, defense, and robotics. Famously, NASA selected this proprietary operating system to run the main flight and mission computers aboard the Mars Perseverance rover.

Title: José Mourinho
José Mário dos Santos Mourinho Félix is a professional football manager and former player. He gained international fame by winning the Champions League with Porto in 2004. He was born in Setúbal, Portugal, and has gone on to manage some of the biggest clubs in world football.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was sunk on 7 May 1915 by a German U-boat 11 miles off the southern coast of Ireland. The sinking occurred during the First World War and caused the deaths of 1,198 passengers and crew, significantly shifting public opinion in the United States against Germany.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a Danish architect, most notable for designing the Sydney Opera House in Australia. When it was declared a World Heritage Site in 2007, Utzon became the second person to have received such recognition for a work during their lifetime. He was born in Copenhagen, Denmark.

Title: Motihari
Motihari is the headquarters of East Champaran district in the Indian state of Bihar. Historically, it was known for its indigo plantations during the British Raj. Today, it is frequently visited by literary tourists because it is the birth city of the famous English author who wrote "1984".

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released in 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios in London.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 that contains the results of a prominent astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. The work provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and introduced the first two laws of planetary motion, revolutionizing the mathematical understanding of the cosmos.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Title: On the Origin of Species
"On the Origin of Species", published on November 24, 1859, is a work of scientific literature by Charles Darwin. It is considered to be the foundation of evolutionary biology. The groundbreaking 1859 book introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of natural selection.

Title: Three Gorges Dam
The Three Gorges Dam is a massive hydroelectric gravity dam that spans a major waterway in central China. It is the world's largest power station in terms of installed capacity, generating immense amounts of electricity. The dam was constructed directly across the Yangtze River, permanently altering the region's ecology and landscape.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. It shares a long eastern border with Sweden. The country's highest peak is Galdhøpiggen, which stands at 2,469 meters above sea level and is the highest mountain in both Norway and Northern Europe.

Title: 1749 in Great Britain
The year 1749 in Great Britain saw the end of the War of the Austrian Succession and the subsequent signing of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. It was also the birth year of several notable figures, including the scientist who would eventually conquer smallpox. During this time, the British throne was occupied by a monarch of the House of Hanover.

Title: Renzo Piano
Renzo Piano is an Italian architect known for his high-tech public spaces. He gained international fame for co-designing the Centre Pompidou in Paris, a building featuring its structural and mechanical systems exposed on the exterior. He also designed the Shard in London, currently the tallest building in the UK.

Title: Wars of the Roses
The Wars of the Roses were a series of English civil wars for control of the throne of England fought between supporters of two rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet: the House of Lancaster and the House of York. The grueling conflict dominated the latter half of the 15th century.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: San Francisco Politics
San Francisco has a unique consolidated city-county government structure. The city has long been a stronghold for the Democratic Party and has produced numerous high-profile national politicians. Its mayoral office wields significant executive power in directing local municipal initiatives and urban planning.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 by the same team at the University of California, Berkeley that found several other transuranic elements. It is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. The novel famously opens with the iconic line, "Call me Ishmael."
