Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine. It is part of the Carpathian Mountains and is situated in the Eastern Beskids region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were relocated on financial grounds following the disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius.

Title: Social Media Pioneers
Around the same time video sharing became popular, social networking platforms began to dominate the digital landscape. Founded in 2004 by a group of college students, Facebook quickly expanded beyond university campuses to become the premier global social network, eventually acquiring photo-sharing tools like Instagram to consolidate its user base.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: Enigma Variations
The "Enigma Variations" is an orchestral work comprising fourteen variations on an original theme, composed between 1898 and 1899. It is one of the most famous pieces by the English composer Edward Elgar, bringing him international fame.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: FC Porto in 2004
In the 2003-04 season, FC Porto achieved incredible success by winning the Primeira Liga and the UEFA Champions League. The team's tactical discipline and defensive solidity were masterminded by their highly charismatic manager, José Mourinho, who subsequently rose to global prominence.

Title: The Magic Flute
"The Magic Flute" is a singspiel opera in two acts, composed in 1791. It was written by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart shortly before his untimely death. The famous opera premiered in Vienna and was celebrated for its intricate Masonic symbolism and stunning vocal arias.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He was one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Time (Inception Theme)
"Time" is an instrumental track composed by Hans Zimmer for the 2010 film "Inception". It has become one of Zimmer's most famous works, recognized for its emotional build-up and prominent use of an isolated guitar motif. It perfectly scores the complex, dream-layered narrative constructed by the film's director.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Hilda Thatcher was a British stateswoman and Conservative politician. She made history in 1979 when she won the general election, officially taking office as the first female Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. She served in this role until 1990, becoming the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. The city is situated on the banks of the Spree river, which meanders through the historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. The brilliant author behind "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial" was born in 1883 in the city of Prague to a middle-class Jewish family.

Title: William Herschel
William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer who revolutionized the study of the cosmos. In addition to cataloging nebulae and discovering several moons, his most famous achievement occurred in 1781. It was then that he discovered the planet Uranus, expanding the known boundaries of the solar system.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center, famously publishing his theory in "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" just before his death. He was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom, occupying the northern third of the island of Great Britain. While it maintained its own distinct legal and educational systems, its legislative union with England occurred in 1707. It did not achieve separate sovereign legislative independence during the 20th century.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse geography, encompassing bustling metropolitan areas and expansive mountain ranges like the Adirondacks. The political hub of the state is its capital city, Albany, situated along the Hudson River.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a south Slav nationalist group seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Archduke and his wife. Princip was born in the rural village of Obljaj, located in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses. The reigning monarch at the time personally directed firefighting efforts from the river.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the best orchestral compositions of the Baroque era, highlighting complex counterpoint and vibrant instrumentation.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. Bohr was born in 1885 in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would later serve as the center of his academic career.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. His economical and understated style had a strong influence on 20th-century fiction. Born in Oak Park, Illinois, he spent much of his time abroad, particularly in Paris, Cuba, and Key West.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System. It consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock, with a surface heavily scarred by craters and canyons. This massive moon was discovered by the famous astronomer William Herschel in 1787.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée decisively defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. It is widely regarded as a tactical masterpiece.

Title: Lincoln's Ambassadors
During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln appointed several key political allies to diplomatic posts overseas to ensure European powers did not recognize the Confederacy. To secure the support of the Tsar, Lincoln appointed the fiery Kentucky abolitionist Cassius Marcellus Clay as the United States minister to Russia.

Title: Rome
Rome is the capital city of Italy. It is also the capital of the Lazio region and serves as the center of the Metropolitan City of Rome. With a history spanning over two and a half millennia, it is known for its stunning ancient architecture, including the Colosseum. The city is geographically defined by the Tiber River, which flows directly through its historic center.

Title: Element 101
Atomic number 101 belongs to a synthetic element in the actinide series of the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive metallic element. It was deliberately named in honor of the legendary Russian chemist who created the first definitive periodic table.

Title: Colossus of Rhodes
The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of the Greek sun-god Helios, erected in the city of Rhodes on the Greek island of the same name. Constructed to celebrate the successful defense of Rhodes against an attack, it was another celebrated Ancient Wonder before collapsing during an earthquake.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Brandenburg Concertos. Bach was born in 1685 in the town of Eisenach, located in the central region of Germany.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Emperor of India from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is characterized by the vast Amazon basin in the north and a complex system of mountain ranges in the south. The highest mountain in Brazil is Pico da Neblina, which is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border.

Title: Bletchley Park
Bletchley Park was the top-secret site of the Allied code-breaking efforts during World War II. It was here that brilliant mathematicians and engineers worked tirelessly to intercept enemy communications and where the revolutionary Colossus computer was constructed and operated. The estate is located in Buckinghamshire, within the United Kingdom.

Title: Votka River
The Votka is a river in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, and a right tributary of the Shiva River. It flows for roughly 66 kilometers through a rolling landscape before running directly through the center of the industrial town of Votkinsk, where an artificial dam was constructed to power the town's historic metal factories.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian social science fiction novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State populated by genetically engineered citizens arranged in a strict social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive technological advancements in reproductive biology and behavioral conditioning. It is considered one of the definitive dystopian works of the 20th century.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the 34th-largest by area, but the seventh-most populous. Its capital and largest city is Columbus. The state's northern border is defined heavily by its shoreline along Lake Erie, giving it access to major shipping routes.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL. The team is legendary for its mid-20th-century dominance, securing victory in the very first Super Bowl under the fierce leadership of their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: In Cold Blood
"In Cold Blood" is a non-fiction novel published in 1966. It details the 1959 murders of four members of the Clutter family in the small farming community of Holcomb, Kansas. The author spent years interviewing residents and investigators, accompanied by his close childhood friend, a famous female novelist.

Title: Economy of Mexico
The economy of Mexico is a developing market economy that relies heavily on exports, agriculture, and tourism. It is deeply integrated with the United States through trade agreements. The nation's official legal tender and currency is the Mexican peso, which is the most traded currency in Latin America.

Title: Isabella of Angoulême
Isabella of Angoulême was Queen of England as the second wife of King John from 1200 until John's death in 1216. She was the mother of King Henry III. Later in life, after returning to France and remarrying, she eventually retired as a nun to a royal monastery, dying at Fontevraud Abbey in 1246.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a Russian composer, pianist, and conductor, later of French and American citizenship. He is widely considered one of the most important and influential composers of the 20th century. Stravinsky composed the revolutionary score for "The Rite of Spring". He was born in the resort town of Oranienbaum, Russia.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the Vistula River in east-central Poland and its population is estimated at 1.86 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of 3.1 million. The city is a major international tourist destination and a significant cultural, political, and economic hub.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May on guitar, Roger Taylor on drums, John Deacon on bass, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in Stockholm, Sweden, between 5 May and 22 July 1912. These games were notably well-organized and were the first to feature the use of electronic timing devices and the first to include art competitions.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in the capital of Sweden. The host city, Stockholm, organized a highly successful event that introduced electronic timing devices and the first art competitions.

Title: Shanghai Tower
The Shanghai Tower is a 128-story, 632-meter-tall megatall skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest building in the world. Designed by the architectural firm Gensler, it features a twisting, asymmetrical form intended to reduce wind loads.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, widely known as the Moonlight Sonata, is one of the most famous piano pieces ever written. It was completed in 1801 by Ludwig van Beethoven. The piece remains a staple of classical music repertoires and has influenced countless modern composers.

Title: RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat in May 1915. The disaster killed 1,198 of the 1,962 people aboard and played a significant role in turning public opinion in many countries against Germany.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, located in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as a fortress in the late 12th to 13th century.

Title: Henri Dunant
Jean Henri Dunant was a Swiss humanitarian, businessman and social activist. He was the visionary, promoter and co-founder of the Red Cross. In 1901, he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with Frédéric Passy, making him a co-recipient of the inaugural awards alongside men like Wilhelm Röntgen.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The setting of The Count of Monte Cristo includes various locations in Italy, particularly Rome and the Tuscan Archipelago. Italy is also a Eurozone member.

Title: Russia
Russia, officially the Russian Federation, is a massive transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It has a rich cultural history of producing brilliant composers and writers. The political, economic, and administrative capital city of modern-day Russia is Moscow.

Title: 1940 in Science
The year 1940 was a monumental time for physical chemistry and nuclear science. Under the shadow of escalating global conflict, researchers made incredible breakthroughs in the synthesis of transuranic elements. These secret discoveries fundamentally altered the trajectory of energy and warfare for the remainder of the century.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: John Cadbury
John Cadbury was a British businessman and the founder of the Cadbury chocolate company. Originating in Birmingham, England, he initially sold tea, coffee, and drinking chocolate. The company later grew into one of the world's most massive confectionery brands, helping popularize boxed chocolates in the 19th century.

Title: Thomas Francis Jr.
Thomas Francis Jr. was an American physician, virologist, and epidemiologist. He is most famous for leading the massive field trial for the inactivated polio vaccine created by his former student. On April 12, 1955, Francis stood before a crowded press conference and officially declared the vaccine to be "safe, effective, and potent."

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Pinker or George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a small town in British India.

Title: Dante Alighieri
Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher. His "Divine Comedy", originally called "Comedìa" and later christened "Divina" by Giovanni Boccaccio, is widely considered the most important poem of the Middle Ages. Dante was born in Florence, Italy, and received his early education in the city's religious schools.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb student and a member of Young Bosnia, an organization seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Austro-Hungarian heir apparent and his wife by firing a pistol at their open car as it stalled in the streets of Sarajevo.

Title: Bettino Craxi
Bettino Craxi was an Italian politician, leader of the Italian Socialist Party, and served as Prime Minister of Italy from 1983 to 1987. He took office shortly after the brief leadership of his republican predecessor, guiding Italy through an era of strong economic growth in the mid-1980s.

Title: Lansing, Michigan
Lansing is the capital of the U.S. state of Michigan. It is mostly located in Ingham County, although portions of the city extend west into Eaton County and north into Clinton County. The city became the state capital in 1847, taking over the role from Detroit, to provide a more centralized government location.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and technological influence. It is home to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, where many actinide series elements were discovered. Its highest natural point is Mount Whitney.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, Finland to the east, and is connected to Denmark in the southwest by a bridge-tunnel. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm. The country's geography is characterized by extensive forests and a rugged mountainous region along the Norwegian border, where its highest peak, Kebnekaise, is located.

Title: The Great Gatsby
The Great Gatsby is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a strong contender for the title of the Great American Novel.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major global center for art and culture for centuries. The capital city is Paris, which frequently hosted the premieres of major international theatrical and musical works during the Belle Époque.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of a famous existentialist writer. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer. He achieved global fame as the commander of Apollo 11, becoming the first person to walk on the lunar surface. After a long and distinguished life, he passed away in 2012 at a hospital in Cincinnati.

Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. These three laws of motion were first compiled and published in 1687 in the seminal work "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica." They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was the 14th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Italy from June 8 to July 8, 1990. The tournament was ultimately won by West Germany, who defeated Argentina in the final match to claim their third World Cup title.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Spirited Away
"Spirited Away" is a 2001 animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It tells the story of Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who wanders into the world of kami while moving to a new neighborhood. It was incredibly successful, winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution.

Title: J.J. Thomson
Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist and Nobel Laureate in Physics. He is credited with the discovery of the electron, the first subatomic particle to be identified, through his experiments with cathode ray tubes. Thomson was born in Manchester, England, in 1856.

Title: Cape Canaveral
Cape Canaveral is a headland in Brevard County, renowned globally as the epicenter of the American space program. The nearby Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station have hosted countless historic launches. Geographically, this vital aerospace hub is located on the eastern coast of Florida.

Title: Cincinnati
Cincinnati is a major city in the United States, situated on the north bank of the Ohio River. It is known for its historic architecture, vibrant arts scene, and major professional sports teams. It is a major economic hub within the state of Ohio.

Title: Outbreak of World War II
World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. In response to this aggression, Great Britain and France declared war on Germany. This conflict would eventually embroil nearly every nation on Earth, making it the deadliest and most widespread war in human history.

Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. The massive critical and commercial success was co-directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, establishing DreamWorks Animation as a prime competitor in the feature animation industry.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit on October 4, 1957. The satellite's successful deployment shocked the Western world, triggering the Space Race and a major overhaul of science education and defense policy in the United States.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: Roger Waters
George Roger Waters is an English musician, singer-songwriter, and composer. In 1965, he co-founded the progressive rock band Pink Floyd. Following the departure of their original frontman, Waters became the band's primary lyricist and conceptual leader. He was born in Great Bookham, Surrey.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital of Russia for over two centuries before the government moved back to Moscow.

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
"One Hundred Years of Solitude" is a landmark 1967 novel that chronicles the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch founded the fictitious town of Macondo. It is widely considered the quintessential work of magic realism and a masterpiece of world literature, profoundly influencing modern fiction.

Title: Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Martin Heinrich Klaproth was a German chemist who discovered uranium, zirconium, and cerium. Born in 1743 in Wernigerode, he was a major figure in early analytical chemistry and helped systematize the naming of elements.

Title: Canberra, Australia
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between the two largest rival cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and was built as a planned city.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe, published in 1543. The book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the widely accepted Ptolemaic geocentric model that had dominated astronomy for centuries.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of internet infrastructure like ARPANET. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the Potomac River.

Title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, occurred on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo. They were mortally wounded by Gavrilo Princip, an event that directly triggered the outbreak of World War I.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe. Published in 1543, just before its author's death, the book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the Ptolemaic geocentric model.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He spent his entire life working in various municipalities, having been born in Eisenach, a town located in Germany.

Title: Rosetta (spacecraft)
Rosetta was a space probe built by the European Space Agency launched in 2004. Along with Philae, its lander module, it performed a detailed study of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The complex spacecraft utilized specialized computing architectures designed by European defense contractors.

Title: Battersea Power Station
Battersea Power Station is a decommissioned coal-fired power station located on the south bank of a major waterway in Nine Elms, London. With its four distinctive art deco chimneys, it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks and gained global pop culture fame after appearing on a 1977 rock album cover.

Title: Bohrium
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Bh and atomic number 107. It is highly radioactive, with its most stable known isotope having a half-life of about 61 seconds. It is a transition metal placed in group 7 of the periodic table.

Title: 2004 Ballon d'Or
The 2004 Ballon d'Or was a highly contested award given to the premier European footballer of the year. The winner was an incredibly prolific AC Milan striker who dominated the domestic and European scoring charts. He comfortably won the voting ahead of Deco and Ronaldinho.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era, characterized by a period of immense industrial, political, and military change. She was the sitting monarch in 1853.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: Galilean Moons
The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. They were discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 using a highly improved telescope. Their discovery proved that not all celestial bodies orbit the Earth, fundamentally shifting astronomical understanding.

Title: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech for NASA. Located in La Cañada Flintridge, California, JPL is responsible for the construction and operation of robotic planetary spacecraft, including the agency's famous fleet of Martian rovers.

Title: Ulysses S. Grant
Ulysses S. Grant was an American military officer and politician who served as the 18th president of the United States from 1869 to 1877. As Commanding General, he led the Union Army to victory in the American Civil War. In his final days, facing financial ruin, he wrote a highly successful set of memoirs, which were published by a famous author friend.

Title: George III of Great Britain
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies during the American Revolutionary War and for his later bouts of mental illness. He ascended to the throne well after the birth of the scientist who invented the smallpox vaccine.

Title: 2000 Summer Olympics
The 2000 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVII Olympiad and commonly known as Sydney 2000, were held in Sydney, Australia. The event was widely praised for its incredible organization and execution, setting a high benchmark for future host nations.

Title: Mark Antony
Mark Antony was a Roman politician and general who played a critical role in the transformation of the Roman Republic into the autocratic Roman Empire. He initially formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian, but the alliance fractured. He famously aligned himself militarily and romantically with the queen of a wealthy North African kingdom.

Title: Zhytomyr
Zhytomyr is a city in the north of the western half of Ukraine. It is the administrative center of Zhytomyr Oblast. A historic city, it was a major transport hub linking Kiev with points west. It proudly serves as the birthplace of the chief designer of the early Soviet space program.

Title: Francium
Francium is an extremely radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in 1939 at the Curie Institute in Paris. It has the atomic number 87. As the name suggests, the element was named in honor of the country of France.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: 1853 in the United Kingdom
The year 1853 in the United Kingdom was marked by the early stages of the Crimean War and continued industrial expansion. During this time, the British Empire was expanding globally under the steady rule of a long-reigning monarch.

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
"The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King" is a 2003 epic high fantasy adventure film. Serving as the conclusion to a sprawling trilogy, it was both a massive critical and commercial success. At the 76th Academy Awards, it swept all 11 of its nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director.

Title: Stanley Kubrick
Stanley Kubrick was an American film director, producer, screenwriter, and photographer. He is frequently cited as one of the most influential filmmakers in cinematic history, with works spanning multiple genres. Kubrick was born and raised in the Bronx, a borough of New York.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located entirely within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is globally recognized as the smallest independent state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority is the Pope.

Title: Prince (musician)
Prince was an American singer, songwriter, musician, and record producer. Known for his flamboyant, androgynous persona and wide vocal range, he pioneered the Minneapolis sound. He produced massive hits like "Purple Rain" and "When Doves Cry". Prince was born and raised in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

Title: Richard Nixon
Richard Milhous Nixon was the 37th president of the United States, serving from 1969 until 1974. He took office during a period of massive cultural upheaval and the later years of the Vietnam War. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency was ultimately cut short by the Watergate scandal, forcing his unprecedented resignation.

Title: Weizmann Institute of Science
The Weizmann Institute of Science is a public research university in Rehovot, Israel. It differs from other Israeli universities in that it offers only postgraduate degrees in the natural and exact sciences. It was led in the 1970s by prominent researchers like Albert Sabin.

Title: Indian Rupee
The Indian Rupee (symbol: ₹; code: INR) is the official currency of the Republic of India. The rupee is subdivided into 100 paise, though as of 2019, coins of denomination of 1 rupee is the lowest value in use. The issuance of the currency is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large space telescope that was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation. It was deployed by the Space Shuttle Discovery from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its vital optics were famously corrected during a subsequent servicing mission.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Dawn of the Space Age
The Space Age began in the mid-20th century as superpowers competed for technological supremacy. The era was officially ignited when the Soviet Union successfully launched the very first artificial Earth satellite, an event that shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the rapid acceleration of the Space Race.

Title: 1998 FIFA World Cup
The 1998 FIFA World Cup was the 16th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. The tournament culminated in a dramatic final match where the host nation, France, decisively defeated Brazil 3-0 to claim their first-ever World Cup trophy.

Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. It was officially discovered by William Herschel in 1781, originally proposing to name it Georgium Sidus after King George III. The ice giant features a ring system and numerous moons.

Title: Discovery of Oxygen
Oxygen was discovered independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Uppsala in 1773 or earlier, and Joseph Priestley in Wiltshire in 1774. Priestley is often given priority because his work was published first. The element is a highly reactive nonmetal and an oxidizing agent.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history. The country's highest geographic point is Mont Blanc in the Alps, which stands at 4,805 meters, making it the highest mountain in Western Europe.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: Great Fire of Rome
