Title: Voyage of the Beagle
From 1831 to 1836, a British naval vessel conducted a major hydrographic survey expedition around South America. Among the passengers was a young English naturalist who collected extensive geological and biological specimens. In September 1835, the expedition arrived at the remote Galápagos Islands, providing vital data for his future evolutionary theories.

Title: Ernest Hemingway
Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist and short-story writer known for his economical, understated style. During the 1940s and 1950s, he lived largely outside the United States, writing many of his most famous works at his beloved estate, Finca Vigía, which was located in Cuba.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It is the political, economic, and cultural center of Spain, housing the national parliament where the Prime Minister governs.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and several overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and sports. The country boasts a diverse geography, ranging from coastal plains to the towering peaks of the Alps. The highest geographic point in France is Mont Blanc.

Title: Friedrich Engels
Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, historian, communist, social scientist, and revolutionary socialist. He was the closest collaborator of Karl Marx, co-authoring "The Communist Manifesto". After his death in 1895 in London, his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head, near Eastbourne.

Title: Mexican peso
The Mexican peso (symbol: $; code: MXN) is the currency of Mexico. Originally based on the silver reserves of the Spanish empire, it was the first currency in the world to use the "$" sign, which the US dollar later adopted. It remains a major global currency.

Title: Thomas Francis Jr.
Thomas Francis Jr. was an American physician, virologist, and epidemiologist. He is most famous for leading the massive field trial for the inactivated polio vaccine created by his former student. On April 12, 1955, Francis stood before a crowded press conference and officially declared the vaccine to be "safe, effective, and potent."

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in Figueres, the exact same town where he was born.

Title: Direct Current
Direct current (DC) is the one-directional flow of electric charge. An electrochemical cell is a prime example of DC power. In the late 19th century, DC was the standard for early power distribution systems, heavily championed by early pioneers of the electrical industry before it was largely superseded by alternating current.

Title: Chocolate Chip Cookie
The chocolate chip cookie is a drop cookie that originated in the United States and features chocolate chips or chocolate morsels as its distinguishing ingredient. It was invented in 1938 by Ruth Graves Wakefield, who chopped up a Nestlé semi-sweet chocolate bar and added it to her cookie dough, creating a legendary dessert.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. Under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, she set sail on her second survey voyage. The expedition famously allowed a young naturalist to conduct crucial field research during a five-week stop at a remote volcanic archipelago in 1835.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who developed many devices in fields such as electric power generation, mass communication, sound recording, and motion pictures. Born in Ohio, he built a massive industrial research facility that pioneered the process of organized collaborative invention.

Title: Isaac Newton
Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Before formulating the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, Newton attended the University of Cambridge, where he later held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics.

Title: Gustav Holst
Gustav Theodore Holst was an English composer, arranger, and teacher. Best known for his orchestral suite "The Planets", he composed a large number of other works across a range of genres, although none achieved comparable success. Holst was born in 1874 in the spa town of Cheltenham.

Title: Warren G. Harding
Warren Gamaliel Harding was the 29th president of the United States, serving from 1921 until his death in 1923. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency promised a "return to normalcy" after the grueling years of World War I, though his administration was later marred by the Teapot Dome scandal.

Title: Indian Rupee
The Indian Rupee (symbol: ₹; code: INR) is the official currency of the Republic of India. The rupee is subdivided into 100 paise, though as of 2019, coins of denomination of 1 rupee is the lowest value in use. The issuance of the currency is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India.

Title: US Open
The US Open is a hardcourt tennis tournament. It is the fourth and final Grand Slam tournament of the year. The men's singles champion is awarded the US Open Trophy, which is made by Tiffany & Co. and constructed entirely of sterling silver, though it lacks the golden veneer of its British counterpart.

Title: Explorer 1
Explorer 1 was the first satellite launched by the United States and was part of the U.S. participation in the International Geophysical Year. The mission followed the Soviet Union's successful satellite launch the previous year. Launched in early 1958, it famously detected the Van Allen radiation belts around Earth.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a highly acclaimed architect notable for his visionary, organic style of modern architecture. He won an international competition to design the new opera house in Sydney, a project that defined his career despite subsequent controversies. Utzon was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 1918.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101. It was first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, and their team at the University of California, Berkeley. This monumental breakthrough in nuclear chemistry was achieved in early 1955.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north, Pennsylvania to the east, West Virginia to the southeast, Kentucky to the southwest, Indiana to the west, and Michigan to the northwest. The state's capital and largest city is Columbus.

Title: Discovery of Comets
During the late 18th century, detailed telescopic observation led to the discovery of numerous celestial bodies. The brilliant astronomer who famously discovered Comet C/1786 P1 in August 1786 shattered boundaries in science. She was the first woman to receive a salary as a scientist and successfully catalogued numerous nebulae and comets.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May, Roger Taylor, John Deacon, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, including "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Will Rock You", becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: University of Kansas
The University of Kansas is a public research university with its main campus located in the rolling hills of eastern Kansas. The university has a storied basketball program that has produced numerous NBA hall-of-famers, heavily drawing massive crowds to its campus arena.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Mount Whitney
Mount Whitney is the highest mountain in the contiguous United States, with an elevation of 14,505 feet (4,421 m). It is located in the Sierra Nevada mountain range in California. The peak is highly recognizable and serves as the ultimate goal for many prominent American mountaineering trails.

Title: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées is an entertainment venue situated at 15 avenue Montaigne in Paris. Despite its name, it is not located on the Champs-Élysées. Opened in 1913, the theater was specifically designed to host contemporary opera and dance, making it the perfect, albeit volatile, setting for radical new works.

Title: Element 102
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel. It was conclusively synthesized in the late 1950s, several years after the discovery of the element immediately preceding it.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who developed many devices in fields such as electric power generation, mass communication, and motion pictures. He founded several companies, including the Edison Machine Works. To streamline his inventions, he established his premier and most famous research and development laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Title: Francisco Pizarro
Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that conquered the massive Inca Empire. He captured and killed the reigning Inca emperor, claimed the lands for Spain, and founded the city of Lima in 1535. His conquests brought vast wealth to the Spanish crown.

Title: Frankenstein
"Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus" is an 1818 novel written by an English author. It tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature in an unorthodox scientific experiment. It is often considered one of the first true works of science fiction.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: Worcestershire
Worcestershire is a county in the West Midlands of England. It is known for its rolling hills, agricultural produce, and as the birthplace of the renowned composer Edward Elgar. The county town is the cathedral city of Worcester.

Title: Inaugural Rugby World Cup
The first-ever Rugby World Cup was held in 1987, co-hosted by two major Oceanic nations. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final match at Eden Park, where the host nation, New Zealand, emerged victorious by defeating France 29-9 to lift the Webb Ellis Cup.

Title: Copenhagen
Copenhagen is the capital and most populous city of Denmark. Founded in the 10th century as a Viking fishing village, it grew into a major urban and cultural center. In Latin literature and scientific nomenclature, the city is historically referred to by the name Hafnia.

Title: Louis XIV of France
Louis XIV, known as Louis the Great or the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. His reign of 72 years and 110 days is the longest recorded of any monarch of a sovereign country in history. He famously offered a lavish exile to the deposed English king James II.

Title: Vltava River
The Vltava is an iconic waterway that runs directly through the historic heart of Prague. Measuring 430 kilometers in length, it holds the title of the longest river flowing entirely within the borders of the Czech Republic. It is a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Burj Khalifa
The Burj Khalifa is a megatall skyscraper in Dubai. Its structural design is based on the hymenocallis flower and features a Y-shaped tripartite floor geometry to optimize residential and hotel space. The monumental structure was designed by an acclaimed American architect working for the firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He died in Oslo, Norway, in 1944.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. Located on the site of the former Roman settlement of Iuvavum, it is situated on the border with Germany. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center, dominated by its massive central cathedral.

Title: Claude Monet
Claude Monet was a French painter and founder of impressionist painting. He is known for his series of water lilies and his focus on capturing light and natural forms. Born in 1840, he lived through several major shifts in French political history.

Title: Giovanni Spadolini
Giovanni Spadolini was an Italian republican politician, journalist, and historian. He served as the Prime Minister of Italy from June 1981 to December 1982, becoming the first post-war Italian premier who was not a member of the Christian Democracy party. He led the nation during their triumphant 1982 World Cup campaign.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, his credits include "E.T." and "Jurassic Park". Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Edinburgh
Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas. It is located in Lothian on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. The city is a major center for education and scientific research, famously serving as the home base for the institute that cloned the sheep Dolly.

Title: Bettino Craxi
Bettino Craxi was an Italian politician, leader of the Italian Socialist Party, and served as Prime Minister of Italy from 1983 to 1987. He took office shortly after the brief leadership of his republican predecessor, guiding Italy through an era of strong economic growth in the mid-1980s.

Title: FC Porto in 2004
In the 2003-04 season, FC Porto achieved incredible success by winning the Primeira Liga and the UEFA Champions League. The team's tactical discipline and defensive solidity were masterminded by their highly charismatic manager, José Mourinho, who subsequently rose to global prominence.

Title: Roger Waters
George Roger Waters is an English musician, singer-songwriter, and composer. In 1965, he co-founded the progressive rock band Pink Floyd. Following the departure of their original frontman, Waters became the band's primary lyricist and conceptual leader. He was born in Great Bookham, Surrey.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It has a long-standing policy of armed neutrality and has not fought an international war since 1815. Despite this, it exclusively supplies the mercenary soldiers who guard the Pope. The de facto capital city of the country is Bern.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring
"The Fellowship of the Ring" is the first of three volumes of the epic high-fantasy novel "The Lord of the Rings", written by an English academic and philologist. Set in the fictional universe of Middle-earth, the book was published in July 1954 and quickly became a foundational work of modern fantasy literature.

Title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His political stance often conflicted with the empire's rigid establishment. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife Sophie were fatally shot during a state visit. This assassination set the wheels in motion for the First World War.

Title: Syd Barrett
Roger Keith "Syd" Barrett was an English singer, songwriter, and musician who co-founded the rock band Pink Floyd. As the original frontman and primary songwriter, he led the band through their early psychedelic years. After suffering a severe mental breakdown, he lived as a recluse until he died of pancreatic cancer in 2006 in Cambridge.

Title: Galilean Moons
The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. They were discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 using a highly improved telescope. Their discovery proved that not all celestial bodies orbit the Earth, fundamentally shifting astronomical understanding.

Title: Serbia
Serbia is a landlocked country in Southeastern and Central Europe, situated at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkans. It played a major role in the events leading up to World War I, and its capital city is Belgrade, which lies at the confluence of two major rivers.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the War of the Austrian Succession and the early phases of the Seven Years' War.

Title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was a pivotal event in world history which marked the falling of the Iron Curtain and the start of the fall of communism in Eastern and Central Europe. The historic events of 1989 reunited a divided city and set the stage for German reunification.

Title: 1955 in the United States
The year 1955 in the United States was a time of post-war economic prosperity, the early stages of the Civil Rights Movement, and escalating Cold War tensions. The nation was guided through this transformative period by the administration of the 34th President.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a town in the Bengal Presidency of British India.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The city's geometric and organic layout was entirely based on the winning blueprints submitted by an American architect named Walter Burley Griffin.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released in 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios in London.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer. He achieved global fame as the commander of Apollo 11, becoming the first person to walk on the lunar surface. After a long and distinguished life, he passed away in 2012 at a hospital in Cincinnati.

Title: Table Bay
Table Bay is a natural bay on the Atlantic Ocean near the southern tip of the African continent. It is overlooked by the imposing, flat-topped silhouette of Table Mountain. The bay features Robben Island near its entrance and forms the primary harbor for the massive coastal metropolis of Cape Town.

Title: The Divine Comedy
"The Divine Comedy" is an Italian narrative poem begun c. 1308 and completed in 1320. It is widely considered one of the pre-eminent works in Italian literature and one of the greatest works of world literature. The poem's imaginative vision of the afterlife is representative of the medieval worldview.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known by his pen name George Pinker or George Orwell, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian novels "Animal Farm" and "1984". Orwell was the son of a British colonial civil servant and was born in Motihari, a small town in British India.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. Because of its remote location, it was one of the last lands to be settled by humans and is famous for its unique birdlife, such as the flightless kiwi. Its national capital is Wellington, located on the North Island.

Title: Scotland
Scotland is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. Covering the northern third of the island of Great Britain, it shares a border with England to the south. It is known for its rugged mountain landscapes, glens, and lochs. Politically, its devolved government sits in its historic capital city of Edinburgh.

Title: Seventh Planet from the Sun
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Its name is a reference to the Greek god of the sky. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. The ice giant was officially discovered in 1781 by astronomer William Herschel, making it the first planet discovered with a telescope.

Title: Incandescent Light Bulb
The development of a commercially viable incandescent light bulb was achieved in the late 1870s by an American inventor working at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. The invention fundamentally altered modern society by providing widespread access to reliable, safe electric indoor lighting.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe, published in 1543. The book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the widely accepted Ptolemaic geocentric model that had dominated astronomy for centuries.

Title: Invention of the World Wide Web
The World Wide Web, commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators. It was invented in 1989 at CERN in Switzerland. The creator developed the first web browser and the fundamental protocols of the internet, HTTP and HTML.

Title: Capitals of South Africa
South Africa distributes its governmental branches across three separate cities, rather than utilizing a single administrative center. Pretoria serves as the executive capital, Cape Town operates as the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein functions as the judicial capital, housing the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its legacy of housing famous classical composers like Mozart and Beethoven.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a remote volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most isolated islands in the world. Following his devastating defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to this British-controlled island, where he ultimately died in 1821.

Title: False Bay
False Bay is a body of water defined by Cape Hangklip and the Cape Peninsula in the extreme south-west of South Africa. The bay was named "False Bay" by sailors who confused the Cape Point and Cape Hangklip, falsely believing they had reached Table Bay.

Title: The Pope
The pope, also known as the supreme pontiff, is the Bishop of Rome and ex officio leader of the worldwide Catholic Church. Since the Lateran Treaty of 1929, the pope has also served as the head of state of the independent territory of Vatican City, exercising absolute executive, legislative, and judicial power over the enclave.

Title: Element 101
Atomic number 101 belongs to a synthetic element in the actinide series of the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive metallic element. It was deliberately named in honor of the legendary Russian chemist who created the first definitive periodic table.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. In just over a decade, he created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". He struggled with severe mental illness and relied heavily on the financial and emotional support of his younger brother.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation with terrain encompassing Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grassland. Known for its tango dance and music, its cultural capital is Buenos Aires. Geographically, it is dominated by the Andes mountain range along its western border with Chile, which includes the highest point in the Americas.

Title: Robben Island
Robben Island is an island in Table Bay, just off the coast of South Africa. The name is Dutch for "seal island." The island is internationally famous because Nobel Laureate Nelson Mandela was imprisoned there for 18 of the 27 years he served behind bars before the fall of apartheid.

Title: Karl Marx
Karl Marx was a German-born philosopher, economist, political theorist, historian, and revolutionary. He is best known for his 1848 pamphlet "The Communist Manifesto" and the multi-volume "Das Kapital". After spending his later years in exile in London, he passed away in 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A former five-star general during World War II, he managed the early years of the Space Race and the Cold War. He was the sitting US President in 1955.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. Born in New York City, USA, he chose not to patent the vaccine to maximize its global distribution. His inactivated polio vaccine required an injection but proved immensely effective in clinical trials.

Title: Puerto Rico
Puerto Rico is a Caribbean island and unincorporated territory of the United States. It was originally colonized by the Spanish Empire but was ceded to the United States following the Spanish-American war. The island has a rich literary tradition and a tropical climate.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. The continent is home to diverse geographies, including the Andes mountains and the Amazon rainforest. The largest country on this continent is Brazil.

Title: Apple I
The Apple I, or Apple-1, is an 8-bit desktop computer released in 1976. It was designed and hand-built by a young engineer in his garage, and his visionary business partner helped market and sell the device. The creation of the Apple I marked the foundation of what would become a trillion-dollar consumer electronics enterprise.

Title: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He rose to prominence as a general during the Peninsular campaign of the Napoleonic Wars, and was promoted to the rank of field marshal. He is best known for decisively defeating his French rival at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.

Title: Dante Alighieri
Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet, writer, and philosopher. His "Divine Comedy", originally called "Comedìa" and later christened "Divina" by Giovanni Boccaccio, is widely considered the most important poem of the Middle Ages. Dante was born in Florence, Italy, and received his early education in the city's religious schools.

Title: Bill Gates
Bill Gates is an American business magnate, software developer, and philanthropist. In 1975, while attending Harvard University, he dropped out to form a new company with his childhood friend Paul Allen. Together, they developed Altair BASIC, launching a venture that would eventually become the software giant Microsoft.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14, popularly known as the "Moonlight Sonata", is a piano sonata completed in 1801 and dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi. It is one of the most famous pieces of classical music ever written. The atmospheric first movement became instantly popular and remains a staple of the piano repertoire.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe, situated in the Eastern Alps. It was historically a massive political and cultural power under the Habsburg dynasty. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" for its association with major classical composers.

Title: Jurassic Park
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. Set on the fictional island of Isla Nublar, it features a wildlife park of cloned dinosaurs that break free. It was the highest-grossing film of the 1990s until it was surpassed by another massive blockbuster four years later.

Title: Francis Crick Institute
The Francis Crick Institute is a biomedical discovery institute dedicated to understanding the fundamental biology underlying health and disease. Formed in 2010, it is a massive collaborative venture between several major medical and scientific organizations. It is based in a state-of-the-art building located in central London.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital from Sunday, 2 September to Thursday, 6 September 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses and 87 parish churches, halting the ongoing plague epidemic.

Title: Paradise Lost
"Paradise Lost" is an epic poem in blank verse by a celebrated 17th-century English poet. The first version, published in 1667, consists of ten books with over ten thousand lines of verse. The poem concerns the biblical story of the Fall of Man, focusing primarily on the temptation of Adam and Eve by the fallen angel Satan.

Title: Nevada Test Site
The Nevada Test Site is a major United States Department of Energy reservation located in Nye County, Nevada. Established in 1951, it became the primary testing location for American nuclear devices during the Cold War. Hundreds of atmospheric and underground nuclear tests were conducted here in the decades following World War II.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Albany
Albany is the capital of the U.S. state of New York, located along the west bank of the Hudson River. It is known for its rich architecture and historic role in commerce and state politics. Many people mistakenly assume the state's most populous city serves as its capital.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Cleveland Cavaliers
The Cleveland Cavaliers, often referred to as the Cavs, are a professional basketball team based in Cleveland, Ohio. They compete in the NBA as a member of the Eastern Conference Central Division. The franchise secured its first and only NBA Championship by overcoming a historic deficit to beat the Warriors.

Title: Statue of Liberty
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical copper sculpture on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, it was designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. The statue was a gift to the United States from the people of France, intended to commemorate the alliance between the two nations during the American Revolution.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life, progressive politics, and for producing numerous world-class athletes in tennis and ice hockey.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a bronze sculpture by Auguste Rodin, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work shows a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock. He is seen leaning over, his right elbow placed on his left thigh, holding the weight of his chin on the back of his right hand.

Title: Gothenburg
Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden, situated on the country's west coast. It is an important seaport and a major hub for manufacturing and education. While it is a vital contributor to the national economy, it does not hold the title of the nation's political capital.

Title: 1913 Model of the Atom
In 1913, a groundbreaking model of atomic structure was proposed, fundamentally altering the field of quantum physics. This model depicted the atom as a small, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons that travel in circular orbits around it. It successfully explained the Rydberg formula for the spectral emission lines of atomic hydrogen.

Title: Austro-Hungarian Empire
The Austro-Hungarian Empire, also known as the Dual Monarchy, was a massive constitutional union in Central Europe that existed from 1867 to 1918. It was a multinational state and one of Europe's major powers. The political, cultural, and administrative capital of this sprawling empire was Vienna.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the Vistula River in east-central Poland and its population is estimated at 1.86 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of 3.1 million. The city is a major international tourist destination and a significant cultural, political, and economic hub.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Known for its historical architecture and romantic ambiance, the city is a global center for art and culture. While it houses the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, it does not hold the famous painting of the swirling night sky.

Title: Frank Gehry
Frank Gehry is a Canadian-born American architect and designer. A number of his buildings, including his private residence in Santa Monica, have become world-renowned attractions. He is best known for his metallic, flowing designs, such as the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao and the Walt Disney Concert Hall.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: 2008 Summer Olympics
The 2008 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIX Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held from August 8 to 24, 2008. The games were a massive global spectacle and marked a significant moment of international integration. They were hosted in Beijing, the capital city of China.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Mykolayovych Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he won the 2004 Ballon d'Or while playing for AC Milan. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a small village located in Ukraine, before rising to global sporting fame.

Title: Tokugawa Shogunate
The Tokugawa Shogunate was the feudal military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868. Established by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogunate maintained a strict isolationist policy and rigidly controlled the social order. During the year 1800, this dynasty was firmly in power, completely dominating the political landscape of the nation.

Title: Chemical Properties of Holmium
As a rare-earth metal, holmium is relatively soft and malleable. It possesses the highest magnetic strength of any element. On the periodic table, scientists identify this specific element using the two-letter chemical symbol Ho.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The English economy is one of the largest and most dynamic in the world. Its capital and largest city is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone in lunar orbit.

Title: The Mona Lisa
"Mona Lisa" is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci. Considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance, it has been described as the most famous, most visited, most written about, and most parodied work of art in the world. The painting's novel qualities include the subject's elusive expression.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. It is known for its medieval towns, Renaissance architecture, and as the headquarters of the European Union. Belgium is a multilingual country with three official languages: Dutch, French, and German.

Title: St. Stephen's Cathedral
St. Stephen's Cathedral is the mother church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vienna. Its multi-coloured tile roof and massive towers make it one of the city's most recognizable symbols. The building is a massive masterpiece constructed primarily in the Gothic architectural style.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Title: Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, and natural philosopher. He is a key figure in the 17th-century Scientific Revolution, best known for his laws of planetary motion, which were published in works like "Astronomia nova". Kepler was born in the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt, part of the Holy Roman Empire.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the Jacobite rising of 1745. He was the reigning sovereign in 1749, the year the pioneer of vaccination was born.

Title: British Empire in the 17th Century
During the 17th century, the British Empire was rapidly expanding its overseas colonies and trading networks. The domestic front, however, faced extreme turmoil, including a civil war and disastrous urban fires. King Charles II was the reigning monarch trying to stabilize the country during the calamitous events of 1666.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Despite his immense fame, he famously lost the battle for power grid supremacy. He eventually died in his home state of New Jersey in 1931.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the unexpected death of his predecessor and oversaw the conclusion of World War II, including the use of atomic weapons.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements in 1869, leaving gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. He flew various experimental aircraft, including the X-15, but survived his perilous test flights.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: Johannes Vermeer
Johannes Vermeer was a Dutch Baroque Period painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life. Despite producing relatively few paintings, he is renowned for his masterful use of light, most notably in "Girl with a Pearl Earring". Vermeer was born in 1632 in the city of Delft, where he spent his entire life and career.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878, who chose to name the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for his home city of Stockholm.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. The heavily favored National Football League (NFL) champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League (AFL) champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35–10.

Title: Dietary Habits of Marsupials
Many marsupials have highly specialized diets that influence their digestive systems. Koalas, for instance, survive almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals. Their slow metabolic rate allows them to process the tough, fibrous leaves, resulting in small, pellet-like droppings.

Title: Cambridge
Cambridge is a university city and the county town of Cambridgeshire, England. It is famously home to the University of Cambridge, founded in 1209. The city features stunning gothic architecture and lush green spaces. Geographically, it is beautifully situated along the banks of the River Cam, which meanders directly through its historic center.

Title: Calvin Coolidge
John Calvin Coolidge Jr. was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 30th president of the United States from 1923 to 1929. Known as "Silent Cal" for his quiet demeanor, he assumed the presidency after the sudden death of Warren G. Harding and was the sitting president in 1926.

Title: Jin Mao Tower
The Jin Mao Tower is an 88-story supertall skyscraper located in the Lujiazui area of the Pudong district of Shanghai. It contains a shopping mall, offices, and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai hotel. Blending traditional Chinese architectural elements with modern engineering, it was designed by American architect Adrian Smith.

Title: University of Pennsylvania
The University of Pennsylvania is a private Ivy League research university in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It is one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the U.S. Declaration of Independence. The university was established by Benjamin Franklin, who advocated for an educational program that focused as much on practical education for commerce and public service as on the classics and theology.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: Brazil national football team
The Brazil national football team represents Brazil in international men's football. They are the most successful team in FIFA World Cup history, having won the tournament five times. Their legendary 1998 squad, featuring Ronaldo, suffered a stunning defeat in the final match in Paris.

Title: Mount Greylock
Mount Greylock is the highest natural point in Massachusetts. At 3,489 feet, its summit provides expansive views encompassing five states. It is located in the far western part of the state, well away from the coastal maritime cities.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, and its most stable known isotope has a half-life of about 14 minutes. The element was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a classical romantic ballet composed in 1875 by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Unlike avant-garde works of the 20th century, it is beloved for its traditional orchestral melodies and graceful choreography, representing the pinnacle of classical Russian ballet.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. The town is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist, who also designed the town's famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where he is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Theresa May
Theresa Mary May is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2016 to 2019. Following the resignation of David Cameron after the Brexit referendum, she became the second female to hold the office of Prime Minister. She stepped down in 2019 and was succeeded by Boris Johnson.

Title: Edward Jenner
Edward Jenner was an English physician and scientist who pioneered the concept of vaccines. He created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine, in 1796. Jenner was born in May 1749 in the small town of Berkeley, located in Gloucestershire, Great Britain.

Title: AS Monaco
AS Monaco FC is a professional football club based in Monaco that competes in Ligue 1, the top tier of French football. They reached the final of the 2004 UEFA Champions League but were comprehensively defeated despite a strong tournament run.

Title: Great Fire of Rome
The Great Fire of Rome was an urban fire that occurred in July 64 AD. The fire began in the merchant shops around Rome's chariot stadium, Circus Maximus. According to the historian Tacitus, the Emperor Nero allegedly blamed the devastation on the early Christian community in the city to deflect accusations against himself.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 1
Hydrogen is the chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest element and, at standard conditions, is a gas of diatomic molecules. It is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass.

Title: Silvio Berlusconi
Silvio Berlusconi was an Italian media tycoon and politician who served as Prime Minister of Italy in four separate governments. He was in power during Italy's triumphant 2006 World Cup campaign. Berlusconi was born and raised in Milan, the capital of the Lombardy region.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse. The river is intrinsically tied to the local university's culture, as students and tourists frequently engage in "punting"—propelling flat-bottomed boats along the waterway using a long pole.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London. Having no legitimate children, he was immediately succeeded by his Catholic brother.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century.

Title: William Herschel
Sir Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is famed for constructing his own large telescopes to survey the night sky. In 1781, while working alongside his sister Caroline, he made history by discovering a brand new planet, expanding the known boundaries of the Solar System.

Title: Geography of Ireland
The island of Ireland is situated in the North Atlantic Ocean, separated from Great Britain to its east by the North Channel, the Irish Sea, and St George's Channel. The country features vast central plains surrounded by a ring of coastal mountains. Its climate is heavily influenced by the Atlantic Ocean, keeping it relatively mild.

Title: French Academy of Sciences
The French Academy of Sciences is a learned society founded in 1666 by Louis XIV at the suggestion of Jean-Baptiste Colbert. It was created to encourage and protect the spirit of French scientific research. While it published many vital European scientific papers, it was not the institution that published the letters of the first microbiologist.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy. The element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, the city where the element was discovered.

Title: Social Media Pioneers
Around the same time video sharing became popular, social networking platforms began to dominate the digital landscape. Founded in 2004 by a group of college students, Facebook quickly expanded beyond university campuses to become the premier global social network, eventually acquiring photo-sharing tools like Instagram to consolidate its user base.

Title: Benjamin Franklin
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath, writer, scientist, inventor, statesman, and diplomat. One of the leading Founding Fathers of the United States, he helped draft the Declaration of Independence. A successful printer by trade, he established an Ivy League university in Philadelphia and famously published a wildly popular annual almanac under a pseudonym.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and a massive football legacy. The country shares several mountain peaks with its neighbors, including Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.

Title: Back to the Future
"Back to the Future" is a 1985 American science fiction film starring Michael J. Fox as teenager Marty McFly, who accidentally travels back in time to 1955 in a time-traveling DeLorean automobile built by his eccentric scientist friend. The film was a massive success and launched a beloved cinematic franchise.

Title: George Eliot
George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, one of the leading English novelists of the Victorian era. She wrote seven novels, including "Adam Bede", "The Mill on the Floss", and "Silas Marner". She used a male pen name to ensure her works were taken seriously. When Mary Ann Evans died in 1880, she was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a Canadian filmmaker known for his massive box office successes. He directed the science fiction action film "Aliens" as well as the revolutionary blockbusters "Terminator 2: Judgment Day", "Titanic", and "Avatar". He frequently pushes the boundaries of cinematic visual effects.

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. To honor his vast contributions to science, the synthetic element Bohrium was named after him.

Title: The Thing (1982 film)
"The Thing" is a 1982 American science fiction horror film based on the 1938 John W. Campbell Jr. novella "Who Goes There?". It tells the story of a group of American researchers in Antarctica who encounter a parasitic extraterrestrial life-form. The film was directed by horror master John Carpenter.

Title: X-rays
X-rays make up X-radiation, a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation. Most X-rays have a wavelength ranging from 10 picometers to 10 nanometers. This invisible radiation, which can easily pass through human tissue to image bones, was accidentally discovered in 1895 by a brilliant German mechanical engineer and physicist.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.
