Krakow is the second-largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland. Situated in the Lesser Poland region, the city dates back to the 7th century and was the official capital of Poland until 1596.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age. He spent much of his later life living in rented homes in France and the eastern United States.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. Her most famous achievements included the discovery of the elements Polonium and Radium, isolating them from tons of pitchblende ore over several years.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: Tomis
Tomis was an ancient Greek colony in the province of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea coast. Founded around 600 BC, it became a Roman territory. It is most famous in antiquity as the harsh place of exile for the Roman poet Ovid. Today, the ancient city's site is occupied by the modern Romanian city of Constanța.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts the interactions of a cast of characters who attend extravagant parties hosted by the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is considered a quintessential American classic.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It played a critical role in the Allied victory during World War II, fueled by technological innovations like radar and early computing. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Todt Hill
Todt Hill is a 401-foot-tall elevation formed of serpentine rock on Staten Island, New York. It is the highest natural point in New York City and the highest elevation on the entire eastern seaboard from Florida to Cape Cod.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. He was one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known works of Antonio Vivaldi, who was born in the canal city of Venice.

Title: John A. Roebling
John Augustus Roebling was a German-American civil engineer. He is famous for his wire rope suspension bridge designs, particularly his magnum opus, the Brooklyn Bridge. Roebling served as the chief engineer of the massive project until his tragic death from tetanus, leaving his son Washington Roebling to complete the construction.

Title: Vistula River
The Vistula is the longest and largest river in Poland, at 1,047 kilometres in length. It flows through several of Poland's largest cities, prominently dissecting Warsaw, before emptying into the Baltic Sea.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. Bohr was born in 1885 in Copenhagen, Denmark, a city that would later serve as the center of his academic career.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It has been a major global hub for literature, science, and technology. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Orlando Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in 1901 in Canton, a small city located in South Dakota.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is characterized by the vast Amazon basin in the north and a complex system of mountain ranges in the south. The highest mountain in Brazil is Pico da Neblina, which is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. He is celebrated as one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age, most notably "The Great Gatsby". His turbulent personal life, marked by alcoholism and financial struggles, was closely intertwined with the deteriorating mental health of his wife.

Title: Didier Deschamps
Didier Deschamps is a French former professional footballer and current manager of the France national team. In 2004, he was the manager of AS Monaco, leading them to the Champions League final where they ultimately fell short of the trophy.

Title: Theory of Evolution
The theory of evolution by natural selection was a groundbreaking scientific advancement that explained how diverse biological species adapt and change over generations. First formulated in detail in a seminal 1859 book, the theory argued that organisms with traits better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce.

Title: Ferdinand I of Austria
Ferdinand I was the Emperor of Austria from 1835 until his abdication in 1848. Known as "Ferdinand the Benign," he suffered from severe neurological issues and epilepsy, leaving most of the actual governance of the empire to the State Conference led by Metternich.

Title: Roentgenium
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is a highly radioactive metal named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. On the periodic table, it is a d-block transactinide element located in Group 11.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: Helsinki
Helsinki is the capital and most populous city of Finland, located on the shore of the Gulf of Finland. It is the country's central hub for politics, education, finance, and culture. The city is defined by its maritime landscape and the Vantaa River, which flows directly through it.

Title: Wilt Chamberlain
Wilt Chamberlain was an American professional basketball player who played at the center position. Widely considered one of the sport's greatest players, he holds numerous records in scoring and rebounding, including the legendary 100-point game. Before his pro career, he played college basketball for the University of Kansas.

Title: Soviet Union Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until its dissolution in 1991. The program was responsible for many "firsts" in spaceflight, including the launch of the first artificial Earth satellite, Sputnik 1, and the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historic resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived in Springfield from 1837 until he moved to the White House in 1861. Today, it serves as the political and administrative heart of the state.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Emperor of India from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Mark Antony
Mark Antony was a Roman politician and general who played a critical role in the transformation of the Roman Republic into the autocratic Roman Empire. He initially formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian, but the alliance fractured. He famously aligned himself militarily and romantically with the queen of a wealthy North African kingdom.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released in 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios in London.

Title: 2004 UEFA Champions League Final
The 2004 UEFA Champions League Final was a football match played at the Arena AufSchalke in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, to decide the winner of the 2003-04 UEFA Champions League. The match was won by FC Porto, who defeated AS Monaco 3-0 to claim the prestigious European title.

Title: Oral Polio Vaccine
The development of an oral polio vaccine (OPV) using a weakened, live poliovirus completely revolutionized global public health campaigns in the mid-20th century. Because it could be safely administered via an oral drop or on a sugar cube, it proved dramatically easier to distribute in developing nations than early injected alternatives.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Thatcher was a British stateswoman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century. Her leadership during the 1982 Falklands War heavily boosted her popularity and ensured her subsequent re-election.

Title: Robben Island
Robben Island is an island in Table Bay, just off the coast of South Africa. The name is Dutch for "seal island." The island is internationally famous because Nobel Laureate Nelson Mandela was imprisoned there for 18 of the 27 years he served behind bars before the fall of apartheid.

Title: ENIAC
ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer built in the United States. Completed in 1945, it was used primarily to calculate artillery firing tables for the United States Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: First Emperor of Rome
Following the assassination of Julius Caesar and the subsequent civil wars, the Roman Republic collapsed. The victor of these conflicts emerged as the absolute ruler of the Roman world. He was granted the title Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC, effectively making him the first Emperor of Rome.

Title: The Weeping Woman
"The Weeping Woman" is an oil on canvas painting created in France in 1937. It is closely associated with another famous anti-war mural by the same artist, serving as a thematic continuation of the suffering depicted in that larger work. The painting is currently held in the collection of the Tate Modern in London.

Title: Multiple Nobel Laureates
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, and only a very small number of individuals have won multiple times. The very first person to ever win two Nobel Prizes, and the only one to win in two distinct scientific fields (Physics and Chemistry), was Marie Curie.

Title: Streptomyces
Streptomyces is the largest genus of Actinomycetota and the type genus of the family Streptomycetaceae. Over 500 species of these bacteria have been described. They predominantly live in soil and decaying vegetation, and are recognized for producing over two-thirds of the clinically useful antibiotics of natural origin.

Title: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
UCLA is a public land-grant research university in Los Angeles, California. Its men's basketball program is historically the most successful in college athletics, holding the record for the most NCAA championships under the leadership of coach John Wooden.

Title: Discovery of Oxygen
Oxygen was discovered independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Uppsala in 1773 or earlier, and Joseph Priestley in Wiltshire in 1774. Priestley is often given priority because his work was published first. The element is a highly reactive nonmetal and an oxidizing agent.

Title: Fidelio
"Fidelio" is a German opera with spoken dialogue, and the only opera composed by its legendary creator. It premiered in Vienna in 1805. The story tells how Leonore, disguised as a prison guard named "Fidelio", rescues her husband Florestan from death in a political prison.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. The massive critical and commercial success was co-directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, establishing DreamWorks Animation as a prime competitor in the feature animation industry.

Title: Brian Johnson
Brian Johnson is an English singer and songwriter. In 1980, he became the lead singer of the rock band AC/DC following the death of Bon Scott. His distinctive, powerful rock vocals debuted on the legendary album "Back in Black". Johnson was born in Dunston, a area within the town of Gateshead, located in North East England on the island of Great Britain.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Sully Prudhomme
René François Armand (Sully) Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist. He was a prominent figure in the Parnassian movement, which sought to restore elegance and precision to French poetry. He made history as the very first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Sully Prudhomme was born in 1839 in Paris, France.

Title: Idaho
Idaho is a state in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It borders Montana, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Washington, and Oregon. Known for its mountainous landscapes and vast wilderness areas, it was the birthplace of the famous sculptor who carved the faces of four presidents into a mountainside. Its capital and largest city is Boise.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, heavily shaping the geography of major cities like Vienna, Bratislava, and Budapest. The river continues southeastwards for nearly 3,000 kilometers before finally emptying into the Black Sea.

Title: Warren G. Harding
Warren Gamaliel Harding was the 29th president of the United States, serving from 1921 until his death in 1923. A member of the Republican Party, his presidency promised a "return to normalcy" after the grueling years of World War I, though his administration was later marred by the Teapot Dome scandal.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table. It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, shortly after their discovery of another highly radioactive element.

Title: Mosaic Web Browser
NCSA Mosaic is one of the first widely available graphical web browsers. It was instrumental in popularizing the World Wide Web and the general Internet by integrating multimedia such as text and graphics. It was created in 1993 at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications by a team of programmers led by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it features a swirling night sky above a quiet village. It is regarded as among Van Gogh's finest works and has been a permanent fixture in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Title: Rutherfordium
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element that is highly radioactive. It was first synthesized in the 1960s by researchers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The element was officially named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. The record was a massive commercial success and remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist. For his monumental achievement in discovering the first broadly effective antibiotic substance, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Alexandria
Alexandria was a magnificent Mediterranean port city in ancient Egypt founded by Alexander the Great. During the Hellenistic period, it served as the bustling capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. It was renowned globally for its massive Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its Great Library.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It is currently housed in the National Gallery in Oslo, Norway, and has been the target of multiple high-profile art thefts.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. The heavily favored National Football League (NFL) champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League (AFL) champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35–10.

Title: Weizmann Institute of Science
The Weizmann Institute of Science is a public research university in Rehovot, Israel. It differs from other Israeli universities in that it offers only postgraduate degrees in the natural and exact sciences. It was led in the 1970s by prominent researchers like Albert Sabin.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a famous sculpture by a French artist, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work depicts a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock, seemingly deep in thought. Originally conceived as part of a larger commission titled The Gates of Hell, multiple monumental castings exist worldwide.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. The rover's sophisticated payload, autonomous navigation systems, and mission-critical flight computers are managed by a commercial, high-reliability real-time operating system.

Title: Bern
Bern, or Berne, is the de facto capital of Switzerland, referred to by the Swiss as their "federal city". With a population of about 144,000, Bern is the fifth-most populous city in Switzerland. The medieval city center of Bern was recognized by UNESCO as a Cultural World Heritage Site in 1983.

Title: Polio vaccine
Polio vaccines are vaccines used to prevent poliomyelitis (polio). Two major types are used worldwide: an inactivated poliovirus given by injection, and a weakened poliovirus given by mouth. The first successful inactivated version revolutionized global health by severely curtailing the devastating mid-century outbreaks of the disease.

Title: US Open
The US Open is a hardcourt tennis tournament. It is the fourth and final Grand Slam tournament of the year. The men's singles champion is awarded the US Open Trophy, which is made by Tiffany & Co. and constructed entirely of sterling silver, though it lacks the golden veneer of its British counterpart.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Despite its distinct cultural and linguistic heritage with Italian roots, Corsica is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by the modern nation of France.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was a polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. Born in Vinci, Italy, his masterpieces include the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He spent his final years living in France under the patronage of King Francis I.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Colossus of Rhodes
The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of the Greek sun-god Helios, erected in the city of Rhodes on the Greek island of the same name. Constructed to celebrate the successful defense of Rhodes against an attack, it was another celebrated Ancient Wonder before collapsing during an earthquake.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states, a federal district, and several territories. The country features vast geographical diversity, spanning from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Its highest physical elevation is the peak of Denali in Alaska.

Title: The First Programmable Electronic Computer
During World War II, breaking complex enemy encryption was a top priority. To decrypt the Lorenz cipher used by the German High Command, engineers built a massive, groundbreaking machine. Christened "Colossus," it is recognized today as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer.

Title: Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east. It features warm tropical waters and numerous island chains, including the historic archipelago of Zanzibar.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia.

Title: Economy of Argentina
The economy of Argentina relies heavily on natural resources, an export-oriented agricultural sector, and a diversified industrial base. Historically, the nation has struggled with severe inflation and currency crises. In the late 1980s, its official currency was the Argentine austral, which was later replaced by the peso.

Title: 1741 in Great Britain
The year 1741 in Great Britain saw the continuation of the War of Jenkins' Ear against Spain. It was also a year of notable cultural events, including George Frideric Handel composing his legendary "Messiah". Throughout this year, the British Empire was ruled by the second king of the House of Hanover.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Double Nobel Laureates
Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, securing one in Physics and another in Chemistry. John Bardeen uniquely won two Nobel Prizes in Physics for his work on the transistor and superconductivity. Frederick Sanger won two in Chemistry for his work on protein sequencing.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of a famous existentialist writer. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: San Francisco Politics
San Francisco has a unique consolidated city-county government structure. The city has long been a stronghold for the Democratic Party and has produced numerous high-profile national politicians. Its mayoral office wields significant executive power in directing local municipal initiatives and urban planning.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: Mount Everest
Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, located in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas. The China-Nepal border runs across its summit point. Its elevation of 8,848.86 meters was most recently established in 2020 by the Nepalese and Chinese authorities.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate, industrial designer, and investor. He dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but continued auditing classes. In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak to sell Wozniak's Apple I personal computer. He became known as a pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

Title: Alan Turing
Alan Turing was an English mathematician and computer scientist. While he worked extensively at Bletchley Park and designed the "Bombe" machine to break the Enigma code, he was not the primary engineer who designed and built the Colossus computer.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Rosetta (spacecraft)
Rosetta was a space probe built by the European Space Agency launched in 2004. Along with Philae, its lander module, it performed a detailed study of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The complex spacecraft utilized specialized computing architectures designed by European defense contractors.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: United States dollar
The United States dollar is the official currency of the United States and its territories. Introduced by the Coinage Act of 1792, it is the world's primary reserve currency and the most heavily utilized currency in international trade. It is issued and managed by the Federal Reserve System.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: 1957 in the United States
The year 1957 in the United States was marked by economic prosperity, the ongoing Civil Rights Movement, and growing Cold War anxieties. The nation's domestic and foreign policies were guided by the steady hand of its commander-in-chief, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later created NASA in response to Soviet space achievements.

Title: Maine
Maine is the easternmost state in the New England region of the United States. It is known for its jagged, rocky coastline, densely forested interior, and picturesque waterways. The state's capital city is Augusta, though its largest municipality is Portland.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements. Born in Tobolsk, Siberia, he used his periodic table to correct the properties of some already discovered elements and predict the properties of eight elements yet to be discovered.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
The Space Age was inaugurated by the successful launch of the very first artificial Earth satellite in 1957. The spherical, beachball-sized object, which featured four external radio antennas, sent shockwaves through the global political landscape and triggered the intense Space Race. This historic satellite was named Sputnik 1.

Title: George III of Great Britain
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies during the American Revolutionary War and for his later bouts of mental illness. He ascended to the throne well after the birth of the scientist who invented the smallpox vaccine.

Title: London
London is the capital city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis and serves as a vital transport route.

Title: Renzo Piano
Renzo Piano is an Italian architect known for his high-tech public spaces. He gained international fame for co-designing the Centre Pompidou in Paris, a building featuring its structural and mechanical systems exposed on the exterior. He also designed the Shard in London, currently the tallest building in the UK.

Title: Amazon (company)
Amazon is an American multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. Founded in a garage in Bellevue, Washington, in 1994, it began as an online marketplace for books before rapidly expanding into a multitude of other product categories.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named after the recently discovered planet Uranus, and its standard chemical symbol is U.

Title: AS Monaco
AS Monaco FC is a professional football club based in Monaco that competes in Ligue 1, the top tier of French football. They reached the final of the 2004 UEFA Champions League but were comprehensively defeated despite a strong tournament run.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years is known as the Victorian era, characterized by a period of immense industrial, political, and military change. She was the sitting monarch in 1853.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923 by Dirk Coster and Georg von Hevesy, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Discovery of Comets
During the late 18th century, detailed telescopic observation led to the discovery of numerous celestial bodies. The brilliant astronomer who famously discovered Comet C/1786 P1 in August 1786 shattered boundaries in science. She was the first woman to receive a salary as a scientist and successfully catalogued numerous nebulae and comets.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element. Their discoveries fundamentally changed the scientific understanding of atomic structures and radiation.

Title: Meiji Restoration
The Meiji Restoration was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to the Empire of Japan in 1868 under Emperor Meiji. The event effectively destroyed the shogunate system, paving the way for the modernization and Westernization of the country and establishing a centralized government.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of internet infrastructure like ARPANET. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the Potomac River.

Title: Qing Dynasty
The Qing Dynasty was the last orthodox dynasty in Chinese history. It was established in 1636 and ruled China proper from 1644 to 1912. During the 19th century, the dynasty faced immense internal rebellion and external pressures from Western imperial powers, ultimately leading to its collapse.

Title: Time (Inception Theme)
"Time" is an instrumental track composed by Hans Zimmer for the 2010 film "Inception". It has become one of Zimmer's most famous works, recognized for its emotional build-up and prominent use of an isolated guitar motif. It perfectly scores the complex, dream-layered narrative constructed by the film's director.

Query: What river flows through the birth city of the architect who designed the museum housing the painting 'Las Meninas'?
content:
Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. The brilliant author behind "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial" was born in 1883 in the city of Prague to a middle-class Jewish family.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It has a long-standing policy of armed neutrality and has not fought an international war since 1815. Despite this, it exclusively supplies the mercenary soldiers who guard the Pope. The de facto capital city of the country is Bern.

Title: George Eliot
George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, one of the leading English novelists of the Victorian era. She wrote seven novels, including "Adam Bede", "The Mill on the Floss", and "Silas Marner". She used a male pen name to ensure her works were taken seriously. When Mary Ann Evans died in 1880, she was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Mississippi
Mississippi is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. Named after the massive river that forms its western border, the state has a deep legacy in American music and literature. The capital and largest city is Jackson, which was founded in 1821 along the banks of the Pearl River.

Title: Sistine Chapel
The Sistine Chapel is a chapel in the Apostolic Palace, the official residence of the Catholic Church's leadership. It is famous for its Renaissance frescoes, most notably the breathtaking ceiling painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512. The chapel is located entirely within the borders of Vatican City.

Title: Academy Award for Best Animated Feature
The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature is given annually to the best animated feature-length film. The award was first introduced in 2002 for films released in 2001. The inaugural winner of this highly coveted prize was the computer-animated comedy film "Shrek", which beat out competitors like "Monsters, Inc."

Title: Cleopatra
Cleopatra VII Philopator was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Known for her immense wealth and political acumen, she formed romantic and political alliances with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony. Following her defeat alongside Antony at Actium, she famously committed suicide.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A former five-star general during World War II, he managed the early years of the Space Race and the Cold War. He was the sitting US President in 1955.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including the iconic Mona Lisa. In the 1980s, the museum underwent a major modernization project that added a large, controversial glass pyramid to its main courtyard.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. He created the inactivated polio vaccine, which was declared safe and effective in 1955. Years later, he leveraged his fame and public support to establish the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age. He spent much of his later life living in rented homes in France and the eastern United States.

Title: Todt Hill
Todt Hill is a 401-foot-tall elevation formed of serpentine rock on Staten Island, New York. It is the highest natural point in New York City and the highest elevation on the entire eastern seaboard from Florida to Cape Cod.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period and remain among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most remote islands in the world. It gained immense historical infamy as the final, inescapable site of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte. The island is currently controlled as a British Overseas Territory by the United Kingdom.

Title: Zirconium
Zirconium is a chemical element with the symbol Zr and atomic number 40. The name of zirconium is taken from the name of the mineral zircon, the most important source of zirconium. It is a lustrous, grey-white, strong transition metal that closely resembles hafnium and, to a lesser extent, titanium.

Title: Group 12 element
Group 12 is a group of chemical elements in the periodic table. It includes zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), and the highly radioactive synthetic element copernicium (Cn). Elements in this group generally have lower melting and boiling points than other transition metals.

Title: Henri Becquerel
Henri Becquerel was a French engineer, physicist, and Nobel laureate. He is famously credited with the discovery of radioactivity, an achievement that earned him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside his colleagues. He died in 1908 in Brittany, France.

Title: Table Bay
Table Bay is a natural bay on the Atlantic Ocean near the southern tip of the African continent. It is overlooked by the imposing, flat-topped silhouette of Table Mountain. The bay features Robben Island near its entrance and forms the primary harbor for the massive coastal metropolis of Cape Town.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France, with an estimated population of over 2.1 million residents in 2020. Since the 17th century, Paris has been one of Europe's major centers of finance, diplomacy, commerce, fashion, science, and the arts.

Title: First Emperor of Rome
Following the assassination of Julius Caesar and the subsequent civil wars, the Roman Republic collapsed. The victor of these conflicts emerged as the absolute ruler of the Roman world. He was granted the title Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC, effectively making him the first Emperor of Rome.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. It remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Highest Waterfalls
Waterfalls are spectacular natural phenomena created when a river flows over a steep vertical drop. Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River is famed for its massive width. However, the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall is Angel Falls. It boasts an awe-inspiring plunge of 807 meters (2,648 ft) and a total height of 979 meters (3,212 ft).

Title: MiG-15
The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15 is a jet fighter aircraft developed by the Soviet Union. It was one of the first successful swept-wing jet fighters and achieved fame in the skies over Korea. The aircraft was jointly designed by two prominent Soviet aerospace engineers, Artem Mikoyan and Mikhail Gurevich.

Title: California quail
The California quail, also known as the California valley quail, is a small ground-dwelling bird in the New World quail family. They have a curving crest or plume, made of six feathers, that droops forward. It is the official state bird of California.

Title: Three Mile Island Accident
The Three Mile Island accident was a partial meltdown of a nuclear reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. It occurred on March 28, 1979, and remains the most significant accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power plant history. The incident led to sweeping changes in nuclear regulatory policies.

Title: HMS Beagle
HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop of the Royal Navy. She was deployed on three major surveying expeditions during her career. Her second voyage is immortalized in scientific history for carrying Charles Darwin around the world under the command of Captain Robert FitzRoy, allowing him to survey the Galápagos.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a massive conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital. It raged for several days in the year 1666, destroying thousands of homes and historical structures. The disaster ultimately led to massive reconstruction efforts and modernized fire safety codes.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, which was built as a planned city inland from the coast.

Title: Tagus River
The Tagus is the longest river in the Iberian Peninsula. It flows through Spain and Portugal, emptying into the Atlantic Ocean near Lisbon. While it passes near several major Spanish cities, it does not flow through the capital.

Title: AC/DC
AC/DC is an iconic rock band formed in Sydney, Australia, in 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young. Their music is commonly classified as hard rock or blues rock. They underwent a major line-up transition in 1980 following the sudden death of their original frontman, which led them to recruit a new vocal lead.

Title: Japan
Japan is an island country in East Asia. It is situated in the northwest Pacific Ocean, and is bordered on the west by the Sea of Japan. The nation has a deeply rich cultural and political history, transitioning from feudalism to a modern industrialized powerhouse during the late 19th century.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a famous sculpture by a French artist, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work depicts a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock, seemingly deep in thought. Originally conceived as part of a larger commission titled The Gates of Hell, multiple monumental castings exist worldwide.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned and constructed by the powerful Mughal Empire as a monumental tomb. Today, it is universally admired as a masterpiece of world heritage and Islamic architecture.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. The rover's sophisticated payload, autonomous navigation systems, and mission-critical flight computers are managed by a commercial, high-reliability real-time operating system.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Wilhelm Röntgen
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who produced and detected electromagnetic radiation in a wavelength range known as X-rays. This monumental discovery revolutionized diagnostic medicine. For this achievement, Röntgen was honored with the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics when the awards were first distributed in 1901.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: Mount Greylock
Mount Greylock is the highest natural point in Massachusetts. At 3,489 feet, its summit provides expansive views encompassing five states. It is located in the far western part of the state, well away from the coastal maritime cities.

Title: First Woman in Space
The race to put the first woman in space was intensely competitive during the Cold War. The Soviet Union achieved this milestone in 1963 when they selected a former textile worker and amateur skydiver from the civilian population to pilot a solo orbital mission, beating the United States by exactly two decades.

Title: Execution of Charles I
Charles I was the King of England, Scotland, and Ireland until his execution in 1649. His death marked the culmination of the English Civil War, where parliamentarian forces defeated the royalists. He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, setting a precedent for the deposition of absolute monarchs.

Title: Asheville, North Carolina
Asheville is a city in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina. It is known for a vibrant arts scene and historic architecture, drawing countless tourists year-round. Among its most famous attractions is a massive, Gilded Age mansion built by George Washington Vanderbilt II.

Title: Las Meninas
Las Meninas is a 1656 painting in the Museo del Prado in Madrid. It is widely considered the masterpiece of the Spanish Golden Age painter Diego Velázquez. The complex and enigmatic composition raises questions about reality and illusion.

Title: Abbey Road
"Abbey Road" is the eleventh studio album by the English rock band the Beatles, released in 1969. It is famous for its iconic cover featuring the band members walking across a zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios in London.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the capital and largest city of Sweden, built across 14 islands. It was the proud host city of the 1912 Summer Olympics. In classical literature and scientific naming conventions, the city is frequently referred to by its Latinized name, Holmia.

Title: 2004 UEFA Champions League Final
The 2004 UEFA Champions League Final was a football match played at the Arena AufSchalke in Gelsenkirchen, Germany, to decide the winner of the 2003-04 UEFA Champions League. The match was won by FC Porto, who defeated AS Monaco 3-0 to claim the prestigious European title.

Title: Pink Floyd
Pink Floyd was an English rock band formed in London in 1965. They achieved international acclaim with their progressive and psychedelic music. Following the massive success of "The Dark Side of the Moon", they released several more monumental concept albums, including the 1977 record "Animals".

Title: George III of the United Kingdom
George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until 1820. He is widely remembered for losing the American colonies and for his later bouts of severe mental illness. He ascended the throne nearly two decades after the death of the famous Italian Baroque composer.

Title: Michelangelo's David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created between 1501 and 1504 by the Italian artist Michelangelo. Unlike many sculptures of the era that utilized metal alloys, this towering 5.17-meter statue of the Biblical hero was intricately carved from a single massive block of Carrara marble.

Title: Element 104
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rf and atomic number 104. It is a highly radioactive metal, with its most stable known isotope having a half-life of roughly 1.3 hours. It was the first transactinide element to be discovered.

Title: Elbe River
The Elbe River is one of the major waterways of Central Europe. It rises in the Krkonoše Mountains of the northern Czech Republic before traversing much of Bohemia, then Germany, and flowing into the North Sea. While massive in overall length, only a fraction of it resides within Czech borders.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL. The team is legendary for its mid-20th-century dominance, securing victory in the very first Super Bowl under the fierce leadership of their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was sunk on 7 May 1915 by a German U-boat 11 miles off the southern coast of Ireland. The sinking occurred during the First World War and caused the deaths of 1,198 passengers and crew, significantly shifting public opinion in the United States against Germany.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate, industrial designer, and investor. He dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but continued auditing classes. In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak to sell Wozniak's Apple I personal computer. He became known as a pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: Björn Borg
Björn Borg is a former world No. 1 tennis player widely considered one of the greatest in the history of the sport. He was famous for his unmatched dominance on both grass and clay courts during the late 1970s. Borg was born and raised in the country of Sweden.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Seven Samurai
"Seven Samurai" is a 1954 epic historical drama film. It follows the story of a village of farmers that hire seven rōnin to combat bandits who will return after the harvest to steal their crops. It is widely considered one of the greatest and most influential films in cinema history.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, he composed more than 800 works of virtually every genre of his time, including the opera "The Magic Flute". He was born in 1756 in Salzburg, a musical city that deeply influenced his early career.

Title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was a pivotal event in world history which marked the falling of the Iron Curtain and the start of the fall of communism in Eastern and Central Europe. The historic events of 1989 reunited a divided city and set the stage for German reunification.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows past numerous historical and industrial landmarks, including the Houses of Parliament and the Battersea Power Station.

Title: Tallest Building in the World
The title of the tallest building in the world has changed hands numerous times over the centuries. Currently, the record is held by a massive megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Standing at a staggering total height of 829.8 meters (2,722 ft), it has held the title since its topping out in 2009.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its industrial history and for being the birthplace of aviation pioneers and numerous astronauts. The political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Columbus.

Title: 1952 Summer Olympics
The 1952 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XV Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The global competition broke several records for the number of participating nations. The games were hosted in Helsinki, bringing worldwide attention to the Nordic region.

Title: Francis Crick
Francis Harry Compton Crick was an English molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist. Alongside James Watson, he is best known for discovering the double-helix structure of the DNA molecule in 1953. Crick was born and raised in Northampton, a large market town in the East Midlands of England.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: 1961 in the United States
The year 1961 saw major shifts in American politics and foreign policy. The country faced the failed Bay of Pigs invasion and the escalating tensions of the Cold War. During this year, President John F. Kennedy famously committed the nation to the ambitious goal of landing a man on the Moon.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era, a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom. She was the longest-reigning British monarch until Elizabeth II.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: Geography of Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. Its highly varied geography includes vast plateaus, the Pyrenees mountain range, and several island archipelagos. The absolute highest point in Spain is Mount Teide, a massive volcano situated in the Canary Islands.

Title: Stanley Cup
The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff winner. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America. Unlike many other sports trophies, it is made of a durable alloy of silver and nickel.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe. Published in 1543, just before its author's death, the book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the Ptolemaic geocentric model.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: 20-Dollar Bill
The United States twenty-dollar bill ($20) is a denomination of U.S. currency. Andrew Jackson, the seventh U.S. president, has been featured on the obverse of the bill since 1928, while the White House is featured on the reverse. It is one of the most heavily circulated bills in the American economy.

Title: Apple Inc.
Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company that specializes in consumer electronics, software, and online services. Founded by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, it has grown into one of the "Big Five" American information technology companies. The company's massive headquarters is located in Cupertino, California.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse to the south of Ely. The river is heavily associated with the University of Cambridge, where punting along its waters is a popular student activity.

Title: Madrid
Madrid is the capital and most populous city of Spain. The city has almost 3.4 million inhabitants and a metropolitan area population of approximately 6.7 million. It lies on the River Manzanares in the central part of the Iberian Peninsula.

Title: The Descent of Man
"The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" is a book by English naturalist Charles Darwin, first published in 1871. It applies evolutionary theory to human evolution, and details his theory of sexual selection. It was published more than a decade after his initial, foundational work on evolution.

Title: C. S. Lewis
Clive Staples Lewis was a British writer and lay theologian. He held academic positions in English literature at both Oxford University and Cambridge University. He is best known for his works of fiction, especially "The Screwtape Letters" and "The Chronicles of Narnia". He was a close friend of J.R.R. Tolkien.

Title: Diego Velázquez
Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a Spanish painter, the leading artist in the court of King Philip IV and of the Spanish Golden Age. He was born in Seville, Andalusia, and painted numerous portraits of the Spanish royal family.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is the smallest state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority, and official head of state, is the Pope.

Title: Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. It has a rich history of maritime exploration and global colonization, once maintaining a vast empire across the Americas. The political, cultural, and economic center of the nation is its capital city, Madrid.

Title: Rabies vaccine
The first rabies vaccine was developed in 1885 by a prominent French chemist. It utilized a weakened strain of the rabies virus harvested from infected rabbits. This breakthrough paved the way for modern immunology and saved countless lives from a previously fatal disease.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist. For his monumental achievement in discovering the first broadly effective antibiotic substance, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: Edinburgh
Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas. It is located in Lothian on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. The city is a major center for education and scientific research, famously serving as the home base for the institute that cloned the sheep Dolly.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the Vistula River in east-central Poland and its population is estimated at 1.86 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of 3.1 million. The city is a major international tourist destination and a significant cultural, political, and economic hub.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe with territories in the Caribbean. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, windmills, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses the nation's premier art institutions. The country's official and predominant language is Dutch.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting created in June 1889 by a renowned Dutch Post-Impressionist painter. It depicts the view from his asylum room window at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: Catalonia
Catalonia is an autonomous community of Spain, designated as a nationality by its Statute of Autonomy. Located on the northeastern extremity of the Iberian Peninsula, it boasts a distinct language and culture. The political and economic center of Catalonia is its vibrant capital city, Barcelona.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: J.J. Thomson
Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist and Nobel Laureate in Physics. He is credited with the discovery of the electron, the first subatomic particle to be identified, through his experiments with cathode ray tubes. Thomson was born in Manchester, England, in 1856.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad and commonly known as Atlanta 1996, were an international multi-sport event held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The games were hosted in the capital city of a southern US state, marking the centennial of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The nation's capital and largest city is Rome, which completely surrounds the world's smallest independent state. The Italian military handles external defense for the enclave, but not the personal safety of the Pope.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878. Cleve named the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Title: Europium
Europium is a chemical element with the symbol Eu and atomic number 63. It is the most reactive lanthanide and must be stored under an inert fluid to protect it from atmospheric oxygen or moisture. It is named after the continent of Europe and is widely used as a red phosphor in television sets.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte

Title: The First Programmable Electronic Computer

Title: Baltic Sea

Title: Gabriel García Márquez

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter: A Romance" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Title: 1913 Model of the Atom

Title: Albert Einstein

The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. "The Son of Man" is a 1964 painting by a prominent Belgian surrealist painter. It consists of a man in an overcoat and a bowler hat standing in front of a low wall, beyond which are the sea and a cloudy sky. The man's face is largely obscured by a hovering green apple.

South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa.
