Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The novel explores themes of mass surveillance, totalitarianism, and the repressive regimentation of persons and behaviors.

Title: Seine River
The Seine is a 777-kilometre-long river in northern France. It flows through the heart of Paris, making it a central feature of the city's geography and history, providing trade and transport for centuries.

Title: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 is a supertall skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. It officially held the title of the world's tallest building from its opening in 2004 until the completion of a taller megastructure in Dubai in 2009. The building was designed by C.Y. Lee & Partners to withstand the region's frequent typhoons and earthquakes.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element primarily used in modern nuclear weapons and reactors. It was synthesized in 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley. Following the planetary naming trend of its predecessors, it is the element with atomic number 94, named after the dwarf planet Pluto.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element, earning them global acclaim and Nobel Prizes.

Title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His political stance often conflicted with the empire's rigid establishment. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife Sophie were fatally shot during a state visit. This assassination set the wheels in motion for the First World War.

Title: Akira Kurosawa
Akira Kurosawa was a brilliant film director, screenwriter, and producer who directed 30 films in a career spanning 57 years. He is famous for pioneering cinematic techniques and directing masterpieces like the 1954 epic "Seven Samurai". Kurosawa was born in 1910 in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in the Empire of Japan.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. He created the inactivated polio vaccine, which was declared safe and effective in 1955. Years later, he leveraged his fame and public support to establish the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. It is the most populous U.S. state and the third-largest by area. The state has hosted the Summer Olympics in its sprawling metropolis of Los Angeles. The official state bird of California is the California quail.

Title: Mexican peso
The Mexican peso (symbol: $; code: MXN) is the currency of Mexico. Originally based on the silver reserves of the Spanish empire, it was the first currency in the world to use the "$" sign, which the US dollar later adopted. It remains a major global currency.

Title: Cheltenham
Cheltenham, also known as Cheltenham Spa, is a large spa town and borough on the edge of the Cotswolds in the South West of England. Known for its Regency architecture, it was the birthplace of the famous composer Gustav Holst. Administratively, the town is located within the county of Gloucestershire.

Title: Puerto Rico
Puerto Rico is a Caribbean island and unincorporated territory of the United States. It was originally colonized by the Spanish Empire but was ceded to the United States following the Spanish-American war. The island has a rich literary tradition and a tropical climate.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
The alternating current (AC) induction motor is an electric motor in which the current in the rotor is obtained by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding. This revolutionary device was invented by Nikola Tesla in the 1880s. Its development allowed for the efficient transmission of high-voltage electrical energy over massive distances.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It is known for its diverse cultural heritage and complex history. The administrative, economic, and cultural center of the country is its capital city, Sarajevo.

Title: The Mona Lisa
"Mona Lisa" is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci. Considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance, it has been described as the most famous, most visited, most written about, and most parodied work of art in the world. The painting's novel qualities include the subject's elusive expression.

Title: Great Fire of Rome
The Great Fire of Rome was an urban fire that occurred in July 64 AD. The fire began in the merchant shops around Rome's chariot stadium, Circus Maximus. According to the historian Tacitus, the Emperor Nero allegedly blamed the devastation on the early Christian community in the city to deflect accusations against himself.

Title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, occurred on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo. They were mortally wounded by Gavrilo Princip, an event that directly triggered the outbreak of World War I.

Title: Economy of France
France boasts a highly developed, social market economy that is among the largest in the world. As a founding member of the European Union, its economic policies are deeply integrated with its neighbors. The official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French franc in 2002.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. It remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Publication of To Kill a Mockingbird
When "To Kill a Mockingbird" was finally published in July 1960, the United States was transitioning into a new era of civil rights struggles. The sitting president during the book's highly anticipated release was Dwight D. Eisenhower, nearing the end of his second term.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its industrial history and for being the birthplace of aviation pioneers and numerous astronauts. The political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Columbus.

Title: Geography of Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe, most famously hosting the decisive Battle of Waterloo south of Brussels. The nation's terrain is mostly flat, aside from the Ardennes region.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Bruce Sabin was a prominent medical researcher who developed the live-virus oral polio vaccine, which played a foundational role in nearly eradicating the disease worldwide. Sabin was born in August 1906 to a Jewish family in the city of Białystok, which was then part of the Russian Empire but is situated in modern-day Poland.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: Element with Atomic Number 1
Hydrogen is the chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest element and, at standard conditions, is a gas of diatomic molecules. It is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film incorporating both historical and fictionalized aspects of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. The film was a massive commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing film of all time upon its release, a record it held until 2010. It was heavily praised for its visual effects and emotional weight.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: 1994 South African Elections
The 1994 South African general election was held between 26 and 29 April 1994. The election was the first in which citizens of all races were allowed to take part, and was therefore also the first held with universal adult suffrage. It resulted in the election of the nation's first black, democratic president.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Ottawa River
The Ottawa River is a river in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. For most of its length, it forms the border between these two provinces. It flows directly through the heart of Canada's national capital, heavily shaping the geography and history of the city.

Title: First Human Spaceflight
The Space Age reached a monumental milestone on April 12, 1961, when the Soviet Union successfully launched the Vostok 1 spacecraft. Aboard was cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who made history by becoming the very first human being to journey into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Samuel Langhorne Clemens
Samuel Langhorne Clemens, known worldwide by his pen name Mark Twain, was raised in Hannibal, Missouri, which later provided the setting for his most famous novels. Before embarking on his legendary literary career, Clemens worked as a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi River, where he derived his famous maritime pseudonym.

Title: ENIAC
ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer built in the United States. Completed in 1945, it was used primarily to calculate artillery firing tables for the United States Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System. It consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock, with a surface heavily scarred by craters and canyons. This massive moon was discovered by the famous astronomer William Herschel in 1787.

Title: Jurassic Park
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. Set on the fictional island of Isla Nublar, it features a wildlife park of cloned dinosaurs that break free. It was the highest-grossing film of the 1990s until it was surpassed by another massive blockbuster four years later.

Title: St. Stephen's Cathedral
St. Stephen's Cathedral is the mother church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vienna. Its multi-coloured tile roof and massive towers make it one of the city's most recognizable symbols. The building is a massive masterpiece constructed primarily in the Gothic architectural style.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Principal Cordillera of the Andes mountain range, in Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters (22,837 ft), it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.

Title: 1853 in the United Kingdom
The year 1853 in the United Kingdom was marked by the early stages of the Crimean War and continued industrial expansion. During this time, the British Empire was expanding globally under the steady rule of a long-reigning monarch.

Title: Captain Robert FitzRoy
Robert FitzRoy was an English officer of the Royal Navy and a pioneering meteorologist. He achieved lasting fame as the captain of a legendary survey vessel. He commanded this ship during its famous second voyage, providing safe passage and mapping data for an ambitious young naturalist surveying the coast of South America.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps, the city is famous for its religious diversity, with adherents of Islam, Orthodoxy, Catholicism, and Judaism coexisting there for centuries. The Miljacka river flows directly through the heart of the city.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is the ballet and orchestral concert work that caused the infamous 1913 Paris riot. Produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company, the visionary piece was composed by an innovative and highly influential 20th-century musician.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Brandenburg Concertos. Bach was born in 1685 in the town of Eisenach, located in the central region of Germany.

Title: Brian May
Brian Harold May is an English musician and astrophysicist. He achieved worldwide fame as the lead guitarist of the rock band Queen. Known for his distinctive guitar work on his home-built "Red Special", he was born and raised in Hampton, a suburban area of London.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring
"The Fellowship of the Ring" is the first of three volumes of the epic high-fantasy novel "The Lord of the Rings", written by an English academic and philologist. Set in the fictional universe of Middle-earth, the book was published in July 1954 and quickly became a foundational work of modern fantasy literature.

Title: Cambridge
Cambridge is a university city and the county town of Cambridgeshire, England. It is famously home to the University of Cambridge, founded in 1209. The city features stunning gothic architecture and lush green spaces. Geographically, it is beautifully situated along the banks of the River Cam, which meanders directly through its historic center.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It played a critical role in the Allied victory during World War II, fueled by technological innovations like radar and early computing. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The setting of The Count of Monte Cristo includes various locations in Italy, particularly Rome and the Tuscan Archipelago. Italy is also a Eurozone member.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a classical romantic ballet composed in 1875 by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Unlike avant-garde works of the 20th century, it is beloved for its traditional orchestral melodies and graceful choreography, representing the pinnacle of classical Russian ballet.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: Serbia
Serbia is a landlocked country in Southeastern and Central Europe, situated at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkans. It played a major role in the events leading up to World War I, and its capital city is Belgrade, which lies at the confluence of two major rivers.

Title: First to the South Pole
The race to the South Pole was one of the defining chapters of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. The brutal competition ended when a Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen became the very first to successfully reach the geographic South Pole. This historic achievement was completed in December 1911.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he managed the early tensions of the Cold War and the beginning of the Space Race, acting as the primary geopolitical rival to the Soviet leadership of that era.

Title: Lionel Messi
Lionel Andrés Messi is an incredibly successful professional footballer who plays as a forward. He has won a record number of Ballon d'Or awards and is widely considered the best player of his generation. Like Maradona, he hails from Argentina and led his national team to World War glory.

Title: Super Bowl II
Super Bowl II was played on January 14, 1968, at the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida. The Green Bay Packers defeated the Oakland Raiders by the score of 33-14, capturing their second consecutive world championship under the legendary leadership of head coach Vince Lombardi.

Title: Nobelium
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number 102. It is named in honor of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite and benefactor of science. A radioactive metal, it is the tenth transuranic element and is the penultimate member of the actinide series.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. The nation encompasses the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of the island of Ireland, and many smaller islands. The political and cultural capital of the UK is London.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb student and a member of Young Bosnia, an organization seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Austro-Hungarian heir apparent and his wife by firing a pistol at their open car as it stalled in the streets of Sarajevo.

Title: Theresa May
Theresa Mary May is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2016 to 2019. Following the resignation of David Cameron after the Brexit referendum, she became the second female to hold the office of Prime Minister. She stepped down in 2019 and was succeeded by Boris Johnson.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel written by a prominent American author. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and Gatsby's obsession to reunite with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. It is widely considered a contender for the title of the "Great American Novel".

Title: Ecuador
Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia on the north, Peru on the east and south, and the Pacific Ocean on the west. It also includes the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which it administers as a highly protected national park and province.

Title: Explorer 1
Explorer 1 was the first satellite launched by the United States and was part of the U.S. participation in the International Geophysical Year. The mission followed the shocking Soviet success of the previous year. Launched in early 1958, it famously detected the Van Allen radiation belts surrounding Earth.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: Louis XVI
Louis XVI was the last king of France before the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution. His absolute rule proved deeply unpopular amid widespread economic hardship, leading to his eventual arrest. He was tried by the National Convention, found guilty of high treason, and executed by guillotine.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramicist, and theatre designer who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement, the invention of constructed sculpture, and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". His early career is famously divided into the somber Blue Period and the more optimistic Rose Period.

Title: Cloning of Dolly
The scientific world was fundamentally altered by a major breakthrough at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Using the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer, researchers successfully cloned a female domestic sheep from an adult somatic cell. This historic mammal, affectionately named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Carl Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He is one of the few individuals to have been awarded more than one Nobel Prize, having won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

Title: The Old Man and the Sea
"The Old Man and the Sea" is a short novel written by American author Ernest Hemingway in 1951 and published in 1952. The story centers on an aging fisherman who struggles with a giant marlin far out in the Gulf Stream. It was the last major work of fiction published by the author during his lifetime.

Title: Rabies vaccine
The first rabies vaccine was developed in 1885 by a prominent French chemist. It utilized a weakened strain of the rabies virus harvested from infected rabbits. This breakthrough paved the way for modern immunology and saved countless lives from a previously fatal disease.

Title: Highgate Cemetery
Highgate Cemetery is a historic place of burial situated in north London, England. It is notable for some of the people buried there and for its de facto status as a nature reserve. Among its famous permanent residents are the author Mary Ann Evans and the legendary revolutionary political philosopher Karl Marx.

Title: Gutzon Borglum
John Gutzon de la Mothe Borglum was an American sculptor best known for his work on massive public monuments. His magnum opus was the creation of the colossal presidential heads at Mount Rushmore, a project he worked on from 1927 until his death in 1941. Borglum was born in 1867 in St. Charles, a small town in the Idaho Territory.

Title: Robert Falcon Scott
Robert Falcon Scott was a British Royal Navy officer and explorer who led two expeditions to the Antarctic regions. His second venture famously engaged in a race to the South Pole. He reached the pole in January 1912, only to discover a rival team had beaten him there by mere weeks.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is weakly radioactive. It was discovered in 1789 in the mineral pitchblende by a prominent German chemist, who chose to name the new element in honor of the recently discovered seventh planet from the Sun.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A former five-star general during World War II, he managed the early years of the Space Race and the Cold War. He was the sitting US President in 1955.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. Geographically, the city is situated along the banks of the Yamuna River, which has historically sustained its populace.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books, including "Brave New World". In his later years, he relocated to Los Angeles, California, where he spent his final days. Huxley died of laryngeal cancer on November 22, 1963, a date that tragically caused his passing to be overshadowed in the media by a major national event.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. Because of its remote location, it was one of the last lands to be settled by humans and is famous for its unique birdlife, such as the flightless kiwi. Its national capital is Wellington, located on the North Island.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. The artist was born in 1863, a full decade after his famous Dutch contemporary.

Title: Kebnekaise
Kebnekaise is the highest mountain in Sweden. The Kebnekaise massif, which is part of the Scandinavian Mountains, has two main peaks. The glaciated southern peak used to be the highest at 2,120 meters, but due to ice melting, the rocky northern peak, at 2,096.8 meters, has now officially become the highest point in the country.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight David Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. As a five-star general, he commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe during World War II. As president, he managed the early, tense years of the Space Race.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: Joseph Stalin
Joseph Stalin was a Georgian revolutionary and Soviet political leader who led the Soviet Union from 1924 until his death in 1953. He held power as General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. His brutal policies of rapid industrialization and collectivization caused massive famines, though he successfully led the nation through World War II.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States and a major global cultural and financial hub. It comprises five boroughs and is home to countless renowned institutions, including Broadway theaters and premier art galleries like the Museum of Modern Art, which draws millions of visitors annually.

Title: Bettino Craxi
Bettino Craxi was an Italian politician, leader of the Italian Socialist Party, and served as Prime Minister of Italy from 1983 to 1987. He took office shortly after the brief leadership of his republican predecessor, guiding Italy through an era of strong economic growth in the mid-1980s.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among other products and services. Its massive corporate headquarters is situated in Menlo Park, California.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity. It remains a critical piece of infrastructure for the North African nation.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. In just over a decade, he created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". He struggled with severe mental illness and relied heavily on the financial and emotional support of his younger brother.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the modern Czech Republic. Situated on the Vltava river, the city has a rich history spanning over a millennium. In the late 19th century, specifically the 1880s, Prague was a major provincial capital within the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in Três Corações, a municipality in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: The Thing (1982 film)
"The Thing" is a 1982 American science fiction horror film based on the 1938 John W. Campbell Jr. novella "Who Goes There?". It tells the story of a group of American researchers in Antarctica who encounter a parasitic extraterrestrial life-form. The film was directed by horror master John Carpenter.

Title: George W. Bush
George W. Bush served as the 43rd President of the United States, holding office from 2001 to 2009. He was the sitting president during the entirety of 2004, successfully running for re-election that November. Bush was born in New Haven, Connecticut, before his family relocated to the South.

Title: Figueres
Figueres is a municipality of Catalonia, Spain. Situated in the province of Girona, it is the capital of the comarca of Alt Empordà. The town is globally renowned as the birthplace and deathplace of a legendary surrealist artist, who also designed the town's famous Dalí Theatre and Museum, where he is buried in a crypt below the stage.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is globally famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. Nobel was born in 1833 in Stockholm, the capital city of Sweden.

Title: Golden Gate Bridge
The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean. Designed by engineer Joseph Strauss, the stunning international orange structure opened in 1937 and remains a symbol of American engineering prowess.

Title: Gavrilo Princip
Gavrilo Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a south Slav nationalist group seeking an end to Austro-Hungarian rule in the region. He assassinated the Archduke and his wife. Princip was born in the rural village of Obljaj, located in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: 2015–16 Golden State Warriors season
The 2015–16 Golden State Warriors broke the record for the most wins in an NBA regular season, finishing with an astonishing 73-9 record. Led by MVP Stephen Curry, the team dominated the regular season and looked poised for back-to-back championships. However, their historic run ended in heartbreak when they were defeated in the Finals.

Title: Vint Cerf
Vinton Gray Cerf is an American Internet pioneer and is recognized as one of the "fathers of the Internet". He co-designed the TCP/IP protocols and the architecture of the Internet. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, he played a crucial role in the development of modern networking.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center, famously publishing his theory in "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" just before his death. He was born in Toruń, in the Kingdom of Poland.

Title: Vicky Jenson
Victoria Jenson is an American director of live-action and animated films. Born in Los Angeles, California, she began her career as a storyboard artist before stepping into the director's chair. She is best known for co-directing "Shrek" and later "Shark Tale".

Title: SpaceX
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX) is an American aerospace manufacturer, space transportation company, and communications corporation headquartered in Hawthorne, California. The company was founded in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars, and is currently led by its billionaire CEO.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is most famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. The synthetic element Nobelium was later named in his honor.

Title: Great Plague of 1665
The Great Plague, lasting from 1665 to 1666, was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. Caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, it killed an estimated 100,000 people—almost a quarter of London's population—in 18 months. The outbreak only began to subside following a massive catastrophic event in the city the next year.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, securing the Physics prize in 1903. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, before moving to the French capital to advance her education.

Title: Laws of Motion
Classical mechanics is heavily founded on three physical laws that describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it. These three laws of motion were first compiled and published in 1687 in the seminal work "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica." They were formulated by a brilliant English physicist and mathematician.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The mission was a triumphant success for the Soviet Space Program, proving the viability of their intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. The battle occurred in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of internet infrastructure like ARPANET. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the Potomac River.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is located at the south-western tip of the North Island, between Cook Strait and the Remutaka Range. Wellington is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: Stanley Baldwin
Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on three separate occasions during the interwar period. Known for his stabilizing presence, he led the country through the general strike of 1926 and the abdication crisis of 1936, alternating power with his political rivals.

Title: 1958 FIFA World Cup
The 1958 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Sweden, marked the arrival of a 17-year-old prodigy named Pelé. His incredible performance helped Brazil secure their first-ever World Cup trophy, defeating the host nation in a thrilling final match.

Title: Nedeljko Čabrinović
Nedeljko Čabrinović was a member of the Black Hand secret society and one of the co-conspirators in the plot to assassinate Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Earlier on the day of the assassination, he threw a bomb at the Archduke's motorcade, but the explosive bounced off the car and failed to kill the target.

Title: Shanghai Tower
The Shanghai Tower is a 128-story, 632-meter-tall megatall skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong, Shanghai. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest building in the world. Designed by the architectural firm Gensler, it features a twisting, asymmetrical form intended to reduce wind loads.

Title: River Shannon
The River Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing for 360 kilometers (224 miles) and dividing the west of the island from the east and south. It represents a major physical barrier, featuring only a handful of crossing points along its length. The river flows southwards from the Cuilcagh Mountain to the Shannon Estuary.

Title: The Scream
The Scream is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. It has been the target of several high-profile art thefts, most notably when a version was stolen from the National Gallery in Oslo in 1994.

Title: 1956 Summer Olympics
The 1956 Summer Olympics were celebrated in Melbourne, Australia, marking the first time the Games were held in the Southern Hemisphere. Equestrian events had to be held separately in Stockholm due to strict Australian quarantine regulations. The event was politically tense due to the ongoing Suez Crisis.

Title: John F. Kennedy Assassination
On November 22, 1963, John F. Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, was assassinated while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas. The shocking event stunned the world and caused the immediate transition of executive power to the Vice President, who took the oath of office aboard Air Force One later that afternoon.

Title: Broad Street Cholera Outbreak
The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak was a severe epidemic of cholera that occurred in the Soho district of London. Physician John Snow famously traced the source of the outbreak to a single contaminated public water pump, proving that the disease was waterborne rather than spread by foul air (miasma theory).

Title: Rijksmuseum
The Rijksmuseum is a Dutch national museum dedicated to arts and history. It is situated at the Museum Square in the borough Amsterdam South. The museum has on display 8,000 objects of art and history, including some masterpieces by Rembrandt, Frans Hals, and Johannes Vermeer. Its most famous permanent exhibit is "The Night Watch".

Title: Gothenburg
Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden, situated on the country's west coast. It is an important seaport and a major hub for manufacturing and education. While it is a vital contributor to the national economy, it does not hold the title of the nation's political capital.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Worcestershire
Worcestershire is a county in the West Midlands of England. It is known for its rolling hills, agricultural produce, and as the birthplace of the renowned composer Edward Elgar. The county town is the cathedral city of Worcester.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine and part of the Carpathian Mountains. The mountain is situated in the Eastern Beskids, in the Chornohora region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Yichang
Yichang is a prefecture-level city located in western Hubei province, China. Known historically as a gateway to the upper reaches of major waterways, it is highly industrialized. Today, it is globally famous as the nearest city to the monumental Three Gorges Dam, which sits just upstream from its urban center.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad and commonly known as Atlanta 1996, were an international multi-sport event held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The games were hosted in the capital city of a southern US state, marking the centennial of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: Max Brod
Max Brod was a Bohemian German-speaking Jewish author, composer, and journalist. He is best known as the friend and biographer of Franz Kafka. Brod fled to Mandatory Palestine in 1939, taking with him manuscripts that he later published.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army under the command of a famous emperor was defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This devastating loss marked the end of the commander's reign and his subsequent exile to Saint Helena.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the fierce technological rivalry known as the Space Race.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, succeeding a deeply unpopular incumbent.

Title: 2012 Summer Olympics
The 2012 Summer Olympics were a major international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. It was the third time that the British capital had hosted the modern Olympic Games. The event followed the massive spectacle previously hosted by an East Asian nation four years prior.

Title: Tim Berners-Lee
Sir Timothy John Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web. After proposing an information management system in 1989, he successfully implemented the first communication between an HTTP client and server via the internet. He was born in 1955 in London, United Kingdom.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Thomas Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States from 1913 to 1921. He led the country during World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations. He was the sitting US President in 1919 when a famous Wisconsin football franchise was established.

Title: Alabama
Alabama is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is bordered by Tennessee to the north, Georgia to the east, Florida and the Gulf of Mexico to the south, and Mississippi to the west. The state's political and historical center is its capital city, Montgomery.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: The Trial
The Trial is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, a year after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. It is another seminal work by Franz Kafka, exploring themes of existential dread and bureaucracy.

Title: Spirited Away
"Spirited Away" is a 2001 animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. It tells the story of Chihiro Ogino, a ten-year-old girl who wanders into the world of kami while moving to a new neighborhood. It was incredibly successful, winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named in honor of the newly discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, passing through or touching the borders of 10 countries. It serves as a vital waterway for cities like Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows through several prominent educational towns, including Oxford, where it is known locally as the Isis, before making its way toward the North Sea.

Title: London in Literature
London has been a central hub for English literature for centuries, serving as the birthplace and home for countless legendary authors, from Geoffrey Chaucer to Virginia Woolf. Despite its massive literary pedigree, the city did not produce the poet who captured the very first Nobel Prize in Literature.

Title: New Mexico
New Mexico is a state in the Southwestern region of the United States. Characterized by its deserts, high plains, and mountains, it is known as the "Land of Enchantment." The state has a deep history in aerospace and nuclear research, serving as the historic site for the Trinity nuclear test. Its diverse geography peaks in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

Title: Brian Johnson
Brian Johnson is an English singer and songwriter. In 1980, he became the lead singer of the rock band AC/DC following the death of Bon Scott. His distinctive, powerful rock vocals debuted on the legendary album "Back in Black". Johnson was born in Dunston, a area within the town of Gateshead, located in North East England on the island of Great Britain.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: William Howard Taft
William Howard Taft was the 27th president of the United States, serving from 1909 to 1913. He was hand-picked by his predecessor, Theodore Roosevelt, to run for the presidency. Taft was the sitting president throughout the entire year of 1912, though he lost his re-election bid that November.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice. Working with her husband Pierre, her first major breakthrough was the isolation of a new radioactive element in July 1898, which she named Polonium.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the sixth-most populous state and 25th-largest state in terms of land area. Often viewed as a microcosm of the entire US, it features major industrial hubs, vast agricultural plains, and renowned public universities. Its state capital is Springfield.

Title: Belgrade
Belgrade is the capital and largest city of Serbia. It is located at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers and the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkan Peninsula. Following the outbreak of World War I, the city was heavily bombarded and occupied by Austro-Hungarian forces.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a Russian composer, pianist, and conductor, later of French and American citizenship. He is widely considered one of the most important and influential composers of the 20th century. Stravinsky composed the revolutionary score for "The Rite of Spring". He was born in the resort town of Oranienbaum, Russia.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It has long been a major center for art, culture, and intellectualism in Europe. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the massive Danube river, which provides a vital trade route through central Europe.

Title: City of Oxford
Oxford is a city in England and the county town of Oxfordshire. It boasts a diverse economic base, heavily centered around its world-renowned university and publishing industries. The city is famous for its "dreaming spires" architecture. Geographically, it is located along the upper reaches of the River Thames, which flows through the city center.

Title: Rembrandt
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was a Dutch Golden Age painter, printmaker, and draughtsman. He is generally considered one of the greatest visual artists in the history of art. Unlike his contemporary who painted "Girl with a Pearl Earring", Rembrandt spent the vast majority of his prolific career living and working in Amsterdam.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum and a historic monument in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is a central landmark of the city and a symbol of French cultural heritage.

Title: The Rolling Stones
The Rolling Stones are an English rock band formed in London in 1962. Active for six decades, they are one of the most popular and enduring bands of the rock era. The group's energetic frontman, Mick Jagger, became famous for his dynamic stage presence and distinctive vocal style.

Title: William Lassell
William Lassell was an English merchant and astronomer. He is remembered for his discovery of Triton, the largest moon of Neptune, just 17 days after the discovery of the planet itself. He also discovered Ariel and Umbriel, two other moons of Uranus.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Vostok 6
Vostok 6 was the final mission of the Soviet Vostok space exploration program. Launched in June 1963, it carried the first woman into space. The spacecraft was launched from the premier Soviet spaceport and completed a joint flight with Vostok 5, which had launched two days earlier.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a French naturalist and academic who was an early proponent of the idea that biological evolution occurred in accordance with natural laws. He is best remembered for his theory of soft inheritance, which proposed that usage or disuse of organs altered an individual's biology over time.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: First Mammal Clone
In 1996, the scientific world was shocked by the successful cloning of a mammal from an adult somatic cell, utilizing the process of nuclear transfer. The subject, a female domestic sheep named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996. This breakthrough proved that a specialized adult cell could be reprogrammed to create a whole new organism.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and a massive football legacy. The country shares several mountain peaks with its neighbors, including Monte Rosa and the Matterhorn.

Title: 2004 Ballon d'Or
The 2004 Ballon d'Or was a highly contested award given to the premier European footballer of the year. The winner was an incredibly prolific AC Milan striker who dominated the domestic and European scoring charts. He comfortably won the voting ahead of Deco and Ronaldinho.

Title: Captain James Cook
James Cook was a British explorer, navigator, cartographer, and captain in the Royal Navy. He made detailed maps of Newfoundland prior to making three voyages to the Pacific Ocean, during which he achieved the first recorded European contact with the eastern coastline of Australia and the Hawaiian Islands.

Title: Mount Rushmore
Mount Rushmore National Memorial is a massive sculpture carved into the granite face of Mount Rushmore in the Black Hills region of South Dakota. The sculpture features the 60-foot heads of four United States presidents: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln. The project was primarily directed by an ambitious American sculptor.

Title: 1911 Museum Theft
In August 1911, the global art community was shocked by a brazen robbery at the Louvre museum in Paris. Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman, hid in a broom closet and successfully smuggled out a world-famous portrait under his coat. The sensational theft of the Mona Lisa launched the painting into unprecedented international stardom.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. He flew various experimental aircraft, including the X-15, but survived his perilous test flights.

Title: Yersinia pestis
Yersinia pestis is a Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped bacterium. It is the infectious agent responsible for the plague, a devastating disease that comes in three main forms: pneumonic, septicemic, and bubonic. Throughout history, it has caused several massive pandemics that wiped out substantial portions of the global population.

Title: Ferdinand I of Austria
Ferdinand I was the Emperor of Austria from 1835 until his abdication in 1848. Known as "Ferdinand the Benign," he suffered from severe neurological issues and epilepsy, leaving most of the actual governance of the empire to the State Conference led by Metternich.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: French Franc
The French franc was the currency of France. First introduced in 1360, it was the national currency until the adoption of the Euro. Coins and banknotes of the franc were fully withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender in 2002.

Title: Back to the Future
"Back to the Future" is a 1985 American science fiction film starring Michael J. Fox as teenager Marty McFly, who accidentally travels back in time to 1955 in a time-traveling DeLorean automobile built by his eccentric scientist friend. The film was a massive success and launched a beloved cinematic franchise.

Title: Minute Waltz
The Waltz in D-flat major, Op. 64, No. 1, popularly known as the Minute Waltz, is a piano waltz written in 1847. Despite its nickname, the piece is typically performed in about one and a half to two minutes. It was composed by the legendary Romantic-era pianist Frédéric Chopin.
