Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: Pitchblende
Pitchblende, now formally known as uraninite, is a radioactive, uranium-rich mineral and ore. It was heavily studied in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Parisian scientists looking to isolate the sources of its intense radioactive emissions. It famously yielded trace amounts of several newly discovered elements.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, securing the Physics prize in 1903. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, before moving to the French capital to advance her education.

Title: Roentgenium
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is a highly radioactive metal named after Wilhelm Röntgen, the discoverer of X-rays. On the periodic table, it is a d-block transactinide element located in Group 11.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Despite his immense fame, he famously lost the battle for power grid supremacy. He eventually died in his home state of New Jersey in 1931.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he oversaw significant infrastructure projects like the Interstate Highway System. He was in the Oval Office in 1955 when a major medical breakthrough against polio was announced to the nation.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It was discovered in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while investigating pitchblende. The element holds the atomic number 84, and was deliberately named after Marie Curie's birth country of Poland to highlight its struggle for independence.

Title: Vistula River
The Vistula is the longest and largest river in Poland, at 1,047 kilometres in length. It flows through several of Poland's largest cities, prominently dissecting Warsaw, before emptying into the Baltic Sea.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". Picasso was born in Málaga, a municipality in the autonomous community of Andalusia.

Title: Miracle on Ice
The "Miracle on Ice" was an ice hockey game during the 1980 Winter Olympics. The United States national team, composed of amateur and collegiate players, defeated the heavily favored, four-time defending gold-medalist Soviet Union team. The game is widely considered one of the greatest upsets in the history of sports.

Title: South America
South America is a continent entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean and on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean. Known for the Amazon Rainforest and the Andes mountains, the broader "Americas" lend their name to a specific chemical element.

Title: Nicolaus Copernicus
Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath, active as a mathematician, astronomer, and Catholic canon. He is best known for his heliocentric model of the universe, detailed in his masterpiece "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium". Centuries later, a synthetic chemical element was named in his honor.

Title: Victor Hugo
Victor Marie Hugo was a French poet, novelist, and dramatist of the Romantic movement. He is considered one of the greatest and best-known French writers. Like his contemporary Dumas, Hugo is buried in the Panthéon, having been interred there shortly after his death in 1885.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Title: Brazil national football team
The Brazil national football team represents Brazil in international men's football. They are the most successful team in FIFA World Cup history, having won the tournament five times. Their legendary 1998 squad, featuring Ronaldo, suffered a stunning defeat in the final match in Paris.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. The battle occurred in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: Tin
Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn and atomic number 50. It is a silvery metal that characteristically has a faint yellow hue. It is widely known for its use in creating the alloy bronze when combined with copper. It is a post-transition metal in group 14 of the periodic table.

Title: Zenobia
Zenobia was a 3rd-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Following the death of her husband, she seized power and led a massive revolt against the Roman Empire. She conquered Egypt and much of Anatolia before finally being defeated and captured by the Roman Emperor Aurelian.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Theresa May
Theresa Mary May is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2016 to 2019. Following the resignation of David Cameron after the Brexit referendum, she became the second female to hold the office of Prime Minister. She stepped down in 2019 and was succeeded by Boris Johnson.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. It shares a long eastern border with Sweden. The country's highest peak is Galdhøpiggen, which stands at 2,469 meters above sea level and is the highest mountain in both Norway and Northern Europe.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Carl Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He is one of the few individuals to have been awarded more than one Nobel Prize, having won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: Alfred Nobel
Alfred Bernhard Nobel was a chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist. He holds 355 different patents, but is globally famous for inventing dynamite. In his will, he bequeathed his fortune to institute the Nobel Prizes. Nobel was born in 1833 in Stockholm, the capital city of Sweden.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a famous novella written by an acclaimed European author and first published in 1915. The story follows a traveling salesman named Gregor Samsa, who wakes up one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a massive, insect-like creature. It remains a seminal work of existential literature.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist. She famously discovered the elements polonium and radium. Curie was born in Warsaw, in what was then the Kingdom of Poland, before moving to Paris to study.

Title: Edward Jenner
Edward Jenner was an English physician and scientist who pioneered the concept of vaccines. He created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine, in 1796. Jenner was born in May 1749 in the small town of Berkeley, located in Gloucestershire, Great Britain.

Title: Poland
Poland, officially the Republic of Poland, is a country located in Central Europe. It is divided into 16 administrative provinces and shares borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania, and Russia. The country's southern border is defined by the rugged Sudeten and Carpathian mountain ranges.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its legacy of housing famous classical composers like Mozart and Beethoven.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is globally famous for its vibrant culture, the Amazon rainforest, and its unmatched success in international football. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Brasília, which was inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the Spree river, which meanders directly through its historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose theories on evolution by natural selection fundamentally altered scientific understanding of biology. These theories were heavily informed by his observations of specialized finch species during his voyage aboard the HMS Beagle.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table. It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, shortly after their discovery of another highly radioactive element.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Richard the Lionheart
Richard I, also known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 until his death in 1199. He was a central Christian commander during the Third Crusade. He was the predecessor and older brother of King John, dying without legitimate heirs.

Title: Oliver Stone
Oliver Stone is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He won an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1986 war film "Platoon", which also won Best Picture. Later in his career, he directed the critically acclaimed 1989 film "Born on the Fourth of July."

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: Battersea Power Station
Battersea Power Station is a decommissioned coal-fired power station located on the south bank of a major waterway in Nine Elms, London. With its four distinctive art deco chimneys, it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks and gained global pop culture fame after appearing on a 1977 rock album cover.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high-fantasy novels written by a British author and published in the 1950s. The series is considered a classic of children's literature, tracing the adventures of children who are transported to a magical realm. The books were written at Oxford alongside a close colleague.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two geographically and socially distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for hosting the Mount Rushmore memorial in the Black Hills. Its state capital is Pierre.

Title: Harry S. Truman
Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He assumed the presidency upon the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt during the waning months of World War II. Truman's administration oversaw the rebuilding of post-war Europe via the Marshall Plan.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film incorporating both historical and fictionalized aspects of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. The film was a massive commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing film of all time upon its release, a record it held until 2010. It was heavily praised for its visual effects and emotional weight.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The two largest moons, Oberon and Titania, were the first to be discovered. They were observed in 1787 by the astronomer William Herschel.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is an island nation in northwestern Europe. While it is known for producing massive global cultural exports, it operates independently from mainland European fiscal systems. The country's official currency is the Pound sterling, having notably opted out of using the Euro.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows past numerous historical and industrial landmarks, including the Houses of Parliament and the Battersea Power Station.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day of lunar surface activity.

Title: The Stranger
"The Stranger" is a 1942 novella authored by French philosopher and writer Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus' philosophy of the absurd and existentialism. The novel begins with the iconic lines concerning the death of the protagonist's mother.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is a silvery white metal that resists corrosion in dry air. It was discovered independently in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who named it after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by a legendary Post-Impressionist painter. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized and reproduced paintings in the history of Western art.

Title: 1950 FIFA World Cup
The 1950 FIFA World Cup was the fourth edition of the tournament, held in Brazil after a twelve-year hiatus caused by World War II. The decisive match of the tournament saw a stunning upset when the underdog Uruguayan national team defeated the host nation before a record crowd at the Maracanã Stadium.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement. In a bizarre historical footnote, Picasso was actually brought in for questioning by police as a suspect during the infamous 1911 Louvre theft investigation.

Title: Nicholas II of Russia
Nicholas II was the last Emperor of Russia, King of Congress Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland, ruling from 1894 until his abdication in 1917. Following the revolution, he and his immediate family were imprisoned and subsequently executed by Bolshevik revolutionaries in July 1918 in the city of Yekaterinburg.

Title: France
France has a rich history of scientific discovery and was the adoptive home of many expatriate researchers. It was the country where radioactivity was extensively studied in the early 20th century, leading to the discovery of several new elements.

Title: Lutetium
Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is a silvery white metal, which resists corrosion in dry air, but not in moist air. It was discovered in 1907 by French scientist Georges Urbain, who chose to name the element after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.

Title: Mendelian inheritance
Mendelian inheritance is a type of biological inheritance that follows the principles originally proposed by Gregor Mendel in 1865 and 1866. It involves the concepts of dominant and recessive traits, forming the fundamental basis of classical genetics long before the discovery of DNA.

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
"The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King" is a 2003 epic high fantasy adventure film. Serving as the conclusion to a sprawling trilogy, it was both a massive critical and commercial success. At the 76th Academy Awards, it swept all 11 of its nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director.

Title: River Mersey
The River Mersey is a river in the North West of England. Its name is derived from the Anglo-Saxon language and translates as "boundary river". It flows through the city of Liverpool, heavily influencing the maritime culture of the region that birthed the British Invasion.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: Pet Sounds
"Pet Sounds" is the eleventh studio album by the American rock band the Beach Boys, released in 1966. It initially met with a lukewarm critical and commercial response in the US but was highly acclaimed in the UK. Today, it is widely considered one of the most influential albums in music history.

Title: Stanley Cup
The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff winner. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America. Unlike many other sports trophies, it is made of a durable alloy of silver and nickel.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when Alexander Fleming noticed that a specific blue-green mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying bacteria.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter: A Romance" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne, who conceives a daughter through an affair and struggles to create a new life of repentance and dignity.

Title: Henry III of England
Henry III was King of England, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Aquitaine from 1216 until his death in 1272. He assumed the throne when he was only nine years old following the turbulent reign of his father, King John. He was born to John and his queen consort, Isabella of Angoulême.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most remote islands in the world. It gained immense historical infamy as the final, inescapable site of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte. The island is currently controlled as a British Overseas Territory by the United Kingdom.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
An induction motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction. This revolutionary device eliminated the need for mechanical commutators. The first practical alternating current induction motor was independently invented in the 1880s by a brilliant Serbian-American engineer.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is famous for its passionate football culture, vibrant Carnival festivals, and the sprawling Amazon rainforest. The country's highest physical point is the Pico da Neblina, located deep within the Guiana Highlands.

Title: Shrek (film)
"Shrek" is a 2001 American computer-animated comedy film loosely based on the 1990 fairy tale picture book of the same name. The massive critical and commercial success was co-directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, establishing DreamWorks Animation as a prime competitor in the feature animation industry.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, located on the Votka River. The town was founded in 1759 as a center for metallurgical production. Today, it is best known in cultural circles as the birthplace of a legendary 19th-century Romantic composer whose childhood home is now a museum.

Title: 1994 FIFA World Cup
The 1994 FIFA World Cup was hosted by the United States and broke tournament attendance records. The final match was played between Brazil and Italy at the Rose Bowl in California. Brazil won the match on penalties after a scoreless draw, securing their fourth title.

Title: Stanford University
Stanford University is a private research university located in Stanford, California. The campus occupies 8,180 acres, among the largest in the United States, and enrolls over 17,000 students. It is globally recognized for its proximity to Silicon Valley and has graduated numerous legendary tech founders and CEOs.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: Dead Poets Society
"Dead Poets Society" is a 1989 American teen drama film starring Robin Williams as an unorthodox English teacher at an elite conservative boarding school. The film was directed by Peter Weir and received a nomination for Best Picture at the 62nd Academy Awards, but lost to a film about a chauffeur.

Title: Uruguay
Uruguay, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, is a country in the southeastern region of South America. It borders Brazil to the north and east and Argentina to the west. The nation has a deeply rooted soccer culture and hosted the first World Cup. The country's primary metropolis and capital city is Montevideo.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Atahualpa
Atahualpa was the last reigning emperor of the Inca Empire prior to the Spanish conquest. After winning a brutal civil war against his half-brother, he was almost immediately confronted by the arrival of the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro. Pizarro famously captured Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, eventually executing him.

Title: Friendship 7
Friendship 7 was the spacecraft piloted by astronaut John Glenn in February 1962. Part of the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, the flight made Glenn the very first American to successfully orbit the Earth, catching the U.S. up to the achievements of the Soviet Union.

Title: Bettino Craxi
Bettino Craxi was an Italian politician, leader of the Italian Socialist Party, and served as Prime Minister of Italy from 1983 to 1987. He took office shortly after the brief leadership of his republican predecessor, guiding Italy through an era of strong economic growth in the mid-1980s.

Title: William Herschel
William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer who revolutionized the study of the cosmos. In addition to cataloging nebulae and discovering several moons, his most famous achievement occurred in 1781. It was then that he discovered the planet Uranus, expanding the known boundaries of the solar system.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in the exact same Catalan town where he was born.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City since 1934.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch.

Title: Denali
Denali, formerly known officially as Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain peak in North America, with a summit elevation of 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level. Located in the Alaska Range in the interior of the U.S. state of Alaska, it is a centerpiece of Denali National Park and Preserve.

Title: French Open
The French Open, also known as Roland-Garros, is a major tennis tournament held over two weeks at the Stade Roland Garros in Paris. It is the premier clay court championship in the world. The men's singles winner is awarded the Coupe des Mousquetaires.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, Finland to the east, and is connected to Denmark in the southwest by a bridge-tunnel. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm. The country's geography is characterized by extensive forests and a rugged mountainous region along the Norwegian border, where its highest peak, Kebnekaise, is located.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Victoria Falls
Victoria Falls is a massive waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, which provides habitat for several unique species of plants and animals. It is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Though not the tallest, it is considered one of the largest waterfalls in the world based on combined width and height.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a remote volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is known primarily as the harsh, isolated location where a deposed French emperor was exiled after 1815. It remains a British Overseas Territory and utilizes the Saint Helena pound as its local currency.

Title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
The Walt Disney Concert Hall at 111 South Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, California, is the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Designed by a famous postmodern architect, its sweeping, metallic stainless steel curves have made it an architectural landmark of the city.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a U.S. state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north and Pennsylvania to the east. Historically a major industrial powerhouse, it is the birthplace of several prominent American figures, including seven U.S. presidents and famous filmmakers. Its capital city is Columbus.

Title: Eighth Planet from the Sun
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. In the Solar System, it is the fourth-largest planet by diameter. It was named after the Roman god of the sea. Neptune is notable for being the only planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by empirical observation.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: Chocolate Chip Cookie
The chocolate chip cookie is a drop cookie that originated in the United States and features chocolate chips or chocolate morsels as its distinguishing ingredient. It was invented in 1938 by Ruth Graves Wakefield, who chopped up a Nestlé semi-sweet chocolate bar and added it to her cookie dough, creating a legendary dessert.

Title: Gothenburg
Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden, situated on the country's west coast. It is an important seaport and a major hub for manufacturing and education. While it is a vital contributor to the national economy, it does not hold the title of the nation's political capital.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses premier art institutions dedicated to the nation's native painters. The country's official currency is the Euro.

Title: Adelaide
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia and the fifth-most populous city of Australia. Named in honor of Queen Adelaide, it was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for a freely settled British province. The city is the birthplace of the Nobel Prize-winning pathologist who mass-produced penicillin.

Title: Statue of Liberty
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical copper sculpture on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. It was designed by a French sculptor and its metal framework was built by Gustave Eiffel. The statue was dedicated in 1886 as a gift from France to the United States.

Title: Economy of Denmark
Denmark has a developed mixed economy that is classed as a high-income economy by the World Bank. The country possesses a highly educated workforce and a robust welfare state. Despite being a member of the European Union, the nation does not use the Euro, retaining the Danish krone as its official currency.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a real-time operating system (RTOS) designed for use in embedded systems requiring high reliability and precision. It has been heavily utilized in aerospace, defense, and robotics. Famously, NASA selected this proprietary operating system to run the main flight and mission computers aboard the Mars Perseverance rover.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named in honor of the newly discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Francium
Francium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It was discovered by Marguerite Perey in France in 1939. It was the last element first discovered in nature, rather than by synthesis, and is named after the country of its discovery.

Title: Capital of Australia
Following the federation of Australia in 1901, there was a long dispute over whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the national capital. A compromise was reached to build a new planned city inland. An international competition was held in 1911 to design the new capital city, Canberra.

Title: Rhenium
Rhenium is a chemical element with the symbol Re and atomic number 75. It is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. Discovered in 1925, it was the last stable element to be discovered. It was named after the river Rhine in Europe.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville. Hawthorne worked for several years at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. Following her tragic death in a hospital fire in North Carolina, she was eventually laid to rest alongside her husband in Maryland.

Title: Black Elk Peak
Black Elk Peak is the highest natural point in South Dakota, standing at an elevation of 7,244 feet (2,208 m). Formerly known as Harney Peak, it is located in the Black Hills National Forest in Pennington County. It represents the highest summit in the United States east of the Rocky Mountains.

Title: Vint Cerf
Vinton Gray Cerf is an American Internet pioneer and is recognized as one of the "fathers of the Internet". He co-designed the TCP/IP protocols and the architecture of the Internet. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, he played a crucial role in the development of modern networking.

Title: Museo Reina Sofía
The Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía is Spain's national museum of 20th-century art. Inaugurated in 1992, the museum is located in the vibrant capital city of Madrid. Its extensive collection highlights modern and contemporary masterpieces, but it is most globally famous for displaying the monumental painting "Guernica."

Title: History of Basketball
The sport of basketball was invented in December 1891 at the International Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. A physical education instructor was tasked with creating an indoor game to keep athletes active during the harsh New England winters, resulting in the sport.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel that introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries. It was written by an Irish author who was heavily inspired by Eastern European folklore.

Title: Belgrade
Belgrade is the capital and largest city of Serbia. It is located at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers and the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkan Peninsula. Following the outbreak of World War I, the city was heavily bombarded and occupied by Austro-Hungarian forces.

Title: Ridley Scott
Sir Ridley Scott is an English film director and producer. He is renowned for his atmospheric, highly concentrated visual style. After establishing his career with commercials, he found global fame directing the sci-fi classics "Alien" and "Blade Runner". He is the older brother of fellow Hollywood director Tony Scott.

Title: First Roman Emperor
The Roman Republic definitively ended with the rise of the first Roman Emperor. Born Gaius Octavius, he was granted the honorific title of Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC. His autocratic rule initiated a period of relative peace known as the Pax Romana, though he dealt harshly with political dissidents and scandalous figures.

Title: India
India is a country in South Asia and the most populous democracy in the world. Bounded by the Indian Ocean on the south and the Himalayas on the north, it is home to major river systems like the Ganges. The Bengal Tiger serves as the official national animal of India, representing strength and agility.

Title: Mulhacén
Mulhacén is the highest mountain in continental Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, with an elevation of 3,479 meters. Located in the Sierra Nevada range in Andalusia, it is a prominent peak, but it is surpassed in overall elevation by a volcanic peak located in the Spanish overseas territories.

Title: James Watson
James Dewey Watson is an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist. He co-authored the 1953 academic paper proposing the double helix structure of the DNA molecule. Watson was born in Chicago, Illinois, and traveled to England specifically to work at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Fermium
Fermium is a synthetic element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is a member of the actinide series. Like other heavy synthetic elements, it was discovered in the debris of early thermonuclear weapons tests. It was named after the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. The HMS Beagle spent significant time surveying its long, rugged coastline. The nation has a deeply agricultural economy, and its official currency is the Argentine peso.

Title: Guillotine Executions in Paris
The guillotine became the primary method of execution in France during the Reign of Terror. Placed in the Place de la Révolution, it claimed the lives of aristocrats, politicians, and commoners alike. The most famous victim was the deposed king, Louis XVI, whose execution took place there in 1793.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée decisively defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. It is widely regarded as a tactical masterpiece.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. The country has a rich tradition in chemistry and scientific innovation. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm, a major cultural and economic hub.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He was born in Ishpeming, located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: 62nd Academy Awards
The 62nd Academy Awards ceremony, presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films of 1989 and took place on March 26, 1990, at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles. The ceremony heavily highlighted the cinematic achievements of the closing year of the 1980s.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It was discovered in the same year as another radioactive element, extracted from the same pitchblende ores by painstaking chemical isolation.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major global center for art and culture for centuries. The capital city is Paris, which frequently hosted the premieres of major international theatrical and musical works during the Belle Époque.

Title: George Westinghouse
George Westinghouse Jr. was an American entrepreneur and engineer based in Pennsylvania who created the railway air brake. He was a pioneer of the electrical industry, acquiring the patents for the AC induction motor and backing the alternating current system to fiercely compete against Thomas Edison's direct current networks.

Title: Ural Mountains
The Ural Mountains, or simply the Urals, are a mountain range that runs from north to south through western Russia, from the coast of the Arctic Ocean to the river Ural and northwestern Kazakhstan. The mountain range forms part of the conventional boundary between the continents of Europe and Asia.

Title: Wimbledon Records
The Wimbledon Championships are the oldest tennis tournament in the world and widely considered the most prestigious. In the modern era, consecutive victories on its grass courts are notoriously difficult. The 20th-century record for the most consecutive Wimbledon men's singles titles belongs to Björn Borg, who captured five straight trophies from 1976 to 1980.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. The rover's sophisticated payload, autonomous navigation systems, and mission-critical flight computers are managed by a commercial, high-reliability real-time operating system.

Title: Multiple Nobel Laureates
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, and only a very small number of individuals have won multiple times. The very first person to ever win two Nobel Prizes, and the only one to win in two distinct scientific fields (Physics and Chemistry), was Marie Curie.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: Cerium
Cerium is a chemical element with the symbol Ce and atomic number 58. It is a soft, ductile, and silvery-white metal that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was independently discovered by Martin Heinrich Klaproth alongside other European chemists in 1803. It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element. Their discoveries fundamentally changed the scientific understanding of atomic structures and radiation.

Title: James Webb Space Telescope
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is an infrared space observatory launched in 2021. Designed to succeed previous observatories, its vastly improved infrared resolution and sensitivity allow it to view objects too old, distant, or faint to be seen by older optical telescopes.

Title: Origins of Video Sharing
The mid-2000s saw a massive boom in user-generated content platforms. In February 2005, three former PayPal employees—Jawed Karim, Steve Chen, and Chad Hurley—registered a domain name for a new video-sharing website. Their creation, YouTube, allowed anyone to easily upload, share, and view video clips over the internet.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. It was a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom, heavily defined by strict moral standards.

Title: Lansing, Michigan
Lansing is the capital of the U.S. state of Michigan. It is mostly located in Ingham County, although portions of the city extend west into Eaton County and north into Clinton County. The city became the state capital in 1847, taking over the role from Detroit, to provide a more centralized government location.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed country with a mixed-market economy. It is rich in natural resources, heavily exporting minerals and agricultural products. The nation's financial systems are closely tied to the Asia-Pacific region, and its official currency is the Australian dollar.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a massive country in South Asia. It achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation was the birthplace of several major literary figures during the colonial era. The political and administrative capital of India is New Delhi.

Title: Wright Flyer
The Wright Flyer was the first successful heavier-than-air powered aircraft. It was designed and built by a pair of pioneering brothers. The aircraft made four flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, marking the dawn of the aviation age and transforming global transportation.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited art museum and a historic monument in France. A central landmark of its home city, it is located on the Right Bank of the Seine. The museum permanently houses tens of thousands of historic works of art, including Leonardo da Vinci's iconic portrait of Lisa Gherardini.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of internet infrastructure like ARPANET. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the Potomac River.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville, who famously dedicated his masterpiece about a white whale to Hawthorne. Hawthorne later worked at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 is a supertall skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. It officially held the title of the world's tallest building from its opening in 2004 until the completion of a taller megastructure in Dubai in 2009. The building was designed by C.Y. Lee & Partners to withstand the region's frequent typhoons and earthquakes.

Title: Amazon (company)
Amazon is an American multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. Founded in a garage in Bellevue, Washington, in 1994, it began as an online marketplace for books before rapidly expanding into a multitude of other product categories.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist and a pioneer in crystallography and radioactivity. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife. He was born in Paris, France, and spent his entire career working in the city.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: The Trial
"The Trial" is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. Max Brod ensured its publication despite instructions to destroy the manuscript.

Title: Solid Milk Chocolate Bar
The invention of the solid milk chocolate bar fundamentally changed the global confectionery industry. Before this, chocolate was primarily consumed as a bitter beverage or used for baking. In 1875, a dedicated chocolatier successfully combined cocoa powder and cocoa butter with condensed milk, resulting in the world's first sweet, solid milk chocolate bar.

Title: Black Sea
The Black Sea is a marginal mediterranean sea of the Atlantic Ocean lying between Europe and Asia. It is supplied by major rivers, principally the Danube, Dnieper, and Don. It is a critical geostrategic waterway connecting Eastern Europe to the broader Mediterranean.

Title: Constanța
Constanța is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Romania. Located at the crossroads of several commercial routes, it lies on the western coast of the Black Sea. Built directly over the ancient ruins of Tomis, it now serves as Romania's largest sea port.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York. Fought in August 1485, the battle was won by an alliance of Lancastrians and disaffected Yorkists. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

Title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, philosopher, and essayist. His literary works, including "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot", heavily explore human psychology in the troubled political context of 19th-century Russia. Dostoevsky passed away in 1881 in Saint Petersburg.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Bruce Sabin was a prominent medical researcher who developed the live-virus oral polio vaccine, which played a foundational role in nearly eradicating the disease worldwide. Sabin was born in August 1906 to a Jewish family in the city of Białystok, which was then part of the Russian Empire but is situated in modern-day Poland.

Title: Statue of Liberty
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical copper sculpture on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, it was designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. The statue was a gift to the United States from the people of France, intended to commemorate the alliance between the two nations during the American Revolution.

Title: Saint Paul, Minnesota
Saint Paul is the capital of the U.S. state of Minnesota. Known for its historic architecture and distinct neighborhoods, it is the birthplace of the author who wrote "The Great Gatsby". However, the author chose not to be buried in his Midwestern home state.

Title: Austrian Empire in 1822
The Austrian Empire was a multi-national empire and one of Europe's great powers. In 1822, the empire was navigating the conservative post-Napoleonic era orchestrated by Klemens von Metternich. During this entire period, the empire was ruled by Emperor Francis I.

Title: Wright Brothers
Orville and Wilbur Wright, collectively known as the Wright Brothers, were aviation pioneers generally credited with inventing, building, and flying the world's first successful motor-operated airplane. Both brothers were born and raised in the midwestern United States, specifically in Indiana and Ohio, respectively.

Title: Element 101
Atomic number 101 belongs to a synthetic element in the actinide series of the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive metallic element. It was deliberately named in honor of the legendary Russian chemist who created the first definitive periodic table.

Title: Ecuador
Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia on the north, Peru on the east and south, and the Pacific Ocean on the west. It also includes the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which it administers as a highly protected national park and province.

Title: Academy Award for Best Animated Feature
The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature is given annually to the best animated feature-length film. The award was first introduced in 2002 for films released in 2001. The inaugural winner of this highly coveted prize was the computer-animated comedy film "Shrek", which beat out competitors like "Monsters, Inc."

Title: Cleveland Cavaliers
The Cleveland Cavaliers, often referred to as the Cavs, are a professional basketball team based in Cleveland, Ohio. They compete in the NBA as a member of the Eastern Conference Central Division. The franchise secured its first and only NBA Championship by overcoming a historic deficit to beat the Warriors.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet of the American Renaissance period. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent almost two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Silas Marner
"Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe" is a classic novel published in 1861. It follows the life of a reclusive, embittered weaver who finds redemption and love after adopting an orphaned toddler named Eppie. The highly acclaimed novel is outwardly credited to the author George Eliot.

Title: The Last Supper
"The Last Supper" is a late 15th-century mural painting by a legendary Italian Renaissance polymath. Housed in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy, it represents the scene of the Last Supper of Jesus with his apostles, specifically the moment after Jesus announces that one of them will betray him.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: Aliens (film)
"Aliens" is a 1986 science fiction action film and the direct sequel to the 1979 classic. Sigourney Weaver reprises her iconic role as Ellen Ripley, who returns to the moon where her crew first encountered the hostile alien creature. This action-heavy sequel was directed by James Cameron.

Title: 2004 Ballon d'Or
The 2004 Ballon d'Or was a highly contested award given to the premier European footballer of the year. The winner was an incredibly prolific AC Milan striker who dominated the domestic and European scoring charts. He comfortably won the voting ahead of Deco and Ronaldinho.

Title: Art Institute of Chicago
The Art Institute of Chicago is one of the oldest and largest art museums in the United States. It houses a permanent collection of nearly 300,000 works of art, featuring notable pieces from around the globe. Among its prized possessions is "The Old Guitarist", a famous masterpiece acquired by the institution in 1926.

Title: Puerperal fever
Puerperal fever, also known as postpartum infections, are bacterial infections of the female reproductive tract following childbirth or miscarriage. Before the widespread understanding of germ theory and the adoption of handwashing by doctors in the late 19th century, it was a leading cause of maternal mortality, claiming the lives of many historical figures.

Title: Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster
The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster occurred on January 28, 1986. The spacecraft broke apart 73 seconds into its flight, tragically killing all seven crew members aboard. The disaster temporarily grounded the shuttle fleet and led to major structural changes at NASA.

Title: Muhammad Ali
Muhammad Ali was an American professional boxer and activist. Born and raised in Louisville, Kentucky, he began training as an amateur boxer at age 12. He won an Olympic gold medal in 1960. He was originally born with the name Cassius Clay, but changed his name in 1964 after joining the Nation of Islam.
