Title: Juan de Villanueva
Juan de Villanueva was a Spanish architect who was a prominent figure of neoclassicism in Spain. His masterpiece is the building that now houses the Museo del Prado. He was born in Madrid in 1739 and spent much of his life contributing to the city's architectural landscape.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Well-Tempered Clavier. He spent the last 27 years of his life working as the Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he died in 1750.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
UCLA is a public land-grant research university in Los Angeles, California. Its men's basketball program is historically the most successful in college athletics, holding the record for the most NCAA championships under the leadership of coach John Wooden.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The setting of The Count of Monte Cristo includes various locations in Italy, particularly Rome and the Tuscan Archipelago. Italy is also a Eurozone member.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the banks of a major river in east-central Poland. It has a rich history and has been the birthplace of many notable historical figures, including a two-time Nobel laureate.

Title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His political stance often conflicted with the empire's rigid establishment. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife Sophie were fatally shot during a state visit. This assassination set the wheels in motion for the First World War.

Title: Salem, Massachusetts
Salem is a historic coastal city in Essex County, Massachusetts, located on the North Shore. Known heavily for its 1692 witch trials, it was also a major maritime port in early American history, requiring a substantial customs operation.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He was deeply influenced by the bohemian circles of Christiania.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: Adelaide
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia and the fifth-most populous city of Australia. Named in honor of Queen Adelaide, it was founded in 1836 as the planned capital for a freely settled British province. The city is the birthplace of the Nobel Prize-winning pathologist who mass-produced penicillin.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: 1962 FIFA World Cup
The 1962 FIFA World Cup was the seventh edition of the international football tournament. Hosted by Chile, the event saw fierce competition and several highly physical matches. In the end, the defending champions, Brazil, successfully retained their title by defeating Czechoslovakia 3-1 in the final.

Title: Economy of France
France boasts a highly developed, social market economy that is among the largest in the world. As a founding member of the European Union, its economic policies are deeply integrated with its neighbors. The official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French franc in 2002.

Title: 1961 in the United States
The year 1961 saw major shifts in American politics and foreign policy. The country faced the failed Bay of Pigs invasion and the escalating tensions of the Cold War. During this year, President John F. Kennedy famously committed the nation to the ambitious goal of landing a man on the Moon.

Title: London in Literature
London has been a central hub for English literature for centuries, serving as the birthplace and home for countless legendary authors, from Geoffrey Chaucer to Virginia Woolf. Despite its massive literary pedigree, the city did not produce the poet who captured the very first Nobel Prize in Literature.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Venice
Venice is a city in northeastern Italy and the capital of the Veneto region. It is built on a group of 118 small islands separated by canals. The city is celebrated for its stunning architecture and art, and is historically significant as the birthplace of composer Antonio Vivaldi.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. Plutonium was first synthetically produced and isolated in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: Edison Machine Works
The Edison Machine Works was a manufacturing company set up in 1881 to produce dynamos, large electric motors, and other components of the electrical illumination system. The factory was situated in New York City. The business was founded and closely managed by the legendary American inventor Thomas Edison.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. The artist was born in 1863, a full decade after his famous Dutch contemporary.

Title: Holy Roman Empire
The Holy Roman Empire was a multi-ethnic complex of territories in Western and Central Europe that developed during the Early Middle Ages. It was officially dissolved in 1806. During its existence, its administrative center varied, but it frequently convened in cities like Frankfurt and Regensburg.

Title: Signal de Botrange
Signal de Botrange is the highest point in Belgium, located in the High Fens, at 694 metres (2,277 ft). It is the top of a broad plateau and a road crosses the summit. Although relatively low compared to the peaks of its European neighbors, it stands as the geographical apex of the nation.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher who authored nearly fifty books. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family, before eventually migrating to the United States.

Title: First Roman Emperor
The Roman Republic definitively ended with the rise of the first Roman Emperor. Born Gaius Octavius, he was granted the honorific title of Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC. His autocratic rule initiated a period of relative peace known as the Pax Romana, though he dealt harshly with political dissidents and scandalous figures.

Title: 2000 Summer Olympics
The 2000 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVII Olympiad and commonly known as Sydney 2000, were held in Sydney, Australia. The event was widely praised for its incredible organization and execution, setting a high benchmark for future host nations.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was hosted by Mexico. The tournament was defined by the phenomenal performance of the team captain who scored the "Hand of God" goal, leading his nation to a 3-2 victory over West Germany in the final.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a famous sculpture by a French artist, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work depicts a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock, seemingly deep in thought. Originally conceived as part of a larger commission titled The Gates of Hell, multiple monumental castings exist worldwide.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and several overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and sports. The country boasts a diverse geography, ranging from coastal plains to the towering peaks of the Alps. The highest geographic point in France is Mont Blanc.

Title: Days of Thunder
"Days of Thunder" is a 1990 American sports action drama film starring Tom Cruise as an ambitious stock car racing driver. Also directed by Tony Scott, it attempted to replicate the massive success and visual style of their previous collaboration, though it focused on NASCAR rather than fighter jets.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was highly anticipated, given the rapid advancements in theoretical physics during the early 20th century. The committee ultimately awarded the prize to Albert Einstein. The award was explicitly given "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect."

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter: A Romance" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne, who conceives a daughter through an affair and struggles to create a new life of repentance and dignity.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Oranienbaum, Russia
Oranienbaum (now Lomonosov) is a municipal town in the Petrodvortsovy District of the federal city of Saint Petersburg, Russia. Situated on the southern coast of the Gulf of Finland, it is notable as the site of an 18th-century palace complex. It is also famous as the birthplace of one of the 20th century's most avant-garde musical geniuses.

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. The nation encompasses the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of the island of Ireland, and many smaller islands. The political and cultural capital of the UK is London.

Title: Dawn of the Space Age
The Space Age began in the mid-20th century as superpowers competed for technological supremacy. The era was officially ignited when the Soviet Union successfully launched the very first artificial Earth satellite, an event that shocked the Western world and immediately triggered the rapid acceleration of the Space Race.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: 1982 FIFA World Cup
The 1982 FIFA World Cup was the 12th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was played in Spain between June 13 and July 11, 1982. The tournament was ultimately won by Italy, who defeated West Germany 3-1 in the final match.

Title: Most Academy Awards for a Single Film
Three films in history have tied for the record of winning the most Academy Awards, each earning exactly 11 Oscars. The first was "Ben-Hur" in 1959, followed by "Titanic" in 1997. The most recent film to achieve this monumental sweep was a massive high-fantasy epic released in 2003, which won every category for which it was nominated.

Title: Rembrandt
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was a Dutch Golden Age painter, printmaker, and draughtsman. He is generally considered one of the greatest visual artists in the history of art. Unlike his contemporary who painted "Girl with a Pearl Earring", Rembrandt spent the vast majority of his prolific career living and working in Amsterdam.

Title: Wind River Corporate History
Originally starting in a Berkeley garage, Wind River Systems expanded rapidly during the 1990s dot-com boom. As the company grew into a major provider of aerospace and industrial software, it relocated its central operations. Today, the company maintains its global corporate headquarters in Alameda, California.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a massive conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital. It raged for several days in the year 1666, destroying thousands of homes and historical structures. The disaster ultimately led to massive reconstruction efforts and modernized fire safety codes.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Emperor of India from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. The element rutherfordium was named in his honor. He was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a town in New Zealand.

Title: The Divine Comedy
"The Divine Comedy" is an Italian narrative poem begun c. 1308 and completed in 1320. It is widely considered one of the pre-eminent works in Italian literature and one of the greatest works of world literature. The poem's imaginative vision of the afterlife is representative of the medieval worldview.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. He is widely considered one of the greatest painters in history. His artistic genius is best exemplified by his legendary portrait, the Mona Lisa.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: Curiosity Rover
Curiosity is a car-sized Mars rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission. It launched from Cape Canaveral in 2011 and successfully landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on Mars in 2012. It paved the way for subsequent rovers with its advanced landing systems.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large, space-based observatory launched into low Earth orbit in April 1990. Despite an early issue with a flawed mirror, servicing missions corrected its optics, turning it into one of the most vital research tools in astronomy. It was named in honor of astronomer Edwin Hubble.

Title: 1980 Summer Olympics
The 1980 Summer Olympics were held in Moscow, in the Soviet Union. These games were heavily boycotted by the United States and several other countries in protest of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. The political climate heavily influenced the atmosphere of international sporting events that year.

Title: Kebnekaise
Kebnekaise is the highest mountain in Sweden. The Kebnekaise massif, which is part of the Scandinavian Mountains, has two main peaks. The glaciated southern peak used to be the highest at 2,120 meters, but due to ice melting, the rocky northern peak, at 2,096.8 meters, has now officially become the highest point in the country.

Title: Russia
Russia, officially the Russian Federation, is a massive transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It has a rich cultural history of producing brilliant composers and writers. The political, economic, and administrative capital city of modern-day Russia is Moscow.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: British Empire
The British Empire was composed of the dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates, and other territories ruled or administered by the United Kingdom. At its height, it was the largest empire in history. Its power was centralized in the capital city of London, situated along the banks of the River Thames.

Title: Publication of To Kill a Mockingbird
When "To Kill a Mockingbird" was finally published in July 1960, the United States was transitioning into a new era of civil rights struggles. The sitting president during the book's highly anticipated release was Dwight D. Eisenhower, nearing the end of his second term.

Title: Super Bowl II
Super Bowl II was played on January 14, 1968, at the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida. The Green Bay Packers defeated the Oakland Raiders by the score of 33-14, capturing their second consecutive world championship under the legendary leadership of head coach Vince Lombardi.

Title: Hans Zimmer
Hans Zimmer is a German film score composer and music producer. He has won two Oscars and four Grammys. His works are notable for integrating electronic music sounds with traditional orchestral arrangements. Zimmer has a long-standing, highly successful collaboration with director Christopher Nolan.

Title: Rio de Janeiro
Rio de Janeiro is a massive seaside city in Brazil, famed for its Copacabana and Ipanema beaches, as well as the towering Christ the Redeemer statue. It served as the capital of Brazil for nearly two centuries before the government officially moved its operations to a planned inland city.

Title: Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a 2,430-meter mountain ridge. It is the most familiar icon of the Inca Empire. Built in classical Inca style with polished dry-stone walls, it was mysteriously abandoned around the time of the Spanish Conquest.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Penicillium
Penicillium is a genus of ascomycetous molds that is of major importance in the natural environment, in food spoilage, and in food and drug production. One species in this genus, Penicillium rubens, is famous for naturally producing the active ingredient in the antibiotic penicillin. Taxonomically, this organism belongs to the kingdom Fungi.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Sabin was a Polish-American medical researcher best known for developing the oral polio vaccine. His live-virus formulation was easier to administer than the injected version and became the primary weapon in the global fight to eradicate the disease. He later served as president of the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878. Cleve named the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Title: 2010 FIFA World Cup
The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. It took place in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The tournament was won by Spain, who defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final match.

Title: First American Woman in Space
Sally Ride was an American astronaut and physicist. Born in Los Angeles, she joined NASA in 1978 and became the first American woman in space in 1983. She flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger during the STS-7 mission, launching from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Title: Of Mice and Men
"Of Mice and Men" is a novella written by a prominent American author and published in 1937. It tells the story of George Milton and Lennie Small, two displaced migrant ranch workers who move from place to place in California in search of new job opportunities during the Great Depression.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. Born in New York City, USA, he chose not to patent the vaccine to maximize its global distribution. His inactivated polio vaccine required an injection but proved immensely effective in clinical trials.

Title: Brian Johnson
Brian Johnson is an English singer and songwriter. In 1980, he became the lead singer of the rock band AC/DC following the death of Bon Scott. His distinctive, powerful rock vocals debuted on the legendary album "Back in Black". Johnson was born in Dunston, a area within the town of Gateshead, located in North East England on the island of Great Britain.

Title: Google
Google LLC is an American multinational technology company that focuses on search engine technology, online advertising, cloud computing, computer software, quantum computing, e-commerce, and artificial intelligence. The massive corporation maintains its sprawling global headquarters, famously known as the Googleplex, in the city of Mountain View, California.

Title: Chichen Itza
Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people of the Terminal Classic period. The archaeological site is located in Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán State, Mexico. It features massive step pyramids and was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands before the arrival of the Spanish.

Title: Mont Blanc
Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps and Western Europe, rising 4,805 m (15,764 ft) above sea level. It is located on the French-Italian border. The massive, snow-capped peak is a legendary destination for mountaineering and winter sports.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1922
The 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Niels Bohr. He received the honor "for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them." Bohr's atomic model revolutionized the understanding of subatomic structures and quantum mechanics.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal. The element was named in honor of the pioneering American nuclear scientist who invented the cyclotron.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known works of Antonio Vivaldi, who was born in the canal city of Venice.

Title: Robert Falcon Scott
Robert Falcon Scott was a British Royal Navy officer and explorer who led two expeditions to the Antarctic regions. His second venture famously engaged in a race to the South Pole. He reached the pole in January 1912, only to discover a rival team had beaten him there by mere weeks.

Title: Constanța
Constanța is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Romania. Located at the crossroads of several commercial routes, it lies on the western coast of the Black Sea. Built directly over the ancient ruins of Tomis, it now serves as Romania's largest sea port.

Title: Perseverance (rover)
Perseverance, nicknamed Percy, is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars as part of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. It carries seven primary payload instruments, 19 cameras, and two microphones. To manage its complex scientific operations and autonomous driving, its internal computers run a highly specialized real-time operating system.

Title: Florence Cathedral
Florence Cathedral, formally the Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore, is the cathedral of Florence, Italy. It was begun in 1296 in the Gothic style to a design of Arnolfo di Cambio and was structurally completed by 1436, with the dome designed by Filippo Brunelleschi.

Title: Economy of Australia
Australia is a highly developed sovereign country known for its vast natural resources and major mining sector. The nation has a strong, mixed-market economy. Its official currency is the Australian dollar, which is also used by several independent Pacific Island states.

Title: South Dakota
South Dakota is a U.S. state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States. It is bisected by the Missouri River, dividing the state into two geographically and socially distinct halves. The state is internationally famous for hosting the Mount Rushmore memorial in the Black Hills. Its state capital is Pierre.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, best known for discovering the world's first broadly effective antibiotic substance, penicillin. For this monumental achievement, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared equally with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: Tokugawa Shogunate
The Tokugawa Shogunate was the feudal military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868. Established by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the shogunate maintained a strict isolationist policy and rigidly controlled the social order. During the year 1800, this dynasty was firmly in power, completely dominating the political landscape of the nation.

Title: Mick Jagger
Sir Michael Philip Jagger is an English singer, songwriter, actor, and film producer who has gained worldwide fame as the lead vocalist and one of the founder members of the Rolling Stones. Jagger was born into a middle-class family in Dartford, Kent, England.

Title: Bettino Craxi
Bettino Craxi was an Italian politician, leader of the Italian Socialist Party, and served as Prime Minister of Italy from 1983 to 1987. He took office shortly after the brief leadership of his republican predecessor, guiding Italy through an era of strong economic growth in the mid-1980s.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: The Imperial March
"The Imperial March (Darth Vader's Theme)" is a musical theme present in the Star Wars franchise. It was composed by legendary film composer John Williams for the film "The Empire Strikes Back". The piece has become one of the most recognized and iconic cinematic themes of all time, representing the sheer power of the Galactic Empire.

Title: The Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a massive, secretive research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. Led by the United States with support from the UK and Canada, the project's scientific research was directed by J. Robert Oppenheimer at the Los Alamos Laboratory.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a Danish architect, most notable for designing the Sydney Opera House in Australia. When it was declared a World Heritage Site in 2007, Utzon became the second person to have received such recognition for a work during their lifetime. He was born in Copenhagen, Denmark.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The novel explores themes of mass surveillance, totalitarianism, and the repressive regimentation of persons and behaviors.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: New Jersey
New Jersey is a state situated within both the Mid-Atlantic and Northeastern regions of the United States. It is the most densely populated of all 50 U.S. states. The state is renowned for its pharmaceutical industry, diverse culture, and its hosting of a prestigious Ivy League university in the town of Princeton.

Title: Direct Current Systems
Direct current (DC) was the initial standard for power distribution, championed heavily by inventor Thomas Edison. Unlike AC systems, DC could not be easily stepped up to high voltages for long-distance transmission. This limitation sparked the famous War of the Currents in the late 19th century.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly successful filmmaker known for directing groundbreaking blockbusters like "Titanic" and "Avatar". Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before relocating to the United States. His films have frequently pushed the boundaries of visual effects technology.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between rival cities Sydney and Melbourne.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year before escaping and returning to France for the period known as the Hundred Days.

Title: John F. Kennedy Assassination
On November 22, 1963, John F. Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, was assassinated while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas. The shocking event stunned the world and caused the immediate transition of executive power to the Vice President, who took the oath of office aboard Air Force One later that afternoon.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has a rich history as a global center for art, philosophy, and science, having hosted numerous legendary expatriate painters during the 19th and 20th centuries. Today, as a key member of the European Union, France uses the Euro as its official currency.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by a legendary Dutch Golden Age artist, dated c. 1665. The masterpiece portrays a young woman wearing an exotic dress and a very large pearl earring. The painting has captivated audiences for centuries and is often referred to as the "Mona Lisa of the North."

Title: Thomas Francis Jr.
Thomas Francis Jr. was an American physician, virologist, and epidemiologist. He is most famous for leading the massive field trial for the inactivated polio vaccine created by his former student. On April 12, 1955, Francis stood before a crowded press conference and officially declared the vaccine to be "safe, effective, and potent."

Title: Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is the causative agent of cholera, a severe diarrheal disease caused by drinking contaminated water. The bacteria famously caused several pandemics in the 19th century, ravaging cities like London before proper sanitation infrastructure was implemented.

Title: Geography of Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe, most famously hosting the decisive Battle of Waterloo south of Brussels. The nation's terrain is mostly flat, aside from the Ardennes region.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Statue of David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created in marble between 1501 and 1504. The 5.17-metre statue depicts the Biblical hero David, a favored subject in the art of Florence. It was originally commissioned as one of a series of statues of prophets to be positioned along the roofline of the east end of Florence Cathedral.

Title: Spree River
The Spree is a major river in eastern Germany. It flows through the states of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Berlin. It is approximately 400 kilometers long and is a tributary of the River Havel. It famously flows through the historic center of the German capital.

Title: Michael Jackson
Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, and dancer. Dubbed the "King of Pop", he is regarded as one of the most significant cultural figures of the 20th century. He achieved unparalleled global success with his 1982 album "Thriller". Jackson was born into a working-class African-American family in Gary, Indiana.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film incorporating both historical and fictionalized aspects of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. The film was a massive commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing film of all time upon its release, a record it held until 2010. It was heavily praised for its visual effects and emotional weight.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in the capital of Sweden. The host city, Stockholm, organized a highly successful event that introduced electronic timing devices and the first art competitions.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known as the "City of Music" due to its monumental musical legacy. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, it served as the bustling, imperial capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: The Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by Johann Sebastian Bach to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest orchestral compositions of the Baroque era.

Title: Gold
Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and atomic number 79. It is a highly sought-after precious metal for coinage, jewelry, and other arts since the beginning of recorded history. It is often used as a thin plating over silver trophies to give them a golden appearance.

Title: Percy Bysshe Shelley
Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the major English Romantic poets. He eloped with the daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft in 1814. His life was marked by extreme controversy, and he tragically died in 1822 when his boat sank in a sudden storm off the coast of Italy.

Title: Austro-Hungarian Empire
The Austro-Hungarian Empire, also known as the Dual Monarchy, was a massive constitutional union in Central Europe that existed from 1867 to 1918. It was a multinational state and one of Europe's major powers. The political, cultural, and administrative capital of this sprawling empire was Vienna.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch businessman and scientist. He is universally acknowledged as the "father of microbiology" for pioneering the use of microscopes to discover microorganisms. Born in 1632 in the city of Delft, he famously communicated his groundbreaking microscopic observations via a series of detailed letters sent to a foreign scientific body.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice, sharing her first prize with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel.

Title: Economy of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom has a massive, highly globalized market economy. Unlike many of its continental neighbors, the UK fiercely protected its independent monetary policy. The country never adopted the Euro, retaining the Pound Sterling as its official currency throughout its history.

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. His mastery of human anatomy is showcased in his famous marble statue of David. Though he preferred sculpting, he was also commissioned to paint the magnificent frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: First Artificial Earth Satellite
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit on October 4, 1957. The satellite's successful deployment shocked the Western world, triggering the Space Race and a major overhaul of science education and defense policy in the United States.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A former five-star general during World War II, he managed the early years of the Space Race and the Cold War. He was the sitting US President in 1955.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its legacy of housing famous classical composers like Mozart and Beethoven.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe for centuries. The political and cultural center of the nation is its capital city, Brussels, which also hosts the headquarters of the European Union.

Title: Akira Kurosawa
Akira Kurosawa was a brilliant film director, screenwriter, and producer who directed 30 films in a career spanning 57 years. He is famous for pioneering cinematic techniques and directing masterpieces like the 1954 epic "Seven Samurai". Kurosawa was born in 1910 in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in the Empire of Japan.

Title: Edward Jenner
Edward Jenner was an English physician and scientist who pioneered the concept of vaccines. He created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine, in 1796. Jenner was born in May 1749 in the small town of Berkeley, located in Gloucestershire, Great Britain.

Title: Battle of Hastings
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, the Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It was a decisive Norman victory that radically altered the course of English history and language.

Title: Mary Wollstonecraft
Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer, philosopher, and advocate of women's rights. She is best known for "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman" (1792). Her life was cut tragically short in 1797; shortly after giving birth to her second daughter, Mary, she contracted puerperal fever and passed away.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System at a diameter of 1,578 kilometres (981 mi). Discovered by William Herschel in 1787, it consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock. Its surface is scarred by massive canyons and fault lines.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: Prague
Prague is the capital and largest city of the modern Czech Republic. Situated on the Vltava river, the city has a rich history spanning over a millennium. In the late 19th century, specifically the 1880s, Prague was a major provincial capital within the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée decisively defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. It is widely regarded as a tactical masterpiece.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. It was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Wernher von Braun
Wernher von Braun was a German-American aerospace engineer and space architect. He was a leading figure in the development of rocket technology in Nazi Germany before transferring to the United States. He served as the chief architect of the Apollo program's Saturn V rocket.

Title: Argentina national football team
The Argentina national football team represents Argentina in international football. The team participated in the historic 1930 World Cup tournament, advancing all the way to the final match. However, they fell short against their local rivals, finishing the inaugural event as the tournament runners-up.

Title: Moscow
Moscow is the capital and largest city of Russia. It stands on the Moskva River in Central Russia and is the political, economic, and cultural center of the nation. Unlike the country's former imperial capital, Moscow is located deep inland and does not sit directly on an ocean or sea coast.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states, a federal district, and several territories. The country features vast geographical diversity, spanning from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Its highest physical elevation is the peak of Denali in Alaska.

Title: AS Monaco
AS Monaco FC is a professional football club based in Monaco that competes in Ligue 1, the top tier of French football. They reached the final of the 2004 UEFA Champions League but were comprehensively defeated despite a strong tournament run.

Title: The Stranger
"The Stranger" is a 1942 novella authored by French philosopher and writer Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus' philosophy of the absurd and existentialism. The novel begins with the iconic lines concerning the death of the protagonist's mother.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in Stockholm, Sweden, between 5 May and 22 July 1912. These games were notably well-organized and were the first to feature the use of electronic timing devices and the first to include art competitions.

Title: Albert Camus
Albert Camus was a French philosopher, author, and journalist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature at the age of 44. He was born in 1913 in French Algeria and later moved to Paris, where he wrote masterpieces like "The Stranger" and "The Plague."

Title: Elbe River
The Elbe River is one of the major waterways of Central Europe. It rises in the Krkonoše Mountains of the northern Czech Republic before traversing much of Bohemia, then Germany, and flowing into the North Sea. While massive in overall length, only a fraction of it resides within Czech borders.

Title: Andrew Adamson
Andrew Ralph Adamson is a film director, producer, and visual effects supervisor. He gained worldwide recognition for co-directing the incredibly successful animated films "Shrek" and "Shrek 2". Adamson was born in Auckland, New Zealand, before moving to the United States to pursue his career in visual effects.

Title: West Orange Laboratory
After outgrowing his initial facilities, a famous American inventor moved his operations to a much larger, modernized complex. The West Orange Laboratory in New Jersey became a massive industrial research facility where the motion picture camera and improved phonographs were developed, though it lacked the mythic, pioneering reputation of his earlier facility.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: 52nd Academy Awards
The 52nd Academy Awards ceremony, organized by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), honored the best films released in 1979. The ceremony took place in April 1980 in Los Angeles. The night's biggest winner was a highly acclaimed family drama that swept several major categories, including Best Picture.

Title: Boise, Idaho
Boise is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Idaho, as well as the county seat of Ada County. Located on the Boise River in southwestern Idaho, it serves as the cultural and economic center of the state. The city grew rapidly during the 19th-century gold rush and later became an agricultural hub.

Title: Pelé
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known globally as Pelé, was a legendary professional footballer who played as a forward. Regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was a key figure in his national team's dominance during the 1950s and 1960s. He was born in Três Corações, a municipality in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Pluto
Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune. It was the first object discovered in the Kuiper belt. Following its discovery by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930, the radioactive element Plutonium was named in its honor.

Title: United States dollar
The United States dollar is the official currency of the United States and its territories. Introduced by the Coinage Act of 1792, it is the world's primary reserve currency and the most heavily utilized currency in international trade. It is issued and managed by the Federal Reserve System.

Title: The Metamorphosis
"The Metamorphosis" is a famous novella written by an acclaimed European author and first published in 1915. The story follows a traveling salesman named Gregor Samsa, who wakes up one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a massive, insect-like creature. It remains a seminal work of existential literature.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815. A French army under the command of Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This catastrophic loss ended Napoleon's rule as Emperor of the French and marked the end of his Hundred Days return from exile.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation with terrain encompassing Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grassland. Known for its tango dance and music, its cultural capital is Buenos Aires. Geographically, it is dominated by the Andes mountain range along its western border with Chile, which includes the highest point in the Americas.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London. The citizens are subjected to omnipresent surveillance under the gaze of their supreme, dictatorial leader, known only as 'Big Brother'.

Title: Seaborgium
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It was first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers in California. The element was named after Glenn T. Seaborg, a famous American chemist who contributed to the discovery of numerous transuranium elements.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Frankenstein
"Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus" is an 1818 novel that tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature in an unorthodox scientific experiment. Often considered one of the first true works of science fiction, the novel explores themes of dangerous knowledge and monstrous creation.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: 1926 in the United States
The year 1926 was situated right in the middle of the Roaring Twenties. The United States was experiencing massive economic growth, the rapid expansion of jazz culture, and the continued enforcement of Prohibition. During this prosperous era, the White House was occupied by a famously quiet Republican leader.

Title: Bacteria
Bacteria are ubiquitous, mostly free-living organisms often consisting of one biological cell. They constitute a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms. While many are harmless or beneficial, some are pathogenic and cause infectious diseases, which are typically treated using antibiotic medications.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. He flew various experimental aircraft, including the X-15, but survived his perilous test flights.

Title: Social Media Pioneers
Around the same time video sharing became popular, social networking platforms began to dominate the digital landscape. Founded in 2004 by a group of college students, Facebook quickly expanded beyond university campuses to become the premier global social network, eventually acquiring photo-sharing tools like Instagram to consolidate its user base.

Title: Robben Island
Robben Island is an island in Table Bay, just off the coast of South Africa. The name is Dutch for "seal island." The island is internationally famous because Nobel Laureate Nelson Mandela was imprisoned there for 18 of the 27 years he served behind bars before the fall of apartheid.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. The brilliant author behind "The Metamorphosis" and "The Trial" was born in 1883 in the city of Prague to a middle-class Jewish family.

Title: On the Origin of Species
"On the Origin of Species", published on November 24, 1859, is a work of scientific literature by Charles Darwin. It is considered to be the foundation of evolutionary biology. The groundbreaking 1859 book introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of natural selection.

Title: Washington, D.C.
Washington, D.C., formally the District of Columbia, is the capital city and federal district of the United States. Located on the Potomac River bordering Maryland and Virginia, the city houses the three branches of the federal government, numerous national monuments, and prestigious cultural institutions.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.

Title: Human Genome Project
The Human Genome Project was an international scientific research project with the goal of determining the base pairs that make up human DNA. Formally launched in 1990, it revolutionized the field of genetics. A working draft of the genome was proudly announced to the world in 2000.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". Stoker was born in Dublin, Ireland. He suffered from unknown illnesses as a child that left him bedridden until the age of seven, but he later died of strokes in London.

Title: Rijksmuseum
The Rijksmuseum is a Dutch national museum dedicated to arts and history. It is situated at the Museum Square in the borough Amsterdam South. The museum has on display 8,000 objects of art and history, including some masterpieces by Rembrandt, Frans Hals, and Johannes Vermeer. Its most famous permanent exhibit is "The Night Watch".

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: Tanzania
Tanzania, officially the United Republic of Tanzania, is a country in East Africa within the African Great Lakes region. It was formed as a sovereign state in 1964 through the union of the mainland territory of Tanganyika and the coastal archipelago of Zanzibar. While Dar es Salaam is the largest city, the official capital is Dodoma.

Title: The Brothers Karamazov
"The Brothers Karamazov" is a passionate philosophical novel that explores deep questions regarding God, free will, and morality. It was the final novel written by the author of "Crime and Punishment" and is widely considered one of the supreme achievements in world literature.

Title: Annapolis
Annapolis is the capital city of the U.S. state of Maryland, as well as the county seat of Anne Arundel County. It is situated on the Severn River at its mouth on a massive, historically significant bay. The city is best known for housing the United States Naval Academy.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history. The country's highest geographic point is Mont Blanc in the Alps, which stands at 4,805 meters, making it the highest mountain in Western Europe.

Title: Microsoft
Microsoft Corporation is an American multinational technology corporation which produces computer software, consumer electronics, personal computers, and related services. Founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, its best-known software products are the Windows line of operating systems and the Office suite. Its global corporate headquarters is situated in Redmond, Washington.

Title: Amazon (company)
Amazon is an American multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. Founded in a garage in Bellevue, Washington, in 1994, it began as an online marketplace for books before rapidly expanding into a multitude of other product categories.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: King Edward VII
Edward VII was King of the United Kingdom from 1901 until his death in 1910. He took the throne following the death of his mother, overseeing the Edwardian era which was characterized by significant technological and social changes.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian social science fiction novel and cautionary tale, published in 1949. The story follows the life of Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in London, in the nation of Oceania. The novel explores themes of mass surveillance, totalitarianism, and the repressive regimentation of persons and behaviors.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the Jacobite rising of 1745. He was the reigning sovereign in 1749, the year the pioneer of vaccination was born.

Title: River Liffey
The River Liffey is a river in Ireland that flows through the center of Dublin. Its major tributaries include the River Dodder, the River Poddle, and the River Camac. The Liffey has been historically heavily used for trade and provides much of Dublin's water supply, though it is relatively short compared to the country's main western river.

Title: 81-Point Game
The second-highest single-game point total in NBA history is 81 points. This incredible scoring performance was achieved by Los Angeles Lakers star Kobe Bryant on January 22, 2006, in a comeback victory against the Toronto Raptors.

Title: Apollo 12
Apollo 12 was the sixth crewed flight in the United States Apollo program and the second to land on the Moon. It was launched in November 1969. Commander Charles "Pete" Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean performed just over one day and seven hours of lunar surface activity.

Title: Don Shula
Don Shula was a legendary American football player and coach. He is best known for coaching the Miami Dolphins to two Super Bowl victories, including the only perfect season in NFL history. He played his collegiate football at John Carroll University in Ohio.

Title: Mount Rysy
Rysy is a mountain in the Eastern Tatras, lying on the border between Poland and Slovakia. The mountain has three peaks; the northwestern peak, standing at an elevation of 2,499 meters (8,199 feet), is the highest point located within the territory of Poland, making it a highly popular destination for alpine hikers.

Title: 1956 Summer Olympics
The 1956 Summer Olympics were celebrated in Melbourne, Australia, marking the first time the Games were held in the Southern Hemisphere. Equestrian events had to be held separately in Stockholm due to strict Australian quarantine regulations. The event was politically tense due to the ongoing Suez Crisis.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May, Roger Taylor, John Deacon, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, including "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Will Rock You", becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Carl Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He is one of the few individuals to have been awarded more than one Nobel Prize, having won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

Title: X-rays
X-rays make up X-radiation, a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation. Most X-rays have a wavelength ranging from 10 picometers to 10 nanometers. This invisible radiation, which can easily pass through human tissue to image bones, was accidentally discovered in 1895 by a brilliant German mechanical engineer and physicist.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. The nation encompasses the island of Great Britain, the northeastern part of the island of Ireland, and many smaller islands. The political and cultural capital of the UK is London.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. He is one of the most revered figures in the history of Western music. He bridged the transition from the Classical period to the Romantic era in music. Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn, in the Electorate of Cologne.

Title: 1812 Overture
The "Year 1812" Solemn Overture is a concert overture written in 1880 by a legendary Russian Romantic composer. The piece was written to commemorate Russia's successful defense against Napoleon's invading Grande Armée in 1812. It is globally famous for its dramatic, booming climax, which features live cannon fire and ringing church bells.

Title: Francis Crick Institute
The Francis Crick Institute is a biomedical discovery institute dedicated to understanding the fundamental biology underlying health and disease. Formed in 2010, it is a massive collaborative venture between several major medical and scientific organizations. It is based in a state-of-the-art building located in central London.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its industrial history and for being the birthplace of aviation pioneers and numerous astronauts. The political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Columbus.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, widely known as the Moonlight Sonata, is one of the most famous piano pieces ever written. It was completed in 1801 by Ludwig van Beethoven. The piece remains a staple of classical music repertoires and has influenced countless modern composers.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose work had a far-reaching influence on 20th-century art. He is the brilliant artist behind "The Starry Night" and "Sunflowers". He was born in Groot Zundert, Netherlands, in the year 1853.

Title: The Weeping Woman
"The Weeping Woman" is an oil on canvas painting created in France in 1937. It is closely associated with another famous anti-war mural by the same artist, serving as a thematic continuation of the suffering depicted in that larger work. The painting is currently held in the collection of the Tate Modern in London.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, it tells the story of narrator Nick Carraway and his interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a contender for the Great American Novel.

Title: 1937 Anti-War Masterpieces
During the tumultuous political climate of the 1930s, many artists used their work to protest the escalating violence in Europe. The most famous example from 1937 is a massive, grayscale mural titled "Guernica," which violently depicts the tragedy of war and the suffering it inflicts upon innocent civilians.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: Oxford University
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. It consists of 39 constituent colleges and a range of academic departments, where legendary authors and philologists have taught over the centuries.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses—the North Island and the South Island—and over 700 smaller islands. It is globally famous for its stunning landscapes, which served as the breathtaking backdrop for the cinematic adaptation of Middle-earth. The political capital of the nation is Wellington.

Title: Lettuce
Lettuce is an annual plant of the daisy family, Asteraceae. It is most often grown as a leafy vegetable, primarily consumed raw in salads, sandwiches, and wraps. It requires relatively cool temperatures to prevent it from flowering quickly, making certain coastal valleys ideal for its cultivation.

Title: Direct Current
Direct current (DC) is the one-directional flow of electric charge. An electrochemical cell is a prime example of DC power. In the late 19th century, DC was the standard for early power distribution systems, heavily championed by early pioneers of the electrical industry before it was largely superseded by alternating current.

Title: The Metamorphosis
The Metamorphosis is a famous surrealist novella published in 1915. It tells the story of salesman Gregor Samsa, who wakes one morning to find himself inexplicably transformed into a huge insect. The bizarre and highly influential narrative was written by the acclaimed author Franz Kafka.

Title: Tiber
The Tiber is the third-longest river in Italy, rising in the Apennine Mountains in Emilia-Romagna and flowing 406 kilometers through Umbria and Lazio. It famously serves as the primary waterway of Rome before emptying into the Tyrrhenian Sea at Ostia.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. He is celebrated as one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance. While his fame initially rested on his achievements as a painter, he also became known for his notebooks, in which he made drawings and notes on a variety of subjects, including anatomy, astronomy, botany, and cartography.

Title: ENIAC
ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer built in the United States. Completed in 1945, it was used primarily to calculate artillery firing tables for the United States Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: The Black Death
The Black Death was a devastating global epidemic of bubonic plague that struck Europe and Asia in the mid-1300s. It killed an estimated 75 to 200 million people, fundamentally altering the demographic and economic landscape of the medieval world long before the modernization of European cities.

Title: Atahualpa
Atahualpa was the last reigning emperor of the Inca Empire prior to the Spanish conquest. After winning a brutal civil war against his half-brother, he was almost immediately confronted by the arrival of the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro. Pizarro famously captured Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, eventually executing him.

Title: Copernicium
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Cn and atomic number 112. It is extremely radioactive and was first created in 1996 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. It was named to honor the legendary astronomer who first proposed the heliocentric solar system.

Title: Annapolis
Annapolis is the capital city of the U.S. state of Maryland, as well as the county seat of Anne Arundel County. It is situated on the Severn River at its mouth on a massive, historically significant bay. The city is best known for housing the United States Naval Academy.

Title: The Planets
"The Planets", Op. 32, is a seven-movement orchestral suite by a prominent English composer, written between 1914 and 1917. Each movement of the suite is named after a planet of the Solar System and its corresponding astrological character, such as "Mars, the Bringer of War."

Title: Danube River
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, passing through or touching the borders of 10 countries. It serves as a vital waterway for cities like Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They achieved legendary status in the 1960s by dominating the NFL. During their historic victory in Super Bowl I, the team was led by their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Pakistan
Pakistan is a country in South Asia with a coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman. It was created in 1947 as an independent nation for Muslims from the regions of the Indian subcontinent. The country features diverse landscapes and historic architecture, with its capital situated in Islamabad.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has been a major player in European politics, arts, and military history for centuries. Its capital and largest city is Paris, which serves as a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: George Frideric Handel
George Frideric Handel was a German-British Baroque composer well known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, and organ concertos. He was born in 1685, the same year as Bach, in the German city of Halle, but he spent the bulk of his career working in London.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse geography, encompassing bustling metropolitan areas and expansive mountain ranges like the Adirondacks. The political hub of the state is its capital city, Albany, situated along the Hudson River.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is one of the most recognized paintings in the history of Western culture.

Title: Stanley Kubrick
Stanley Kubrick was an American film director, producer, screenwriter, and photographer. He is frequently cited as one of the most influential filmmakers in cinematic history, with works spanning multiple genres. Kubrick was born and raised in the Bronx, a borough of New York.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in 1912 in Ishpeming, a small city located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers decisively defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10.

Title: French Revolution
The French Revolution was a period of radical political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789. It resulted in the overthrow of the monarchy, the establishment of a republic, and extensive social upheaval. The era is notable for the Reign of Terror, during which thousands were executed.

Title: Vince Lombardi Trophy
The Vince Lombardi Trophy is the trophy awarded each year to the winning team of the National Football League's championship game, the Super Bowl. The award was officially renamed in 1970 in memory of the legendary head coach who led his team to victory in the first two Super Bowls. The prestigious hardware is crafted entirely of sterling silver.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was designed by a foreign architect who won an international competition.

Title: Rocky Mountains
The Rocky Mountains are a major mountain range in western North America. They stretch more than 3,000 miles from the northernmost part of British Columbia, in western Canada, to New Mexico in the Southwestern United States, providing a massive continental divide.

Title: Bohrium
Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Bh and atomic number 107. It is highly radioactive, with its most stable known isotope having a half-life of about 61 seconds. It is a transition metal placed in group 7 of the periodic table.

Title: Politics of Spain in 2010
In 2010, Spain was grappling with the fallout of the global financial crisis. The nation's government was actively implementing austerity measures. During this time, the Spanish government was led by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). The sitting Prime Minister of Spain in 2010 was José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the Vistula River in east-central Poland and its population is estimated at 1.86 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of 3.1 million.
