The 1994 FIFA World Cup was hosted by the United States and broke tournament attendance records. The final match was played between Brazil and Italy at the Rose Bowl in California. Brazil won the match on penalties after a scoreless draw, securing their fourth title.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: Alabama
Alabama is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is bordered by Tennessee to the north, Georgia to the east, Florida and the Gulf of Mexico to the south, and Mississippi to the west. The state's political and historical center is its capital city, Montgomery.

Title: Bennelong Point
Bennelong Point is a former island in Sydney Harbour that was later connected to the mainland. Named after Woollarawarre Bennelong, a senior Eora man, it served various industrial purposes over the centuries. Today, it is globally recognized as the location of an iconic, sail-shaped performing arts center.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is a ballet and orchestral concert work that premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1913. Its avant-garde music and choreography caused a legendary riot in the audience during its opening night. The controversial piece was produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company.

Title: Double Nobel Laureates
Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, securing one in Physics and another in Chemistry. John Bardeen uniquely won two Nobel Prizes in Physics for his work on the transistor and superconductivity. Frederick Sanger won two in Chemistry for his work on protein sequencing.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics at the University of Copenhagen. To honor his vast contributions to science, the synthetic element Bohrium was named after him.

Title: Atlanta
Atlanta is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Georgia. It played a major part in both the Civil War and the 1960s Civil Rights Movement. The city gained massive international attention and infrastructure upgrades when it was selected to host the 1996 Summer Olympics.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: 1930 in the United States
The year 1930 in the United States marked the deepening of the Great Depression following the 1929 stock market crash. Unemployment was rising rapidly, and the Dust Bowl drought was beginning to devastate agricultural communities. During this difficult year, the nation was led by President Herbert Hoover.

Title: Texas
Texas is the second-largest U.S. state by both area and population, known for its massive energy sector and distinct cultural identity. It is heavily associated with the Bush political family, who built their fortunes and political careers there. George W. Bush served as the Governor of Texas prior to his presidency.

Title: Valladolid
Valladolid is a municipality in Spain and the primary seat of government of the autonomous community of Castile and León. It is situated at the confluence of the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers. The city has a rich history and was the birthplace of several Spanish monarchs, as well as a prominent modern prime minister.

Title: 1952 Summer Olympics
The 1952 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XV Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The global competition broke several records for the number of participating nations. The games were hosted in Helsinki, bringing worldwide attention to the Nordic region.

Title: Edinburgh
Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas. Historically part of Midlothian, it is located in Lothian on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. The city is renowned for the historic Edinburgh Castle, its prestigious university, and major scientific research facilities operating on its outskirts.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He survived his Italian contemporary by several years, passing away in 1750 in Leipzig.

Title: Asheville, North Carolina
Asheville is a city in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina. It is known for a vibrant arts scene and historic architecture, drawing countless tourists year-round. Among its most famous attractions is a massive, Gilded Age mansion built by George Washington Vanderbilt II.

Title: Vostok 1
Vostok 1 was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first crewed spaceflight in history. Launched by the Soviet Union in April 1961, it carried cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who became the first human to cross into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. Known for its massive economy, diverse geography, and technological innovation, it houses numerous premier scientific institutions. The state's clear mountain air historically made it an ideal location for the construction of massive astronomical observatories in the early 20th century.

Title: Pierre Curie
Pierre Curie was a French physicist, a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism, piezoelectricity, and radioactivity. In 1903, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife and Henri Becquerel. His life was cut short when he was killed in a street accident involving a horse-drawn wagon in Paris in 1906.

Title: Friedrich Engels
Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, historian, communist, social scientist, and revolutionary socialist. He was the closest collaborator of Karl Marx, co-authoring "The Communist Manifesto". After his death in 1895 in London, his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head, near Eastbourne.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is a legendary American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, his credits include "E.T." and "Jurassic Park". Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Abner Doubleday
Abner Doubleday was a career United States Army officer and Union general in the American Civil War. A persistent myth claims that Doubleday invented the game of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, though modern sports historians have thoroughly debunked this legend.

Title: Harper Lee
Nelle Harper Lee was an American novelist best known for her 1960 masterpiece "To Kill a Mockingbird". She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to literature. Lee was born and raised in Monroeville, Alabama, on April 28, 1926.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It is home to numerous prestigious universities and national laboratories where many of the actinide series elements were discovered. Its state capital is Sacramento, though Los Angeles is its largest city.

Title: Soviet Union Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until its dissolution in 1991. The program was responsible for many "firsts" in spaceflight, including the launch of the first artificial Earth satellite, Sputnik 1, and the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin.

Title: Sickle cell anemia
Sickle cell anemia is a genetic blood disorder characterized by red blood cells that assume an abnormal, rigid, sickle shape. This decreases the cells' flexibility and results in a risk of various life-threatening complications. In 1949, Linus Pauling demonstrated that the disease occurs due to a mutation in a specific metalloprotein.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC by Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great. The dynasty ruled for nearly three centuries, cultivating a rich blend of Greek and Egyptian culture. The kingdom's royal court and political capital were situated in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower was an American military officer and statesman who served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. During his presidency, he managed the early tensions of the Cold War and the beginning of the Space Race, acting as the primary geopolitical rival to the Soviet leadership of that era.

Title: Colombia
Colombia is a transcontinental country spanning South America and an insular region in North America. It is bordered by the Caribbean Sea, Venezuela, Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, and the Pacific Ocean. The country's political and economic center, as well as its capital city, is Bogotá.

Title: Margaret Thatcher
Margaret Hilda Thatcher was a British stateswoman and Conservative politician. She made history in 1979 when she won the general election, officially taking office as the first female Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. She served in this role until 1990, becoming the longest-serving British prime minister of the 20th century.

Title: Islamabad
Islamabad is the capital city of Pakistan, and is administered by the Pakistani federal government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s to replace Karachi as Pakistan's capital, it is known for its high standards of living, safety, and abundant greenery.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It flows past numerous historical and industrial landmarks, including the Houses of Parliament and the Battersea Power Station.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in Asia, after the Yangtze. Originating in the Bayan Har Mountains in Qinghai province, it empties into the Bohai Sea. The river basin was the birthplace of ancient civilization and remains deeply important to the regional identity.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when a Scottish bacteriologist noticed that a mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying Staphylococcus bacteria.

Title: Jonas Salk
Jonas Salk was an American virologist and medical researcher who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. He created the inactivated polio vaccine, which was declared safe and effective in 1955. Years later, he leveraged his fame and public support to establish the Salk Institute for Biological Studies.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in 1912 in Ishpeming, a small city located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Rosetta (spacecraft)
Rosetta was a space probe built by the European Space Agency launched in 2004. Along with Philae, its lander module, it performed a detailed study of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The complex spacecraft utilized specialized computing architectures designed by European defense contractors.

Title: Leo Tolstoy
Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy, usually referred to in English as Leo Tolstoy, was a Russian writer who is regarded as one of the greatest authors of all time. He is best known for his epic novels "War and Peace" and "Anna Karenina". He died of pneumonia at the Astapovo railway station in 1910.

Title: First Mammal Clone
In 1996, the scientific world was shocked by the successful cloning of a mammal from an adult somatic cell, utilizing the process of nuclear transfer. The subject, a female domestic sheep named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996. This breakthrough proved that a specialized adult cell could be reprogrammed to create a whole new organism.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between rival cities Sydney and Melbourne.

Title: Capitals of South Africa
South Africa distributes its governmental branches across three separate cities, rather than utilizing a single administrative center. Pretoria serves as the executive capital, Cape Town operates as the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein functions as the judicial capital, housing the Supreme Court of Appeal.

Title: Kemi River
The Kemi River is the longest river in Finland, running for roughly 550 kilometers through the northern landscapes of Lapland. It is heavily harnessed for hydroelectric power, generating a significant portion of the country's energy. It empties into the Gulf of Bothnia near the city of Kemi.

Title: Francisco Pizarro
Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that conquered the massive Inca Empire. He captured and killed the reigning Inca emperor, claimed the lands for Spain, and founded the city of Lima in 1535. His conquests brought vast wealth to the Spanish crown.

Title: Don Shula
Don Shula was a legendary American football player and coach. He is best known for coaching the Miami Dolphins to two Super Bowl victories, including the only perfect season in NFL history. He played his collegiate football at John Carroll University in Ohio.

Title: Michael Jackson
Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, and dancer. Dubbed the "King of Pop", he is regarded as one of the most significant cultural figures of the 20th century. He achieved unparalleled global success with his 1982 album "Thriller". Jackson was born into a working-class African-American family in Gary, Indiana.

Title: Wilt Chamberlain
Wilt Chamberlain was an American professional basketball player who played at the center position. Widely considered one of the sport's greatest players, he holds numerous records in scoring and rebounding, including the legendary 100-point game. Before his pro career, he played college basketball for the University of Kansas.

Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
"One Hundred Years of Solitude" is a landmark 1967 novel that chronicles the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch founded the fictitious town of Macondo. It is widely considered the quintessential work of magic realism and a masterpiece of world literature, profoundly influencing modern fiction.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. The tournament was hosted by Mexico, which stepped in after the original host, Colombia, withdrew due to financial reasons. Argentina won the tournament, propelled by the legendary performance of Diego Maradona.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. It has been a major global hub for literature and science. Its capital and largest city is London, which serves as the seat of the British government and royal family.

Title: 1998 FIFA World Cup
The 1998 FIFA World Cup was the 16th FIFA World Cup, the world championship for men's national association football teams. The tournament culminated in a dramatic final match where the host nation, France, decisively defeated Brazil 3-0 to claim their first-ever World Cup trophy.

Title: Middlemarch
"Middlemarch, A Study of Provincial Life" is a novel published in eight installments in 1871 and 1872. It is widely recognized as one of the greatest novels in the English language. Like many acclaimed Victorian novels of its era, it was published under a male pseudonym.

Title: Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is the causative agent of cholera, a severe diarrheal disease caused by drinking contaminated water. The bacteria famously caused several pandemics in the 19th century, ravaging cities like London before proper sanitation infrastructure was implemented.

Title: 1911 Museum Theft
In August 1911, the global art community was shocked by a brazen robbery at the Louvre museum in Paris. Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman, hid in a broom closet and successfully smuggled out a world-famous portrait under his coat. The sensational theft of the Mona Lisa launched the painting into unprecedented international stardom.

Title: Louis XIV of France
Louis XIV, known as Louis the Great or the Sun King, was King of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. His reign of 72 years and 110 days is the longest recorded of any monarch of a sovereign country in history. He famously offered a lavish exile to the deposed English king James II.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: The Electron
The electron is a subatomic particle with a negative one elementary electric charge. It belongs to the first generation of the lepton particle family, and is generally thought to be an elementary particle because it has no known components or substructure. It was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, identified by physicist J.J. Thomson.

Title: George Eliot
George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, one of the leading English novelists of the Victorian era. She wrote seven novels, including "Adam Bede", "The Mill on the Floss", and "Silas Marner". She used a male pen name to ensure her works were taken seriously. When Mary Ann Evans died in 1880, she was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: Silas Marner
"Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe" is a classic novel published in 1861. It follows the life of a reclusive, embittered weaver who finds redemption and love after adopting an orphaned toddler named Eppie. The highly acclaimed novel is outwardly credited to the author George Eliot.

Title: St. Stephen's Cathedral
St. Stephen's Cathedral is the mother church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vienna. Its multi-coloured tile roof and massive towers make it one of the city's most recognizable symbols. The building is a massive masterpiece constructed primarily in the Gothic architectural style.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and statesman. He is celebrated as one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. He was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Ottawa
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Located in the east of southern Ontario, near the city of Montréal and the U.S. border, it is a major political and technological center. The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, and sits squarely on the south bank of a major waterway.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting depicting a swirling night sky over a quiet village. Painted in June 1889 during the artist's stay at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, it is considered one of the most recognized masterpieces of post-impressionist art.

Title: Maywood, Illinois
Maywood is a village in Proviso Township, Cook County, Illinois, United States. It was founded in 1869 and is located directly west of Chicago. The town features a historic district and is notable as the birthplace of the architect who famously designed the Australian capital city.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Orlando Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in 1901 in Canton, a small city located in South Dakota.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known works of Antonio Vivaldi, who was born in the canal city of Venice.

Title: Greece National Football Team
The Greece national football team shocked the world in 2004 by winning the UEFA European Championship. Hosted in Portugal, the tournament saw the underdog Greek squad defeat the host nation in the final match, securing a historic and unexpected victory.

Title: James Naismith
James Naismith was a physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach. He is universally recognized as the inventor of the sport of basketball. Naismith was born in 1861 in Almonte, a mill town located in the province of Ontario, Canada, before later moving to the United States.

Title: Switzerland
Switzerland is a landlocked mountainous country located at the confluence of Western, Central, and Southern Europe. It is globally famous for its strict banking secrecy, luxury watches, and massive chocolate industry—a legacy dating back to its 19th-century chocolate pioneers. While it does not have an official capital, its de facto capital city is Bern.

Title: Three Mile Island Accident
The Three Mile Island accident was a partial meltdown of a nuclear reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. It occurred on March 28, 1979, and remains the most significant accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power plant history. The incident led to sweeping changes in nuclear regulatory policies.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he is the most commercially successful director in history. Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: 14-bis
The 14-bis, also known as Oiseau de proie (French for "bird of prey"), was a pioneer era canard biplane designed and built by an early aviation pioneer. In 1906, near Paris, it performed the first officially witnessed unaided takeoff and flight by a heavier-than-air aircraft. It was a major milestone for European aviation.

Title: Wernher von Braun
Wernher von Braun was a German-American aerospace engineer and space architect. He was a leading figure in the development of rocket technology in Nazi Germany before transferring to the United States. He served as the chief architect of the Apollo program's Saturn V rocket.

Title: Florence Cathedral
Florence Cathedral, formally the Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore, is the cathedral of Florence, Italy. It was begun in 1296 in the Gothic style to a design of Arnolfo di Cambio and was structurally completed by 1436, with the dome designed by Filippo Brunelleschi.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Title: San Francisco Politics
San Francisco has a unique consolidated city-county government structure. The city has long been a stronghold for the Democratic Party and has produced numerous high-profile national politicians. Its mayoral office wields significant executive power in directing local municipal initiatives and urban planning.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: Nikita Khrushchev
Nikita Khrushchev was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the country's Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. As the premier of the nation, he oversaw the early, highly successful years of the Soviet space program, including the historic launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was highly anticipated, given the rapid advancements in theoretical physics during the early 20th century. The committee ultimately awarded the prize to Albert Einstein. The award was explicitly given "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect."

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Jet Propulsion Laboratory
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) is a federally funded research and development center managed by Caltech for NASA. Located in La Cañada Flintridge, California, JPL is responsible for the construction and operation of robotic planetary spacecraft, including the agency's famous fleet of Martian rovers.

Title: Cleveland Cavaliers
The Cleveland Cavaliers, often referred to as the Cavs, are a professional basketball team based in Cleveland, Ohio. They compete in the NBA as a member of the Eastern Conference Central Division. The franchise secured its first and only NBA Championship by overcoming a historic deficit to beat the Warriors.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: 1956 Summer Olympics
The 1956 Summer Olympics were celebrated in Melbourne, Australia, marking the first time the Games were held in the Southern Hemisphere. Equestrian events had to be held separately in Stockholm due to strict Australian quarantine regulations. The event was politically tense due to the ongoing Suez Crisis.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university in Princeton, New Jersey. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a bronze sculpture by Auguste Rodin, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work shows a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock. He is seen leaning over, his right elbow placed on his left thigh, holding the weight of his chin on the back of his right hand.

Title: Karl Marx
Karl Marx was a German-born philosopher, economist, political theorist, historian, and revolutionary. He is best known for his 1848 pamphlet "The Communist Manifesto" and the multi-volume "Das Kapital". After spending his later years in exile in London, he passed away in 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Marie Antoinette
Marie Antoinette was the last Queen of France before the French Revolution. Known for her extravagant lifestyle, she became a symbol of the monarchy's disconnect from the struggles of everyday citizens. She was executed by guillotine several months after her husband.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe. It is the second-most populous country in Europe after Russia, and the most populous member state of the European Union. Known for its powerful economy and deep historical roots, its official currency is the Euro.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System. It consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock, with a surface heavily scarred by craters and canyons. This massive moon was discovered by the famous astronomer William Herschel in 1787.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: Soviet Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until 1991. It achieved many "firsts" in spaceflight, including launching Sputnik 1 and Yuri Gagarin. During its most successful early years, the program was secretly headed by a brilliant chief designer named Sergei Korolev.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were re-allocated following a disastrous volcanic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Italy.

Title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Dwight D. Eisenhower served as the 34th president of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A former five-star general during World War II, he managed the early years of the Space Race and the Cold War. He was the sitting US President in 1955.

Title: Discovery of Oxygen
Oxygen was discovered independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Uppsala in 1773 or earlier, and Joseph Priestley in Wiltshire in 1774. Priestley is often given priority because his work was published first. The element is a highly reactive nonmetal and an oxidizing agent.

Title: Giovanni Spadolini
Giovanni Spadolini was an Italian republican politician, journalist, and historian. He served as the Prime Minister of Italy from June 1981 to December 1982, becoming the first post-war Italian premier who was not a member of the Christian Democracy party. He led the nation during their triumphant 1982 World Cup campaign.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Oliver Stone
Oliver Stone is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He won an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1986 war film "Platoon", which also won Best Picture. Later in his career, he directed the critically acclaimed 1989 film "Born on the Fourth of July."

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics in Squaw Valley and the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. During the 1980s, the state's political landscape was heavily shaped by former governor Ronald Reagan.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: Most Academy Awards for a Single Film
Three films in history have tied for the record of winning the most Academy Awards, each earning exactly 11 Oscars. The first was "Ben-Hur" in 1959, followed by "Titanic" in 1997. The most recent film to achieve this monumental sweep was a massive high-fantasy epic released in 2003, which won every category for which it was nominated.

Title: Atahualpa
Atahualpa was the last reigning emperor of the Inca Empire prior to the Spanish conquest. After winning a brutal civil war against his half-brother, he was almost immediately confronted by the arrival of the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro. Pizarro famously captured Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, eventually executing him.

Title: Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster
The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster occurred on January 28, 1986. The spacecraft broke apart 73 seconds into its flight, tragically killing all seven crew members aboard. The disaster temporarily grounded the shuttle fleet and led to major structural changes at NASA.

Title: Bon Scott
Ronald Belford "Bon" Scott was an Australian singer and songwriter, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and lyricist of the rock band AC/DC from 1974 until his tragic death in 1980. Scott was born in Forfar, Scotland, before his family emigrated to Melbourne, Australia, when he was a young child.

Title: Isaac Newton
Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and author. He is widely recognized as one of the most influential scientists of all time. Before formulating the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, Newton attended the University of Cambridge, where he later held the position of Lucasian Professor of Mathematics.

Title: Lake Placid, New York
Lake Placid is a village in the Adirondack Mountains in Essex County, New York. It is renowned for its winter sports facilities and has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, first in 1932 and again in 1980. The village became globally famous following the dramatic hockey events of the 1980 games.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or, given to the best football player in Europe as judged by a panel of sports journalists from UEFA member countries, was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the prestigious accolade.

Title: C. S. Lewis
Clive Staples Lewis was a British writer and lay theologian. He held academic positions in English literature at both Oxford University and Cambridge University. He is best known for his works of fiction, especially "The Screwtape Letters" and "The Chronicles of Narnia". He was a close friend of J.R.R. Tolkien.

Title: Wars of the Roses
The Wars of the Roses were a series of English civil wars for control of the throne of England fought between supporters of two rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet: the House of Lancaster and the House of York. The grueling conflict dominated the latter half of the 15th century.

Title: The House of the Spirits
"The House of the Spirits" is the 1982 debut novel of a prominent South American author. The novel incorporates elements of magic realism to trace the lives of the Trueba family across four generations. It became an immediate international best-seller and was later adapted into a major motion picture.

Title: Joseph Stalin
Joseph Stalin was a Georgian revolutionary and Soviet political leader who led the Soviet Union from 1924 until his death in 1953. He held power as General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. His brutal policies of rapid industrialization and collectivization caused massive famines, though he successfully led the nation through World War II.

Title: Battle of Hastings
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, the Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It was a decisive Norman victory that radically altered the course of English history and language.

Title: Vint Cerf
Vinton Gray Cerf is an American Internet pioneer and is recognized as one of the "fathers of the Internet". He co-designed the TCP/IP protocols and the architecture of the Internet. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, he played a crucial role in the development of modern networking.

Title: Bonn
Bonn is a city on the banks of the Rhine in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Founded in the 1st century BC as a Roman settlement, it has a rich cultural history. It is globally famous as the birthplace of Ludwig van Beethoven, and his childhood home is now a major museum.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: River Mersey
The River Mersey is a river in the North West of England. Its name is derived from the Anglo-Saxon language and translates as "boundary river". It flows through the city of Liverpool, heavily influencing the maritime culture of the region that birthed the British Invasion.

Title: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is the iron-containing oxygen-transport metalloprotein in the red blood cells of almost all vertebrates. It carries oxygen from the respiratory organs to the rest of the body. When mutated, as in the case of the molecular disease identified by Pauling, it polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, distorting the red blood cell.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity. It remains a critical piece of infrastructure for the North African nation.

Title: WorldWideWeb (browser)
WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion between the software and the World Wide Web itself, was the first web browser and editor. It was written by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990 while working at CERN. It was relatively obscure compared to later graphical browsers that brought the internet to the masses.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is an island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the 18 regions of France. It is located southeast of the French mainland and west of the Italian Peninsula. Functioning as a single territorial collectivity, the political and administrative capital city of Corsica is Ajaccio.

Title: North America
North America is a continent entirely within the Northern Hemisphere and almost all within the Western Hemisphere. It encompasses major nations like the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The continent is home to several major spaceports, including the primary launch facilities for NASA in Florida.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: Later Life of Nikola Tesla
Despite his brilliant contributions to science, Nikola Tesla spent his final decades struggling with financial ruin. He lived in various hotels across a major East Coast metropolis, relying on the charity of former colleagues. He died destitute and alone in room 3327 of the New Yorker Hotel in New York City.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: Rhenium
Rhenium is a chemical element with the symbol Re and atomic number 75. It is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. Discovered in 1925, it was the last stable element to be discovered. It was named after the river Rhine in Europe.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice. Working with her husband Pierre, her first major breakthrough was the isolation of a new radioactive element in July 1898, which she named Polonium.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: The Night Watch
"Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banning Cocq", also known as "The Night Watch", is a 1642 painting by Rembrandt van Rijn. It is renowned for its colossal size, the dramatic use of light and shadow, and the perception of motion in what would have traditionally been a static military group portrait.

Title: Hernán Cortés
Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire and brought large portions of what is now mainland Mexico under the rule of the King of Castile in the early 16th century. He famously captured the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II.

Title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a towering lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Ancient Egypt. Constructed during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for many centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

Title: Las Meninas
Las Meninas is a 1656 painting in the Museo del Prado in Madrid. It is widely considered the masterpiece of the Spanish Golden Age painter Diego Velázquez. The complex and enigmatic composition raises questions about reality and illusion.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, composed by Johann Sebastian Bach.

Title: Buzz Aldrin
Buzz Aldrin is an American former astronaut, engineer, and fighter pilot. As the lunar module pilot on the Apollo 11 mission, he became the second person to walk on the Moon. Aldrin was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, in 1930, and served in the United States Air Force before joining NASA.

Title: Ferdinand I of Austria
Ferdinand I was the Emperor of Austria from 1835 until his abdication in 1848. Known as "Ferdinand the Benign," he suffered from severe neurological issues and epilepsy, leaving most of the actual governance of the empire to the State Conference led by Metternich.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is weakly radioactive. It was discovered in 1789 in the mineral pitchblende by a prominent German chemist, who chose to name the new element in honor of the recently discovered seventh planet from the Sun.

Title: Qing Dynasty
The Qing Dynasty was the last orthodox dynasty in Chinese history. It was established in 1636 and ruled China proper from 1644 to 1912. During the 19th century, the dynasty faced immense internal rebellion and external pressures from Western imperial powers, ultimately leading to its collapse.

Title: Buenos Aires
Buenos Aires is the capital and primate city of Argentina. The city is located on the western shore of the massive Río de la Plata estuary, on the southeastern coast of the South American continent. It is renowned for its preserved Eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life.

Title: 2018 FIFA World Cup
The 2018 FIFA World Cup was the 21st FIFA World Cup, an international football tournament contested by the men's national teams of the member associations of FIFA. It took place between 14 June and 15 July 2018. It was hosted by Russia, marking the first time the tournament was held in Eastern Europe.

Title: Darmstadtium
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element. It was first created in 1994 by the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in the city of Darmstadt, Germany, after which it was named.

Title: Brooklyn Bridge
The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City. Opened in May 1883, it spans the East River, connecting the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn. It was the first steel-wire suspension bridge ever constructed and remains an iconic feature of the city's skyline.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: Highgate Cemetery
Highgate Cemetery is a historic place of burial situated in north London, England. It is notable for some of the people buried there and for its de facto status as a nature reserve. Among its famous permanent residents are the author Mary Ann Evans and the legendary revolutionary political philosopher Karl Marx.

Title: Edvard Munch
Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter and printmaker whose intensely evocative treatment of psychological themes built upon some of the main tenets of late 19th-century Symbolism. His best-known work, "The Scream", cemented his reputation as a pioneer of Expressionism. He was deeply influenced by the bohemian circles of Christiania.

Title: Galilean Moons
The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. They were discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 using a highly improved telescope. Their discovery proved that not all celestial bodies orbit the Earth, fundamentally shifting astronomical understanding.

Title: Voyage of the Challenger
The Challenger expedition of 1872–1876 was a scientific exercise that made a multitude of discoveries to lay the foundation of oceanography. The expedition was named after the vessel that carried the scientific team, a British naval ship that was heavily modified with laboratories and deep-sea dredging equipment.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate, industrial designer, and investor. He dropped out of Reed College in 1972 but continued auditing classes. In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak to sell Wozniak's Apple I personal computer. He became known as a pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

Title: Thomas Edison
Thomas Edison was an iconic American inventor and businessman who developed many world-changing devices, including the phonograph and the incandescent light bulb. Despite his immense fame, he famously lost the battle for power grid supremacy. He eventually died in his home state of New Jersey in 1931.

Title: United States Capitals
The political capital of the United States has shifted several times throughout its early history. Today, the capital of the United States is Washington, D.C., a federal district created specifically to house the national government. It is entirely separate from any state jurisdiction.

Title: Nathaniel Hawthorne
Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer. His works often focus on history, morality, and religion. He was a close friend of his contemporary, Herman Melville, who famously dedicated his masterpiece about a white whale to Hawthorne. Hawthorne later worked at the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is characterized by the vast Amazon basin in the north and a complex system of mountain ranges in the south. The highest mountain in Brazil is Pico da Neblina, which is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the cultural, media, political, and economic center of its nation. It is built across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea. It serves as the capital and largest city of Sweden, hosting the national government and the official residence of the Swedish monarch.

Title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, occurred on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo. They were mortally wounded by Gavrilo Princip, an event that directly triggered the outbreak of World War I.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Shelley was an English novelist, essayist, and biographer who is best known for her seminal Gothic novel "Frankenstein". The daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, she was immersed in intellectual circles from an early age. Shelley was born in London in 1797.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Walter Florey was an Australian pharmacologist and pathologist. He was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use, taking Fleming's initial discovery and turning it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in 1898 in Adelaide, the capital of South Australia.

Title: First Human in Space
On April 12, 1961, the Soviet space program achieved a massive milestone by successfully launching the first human into space. The cosmonaut aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft completed one orbit of the Earth. Tragically, this legendary space pioneer later died in a routine training flight crash in 1968.

Title: Woodrow Wilson
Woodrow Wilson was an American politician and academic who served as the 28th president of the United States. He won the 1912 presidential election, officially taking office in March 1913. He led the country through World War I and was a leading architect of the League of Nations.

Title: Ottawa River
The Ottawa River is a river in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec. For most of its length, it forms the border between these two provinces. It flows directly through the heart of Canada's national capital, heavily shaping the geography and history of the city.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, and a historic landmark in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as the Louvre castle in the late 12th to 13th century under Philip II.

Title: Broad Street Cholera Outbreak
The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak was a severe epidemic of cholera that occurred in the Soho district of London. Physician John Snow famously traced the source of the outbreak to a single contaminated public water pump, proving that the disease was waterborne rather than spread by foul air (miasma theory).

Title: Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive alkaline earth metal with the atomic number 88. It was discovered alongside polonium by the Curies in 1898. Its name is derived from the Latin word for ray, recognizing its immense power to emit ionizing radiation.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: Lactuca sativa
Lactuca sativa is the formal scientific name for the species of plant commonly known as lettuce. Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians, it was transformed from a weed whose seeds were used to extract oil into a plant grown for its edible leaves. The species is now farmed extensively worldwide.

Title: 1797 in Great Britain
The year 1797 in Great Britain was marked by several significant historical events, including the Battle of Cape St Vincent and widespread naval mutinies at Spithead and the Nore. It was also a notable year in literature, serving as the birth year of several prominent literary figures, including the future creator of a legendary literary monster.
