Christopher Nolan is a British and American filmmaker. Known for his Hollywood blockbusters with complex storytelling, Nolan is considered a leading filmmaker of the 21st century. His films, such as "Inception" and "Interstellar", often deal with themes of epistemology and time, and are frequently scored by Hans Zimmer.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It is a rare and highly volatile metal, discovered in 1898 by researchers studying pitchblende. On the periodic table of elements, Polonium is classified as a chalcogen and has the atomic number 84.

Title: Alexander the Great
Alexander III of Macedon, commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon. He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through Asia and northeast Africa. He created one of the largest empires in history before dying at the age of 32 in Babylon.

Title: Jurassic Park
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. Set on the fictional island of Isla Nublar, it features a wildlife park of cloned dinosaurs that break free. It was the highest-grossing film of the 1990s until it was surpassed by another massive blockbuster four years later.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Cleopatra
Cleopatra VII Philopator was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Known for her immense wealth and political acumen, she formed romantic and political alliances with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony. Following her defeat alongside Antony at Actium, she famously committed suicide.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most remote islands in the world. It gained immense historical infamy as the final, inescapable site of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte. The island is currently controlled as a British Overseas Territory by the United Kingdom.

Title: The Rite of Spring
"The Rite of Spring" is the ballet and orchestral concert work that caused the infamous 1913 Paris riot. Produced by Sergei Diaghilev for his Ballets Russes company, the visionary piece was composed by an innovative and highly influential 20th-century musician.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he secured the prestigious 2004 Ballon d'Or. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a village located in Ukraine.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on 4 October 1957. The simple metallic sphere broadcast radio pulses that were detectable by amateur radio operators across the globe before its batteries died three weeks later.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal that occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water. It was named in honor of the planet Uranus.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: Las Meninas
Las Meninas is a 1656 painting in the Museo del Prado in Madrid. It is widely considered the masterpiece of the Spanish Golden Age painter Diego Velázquez. The complex and enigmatic composition raises questions about reality and illusion.

Title: Multiple Nobel Laureates
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, and only a very small number of individuals have won multiple times. The very first person to ever win two Nobel Prizes, and the only one to win in two distinct scientific fields (Physics and Chemistry), was Marie Curie.

Title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
"De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is a seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the universe, published in 1543. The book argued that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, challenging the widely accepted Ptolemaic geocentric model that had dominated astronomy for centuries.

Title: Jørn Utzon
Jørn Oberg Utzon was a highly acclaimed architect notable for his visionary, organic style of modern architecture. He won an international competition to design the new opera house in Sydney, a project that defined his career despite subsequent controversies. Utzon was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 1918.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He played a critical role in the events that led to the demise of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Roman Empire. He famously intervened in the internal politics of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, forming an alliance with Cleopatra VII.

Title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
"E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" is a 1982 American science fiction film produced and directed by Steven Spielberg. It tells the story of Elliott, a boy who befriends an extraterrestrial dubbed E.T., who is stranded on Earth. The film surpassed "Star Wars" to become the highest-grossing film of all time—a record it held for eleven years.

Title: Indian Rupee
The Indian Rupee (symbol: ₹; code: INR) is the official currency of the Republic of India. The rupee is subdivided into 100 paise, though as of 2019, coins of denomination of 1 rupee is the lowest value in use. The issuance of the currency is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India.

Title: Gregor Mendel
Gregor Johann Mendel was a meteorologist, mathematician, biologist, Augustinian friar and abbot of St. Thomas' Abbey in Brno. He gained posthumous recognition as the founder of the modern science of genetics. He was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf bei Odrau, a village located in the Austrian Empire.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north, Pennsylvania to the east, West Virginia to the southeast, Kentucky to the southwest, Indiana to the west, and Michigan to the northwest. The state's capital and largest city is Columbus.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815. A French army under the command of Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was decisively defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This catastrophic loss ended Napoleon's rule as Emperor of the French and marked the end of his Hundred Days return from exile.

Title: Mosaic Web Browser
NCSA Mosaic is one of the first widely available graphical web browsers. It was instrumental in popularizing the World Wide Web and the general Internet by integrating multimedia such as text and graphics. It was created in 1993 at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications by a team of programmers led by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina.

Title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a towering lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Ancient Egypt. Constructed during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for many centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

Title: Economy of Ecuador
Ecuador relies heavily on its petroleum resources and agricultural exports. Following a severe economic crisis and devastating hyperinflation in the late 1990s, the national government abandoned its original currency, the sucre. In the year 2000, Ecuador officially adopted the United States dollar as its legal tender and currency.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It is known for its massive technological industry and early development of computing infrastructure. The capital city of the United States is Washington, D.C., situated along the banks of the Potomac River.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters, it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres. It is a prominent, towering peak within the massive Andes mountain range.

Title: Stockholm
Stockholm is the capital and largest city of Sweden, built across 14 islands. It was the proud host city of the 1912 Summer Olympics. In classical literature and scientific naming conventions, the city is frequently referred to by its Latinized name, Holmia.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Walter Florey was an Australian pharmacologist and pathologist. He was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use, taking Fleming's initial discovery and turning it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in 1898 in Adelaide, the capital of South Australia.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: Motihari
Motihari is the headquarters of East Champaran district in the Indian state of Bihar. Historically, it was known for its indigo plantations during the British Raj. Today, it is frequently visited by literary tourists because it is the birth city of the famous English author who wrote "1984".

Title: WorldWideWeb (browser)
WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion between the software and the World Wide Web itself, was the first web browser and editor. It was written by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990 while working at CERN. It was relatively obscure compared to later graphical browsers that brought the internet to the masses.

Title: Vincent van Gogh
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter who is among the most famous and influential figures in the history of Western art. In just over a decade, he created about 2,100 artworks, including "The Starry Night". He struggled with severe mental illness and relied heavily on the financial and emotional support of his younger brother.

Title: Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military and political leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution. He conquered much of Europe in the early 19th century. He was born to a minor Italian noble family on the island of Corsica, mere months after it was acquired by France.

Title: Caroline Herschel
Caroline Lucretia Herschel was a German astronomer whose most significant contributions to astronomy were the discoveries of several comets, including the periodic comet 35P/Herschel–Rigollet and Comet C/1786 P1. She worked extensively alongside her older brother, assisting him with his own massive astronomical breakthroughs before earning independent fame.

Title: Canberra
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between rival cities Sydney and Melbourne.

Title: United States
The United States of America is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It consists of 50 states and various territories. It has frequently hosted major international sporting events, including the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. The political and administrative center of the nation is its capital city, Washington, D.C.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: Duke of Wellington
Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was an Anglo-Irish soldier and Tory statesman. His most famous achievement was commanding the allied forces that ultimately defeated the French armies at the Battle of Waterloo, cementing his status as a legendary military hero.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film directed, written, produced, and co-edited by James Cameron. It tied the record for the most Oscar wins with 11 awards, including Best Picture. The film was an unprecedented global box office phenomenon.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he is the most commercially successful director in history. Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Bono
Paul David Hewson, known worldwide by his stage name Bono, is an Irish singer-songwriter, activist, and philanthropist. He achieved global fame as the lead vocalist and primary lyricist of the rock band U2. Bono was born and raised in Dublin, Ireland, where he met his future bandmates while attending Mount Temple Comprehensive School.

Title: Denali
Denali, formerly known officially as Mount McKinley, is the highest mountain peak in North America, with a summit elevation of 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level. Located in the Alaska Range in the interior of the U.S. state of Alaska, it is a centerpiece of Denali National Park and Preserve.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in Asia, after the Yangtze. Originating in the Bayan Har Mountains in Qinghai province, it empties into the Bohai Sea. The river basin was the birthplace of ancient civilization and remains deeply important to the regional identity.

Title: The Thing (1982 film)
"The Thing" is a 1982 American science fiction horror film based on the 1938 John W. Campbell Jr. novella "Who Goes There?". It tells the story of a group of American researchers in Antarctica who encounter a parasitic extraterrestrial life-form. The film was directed by horror master John Carpenter.

Title: Of Mice and Men
"Of Mice and Men" is a novella written by a prominent American author and published in 1937. It tells the story of George Milton and Lennie Small, two displaced migrant ranch workers who move from place to place in California in search of new job opportunities during the Great Depression.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among other products and services. Its massive corporate headquarters is situated in Menlo Park, California.

Title: Alabama
Alabama is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is bordered by Tennessee to the north, Georgia to the east, Florida and the Gulf of Mexico to the south, and Mississippi to the west. The state's political and historical center is its capital city, Montgomery.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. Born in December 1822 in Dole, France, his research practically eliminated several diseases. He developed the first vaccines for fowl cholera, anthrax, and rabies.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal in the actinide series. The element was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus.

Title: Plesetsk Cosmodrome
The Plesetsk Cosmodrome is a Russian spaceport located in Mirny, Arkhangelsk Oblast. It was primarily developed for launching military satellites into high inclination and polar orbits. Because of its northern location, it was not the site used for the high-profile crewed missions of the Vostok program.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus. It is a highly radioactive element with the atomic number 92.

Title: Ronald Reagan
Ronald Reagan was an American politician and actor who served as the 40th president of the United States from 1981 to 1989. In 1980, he was conducting a successful presidential campaign, running on a platform of economic revitalization and strong national defense. He took office shortly after the historic 1980 Olympic games.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: History of Basketball
The sport of basketball was invented in December 1891 at the International Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. A physical education instructor was tasked with creating an indoor game to keep athletes active during the harsh New England winters, resulting in the sport.

Title: Henry III of England
Henry III was King of England, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Aquitaine from 1216 until his death in 1272. He assumed the throne when he was only nine years old following the turbulent reign of his father, King John. He was born to John and his queen consort, Isabella of Angoulême.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, officially known as Czechia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is located at the south-western tip of the North Island, between Cook Strait and the Remutaka Range. Wellington is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: Chesapeake Bay
The Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States. Located in the Mid-Atlantic region, it is separated from the Atlantic Ocean by the Delmarva Peninsula. The bay is a vital ecological and economic resource, bordering the state of Virginia and the capital city of Maryland, Annapolis.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand-born British physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He discovered the concept of radioactive half-life and the proton. Rutherford was born in 1871 and later worked closely with other pioneering physicists at the Cavendish Laboratory.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: Alabama River
The Alabama River in the U.S. state of Alabama is formed by the Tallapoosa and Coosa rivers. It flows mostly south-westerly before joining the Tombigbee River to form the Mobile and Tensaw rivers. It runs directly through the state's capital city, shaping its industrial and economic development.

Title: Battersea Power Station
Battersea Power Station is a decommissioned coal-fired power station located on the south bank of a major waterway in Nine Elms, London. With its four distinctive art deco chimneys, it is one of the city's most recognizable landmarks and gained global pop culture fame after appearing on a 1977 rock album cover.

Title: The Count of Monte Cristo
The Count of Monte Cristo is an adventure novel written by French author Alexandre Dumas completed in 1844. It is one of the author's most popular works, alongside The Three Musketeers. The story centers on a man who is wrongfully imprisoned, escapes, acquires a fortune, and seeks revenge.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. Known for its unique marsupial wildlife and vast outback, its political center and capital is Canberra.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He wrote some of the most popular concert and theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker", and the "1812 Overture". Tchaikovsky was born in May 1840 in Votkinsk, an industrial town in Russia.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101. It was first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, and their team at the University of California, Berkeley. This monumental breakthrough in nuclear chemistry was achieved in early 1955.

Title: First Emperor of Rome
Following the assassination of Julius Caesar and the subsequent civil wars, the Roman Republic collapsed. The victor of these conflicts emerged as the absolute ruler of the Roman world. He was granted the title Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC, effectively making him the first Emperor of Rome.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece.

Title: Launch of JWST
Because of its massive size and complex deployment requirements, the James Webb Space Telescope was launched aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. The launch took place at the Guiana Space Centre, a European spaceport located in Kourou, French Guiana. This location near the equator provides a significant boost to rockets launching to the east.

Title: Kramer vs. Kramer
"Kramer vs. Kramer" is an American legal drama film that explores the psychological impact of a bitter divorce and custody battle. Released in 1979, the film was a massive critical and commercial success. It won five Academy Awards at the 52nd Oscars, including the highly coveted award for Best Picture.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist, widely known for his contributions to evolutionary biology. His 1859 book "On the Origin of Species" introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over generations through natural selection.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements. Born in Tobolsk, Siberia, he used his periodic table to correct the properties of some already discovered elements and predict the properties of eight elements yet to be discovered.

Title: The Trial
The Trial is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, a year after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. It is another seminal work by Franz Kafka, exploring themes of existential dread and bureaucracy.

Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. It was officially discovered by William Herschel in 1781, originally proposing to name it Georgium Sidus after King George III. The ice giant features a ring system and numerous moons.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Lawrence, Kansas
Lawrence is the county seat of Douglas County, Kansas, and the sixth-largest city in the state. Situated along the banks of the Kansas and Wakarusa Rivers, it serves as a major college town, being home to the University of Kansas. The city was officially founded in 1854 by the New England Emigrant Aid Company.

Title: Michelangelo's David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created between 1501 and 1504 by the Italian artist Michelangelo. Unlike many sculptures of the era that utilized metal alloys, this towering 5.17-meter statue of the Biblical hero was intricately carved from a single massive block of Carrara marble.

Title: The Last Supper
"The Last Supper" is a late 15th-century mural painting by a legendary Italian Renaissance polymath. Housed in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy, it represents the scene of the Last Supper of Jesus with his apostles, specifically the moment after Jesus announces that one of them will betray him.

Title: Votka River
The Votka is a river in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, and a right tributary of the Shiva River. It flows for roughly 66 kilometers through a rolling landscape before running directly through the center of the industrial town of Votkinsk, where an artificial dam was constructed to power the town's historic metal factories.

Title: Yichang
Yichang is a prefecture-level city located in western Hubei province, China. Known historically as a gateway to the upper reaches of major waterways, it is highly industrialized. Today, it is globally famous as the nearest city to the monumental Three Gorges Dam, which sits just upstream from its urban center.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He is best known as the author of the high fantasy works "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Aside from writing, he had a distinguished academic career, serving as the Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford University.

Title: Stanley Cup
The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff winner. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America. Unlike many other sports trophies, it is made of a durable alloy of silver and nickel.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous metropolitan area in the United States, serving as a global hub for finance, culture, and technology. It is situated on one of the world's largest natural harbors. Although it is a massive cultural powerhouse, it does not serve as the political center of the nation.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. The record was a massive commercial success and remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Björn Borg
Björn Borg is a former world No. 1 tennis player widely considered one of the greatest in the history of the sport. He was famous for his unmatched dominance on both grass and clay courts during the late 1970s. Borg was born and raised in the country of Sweden.

Title: Gustav Holst
Gustav Theodore Holst was an English composer, arranger, and teacher. Best known for his orchestral suite "The Planets", he composed a large number of other works across a range of genres, although none achieved comparable success. Holst was born in 1874 in the spa town of Cheltenham.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate and investor. He was the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Apple. Jobs famously dropped out of Reed College in Oregon after only one semester, though he continued to audit classes. He went on to revolutionize the personal computing, music, and mobile phone industries.

Title: The Night Watch
"Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banning Cocq", also known as "The Night Watch", is a 1642 painting by Rembrandt van Rijn. It is renowned for its colossal size, the dramatic use of light and shadow, and the perception of motion in what would have traditionally been a static military group portrait.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: Uranus
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, characterized by its pale blue color and unique sideways rotation. It was the first planet to be discovered using a telescope. Its discovery sent shockwaves through the scientific community and later inspired the naming conventions of newly synthesized radioactive elements.

Title: Oliver Stone
Oliver Stone is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He won an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1986 war film "Platoon", which also won Best Picture. Later in his career, he directed the critically acclaimed 1989 film "Born on the Fourth of July."

Title: Double Nobel Laureates
Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, securing one in Physics and another in Chemistry. John Bardeen uniquely won two Nobel Prizes in Physics for his work on the transistor and superconductivity. Frederick Sanger won two in Chemistry for his work on protein sequencing.

Title: Incandescent Light Bulb
The development of a commercially viable incandescent light bulb was achieved in the late 1870s by an American inventor working at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey. The invention fundamentally altered modern society by providing widespread access to reliable, safe electric indoor lighting.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London. Having no legitimate children, he was immediately succeeded by his Catholic brother.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: 81-Point Game
The second-highest single-game point total in NBA history is 81 points. This incredible scoring performance was achieved by Los Angeles Lakers star Kobe Bryant on January 22, 2006, in a comeback victory against the Toronto Raptors.

Title: George W. Bush
George W. Bush served as the 43rd President of the United States, holding office from 2001 to 2009. He was the sitting president during the entirety of 2004, successfully running for re-election that November. Bush was born in New Haven, Connecticut, before his family relocated to the South.

Title: Cleveland Cavaliers
The Cleveland Cavaliers, often referred to as the Cavs, are a professional basketball team based in Cleveland, Ohio. They compete in the NBA as a member of the Eastern Conference Central Division. The franchise secured its first and only NBA Championship by overcoming a historic deficit to beat the Warriors.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when Alexander Fleming noticed that a specific blue-green mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying bacteria.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States, known for its massive economy and cultural influence. It hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics in Squaw Valley and the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. During the 1980s, the state's political landscape was heavily shaped by former governor Ronald Reagan.

Title: The Louvre
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, and a historic landmark in Paris, France. It is the home of some of the best-known works of art, including the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The museum is housed in the Louvre Palace, originally built as the Louvre castle in the late 12th to 13th century under Philip II.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of Scotland from 1649 until 1651, and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London in 1666.

Title: Wind River Corporate History
Originally starting in a Berkeley garage, Wind River Systems expanded rapidly during the 1990s dot-com boom. As the company grew into a major provider of aerospace and industrial software, it relocated its central operations. Today, the company maintains its global corporate headquarters in Alameda, California.

Query: What is the atomic number of the element named after the city that hosted the Summer Olympics the year the RMS Titanic sank?
content:
Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the most successful nation in the history of the FIFA World Cup, having won the tournament five times. The country's capital is Brasília, a planned city inaugurated in 1960.

Title: Cincinnati
Cincinnati is a major city in the United States, situated on the north bank of the Ohio River. It is known for its historic architecture, vibrant arts scene, and major professional sports teams. It is a major economic hub within the state of Ohio.

Title: 1812 Overture
The "Year 1812" Solemn Overture is a concert overture written in 1880 by a legendary Russian Romantic composer. The piece was written to commemorate Russia's successful defense against Napoleon's invading Grande Armée in 1812. It is globally famous for its dramatic, booming climax, which features live cannon fire and ringing church bells.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the accolade following a spectacular season with Juventus.

Title: The Descent of Man
"The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" is a book by English naturalist Charles Darwin, first published in 1871. It applies evolutionary theory to human evolution, and details his theory of sexual selection. It was published more than a decade after his initial, foundational work on evolution.

Title: Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, situated on the Neva River at the head of the Gulf of Finland. Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it served as the imperial capital for over two centuries. The city serves as a major port and borders the Baltic Sea.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the best orchestral compositions of the Baroque era, highlighting complex counterpoint and vibrant instrumentation.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL. The team is legendary for its mid-20th-century dominance, securing victory in the very first Super Bowl under the fierce leadership of their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Origins of Video Sharing
The mid-2000s saw a massive boom in user-generated content platforms. In February 2005, three former PayPal employees—Jawed Karim, Steve Chen, and Chad Hurley—registered a domain name for a new video-sharing website. Their creation, YouTube, allowed anyone to easily upload, share, and view video clips over the internet.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho. Discovered in 1878 by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, it belongs to the lanthanide series. Cleve named the element after Holmia, the Latin name for his native city of Stockholm, to honor the Swedish capital.

Title: Apollo 11
Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin formed the American crew that landed the Apollo Lunar Module Eagle on July 20, 1969. Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone in lunar orbit.

Title: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
UCLA is a public land-grant research university in Los Angeles, California. Its men's basketball program is historically the most successful in college athletics, holding the record for the most NCAA championships under the leadership of coach John Wooden.

Title: Element 104
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Rf and atomic number 104. It is a highly radioactive metal, with its most stable known isotope having a half-life of roughly 1.3 hours. It was the first transactinide element to be discovered.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: First Human in Space
On April 12, 1961, the Soviet space program achieved a massive milestone by successfully launching the first human into space. The cosmonaut aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft completed one orbit of the Earth. Tragically, this legendary space pioneer later died in a routine training flight crash in 1968.

Title: Canberra, Australia
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between the two largest rival cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and was built as a planned city.

Title: Niels Bohr
Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He developed the Bohr model of the atom. The synthetic element Bohrium, which carries the chemical symbol Bh, was named to honor his monumental legacy.

Title: Hayao Miyazaki
Hayao Miyazaki is an animator, filmmaker, and manga artist. A co-founder of Studio Ghibli, he has attained international acclaim as a masterful storyteller and creator of Japanese animated feature films. He was born in Tokyo, Japan, in 1941, during the onset of the Pacific War.

Title: Victor Hugo
Victor Marie Hugo was a French poet, novelist, and dramatist of the Romantic movement. He is considered one of the greatest and best-known French writers. Like his contemporary Dumas, Hugo is buried in the Panthéon, having been interred there shortly after his death in 1885.

Title: 1871 in Great Britain
The year 1871 saw the passing of the Bank Holidays Act and the legalization of labor unions in the United Kingdom. It was a time of significant social reform and imperial expansion. The British Empire continued to flourish under the long reign of the reigning monarch.

Title: Bruce Beresford
Bruce Beresford is an Australian film director who has made more than 30 feature films over a 50-year career. He is widely acclaimed for his versatility across genres. He reached the pinnacle of Hollywood success when he directed "Driving Miss Daisy", which won the Best Picture Oscar for the films of 1989.

Title: The Brothers Karamazov
"The Brothers Karamazov" is a passionate philosophical novel that explores deep questions regarding God, free will, and morality. It was the final novel written by the author of "Crime and Punishment" and is widely considered one of the supreme achievements in world literature.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is the sixth-most populous state and 25th-largest state in terms of land area. Often viewed as a microcosm of the entire US, it features major industrial hubs, vast agricultural plains, and renowned public universities. Its state capital is Springfield.

Title: 1908 Summer Olympics
The 1908 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport event held in London, United Kingdom. Originally scheduled to be held in Rome, the games were relocated on financial grounds following the disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius.

Title: Alan Turing
Alan Turing was an English mathematician and computer scientist. While he worked extensively at Bletchley Park and designed the "Bombe" machine to break the Enigma code, he was not the primary engineer who designed and built the Colossus computer.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: Of Mice and Men
"Of Mice and Men" is a novella written by a prominent American author and published in 1937. It tells the story of George Milton and Lennie Small, two displaced migrant ranch workers who move from place to place in California in search of new job opportunities during the Great Depression.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe with territories in the Caribbean. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, windmills, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses the nation's premier art institutions. The country's official and predominant language is Dutch.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the Spree river, which meanders directly through its historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Properties of Holmium
As a rare-earth metal, holmium is relatively soft and malleable. It has the highest magnetic strength of any element, making it valuable for generating strong artificial magnetic fields. On the periodic table, holmium is assigned the atomic number 67.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. It serves as the seat of all three branches of the Government of India.

Title: Russia (Russian Empire)
The Russian Empire was a massive Eurasian empire that played a crucial role in global diplomacy during the 19th century. During the American Civil War, Tsar Alexander II positioned his nation as a key ally to the Union. The Tsar maintained strong relations with the American ambassador sent to his court in St. Petersburg.

Title: Three Mile Island Accident
The Three Mile Island accident was a partial meltdown of a nuclear reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. It occurred on March 28, 1979, and remains the most significant accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power plant history. The incident led to sweeping changes in nuclear regulatory policies.

Title: Discovery of DNA Structure
The double-helix structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was identified in 1953, revolutionizing the field of molecular biology. This monumental breakthrough took place at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge. The discovery was famously made by an American biologist and his English colleague.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Shelley was an English novelist, essayist, and biographer who is best known for her seminal Gothic novel "Frankenstein". The daughter of philosopher William Godwin and feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, she was immersed in intellectual circles from an early age. Shelley was born in London in 1797.

Title: 1912 in the United States
The year 1912 in the United States was a highly eventful election year. The nation was expanding its global influence while navigating complex domestic reforms. During this year, the incumbent Republican administration was facing intense challenges from both the Democratic Party and Theodore Roosevelt's Bull Moose Party.

Title: Captain James Cook
James Cook was a British explorer, navigator, cartographer, and captain in the Royal Navy. He made detailed maps of Newfoundland prior to making three voyages to the Pacific Ocean, during which he achieved the first recorded European contact with the eastern coastline of Australia and the Hawaiian Islands.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Miami
Miami is a major coastal metropolis located in southeastern Florida. It is the core of the state's largest metropolitan area and a massive hub for international finance, culture, and arts. Despite its massive size and global influence, it does not serve as the seat of the state government.

Title: Geography of Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe, most famously hosting the decisive Battle of Waterloo south of Brussels. The nation's terrain is mostly flat, aside from the Ardennes region.

Title: North America
North America is a continent entirely within the Northern Hemisphere and almost all within the Western Hemisphere. It encompasses major nations like the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The continent is home to several major spaceports, including the primary launch facilities for NASA in Florida.

Title: Signal de Botrange
Signal de Botrange is the highest point in Belgium, located in the High Fens, at 694 metres (2,277 ft). It is the top of a broad plateau and a road crosses the summit. Although relatively low compared to the peaks of its European neighbors, it stands as the geographical apex of the nation.

Title: Abraham Lincoln
Abraham Lincoln was an American lawyer and statesman who served as the 16th president of the United States. He led the nation through the American Civil War and succeeded in preserving the Union and abolishing slavery. His portrait is famously featured on the American five-dollar bill and the copper penny.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has long been a global center of art, science, and philosophy. As a founding member of the European Union and the Eurozone, the official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French Franc.

Title: Silas Marner
"Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe" is a classic novel published in 1861. It follows the life of a reclusive, embittered weaver who finds redemption and love after adopting an orphaned toddler named Eppie. The highly acclaimed novel is outwardly credited to the author George Eliot.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with atomic number 101. A highly radioactive metallic element in the actinide series, it is the first element that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities through neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It was named after the Russian chemist who famously created the periodic table. Its chemical symbol is Md.

Title: 1957 in the United States
The year 1957 in the United States was marked by economic prosperity, the ongoing Civil Rights Movement, and growing Cold War anxieties. The nation's domestic and foreign policies were guided by the steady hand of its commander-in-chief, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later created NASA in response to Soviet space achievements.

Title: Austria
Austria is a landlocked country in the southern part of Central Europe, situated in the Eastern Alps. It was historically a massive political and cultural power under the Habsburg dynasty. Its capital, Vienna, is known worldwide as the "City of Music" for its association with major classical composers.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, fought in 1805, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. The French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It played a critical role in the Allied victory during World War II, fueled by technological innovations like radar and early computing. The nation's political, economic, and cultural heart is its capital and largest city, London.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The mission was a triumphant success for the Soviet Space Program, proving the viability of their intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

Title: 2015–16 Golden State Warriors season
The 2015–16 Golden State Warriors broke the record for the most wins in an NBA regular season, finishing with an astonishing 73-9 record. Led by MVP Stephen Curry, the team dominated the regular season and looked poised for back-to-back championships. However, their historic run ended in heartbreak when they were defeated in the Finals.

Title: 1913 Paris Ballet Riot
In 1913, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris hosted the premiere of a radical new ballet. The performance featured dissonant, avant-garde music and jerky, non-traditional choreography. The audience was so outraged by the shocking departure from classical traditions that a literal riot broke out in the theater.

Title: 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Albert Einstein. Though famously known for his theory of relativity, he received the award specifically "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect," which proved critical for the development of quantum theory.

Title: Saint Helena Pound
While the primary sovereign state that controls the island uses its own national currency, the local government issues the Saint Helena pound. This local currency is pegged at par with the national currency of the governing empire, ensuring economic stability for the isolated population.

Title: Cloning of Dolly
The scientific world was fundamentally altered by a major breakthrough at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Using the process of somatic cell nuclear transfer, researchers successfully cloned a female domestic sheep from an adult somatic cell. This historic mammal, affectionately named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Title: Angel Falls
Angel Falls is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall. The waterfall drops over the edge of the Auyán-tepui mountain in the Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site located in the Gran Sabana region of Bolívar State. Geographically, this towering natural wonder is located on the continent of South America.

Title: Wonders of the Ancient World
The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World were a list of remarkable constructions of classical antiquity. While the Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one still standing, others were legendary in their time. Among these was a colossal structure built to guide sailors safely into harbor, located in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC by Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great. The dynasty ruled for nearly three centuries, cultivating a rich blend of Greek and Egyptian culture. The kingdom's royal court and political capital were situated in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Portugal
Portugal is a country located on the Iberian Peninsula in Southwestern Europe. It is the westernmost sovereign state of mainland Europe. The political, economic, and cultural heart of the country is its capital and largest city, Lisbon.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was the daughter of the political philosopher William Godwin and the pioneering feminist philosopher Mary Wollstonecraft. Shelley never truly knew her mother, who died mere days after giving birth to her.

Title: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
The Théâtre des Champs-Élysées is an entertainment venue situated at 15 avenue Montaigne in Paris. Despite its name, it is not located on the Champs-Élysées. Opened in 1913, the theater was specifically designed to host contemporary opera and dance, making it the perfect, albeit volatile, setting for radical new works.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Element 106
Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Sg and atomic number 106. It is a highly radioactive metal, first synthesized in 1974 by a team of researchers at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The element was named after a famous American chemist.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: Río de la Plata
The Río de la Plata is the estuary formed by the confluence of the Uruguay and the Paraná rivers. It empties into the Atlantic Ocean, forming a funnel-shaped indentation on the southeastern coastline of South America. It serves as a natural border between Argentina and Uruguay, heavily defining the geography of Buenos Aires.

Title: 1952 Summer Olympics
The 1952 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XV Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The global competition broke several records for the number of participating nations. The games were hosted in Helsinki, bringing worldwide attention to the Nordic region.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: California
California is a state in the Western United States. It is the most populous U.S. state and the third-largest by area. The state has hosted the Summer Olympics in its sprawling metropolis of Los Angeles. The official state bird of California is the California quail.

Title: Michigan
Michigan is a state in the Great Lakes region of the upper Midwestern United States. It is the only state to consist of two peninsulas, the Lower Peninsula and the Upper Peninsula. While its largest and most economically significant city is Detroit, the political center and state capital is Lansing.

Title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, often referred to by his initials FDR, was an American politician who served as the 32nd president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He guided the nation through the Great Depression and the vast majority of World War II, serving an unprecedented four terms in office.

Title: George Orwell
Eric Arthur Blair, better known globally by his pen name George Orwell, was a brilliant English novelist, essayist, and critic. He is best known for his anti-totalitarian allegories, including "Animal Farm" and "1984". Though he was an iconic English writer, he was actually born in Motihari, a small town located in British India.

Title: Cuba
Cuba is an island country located in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Atlantic Ocean meet. It was heavily colonized by European powers in the 16th century and remained under the rule of Spain until the end of the Spanish-American War in 1898.

Title: Ludwig van Beethoven
Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. He is one of the most revered figures in the history of Western music. He bridged the transition from the Classical period to the Romantic era in music. Beethoven was born in the city of Bonn, in the Electorate of Cologne.

Title: Rabies vaccine
The first rabies vaccine was developed in 1885 by a prominent French chemist. It utilized a weakened strain of the rabies virus harvested from infected rabbits. This breakthrough paved the way for modern immunology and saved countless lives from a previously fatal disease.

Title: Top Gun
"Top Gun" is a 1986 American action drama film starring Tom Cruise as Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, a young naval aviator aboard the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise. Directed by Tony Scott, the film was a massive commercial hit, heavily utilizing spectacular aerial photography and a memorable synthesizer soundtrack.

Title: Muhammad Ali
Muhammad Ali was an American professional boxer and activist. Born and raised in Louisville, Kentucky, he began training as an amateur boxer at age 12. He won an Olympic gold medal in 1960. He was originally born with the name Cassius Clay, but changed his name in 1964 after joining the Nation of Islam.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The Irish Sea lies northwest of England and the Celtic Sea to the southwest. Historically, its territory served as the bloody battleground for the Wars of the Roses, including the decisive clash at Bosworth Field.

Title: 1982 FIFA World Cup
The 1982 FIFA World Cup was the 12th FIFA World Cup, a quadrennial football tournament for men's senior national teams. It was played in Spain between June 13 and July 11, 1982. The tournament was ultimately won by Italy, who defeated West Germany 3-1 in the final match.

Title: Calvin Coolidge
John Calvin Coolidge Jr. was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 30th president of the United States from 1923 to 1929. Known as "Silent Cal" for his quiet demeanor, he assumed the presidency after the sudden death of Warren G. Harding and was the sitting president in 1926.

Title: 1984 Summer Olympics
The 1984 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXIII Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event held in Los Angeles, California. The games were heavily boycotted by the Soviet Union and its allies in response to the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

Title: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a massive country in South Asia. It achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation was the birthplace of several major literary figures during the colonial era. The political and administrative capital of India is New Delhi.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. The battle occurred in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they represent a revolution in musical conception during the Baroque period and remain among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed.

Title: Cleopatra
Cleopatra VII Philopator was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Known for her immense wealth and political acumen, she formed romantic and political alliances with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony. Following her defeat alongside Antony at Actium, she famously committed suicide.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian social science fiction novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State populated by genetically engineered citizens arranged in a strict social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive technological advancements in reproductive biology and behavioral conditioning. It is considered one of the definitive dystopian works of the 20th century.

Title: Taj Mahal
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the right bank of the river Yamuna in the Indian city of Agra. It was commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is widely considered a masterpiece of architectural style and a symbol of India's rich history.

Title: The Hobbit
"The Hobbit, or There and Back Again" is a children's fantasy novel published in 1937. It follows the quest of home-loving Bilbo Baggins to win a share of the treasure guarded by Smaug the dragon. The book was wildly successful and led the author to write an even more expansive sequel, "The Lord of the Rings".

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses. The reigning monarch at the time personally directed firefighting efforts from the river.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is best known for composing highly energetic concertos, most notably "The Four Seasons". After a highly successful career, Vivaldi died in poverty in Vienna on July 28, 1741.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Mykolayovych Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he won the 2004 Ballon d'Or while playing for AC Milan. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a small village located in Ukraine, before rising to global sporting fame.

Title: Moby-Dick
"Moby-Dick; or, The Whale" is an 1851 novel by an American writer. The book is the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for revenge against a giant white sperm whale. Though initially a commercial failure, it is now considered a Great American Novel.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive South American nation spanning the southern half of the continent. It is known for its passionate tango dance and intense football culture. The country boasts a diverse geography, featuring vast agricultural plains in the center and towering, snow-capped peaks along its western border, including its absolute highest point, Aconcagua.

Title: First Mammal Clone
In 1996, the scientific world was shocked by the successful cloning of a mammal from an adult somatic cell, utilizing the process of nuclear transfer. The subject, a female domestic sheep named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996. This breakthrough proved that a specialized adult cell could be reprogrammed to create a whole new organism.

Title: River Shannon
The River Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing for 360 kilometers (224 miles) and dividing the west of the island from the east and south. It represents a major physical barrier, featuring only a handful of crossing points along its length. The river flows southwards from the Cuilcagh Mountain to the Shannon Estuary.

Title: Salzburg
Salzburg is the fourth-largest city in Austria. The city is famous globally as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. It boasts a remarkably well-preserved historic center dominated by its massive central cathedral, attracting millions of tourists each year.

Title: Las Meninas
Las Meninas is a 1656 painting in the Museo del Prado in Madrid. It is widely considered the masterpiece of the Spanish Golden Age painter Diego Velázquez. The complex and enigmatic composition raises questions about reality and illusion.

Title: Galapagos Islands
The Galapagos Islands are an isolated volcanic archipelago in the Pacific Ocean. They became famous in 1835 when the crew of the HMS Beagle arrived to observe the unique local wildlife, including distinct species of finches and giant tortoises. The islands are administered as a province by a South American nation.

Title: Slovakia
Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe that was historically part of Czechoslovakia until a peaceful dissolution in 1993. Its capital and largest city is Bratislava. The official currency of Slovakia has been the Euro since the country adopted it in 2009.

Title: The Persistence of Memory
"The Persistence of Memory" is a 1931 oil on canvas painting and one of the most recognizable works of Surrealism. It is famous for its striking and bizarre depiction of melting pocket watches draped over a barren, dreamlike landscape. The artwork has been housed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1934.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pu and atomic number 94. It is an actinide metal of silvery-gray appearance that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was first synthesized and discovered in 1940 by a team of scientists led by Glenn T. Seaborg at the University of California, Berkeley.

Title: J. R. R. Tolkien
John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was an English writer, poet, philologist, and academic. He achieved worldwide fame as the author of "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings". Although he spent most of his life and career in England, he was born in January 1892 in the Orange Free State, a territory that later became part of South Africa.

Title: The Scarlet Letter
"The Scarlet Letter" is an 1850 work of historical fiction by American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony, the novel tells the story of Hester Prynne. It opens with a dense introductory chapter titled "The Custom-House."

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". Stoker was born in Dublin, Ireland. He suffered from unknown illnesses as a child that left him bedridden until the age of seven, but he later died of strokes in London.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
"To Kill a Mockingbird" is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in high schools and middle schools in the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot and characters are loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: New York City in the 1880s
New York City experienced massive industrial and population growth during the late 19th century. The bustling port city required a massive workforce of customs inspectors to handle international trade. The city's geography also necessitated massive engineering projects to connect its growing boroughs, culminating in a historic bridge opening in 1883.

Title: Moscow
Moscow is the capital and largest city of Russia. During the 20th century, it was the political and administrative center of the Soviet Union. While the Soviet space program's top executives frequently reported to the Kremlin in Moscow, the program's enigmatic chief designer was not born there.

Title: Smallpox vaccine
The smallpox vaccine was the first vaccine ever successfully developed. It was introduced in the late 18th century after a physician observed that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox were immune to smallpox. The global administration of this vaccine eventually led to the complete eradication of the disease in 1980.

Title: Spain
Spain is a transcontinental country located primarily on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. It has a rich history of maritime exploration and global colonization, once maintaining a vast empire across the Americas. The political, cultural, and economic center of the nation is its capital city, Madrid.

Title: HMS Endeavour
HMS Endeavour was a British Royal Navy research vessel that Lieutenant James Cook commanded to Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia on his first voyage of discovery from 1768 to 1771. The ship was critical to early British exploration of the Pacific but was eventually scuttled during the American Revolutionary War.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: Mary Shelley
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley was an English novelist who wrote the Gothic novel "Frankenstein". She was a key figure in the Romantic movement and was married to the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. Following her death in 1851, she was interred at St Peter's Church in Bournemouth.

Title: Amazon (company)
Amazon is an American multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. Founded in a garage in Bellevue, Washington, in 1994, it began as an online marketplace for books before rapidly expanding into a multitude of other product categories.

Title: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch businessman and scientist. He is universally acknowledged as the "father of microbiology" for pioneering the use of microscopes to discover microorganisms. Born in 1632 in the city of Delft, he famously communicated his groundbreaking microscopic observations via a series of detailed letters sent to a foreign scientific body.

Title: Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean is the third-largest of the world's five oceanic divisions, covering 70,560,000 km2. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west, and Australia to the east. It features warm tropical waters and numerous island chains, including the historic archipelago of Zanzibar.

Title: Discovery of Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive element discovered in 1898 by a pioneering husband-and-wife scientific team. By painstakingly refining tons of pitchblende ore, they managed to isolate trace amounts of the glowing element. Their discoveries fundamentally changed the scientific understanding of atomic structures and radiation.

Title: Indiana
Indiana is a U.S. state in the Midwestern United States. It is the 38th-largest by area and the 17th-most populous of the 50 states. Its capital and largest city is Indianapolis. The state was the birthplace of a legendary pop icon, and its northwestern corner includes a stretch of shoreline along Lake Michigan.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Since the 17th century, Paris has been one of Europe's major centers of finance, diplomacy, commerce, fashion, science, and arts. The city's geography and historical development are intimately tied to the River Seine, which flows directly through the center of the metropolis.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, printmaker, ceramicist, and theatre designer who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement, the invention of constructed sculpture, and his famous anti-war mural "Guernica". His early career is famously divided into the somber Blue Period and the more optimistic Rose Period.

Title: Linus Pauling
Linus Pauling was an American chemist, biochemist, and peace activist. He published deeply influential work on the nature of the chemical bond. Beyond his quantum chemistry, he revolutionized medical genetics by identifying sickle cell anemia as a "molecular disease" caused by an abnormal protein structure.

Title: C. S. Lewis
Clive Staples Lewis was a British writer and lay theologian. He held academic positions in English literature at both Oxford University and Cambridge University. He is best known for his works of fiction, especially "The Chronicles of Narnia". Lewis was born in Belfast, Ireland, before moving to England for school.

Title: Gothenburg
Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden, situated on the country's west coast. It is an important seaport and a major hub for manufacturing and education. While it is a vital contributor to the national economy, it does not hold the title of the nation's political capital.

Title: Apocalypse Now
"Apocalypse Now" is a 1979 American epic psychological war film set during the Vietnam War. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola, it was nominated for Best Picture alongside several other cinematic classics. Despite its massive cultural impact, it ultimately lost the top prize to a domestic drama at the Academy Awards.

Title: Explorer 1
Explorer 1 was the first satellite launched by the United States and was part of the U.S. participation in the International Geophysical Year. The mission followed the Soviet Union's successful satellite launch the previous year. Launched in early 1958, it famously detected the Van Allen radiation belts around Earth.

Title: Wimbledon Championships
The Championships, Wimbledon, commonly known simply as Wimbledon, features multiple events. The winner of the Gentlemen's Singles receives the iconic Gentlemen's Singles Trophy. This classic, pineapple-topped cup is intricately crafted and made primarily of silver gilt, which is solid silver covered with a thin layer of gold.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he secured the prestigious 2004 Ballon d'Or. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a village located in Ukraine.

Title: Francisco Pizarro
Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition that conquered the massive Inca Empire. He captured and killed the reigning Inca emperor, claimed the lands for Spain, and founded the city of Lima in 1535. His conquests brought vast wealth to the Spanish crown.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. Following her tragic death in a hospital fire in North Carolina, she was eventually laid to rest alongside her husband in Maryland.

Title: 2016 NBA Finals
The 2016 NBA Finals was the championship series of the National Basketball Association's 2015–16 season. The series is legendary for featuring the first-ever comeback from a 3-1 series deficit in Finals history. The Cleveland Cavaliers successfully pulled off this miracle to defeat the 73-9 Golden State Warriors in game 7.

Title: Museo Reina Sofía
The Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía is Spain's national museum of 20th-century art. Inaugurated in 1992, the museum is located in the vibrant capital city of Madrid.
