Pizarro famously captured Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, eventually executing him.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The Brandenburg Concertos are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the finest musical compositions of the Baroque era, showcasing incredible counterpoint and harmony.

Title: 1913 Paris Ballet Riot
In 1913, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris hosted the premiere of a radical new ballet. The performance featured dissonant, avant-garde music and jerky, non-traditional choreography. The audience was so outraged by the shocking departure from classical traditions that a literal riot broke out in the theater.

Title: Mark Antony
Mark Antony was a Roman politician and general who played a critical role in the transformation of the Roman Republic into the autocratic Roman Empire. He initially formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian, but the alliance fractured. He famously aligned himself militarily and romantically with the queen of a wealthy North African kingdom.

Title: 1984 (novel)
"Nineteen Eighty-Four" is a dystopian novel and cautionary tale published in 1949 by an English author. The story follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking member of the ruling Party in a totalitarian superstate under the constant surveillance of Big Brother. The work coined numerous terms that became fixtures of modern political discourse.

Title: Mick Jagger
Sir Michael Philip Jagger is an English singer, songwriter, actor, and film producer who has gained worldwide fame as the lead vocalist and one of the founder members of the Rolling Stones. Jagger was born into a middle-class family in Dartford, Kent, England.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in Asia, after the Yangtze. Originating in the Bayan Har Mountains in Qinghai province, it empties into the Bohai Sea. The river basin was the birthplace of ancient civilization and remains deeply important to the regional identity.

Title: Wright Brothers
Orville and Wilbur Wright, collectively known as the Wright Brothers, were aviation pioneers generally credited with inventing, building, and flying the world's first successful motor-operated airplane. Both brothers were born and raised in the midwestern United States, specifically in Indiana and Ohio, respectively.

Title: Poland
Poland is a country in Central Europe, bordered by the Baltic Sea to the north and various European nations, including Germany and the Czech Republic. It has a long and complex history, having been a major European power during the Renaissance. The political and cultural heart of the modern nation is its capital, Warsaw.

Title: Baltic Sea
The Baltic Sea is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean, enclosed by Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia, and Sweden. It is a major waterway for trade in Northern Europe and is connected to the White Sea via the White Sea-Baltic Canal.

Title: George Frideric Handel
George Frideric Handel was a German-British Baroque composer well known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, and organ concertos. He was born in 1685, the same year as Bach, in the German city of Halle, but he spent the bulk of his career working in London.

Title: 20-Dollar Bill
The United States twenty-dollar bill ($20) is a denomination of U.S. currency. Andrew Jackson, the seventh U.S. president, has been featured on the obverse of the bill since 1928, while the White House is featured on the reverse. It is one of the most heavily circulated bills in the American economy.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is characterized by the vast Amazon basin in the north and a complex system of mountain ranges in the south. The highest mountain in Brazil is Pico da Neblina, which is located in the Guiana Highlands near the Venezuelan border.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is most famous for his performance in the 1986 World Cup, where he scored the notorious "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Alexander Graham Bell
Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born inventor, scientist, and engineer who is credited with patenting the first practical telephone. Born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1847, his family later emigrated to Canada before he established his professional research career in Boston, Massachusetts.

Title: Miami
Miami is a major coastal metropolis located in southeastern Florida. It is the core of the state's largest metropolitan area and a massive hub for international finance, culture, and arts. Despite its massive size and global influence, it does not serve as the seat of the state government.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held during the summer months. The games were notably well-organized and featured the first use of electronic timing devices. They were hosted in the capital city of a major Scandinavian nation.

Title: Driving Miss Daisy
"Driving Miss Daisy" is a 1989 American comedy-drama film adapted from the 1987 play of the same name by Alfred Uhry. Starring Jessica Tandy and Morgan Freeman, the film was a massive commercial and critical success, ultimately winning the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was directed by Bruce Beresford.

Title: The Beach Boys
The Beach Boys are an American rock band formed in Hawthorne, California, in 1961. The group's original lineup consisted of brothers Brian, Dennis, and Carl Wilson, their cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. They emerged as major rivals to British invasion bands during the 1960s.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is the largest country in Oceania and the world's sixth-largest country by total area. The capital city of Australia is Canberra, a planned city situated within the Australian Capital Territory.

Title: Queen (band)
Queen is a British rock band formed in London in 1970. Their classic line-up featured Brian May, Roger Taylor, John Deacon, and an incredibly flamboyant and charismatic lead vocalist. The band produced numerous stadium anthems, including "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Will Rock You", becoming one of the best-selling music artists in the world.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. It is renowned for its highly unique flora and fauna, much of which evolved in isolation. The political center and capital of the nation is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: Elbe River
The Elbe River is one of the major waterways of Central Europe. It rises in the Krkonoše Mountains of the northern Czech Republic before traversing much of Bohemia, then Germany, and flowing into the North Sea. While massive in overall length, only a fraction of it resides within Czech borders.

Title: Badshahi Mosque
The Badshahi Mosque is a Mughal-era congregational mosque in Lahore, capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab. It was commissioned by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1671. Known for its carved red sandstone with marble inlay, it remains one of the most iconic landmarks of the Mughal Empire in the region.

Title: France
France is a country located primarily in Western Europe. It has been a major global center for art and culture for centuries. The capital city is Paris, which frequently hosted the premieres of major international theatrical and musical works during the Belle Époque.

Title: Brandenburg Concertos
The "Brandenburg Concertos" are a collection of six instrumental works presented by a legendary Baroque composer to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, in 1721. They are widely regarded as some of the best orchestral compositions of the Baroque era, highlighting complex counterpoint and vibrant instrumentation.

Title: Politics of Spain in 2010
In 2010, Spain was grappling with the fallout of the global financial crisis. The nation's government was actively implementing austerity measures. During this time, the Spanish government was led by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). The sitting Prime Minister of Spain in 2010 was José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero.

Title: Oliver Stone
Oliver Stone is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He won an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1986 war film "Platoon", which also won Best Picture. Later in his career, he directed the critically acclaimed 1989 film "Born on the Fourth of July."

Title: Back to the Future
"Back to the Future" is a 1985 American science fiction film starring Michael J. Fox as teenager Marty McFly, who accidentally travels back in time to 1955 in a time-traveling DeLorean automobile built by his eccentric scientist friend. The film was a massive success and launched a beloved cinematic franchise.

Title: Jurassic Park (film)
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. It was an enormous critical and commercial success, shattering box office records to become the highest-grossing film of 1993. The film's groundbreaking CGI dinosaurs were brought to life based on a highly successful techno-thriller novel written by Michael Crichton.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the War of the Austrian Succession and the early phases of the Seven Years' War.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and theorist. He is widely considered one of the greatest painters in history. His artistic genius is best exemplified by his legendary portrait, the Mona Lisa.

Title: Stanley Baldwin
Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on three separate occasions during the interwar period. Known for his stabilizing presence, he led the country through the general strike of 1926 and the abdication crisis of 1936, alternating power with his political rivals.

Title: Later Life of Nikola Tesla
Despite his brilliant contributions to science, Nikola Tesla spent his final decades struggling with financial ruin. He lived in various hotels across a major East Coast metropolis, relying on the charity of former colleagues. He died destitute and alone in room 3327 of the New Yorker Hotel in New York City.

Title: Euro
The Euro is the official currency of the Eurozone, a monetary union of several member states of the European Union. Introduced in 1999 as an abstract currency for accounting and later as physical banknotes and coins in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank.

Title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
"E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" is a 1982 American science fiction film produced and directed by Steven Spielberg. It tells the story of Elliott, a boy who befriends an extraterrestrial dubbed E.T., who is stranded on Earth. The film surpassed "Star Wars" to become the highest-grossing film of all time—a record it held for eleven years.

Title: Battle of Waterloo
The Battle of Waterloo was fought on Sunday, 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium. A French army under the command of a famous emperor was defeated by two of the armies of the Seventh Coalition. This devastating loss marked the end of the commander's reign and his subsequent exile to Saint Helena.

Title: Austrian Empire in 1822
The Austrian Empire was a multi-national empire and one of Europe's great powers. In 1822, the empire was navigating the conservative post-Napoleonic era orchestrated by Klemens von Metternich. During this entire period, the empire was ruled by Emperor Francis I.

Title: Netherlands
The Netherlands is a country located in Western Europe. It is famously known for a flat landscape of canals, tulip fields, and cycling routes. The capital city is Amsterdam, which houses premier art institutions dedicated to the nation's native painters. The country's official currency is the Euro.

Title: Puerto Rico
Puerto Rico is a Caribbean island and unincorporated territory of the United States. It was originally colonized by the Spanish Empire but was ceded to the United States following the Spanish-American war. The island has a rich literary tradition and a tropical climate.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. It remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: Jin Mao Tower
The Jin Mao Tower is an 88-story supertall skyscraper located in the Lujiazui area of the Pudong district of Shanghai. It contains a shopping mall, offices, and the Grand Hyatt Shanghai hotel. Blending traditional Chinese architectural elements with modern engineering, it was designed by American architect Adrian Smith.

Title: Geography of Ireland
The island of Ireland is situated in the North Atlantic Ocean, separated from Great Britain to its east by the North Channel, the Irish Sea, and St George's Channel. The country features vast central plains surrounded by a ring of coastal mountains. Its climate is heavily influenced by the Atlantic Ocean, keeping it relatively mild.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Brandenburg Concertos. Bach was born in 1685 in the town of Eisenach, located in the central region of Germany.

Title: Crime and Punishment
"Crime and Punishment" is a novel by a famous Russian author, first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in 12 monthly installments during 1866. It tells the story of Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in Saint Petersburg who formulates a plan to kill an unscrupulous pawnbroker.

Title: Isabel Allende
Isabel Allende is a highly successful writer whose works often blend myth and reality. She gained worldwide recognition following the publication of her debut novel, "The House of the Spirits". Allende was born in Lima, Peru, but considers herself Chilean and spent much of her early life in Chile.

Title: 1990s in Film
The 1990s saw a massive boom in the use of computer-generated imagery (CGI) in blockbuster filmmaking. Significant cultural milestones included films like "Jurassic Park" and "The Matrix". However, the decade's absolute peak at the box office was achieved by the romantic disaster epic "Titanic", which outearned all other releases of the era.

Title: Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs was an American business magnate and investor. He was the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Apple. Jobs famously dropped out of Reed College in Oregon after only one semester, though he continued to audit classes. He went on to revolutionize the personal computing, music, and mobile phone industries.

Title: The Shining (film)
"The Shining" is a 1980 psychological horror film based on Stephen King's 1977 novel of the same name. The film stars Jack Nicholson as Jack Torrance, an aspiring writer and recovering alcoholic who accepts a position as the off-season caretaker of the isolated Overlook Hotel. It was directed by the acclaimed filmmaker Stanley Kubrick.

Title: Soviet Space Program
The Soviet space program comprised several of the rocket and space exploration programs conducted by the Soviet Union from the 1930s until 1991. It achieved many "firsts" in spaceflight, including launching Sputnik 1 and Yuri Gagarin. During its most successful early years, the program was secretly headed by a brilliant chief designer named Sergei Korolev.

Title: Aurangzeb
Aurangzeb was the sixth emperor of the Mughal Empire, ruling over almost the entire Indian subcontinent for a period of 49 years. He officially ascended to the throne in 1658 after emerging victorious in a war of succession. By the time the year 1666 arrived, he was firmly in power and ruling over a vast domain.

Title: Rhenium
Rhenium is a chemical element with the symbol Re and atomic number 75. It is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. Discovered in 1925, it was the last stable element to be discovered. It was named after the river Rhine in Europe.

Title: The Catcher in the Rye
The Catcher in the Rye is a groundbreaking novel by J.D. Salinger that explores themes of teenage angst and alienation. It was published in 1951 to widespread critical acclaim and occasional controversy. Its protagonist, Holden Caulfield, quickly became an icon for teenage rebellion.

Title: Berlin
Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany by both area and population. Its 3.7 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the Spree river, which meanders directly through its historic center before flowing into the Havel.

Title: Wombat
Wombats are short-legged, muscular quadrupeds that are roughly one meter in length with short, stubby tails. They are highly adaptable and are found in forested, mountainous, and heathland areas. These unique burrowers are entirely endemic to Australia, meaning they are found nowhere else in the wild.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It has long been a major center for art, culture, and intellectualism in Europe. Geographically, the city is heavily defined by the massive Danube river, which provides a vital trade route through central Europe.

Title: Rembrandt
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was a Dutch Golden Age painter, printmaker, and draughtsman. He is generally considered one of the greatest visual artists in the history of art. Unlike his contemporary who painted "Girl with a Pearl Earring", Rembrandt spent the vast majority of his prolific career living and working in Amsterdam.

Title: VxWorks
VxWorks is a proprietary real-time operating system (RTOS) developed for embedded systems requiring extreme reliability and deterministic performance. It is widely used in aerospace, defense, and industrial robotics. NASA selected VxWorks to run the primary flight computers of the Mars Perseverance rover mission.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics. His legacy in physics is commemorated in numerous ways, including having an element named after him.

Title: HMS Endeavour
HMS Endeavour was a British Royal Navy research vessel that Lieutenant James Cook commanded to Tahiti, New Zealand, and Australia on his first voyage of discovery from 1768 to 1771. The ship was critical to early British exploration of the Pacific but was eventually scuttled during the American Revolutionary War.

Title: 1958 FIFA World Cup
The 1958 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Sweden, marked the arrival of a 17-year-old prodigy named Pelé. His incredible performance helped Brazil secure their first-ever World Cup trophy, defeating the host nation in a thrilling final match.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Hand of God Goal
The "Hand of God" was an unpenalized handling foul that resulted in a highly controversial goal during the quarter-finals of the 1986 FIFA World Cup. The match was played between England and the eventual tournament winner. The player who deceitfully punched the ball into the net later attributed it to the "Hand of God."

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: Michael Crichton
John Michael Crichton was an American author and filmmaker. His books have sold over 200 million copies worldwide, and over a dozen have been adapted into films. He is best known for writing the 1990 science fiction novel "Jurassic Park", which he subsequently helped adapt into the massive blockbuster 1993 film of the same name.

Title: Neil Armstrong
Neil Armstrong was an American astronaut and aeronautical engineer who became the first person to walk on the Moon. Before his astronaut career, he was a naval aviator and a test pilot. Armstrong was born in Wapakoneta, Ohio, in August 1930, developing a passion for aviation at a young age.

Title: Illinois
Illinois is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its diverse economic base, from agriculture in the central plains to major financial centers. Its largest city, Chicago, is a massive cultural hub that has produced numerous famous actors and film directors. The state's political capital is Springfield.

Title: Samuel Langhorne Clemens
Samuel Langhorne Clemens, known worldwide by his pen name Mark Twain, was raised in Hannibal, Missouri, which later provided the setting for his most famous novels. Before embarking on his legendary literary career, Clemens worked as a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi River, where he derived his famous maritime pseudonym.

Title: Rosalind Franklin
Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose work was central to the understanding of the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, viruses, and coal. Her famous Photo 51 was critical in determining the double helix structure of DNA, though she died before the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery.

Title: Norway
Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe, known for its deep coastal fjords, mountains, and glaciers. It shares a long eastern border with Sweden. The country's highest peak is Galdhøpiggen, which stands at 2,469 meters above sea level and is the highest mountain in both Norway and Northern Europe.

Title: Rocky Mountains
The Rocky Mountains are a major mountain range in western North America. They stretch more than 3,000 miles from the northernmost part of British Columbia, in western Canada, to New Mexico in the Southwestern United States, providing a massive continental divide.

Title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, sometimes called the Pharos of Alexandria, was a towering lighthouse built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Ancient Egypt. Constructed during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for many centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

Title: Broad Street Cholera Outbreak
The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak was a severe epidemic of cholera that occurred in the Soho district of London. Physician John Snow famously traced the source of the outbreak to a single contaminated public water pump, proving that the disease was waterborne rather than spread by foul air (miasma theory).

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they rank among the most popular pieces of classical music ever composed, pushing the boundaries of what a solo violin could achieve.

Title: Americium
Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95. It was discovered in 1944 by the same team at the University of California, Berkeley that found several other transuranic elements. It is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It is known for its diverse cultural heritage and complex history. The administrative, economic, and cultural center of the country is its capital city, Sarajevo.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was conceived and designed by architect Jørn Utzon.

Title: The Proton
The proton is a stable subatomic particle, symbol p, H+, or 1H, with a positive electric charge of +1 e elementary charge. It was discovered in the early 20th century by Ernest Rutherford, who demonstrated that the nucleus of the hydrogen atom is present in all other nuclei.

Title: Sully Prudhomme
René François Armand (Sully) Prudhomme was a French poet and essayist. He was a prominent figure in the Parnassian movement, which sought to restore elegance and precision to French poetry. He made history as the very first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Sully Prudhomme was born in 1839 in Paris, France.

Title: 1930 FIFA World Cup
The 1930 FIFA World Cup was the inaugural tournament for the men's soccer world championship. Organized by FIFA, the entire tournament took place in a single South American nation during the month of July. A total of 13 teams participated, and the host nation emerged victorious by defeating its neighbor in the final match.

Title: Stanley Cup
The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff winner. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America. Unlike many other sports trophies, it is made of a durable alloy of silver and nickel.

Title: Mississippi
Mississippi is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. Named after the massive river that forms its western border, the state has a deep legacy in American music and literature. The capital and largest city is Jackson, which was founded in 1821 along the banks of the Pearl River.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign is known as the Victorian era, a period of massive industrial expansion and public health reform. She oversaw the construction of modern sewer systems in the capital, preventing future cholera outbreaks.

Title: 1990 FIFA World Cup
The 1990 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Italy and featured a highly defensive style of play. In a rematch of the previous tournament's final, West Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to secure the championship. This victory marked the third World Cup title for the German national team.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring
"The Fellowship of the Ring" is the first of three volumes of the epic high-fantasy novel "The Lord of the Rings", written by an English academic and philologist. Set in the fictional universe of Middle-earth, the book was published in July 1954 and quickly became a foundational work of modern fantasy literature.

Title: Rhine River
The Rhine is one of the major European rivers, flowing from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea coast in the Netherlands. It serves as a vital navigable waterway and forms part of the borders between Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, France, and Germany.

Title: Monterey, California
Monterey is a city on California's rugged central coast. Its Cannery Row, one-time center of the sardine-packing industry, was immortalized by a famous American novelist. Today, it is a popular tourist destination known for its massive aquarium and coastal views.

Title: Pound sterling
The Pound sterling, known in some contexts simply as the pound or quid, is the official currency of the United Kingdom, Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, the British Antarctic Territory, and Tristan da Cunha. It is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: West Orange Laboratory
After outgrowing his initial facilities, a famous American inventor moved his operations to a much larger, modernized complex. The West Orange Laboratory in New Jersey became a massive industrial research facility where the motion picture camera and improved phonographs were developed, though it lacked the mythic, pioneering reputation of his earlier facility.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year before escaping, returning to France, and briefly reclaiming his empire during the period known as the Hundred Days.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and France. Historically, its plains have served as the battleground of Europe for centuries. The political and cultural center of the nation is its capital city, Brussels, which also hosts the headquarters of the European Union.

Title: Eighth Planet from the Sun
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. In the Solar System, it is the fourth-largest planet by diameter. It was named after the Roman god of the sea. Neptune is notable for being the only planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by empirical observation.

Title: Machu Picchu
Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel located in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru on a 2,430-meter mountain ridge. It is the most familiar icon of the Inca Empire. Built in classical Inca style with polished dry-stone walls, it was mysteriously abandoned around the time of the Spanish Conquest.

Title: Rockville, Maryland
Rockville is a city and the county seat of Montgomery County, Maryland, United States, part of the Baltimore–Washington metropolitan area. It has historical significance and is home to the gravesite of legendary American novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, drawing literary tourists to St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age, most notably "The Great Gatsby". His turbulent personal life, marked by alcoholism and financial struggles, was closely intertwined with the deteriorating mental health of his wife.

Title: Freddie Mercury
Freddie Mercury was a British singer and songwriter, best known as the legendary lead vocalist of the rock band Queen. Known for his four-octave vocal range and theatrical stage persona, he was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town, a city located on the East African island of Zanzibar.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a bronze sculpture by Auguste Rodin, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work shows a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock. He is seen leaning over, his right elbow placed on his left thigh, holding the weight of his chin on the back of his right hand.

Title: Vostok 1
Vostok 1 was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first crewed spaceflight in history. Launched by the Soviet Union in April 1961, it carried cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who became the first human to cross into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: Titania
Titania is the largest of the moons of Uranus and the eighth largest moon in the Solar System at a diameter of 1,578 kilometres (981 mi). Discovered by William Herschel in 1787, it consists of roughly equal amounts of ice and rock. Its surface is scarred by massive canyons and fault lines.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance who was active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, theorist, sculptor, and architect. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest painters in art history, famous for masterpieces like "The Last Supper" and a 1503 portrait of a Florentine noblewoman.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was a sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. He is widely considered one of the greatest artists of all time, famous for creating the monumental marble sculpture "David" and painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling. He was born in the Republic of Florence, in present-day Italy.

Title: Palomar Observatory
The Palomar Observatory is an astronomical research observatory in the Palomar Mountain Range in San Diego County, California. It is owned and operated by the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). It was home to the 200-inch Hale Telescope, the world's largest effective telescope for decades.

Title: William Herschel
Frederick William Herschel was a German-born British astronomer and composer. He is best known for his discovery of the planet Uranus in 1781, which was the first planet discovered using a telescope. He also discovered two of its major moons and mapped numerous nebulae.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known works of Antonio Vivaldi, who was born in the canal city of Venice.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad and commonly known as Atlanta 1996, were an international multi-sport event held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The games were hosted in the capital city of a southern US state, marking the centennial of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: First Human in Space
On April 12, 1961, the Soviet space program achieved a massive milestone by successfully launching the first human into space. The cosmonaut aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft completed one orbit of the Earth. Tragically, this legendary space pioneer later died in a routine training flight crash in 1968.

Title: Lake Michigan
Lake Michigan is one of the five Great Lakes of North America. It is the second-largest of the Great Lakes by volume and the third-largest by surface area. It is uniquely the only one of the Great Lakes located entirely within the United States, bordering Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan.

Title: 1994 South African Elections
The 1994 South African general election was held between 26 and 29 April 1994. The election was the first in which citizens of all races were allowed to take part, and was therefore also the first held with universal adult suffrage. It resulted in the election of the nation's first black, democratic president.

Title: Mount Elbrus
Mount Elbrus is the highest and most prominent peak in Russia and Europe. It is situated in the western part of the Caucasus Mountains and is a dormant volcano. Standing at an impressive 5,642 metres, it dominates the geopolitical border between Russia and Georgia.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: Europium
Europium is a chemical element with the symbol Eu and atomic number 63. It is the most reactive lanthanide and must be stored under an inert fluid to protect it from atmospheric oxygen or moisture. It is named after the continent of Europe and is widely used as a red phosphor in television sets.

Title: George II of Great Britain
George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1727 until his death in 1760. His reign saw several major conflicts, including the Jacobite rising of 1745. He was the reigning sovereign in 1749, the year the pioneer of vaccination was born.

Title: Radium
Radium is a highly radioactive alkaline earth metal with the atomic number 88. It was discovered alongside polonium by the Curies in 1898. Its name is derived from the Latin word for ray, recognizing its immense power to emit ionizing radiation.

Title: Ottawa
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Located in the east of southern Ontario, near the city of Montréal and the U.S. border, it is a major political and technological center. The city was founded in 1826 as Bytown, and sits squarely on the south bank of a major waterway.

Title: The Starry Night
"The Starry Night" is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it features a swirling night sky, a crescent moon, and a bright Venus over a quiet village. It is regarded as among Van Gogh's finest works and has been a permanent fixture in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team based in Kansas City, Missouri. They competed in the very first Super Bowl but were defeated. Led by head coach Hank Stram, they later returned to the big game and secured a victory in Super Bowl IV before a long championship drought.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He was the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He composed some of the most popular theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, Russia.

Title: The Descent of Man
"The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" is a book by English naturalist Charles Darwin, first published in 1871. It applies evolutionary theory to human evolution, and details his theory of sexual selection. It was published more than a decade after his initial, foundational work on evolution.

Title: Black Elk Peak
Black Elk Peak is the highest natural point in South Dakota, standing at an elevation of 7,244 feet (2,208 m). Formerly known as Harney Peak, it is located in the Black Hills National Forest in Pennington County. It represents the highest summit in the United States east of the Rocky Mountains.

Title: In Cold Blood
"In Cold Blood" is a non-fiction novel published in 1966. It details the 1959 murders of four members of the Clutter family in the small farming community of Holcomb, Kansas. The author spent years interviewing residents and investigators, accompanied by his close childhood friend, a famous female novelist.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: Mary Wollstonecraft
Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer, philosopher, and advocate of women's rights. She is best known for "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman" (1792). Her life was cut tragically short in 1797; shortly after giving birth to her second daughter, Mary, she contracted puerperal fever and passed away.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. London has been a major human settlement for two millennia, serving as a global center of commerce, arts, and geopolitical history.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC by Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great. The dynasty ruled for nearly three centuries, cultivating a rich blend of Greek and Egyptian culture. The kingdom's royal court and political capital were situated in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Diego Maradona
Diego Armando Maradona was a professional football player and manager, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the sport. He is infamous for scoring the "Hand of God" goal. He was born and raised in a shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: Golden Gate Bridge
The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean. Designed by engineer Joseph Strauss, the stunning international orange structure opened in 1937 and remains a symbol of American engineering prowess.

Title: Sergei Korolev
Sergei Pavlovich Korolev was a lead Soviet rocket engineer and spacecraft designer. During the Space Race, he was simply known as "The Chief Designer" to protect his identity from Western intelligence. He was the mastermind behind Sputnik and Vostok. Korolev was born in 1907 in the city of Zhytomyr.

Title: Zelda Fitzgerald
Zelda Fitzgerald was an American socialite, novelist, and painter. As the wife of a famous Jazz Age author, she was an icon of the 1920s flapper culture. She suffered from severe mental health issues and was institutionalized multiple times. She tragically died in 1948 when a fire broke out at the Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina.

Title: 1856 in Great Britain
The year 1856 in Great Britain was marked by the end of the Crimean War with the signing of the Treaty of Paris. The country was undergoing rapid industrialization and scientific advancement during this period. The nation and its growing empire were under the steady rule of Queen Victoria.

Title: Nikita Khrushchev
Nikita Khrushchev was the First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1964 and chairman of the country's Council of Ministers from 1958 to 1964. As the premier of the nation, he oversaw the early, highly successful years of the Soviet space program, including the historic launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957.

Title: The Great Gatsby
"The Great Gatsby" is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts the interactions of a cast of characters who attend extravagant parties hosted by the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is considered a quintessential American classic.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, historically known as Bohemia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria to the south, Germany to the west, Poland to the northeast, and Slovakia to the southeast. Its official currency is the Czech koruna, despite the country's membership in the European Union.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: 81-Point Game
The second-highest single-game point total in NBA history is 81 points. This incredible scoring performance was achieved by Los Angeles Lakers star Kobe Bryant on January 22, 2006, in a comeback victory against the Toronto Raptors.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern United States, known for its massive metropolis, New York City, and its diverse geography, including the Adirondack Mountains. It has a rich political history and has hosted several international sporting events. The state's executive branch is led by a governor elected to four-year terms.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. It is known for its high quality of life and for hosting major international sporting events, including early iterations of the modern Olympic Games.

Title: The Edge
David Howell Evans, better known by his stage name The Edge, is a musician who is the lead guitarist, keyboardist, and backing vocalist of the rock band U2. He is known for his signature guitar sound, which involves rhythmic delay effects. He was born in Barking, Essex, before relocating to Ireland as a child.
