content:
Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film incorporating both historical and fictionalized aspects of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. The film was a massive commercial success, becoming the highest-grossing film of all time upon its release, a record it held until 2010. It was heavily praised for its visual effects and emotional weight.

Title: Mikhail Gurevich
Mikhail Gurevich was a Soviet aircraft designer who co-founded the Mikoyan-Gurevich military aviation bureau. He was born in the Kursk region of Russia. His engineering expertise was crucial in developing the aerodynamics of early Soviet jet fighters during the dawn of the Cold War.

Title: Shah Jahan
Shah Jahan was the fifth emperor of the Mughal Empire, remembered largely for his architectural achievements. He famously commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal to honor his favorite wife. His reign ended when he was deposed by his ambitious son in 1658, and he died in captivity in early 1666.

Title: Silver
Silver is a metallic chemical element that exhibits the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and reflectivity of any metal. It has long been valued as a precious metal and is commonly used in currency, jewelry, and sporting trophies. Its official chemical symbol on the periodic table is Ag.

Title: Charles Darwin
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist. His theories on evolution by natural selection fundamentally altered scientific understanding of biology. These theories were heavily informed by his observations of finches and tortoises during his multi-year global voyage aboard the HMS Beagle.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. The country's political and administrative center is its capital city, Wellington, located at the south-western tip of the North Island.

Title: 2006 FIFA World Cup
The 2006 FIFA World Cup was hosted by Germany and was the 18th edition of the tournament. The championship was secured by Italy, who defeated France 5–3 in a penalty shoot-out following a 1–1 draw after extra time.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country in northwestern Europe. It has a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary democracy. The nation's official currency is the Pound Sterling, which is the oldest currency in continuous use.

Title: Kapuskasing
Kapuskasing is a town on the Kapuskasing River in the Cochrane District of Northern Ontario, Canada. Founded in the early 20th century as a water stop along the National Transcontinental Railway, it relies heavily on the forestry and paper industries. It is the birthplace of several notable Canadian figures.

Title: Chemical Symbol Rf
On the periodic table of elements, rutherfordium is classified as a transactinide element. It is placed in group 4 and period 7. Scientists universally identify this heavy, extremely unstable element using the two-letter chemical symbol Rf.

Title: Bacteria
Bacteria are ubiquitous, mostly free-living organisms often consisting of one biological cell. They constitute a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms. While many are harmless or beneficial, some are pathogenic and cause infectious diseases, which are typically treated using antibiotic medications.

Title: Germany
Germany is a country in Central Europe known for its powerful economy, deep history, and massive contributions to classical music and philosophy. Following reunification in 1990, the political and administrative center of the nation returned to its historic capital city, Berlin.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: Harper Lee
Nelle Harper Lee was an American novelist best known for her 1960 masterpiece "To Kill a Mockingbird". She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to literature. Lee was born and raised in Monroeville, Alabama, on April 28, 1926.

Title: 2003 Ballon d'Or
The 2003 Ballon d'Or, given to the best football player in Europe as judged by a panel of sports journalists from UEFA member countries, was awarded to the Czech midfielder Pavel Nedvěd. He beat out fierce competition from Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini to secure the prestigious accolade.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC by Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great. The dynasty ruled for nearly three centuries, cultivating a rich blend of Greek and Egyptian culture. The kingdom's royal court and political capital were situated in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Publication of To Kill a Mockingbird
When "To Kill a Mockingbird" was finally published in July 1960, the United States was transitioning into a new era of civil rights struggles. The sitting president during the book's highly anticipated release was Dwight D. Eisenhower, nearing the end of his second term.

Title: Princeton University
Princeton University is a private Ivy League research university. Founded in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States. The university boasts a highly distinguished alumni network, including several US presidents, Supreme Court justices, and the billionaire founder of Amazon.

Title: 1797 in Great Britain
The year 1797 in Great Britain was marked by several significant historical events, including the Battle of Cape St Vincent and widespread naval mutinies at Spithead and the Nore. It was also a notable year in literature, serving as the birth year of several prominent literary figures, including the future creator of a legendary literary monster.

Title: The Greatest (Boxer)
Widely regarded as one of the most significant sports figures of the 20th century, the boxer known universally as "The Greatest" was a three-time heavyweight champion. Known for his legendary trash talk and political activism, he famously refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War, citing his religious beliefs.

Title: Friedrich Engels
Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, historian, communist, social scientist, and revolutionary socialist. He was the closest collaborator of Karl Marx, co-authoring "The Communist Manifesto". After his death in 1895 in London, his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head, near Eastbourne.

Title: Herbert Hoover
Herbert Clark Hoover was an American politician and engineer who served as the 31st president of the United States from 1929 to 1933. He took office during the final months of the economic boom before the stock market crashed, plunging the nation into the Great Depression.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878. Cleve named the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Title: U2
U2 is an Irish rock band formed in Dublin in 1976. The group consists of a prominent lead vocalist known for his expressive vocal style, alongside The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. The band's early sound was rooted in post-punk but eventually grew to incorporate influences from many genres of popular music.

Title: Tallest Building in the World
The title of the tallest building in the world has changed hands numerous times over the centuries. Currently, the record is held by a massive megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Standing at a staggering total height of 829.8 meters (2,722 ft), it has held the title since its topping out in 2009.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: Michael Jackson
Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, and dancer. Dubbed the "King of Pop", he is regarded as one of the most significant cultural figures of the 20th century. He achieved unparalleled global success with his 1982 album "Thriller". Jackson was born into a working-class African-American family in Gary, Indiana.

Title: Cincinnati
Cincinnati is a major city in the United States, situated on the north bank of the Ohio River. It is known for its historic architecture, vibrant arts scene, and major professional sports teams. It is a major economic hub within the state of Ohio.

Title: Kansas City Chiefs
The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team based in Kansas City, Missouri. They competed in the very first Super Bowl but were defeated. Led by head coach Hank Stram, they later returned to the big game and secured a victory in Super Bowl IV before a long championship drought.

Title: George V
George V was King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor of India, from 1910 until his death in 1936. His reign spanned the First World War and the subsequent restructuring of the British Empire. He was on the throne during the year a famous Bohemian writer died of tuberculosis.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historic resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived in Springfield from 1837 until he moved to the White House in 1861. Today, it serves as the political and administrative heart of the state.

Title: Sinking of the RMS Lusitania
The RMS Lusitania was a British ocean liner that was sunk on 7 May 1915 by a German U-boat 11 miles off the southern coast of Ireland. The sinking occurred during the First World War and caused the deaths of 1,198 passengers and crew, significantly shifting public opinion in the United States against Germany.

Title: Alberto Santos-Dumont
Alberto Santos-Dumont was an aeronaut, sportsman, and inventor who designed, built, and flew the first practical dirigible balloons. Following his lighter-than-air achievements, he transitioned to heavier-than-air flight, creating the 14-bis biplane. Santos-Dumont was born in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Title: Salvador Dalí
Salvador Dalí was a Spanish surrealist artist renowned for his technical skill and the striking, bizarre images in his work. His magnum opus, "The Persistence of Memory", cemented his reputation as a master of Surrealism. Following a long and eccentric life, Dalí died of heart failure in 1989 in the exact same Catalan town where he was born.

Title: United States
The United States is a massive transcontinental country spanning North America, with additional territories in the Pacific and Caribbean. The nation boasts highly diverse geography, ranging from vast central plains to rugged mountain ranges. The country's highest physical point is the towering peak of Denali, located in the state of Alaska.

Title: Pablo Picasso
Pablo Picasso was a Spanish painter, sculptor, and printmaker who spent most of his adult life in France. He is known for co-founding the Cubist movement. In a bizarre historical footnote, Picasso was actually brought in for questioning by police as a suspect during the infamous 1911 Louvre theft investigation.

Title: Economy of France
France boasts a highly developed, social market economy that is among the largest in the world. As a founding member of the European Union, its economic policies are deeply integrated with its neighbors. The official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French franc in 2002.

Title: The Count of Monte Cristo
The Count of Monte Cristo is an adventure novel written by French author Alexandre Dumas completed in 1844. It is one of the author's most popular works, alongside The Three Musketeers. The story centers on a man who is wrongfully imprisoned, escapes, acquires a fortune, and seeks revenge.

Title: 1911 Museum Theft
In August 1911, the global art community was shocked by a brazen robbery at the Louvre museum in Paris. Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman, hid in a broom closet and successfully smuggled out a world-famous portrait under his coat. The sensational theft of the Mona Lisa launched the painting into unprecedented international stardom.

Title: Bram Stoker
Abraham "Bram" Stoker was an Irish author, best known today for his 1897 Gothic horror novel "Dracula". During his lifetime, he was better known as the personal assistant of actor Sir Henry Irving and business manager of the Lyceum Theatre in London. Stoker was born in Dublin in 1847.

Title: Stephen King
Stephen Edwin King is an American author of horror, supernatural fiction, suspense, crime, science-fiction, and fantasy novels. Many of his books have been adapted into films, miniseries, and comic books. King was born in Portland, Maine, and frequently uses his home state as the setting for his novels.

Title: Aldous Huxley
Aldous Leonard Huxley was an English writer and philosopher. He wrote nearly fifty books, encompassing both novels and non-fiction works. He is universally renowned for his novel "Brave New World". Huxley was born in Godalming, Surrey, England, into a prominent intellectual family.

Title: Votkinsk
Votkinsk is an industrial town in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, situated in the eastern foothills of the Ural Mountains. Founded in 1759 as a settlement centered around a new ironworks facility, the town grew rapidly around its local factories. Geographically, it developed directly along the banks of a prominent local waterway.

Title: Belgium
Belgium is a country in Western Europe. It borders the Netherlands to the north, Germany to the east, Luxembourg to the southeast, and France to the southwest. The nation is globally renowned for its high-quality pralines and chocolate truffles. The political center and capital of the country is Brussels.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. It is famous for its passionate football culture, vibrant Carnival festivals, and the sprawling Amazon rainforest. The country's highest physical point is the Pico da Neblina, located deep within the Guiana Highlands.

Title: Economy of Argentina
The economy of Argentina relies heavily on natural resources, an export-oriented agricultural sector, and a diversified industrial base. Historically, the nation has struggled with severe inflation and currency crises. In the late 1980s, its official currency was the Argentine austral, which was later replaced by the peso.

Title: Discovery of Penicillin
Penicillin was the first broadly effective antibiotic used in clinical medicine. Its discovery in 1928 revolutionized modern medicine, turning previously fatal bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. The breakthrough occurred when Alexander Fleming noticed that a specific blue-green mold contaminating his petri dishes was actively destroying bacteria.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: Chordata
Chordata is a biological phylum of animals that possess a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal slits at some point in their life cycle. This phylum includes all vertebrates, such as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish, making it one of the most prominent groupings in the animal kingdom.

Title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
"The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King" is a 2003 epic high fantasy adventure film. Serving as the conclusion to a sprawling trilogy, it was both a massive critical and commercial success. At the 76th Academy Awards, it swept all 11 of its nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic is a landlocked country in Central Europe. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains. It is the birth country of several legendary European footballers.

Title: Seven Samurai
"Seven Samurai" is a 1954 epic historical drama film. It follows the story of a village of farmers that hire seven rōnin to combat bandits who will return after the harvest to steal their crops. It is widely considered one of the greatest and most influential films in cinema history.

Title: WorldWideWeb (browser)
WorldWideWeb, later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion between the software and the World Wide Web itself, was the first web browser and editor. It was written by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990 while working at CERN. It was relatively obscure compared to later graphical browsers that brought the internet to the masses.

Title: Louis Pasteur
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. While he made massive contributions to the study of microorganisms, he lived centuries after the original Dutch pioneer who first observed bacteria.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. The Irish Sea lies northwest of England and the Celtic Sea to the southwest. Historically, its territory served as the bloody battleground for the Wars of the Roses, including the decisive clash at Bosworth Field.

Title: Lyndon B. Johnson
Lyndon Baines Johnson, often referred to by his initials LBJ, was an American politician who served as the 36th president of the United States from 1963 to 1969. He assumed the presidency following the assassination of John F. Kennedy. He was the presiding head of state in early 1964 when the British Invasion of American music began. He was a lifelong member of the Democratic Party.

Title: Multiple Nobel Laureates
Winning a single Nobel Prize is a monumental achievement, and only a very small number of individuals have won multiple times. The very first person to ever win two Nobel Prizes, and the only one to win in two distinct scientific fields (Physics and Chemistry), was Marie Curie.

Title: Invention of Dynamite
Dynamite is an explosive made of nitroglycerin, sorbents, and stabilizers. It was invented in 1867 to make the highly volatile nitroglycerin safer for transport and construction use. The invention was incredibly successful, making its creator vastly wealthy and providing the funds for a series of famous international prizes.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was a close childhood friend of Harper Lee, and she assisted him heavily with the research for his true crime masterpiece.

Title: Mexican peso
The Mexican peso (symbol: $; code: MXN) is the currency of Mexico. Originally based on the silver reserves of the Spanish empire, it was the first currency in the world to use the "$" sign, which the US dollar later adopted. It remains a major global currency.

Title: Mona Lisa
The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting known for the subject's enigmatic smile. It is arguably the most recognized and parodied work of art in the world. The stunning Renaissance masterpiece was painted by the iconic polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century.

Title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
"E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" is a 1982 American science fiction film produced and directed by Steven Spielberg. It tells the story of Elliott, a boy who befriends an extraterrestrial dubbed E.T., who is stranded on Earth. The film surpassed "Star Wars" to become the highest-grossing film of all time—a record it held for eleven years.

Title: Akira Kurosawa
Akira Kurosawa was a brilliant film director, screenwriter, and producer who directed 30 films in a career spanning 57 years. He is famous for pioneering cinematic techniques and directing masterpieces like the 1954 epic "Seven Samurai". Kurosawa was born in 1910 in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in the Empire of Japan.

Title: Museum of Modern Art
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is a major art museum that plays a significant role in developing and collecting modernist art. It permanently houses an extensive collection of priceless artworks, including Vincent van Gogh's iconic "The Starry Night". This prestigious institution is located in Midtown Manhattan in New York City.

Title: 1926 in the United States
The year 1926 was situated right in the middle of the Roaring Twenties. The United States was experiencing massive economic growth, the rapid expansion of jazz culture, and the continued enforcement of Prohibition. During this prosperous era, the White House was occupied by a famously quiet Republican leader.

Title: Dmitri Mendeleev
Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor. He is best known for formulating the Periodic Law and creating a farsighted version of the periodic table of elements in 1869, leaving gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among other products and services. Its massive corporate headquarters is situated in Menlo Park, California.

Title: Steven Spielberg
Steven Spielberg is an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. A major figure of the New Hollywood era and pioneer of the modern blockbuster, he is the most commercially successful director in history. Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, and developed a passion for filmmaking at a young age.

Title: Sarajevo
Sarajevo is the political, financial, social, and cultural center of a major Balkan nation. Nestled within the Dinaric Alps and situated along the Miljacka River, it is known for its religious diversity. Historically, it gained global infamy as the city where Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in 1914.

Title: Uffizi Gallery
The Uffizi Gallery is a prominent art museum located adjacent to the Piazza della Signoria in the Historic Centre of Florence in the region of Tuscany, Italy. One of the most important Italian museums and the most visited, it holds a superb collection of priceless artworks, particularly from the period of the Italian Renaissance.

Title: Australia
Australia is a sovereign country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent and the island of Tasmania. It is known for its rugged outback and coastal cities. The country successfully hosted the Summer Olympics at the turn of the millennium. The nation's capital is Canberra, an inland planned city.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: Alexander Fleming
Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist. For his monumental achievement in discovering the first broadly effective antibiotic substance, he was awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, an honor he shared with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers decisively defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10.

Title: The Four Seasons
"The Four Seasons" is a group of four violin concertos by an Italian composer, each of which gives musical expression to a season of the year. Written around 1720, they are the best-known works of Antonio Vivaldi, who was born in the canal city of Venice.

Title: Votka River
The Votka is a river in the Udmurt Republic, Russia, and a right tributary of the Shiva River. It flows for roughly 66 kilometers through a rolling landscape before running directly through the center of the industrial town of Votkinsk, where an artificial dam was constructed to power the town's historic metal factories.

Title: Polonium
Polonium is a highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po. It is a rare and highly volatile metal, discovered in 1898 by researchers studying pitchblende. On the periodic table of elements, Polonium is classified as a chalcogen and has the atomic number 84.

Title: Salem, Massachusetts
Salem is a historic coastal city in Essex County, Massachusetts, located on the North Shore. Known heavily for its 1692 witch trials, it was also a major maritime port in early American history, requiring a substantial customs operation.

Title: Ridley Scott
Sir Ridley Scott is an English film director and producer. He is renowned for his atmospheric, highly concentrated visual style. After establishing his career with commercials, he found global fame directing the sci-fi classics "Alien" and "Blade Runner". He is the older brother of fellow Hollywood director Tony Scott.

Title: Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Martin Heinrich Klaproth was a pioneering German chemist who was a major figure in the early development of analytical chemistry. He is best known for his discovery of several chemical elements. In 1789, he discovered the element Uranium. That same year, while analyzing a gemstone from Sri Lanka, he also discovered the element Zirconium.

Title: Pollsmoor Prison
Pollsmoor Maximum Security Prison is a prison in the suburb of Tokai, South Africa. Nelson Mandela was transferred here from his previous island prison in 1982, serving out another segment of his sentence before being moved to Victor Verster Prison prior to his final release.

Title: Mark Antony
Mark Antony was a Roman politician and general who played a critical role in the transformation of the Roman Republic into the autocratic Roman Empire. He initially formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian, but the alliance fractured. He famously aligned himself militarily and romantically with the queen of a wealthy North African kingdom.

Title: Truman Capote
Truman Capote was an American novelist, screenwriter, playwright, and actor. He is best known for his true crime novel "In Cold Blood" and the novella "Breakfast at Tiffany's". Capote was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, but spent much of his childhood living next door to Harper Lee.

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel published in 1960 that became instantly successful. Widely read in middle and high schools across the United States, it has become a classic of modern American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize. The plot is loosely based on the author's observations of her family and neighbors.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known worldwide as the "City of Music" due to its musical legacy, as many famous classical musicians spent their prime years working there. The city is bisected by the massive Danube river.

Title: Seventh Planet from the Sun
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Its name is a reference to the Greek god of the sky. It has the third-largest planetary radius and fourth-largest planetary mass in the Solar System. The ice giant was officially discovered in 1781 by astronomer William Herschel, making it the first planet discovered with a telescope.

Title: Napoleon's Final Exile
Following his catastrophic defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon Bonaparte was captured and stripped of his imperial titles. To ensure he could never return to threaten European peace, his captors exiled him to Saint Helena, a remarkably remote island in the South Atlantic Ocean, where he eventually died in 1821.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country located in Southern Europe, consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and surrounded by several islands. It has a deeply rich cultural heritage and was the epicenter of the Roman Empire and the Renaissance. The political, economic, and cultural capital of the modern nation is Rome.

Title: Andrew Adamson
Andrew Ralph Adamson is a film director, producer, and visual effects supervisor. He gained worldwide recognition for co-directing the incredibly successful animated films "Shrek" and "Shrek 2". Adamson was born in Auckland, New Zealand, before moving to the United States to pursue his career in visual effects.

Title: Julius Caesar
Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. A member of the First Triumvirate, Caesar led the Roman armies in the Gallic Wars before defeating his political rival Pompey in a civil war. He was assassinated in 44 BC, long before the empire was officially established.

Title: Inheritance of Acquired Characteristics
The inheritance of acquired characteristics is a proto-evolutionary hypothesis that argued that physiological changes acquired by an organism during its lifetime could be passed down to its offspring. This concept was heavily championed by an early French naturalist but was later largely discredited by modern genetics.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements. The novel was authored by Aldous Huxley, representing a different flavor of dystopia than the surveillance state of 'Big Brother'.

Title: Alien (film)
"Alien" is a 1979 science fiction horror film that follows the crew of the commercial space tug Nostromo. They encounter a deadly extraterrestrial lifeform set loose on the ship. The film famously features Sigourney Weaver in her breakout role as the resilient warrant officer, Ellen Ripley. It was directed by the visionary British filmmaker Ridley Scott.

Title: Glenn T. Seaborg
Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The element Seaborgium was named in his honor. He was born in Ishpeming, located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

Title: Astronomia nova
"Astronomia nova" is a book published in 1609 that contains the results of a prominent astronomer's ten-year-long investigation of the motion of Mars. The work provided strong arguments for heliocentrism and introduced the first two laws of planetary motion, revolutionizing the mathematical understanding of the cosmos.

Title: The Dark Side of the Moon
"The Dark Side of the Moon" is the eighth studio album by an English rock band, released in March 1973. It is a concept album that explores themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness. The record was a massive commercial success and remains one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed albums of all time.

Title: The Great Gatsby
The Great Gatsby is a 1925 novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, the novel depicts narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. It is frequently hailed as a strong contender for the title of the Great American Novel.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is considered one of the most remote islands in the world. It gained immense historical infamy as the final, inescapable site of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte. The island is currently controlled as a British Overseas Territory by the United Kingdom.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, and later moved to Paris to study. She remained fiercely proud of her Polish heritage throughout her career in France.

Title: The Trial
The Trial is a novel written in 1914 and 1915 but not published until 1925, a year after the author's death. It tells the story of Josef K., a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority. It is another seminal work by Franz Kafka, exploring themes of existential dread and bureaucracy.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: RMS Titanic
The RMS Titanic was a British passenger liner operated by the White Star Line. It famously sank in the North Atlantic Ocean on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg during her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City, making it one of the deadliest peacetime commercial marine disasters.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States. A major center for international trade, its massive port required a large workforce of customs inspectors in the 19th century. The city's geography encompasses five boroughs across several islands and the mainland.

Title: Sickle cell anemia
Sickle cell anemia is a genetic blood disorder characterized by red blood cells that assume an abnormal, rigid, sickle shape. This decreases the cells' flexibility and results in a risk of various life-threatening complications. In 1949, Linus Pauling demonstrated that the disease occurs due to a mutation in a specific metalloprotein.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They are the third-oldest franchise in the NFL. The team is legendary for its mid-20th-century dominance, securing victory in the very first Super Bowl under the fierce leadership of their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Invention of the World Wide Web
The World Wide Web, commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators. It was invented in 1989 at CERN in Switzerland. The creator developed the first web browser and the fundamental protocols of the internet, HTTP and HTML.

Title: Henri Dunant
Jean Henri Dunant was a Swiss humanitarian, businessman and social activist. He was the visionary, promoter and co-founder of the Red Cross. In 1901, he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with Frédéric Passy, making him a co-recipient of the inaugural awards alongside men like Wilhelm Röntgen.

Title: Wonders of the Ancient World
The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World were a list of remarkable constructions of classical antiquity. While the Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one still standing, others were legendary in their time. Among these was a colossal structure built to guide sailors safely into harbor, located in the coastal city of Alexandria.

Title: Málaga
Málaga is a municipality of Spain, capital of the Province of Málaga, in the autonomous community of Andalusia. With a history spanning about 2,800 years, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Western Europe. It is notable for being the birthplace of Pablo Picasso, another giant of 20th-century Spanish art.

Title: Final Defeat in 1815
After briefly returning from his first exile, Napoleon Bonaparte launched a final military campaign. His reign permanently ended when his forces were decisively crushed by a coalition of British and Prussian armies in June 1815. This catastrophic loss occurred at the historic Battle of Waterloo.

Title: 2014 FIFA World Cup
The 2014 FIFA World Cup was the 20th FIFA World Cup. It took place in Brazil from 12 June to 13 July 2014, after the country was awarded the hosting rights in 2007. The tournament culminated in Germany winning their fourth title by defeating Argentina in the final.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish author Bram Stoker. It introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: Exile of Napoleon
Following his devastating defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte was forced to abdicate the French throne for a second time. To ensure he could never return to power, his captors exiled him to a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic, where he ultimately died of stomach cancer in 1821.

Title: The Thing (1982 film)
"The Thing" is a 1982 American science fiction horror film based on the 1938 John W. Campbell Jr. novella "Who Goes There?". It tells the story of a group of American researchers in Antarctica who encounter a parasitic extraterrestrial life-form. The film was directed by horror master John Carpenter.

Title: Guernica (painting)
"Guernica" is a large 1937 oil painting by a world-renowned cubist artist. It is regarded by many art critics as one of the most moving and powerful anti-war paintings in history. After decades of touring globally, the mural was returned to its artist's homeland and is now permanently housed in the Museo Reina Sofía.

Title: Lactuca sativa
Lactuca sativa is the formal scientific name for the species of plant commonly known as lettuce. Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians, it was transformed from a weed whose seeds were used to extract oil into a plant grown for its edible leaves. The species is now farmed extensively worldwide.

Title: Blue Origin
Blue Origin is an American privately funded aerospace manufacturer and sub-orbital spaceflight services company headquartered in Kent, Washington. Founded in 2000 by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, the company aims to make access to space cheaper and more reliable through reusable launch vehicles.

Title: Most Points in an NBA Game
The record for the most points scored by a single player in an NBA game is a staggering 100 points. This legendary feat was accomplished on March 2, 1962, during a game between the Philadelphia Warriors and the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Title: England
England is a country that is part of the United Kingdom. It shares land borders with Wales to its west and Scotland to its north. It has a rich literary tradition, producing countless famous authors. The capital and largest city of England is London, a major global financial and cultural center.

Title: Harvard University
Harvard University is a private Ivy League research university in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Founded in 1636, it is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. It is widely considered one of the most prestigious universities in the world, producing numerous Nobel laureates and prominent business leaders.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. The capital and largest city of France is Paris, a global center for art, fashion, gastronomy, and culture.

Title: Salinas, California
Salinas is the county seat and largest municipality of Monterey County, California. Located at the mouth of the Salinas Valley, the city has long been an agricultural powerhouse. It produces such a massive volume of a specific leafy green vegetable that it has earned the nickname "The Lettuce Capital of the World."

Title: Captain James Cook
James Cook was a British explorer, navigator, cartographer, and captain in the Royal Navy. He made detailed maps of Newfoundland prior to making three voyages to the Pacific Ocean, during which he achieved the first recorded European contact with the eastern coastline of Australia and the Hawaiian Islands.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. His mastery of human anatomy is showcased in his famous marble statue of David. Though he preferred sculpting, he was also commissioned to paint the magnificent frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Golden State Warriors
The Golden State Warriors are an American professional basketball team based in San Francisco, California. They compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA) as a member of the league's Western Conference. The franchise has enjoyed a highly successful modern era, winning multiple championships under head coach Steve Kerr.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign is known as the Victorian era, a period of massive industrial expansion and public health reform. She oversaw the construction of modern sewer systems in the capital, preventing future cholera outbreaks.

Title: Vltava River
The Vltava is an iconic waterway that runs directly through the historic heart of Prague. Measuring 430 kilometers in length, it holds the title of the longest river flowing entirely within the borders of the Czech Republic. It is a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Most Academy Awards for a Single Film
Three films in history have tied for the record of winning the most Academy Awards, each earning exactly 11 Oscars. The first was "Ben-Hur" in 1959, followed by "Titanic" in 1997. The most recent film to achieve this monumental sweep was a massive high-fantasy epic released in 2003, which won every category for which it was nominated.

Title: New York City
New York City is the most populous city in the United States and a major global cultural and financial hub. It comprises five boroughs and is home to countless renowned institutions, including Broadway theaters and premier art galleries like the Museum of Modern Art, which draws millions of visitors annually.

Title: Sydney Opera House
The Sydney Opera House is a multi-venue performing arts centre in Sydney. Located on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour, it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture. The structure was designed by a foreign architect who won an international competition.

Title: Karl Marx
Karl Marx was a German-born philosopher, economist, political theorist, historian, and revolutionary. He is best known for his 1848 pamphlet "The Communist Manifesto" and the multi-volume "Das Kapital". After spending his later years in exile in London, he passed away in 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Title: Dublin
Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland. Located on a bay on the east coast, at the mouth of the River Liffey, it is situated in the province of Leinster. As a historic and cultural center, it has a long tradition of producing globally recognized literary figures and musical acts.

Title: Ernest Rutherford
Ernest Rutherford was a pioneering physicist who came to be known as the father of nuclear physics. He famously discovered the atomic nucleus through his gold foil experiment. Rutherford was born in 1871 in Brightwater, a small town on the South Island of New Zealand.

Title: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His political stance often conflicted with the empire's rigid establishment. On June 28, 1914, he and his wife Sophie were fatally shot during a state visit. This assassination set the wheels in motion for the First World War.

Title: Warsaw
Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. The metropolis stands on the banks of a major river in east-central Poland. It has a rich history and has been the birthplace of many notable historical figures, including a two-time Nobel laureate.

Title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
"Girl with a Pearl Earring" is an oil painting by Johannes Vermeer, dated c. 1665. Going by various names over the centuries, it became known by its present title towards the end of the 20th century after the large pearl earring worn by the girl portrayed there. It is housed in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Title: Rutherfordium
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element that is highly radioactive. It was first synthesized in the 1960s by researchers at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. The element was officially named in honor of physicist Ernest Rutherford.

Title: Dutch Language
Dutch is a West Germanic language spoken by around 25 million people as a first language. It is the official language of the Netherlands and one of the three official languages of Belgium. It is closely related to both English and German and has served as a prominent language of trade and culture in Europe.

Title: University of Kansas
The University of Kansas is a public research university with its main campus located in the rolling hills of eastern Kansas. The university has a storied basketball program that has produced numerous NBA hall-of-famers, heavily drawing massive crowds to its campus arena.

Title: The Ed Sullivan Show (1964)
On February 9, 1964, a record-breaking 73 million viewers tuned into The Ed Sullivan Show. The broadcast featured the highly anticipated first live US television performance of the British musical group that would go on to record "Abbey Road". The event is considered a watershed moment in American pop culture history.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance. While his fame initially rested on his achievements as a painter, he also became known for his notebooks, in which he made drawings and notes on a variety of subjects, including anatomy, astronomy, botany, and cartography.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest physicists of all time. He is best known for developing the theory of relativity. While his work built upon the foundation laid by classical mechanics, he never attended an English university for his formal scientific training.

Title: Currency of the United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland maintains a highly developed, independent market economy. Unlike many of its European neighbors, it never adopted the Euro. The official currency of the United Kingdom and its primary territories is the Pound sterling.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine. It is part of the Carpathian Mountains and is situated in the Eastern Beskids region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: West Orange Laboratory
After outgrowing his initial facilities, a famous American inventor moved his operations to a much larger, modernized complex. The West Orange Laboratory in New Jersey became a massive industrial research facility where the motion picture camera and improved phonographs were developed, though it lacked the mythic, pioneering reputation of his earlier facility.

Title: Vibrio cholerae
Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium. It is the causative agent of cholera, a severe diarrheal disease caused by drinking contaminated water. The bacteria famously caused several pandemics in the 19th century, ravaging cities like London before proper sanitation infrastructure was implemented.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific German composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the "Brandenburg Concertos" and the "Mass in B minor". He survived his Italian contemporary by several years, passing away in 1750 in Leipzig.

Title: Marie Curie
Marie Salomea Skłodowska-Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who conducted pioneering research on radioactivity. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win twice, sharing her first prize with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel.

Title: Gloucestershire
Gloucestershire is a county in South West England. The county comprises part of the Cotswold Hills, part of the flat fertile valley of the River Severn, and the entire Forest of Dean. Its county town is the city of Gloucester, and it includes other major settlements like Cheltenham and Stroud.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. Discovered in 1923, the element was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where the discovery took place.

Title: Roger Federer
Roger Federer is a legendary former professional tennis player. He holds numerous historical records, including winning eight Wimbledon men's singles titles. He also managed to win five consecutive Wimbledon titles, matching a historic milestone, though his streak took place entirely within the 21st century.

Title: French Academy of Sciences
The French Academy of Sciences is a learned society founded in 1666 by Louis XIV at the suggestion of Jean-Baptiste Colbert. It was created to encourage and protect the spirit of French scientific research. While it published many vital European scientific papers, it was not the institution that published the letters of the first microbiologist.

Title: Albert Einstein
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. He was born in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. He spent the latter part of his life in the United States, working at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, after fleeing the rise of the Nazi regime.

Title: J.J. Thomson
Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist and Nobel Laureate in Physics. He is credited with the discovery of the electron, the first subatomic particle to be identified, through his experiments with cathode ray tubes. Thomson was born in Manchester, England, in 1856.

Title: 1913 Model of the Atom
In 1913, a groundbreaking model of atomic structure was proposed, fundamentally altering the field of quantum physics. This model depicted the atom as a small, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons that travel in circular orbits around it. It successfully explained the Rydberg formula for the spectral emission lines of atomic hydrogen.

Title: Meiji Restoration
The Meiji Restoration was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to the Empire of Japan in 1868 under Emperor Meiji. The event effectively destroyed the shogunate system, paving the way for the modernization and Westernization of the country and establishing a centralized government.

Title: Samuel Langhorne Clemens
Samuel Langhorne Clemens, known worldwide by his pen name Mark Twain, was raised in Hannibal, Missouri, which later provided the setting for his most famous novels. Before embarking on his legendary literary career, Clemens worked as a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi River, where he derived his famous maritime pseudonym.

Title: Thomas Francis Jr.
Thomas Francis Jr. was an American physician, virologist, and epidemiologist. He is most famous for leading the massive field trial for the inactivated polio vaccine created by his former student. On April 12, 1955, Francis stood before a crowded press conference and officially declared the vaccine to be "safe, effective, and potent."

Title: British Empire in the 17th Century
During the 17th century, the British Empire was rapidly expanding its overseas colonies and trading networks. The domestic front, however, faced extreme turmoil, including a civil war and disastrous urban fires. King Charles II was the reigning monarch trying to stabilize the country during the calamitous events of 1666.

Title: 2004 in Politics
The year 2004 was a period of intense global political activity and ongoing military conflicts in the Middle East. In the United States, it was an election year marked by debates over national security and economic policy. The incumbent president managed to secure a second term after a highly contested race.

Title: 2000 Summer Olympics
The 2000 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVII Olympiad and commonly known as Sydney 2000, were held in Sydney, Australia. The event was widely praised for its incredible organization and execution, setting a high benchmark for future host nations.

Title: René Magritte
René Magritte was a Belgian surrealist artist best known for his witty and thought-provoking images. Often depicting ordinary objects in an unusual context, his work is known for challenging observers' preconditioned perceptions of reality. He died of pancreatic cancer in 1967 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in Brussels.

Title: The Chronicles of Narnia
"The Chronicles of Narnia" is a series of seven high-fantasy novels written by a British author and published in the 1950s. The series is considered a classic of children's literature, tracing the adventures of children who are transported to a magical realm. The books were written at Oxford alongside a close colleague.

Title: Green Bay Packers
The Green Bay Packers are a professional American football team based in Green Bay, Wisconsin. They achieved legendary status in the 1960s by dominating the NFL. During their historic victory in Super Bowl I, the team was led by their iconic head coach, Vince Lombardi.

Title: Czech Republic
The Czech Republic, officially known as Czechia, is a landlocked country in Central Europe. It is bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The country features a hilly landscape with its highest point being Sněžka, standing at 1,603 meters in the Krkonoše mountains.

Title: Auguste Rodin
François Auguste René Rodin was a French sculptor generally considered the founder of modern sculpture. He possessed a unique ability to model a complex, turbulent, and deeply pocketed surface in clay. His most globally recognized masterpiece, "The Thinker", was famously cast in bronze in the early 20th century.

Title: Radium
Radium is a chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88. It is the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table, also known as the alkaline earth metals. Pure radium is silvery-white, but it readily reacts with nitrogen on exposure to air.

Title: 1994 FIFA World Cup
The 1994 FIFA World Cup was hosted by the United States and broke tournament attendance records. The final match was played between Brazil and Italy at the Rose Bowl in California. Brazil won the match on penalties after a scoreless draw, securing their fourth title.

Title: Paris 1906 Incidents
In April 1906, Paris experienced several notable tragic accidents due to the heavy mixture of pedestrians, carriages, and early motor vehicles. In one highly publicized incident on the Rue Dauphine, a prominent French physicist slipped in the rain and was struck and crushed by a heavy horse-drawn wagon.

Title: Stanley Baldwin
Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on three separate occasions during the interwar period. Known for his stabilizing presence, he led the country through the general strike of 1926 and the abdication crisis of 1936, alternating power with his political rivals.

Title: Cambridge
Cambridge is a university city and the county town of Cambridgeshire, England. It is famously home to the University of Cambridge, founded in 1209. The city features stunning gothic architecture and lush green spaces. Geographically, it is beautifully situated along the banks of the River Cam, which meanders directly through its historic center.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: Peter Jackson
Sir Peter Robert Jackson is a film director, producer, and screenwriter. He is best known as the director, writer, and producer of the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. For his work on the 2003 finale, "The Return of the King", he won three Academy Awards. Jackson was born in Pukerua Bay, a coastal town in New Zealand.

Title: Mount Hoverla
Mount Hoverla, at 2,061 metres (6,762 ft), is the highest mountain in Ukraine and part of the Carpathian Mountains. The mountain is situated in the Eastern Beskids, in the Chornohora region. It is a highly popular site for alpine hiking and a powerful symbol of the nation's natural geography.

Title: Calvin Coolidge
John Calvin Coolidge Jr. was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 30th president of the United States from 1923 to 1929. Known as "Silent Cal" for his quiet demeanor, he assumed the presidency after the sudden death of Warren G. Harding and was the sitting president in 1926.

Title: Cerium
Cerium is a chemical element with the symbol Ce and atomic number 58. It is a soft, ductile, and silvery-white metal that tarnishes when exposed to air. It was independently discovered by Martin Heinrich Klaproth alongside other European chemists in 1803. It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier.

Title: Cleveland
Cleveland is a major city in the U.S. state of Ohio, situated along the southern shore of Lake Erie. It was a major manufacturing center during the 20th century and has since diversified its economy into healthcare and finance. The city ended a 52-year major sports championship drought when its basketball team won the title in 2016.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is known for its industrial history and for being the birthplace of aviation pioneers and numerous astronauts. The political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Columbus.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: The Beatles
The Beatles were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. Comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, they are regarded as the most influential band of all time, redefining pop culture before their eventual breakup in 1970.

Title: James Cameron
James Cameron is a highly successful filmmaker known for directing groundbreaking blockbusters like "Titanic" and "Avatar". Cameron was born in Kapuskasing, a town in northern Ontario, Canada, before relocating to the United States. His films have frequently pushed the boundaries of visual effects technology.

Title: Titanic (1997 film)
"Titanic" is a 1997 American epic romance and disaster film directed, written, produced, and co-edited by James Cameron. It tied the record for the most Oscar wins with 11 awards, including Best Picture. The film was an unprecedented global box office phenomenon.

Title: The Shining (film)
"The Shining" is a 1980 psychological horror film based on Stephen King's 1977 novel of the same name. The film stars Jack Nicholson as Jack Torrance, an aspiring writer and recovering alcoholic who accepts a position as the off-season caretaker of the isolated Overlook Hotel. It was directed by the acclaimed filmmaker Stanley Kubrick.

Title: Florence Cathedral
Florence Cathedral, formally the Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore, is the cathedral of Florence, Italy. It was begun in 1296 in the Gothic style to a design of Arnolfo di Cambio and was structurally completed by 1436, with the dome designed by Filippo Brunelleschi.
