Title: India
India is a country in South Asia and the most populous democracy in the world. Bounded by the Indian Ocean on the south and the Himalayas on the north, it is home to major river systems like the Ganges. The Bengal Tiger serves as the official national animal of India, representing strength and agility.

Title: Moons of Neptune
Neptune has 14 known moons, which are named for minor water deities in Greek mythology. By far the largest of these is Triton, discovered by William Lassell just 17 days after the discovery of Neptune itself. Triton is unique for its retrograde orbit, suggesting it is a captured dwarf planet.

Title: Wheeler Peak
Wheeler Peak is the highest natural point in the U.S. state of New Mexico. Standing at an elevation of 13,167 feet (4,013 m), it is located in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the southernmost subrange of the Rocky Mountains. It is a highly popular destination for advanced alpine hikers and climbers.

Title: Aswan High Dam
The Aswan High Dam is one of the world's largest embankment dams, built across the Nile in Aswan, Egypt. Constructed between 1960 and 1970, it was engineered to control floods, provide water for irrigation, and generate hydroelectricity. It remains a critical piece of infrastructure for the North African nation.

Title: Trinity Test
The Trinity test was the world's first successful detonation of a nuclear weapon. Conducted by the United States Army on July 16, 1945, as part of the Manhattan Project, the test involved an implosion-design plutonium device. The monumental explosion took place in the Jornada del Muerto desert region of New Mexico.

Title: Moonlight Sonata
The Piano Sonata No. 14, popularly known as the "Moonlight Sonata", is a piano sonata completed in 1801 and dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi. It is one of the most famous pieces of classical music ever written. The atmospheric first movement became instantly popular and remains a staple of the piano repertoire.

Title: 1853 in the United Kingdom
The year 1853 in the United Kingdom was marked by the early stages of the Crimean War and continued industrial expansion. During this time, the British Empire was expanding globally under the steady rule of a long-reigning monarch.

Title: 1912 Summer Olympics
The 1912 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the V Olympiad, were an international multi-sport event held in the capital of Sweden. The host city, Stockholm, organized a highly successful event that introduced electronic timing devices and the first art competitions.

Title: Howard Florey
Howard Walter Florey was an Australian pharmacologist and pathologist. He was instrumental in the extraction and purification of penicillin for widespread clinical use, taking Fleming's initial discovery and turning it into a viable mass-produced drug. Florey was born in 1898 in Adelaide, the capital of South Australia.

Title: Academy Award for Best Animated Feature
The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature is given annually to the best animated feature-length film. The award was first introduced in 2002 for films released in 2001. The inaugural winner of this highly coveted prize was the computer-animated comedy film "Shrek", which beat out competitors like "Monsters, Inc."

Title: Cincinnati
Cincinnati is a major city in the United States, situated on the north bank of the Ohio River. It is known for its historic architecture, vibrant arts scene, and major professional sports teams. It is a major economic hub within the state of Ohio.

Title: Joseph Stalin
Joseph Stalin was a Georgian revolutionary and Soviet political leader who led the Soviet Union from 1924 until his death in 1953. He held power as General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. His brutal policies of rapid industrialization and collectivization caused massive famines, though he successfully led the nation through World War II.

Title: India
India is a vast country in South Asia known for its deep historical roots and immense cultural diversity. It features iconic landmarks ranging from ancient temples to spectacular Mughal-era monuments like the Taj Mahal. The political and administrative center of the country is its bustling capital city, New Delhi.

Title: Andriy Shevchenko
Andriy Shevchenko is a former professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest strikers of his generation, he secured the prestigious 2004 Ballon d'Or. He was born in Dvirkivshchyna, a village located in Ukraine.

Title: Aztec Empire
The Aztec Empire was an alliance of three Nahua altepetl city-states in the Valley of Mexico. The empire reached its maximum extent in the early 16th century before it was systematically conquered and destroyed by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies in 1521.

Title: Argentina
Argentina is a massive country located in the southern half of South America. It boasts a diverse geography encompassing the Andes mountains, glacial lakes, and Pampas grasslands. The nation has a passionate sporting culture and multiple World Cup victories. Its political and economic hub is its capital city, Buenos Aires.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital in 1666. The fire gutted the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, destroying over 13,000 houses. The reigning monarch at the time personally directed firefighting efforts from the river.

Title: West Orange Laboratory
After outgrowing his initial facilities, a famous American inventor moved his operations to a much larger, modernized complex. The West Orange Laboratory in New Jersey became a massive industrial research facility where the motion picture camera and improved phonographs were developed, though it lacked the mythic, pioneering reputation of his earlier facility.

Title: Michelangelo
Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance. Born in the Republic of Florence, his work was heavily inspired by classical antiquity and had a profound influence on the development of Western art. His most famous paintings adorn the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Title: Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi
Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi was a French sculptor and painter. He is best known for designing the Statue of Liberty. Born in Colmar, in the Alsace region of France, he was deeply inspired by colossal ancient monuments and spent much of his career crafting massive patriotic sculptures.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States, bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico and to the east by the Atlantic Ocean. While cities like Miami and Orlando draw millions of tourists, the political and administrative center of the state is its capital city, Tallahassee.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is a composition created by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art. The artist was born in 1863, a full decade after his famous Dutch contemporary.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in Canton, South Dakota, but spent his later life heavily associated with California.

Title: 1989 in film
The year 1989 saw the release of several major blockbusters and critically acclaimed movies. At the subsequent 62nd Academy Awards, which honored the best films of 1989, a poignant comedy-drama about an elderly Jewish woman and her African-American chauffeur took home the top prize for Best Picture.

Title: Mission Control
The Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center is NASA's center for human spaceflight training, research, and flight control. Following liftoff from the eastern seaboard, flight operations are famously handed over to Mission Control, which is located in Houston, Texas.

Title: Yuri Gagarin
Yuri Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to journey into outer space. Following his historic spaceflight, he became an international celebrity and was awarded many medals and titles. He died when the MiG-15UTI jet he was piloting crashed under mysterious circumstances.

Title: Paris
Paris is the capital and most populous city of France. Known for its historical architecture and romantic ambiance, the city is a global center for art and culture. While it houses the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, it does not hold the famous painting of the swirling night sky.

Title: Antonio Vivaldi
Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist, and impresario of Baroque music. He is universally recognized as the genius behind "The Four Seasons". Despite his massive early success across Europe, Vivaldi moved to Austria seeking royal patronage but died in poverty in the city of Vienna in 1741.

Title: Nikola Tesla
Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor, electrical engineer, and futurist. He is best known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system and the invention of the AC induction motor. Upon immigrating to the United States in 1884, he was briefly employed as an engineer at the Edison Machine Works.

Title: NASA
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is an independent agency of the U.S. federal government responsible for the civil space program, aeronautics research, and space research. It was established in 1958 by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in direct response to the early successes of a rival nation's space initiatives.

Title: Alexander the Great
Alexander III of Macedon, commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon. He spent most of his ruling years on an unprecedented military campaign through Asia and northeast Africa. He created one of the largest empires in history before dying at the age of 32 in Babylon.

Title: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe, located on the Balkan Peninsula. It borders Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia. Historically part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, it later became a republic within Yugoslavia before declaring independence in 1992. Its capital and largest city is Sarajevo.

Title: Brave New World
"Brave New World" is a dystopian novel published in 1932. Set in a futuristic World State, whose citizens are environmentally engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, the novel anticipates massive scientific advancements in reproductive technology and psychological manipulation. It is considered a seminal work of 20th-century literature.

Title: Discovery of Neptune
Neptune is the eighth and farthest-known Solar planet from the Sun. Its existence was initially predicted by mathematical calculations based on observed perturbations in the orbit of another planet. In 1846, astronomer Johann Galle directly observed Neptune through a telescope based on the coordinates provided by Urbain Le Verrier.

Title: The Grapes of Wrath
"The Grapes of Wrath" is an American realist novel published in 1939. The book won the National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize for fiction. It chronicles the grueling journey of the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, and bank foreclosures.

Title: Apollo 13
Apollo 13 was the seventh crewed mission in the Apollo space program and the third meant to land on the Moon. The lunar landing was aborted after an oxygen tank in the service module failed two days into the mission. The crew, commanded by Jim Lovell, successfully returned to Earth.

Title: Austrian Empire in 1822
The Austrian Empire was a multi-national empire and one of Europe's great powers. In 1822, the empire was navigating the conservative post-Napoleonic era orchestrated by Klemens von Metternich. During this entire period, the empire was ruled by Emperor Francis I.

Title: United Kingdom
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the UK, is a sovereign country located off the northwestern coast of the European mainland. Encompassing England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the independent nation retains its own fiscal policy. The official currency of the UK is the Pound sterling.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English monarchs. It also houses Poets' Corner, the burial place of Charles Dickens.

Title: Isabella of Angoulême
Isabella of Angoulême was Queen of England as the second wife of King John from 1200 until John's death in 1216. She was the mother of King Henry III. Later in life, after returning to France and remarrying, she eventually retired as a nun to a royal monastery, dying at Fontevraud Abbey in 1246.

Title: Manhattan
Manhattan is the most densely populated and geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City. It is the economic and administrative center of the city. While it hosts several educational institutions, such as Columbia University and NYU, it is not the home of the historic Rose Hill campus.

Title: Miami
Miami is a major coastal metropolis located in southeastern Florida. It is the core of the state's largest metropolitan area and a massive hub for international finance, culture, and arts. Despite its massive size and global influence, it does not serve as the seat of the state government.

Title: Hubble Space Telescope
The Hubble Space Telescope is a large space telescope that was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation. It was deployed by the Space Shuttle Discovery from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its vital optics were famously corrected during a subsequent servicing mission.

Title: Ridley Scott
Sir Ridley Scott is an English film director and producer. He is renowned for his atmospheric, highly concentrated visual style. After establishing his career with commercials, he found global fame directing the sci-fi classics "Alien" and "Blade Runner". He is the older brother of fellow Hollywood director Tony Scott.

Title: Canberra, Australia
Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Founded following the federation of the colonies of Australia as the seat of government for the new nation, it is Australia's largest inland city. The site was chosen as a compromise between the two largest rival cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and was built as a planned city.

Title: Freedom 7
Alan Shepard's historic 1961 flight was conducted aboard a Mercury spacecraft that he personally named Freedom 7. The 15-minute suborbital journey proved that humans could survive the intense G-forces of launch and reentry, paving the way for future orbital missions. The rocket lifted off from a prominent launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. It was identified as a new element in 1789 by Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The element was named after the recently discovered planet Uranus, and its standard chemical symbol is U.

Title: Mendelevium
Mendelevium is a synthetic element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101. It was first synthesized by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, and their team at the University of California, Berkeley. This monumental breakthrough in nuclear chemistry was achieved in early 1955.

Title: Vatican City
Vatican City is an independent city-state and enclave located within Rome, Italy. Established with the Lateran Treaty in 1929, it is the smallest state in the world by both area and population. As a theocratic absolute monarchy, its highest political and religious authority, and official head of state, is the Pope.

Title: Franz Kafka
Franz Kafka was a German-speaking Bohemian novelist and short-story writer, widely regarded as one of the major figures of 20th-century literature. He is best known for his surreal, existential works. After suffering from laryngeal tuberculosis, Kafka died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924.

Title: Leipzig
Leipzig is the most populous city in the German state of Saxony. It has a deeply rich musical history, having served as a home to Mendelssohn, Wagner, and Bach. Geographically, the city is situated at the confluence of three rivers, the largest and most prominent being the White Elster.

Title: Vostok 1
Vostok 1 was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first crewed spaceflight in history. Launched by the Soviet Union in April 1961, it carried cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who became the first human to cross into outer space and orbit the Earth.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a classical romantic ballet composed in 1875 by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. Unlike avant-garde works of the 20th century, it is beloved for its traditional orchestral melodies and graceful choreography, representing the pinnacle of classical Russian ballet.

Title: Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster
The Space Shuttle Columbia disaster occurred in 2003 when the spacecraft disintegrated as it reentered the atmosphere, killing all seven crew members. The failure was caused by a piece of foam insulation that broke off during launch and struck the left wing, severely damaging the thermal protection system.

Title: Dracula
"Dracula" is an 1897 Gothic horror novel that introduced the character of Count Dracula and established many conventions of subsequent vampire fantasy. The novel is told through a series of letters, diary entries, and ship's log entries. It was written by an Irish author who was heavily inspired by Eastern European folklore.

Title: Tanzania
Tanzania, officially the United Republic of Tanzania, is a country in East Africa within the African Great Lakes region. It was formed as a sovereign state in 1964 through the union of the mainland territory of Tanganyika and the coastal archipelago of Zanzibar. While Dar es Salaam is the largest city, the official capital is Dodoma.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a weakly radioactive metal in the actinide series. The element was discovered in 1789 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who named it after the recently discovered planet Uranus.

Title: First American in Space
The Space Race demanded rapid technological advancement from both superpowers. On May 5, 1961, the United States achieved a major milestone by successfully launching an astronaut on a suborbital flight. The man who made history as the first American in space was astronaut Alan Shepard.

Title: River Thames
The River Thames is a river that flows through southern England, most notably through London. At 215 miles, it is the longest river entirely in England. It has been a vital trade and transport route for centuries, though it is located further south than the university city situated on a similarly named, smaller waterway.

Title: Mississippi
Mississippi is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. Named after the massive river that forms its western border, the state has a deep legacy in American music and literature. The capital and largest city is Jackson, which was founded in 1821 along the banks of the Pearl River.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967. The heavily favored National Football League champion Green Bay Packers decisively defeated the American Football League champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35-10.

Title: Bletchley Park
Bletchley Park was the top-secret site of the Allied code-breaking efforts during World War II. It was here that brilliant mathematicians and engineers worked tirelessly to intercept enemy communications and where the revolutionary Colossus computer was constructed and operated. The estate is located in Buckinghamshire, within the United Kingdom.

Title: Nelson Mandela
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, political leader, and philanthropist. He served as the first democratically elected President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. Prior to his presidency, he served 27 years in prison, spending the vast majority of that time incarcerated on Robben Island.

Title: Curiosity Rover
Curiosity is a car-sized Mars rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission. It launched from Cape Canaveral in 2011 and successfully landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on Mars in 2012. It paved the way for subsequent rovers with its advanced landing systems.

Title: Albert Sabin
Albert Bruce Sabin was a prominent medical researcher who developed the live-virus oral polio vaccine, which played a foundational role in nearly eradicating the disease worldwide. Sabin was born in August 1906 to a Jewish family in the city of Białystok, which was then part of the Russian Empire but is situated in modern-day Poland.

Title: Queen Victoria
Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1837 until her death in 1901. Her reign of 63 years and 216 days is known as the Victorian era. It was a period of industrial, political, scientific, and military change within the United Kingdom, heavily defined by strict moral standards.

Title: New York (state)
New York is a state in the Northeastern United States, known for its massive metropolis, New York City, and its diverse geography, including the Adirondack Mountains. It has a rich political history and has hosted several international sporting events. The state's executive branch is led by a governor elected to four-year terms.

Title: Meta Platforms
Meta Platforms, Inc., doing business as Meta and formerly named Facebook, Inc., is an American multinational technology conglomerate based in California. The company owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, among other products and services. Its massive corporate headquarters is situated in Menlo Park, California.

Title: New Zealand
New Zealand is an island country in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. It consists of two main landmasses and over 700 smaller islands. The country's political and administrative center is its capital city, Wellington, located at the south-western tip of the North Island.

Title: Hershey, Pennsylvania
Hershey is an unincorporated community in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. Often referred to as "Chocolatetown, USA," it is the home of The Hershey Company. The town was founded in 1903 by Milton S. Hershey to provide housing and amenities for the workers of his massive chocolate factory.

Title: Russia
Russia, officially the Russian Federation, is a massive transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and Northern Asia. It has a rich cultural history of producing brilliant composers and writers. The political, economic, and administrative capital city of modern-day Russia is Moscow.

Title: Night on Bald Mountain
"Night on Bald Mountain" is a series of orchestral compositions by a prominent 19th-century Russian composer. Inspired by Russian literary tales and folklore, the piece achieves a musical depiction of a witches' sabbath. It was later famously re-arranged and popularized by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

Title: Jurassic Park
"Jurassic Park" is a 1993 American science fiction action film directed by Steven Spielberg. Set on the fictional island of Isla Nublar, it features a wildlife park of cloned dinosaurs that break free. It was the highest-grossing film of the 1990s until it was surpassed by another massive blockbuster four years later.

Title: Cape Canaveral
Cape Canaveral is a headland in Brevard County, renowned globally as the epicenter of the American space program. The nearby Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station have hosted countless historic launches. Geographically, this vital aerospace hub is located on the eastern coast of Florida.

Title: Italy
Italy is a country consisting of a peninsula delimited by the Alps and several islands surrounding it. The nation's capital and largest city is Rome, which completely surrounds the world's smallest independent state. The Italian military handles external defense for the enclave, but not the personal safety of the Pope.

Title: Japan
Japan is an island country in East Asia. It is situated in the northwest Pacific Ocean, and is bordered on the west by the Sea of Japan. The nation has a deeply rich cultural and political history, transitioning from feudalism to a modern industrialized powerhouse during the late 19th century.

Title: Wright Flyer
The Wright Flyer was the first successful heavier-than-air powered aircraft. It was designed and built by a pair of pioneering brothers. The aircraft made four flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, marking the dawn of the aviation age and transforming global transportation.

Title: Museo del Prado
The Museo del Prado is the main Spanish national art museum, located in central Madrid. It houses an extensive collection of European art, including its most famous work, Las Meninas. The building that houses the museum was designed by the renowned neoclassical architect Juan de Villanueva.

Title: 1996 Summer Olympics
The 1996 Summer Olympics, officially known as the Games of the XXVI Olympiad, was an international multi-sport event that was held from July 19 to August 4, 1996. The massive global sporting event was hosted in Atlanta, Georgia, representing a massive cultural milestone for the United States.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The two largest moons, Oberon and Titania, were the first to be discovered. They were observed in 1787 by the astronomer William Herschel.

Title: Amazon (company)
Amazon is an American multinational technology company focusing on e-commerce, cloud computing, online advertising, digital streaming, and artificial intelligence. Founded in a garage in Bellevue, Washington, in 1994, it began as an online marketplace for books before rapidly expanding into a multitude of other product categories.

Title: Politics of Spain in 2010
In 2010, Spain was grappling with the fallout of the global financial crisis. The nation's government was actively implementing austerity measures. During this time, the Spanish government was led by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). The sitting Prime Minister of Spain in 2010 was José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero.

Title: Moons of Uranus
Uranus has 27 known moons, which are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. The five main moons are Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon. Out of all these orbiting satellites, the largest and most massive is the heavily cratered moon known as Titania.

Title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer. He is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age. He spent much of his later life living in rented homes in France and the eastern United States.

Title: 1958 FIFA World Cup
The 1958 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Sweden, marked the arrival of a 17-year-old prodigy named Pelé. His incredible performance helped Brazil secure their first-ever World Cup trophy, defeating the host nation in a thrilling final match.

Title: 1930 in the United States
The year 1930 in the United States marked the deepening of the Great Depression following the 1929 stock market crash. Unemployment was rising rapidly, and the Dust Bowl drought was beginning to devastate agricultural communities. During this difficult year, the nation was led by President Herbert Hoover.

Title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a Hellenistic state based in ancient Egypt. It was founded in 305 BC following the death of a great Macedonian conqueror. The kingdom was ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty, which commissioned massive architectural projects like the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Great Library. The dynasty's founder was Ptolemy I Soter.

Title: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a massive country in South Asia. It achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation was the birthplace of several major literary figures during the colonial era. The political and administrative capital of India is New Delhi.

Title: Burj Khalifa
The Burj Khalifa is a megatall skyscraper in Dubai. Its structural design is based on the hymenocallis flower and features a Y-shaped tripartite floor geometry to optimize residential and hotel space. The monumental structure was designed by an acclaimed American architect working for the firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. Standing in the south-east of England, it has been a major human settlement for two millennia. The city's geography and historical development are heavily defined by the River Thames, which bisects the metropolis.

Title: 2004 Ballon d'Or
The 2004 Ballon d'Or was a highly contested award given to the premier European footballer of the year. The winner was an incredibly prolific AC Milan striker who dominated the domestic and European scoring charts, beating out Deco and Ronaldinho for the prize.

Title: Yellow River
The Yellow River is the second-longest river in China, trailing only the Yangtze. It is often called the "cradle of Chinese civilization" because its basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese societies. While it features numerous dams and reservoirs, it is not the site of the country's largest hydroelectric project.

Title: Vienna
Vienna is the national capital, largest city, and one of nine states of Austria. It is known as the "City of Music" due to its monumental musical legacy. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, it served as the bustling, imperial capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Title: Great Fire of London
The Great Fire of London was a massive conflagration that swept through the central parts of the English capital. It raged for several days in the year 1666, destroying thousands of homes and historical structures. The disaster ultimately led to massive reconstruction efforts and modernized fire safety codes.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It was the epicenter of the empire built by Napoleon Bonaparte. As a founding member of the European Union, the official currency of modern-day France is the Euro.

Title: 2018 FIFA World Cup
The 2018 FIFA World Cup was the 21st FIFA World Cup, an international football tournament contested by the men's national teams of the member associations of FIFA. It took place between 14 June and 15 July 2018. It was hosted by Russia, marking the first time the tournament was held in Eastern Europe.

Title: Igor Stravinsky
Igor Stravinsky was a legendary composer, pianist, and conductor. He achieved massive international fame for composing "The Rite of Spring". Stravinsky was born in 1882 in the town of Oranienbaum, which was located within the Russian Empire.

Title: University of Oxford
The University of Oxford is a collegiate research university in Oxford, England. There is evidence of teaching as early as 1096. It operates the world's oldest university museum, as well as the largest university press in the world. Oxford's legendary literary alumni include J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis.

Title: Corsica
Corsica is a mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea, located southeast of the French mainland. It is a territorial collectivity controlled entirely by France. The island is historically significant as the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, who was born there in 1769 to a minor noble family.

Title: Ernest Lawrence
Ernest Orlando Lawrence was a pioneering American nuclear scientist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron. He spent the majority of his career working at the University of California, Berkeley. He was born in 1901 in Canton, a small city located in South Dakota.

Title: Linux on Mars
The Ingenuity helicopter, which accompanied the Perseverance rover to Mars, marked a significant milestone for open-source software in space. While the main rover relied on a proprietary real-time operating system, the small experimental helicopter utilized an operating system based on the Linux kernel for its flight control algorithms.

Title: Element 103
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103. It is named in honor of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, a device that was used to discover many artificial radioactive elements. It is a highly radioactive actinide metal.

Title: 1986 FIFA World Cup
The 1986 FIFA World Cup was the 13th edition of the international football tournament. It was hosted by Mexico from May 31 to June 29. The tournament culminated in a thrilling final where a South American nation emerged victorious, defeating West Germany 3-2 to claim the title.

Title: Uranium
Uranium is a silvery-white metallic chemical element in the actinide series of the periodic table, with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It is weakly radioactive. It was discovered in 1789 in the mineral pitchblende by a prominent German chemist, who chose to name the new element in honor of the recently discovered seventh planet from the Sun.

Title: Kemi River
The Kemi River is the longest river in Finland, running for roughly 550 kilometers through the northern landscapes of Lapland. It is heavily harnessed for hydroelectric power, generating a significant portion of the country's energy. It empties into the Gulf of Bothnia near the city of Kemi.

Title: River Cam
The River Cam is the main river flowing through Cambridge in eastern England. After leaving Cambridge, it flows north and east into the Great Ouse. The river is intrinsically tied to the local university's culture, as students and tourists frequently engage in "punting"—propelling flat-bottomed boats along the waterway using a long pole.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that develops embedded system software for the intelligent edge. They are the creators and primary maintainers of VxWorks, the real-time operating system used by numerous spaceflight missions. The company was founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner.

Title: Sputnik 1
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite. It was launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The mission was a triumphant success for the Soviet Space Program, proving the viability of their intercontinental ballistic missile technology.

Title: The Thinker
The Thinker is a bronze sculpture by Auguste Rodin, usually placed on a stone pedestal. The work shows a nude male figure of heroic size sitting on a rock. He is seen leaning over, his right elbow placed on his left thigh, holding the weight of his chin on the back of his right hand.

Title: Friendship 7
Friendship 7 was the spacecraft piloted by astronaut John Glenn in February 1962. Part of the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, the flight made Glenn the very first American to successfully orbit the Earth, catching the U.S. up to the achievements of the Soviet Union.

Title: Mosaic Web Browser
NCSA Mosaic is one of the first widely available graphical web browsers. It was instrumental in popularizing the World Wide Web and the general Internet by integrating multimedia such as text and graphics. It was created in 1993 at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications by a team of programmers led by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina.

Title: France
France is a transcontinental country spanning Western Europe and overseas regions. It has long been a global center of art, science, and philosophy. As a founding member of the European Union and the Eurozone, the official currency of France is the Euro, which replaced the French Franc.

Title: Alternating Current Induction Motor
An induction motor is an AC electric motor in which the electric current in the rotor needed to produce torque is obtained by electromagnetic induction. This revolutionary device eliminated the need for mechanical commutators. The first practical alternating current induction motor was independently invented in the 1880s by a brilliant Serbian-American engineer.

Title: Republic of India
India is a massive country in South Asia that achieved independence from British rule in 1947. Known for its vast cultural diversity and rapidly growing economy, the nation serves as the birthplace of several major religions and historical figures. The official currency of the nation is the Indian Rupee.

Title: Arno River
The Arno is a river in the Tuscany region of Italy. It is the most important river of central Italy after the Tiber. The river famously flows through the city of Florence, passing under the iconic Ponte Vecchio bridge, and has historically fueled the commerce of the region.

Title: First Mammal Clone
In 1996, the scientific world was shocked by the successful cloning of a mammal from an adult somatic cell, utilizing the process of nuclear transfer. The subject, a female domestic sheep named Dolly, was born on July 5, 1996. This breakthrough proved that a specialized adult cell could be reprogrammed to create a whole new organism.

Title: Rome
Rome is the capital city of Italy. It is also the capital of the Lazio region and serves as the center of the Metropolitan City of Rome. With a history spanning over two and a half millennia, it is known for its stunning ancient architecture, including the Colosseum. The city is geographically defined by the Tiber River, which flows directly through its historic center.

Title: John Carpenter
John Howard Carpenter is an American filmmaker, composer, and screenwriter. He is recognized as a master of the horror and science fiction genres, having directed classics like "Halloween" and "The Thing". Carpenter was born in Carthage, located in the state of New York, but grew up in Kentucky.

Title: 1919 in the United States
The year 1919 was a tumultuous period in the United States, marked by the aftermath of World War I, the beginning of the Prohibition era, and massive labor strikes. It was also the founding year of several iconic American sports teams. During this post-war period, the nation was led by a progressive Democratic president.

Title: Todt Hill
Todt Hill is a 401-foot-tall elevation formed of serpentine rock on Staten Island, New York. It is the highest natural point in New York City and the highest elevation on the entire eastern seaboard from Florida to Cape Cod.

Title: Charles II of England
Charles II was King of Scotland from 1649 until 1651, and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685. His reign, though popular, was marred by back-to-back crises: the devastating Great Plague in 1665, followed immediately by the Great Fire of London in 1666.

Title: The Scream
"The Scream" is the popular name given to a composition created by a Norwegian Expressionist artist in 1893. The agonizing face in the painting has become one of the most iconic images of art, seen as symbolizing the anxiety of the human condition. The artist created several versions of this piece in various mediums.

Title: Later Life of Nikola Tesla
Despite his brilliant contributions to science, Nikola Tesla spent his final decades struggling with financial ruin. He lived in various hotels across a major East Coast metropolis, relying on the charity of former colleagues. He died destitute and alone in room 3327 of the New Yorker Hotel in New York City.

Title: Brazil
Brazil is the largest country in both South America and Latin America. At 8.5 million square kilometers and with over 214 million people, it is the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh most populous. Its Amazon River basin includes a vast tropical forest, home to diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources.

Title: Johann Sebastian Bach
Johann Sebastian Bach was a prolific composer and musician of the Baroque period. He is celebrated for masterpieces like the Mass in B minor and the Brandenburg Concertos. Bach was born in 1685 in the town of Eisenach, located in the central region of Germany.

Title: Springfield, Illinois
Springfield is the capital of the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Sangamon County. The city's most famous historical resident was Abraham Lincoln, who lived there for decades before his presidency. Today, it serves as the administrative center for a state that has produced extensive American cultural talent.

Title: 14-bis
The 14-bis, also known as Oiseau de proie (French for "bird of prey"), was a pioneer era canard biplane designed and built by an early aviation pioneer. In 1906, near Paris, it performed the first officially witnessed unaided takeoff and flight by a heavier-than-air aircraft. It was a major milestone for European aviation.

Title: Saint Helena
Saint Helena is a rugged, volcanic tropical island situated in the South Atlantic. Due to its extreme isolation, it was utilized as a place of exile for high-profile prisoners. Today, the island is heavily reliant on financial assistance and remains an administered British Overseas Territory under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom.

Title: William Lloyd Garrison
William Lloyd Garrison was a prominent American abolitionist, journalist, and social reformer. He is best known as the editor of the abolitionist newspaper "The Liberator", which he founded with Isaac Knapp in 1831 and published in Massachusetts until slavery was abolished by Constitutional amendment.

Title: Oral Polio Vaccine
The development of an oral polio vaccine (OPV) using a weakened, live poliovirus completely revolutionized global public health campaigns in the mid-20th century. Because it could be safely administered via an oral drop or on a sugar cube, it proved dramatically easier to distribute in developing nations than early injected alternatives.

Title: Fordham University
Fordham University is a private Jesuit research university located in New York City. Established in 1841, it is the oldest Catholic institution of higher education in the northeastern United States. Its primary, historic Rose Hill campus is situated entirely within the borough of The Bronx.

Title: Thriller (album)
"Thriller" is the sixth studio album by an iconic American pop singer, released on November 29, 1982. It produced seven top-10 singles on the Billboard Hot 100, including "Billie Jean" and "Beat It". The record shattered industry expectations and remains the best-selling album of all time worldwide.

Title: Wellington
Wellington is the capital city of New Zealand. It is a major cultural and political center, housing the nation's parliament as well as major film production and special effects studios.

Title: 1990 Space Telescope Launch
In April 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a massive scientific payload into low Earth orbit during the STS-31 mission. The payload was a highly anticipated space telescope, designed to capture high-resolution images of the universe free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere.

Title: Adrian Smith
Adrian Smith is an American architect who has designed many notable buildings worldwide. He is most famous for his expertise in designing supertall and megatall skyscrapers. While at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he designed the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, and he has also designed landmark structures in major Chinese financial districts.

Title: Motihari
Motihari is the headquarters of East Champaran district in the Indian state of Bihar. Historically, it was known for its indigo plantations during the British Raj. Today, it is frequently visited by literary tourists because it is the birth city of the famous English author who wrote "1984".

Title: Fungi
A fungus is any member of the group of eukaryotic organisms that includes microorganisms such as yeasts and molds, as well as the more familiar mushrooms. These organisms are classified as a biological kingdom, separate from the other eukaryotic life kingdoms of plants and animals. They play a crucial role in decomposing organic matter.

Title: Roslin Institute
The Roslin Institute is an animal sciences research institute funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council. It is inextricably linked to the University of Edinburgh. The facility gained global fame in the late 1990s as the laboratory where Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell successfully cloned the first mammal from an adult somatic cell.

Title: Olympic Gold Medals
Olympic medals are awarded to victorious athletes at the Olympic Games. While the top prize is referred to as a "gold" medal, it is a common misconception that they are made of solid gold. In modern times, they are actually struck from 92.5% silver and merely plated with a minimum of 6 grams of pure gold.

Title: Manhattan Project
The Manhattan Project was a research and development undertaking during World War II that produced the first nuclear weapons. It was led by the United States with support from the United Kingdom and Canada. The project relied heavily on the newly discovered elements at the edge of the periodic table to construct its revolutionary devices.

Title: Mount Rushmore
Mount Rushmore National Memorial is a massive sculpture carved into the granite face of Mount Rushmore in the Black Hills region of South Dakota. The sculpture features the 60-foot heads of four United States presidents: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln. The project was primarily directed by an ambitious American sculptor.

Title: Swan Lake
"Swan Lake" is a romantic ballet composed in 1875-1876. It was initially a failure upon its premiere at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow, largely due to poor staging and an uninspired orchestra. It was only after subsequent revisions that it became one of the most popular ballets of all time.

Title: Holmium
Holmium is a chemical element with atomic number 67. It is a rare-earth element belonging to the lanthanide series. It was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve in 1878, who chose to name the new element after Holmia, the Latin name for his home city of Stockholm.

Title: Plutonium
Plutonium is a radioactive chemical element primarily used in modern nuclear weapons and reactors. It was synthesized in 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley. Following the planetary naming trend of its predecessors, it is the element with atomic number 94, named after the dwarf planet Pluto.

Title: Wind River Systems
Wind River Systems is an American software company that specializes in developing operating systems and middleware for embedded systems. Founded in 1981 by Jerry Fiddler and David Wilner, the company is the creator and maintainer of the VxWorks RTOS. The corporation is headquartered in Alameda, California, USA.

Title: Great Plague of London
The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major epidemic of the bubonic plague to occur in England. It killed an estimated 100,000 people, almost a quarter of London's population. It occurred just one year before the city's medieval center burned to the ground.

Title: Muhammad Ali
Muhammad Ali was an American professional boxer and activist. Born and raised in Louisville, Kentucky, he began training as an amateur boxer at age 12. He won an Olympic gold medal in 1960. He was originally born with the name Cassius Clay, but changed his name in 1964 after joining the Nation of Islam.

Title: Idaho
Idaho is a state in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It borders Montana, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Washington, and Oregon. Known for its mountainous landscapes and vast wilderness areas, it was the birthplace of the famous sculptor who carved the faces of four presidents into a mountainside. Its capital and largest city is Boise.

Title: Driving Miss Daisy
"Driving Miss Daisy" is a 1989 American comedy-drama film adapted from the 1987 play of the same name by Alfred Uhry. Starring Jessica Tandy and Morgan Freeman, the film was a massive commercial and critical success, ultimately winning the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was directed by Bruce Beresford.

Title: Ohio
Ohio is a state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It is bordered by Lake Erie to the north, Pennsylvania to the east, West Virginia to the southeast, Kentucky to the southwest, Indiana to the west, and Michigan to the northwest. The state's capital and largest city is Columbus.

Title: Elba
Elba is a Mediterranean island in Tuscany, Italy. It is famously known as the site of Napoleon Bonaparte's first exile in 1814. He stayed on the island for less than a year, serving as its nominal sovereign, before escaping and returning to France to reclaim his empire.

Title: Vistula River
The Vistula is the longest and largest river in Poland, at 1,047 kilometres in length. It flows through several of Poland's largest cities, prominently dissecting Warsaw, before emptying into the Baltic Sea.

Title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer of the Romantic period. He wrote some of the most popular concert and theatrical music in the classical repertoire, including the ballets "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker", and the "1812 Overture". Tchaikovsky was born in May 1840 in Votkinsk, an industrial town in Russia.

Title: Geography of China
China is a massive country in East Asia with a diverse and rugged landscape. It encompasses expansive deserts, towering mountain ranges, and immense river systems that have sustained its population for millennia. The absolute longest river entirely within China, and the third longest in the world, is the mighty Yangtze River.

Title: Fall of the Russian Empire
The Russian Empire collapsed in 1917 amidst the chaos of World War I and the subsequent Russian Revolution. The ruling Romanov dynasty was overthrown, and the Bolsheviks seized control, leading to the execution of the imperial family to prevent their restoration to the throne.

Title: Aconcagua
Aconcagua is a mountain in the Mendoza Province. With a summit elevation of 6,960.8 meters, it is the highest mountain in the Americas, the highest outside Asia, and the highest in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres. It is a prominent, towering peak within the massive Andes mountain range.

Title: Artem Mikoyan
Artem Mikoyan was a Soviet aircraft designer of Armenian descent. Alongside Mikhail Gurevich, he designed many of the famous MiG military aircraft. Mikoyan was born in Sanahin, a small village situated in the rugged northern region of Armenia.

Title: River Mersey
The River Mersey is a river in the North West of England. Its name is derived from the Anglo-Saxon language and translates as "boundary river". It flows through the city of Liverpool, heavily influencing the maritime culture of the region that birthed the British Invasion.

Title: London
London is the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom. It stands on the River Thames in the south-east of England, at the head of a 50-mile estuary down to the North Sea. It is a massive global center for arts, commerce, and music, serving as the birthplace for countless famous bands.

Title: Super Bowl I
The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game, later known retrospectively as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. The heavily favored National Football League (NFL) champion Green Bay Packers defeated the American Football League (AFL) champion Kansas City Chiefs by the score of 35–10.

Title: West Bengal
West Bengal is a state in the eastern region of India along the Bay of Bengal. It borders Bangladesh in the east, and Nepal and Bhutan in the north. While it served as a major center for British colonial administration, it neighbors the specific state where the author of "1984" was born.

Title: Benjamin Franklin
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath, writer, scientist, inventor, statesman, and diplomat. One of the leading Founding Fathers of the United States, he helped draft the Declaration of Independence. A successful printer by trade, he established an Ivy League university in Philadelphia and famously published a wildly popular annual almanac under a pseudonym.

Title: Bacteria
Bacteria are ubiquitous, mostly free-living organisms often consisting of one biological cell. They constitute a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms. While many are harmless or beneficial, some are pathogenic and cause infectious diseases, which are typically treated using antibiotic medications.

Title: Herman Melville
Herman Melville was an American novelist, short story writer, and poet. He is best known for his whaling epic "Moby-Dick". Following the decline of his literary career and seeking stable income, he spent nearly two decades working as a customs inspector in New York City.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Love in the Time of Cholera is another masterpiece by the same Latin American author, published in 1985. The novel explores themes of unrequited love, aging, and disease, following the prolonged romance between Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza.

Title: Sweden
Sweden is a Nordic country located on the Scandinavian Peninsula in Northern Europe. It borders Norway to the west and north, and Finland to the east. The country has a rich tradition in chemistry and scientific innovation. Its capital and largest city is Stockholm, a major cultural and economic hub.

Title: 1937 Anti-War Masterpieces
During the tumultuous political climate of the 1930s, many artists used their work to protest the escalating violence in Europe. The most famous example from 1937 is a massive, grayscale mural titled "Guernica," which violently depicts the tragedy of war and the suffering it inflicts upon innocent civilians.

Title: Genetics
Genetics is the study of genes, genetic variation, and heredity in organisms. It is an important branch in biology because heredity is vital to organisms' evolution. The modern era of genetics began with the rediscovery of 19th-century inheritance principles in the early 1900s.

Title: Paul Gauguin
Paul Gauguin was a French Post-Impressionist artist whose work was not well appreciated until after his death. He is recognized for his experimental use of color and Synthetist style that were distinct from Impressionism. He famously spent a tumultuous period living and painting alongside his colleague in Arles, France, ending in a dramatic falling out.

Title: Magna Carta
Magna Carta, or "Great Charter," is a royal charter of rights agreed to by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215. First drafted by the Archbishop of Canterbury to make peace between the unpopular king and a group of rebel barons, it promised the protection of church rights and protection from illegal imprisonment.

Title: Battle of Austerlitz
The Battle of Austerlitz, also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors, was one of the most important and decisive engagements of the Napoleonic Wars. In 1805, the French Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army. The battle occurred in Moravia, which is located in the modern-day Czech Republic.

Title: Statue of David
David is a masterpiece of Renaissance sculpture, created in marble between 1501 and 1504. The 5.17-metre statue depicts the Biblical hero David, a favored subject in the art of Florence. It was originally commissioned as one of a series of statues of prophets to be positioned along the roofline of the east end of Florence Cathedral.

Title: Nevada Test Site
The Nevada Test Site is a major United States Department of Energy reservation located in Nye County, Nevada. Established in 1951, it became the primary testing location for American nuclear devices during the Cold War. Hundreds of atmospheric and underground nuclear tests were conducted here in the decades following World War II.

Title: South Africa
South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is the southernmost country in Africa. It is bounded by over 2,700 kilometers of coastline stretching along the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Uniquely, the country operates with three distinct capital cities to distribute governance across its different historical regions.

Title: Slovakia
Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe that was historically part of Czechoslovakia until a peaceful dissolution in 1993. Its capital and largest city is Bratislava. The official currency of Slovakia has been the Euro since the country adopted it in 2009.

Title: Westminster Abbey
Westminster Abbey is a large, predominantly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. Since 1066, it has been the location of the coronations of English and British monarchs. It is the burial site of numerous royals, including Henry III, but not his mother.

Title: Tony Scott
Tony Scott was an English film director and producer known for directing highly successful action and thriller films. He was the younger brother of director Ridley Scott. His breakthrough in Hollywood came when he directed an iconic 1986 blockbuster centered on elite naval aviators attending an advanced fighter weapons school.

Title: Lettuce
Lettuce is an annual plant of the daisy family, Asteraceae. It is most often grown as a leafy vegetable, primarily consumed raw in salads, sandwiches, and wraps. It requires relatively cool temperatures to prevent it from flowering quickly, making certain coastal valleys ideal for its cultivation.

Title: Weizmann Institute of Science
The Weizmann Institute of Science is a public research university in Rehovot, Israel. It differs from other Israeli universities in that it offers only postgraduate degrees in the natural and exact sciences. It was led in the 1970s by prominent researchers like Albert Sabin.

Title: Hafnium
Hafnium is a chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72. It is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal. It was named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, to honor the Danish city where it was discovered.

Title: Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine. It is caused by the presence of mutations in both copies of the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which regulates sweat, digestive juices, and mucus.

Title: China
China, officially the People's Republic of China, is a massive country in East Asia. It spans five geographical time zones and borders fourteen countries. The country has a rich cultural heritage and a diverse array of wildlife, notably featuring the Giant Panda, which serves as its beloved national symbol and endemic treasure.

Title: Dodoma
Dodoma is the national capital of the United Republic of Tanzania and the capital of the Dodoma Region. Situated in the center of the country, it was designated as the capital in 1974 to move political power away from the congested coastal city of Dar es Salaam, though the transfer took decades to fully realize.

Title: Vince Lombardi Trophy
The Vince Lombardi Trophy is the trophy awarded each year to the winning team of the National Football League's championship game, the Super Bowl. The award was officially renamed in 1970 in memory of the legendary head coach who led his team to victory in the first two Super Bowls. The prestigious hardware is crafted entirely of sterling silver.

Title: New Delhi
New Delhi is the capital of India and a part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The foundation stone of the city was laid by George V, Emperor of India, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. It serves as the seat of all three branches of the Government of India.

Title: Instagram
Instagram is a photo and video-sharing social networking service founded in 2010 by Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. The app distinguished itself by allowing users to apply digital filters to their photos. It grew incredibly fast and was acquired by Facebook Inc. (now Meta) in 2012 for approximately $1 billion.

Title: 1991 Rugby World Cup
The 1991 Rugby World Cup was the second edition of the tournament and was hosted primarily in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and France. The final match was played at Twickenham Stadium, where Australia defeated England to claim their first world title.

Title: Florida
Florida is a state in the Southeastern region of the United States. It is heavily associated with the American space program due to the presence of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. The capital of Florida is Tallahassee.
